Welcome. Nebulosa is a Bun-first, ESM-only TypeScript toolkit for numerical astronomy, astrophotography, imaging, I/O, and observatory control.

# 🚀 Installation

Nebulosa runs on [Bun](https://bun.com). Install it from the Git repository; Bun fetches that repository directly. Imports use the path under `nebulosa/src/` and omit the `.ts` extension.

## 💥 Requirements

- Install [Bun](https://bun.com/docs/installation).

## 📦 Add the package

```sh
bun add --trust github:tiagohm/nebulosa.ts
```

`--trust` records `nebulosa` in `trustedDependencies`. Bun runs lifecycle scripts only for packages named there, and the postinstall extracts the native libraries shipped with the package. The command writes:

```json
{
	"dependencies": {
		"nebulosa": "github:tiagohm/nebulosa.ts"
	},
	"trustedDependencies": ["nebulosa"]
}
```

Append `#` and a commit or tag to stay on one revision:

```sh
bun add --trust github:tiagohm/nebulosa.ts#<commit>
```

## 📚 Native libraries

The [postinstall](https://github.com/tiagohm/nebulosa.ts/blob/main/postinstall.ts) script extracts the shared libraries for this platform from zips shipped in `native/`:

- `libwcs.shared` — [WCSLIB](https://www.atnf.csiro.au/computing/software/wcs/), for FITS WCS pixel and sky transforms, from `libwcs-<platform>-<arch>.zip`
- `libturbojpeg.shared` — [TurboJPEG](https://github.com/libjpeg-turbo/libjpeg-turbo), for JPEG compression and decompression, from `libturbojpeg-<platform>-<arch>.zip`
- `libastrometry.shared` — [fork of Astrometry.net](https://github.com/tiagohm/astrometry.net), for local plate solving, from `libastrometry-<platform>-<arch>.zip`

The native libraries are built at [nebulosa.native](https://github.com/tiagohm/nebulosa.native) repository.

## ⭐ Astronomy

Times, coordinates, ephemerides, and events for bodies and observers.

### Affine Origin Frames

A rotation-only `Frame` changes the axes but keeps the origin. An affine frame also moves the origin: a position is first shifted by the origin position `O`, then rotated by `R`, and a velocity is shifted by the origin velocity `Ȯ`. If the frame rotates with time, the velocity gains the extra transport term `W · p`, with `W = dR/dt · Rᵀ`.

```text
p_frame = R · (p − O)
v_frame = R · (v − Ȯ) + W · p_frame
```

Affine frames move absolute positions (AU) or full `[position, velocity]` states (AU, AU/day) between systems whose centers differ, such as barycentric ICRS and a Sun-centered ecliptic system; the base side is always barycentric ICRS/BCRS axes. They only make sense for positions with a real distance: subtracting an origin from a normalized direction is meaningless, so convert directions with a plain `Frame`. Every plain `Frame` is also an affine frame whose origin stays at the base origin.

The heliocentric ecliptic frame has the orientation of the J2000 ecliptic with the origin at the Sun. Its Sun state is supplied by the caller, so the frame works with any ephemeris. The Galactic-center and Local Standard of Rest origins are covered by [Galactocentric Frame](#galactocentric-frame) and [Local Standard of Rest Frames](#local-standard-of-rest-frames).

```ts
import { affineFromBase, affineToAffine, affineToBase, BARYCENTRIC_ECLIPTIC, heliocentricEclipticFrame } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/affine'
import type { PositionAndVelocity } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/astrometry'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Heliocentric ecliptic J2000. The callback returns the Sun's barycentric ICRS state (AU, AU/day) at a time:
// constants here, an ephemeris lookup in practice.
const helio = heliocentricEclipticFrame(() => [
	[0.004, -0.007, -0.003],
	[0.0000035, 0.0000045, 0.000002],
])

// Barycentric ICRS state: position in AU, velocity in AU/day.
const state: PositionAndVelocity = [
	[1.2, 0.3, -0.5],
	[0.002, -0.001, 0.0008],
]

// Base (ICRS) -> frame: shift the origin, then rotate. A bare position (length 3) transforms only the position.
const [p, v] = affineFromBase(state, helio, time)

console.log(p) // [1.196, 0.083972, -0.578106] — AU, Sun-centered ecliptic axes
console.log(v) // [0.0019965, -0.000604, 0.001132] — AU/day

// BARYCENTRIC_ECLIPTIC only rotates the axes; the origin stays at the barycenter.
console.log(affineFromBase(state, BARYCENTRIC_ECLIPTIC, time)[0]) // [1.2, 0.076356, -0.578074] — AU

// Exact inverse, frame -> base.
console.log(affineToBase([p, v], helio, time)[0]) // [1.2, 0.3, -0.5] — AU, the original position

// Frame -> frame through the base: the heliocentric state back at the barycenter, in ecliptic axes.
console.log(affineToAffine([p, v], helio, BARYCENTRIC_ECLIPTIC, time)[0]) // [1.2, 0.076356, -0.578074] — AU
```

### Airmass and Extinction

Airmass is the optical path length through the atmosphere relative to the zenith path. It is 1 at the zenith and grows quickly near the horizon, where the simple `sec(z)` form stops being a good approximation. Atmospheric extinction is the magnitude loss `k · X`, where `k` is the extinction coefficient in magnitudes per airmass and `X` the airmass.

Use these for planning and photometric estimates, not for precise reduction. `airmass` is `sec(z)` from the zenith distance and is only reasonable well above the horizon. `airmassKastenYoung` takes the altitude instead and stays usable near the horizon; it is clamped to a minimum of 1 because the published fit dips slightly below 1 at the zenith. Both are dimensionless and ignore pressure, temperature, and altitude of the site.

```ts
import { airmass, airmassKastenYoung, atmosphericExtinction } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// sec(z). z: zenith distance in radians.
console.log(airmass(deg(60))) // 2.0 — dimensionless airmass

// Kasten-Young. altitude: radians above the horizon, in (0, PI/2].
console.log(airmassKastenYoung(deg(30))) // 1.9943 — dimensionless
console.log(airmassKastenYoung(deg(10))) // 5.5860 — dimensionless

// Magnitude loss = k * X. k: mag/airmass. X: airmass, must be >= 1.
console.log(atmosphericExtinction(0.2, airmassKastenYoung(deg(30)))) // 0.3989 — magnitudes lost
```

### Alt-Az Field Rotation

An alt-az mount keeps the optical axis on the target but not the sky orientation: the field turns about the optical axis at a rate that depends on latitude, azimuth, and altitude, and diverges at the zenith. The rate is `Ω · cos(latitude) · cos(azimuth) / cos(altitude)`, with `Ω` the sidereal rate. It equals minus the rate of the parallactic angle, and a rotator holds the sky orientation by commanding `offset − parallactic angle`.

The rate decides how long a sub-exposure can be before stars far from the rotation center trail by more than a chosen budget, and the derotator angle is what an instrument rotator must follow to cancel the rotation. Angles are radians, azimuth is measured north through east, and rates are radians per SI second. The rate is undefined at the zenith. Nothing here moves hardware, and the derotator track follows the sidereal hour angle only, ignoring the target's own motion.

```ts
import { parallacticAngle } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/astrometry'
import { derotatorAngle, derotatorTrack, fieldRotation, fieldRotationRate } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/field'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Signed rotation rate at latitude 45°, azimuth 30°, altitude 40°.
console.log(fieldRotationRate(deg(45), deg(30), deg(40))) // 5.829e-5 — rad/s

// Adds the longest exposure that keeps the smear within 1 pixel at 2000 px from the rotation center.
const rotation = fieldRotation(deg(45), deg(30), deg(40), 1, 2000)

console.log(rotation?.maxExposureSeconds) // 8.58 — seconds

// Parallactic angle q from hour angle (positive west), declination, and latitude.
console.log(parallacticAngle(hour(2), deg(20), deg(45))) // 0.6606 — radians

// Rotator command, offset − q, for the same target.
console.log(derotatorAngle(hour(2), deg(20), deg(45))) // -0.6606 — radians in (-PI, PI]

// Rotator commands sampled every 300 s over 600 s.
const track = derotatorTrack(hour(2), deg(20), deg(45), 600, 300)

console.log(track.map((s) => s.angle)) // [-0.6606, -0.6757, -0.6899] — radians at 0, 300, 600 s
```

### Angular Separation and Position Angle

Two sky positions are separated by the great-circle angle between them, and the position angle says in which direction one lies from the other, measured from celestial north toward east: 0° is north, 90° east, 180° south, 270° west. Together they describe double stars, offsets from a guide star, and the orientation of a target relative to a reference.

The separation is computed in an `atan2` form that keeps tiny separations accurate, where the classical cosine formula loses precision; a haversine variant exists but is less stable. The position angle is that of the second point as seen from the first, in `[0, 2π)`. For two Cartesian direction vectors instead of equatorial coordinates, use the vector separation. All angles are radians.

```ts
import { separationFrom } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/astrometry'
import { angularDistance, angularDistanceHaversine, positionAngleBetween } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/coordinate'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Right ascension and declination of point 0 and point 1 (radians).
console.log(toDeg(angularDistance(deg(10), deg(20), deg(10), deg(21)))) // 1.0 — degrees

// The same separation with the haversine formula.
console.log(toDeg(angularDistanceHaversine(deg(10), deg(20), deg(10), deg(21)))) // 1.0 — degrees

// Position angle of point 1 from point 0, north through east.
console.log(toDeg(positionAngleBetween(deg(10), deg(20), deg(10), deg(21)))) // 0 — north
console.log(toDeg(positionAngleBetween(deg(10), deg(20), deg(11), deg(20)))) // 89.83 — nearly east

// Angle between two direction vectors (need not be unit length).
console.log(toDeg(separationFrom([1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0]))) // 90 — degrees
```

### Angular Size and Surface Brightness Estimates

Angular diameter is the angle an object of a given size subtends at a given distance, `2 · atan(d / 2D)`. Surface brightness spreads an integrated magnitude over an area in square arcseconds, `m + 2.5 · log10(A)`, so a larger object of the same total magnitude is fainter per unit area.

These are planning helpers for sizing a target in the frame or judging how hard an extended object is to see. The surface brightness is a mean over the area you supply, not a measured profile.

```ts
import { objectAngularDiameter, surfaceBrightness } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'
import { toArcmin } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Diameter and distance must be in the same length unit (here km: Sun and 1 AU).
const theta = objectAngularDiameter(1391400, 149597870.7)

console.log(theta) // 0.0093009 — angular diameter in radians
console.log(toArcmin(theta)) // 31.974 — arcminutes

// Total magnitude 10 spread over 3600 arcsec² (one square arcminute).
console.log(surfaceBrightness(10, 3600)) // 18.8908 — mag/arcsec²
```

### Annual Aberration

Aberration is the apparent shift of a source toward the direction the observer is moving, caused by the observer's velocity relative to the speed of light. For the Earth's orbital speed (about 30 km/s) the shift reaches about 20.5″; the diurnal term from the Earth's rotation is much smaller.

The correction uses the ERFA special-relativistic model (`eraAb`) on a unit direction in ICRS/BCRS axes. It is the complete aberration for whatever velocity you pass: use the Earth's barycentric velocity for the annual term, or the observer's full barycentric velocity (geocenter plus diurnal rotation) for annual plus diurnal. The observer-Sun distance only feeds a tiny light-bending term inside the ERFA model. For a full astrometric-to-apparent chain with deflection and ordering handled for you, see [Apparent Direction](#apparent-direction).

```ts
import { annualAberration } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/correction'
import { kilometerPerSecond } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/velocity'

// direction: unit vector toward the source (ICRS/BCRS axes).
// observerVelocity: AU/day, barycentric. sunDistance: observer-Sun distance in AU.
const apparent = annualAberration([1, 0, 0], [0, kilometerPerSecond(29.78), 0], 1)

console.log(apparent) // [0.99999999507, 0.0000993354, 0] — unit vector, tilted toward +y, the velocity direction
```

### Apparent Direction

The apparent direction of a Solar-System target is where an observer sees it in barycentric ICRS/BCRS axes. It is built in a fixed order: solve light time to get the astrometric direction (the target at emission, the observer at reception), bend the ray by the gravity of any bodies you list, then apply the observer's aberration. Precession, nutation, Earth rotation, horizontal conversion, and refraction are not applied.

There is no hidden ephemeris: the target, observer, Sun, and every deflector are state providers you supply, each a function of `Time` returning a barycentric `[position (AU), velocity (AU/day)]`. Aberration needs the Sun, which supplies the observer-Sun distance. Deflection happens only for the bodies you list, in the order the photon meets them; the Sun is not implied. This path assumes a source at a finite distance; for a star at infinity use [Starlight Deflection](#starlight-deflection). When the light-time solution is already known, the deflection and aberration stages can be applied alone to snapshots.

```ts
import { apparentDirection, applyApparentDirectionCorrections, SUN_LIGHT_DEFLECTOR_LIMITER, SUN_LIGHT_DEFLECTOR_MASS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/apparent'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.TDB)

// target, observer, sun: providers of a barycentric [position (AU), velocity (AU/day)], such as ephemeris lookups.
// Light time, then deflection by the Sun, then the observer's aberration. JUPITER_ and SATURN_LIGHT_DEFLECTOR_MASS
// and _LIMITER describe the giant planets as further deflectors.
const result = apparentDirection(target, observer, time, {
	sun,
	deflectors: [{ mass: SUN_LIGHT_DEFLECTOR_MASS, limiter: SUN_LIGHT_DEFLECTOR_LIMITER, state: sun }],
})

console.log(result?.astrometric) // unit direction after light time
console.log(result?.apparent) // unit direction after deflection and aberration
console.log(result?.distance, result?.lightTime) // AU and days at the retarded solution

// Only the deflection and aberration stages, from snapshots: astrometric unit direction, target position at
// emission (AU), observer position (AU) and velocity (AU/day) at reception, and the light time (days).
const apparent = applyApparentDirectionCorrections(result!.astrometric, targetPosition, observerPosition, observerVelocity, result!.lightTime, { sunPosition })
```

### Approximate Atmospheric Refraction

Refraction bends starlight so an object appears higher than its geometric position, by about 1′ at 45° altitude and several arcminutes near the horizon. `atmosphericRefraction` uses Sæmundsson's formula (Meeus, ch. 16) as a standard-atmosphere planning estimate.

The input is the true (airless) altitude, and the result is the amount to add to it to get the apparent altitude. It is not Bennett's apparent-altitude formula and takes no pressure or temperature, so do not use it when pressure, temperature, humidity, or wavelength matter; see [Refractive Displacement](#refractive-displacement) for that. Valid for altitudes above the horizon.

```ts
import { atmosphericRefraction } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'
import { arcmin, deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// altitude: true geometric altitude in radians, in (0, PI/2].
const r = atmosphericRefraction(deg(10))

console.log(r) // 5.4077 — refraction in arcminutes (not radians)
console.log(atmosphericRefraction(deg(45))) // 1.0127 — arcminutes

// Apparent altitude = true altitude + refraction (converted to radians).
const apparent = deg(10) + arcmin(r)

console.log(apparent) // 0.17611 — apparent altitude in radians
```

### Asteroid and Comet Magnitude Estimates

Apparent magnitude grows with the distances to the Sun and to the observer. Asteroids follow `m = H + 5·log10(r·Δ) + φ`, where `H` is the absolute magnitude and `φ` is a phase correction you supply. Comets follow `m = H + 5·log10(Δ) + k·log10(r)`, where `k` is an activity coefficient you supply.

These are quick planning formulas, not the Mallama and Hilton planetary model, and they do not compute the phase angle or the phase function for you; use [Planetary Apparent Magnitudes (Mallama and Hilton)](#planetary-apparent-magnitudes-mallama-and-hilton) for planets. Distances are positive and in AU.

```ts
import { asteroidMagnitudeEstimate, cometMagnitudeEstimate } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'

// H: absolute magnitude. r: heliocentric distance (AU). delta: geocentric distance (AU).
// phase: magnitude correction already computed by the caller.
console.log(asteroidMagnitudeEstimate(12, 1.5, 0.8, 0.3)) // 12.696 — apparent magnitude

// H: total absolute magnitude. delta, r: AU. k: activity coefficient.
console.log(cometMagnitudeEstimate(8, 0.5, 1.2, 10)) // 7.2867 — apparent magnitude
```

### Asteroid and Comet Orbit Construction

A small body's orbit is described by classical elements referred to a plane and an epoch. Asteroids are normally given by the semi-major axis, eccentricity, inclination, longitude of the ascending node, argument of perihelion, and mean anomaly at an epoch. Comets, whose eccentricity can be 1 or more, are given by perihelion distance and the time of perihelion passage instead, since a parabolic or hyperbolic orbit has no finite semi-major axis or period. Both become a `KeplerOrbit`, a two-body orbit around the Sun whose state the library can propagate (see [Two-Body Kepler Propagation](#two-body-kepler-propagation)).

The elements are heliocentric and referred to the ecliptic and equinox of J2000, as in the MPC files, and the gravitational parameter is the Sun's. The comet constructor takes the semi-latus rectum `p = q(1 + e)`, which stays finite for every conic, rather than the perihelion distance `q`. The state at the epoch is kept in that ecliptic frame, while a propagated state is rotated to equatorial J2000. Orbits can also be built from parsed MPC records (see [MPCORB Parsing](#mpcorb-parsing)), whose epochs are TT, or from a Cartesian state. A hyperbolic orbit has a negative semi-major axis and an infinite period.

```ts
import { asteroid, comet, KeplerOrbit, mpcAsteroid } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/asteroid'
import { mpcorb } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/mpcorb'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const epoch = timeYMDHMS(2025, 5, 5, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Ceres: a (AU), e, i, node, argument of perihelion, and mean anomaly at the epoch (radians).
const ceres = asteroid(2.7660512, 0.0794013, deg(10.5878), deg(80.25221), deg(73.27343), deg(188.70269), epoch)

console.log(ceres.position) // [2.7711, -0.96407, -0.54103] — AU, heliocentric ecliptic J2000 at the epoch
console.log(ceres.periodInDays / 365.25) // 4.600 — years

// Two-body propagation to another instant: [position (AU), velocity (AU/day)] in equatorial J2000.
const [position, velocity] = ceres.at(timeYMDHMS(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT))

// Halley: semi-latus rectum p = q(1 + e) in AU, e, i, node, argument of perihelion, and the perihelion time.
const halley = comet(0.583972 * (1 + 0.967311), 0.967311, deg(162.2146), deg(59.6368), deg(112.547), timeYMDHMS(2061, 8, 31, 19, 50, 18, Timescale.TT))

console.log(halley.periodInDays / 365.25) // 75.5 — years

// The underlying constructors take the semi-latus rectum p = a(1 − e²) and an anomaly: KeplerOrbit.meanAnomaly (used by asteroid),
// KeplerOrbit.periapsis (used by comet, the epoch being the perihelion time), and KeplerOrbit.trueAnomaly.
const e = 0.0794013
console.log(KeplerOrbit.meanAnomaly(2.7660512 * (1 - e * e), e, deg(10.5878), deg(80.25221), deg(73.27343), deg(188.70269), epoch).position) // [2.7711, -0.96407, -0.54103] — AU, Ceres again

// line: the MPCORB.DAT record of Ceres (epoch K2555 = 2025-05-05). mpcComet(mpcorbComet(line)) does the same for CometEls.txt.
console.log(mpcAsteroid(mpcorb(line)!).position) // [2.7711, -0.96407, -0.54103] — AU, the same orbit
```

### Astrometric Sample-Grid Interpolation

A plate-solved image gives the sky position of every pixel through the WCS, but evaluating the projection for each mouse movement or overlay vertex is slow. The interpolator evaluates right ascension and declination once on a coarse, regular grid of pixels and then answers pixel-to-sky queries with a cheap local interpolation (bicubic by default).

Samples are stored as Cartesian unit vectors, so interpolation never jumps across the 0/2π right ascension seam, and the interpolated vector is renormalized before it is converted back to right ascension and declination. Queries outside the sampled extent are clamped to its edge rather than extrapolated, so sample the whole image. This interpolates a precomputed grid; it is not a plate solution, for which see [Plate Solution](#plate-solution).

```ts
import { AstrometricInterpolator } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/interpolation/astrometric'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// ra, dec: width × height samples in radians, row-major, evaluated from the WCS every 10 px in x and 20 px in y.
const interpolator = new AstrometricInterpolator(ra, dec, width, height, 10, 20)

// Sky position of pixel (15, 30): right ascension in [0, 2π) and declination, in radians.
const [rightAscension, declination] = interpolator.pixelToSky(15, 30)

console.log(toDeg(rightAscension), toDeg(declination)) // degrees
```

### Astronomical State Ownership

Position and velocity states are plain pairs of three-component arrays, `[position (AU), velocity (AU/day)]`, in ICRS/BCRS axes, and the types say who may write them. `PositionAndVelocity` is a read-only state you may read but do not own; `PositionAndVelocityMut` is a writable workspace or result whose position and velocity are distinct arrays. `readonly` is only a promise of the type: it does not make the storage a snapshot, and its lifetime belongs to whoever produced it.

This matters because state providers (`PositionAndVelocityOverTime` and its position-only and velocity-only variants), the functions of `Time` that ephemerides and paths expose, may return borrowed storage that they overwrite on their next call. Keeping such a state across calls without copying it silently changes it, and two independent providers must not share output storage. Functions that fill an optional output return that output, so passing the same workspace twice makes the first result alias the second. Light-time solutions are owned snapshots, safe to keep.

The relative state of two providers is their geometric difference `target − origin` at the same instant, with no light time and no aberration: with the Sun as origin it is heliocentric, with the Earth geocentric.

```ts
import { type PositionAndVelocity, type PositionAndVelocityOverTime, relativePositionAndVelocity, zeroPositionAndVelocity } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/astrometry'
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 4, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// A heliocentric Earth state: Earth minus Sun, both barycentric VSOP87E providers, as a new writable state.
const [position, velocity] = relativePositionAndVelocity(earth, sun, time)

console.log(position) // [0.12544, -0.92555, -0.40121] — AU
console.log(velocity) // [0.016787, 0.0018891, 0.00081848] — AU/day

// Any function of Time returning a state is a provider. Copy a borrowed result before calling the provider again.
const fixed: PositionAndVelocityOverTime = (): PositionAndVelocity => [
	[1, 0, 0],
	[0, 0, 0],
]
const kept = fixed(time).map((v) => [...v])

// A fresh writable zero state, never shared with another call.
const workspace = zeroPositionAndVelocity()
```

### Astronomical Time Arithmetic

Differences and offsets between instants are only meaningful inside one time scale. UTC has leap seconds, so a UTC "day" can be 86401 s long, while TAI and TT run uniformly. Elapsed physical time must therefore be measured on TAI or TT, while a UTC difference counts civil days on the quasi-Julian-Date axis and ignores the leap second.

A difference is computed after converting both instants to one scale, by default that of the first. A shift moves an instant by a number of days in its own scale and keeps its location and providers; whole and fractional days can be passed separately so that very large shifts keep the two-part precision. An instant can also be built at an absolute Julian Date in the scale of a reference instant.

```ts
import { Timescale, timeAtJulianDay, timeShift, timeSubtract, timeToDate, timeYMD, timeYMDHMS, tt } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

const newYear = timeYMD(2017, 1, 1)
const eve = timeYMD(2016, 12, 31) // a leap second was inserted at the end of this day

// a - b in days, in the scale of a (UTC) or in an explicit scale.
console.log(timeSubtract(newYear, eve)) // 1 — days, UTC quasi-JD (leap second not counted)
console.log(timeSubtract(newYear, eve, Timescale.TAI) * 86400) // 86401 — elapsed SI seconds

// Move by a number of days (1/24 = one hour). The scale is preserved.
console.log(timeToDate(timeShift(timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0), 1 / 24))) // [2026, 6, 29, 1, 0, 0, 0]

// Instant at an absolute Julian Date, in the scale of the reference (TT here).
console.log(timeToDate(timeAtJulianDay(tt(timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29)), 2461221.25))) // [2026, 6, 29, 18, 0, 0, 0] — TT clock reading
```

### Astronomical Time Representation and Epochs

A `Time` is an instant stored as an integer Julian Date `day`, a `fraction` of a day in `[−0.5, 0.5)`, and a `Timescale` tag (`UT1`, `UTC`, `TAI`, `TT`, `TCG`, `TDB`, `TCB`). A single double holds a Julian Date to only about 40 µs, so the two-part form keeps full precision. The fraction is measured from the nearest integer day: JD 2461220.5 is stored as day 2461221 and fraction −0.5. Read it as `day + fraction`.

Astronomy writes instants in several epoch conventions, and each has a constructor: the Julian Date, the Modified Julian Date (`JD − 2400000.5`), Julian epoch years such as J2000.0 (365.25-day years, on TT by default), Besselian epoch years such as B1950.0 of the older catalogs, counts of units after a reference instant, and GPS seconds (a TAI instant). The tag only labels the instant; converting between scales is a separate step, see [Astronomical Time-Scale Conversion](#astronomical-time-scale-conversion), and calendar construction is under [Civil UTC Timestamps](#civil-utc-timestamps).

```ts
import { time, timeBesselianYear, timeFromEpoch, timeGPS, timeJulianYear, timeMJD, timeNormalize, Timescale, toJulianDay, toJulianEpoch } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

// day: integer Julian Date. fraction: days. Normalized so the fraction is within [-0.5, 0.5); UTC by default.
const t = time(2451545, 0.25)

console.log(t.day, t.fraction) // 2451545 0.25

// The normalization alone: day and fraction re-split so the fraction is within [-0.5, 0.5).
const normalized = timeNormalize(2451545, 0.75)

console.log(normalized.day, normalized.fraction) // 2451546 -0.25

// Epoch conventions.
console.log(toJulianDay(timeMJD(51544.5))) // 2451545 — J2000.0 as a JD
console.log(toJulianDay(timeBesselianYear(1950))) // 2433282.42346 — B1950.0 as a JD in TT
console.log(toJulianEpoch(timeJulianYear(2026.5))) // 2026.5 — Julian epoch year

// 1.5 days (in seconds, 86400 per day) after JD 2451545.0, labeled TAI.
console.log(toJulianDay(timeFromEpoch(86400 * 1.5, 86400, 2451545, 0, Timescale.TAI))) // 2451546.5

// GPS time zero is 1980-01-06 00:00:00 UTC, as a TAI instant.
console.log(toJulianDay(timeGPS(0))) // 2444244.50022 — TAI
```

### Astronomical Time-Scale Conversion

Astronomy uses several time scales. UTC is the civil scale with leap seconds; TAI is atomic time without them; TT is the uniform scale of geocentric ephemerides, `TT = TAI + 32.184 s`; TDB is the barycentric dynamical scale of Solar-System ephemerides, which differs from TT by a periodic term under 2 ms; TCG and TCB are the coordinate scales of relativity, which run faster than TT and TDB; and UT1 follows the Earth's actual rotation. Conversions go through TAI: UTC to TAI adds the leap-second count, and UT1 needs `UT1 − UTC` from the IERS Earth orientation tables.

Each conversion returns a new instant in the target scale. Without loaded IERS tables `UT1 − UTC` is 0, so UT1 silently equals UTC; load them first (see [Earth Orientation Parameters](#earth-orientation-parameters)). TDB − TT is the ERFA model and includes a topocentric term when the instant carries a location. The offsets come from replaceable providers, which an instant can override for itself.

```ts
import { dut1, taiMinusUtc, tdb, tdbMinusTt, tdbMinusTtByFairheadAndBretagnon1990, timeConvert, timeToDate, Timescale, timeYMDHMS, tt, ut1MinusTai, utc } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

const instant = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// One function per target scale (utc, ut1, tai, tt, tcg, tdb, tcb), or timeConvert for any.
const terrestrial = tt(instant)

console.log(timeToDate(terrestrial)) // [2026, 6, 29, 0, 1, 9, 184] — TT clock reading, 69.184 s ahead
console.log(utc(terrestrial).day === instant.day) // true — round trip
console.log(timeConvert(instant, Timescale.TDB).scale === tdb(instant).scale) // true

// The offsets, in seconds.
console.log(taiMinusUtc(instant)) // 37 — leap seconds in force
console.log(tdbMinusTt(terrestrial)) // 0.000174 — TDB - TT
console.log(dut1(instant)) // 0 — UT1 - UTC, 0 when no IERS data is loaded
console.log(ut1MinusTai(instant)) // -37 — UT1 - TAI

// The defaults are in TIME_PROVIDERS. An alternative TDB - TT series (USNO Circular 179), usable as an
// instant's providers.tdbMinusTt.
console.log(tdbMinusTtByFairheadAndBretagnon1990(terrestrial)) // 0.000178 — seconds
```

### B-Plane

During a flyby the small body moves relative to the planet on an approximately two-body hyperbola. The B-plane is the plane through the planet's center perpendicular to the incoming asymptote `S`, and the B-vector runs from the center to where the asymptote pierces it. Its length, the impact parameter, is the perpendicular miss distance of the undeflected path; it exceeds the real closest-approach distance because of gravitational focusing. Its components on the `T` and `R` axes are the standard coordinates for flyby targeting, gravity assists, and impact and keyhole analysis.

The B-plane is formed from the osculating hyperbola of the planetocentric state (body minus planet, in AU and AU/day) near the encounter, where the two-body approximation holds; the relative orbit must be hyperbolic. The axes follow the convention `T = S × pole`, `R = S × T`. The default pole is the `z` axis of the state, the equator for an ICRF state; pass the ecliptic pole in the state's axes for the ecliptic convention, since `T` and `R` components from different conventions are not comparable. The default gravitational parameter is the Earth's.

```ts
import { closeApproachBPlane } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/bplane'
import { kilometer, toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'
import { kilometerPerSecond, toKilometerPerSecond } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/velocity'

// Body minus Earth, inbound at about 300000 km: position in AU, velocity in AU/day.
const position = [kilometer(-300000), kilometer(40000), kilometer(10000)] as const
const velocity = [kilometerPerSecond(12), kilometerPerSecond(-1), kilometerPerSecond(0.5)] as const

const bplane = closeApproachBPlane(position, velocity)

console.log(toKilometer(bplane.impactParameter)) // 27288 — km, |B|
console.log(toKilometer(bplane.bt), toKilometer(bplane.br)) // -15086 -22739 — km, B-vector on T and R
console.log(toKilometerPerSecond(bplane.vInfinity)) // 11.94 — km/s, hyperbolic excess speed
console.log(toKilometer(bplane.periapsisDistance)) // 24636 — km, closest approach (smaller than |B|)

// The same encounter on the ecliptic convention: the ecliptic pole in the state's axes.
const ecliptic = closeApproachBPlane(position, velocity, { pole: [0, -0.3978, 0.9175] })

console.log(toKilometer(ecliptic.bt), toKilometer(ecliptic.br)) // -22880 -14871 — km
```

### Barycentric and Heliocentric Light-Time Correction

Light from a distant source reaches the Earth earlier or later than it would reach the Solar-System barycenter (BJD) or the Sun's center (HJD), depending on where the observer sits along the line of sight. The light-travel-time correction is `(r_obs · n) / c`, with `r_obs` the observer's position relative to the chosen center and `n` the unit direction to the source; it reaches about ±8.5 minutes. Timing work such as eclipse or pulsar timing adds it to the observed time.

The correction is in days, positive when the observer lies on the source's side of the center. The reference center is the one of the Earth state you pass: a barycentric Earth state gives the barycentric correction and a heliocentric one the heliocentric correction. A site adds its topocentric offset to the Earth state. This is the first-order term only; for a complete BJD_TDB with the TDB conversion and the Shapiro delay, see [Barycentric Julian Date](#barycentric-julian-date). The same observer state feeds [Radial Velocity Correction](#radial-velocity-correction).

```ts
import { lightTravelTime, observerState } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/correction'
import { eraEpv00 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/earth'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { tdb, Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// La Silla Observatory: longitude, latitude, elevation.
const location = geodeticLocation(deg(-70.7313), deg(-29.2563), meter(2400))
const time = timeYMDHMS(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Earth's [barycentric, heliocentric] state (AU, AU/day) at the TDB instant.
const t = tdb(time)
const [barycentric, heliocentric] = eraEpv00(t.day, t.fraction)

// Correction for a source at RA 5.5 h, Dec -5° (ICRS, radians), in days.
console.log(lightTravelTime(hour(5.5), deg(-5), time, barycentric, location) * 86400) // 413.66 — seconds, barycentric
console.log(lightTravelTime(hour(5.5), deg(-5), time, heliocentric, location) * 86400) // 410.68 — seconds, heliocentric

// The observer's barycentric [position (AU), velocity (AU/day)]: Earth plus the site's offset and diurnal velocity.
const [position, velocity] = observerState(time, barycentric, location)
```

### Barycentric Julian Date

BJD_TDB is the instant a signal would reach the Solar System barycenter, read on the Barycentric Dynamical Time clock. It removes the observer's orbital and diurnal motion from a time series, which is why transit, eclipse, and pulsar timings are published in it:

```text
BJD_TDB = TDB(t) + Δ_Rømer + Δ_Shapiro
```

The reception instant `t` is first converted to TDB (the Einstein delay). The Rømer delay `(r · n) / c` is the geometric light time between the observer at barycentric position `r` and the barycenter along the source direction `n`; it reaches about ±8.5 min. The solar Shapiro delay is the extra light time of a ray passing the Sun, tens of microseconds within a few tens of degrees of the Sun and about 112 µs at the solar limb. A plane wavefront is assumed unless the source distance is given; the curvature it neglects is at most `(1 AU)² / (2cd)`, about 120 µs at 10 pc.

The observer is an SSB-centered ephemeris path: for a ground site compose an SSB-to-Earth path with the site (see [Ephemeris Path Composition](#ephemeris-path-composition)), for a spacecraft pass its own barycentric path. A path with another center is rejected, because a Sun-centered one would produce an HJD labelled as BJD. The source direction is ICRS at the observation epoch, so apply proper motion first, and the Shapiro term needs a Sun path. The ephemeris sets the floor of the Rømer term: each kilometer of observer position error is 3.3 µs, so use an SPK kernel rather than an analytical Earth for microsecond work. The result is a two-part TDB `Time`, not UTC; the inverse finds the UTC reception instant of a published BJD_TDB, such as a transit center (see [Exoplanet Transit Prediction](#exoplanet-transit-prediction)). The timestamp of an exposure is discussed in [Exposure Timing](#exposure-timing).

```ts
import fs from 'fs/promises'
import { barycentricJulianDate, receptionFromBarycentricJulianDate } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/correction'
import { eraS2c } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/erfa'
import { readDaf } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/daf'
import { Naif } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/naif'
import { readSpk } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/spk'
import { composeEphemerisPaths, customEphemerisEndpoint } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/path'
import { earthObserverEphemerisPath, spkEphemerisPath } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/path.adapter'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { exposureInterval } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/exposure'
import { Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { fileHandleSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/file'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

await using source = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/de421.bsp'))
const spk = readSpk(await readDaf(source))

// SSB -> Earth from DE421, then Earth -> La Silla; and SSB -> Sun for the Shapiro term.
const earth = composeEphemerisPaths((await spkEphemerisPath(spk, Naif.SSB, Naif.EMB))!, (await spkEphemerisPath(spk, Naif.EMB, Naif.EARTH))!)
const sun = (await spkEphemerisPath(spk, Naif.SSB, Naif.SUN))!
const location = geodeticLocation(deg(-70.7313), deg(-29.2563), meter(2400))
const observer = composeEphemerisPaths(earth, earthObserverEphemerisPath(location, customEphemerisEndpoint('la-silla')))

// Midpoint of a 300 s exposure stamped at the open command, with 0.12 s shutter latency; the location adds the topocentric TDB term.
const start = timeYMDHMS(2024, 3, 10, 3, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
start.location = location
const exposure = exposureInterval({ time: start, reference: 'start', duration: 300, openLatency: 0.12 })

// UTC reception -> BJD_TDB for a source at RA 5.5 h, Dec -5° (ICRS unit direction).
const bjd = barycentricJulianDate(exposure.midpoint, eraS2c(hour(5.5), deg(-5)), observer, { sun })

console.log(bjd.time.day, bjd.time.fraction) // 2460380 -0.37232562 — BJD_TDB = 2460379.62767438
console.log(bjd.romer, bjd.shapiro) // 11.82055 2.0e-7 — seconds added

// BJD_TDB -> UTC reception instant at the site: the exposure midpoint, 03:02:30.06.
const reception = receptionFromBarycentricJulianDate(bjd.time, eraS2c(hour(5.5), deg(-5)), observer, location, { sun })

console.log(timeToDate(reception)) // [2024, 3, 10, 3, 2, 30, 60] — UTC
```

### Binary PCK Rotation

A binary PCK (Planetary Constants Kernel) is the NAIF file that stores the high-precision orientation of a body-fixed frame, such as the Moon's principal-axes frame derived with a JPL ephemeris, as Chebyshev series for three Euler angles `φ`, `δ`, `W` against an inertial frame (J2000, NAIF id 1). The rotation is `R = Rz(W) · Rx(δ) · Rz(φ)`, from the inertial frame to the body-fixed frame, and the angular-rate operator `W = dR/dt · Rᵀ` comes from the same polynomials, in radians per day. Only Chebyshev Type 2 segments are supported.

A PCK is read from an already-opened DAF (see [DAF Binary Containers](#daf-binary-containers)) and its segments are looked up by frame class id, such as 31006 for the DE421 lunar principal axes. Coefficient records are read on demand, so the file must stay open, with synchronous reads, while you evaluate. A segment is a `Frame`, so it works with the frame functions as well as directly, at any time scale (converted to TDB) inside its coverage. For the IAU analytical rotation models see [IAU Body Orientation](#iau-body-orientation).

```ts
import fs from 'fs/promises'
import { readDaf } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/daf'
import { readPck } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/pck'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { fileHandleSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/file'

// Lunar principal-axes orientation from the DE421 binary PCK; the source stays open while it is used.
await using source = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/moon_pa_de421_1900-2050.bpc'))
const pck = readPck(await readDaf(source))

// Loads the segment directories.
await pck.initialize()

const moon = pck.segment(31006)!
const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.TDB)

// Inertial -> Moon principal-axes rotation, row-major 3x3.
console.log(moon.rotationAt(time)) // [-0.04874, 0.92578, 0.37490, -0.99873, -0.04988, -0.00666, 0.01254, -0.37475, 0.92704]

// Angular-rate operator W = dR/dt · Rᵀ, radians per day (antisymmetric).
console.log(moon.dRdtTimesRtAt(time)) // [0, 0.22998, -0.0000071, -0.22998, 0, -0.00021533, 0.0000071, 0.00021533, 0]
```

### Body-Surface Solar Illumination

On a rotating body, the local Sun altitude at a surface point is the angle between the Sun direction and the local horizontal plane, which is perpendicular to the reference ellipsoid's normal at that point. It changes as the body rotates, and sunrise and sunset are the times it crosses a chosen horizon altitude. On the Moon or Mars this decides when a landing site, a crater, or a feature for imaging is lit, and how low the Sun stands for relief.

The site is a body-surface location whose frame orients the rotating body (see [Planetary Surface Locations](#planetary-surface-locations)), and the Sun is a function of `Time` returning the body-center-to-Sun vector in the library's base axes. The Sun is treated as a point at infinity seen in parallel across the body: there is no terrain, refraction, solar radius, or surface parallax, and the altitude refers to the solar center. Sunrise and sunset are found by scanning a window with a step small enough that no two crossings share it; an empty list can mean polar day or night. For a feature's incidence, emission, terrain mask, and shadows, see [Surface Feature Illumination](#surface-feature-illumination).

```ts
import { bodyFixedFrame, MOON_ROTATION } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/orientation'
import { moon } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/elpmpp02'
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { bodySurfaceSolarAltitude, bodySurfaceSunEvents } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/surface'
import { bodyShape, bodySurfaceLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/body'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeSubtract, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { kilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const epoch = timeYMDHMS(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Copernicus crater on the Moon: 20.08° W, 9.62° N, on a sphere of radius 1737.4 km.
const radius = kilometer(1737.4)
const location = bodySurfaceLocation(deg(-20.08), deg(9.62), 0, bodyShape([radius, radius, radius]), bodyFixedFrame(MOON_ROTATION))

// Moon-center to Sun, in base axes (geometric, no light time).
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0]), moon(time)[0])

// Altitude of the Sun's center, radians.
console.log(toDeg(bodySurfaceSolarAltitude(location, sunAt, epoch))) // -43.87 — degrees, the Sun is below the horizon

// Sunrise and sunset over 32 days, scanning every 0.5 day.
const events = bodySurfaceSunEvents(location, sunAt, epoch, timeShift(epoch, 32), { step: 0.5 })

console.log(events.map((e) => e.kind)) // ['sunrise', 'sunset']
console.log(events.map((e) => timeSubtract(e.time, epoch))) // [3.674, 18.492] — days after the epoch
```

### Carrington Rotation

The Carrington system numbers the Sun's rotations by a fixed synodic period of about 27.275 days, as seen from Earth, counted from a conventional epoch in 1853. Solar maps and datasets are usually labeled by Carrington rotation number.

`carringtonRotationNumber` returns the integer rotation number whose span contains the given `Time`. It is a linear count with that fixed period; it does not compute the central meridian longitude within the rotation. For the observed Carrington longitude of the disk center (L0), see [Solar Disk Geometry and Heliographic Coordinates](#solar-disk-geometry-and-heliographic-coordinates).

```ts
import { carringtonRotationNumber } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/sun'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

const rotation = carringtonRotationNumber(timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC))

console.log(rotation) // 2302 — Carrington rotation number
```

### Celestial and Terrestrial Reference Frames

A reference frame here is an orientation of the axes, defined relative to a common base (ICRS/GCRS-oriented) by a base-to-frame rotation matrix at a time. Fixed frames never change: ICRS, FK4, FK5, Galactic, Supergalactic, the B1950 equatorial and ecliptic, and the J2000 ecliptic. Dynamical frames depend on time: the mean and true equator and equinox of date, the mean and true ecliptic of date, and the Celestial Intermediate Reference System (CIRS). Earth-fixed frames add the planet's rotation: TIRS, and ITRS (TIRS plus polar motion). TEME, the SGP4 frame, is also provided.

A rotating frame also needs the term `W = dR/dt · Rᵀ`, so that a full state transforms as `v_frame = R · v_base + W · p_frame`; a point at rest in ICRS moves in ITRS. A single precomputed rotation matrix between two frames is fine for positions and inertial pairs but does not include `W`, so it gives wrong velocities in a rotating frame. Frames only rotate: they do not shift the origin (see [Affine Origin Frames](#affine-origin-frames)) and do not apply aberration, deflection, or refraction (see [Apparent Direction](#apparent-direction)). Units are whatever the input carries: AU and AU/day for states.

```ts
import { eraS2c } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/erfa'
import { cirs, ECLIPTIC_J2000, ecliptic, frameAt, frameRotationAt, frameToBase, frameToFrame, GALACTIC, galactic, ICRS, ITRS, supergalactic } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/frame'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Unit direction for RA 10 h, Dec +20° in ICRS.
const direction = eraS2c(hour(10), deg(20))

// Named wrappers: ICRS -> Galactic axes (fixed), ICRS -> ecliptic of date (needs a time).
console.log(galactic(direction)) // [-0.5312, -0.3556, 0.7690]
console.log(ecliptic(direction, time)) // unit vector in ecliptic-of-date axes

// Other fixed wrappers: icrs, fk4, fk5, eclipticJ2000, eclipticB1950, meanEquatorAndEquinoxAtB1950.
console.log(supergalactic(direction)) // [0.1500, 0.8327, -0.5330]

// Other time-dependent wrappers: meanEquatorAndEquinoxOfDate, trueEquatorAndEquinoxOfDate, meanEclipticOfDate,
// tirs, teme, itrs, itrsInstantaneous.
console.log(cirs(direction, time)) // [-0.8147, 0.4698, 0.3399] — CIRS axes

// Generic conversions: between two frames through the base, and back to the base. The Frame constants are ICRS, FK4,
// FK5, GALACTIC, SUPERGALACTIC, ECLIPTIC_J2000, ECLIPTIC_B1950, MEAN_EQUATOR_AND_EQUINOX_AT_B1950,
// MEAN_EQUATOR_AND_EQUINOX_OF_DATE, TRUE_EQUATOR_AND_EQUINOX_OF_DATE, MEAN_ECLIPTIC_OF_DATE, ECLIPTIC, CIRS, TIRS,
// TEME, ITRS, and ITRS_INSTANTANEOUS.
console.log(frameToFrame(direction, ICRS, ECLIPTIC_J2000)) // unit vector in ecliptic J2000 axes
console.log(frameToBase(galactic(direction), GALACTIC, time)) // [-0.8138, 0.4698, 0.3420] — the original direction

// A state (AU, AU/day) fixed in ICRS at 1 AU on +x: in ITRS Earth's spin adds W · p to the velocity.
const state = [
	[1, 0, 0],
	[0, 0, 0],
] as const

const [position, velocity] = frameAt(state, ITRS, time)

console.log(position) // [-0.1261, -0.9920, 0.0026] — AU, Earth-fixed axes
console.log(velocity) // [-6.250, 0.7946, 0] — AU/day

// One matrix for many positions at one instant (no W term).
const rotation = frameRotationAt(ICRS, GALACTIC, time)
```

### Civil UTC Timestamps

Civil time is a calendar date and clock reading in UTC, and Unix time counts seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. UTC includes leap seconds, so a civil day can last 86401 s and the clock can read 23:59:60. The library keeps this exact when you build or read UTC instants: a UTC day is 86400 s plus its leap second, while a day of any other scale is 86400 s, and a date read back is in the clock of the instant's own scale.

Unix time follows POSIX: every day has 86400 labelled seconds, so on a leap-second day a Unix value maps to the same civil clock reading as `Date.UTC`, and the inserted second 23:59:60.x converts to the Unix value of the next midnight. Conversions to Unix time convert the instant to UTC first.

```ts
import { timeNow, timeToDate, timeToUnix, timeToUnixMillis, timeUnix, timeYMD, timeYMDHMS, utcLeapSeconds } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

// Year, month, day, hour, minute, and second (fractional allowed), UTC by default.
const instant = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 12, 30, 15.25)

console.log(timeToDate(instant)) // [2026, 6, 29, 12, 30, 15, 250] — UTC; the last field is rounded milliseconds
console.log(timeToDate(timeYMD(2026, 6, 29, 0.75))) // [2026, 6, 29, 18, 0, 0, 0] — 0.75 of the civil day

// Unix seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, both ways.
console.log(timeToDate(timeUnix(946684800))) // [2000, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]
console.log(timeToUnix(timeYMDHMS(2000, 1, 1))) // 946684800 — seconds
console.log(timeToUnixMillis(timeYMDHMS(2000, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0.25))) // 946684800250 — milliseconds

// A positive leap second: 2016-12-31 23:59:60.
console.log(timeToDate(timeYMDHMS(2016, 12, 31, 23, 59, 60.5))) // [2016, 12, 31, 23, 59, 60, 500]

// Extra length of a UTC civil day in seconds (year, month, day).
console.log(utcLeapSeconds(2016, 12, 31), utcLeapSeconds(2016, 12, 30)) // 1 0

// Current instant from the system clock, UTC.
const now = timeNow()
```

### Constellations

The IAU divides the sky into 88 constellations with boundaries defined along lines of constant right ascension and declination in the B1875 equinox (Delporte, 1930). Because the boundaries are fixed to that equinox, a position of another equinox must be precessed to B1875 before the lookup, otherwise objects near a boundary land in the wrong constellation.

The lookup precesses the position from its equinox (J2000 by default) to B1875 and searches the boundary table. The result is the three-letter uppercase key, which indexes a table of display names, IAU abbreviations, Latin genitives, and short descriptions.

```ts
import { CONSTELLATION_LIST, constellation, CONSTELLATIONS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/constellation'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// J2000 right ascension 5h30m, declination -5° (radians).
const key = constellation(hour(5.5), deg(-5))

console.log(key) // ORI
console.log(CONSTELLATIONS[key].name, CONSTELLATIONS[key].genitive) // Orion Orionis

// Coordinates already on the B1875 equinox: no precession is applied.
console.log(constellation(hour(5.5), deg(-5), false)) // ORI

// All keys, in table order.
console.log(CONSTELLATION_LIST.length) // 88
```

### DAF Binary Containers

DAF (Double precision Array File) is the NAIF binary container underneath SPK ephemeris kernels and binary PCK orientation kernels. A file is a sequence of 1024-byte records holding a header, a chain of segment summaries, and the numeric data, as 64-bit floats in either byte order. Each summary describes one segment: a trimmed name, a few doubles (for SPK and PCK these are the start and end epochs, in TDB seconds past J2000), and integers (ids, data type, and the first and last data word).

Reading a DAF parses only the header and the summary chain from a seekable source; the data stay on disk and are read as 1-based, inclusive ranges of double-words, so the source must stay open while the container is used. Synchronous reads need a source that supports them, which kernel frames require because a rotation cannot await. The container only exposes numbers: interpret the segments with [Binary PCK Rotation](#binary-pck-rotation) or [SPK State Kernels](#spk-state-kernels).

```ts
import fs from 'fs/promises'
import { readDaf } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/daf'
import { fileHandleSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/file'

// The source must be seekable and stay open while you read from the Daf.
await using source = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/moon_pa_de421_1900-2050.bpc'))
const daf = await readDaf(source)

const [summary] = daf.summaries

console.log(summary.name) // de421.nio
console.log(summary.doubles) // [-3155716800, 1609416000] — start and end epochs, TDB seconds past J2000
console.log(summary.ints) // [31006, 1, 2, 641, 221284] — frame id, inertial frame id, data type, first and last double-word

// Double-words 641 to 644 of the segment data (1-based, inclusive); readSync is the synchronous counterpart.
const words = await daf.read(summary.ints[3], summary.ints[3] + 3)
```

### Delta T

Delta T is `TT − UT1`: the gap between the uniform Terrestrial Time scale and Earth-rotation time. It changes irregularly because the Earth's rotation does, so past values come from historical records and future values are extrapolations. It is needed whenever dynamical time must be turned into a civil or rotational clock without IERS data, such as for historical eclipses or events decades ahead.

One model is used per era: the Stephenson, Morrison and Hohenkerk 2016 parabola before year −720, their S15 cubic spline from there to 2019, and the Espenak and Meeus 2006 expressions after 2019. A step of about 1.8 s exists at 2019, where observations hand over to forward prediction, so values after 2019 are model predictions rather than measurements. The Espenak-Meeus polynomial alone is also available.

```ts
import { deltaT, deltaTByEspenakMeeus2006, parabolaOfStephensonMorrisonHohenkerk2016, s15 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/deltat'

// year: decimal calendar year, e.g. 2000.5 is mid-2000. Result in seconds.
console.log(deltaT(2000)) // 63.81 — seconds, from the S15 spline
console.log(deltaT(1900)) // -1.98 — seconds
console.log(deltaT(2100)) // 202.74 — seconds, predicted

// Each model alone: the Espenak-Meeus polynomial, the S15 spline segment of a year, and the long-term
// parabola (parabolaOfStephensonMorrison2004 is the older one).
console.log(deltaTByEspenakMeeus2006(2000)) // 63.86 — seconds
console.log(s15(2000).compute(2000)) // 63.81 — seconds, what deltaT uses here
console.log(parabolaOfStephensonMorrisonHohenkerk2016.compute(-1000)) // 25049.16 — seconds, what deltaT uses before -720
```

### Dew Point and Frost

The dew point is the temperature at which air saturates and water condenses on a surface; the frost point is the same for deposition of ice. Both come from the Magnus approximation. The margin `T − Tdew` says how far the air is from saturation, and optics that cool below the dew point by radiating to the night sky collect dew, which is why dew heaters are driven from it.

Temperatures are °C within the Magnus domain of −100 to 100 °C, and humidity is relative, in percent. The frost point expects the humidity relative to ice, not the water-relative value weather stations report; above freezing the dew point is the relevant temperature. The relative humidity is the inverse of the dew point, and the dew risk is a planning scale from 1 at or below the dew point down to 0 at a clear margin.

```ts
import { dewMargin, dewPoint, dewRisk, dewRiskFromMargin, frostPoint, relativeHumidity } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'

// temperature: °C. humidity: percent over water, in (0, 100].
const td = dewPoint(20, 60)

console.log(td) // 12.0 — dew point in °C
console.log(relativeHumidity(20, td)) // 60 — percent, inverse of dewPoint
console.log(frostPoint(-10, 50)) // -17.58 — °C, humidity relative to ice

// Margin above the dew point (T - Tdew) and the risk on a 0..1 scale.
console.log(dewMargin(20, 60)) // 8.0 — °C
console.log(dewRisk(10, 90, 10)) // 0.8435 — margin of 1.57 °C against a 10 °C clear margin

// The same risk from a margin measured directly (°C), against the default clear margin.
console.log(dewRiskFromMargin(2)) // 0.6
```

### Differential Orbit Correction

Differential correction refines an approximate orbit so that it reproduces a set of astrometric observations. Starting from a state guess at an epoch, the six Cartesian parameters (position and velocity) are adjusted to minimize the weighted squared difference between the observed and predicted right ascension and declination, using a Levenberg-Marquardt least-squares loop with a finite-difference Jacobian. It is a two-body fit around the Sun: it models no planetary perturbations, so it suits short arcs and modest accuracy.

Each observation has its time, right ascension and declination in radians in the same inertial frame as the state, the observer's position at that time in the same frame and units (AU, heliocentric for a heliocentric state), and 1σ uncertainties that weight it. At least three observations are needed for six parameters, and the starting state typically comes from [Gauss Angles-Only Orbit Determination](#gauss-angles-only-orbit-determination). A reduced χ² near 1 means the residuals match the stated uncertainties. The parameter covariance is scaled by the reduced χ² and feeds [Orbit Covariance Propagation](#orbit-covariance-propagation).

```ts
import { fitOrbit } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/fit'
import { Timescale, time } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toArcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const epoch = time(2460787, 0, Timescale.TDB)

// observations: OrbitFitObservation[] — time, RA and Dec (radians), the observer's heliocentric position (AU), and 1σ errors.
// position, velocity: approximate heliocentric state at the epoch (AU, AU/day).
const fit = fitOrbit(observations, epoch, position, velocity)

console.log(fit.converged, fit.reducedChi2) // convergence, and χ² per degree of freedom
console.log(toArcsec(fit.rms)) // arcseconds, RMS angular residual
console.log(fit.state.position, fit.state.velocity) // fitted state, AU and AU/day
console.log(fit.orbit.semiMajorAxis) // AU, from the fitted KeplerOrbit
console.log(fit.covariance) // 6×6 covariance of x, y, z, vx, vy, vz
```

### Differential Refraction and Atmospheric Dispersion

Refraction depends on wavelength: blue light is bent more than red, so the image of a star is stretched into a short spectrum along the vertical, with the blue end toward the zenith. The effect grows toward the horizon and matters for broadband imaging, guiding in a different band from the science camera, and slit spectroscopy, where it moves light out of the slit unless the slit is aligned with the parallactic angle.

Differential refraction is the signed difference between the refractive displacements at two wavelengths, positive when the first is the bluer one. Atmospheric dispersion is the length of the spectrum of a whole band, optionally oriented by the parallactic angle and converted to pixels. Both take the apparent altitude and optional pressure, temperature, and humidity, and are undefined at and below the horizon. For one wavelength, see [Refractive Displacement](#refractive-displacement).

```ts
import { atmosphericDispersion, differentialRefraction } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/refraction'
import { deg, hour, toArcsec, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Blue (0.45 µm) minus red (0.65 µm) at apparent altitude 45°; the sign follows the argument order.
console.log(toArcsec(differentialRefraction(deg(45), 0.45, 0.65)!)) // 0.8669 — arcseconds
console.log(toArcsec(differentialRefraction(deg(10), 0.45, 0.65)!)) // 4.7616 — arcseconds, larger lower down

// A 0.4-0.7 µm band at altitude 40°, oriented by hour angle, declination, and latitude, at 1.5"/pixel.
const dispersion = atmosphericDispersion(deg(40), 0.4, 0.7, { hourAngle: hour(2), declination: deg(20), latitude: deg(-30), arcsecPerPixel: 1.5 })

console.log(dispersion?.arcseconds) // 1.7036 — arcseconds
console.log(toDeg(dispersion!.positionAngle!)) // 149.2 — degrees, parallactic angle: blue end toward the zenith
console.log(dispersion?.pixels) // 1.1357 — pixels
```

### Digital Elevation Model Terrain

A digital elevation model (DEM) is a grid of surface heights, such as the LOLA topography of the Moon. On an airless body, relief decides the look of the surface near the terminator: a crater floor stays dark while its rim is lit, and a peak casts a shadow whose length grows as the Sun drops, roughly `L ≈ h / tan(altitude)` on level ground, the basis of the classical shadow-length measurement of lunar heights. A smooth reference ellipsoid predicts none of this.

The terrain functions work on a caller-supplied grid in body-fixed planetocentric longitude and latitude, with heights in AU above the same reference ellipsoid as the feature's location (for LOLA, a 1737.4 km sphere). They stand a feature on the terrain, march the DEM to build its horizon mask and its facet slope for [Surface Feature Illumination](#surface-feature-illumination), trace a ray toward a direction to tell whether relief blocks it, and find the tip of the shadow a summit or rim casts. The Sun is treated as a point; to bracket the penumbra, offset the solar altitude by its angular radius. All results are only as good as the DEM: ridges and peaks narrower than its spacing can be missed or smoothed.

```ts
import { bodyFixedFrame, MOON_ROTATION } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/orientation'
import { moon } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/elpmpp02'
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { surfaceFeature, surfaceFeatureIllumination } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/surface'
import { type ElevationGrid, terrainElevation, terrainHorizon, terrainModel, terrainOcclusion, terrainShadowTip, terrainSlope, terrainSurfaceLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/surface.terrain'
import { bodyShape } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/body'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { kilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// grid: ElevationGrid — heights in AU above the 1737.4 km sphere on a planetocentric longitude/latitude grid around Copernicus.
declare const grid: ElevationGrid
const dem = terrainModel(grid)

// Interpolated terrain height (AU) at 20.08° W, 9.62° N; undefined off the grid or next to missing data.
console.log(terrainElevation(dem, deg(-20.08), deg(9.62)))

// A feature standing on the terrain, then with the horizon mask and facet the DEM implies.
const radius = kilometer(1737.4)
const floor = surfaceFeature(terrainSurfaceLocation(dem, deg(-20.08), deg(9.62), bodyShape([radius, radius, radius]), bodyFixedFrame(MOON_ROTATION))!)
const feature = surfaceFeature(floor.location, { ...terrainSlope(dem, floor), horizon: terrainHorizon(dem, floor) })

// The local Sun at one instant (Moon-centre to Sun and to the geocenter, AU).
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0]), moon(time)[0])
const earthAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus([0, 0, 0], moon(time)[0])
const light = surfaceFeatureIllumination(feature, sunAt, earthAt, timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 20, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.TDB))

// The first terrain crossing of the ray toward the Sun, or undefined when it is clear of relief.
const blocker = terrainOcclusion(dem, feature, light.solarAltitude, light.solarAzimuth)

console.log(blocker === undefined ? 'sunlit' : 'in a cast shadow')

// The tip of the shadow the feature casts down-Sun: its length along the surface (AU).
console.log(terrainShadowTip(dem, feature, light.solarAltitude, light.solarAzimuth)?.distance)
```

### Earth Occultation of a Finite Target

A satellite or spacecraft can be hidden behind the solid Earth as seen from another one, which decides when an inter-satellite link, a relay, or an observation of one spacecraft from another is possible. The question is whether the straight segment from an observer to a target at a finite distance touches the Earth's reference ellipsoid, and where. This is a geometric test only: there is no atmosphere, terrain, or shadow of the Sun, so it says nothing about visibility under illumination.

Observer and target are geocentric positions in AU, in the same GCRS/ICRS-oriented axes at the same reception time; they are rotated into ITRS and the segment is tested against the ellipsoid (IERS 2010 by default). A surface contact counts as an occultation, and the first contact is reported as a fraction of the segment from the observer. The observer must be outside the solid Earth.

```ts
import { earthOccultation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/occultation.earth'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { kilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// An observer 7000 km from the center on +x, and a target 40000 km on the opposite side: Earth is in the way.
const behind = earthOccultation([kilometer(7000), 0, 0], [kilometer(-40000), 0, 0], time)

console.log(behind.occulted) // true
console.log(behind.intersection) // 0.01323 — fraction of the segment: about 622 km from the observer, at the surface

// Same side: the segment moves away from the Earth.
console.log(earthOccultation([kilometer(7000), 0, 0], [kilometer(40000), 0, 0], time).occulted) // false
```

### Earth Orientation Parameters

The Earth does not rotate uniformly, and its rotation axis wanders slightly inside the crust. The IERS publishes the irregularities as daily Earth orientation parameters: `UT1 − UTC` in seconds and the polar-motion coordinates `x`, `y` in arcseconds. They are needed for UT1, sidereal time, and the GCRS to ITRS rotation, so they are the data behind precise Earth-fixed work and topocentric coordinates.

The library has no built-in tables. You load one of two IERS files into a shared provider, and the time module reads them automatically: the IERS Bulletin A `finals2000A` file (rapid and predicted values extending into the future) or the IERS EOP 14 C04 `eopc04` series (final values); where both cover a date, C04 is preferred. Values are linearly interpolated between daily samples, with the leap-second jump removed from `UT1 − UTC` so it stays continuous, and clamp to the nearest edge outside the table. With nothing loaded they are 0, which silently turns UT1 into UTC, so load a table before computing UT1-dependent results. To use other data for a single instant, replace the providers described in [Astronomical Time-Scale Conversion](#astronomical-time-scale-conversion).

```ts
import { dut1, iersa, iersab, xy } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/iers'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS, ut1 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { readableStreamSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'
import { toArcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// IERS Bulletin A (finals2000A); iersb loads the final C04 series the same way.
await using source = readableStreamSource(Bun.file('data/finals2000A.txt').stream())
await iersa.load(source)

// Use instants created after loading: an offset already computed is cached on its instant.
const time = timeYMDHMS(2020, 10, 7, 12, 34, 56, Timescale.UTC)

console.log(dut1(time)) // -0.17181 — seconds, UT1 - UTC
console.log(xy(time).map(toArcsec)) // [0.18781, 0.31804] — arcseconds, polar motion x and y (returned in radians)
console.log(iersa.covers(time)) // true
console.log(iersa.distance(time)) // 0 — days outside the table's coverage

// iersab, the C04-first combination of iersa and iersb, is what dut1 and xy read; it has the same
// dut1, xy, and covers methods. new IersA(), new IersB(), and new IersAB(a, b) build private tables.
console.log(iersab.dut1(time)) // -0.17181 — seconds

// The time module now applies UT1 - UTC.
const instant = ut1(time)

// Drop the loaded table; lookups fall back to 0.
iersa.clear()
```

### Elliptic Elements to Rectangular State

The analytical satellite theories describe each orbit by slowly varying elliptic elements and need a position and velocity from them. The element set used is equinoctial-style, which stays well defined for small eccentricity and inclination where the classical node and periapsis are undefined: mean longitude `L = Ω + ω + M`, `K = e·cos(Ω + ω)`, `H = e·sin(Ω + ω)`, `Q = sin(i/2)·cos Ω`, and `P = sin(i/2)·sin Ω`. Kepler's equation is solved directly in these variables.

The element array is `[a or n, L, K, H, Q, P]` with the angles in radians, and the state is evaluated a time offset `dt` in days after the elements' epoch. The first element is either the semi-major axis in AU, with the mean motion derived from the gravitational parameter `mu` (AU³/day²), or the mean motion in radians per day, with the semi-major axis derived. Position is in AU and velocity in AU/day, in the frame the elements are referred to. The orbit must be elliptic (`K² + H² < 1`); for hyperbolic or parabolic orbits see [Two-Body Kepler Propagation](#two-body-kepler-propagation).

```ts
import { ellipticToRectangular, ellipticToRectangularA, ellipticToRectangularN } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/ephemeris'
import { GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005, TAU } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'

const mu = GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005 // AU³/day²
const n = Math.sqrt(mu) // radians/day for a = 1 AU, a period of 365.26 days

// Circular, equatorial orbit of a = 1 AU (K = H = Q = P = 0) starting at L = 0 on +x, a quarter of an orbit later.
const [position, velocity] = ellipticToRectangularA(mu, [1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], TAU / n / 4)

console.log(position) // [0, 1, 0] — AU
console.log(velocity) // [-0.017202, 0, 0] — AU/day, counter-clockwise

// The same orbit with the mean motion (radians/day) in place of a.
console.log(ellipticToRectangularN(mu, [n, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], TAU / n / 4)[0]) // [0, 1, 0] — AU

// The general form takes both a (AU) and n (radians/day), and ignores the first element.
console.log(ellipticToRectangular(1, n, [1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], TAU / n / 4)[0]) // [0, 1, 0] — AU
```

### ELP/MPP02 Lunar Theory

ELP/MPP02 is an analytical theory of the Moon's motion. It sums large tables of periodic terms, the main problem plus planetary and other perturbations, for the Moon's ecliptic longitude, latitude, and distance, and ties the result to the ICRF equatorial frame. It needs no data files and works over a wide range of dates, which makes it a good default Moon ephemeris when an SPK kernel is not at hand.

The state is geocentric, in AU and AU/day, in ICRF equatorial axes, at any time scale (converted to TT). Add it to the Earth's barycentric state to get a barycentric Moon (see [Ephemeris Path Composition](#ephemeris-path-composition)), and for a high-precision lunar ephemeris use an SPK kernel instead (see [SPK State Kernels](#spk-state-kernels)).

```ts
import { moon } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/elpmpp02'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// Geocentric [position (AU), velocity (AU/day)] in ICRF axes.
const [position, velocity] = moon(timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.TT))

console.log(position) // [-0.00052834, -0.0023152, -0.0012725] — AU, geocentric ICRF
console.log(velocity) // [0.00055235, -0.000087550, -0.000035530] — AU/day
console.log(toKilometer(Math.hypot(...position))) // 403051 — km, Earth-Moon distance
```

### Ephemeris Observed Positions

Observing a body from another moves through stages, each a distinct kind of position. A geometric position is the same-epoch center-to-target state. An astrometric position is the retarded one: the target is sampled at emission time and the observer at reception, so light time is accounted for. An apparent position then adds the deflection of light by Solar-System bodies and the observer's aberration, while distance and light time stay astrometric. Each stage is an owned snapshot tagged with its kind, in ICRS/BCRS-oriented axes, positions in AU, velocities in AU/day, and light time in days.

This is the path-based counterpart of [Apparent Direction](#apparent-direction): the observer and target are barycentric ephemeris paths (see [Ephemeris Path Composition](#ephemeris-path-composition)), aberration needs a barycentric Sun path, and deflection applies only to the bodies you list. A stage can be read as right ascension, declination, and distance, rotated into another frame, or, for a geometric state, converted to spherical coordinates and rates (see [Spherical State Rates](#spherical-state-rates)). Right ascension and declination here are ICRS, not of date: no precession, nutation, or refraction is applied, and for an observed place use [Topocentric Observed Place](#topocentric-observed-place).

```ts
import { ECLIPTIC_J2000 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/frame'
import { Naif } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/naif'
import { earth, mars, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { ephemerisPath, naifEphemerisEndpoint, SOLAR_SYSTEM_BARYCENTER } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/path'
import { apparentPosition, directionPositionInFrame, ephemerisAt, equatorialPosition, geometricPositionInFrame, geometricSphericalPositionAndVelocity, observeEphemeris } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/position'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toDeg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TDB)

// Barycentric paths from VSOP87E: Earth is the observer, Mars the target, the Sun feeds the aberration term.
const earthPath = ephemerisPath(SOLAR_SYSTEM_BARYCENTER, naifEphemerisEndpoint(Naif.EARTH, 'Earth'), earth)
const marsPath = ephemerisPath(SOLAR_SYSTEM_BARYCENTER, naifEphemerisEndpoint(499, 'Mars'), mars)
const sunPath = ephemerisPath(SOLAR_SYSTEM_BARYCENTER, naifEphemerisEndpoint(Naif.SUN, 'Sun'), sun)

// Geometric: Earth's owned barycentric state.
const geometric = ephemerisAt(earthPath, time)

console.log(geometric.position) // [0.12079, -0.93081, -0.40337] — AU

// The geometric state rotated into another frame, and as spherical coordinates with their rates.
console.log(geometricPositionInFrame(geometric, ECLIPTIC_J2000)[0]) // [0.12079, -1.01445, 0.00016925] — AU, ecliptic J2000
const spherical = geometricSphericalPositionAndVelocity(geometric, ECLIPTIC_J2000)!

console.log(toDeg(spherical.longitude), toDeg(spherical.longitudeRate!)) // 276.79 0.94891 — degrees and degrees/day

// Astrometric: Mars as seen from Earth, with light time.
const astrometric = observeEphemeris(earthPath, marsPath, time)!

console.log(astrometric.distance, astrometric.lightTime) // 2.1124 0.012200 — AU and days

// Apparent: adds aberration (no deflectors listed).
const apparent = apparentPosition(astrometric, { sun: sunPath })
const [ra, dec, distance] = equatorialPosition(apparent)

console.log(toHour(ra), toDeg(dec), distance) // 3.8430 19.780 2.1124 — hours, degrees, AU (ICRS, not of date)

// The unit direction of an astrometric or apparent stage rotated into another frame.
console.log(directionPositionInFrame(apparent, ECLIPTIC_J2000)) // [0.50360, 0.86392, -0.0057048] — unit vector, ecliptic J2000
```

### Ephemeris Path Adapters

The library's state sources differ: a JPL SPK kernel stores Chebyshev segments between NAIF bodies, SGP4 propagates an Earth satellite in the TEME frame, and a ground or planetary-surface site moves with its body's rotation. Adapters turn each into an ephemeris path, so they can be composed and observed uniformly (see [Ephemeris Path Composition](#ephemeris-path-composition)). All paths are synchronous, in AU and AU/day, in ICRS/BCRS-oriented axes.

The SPK adapter is asynchronous only to prepare the segment; evaluating it may still read the file, so keep the DAF source open. It yields nothing when the kernel has no segment for that center and target, and accepts only segments in the J2000 frame, because any other frame would be published as ICRS axes. The SGP4 adapter takes a TLE, an OMM, or a prepared record and converts SGP4's TEME state to ICRS. The site adapters include the diurnal or rotational velocity of the site.

```ts
import fs from 'fs/promises'
import { bodyFixedFrame, MOON_ROTATION } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/orientation'
import { readDaf } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/daf'
import { Naif } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/naif'
import { readSpk } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/spk'
import { customEphemerisEndpoint, naifEphemerisEndpoint } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/path'
import { bodySurfaceEphemerisPath, earthObserverEphemerisPath, sgp4EphemerisPath, spkEphemerisPath } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/path.adapter'
import { bodyShape, bodySurfaceLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/body'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { parseTLE } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/propagation/sgp4'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { fileHandleSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/file'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { kilometer, meter, toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2023, 8, 19, 12, 25, 28, Timescale.UTC)

// SPK: Earth-Moon barycenter -> Earth from DE421 (undefined when the kernel has no such segment).
await using source = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/de421.bsp'))
const earth = (await spkEphemerisPath(readSpk(await readDaf(source)), Naif.EMB, Naif.EARTH))!

// SGP4: Earth -> ISS from a TLE, as a geocentric ICRS path with target id norad:25544.
const iss = sgp4EphemerisPath(parseTLE('1 25544U 98067A   23231.51768399  .00014050  00000+0  25837-3 0  9996', '2 25544  51.6415  14.7889 0003559 325.3396 149.4637 15.49477580411611'))

console.log(iss.stateAt(time)[0].map(toKilometer)) // [-3712, 2990, 4839] — km, geocentric ICRS

// Earth center -> observatory.
const observatory = earthObserverEphemerisPath(geodeticLocation(deg(-70.7313), deg(-29.2563), meter(2400)), customEphemerisEndpoint('lasilla', 'La Silla'))
```
