```ts
console.log(observatory.stateAt(time)[0].map(toKilometer)) // [678, 5529, -3102] — km, geocentric ICRS

// Moon center -> Copernicus crater on a 1737.4 km sphere.
const radius = kilometer(1737.4)
const surface = bodySurfaceLocation(deg(-20.08), deg(9.62), 0, bodyShape([radius, radius, radius]), bodyFixedFrame(MOON_ROTATION))
const crater = bodySurfaceEphemerisPath(naifEphemerisEndpoint(Naif.MOON, 'Moon'), customEphemerisEndpoint('copernicus', 'Copernicus'), surface)

console.log(crater.stateAt(time)[0].map(toKilometer)) // [1639, -565, 107] — km, 1737.4 km from the Moon's center
```

### Ephemeris Path Composition

An ephemeris path is a prepared, synchronous state provider from a center to a target: a function of `Time` returning `[position (AU), velocity (AU/day)]` in ICRS/BCRS-oriented axes, tagged with its two endpoints. Paths can be chained or subtracted like vectors between points: Earth to Moon added to the barycenter to Earth gives the barycenter to Moon, and two paths from the same center give the target relative to any other body. This is how ephemerides from different sources (an SPK kernel, VSOP87, ELP/MPP02, a ground site) are combined into the barycentric observer and target that observation needs.

An endpoint is a NAIF body code or a caller-defined identifier; its name is only a label. Chaining requires the first path's target to be the second path's center, and subtraction requires a common center, so the endpoints catch a mismatched combination. No light time is applied: use [Ephemeris Observed Positions](#ephemeris-observed-positions) for that. The state a path returns is borrowed: each path reuses its own storage, so a later call overwrites an earlier result; copy it, or materialize an owned snapshot with `ephemerisAt`, to keep it.

```ts
import { Naif } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/naif'
import { moon } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/elpmpp02'
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { composeEphemerisPaths, ephemerisPath, naifEphemerisEndpoint, relativeEphemerisPath, reverseEphemerisPath, sameEphemerisEndpoint, SOLAR_SYSTEM_BARYCENTER } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/path'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TDB)

const EARTH = naifEphemerisEndpoint(Naif.EARTH, 'Earth')

// Wrap providers: barycenter -> Earth and -> Sun from VSOP87E, Earth -> Moon from ELP/MPP02 (geocentric).
const earthPath = ephemerisPath(SOLAR_SYSTEM_BARYCENTER, EARTH, earth)
const sunPath = ephemerisPath(SOLAR_SYSTEM_BARYCENTER, naifEphemerisEndpoint(Naif.SUN, 'Sun'), sun)
const moonFromEarth = ephemerisPath(EARTH, naifEphemerisEndpoint(Naif.MOON, 'Moon'), moon)

// Barycenter -> Moon = (barycenter -> Earth) + (Earth -> Moon).
console.log(composeEphemerisPaths(earthPath, moonFromEarth).stateAt(time)[0]) // [0.12060, -0.93320, -0.40464] — AU, barycentric ICRS

// Earth -> Sun from two paths with the same center.
console.log(relativeEphemerisPath(sunPath, earthPath).stateAt(time)[0]) // [-0.12263, 0.92586, 0.40134] — AU

// Earth -> barycenter: center and target swapped, state negated.
console.log(reverseEphemerisPath(earthPath).stateAt(time)[0]) // [-0.12079, 0.93081, 0.40337] — AU

// Endpoints compare by NAIF code or identifier, never by name.
console.log(sameEphemerisEndpoint(earthPath.target, naifEphemerisEndpoint(Naif.EARTH, 'Terra'))) // true
```

### Equation of Time

The equation of time is the difference between apparent solar time (a sundial) and mean solar time (a clock). Here it is the hour-angle difference, apparent Sun minus mean Sun, and it stays within roughly ±16 minutes over a year, positive when the sundial is ahead of the clock. It comes from the eccentricity of the Earth's orbit and the obliquity of the ecliptic.

The result is in radians, wrapped to `[−π, π]`; multiply degrees by 4 to get minutes of time. The caller supplies the apparent right ascension of the Sun, which must be referred to the true equator and equinox of date, the same reference as Greenwich apparent sidereal time. Passing an ICRS/J2000 right ascension adds a spurious precession term of about 50″ per year, so precess and nutate the Sun direction first. Keeping the right ascension as an argument leaves the function independent of the ephemeris model.

```ts
import { equationOfTime } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/sun'
import { equatorial } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/astrometry'
import { equatorialFromJ2000 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/coordinate'
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 11, 3, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Geocentric ICRS direction to the Sun, then its right ascension of date.
const [ra, dec] = equatorial(vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0]))
const [raOfDate] = equatorialFromJ2000(ra, dec, time)

// Apparent minus mean solar hour angle, radians.
console.log(toDeg(equationOfTime(time, raOfDate)) * 4) // 16.42 — minutes of time; the sundial is ahead of the clock
```

### Equatorial Ephemeris Interpolation

A precomputed ephemeris, such as a table of apparent right ascension and declination from an external service, gives positions at discrete times. An interpolator turns those samples into a continuous function of time, from which you read positions at any instant inside the span, for example to track a comet or asteroid between tabulated rows, or resample a denser table. It works on topocentric or apparent equatorial samples, with right ascension unwrapped before fitting so the 0/2π seam causes no jump; consecutive samples must therefore be close enough that the target moves less than π radians in right ascension between them.

Three families are available: piecewise linear, cubic splines (including monotone variants that do not overshoot), and a least-squares Chebyshev polynomial over the whole interval, which is smooth but unsafe to extrapolate. Times may be in any scale and are converted to TT. Outside the sampled span the position is clamped to the nearest end by default. For a pixel grid rather than a time series, see [Astrometric Sample-Grid Interpolation](#astrometric-sample-grid-interpolation).

```ts
import { chebyshevInterpolator, linearInterpolator, splineInterpolator } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/interpolation/ephemeris'
import { Timescale, time, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, hour, toDeg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)
const at = (days: number) => time(start.day, start.fraction + days, Timescale.TT)

// Daily samples over 4 days: { time, rightAscension, declination } in radians.
const points = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4].map((d) => ({ time: at(d), rightAscension: hour(10) + deg(0.5) * d + deg(0.02) * d * d, declination: deg(20) - deg(0.1) * d }))

// Linear interpolation: [ra, dec] in radians at any instant of the span. The factories return
// LinearEphemerisInterpolator, SplineEphemerisInterpolator, and ChebyshevEphemerisInterpolator instances.
const linear = linearInterpolator(points)
const [ra, dec] = linear.compute(at(1.5))

console.log(toHour(ra), toDeg(dec)) // 10.0533 19.85 — hours, degrees

// The same evaluation written into a caller-owned [ra, dec] pair.
const out: [number, number] = [0, 0]
linear.computeInto(at(1.5), out)

// Refit the same interpolator to new samples, here every declination 1° higher.
linear.update(points.map((p) => ({ ...p, declination: p.declination + deg(1) })))

console.log(toDeg(linear.compute(at(1.5))[1])) // 20.85 — degrees

// Natural cubic spline (default type) and a degree-4 Chebyshev fit.
console.log(toHour(splineInterpolator(points).compute(at(1.5))[0])) // 10.0530 — hours
console.log(toHour(chebyshevInterpolator(points, 4).compute(at(1.5))[0])) // 10.0530 — hours

// A denser table.
const table = splineInterpolator(points).resample([at(0.5), at(2.5)])
```

### Equatorial Mount Geometric Pointing Errors

An equatorial mount that is not perfectly built or aligned points slightly away from where its axes say it points. The model here is the six basic geometric terms of TPoint: index offsets in hour angle and declination (`IH`, `ID`), collimation or cone error (`CH`), non-perpendicularity of the polar and declination axes (`NP`), and polar-axis misalignment in azimuth (`MA`) and elevation (`ME`). The error at a mechanical orientation is

```text
ΔH = IH + CH·sec δ + NP·tan δ − MA·cos H·tan δ + ME·sin H·tan δ
Δδ = ID + MA·sin H + ME·cos H
```

`[ΔH, Δδ]` is the amount to add to the mechanical hour angle and declination to get where the optical axis really points; in right ascension, with `H = LST − RA`, the true pointing is `[RA − ΔH, δ + Δδ]`. A polar axis misaligned by knob errors is the special case `MA = azimuth·cos(latitude)` and `ME = −altitude`, plus a constant hour-angle term `azimuth·sin(latitude)`; a positive altitude error means the polar axis points above the true pole. All coefficients are radians. The `sec δ` and `tan δ` terms diverge at the pole, so near it the raw `ΔH` grows large without meaning an on-sky error of that size; the corrected right ascension and declination remain well defined there. Add tube flexure separately with [Tube Flexure Pointing Error](#tube-flexure-pointing-error).

```ts
import { applyEquatorialPointingError, equatorialPointingError, type EquatorialPointingModel, IDENTITY_EQUATORIAL_POINTING_MODEL, isIdentityEquatorialPointingModel, polarAlignmentPointingModel } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/pointing'
import { arcsec, deg, hour, toArcsec, toDeg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const model: EquatorialPointingModel = {
	...IDENTITY_EQUATORIAL_POINTING_MODEL,
	indexHourAngle: arcsec(30), // IH
	indexDeclination: arcsec(-45), // ID
	coneError: arcsec(120), // CH
	axisNonPerpendicularity: arcsec(90), // NP
	polarAzimuthError: arcsec(60), // MA
	polarAltitudeError: arcsec(-60), // ME
}

// Whether every term is zero, so the correction can be skipped.
console.log(isIdentityEquatorialPointingModel(IDENTITY_EQUATORIAL_POINTING_MODEL), isIdentityEquatorialPointingModel(model)) // true false

// [ΔH, Δδ] at hour angle 3 h, declination +45°.
const [deltaHourAngle, deltaDeclination] = equatorialPointingError(hour(3), deg(45), model)

console.log(toArcsec(deltaHourAngle), toArcsec(deltaDeclination)) // 204.85 -45 — arcseconds

// Where the optical axis actually points when the mount reads RA 10 h, Dec +45° at LST 13 h.
const [ra, dec] = applyEquatorialPointingError(hour(10), deg(45), hour(13), model)

console.log(toHour(ra), toDeg(dec)) // 9.9962 44.9875 — hours, degrees

// Model of a polar axis 120" off in azimuth and 300" too low, at latitude +40°.
const polar = polarAlignmentPointingModel(arcsec(120), arcsec(-300), deg(40))

console.log(toArcsec(polar.polarAzimuthError), toArcsec(polar.polarAltitudeError)) // 91.93 300 — MA, ME in arcseconds
```

### Equinoxes and Solstices

The astronomical seasons begin at the two equinoxes and two solstices, the instants when the Sun's apparent ecliptic longitude is 0°, 90°, 180°, and 270°. Here `spring`, `summer`, `autumn`, and `winter` name the starts of the northern-hemisphere seasons: the March equinox, June solstice, September equinox, and December solstice.

`season` uses Meeus' method and is valid for years 1000 to 3000. The instant comes back in dynamical time: the returned `Time` is tagged TT, so convert it with `utc` for a civil clock time, which moves it earlier by [Delta T](#delta-t) (about a minute in the 2020s).

```ts
import { season } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/sun'
import { timeToDate, utc } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

// year: calendar year. name: 'spring' | 'summer' | 'autumn' | 'winter'. The instant is TT.
const june = season(2026, 'summer')

console.log(timeToDate(utc(june)).slice(0, 6)) // [2026, 6, 21, 8, 24, 55] — civil UTC
console.log(timeToDate(utc(season(2026, 'winter'))).slice(0, 6)) // [2026, 12, 21, 20, 50, 13]
```

### ERFA / SOFA Algorithms

SOFA (Standards of Fundamental Astronomy) is the IAU's reference implementation of the models that define time scales, Earth rotation, precession-nutation, reference frames, and astrometry; ERFA (Essential Routines for Fundamental Astronomy) is its openly licensed derivative. Results computed with them agree with other software that follows the IAU resolutions, which is why the rest of the library builds on them. `nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/erfa` is a TypeScript port of ERFA that keeps the `era` prefix of the C names (`eraAtco13`, `eraC2t06a`, `eraNut06a`, and so on); the companion modules `erfa/earth` and `erfa/moon` add `eraEpv00` (Earth position and velocity) and `eraMoon98` (geocentric Moon). The tests of the library reproduce the t_erfa_c reference values.

The port follows the conventions of the original. A date is a two-part Julian Date `(date1, date2)` whose sum is the date, split to keep the precision (`2400000.5` plus an MJD, or `2451545` plus an offset). Angles are radians, distances AU, velocities AU/day, except parameters typed `Velocity`, which are in the library's velocity unit. Rotation matrices are row-major `Mat3` in the sense of the C code. Functions that return several values return a tuple, and a routine whose C version returns a status code returns it as the first element of the tuple or as `false`.

The routines come in families named after ERFA: `Tt`, `Tai`, `Utc`, `Ut1`, `Tdb` and `Tcb` for the time scales; `Nut`, `Pn`, `Pnm`, `Pr`, `Prec`, `Bp`, `Pfw` and `Fw` for precession, bias and nutation (IAU 1976/1980, 2000A/B and 2006); `Gst`, `Gmst`, `Era` and `Ee` for sidereal time; `Xy`, `Xys` and `S` for the CIO locator; `C2i`, `C2t`, `C2ixy` and `C2tcio` for the celestial-to-terrestrial matrices; `Ap` and `At` for the star-independent parameters and the astrometric transformations; `Fk`, `H`, `Icrs` and `G` for the reference frames; `Tp` for the tangent plane; `Ltp` and `Lte` for long-term precession; `Fa` for the fundamental arguments; and `Pv`, `Star` and `Pm` for position/velocity and proper motion. The observer chain goes from ICRS to CIRS to observed azimuth, zenith distance, hour angle, and right ascension and declination, with refraction when the pressure is positive; its star-independent parameters are an `EraAstrom` record that the `eraAp*` routines build and the `eraAt*` routines consume.

```ts
import { eraEpv00 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/earth'
import {
	eraAnpm,
	eraApco13,
	eraAtciq,
	eraAtco13,
	eraAtoc13,
	eraBp06,
	eraC2s,
	eraC2t06a,
	eraCalToJd,
	eraDat,
	eraEra00,
	eraFk425,
	eraGd2Gce,
	eraGmst06,
	eraHd2ae,
	eraIcrs2g,
	eraLtpequ,
	eraNut06a,
	eraObl06,
	eraRefco,
	eraStarpm,
	eraTaiTt,
	eraTpxes,
	eraUtcTai,
	eraUtcUt1,
	eraXys06a,
} from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/erfa'
import { eraMoon98 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/moon'
import { arcsec, deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'
import { kilometerPerSecond } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/velocity'

// Angles and vectors: normalize to [-π, π), and Cartesian to spherical.
console.log(eraAnpm(deg(190))) // -2.96705972839036 (-170°)
console.log(eraC2s(1, 1, 1)) // [0.7853981633974483, 0.6154797086703873]
// Also: eraS2c, eraP2s, eraS2p, eraPv2s, eraS2pv, eraPpsp, eraSeps, eraSepp.

// Calendars: the MJD of 2008-02-29, and TAI - UTC on 2017-01-01 in seconds.
console.log(eraCalToJd(2008, 2, 29)) // 54525
console.log(eraDat(2017, 1, 1, 0.5)) // 37
// Also: eraJdToCal, and the Besselian and Julian epochs eraEpb, eraEpj, eraEpb2jd, eraEpj2jd.

// Time scales: UTC to TAI, TT, and UT1 (with UT1 - UTC = 0.1550675 s); each result is a two-part date.
const tai = eraUtcTai(2456384.5, 0.969254051).slice()
const tt = eraTaiTt(tai[0], tai[1]).slice()
const ut1 = eraUtcUt1(2456384.5, 0.969254051, 0.1550675).slice()

console.log(tt) // [2456384.5, 0.9700316435925925]
// Also: eraTaiUtc, eraTtTai, eraTtTdb, eraTdbTt, eraTdbTcb, eraTcbTdb, eraTtTcg, eraTcgTt, eraTtUt1, eraUt1Tt,
// eraTaiUt1, eraUt1Tai, eraUt1Utc, and TDB - TT eraDtDb.

// Earth rotation angle and GMST 2006 (radians).
console.log(eraEra00(ut1[0], ut1[1]), eraGmst06(ut1[0], ut1[1], tt[0], tt[1])) // 3.1454097152192517 3.14837320809816
// Also: eraGmst00, eraGmst82, eraGst06a, eraGst06, eraGst00a, eraGst00b, eraGst94, the equation of the equinoxes
// eraEe06a, eraEe00, eraEe00a, eraEe00b, eraEect00, eraEqeq94, and the equation of the origins eraEo06a, eraEors.

// Nutation (Δψ, Δε), mean obliquity, and the bias-precession matrices (row-major 3×3).
console.log(eraNut06a(tt[0], tt[1])) // [0.0000621963812079798, -0.000027249381174917327]
console.log(eraObl06(tt[0], tt[1])) // 0.40906250804962774
const [bias, precession, biasPrecession] = eraBp06(tt[0], tt[1])
// Also nutation and obliquity: eraNut00a, eraNut00b, eraNut80, eraNutm80, eraNumat, eraNum06a, eraNum00a, eraNum00b, eraObl80.
// Also precession and bias: eraBp00, eraBi00, eraPmat06, eraPmat00, eraPmat76, eraPrec76, eraPr00, eraPb06, eraP06e,
// eraPfw06, eraFw2m, eraFw2xy, eraBpn2xy, eraPn06, eraPn06a, eraPn00, eraPn00a, eraPn00b, eraPnm06a, eraPnm00a,
// eraPnm00b, eraPnm80.
// Also the fundamental arguments: eraFal03, eraFalp03, eraFaf03, eraFad03, eraFaom03, eraFame03, eraFave03, eraFae03,
// eraFama03, eraFaju03, eraFasa03, eraFaur03, eraFane03, eraFapa03.

// CIP X, Y and the CIO locator s; the celestial-to-terrestrial matrix with polar motion xp, yp and s'.
console.log(eraXys06a(tt[0], tt[1])) // [0.0013122272008502932, -0.000029280862309744027, 3.0574946809250636e-8]
// Also: eraXys00a, eraXys00b, eraXy06, eraS06, eraS06a, eraS00, eraS00a, eraS00b, and the TIO locator eraSp00.
const xp = 2.47230737e-7
const yp = 1.82640464e-6
const sp = -3.01974337e-11
console.log(eraC2t06a(tt[0], tt[1], ut1[0], ut1[1], xp, yp, sp)[0]) // -0.9999918539305882
// Also: eraC2t00a, eraC2t00b, eraC2txy, eraC2tpe, eraC2tcio, eraC2teqx, eraC2i06a, eraC2i00a, eraC2i00b, eraC2ixys,
// eraC2ixy, eraC2ibpn, and the polar-motion matrix eraPom00.

// Refraction constants A and B (radians) for 731 hPa, 12.8 °C, 59 % humidity, and 0.55 µm.
console.log(eraRefco(731, 12.8, 0.59, 0.55)) // [0.0002014187785940397, -2.3614083149436963e-7]

// ICRS star (RA, Dec, proper motions, parallax, radial velocity) to observed place, with the Earth's
// barycentric [pb, vb] and heliocentric ph state and the site: longitude, latitude, height, xp, yp, sp, pressure, temperature, humidity, wavelength.
const pb = [-0.974170437669016342, -0.211520082035387968, -0.091758302425478583] as const
const vb = [0.003643658242375083, -0.015428731944935825, -0.006689220237864495] as const
const ph = [-0.973458265012157486, -0.209215306558769298, -0.090699647709202746] as const
const site = [-0.527800806, -1.2345856, meter(2738), xp, yp, sp, 731, 12.8, 0.59, 0.55] as const
const [aob, zob, hob, rob, dob, astrom] = eraAtco13(tt[0], tt[1], ut1[0], ut1[1], 2.71, 0.174, 1e-5, 5e-6, arcsec(0.1), kilometerPerSecond(55), ...site, [pb, vb], ph)

console.log(aob, zob, hob) // 0.09251774485486736 1.4076614052564997 -0.09265154431530948 — azimuth, zenith distance, hour angle

// The inverse, observed azimuth/zenith distance ('A') to ICRS; and the two stages: parameters, then ICRS to CIRS.
console.log(eraAtoc13('A', aob, zob, tt[0], tt[1], ut1[0], ut1[1], ...site, [pb, vb], ph).slice(0, 2)) // [2.710132222988453, 0.17406641381551874]
console.log(eraAtciq(2.71, 0.174, 1e-5, 5e-6, arcsec(0.1), kilometerPerSecond(55), eraApco13(tt[0], tt[1], ut1[0], ut1[1], ...site, [pb, vb], ph))) // [2.7102974865123404, 0.17283379216905348]
// Also parameters: eraApci13, eraApci, eraApcg, eraApcs, eraApco, eraApio13, eraApio, eraPvtob.
// Also transformations: eraAtci13, eraAtciqz, eraAtciqn, eraAtccq, eraAtcc13, eraAtic13, eraAticq, eraAticqn,
// eraAtio13, eraAtioq, eraAtoi13, eraAtoiq; aberration eraAb and light deflection eraLd, eraLdn, eraLdSun.

// Horizontal: azimuth and elevation from hour angle, declination, and latitude.
console.log(eraHd2ae(1.1, 1.2, 0.3)) // [5.916889243730066, 0.4472186304990486]
// Also: eraAe2hd, and the parallactic angle eraHd2pa.

// Frames: ICRS to Galactic, and FK4 B1950 to FK5 J2000 (position, proper motion, parallax, radial velocity).
console.log(eraIcrs2g(0, 0)) // [1.6814025947831113, -1.0504884265315022]
console.log(eraFk425(0.1, 0.2, 1e-6, 2e-6, 0.1, 10)) // [0.11128743449126417, 0.20483107183314778, 5.1259e-9, -9.7198e-9, 5.4752e-6, 10.000213636167985]
// Also: eraG2icrs, eraFk524, eraFk45z, eraFk54z, eraFk5hz, eraFk52h, eraH2fk5, eraHfk5z, and the ecliptic eraEqec06,
// eraEceq06, eraEcm06.

// Long-term precession: the mean pole of the equator at Julian epoch -11000, in J2000 axes.
console.log(eraLtpequ(-11000)) // [-0.0011076, -0.75567, 0.65495] — 49° from the J2000 pole
// Also: eraLtp, eraLtpb, eraLtpecl, eraLtecm, eraLteqec, eraLteceq.

// Proper motion of a star from one epoch to another (two-part dates).
console.log(eraStarpm(0.01, 0.02, 1e-6, 2e-6, 0.05, 10, 2451545, 0, 2460000, 0)) // [0.010000005637155604, 0.020000011274311204, ...]
// Also: eraStarpv, eraStarpmpv, eraPvstar, eraPmpx.

// Geodetic to geocentric [x, y, z] in meters for radius 6378136.6 m and flattening 1/298.25642.
console.log(eraGd2Gce(6378136.6, 1 / 298.25642, 3, -0.5, 1000)) // [-5546462.988430975, 790629.1252902636, -3040190.092955975]
// Also the inverse eraGc2Gde.

// Tangent plane: status and standard coordinates ξ, η of a star relative to a tangent point.
console.log(eraTpxes(1.2, 0.5, 1.0, 0.4)) // [0, 0.17810827845499125, 0.10894523228859818]
// Also: eraTpxev, eraTpsts, eraTpstv, eraTpors, eraTporv.

// Barycentric Earth position and the geocentric Moon (AU).
console.log(eraEpv00(2400000.5, 53411.52501161)[0][0]) // [-0.7714104440491069, 0.5598412061824241, 0.24259962777224825]
console.log(eraMoon98(2400000.5, 54282.5)[0]) // [0.0008944441964973188, -0.002147741375955652, -0.0011168576496977227]
// Also the planets eraPlan94.
```

### Exoplanet Transit Light Curves

A transiting planet hides the part of the stellar disk behind it. The star is limb darkened, brighter at the center than at the edge, so the dip is rounded rather than box-shaped: the flux falls between the first and second contacts (ingress), curves through the bottom while the planet is wholly inside the disk, and recovers between the third and fourth contacts (egress). The quadratic law describes the intensity as `I(μ) / I(1) = 1 − u1 (1 − μ) − u2 (1 − μ)²`, with `μ` the cosine of the angle between the line of sight and the stellar surface normal; it is positive and darkens monotonically toward the limb when `u1 >= 0`, `u1 + u2 <= 1` and `u1 + 2 u2 >= 0`.

The forward model is the analytic solution of Mandel & Agol (2002) for a dark disk of radius ratio `p = Rp / R*` at a separation `z` (in stellar radii) from the star's center; the tests compare it with exoplanet-core and batman. The orbit is circular and is described by the mid-transit epoch and period (in one uniform scale, such as BJD_TDB, see [Barycentric Julian Date](#barycentric-julian-date)), the radius ratio, the impact parameter `b = (a/R*) cos i`, the scaled semi-major axis `a/R*`, and the limb darkening. The total (T14) and full (T23) durations and the inclination follow from the geometry (Seager & Mallén-Ornelas 2003). Long exposures smear ingress and egress, so the model averages the flux over the exposure time: for a 1% transit with 29.4-minute exposures, instantaneous samples are off by up to 1.5e-3. There is no eccentricity, planetary light, secondary eclipse, light-travel time, spots, or gravity darkening.

The fit adjusts the epoch, radius ratio, impact parameter, `a/R*`, and the out-of-transit baseline to photometry by weighted least squares, starting from an initial guess such as a [Box Least Squares Transit Search](#box-least-squares-transit-search) candidate; the search is local, so a poor initial epoch or duration can converge elsewhere. The period and limb darkening are fixed by default, because a single transit does not constrain the period and the limb darkening is degenerate with `p` and `b` at modest signal-to-noise. The uncertainties are first-order (from the Fisher matrix) and describe a well-constrained minimum; for grazing or shallow transits, or the strong `b`–`a/R*` correlation, resampling or a Markov chain gives better intervals. The fit infers geometry only: a planet radius or mass needs an independent stellar radius and radial velocities.

```ts
import { fitTransit, quadraticTransitFlux, scaledSemiMajorAxisFromDuration, transitFlux, transitFullDuration, transitInclination, transitLightCurve, transitSeparation, transitTotalDuration } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/exoplanet.lightcurve'

// A hot Jupiter (BJD_TDB days): Rp/R* = 0.1, b = 0.3, a/R* = 9, P = 3.5 d and Sun-like limb darkening [u1, u2].
const planet = { epoch: 2460000.5, period: 3.5, radiusRatio: 0.1, impactParameter: 0.3, scaledSemiMajorAxis: 9, limbDarkening: [0.4, 0.26] } as const

// Relative flux with the planet 0.3 stellar radii from the center (1 unocculted).
console.log(quadraticTransitFlux(0.3, 0.1, planet.limbDarkening)) // 0.98810

// T14, T23 (days), and the inclination (radians).
console.log(transitTotalDuration(planet), transitFullDuration(planet), transitInclination(planet)) // 0.13138 0.10525 1.53746

// a/R* from a measured T14 (days), the period, Rp/R*, and b: the inverse of transitTotalDuration.
console.log(scaledSemiMajorAxisFromDuration(3.5, transitTotalDuration(planet), 0.1, 0.3)) // 9

// Projected separation z (stellar radii) 0.05 days before mid-transit, just inside second contact; undefined behind the star.
console.log(transitSeparation(2460000.45, planet)) // 0.86031

// Flux at that time: an instantaneous sample and a 29.4-minute (0.0204-day) exposure, which also averages part of the ingress.
console.log(transitFlux(2460000.45, planet), transitFlux(2460000.45, planet, { exposureTime: 0.0204 })) // 0.99112 0.99198

// Model fluxes for an array of times (days).
const model = transitLightCurve(times, planet)

// time, flux: observed photometry; 2.04e-4 is the 1σ flux error. Start from a rough guess.
const result = fitTransit(time, flux, 2.04e-4, { ...planet, epoch: 2460000.503, radiusRatio: 0.09, impactParameter: 0.5, scaledSemiMajorAxis: 8 })

console.log(result.status, result.flags) // convergence, and warnings such as a strong degeneracy
console.log(result.parameters, result.uncertainties) // fitted parameters and their 1σ errors
console.log(result.baseline, result.reducedChiSquare) // out-of-transit level in flux units, and χ² per degree of freedom
```

### Exoplanet Transit Prediction

A transiting exoplanet dims its star once per orbit. Published ephemerides give a reference mid-transit epoch `T0`, usually in BJD_TDB (see [Barycentric Julian Date](#barycentric-julian-date)), a period `P`, and a total duration `T14` from first to fourth contact. Cycle `n` is centered at `Tn = T0 + n·P`, and its 1σ timing uncertainty grows with the distance from `T0`:

```text
σ²(Tn) = σ²(T0) + n²·σ²(P) + 2n·Cov(T0, P)
```

Planning an observation turns these barycentric predictions into local clock times and checks whether each transit, with some baseline before and after, is observable: the target high enough, the sky dark, and the Moon far enough (the limits of [Observing Visibility Windows](#observing-visibility-windows)). Each predicted contact is moved from BJD_TDB to the UTC instant its light reaches the site, so the observed transit differs from `T14` by the change of the light time across it, about 1 s for a 3 h transit. The required span is widened by the timing uncertainty, and an event is feasible only when enough of the transit itself is visible; baselines alone never qualify it.

The clock of the ephemeris matters. A TDB epoch is used as is; UTC, TAI, TT, and UT1 epochs are moved to TDB and their days taken as TDB days, so leap seconds after `T0` are not counted as elapsed time; TCB and TCG days are longer than TDB days (by `L_B = 1.550519768e-8` and `L_G = 6.969290134e-10`), so their periods are rescaled, otherwise a one-day BJD_TCB period would drift by about 4.9 s in ten years. A heliocentric (HJD) ephemeris advances on the Sun's clock and needs a Sun path to move each prediction to BJD. The NASA Exoplanet Archive labels each row's time reference; plain `BJD` is taken as BJD_TDB and plain `HJD` as HJD_UTC, and the archive publishes no covariance. Rows can be fetched with [NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP Queries](#nasa-exoplanet-archive-tap-queries). The ephemeris is strictly periodic: transit-timing variations and orbital decay are not modeled.

```ts
import { exoplanetArchiveTransitEphemeris } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/catalogs/exoplanet.archive'
import { eraS2c } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/erfa'
import { Naif } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/naif'
import { moon } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/elpmpp02'
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { composeEphemerisPaths, customEphemerisEndpoint, ephemerisPath, naifEphemerisEndpoint, SOLAR_SYSTEM_BARYCENTER } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/path'
import { earthObserverEphemerisPath } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/path.adapter'
import { exoplanetTransits, transitEphemerisUncertainty, transitTimingUncertainty } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/exoplanet'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// row: one NASA Exoplanet Archive ps or pscomppars row (pl_tranmid, pl_orbper, pl_trandur, their errors, and the time reference).
const result = exoplanetArchiveTransitEphemeris(row)
if (!result.success) throw new Error(result.reason)

// The site, its SSB-centered path, and the geocentric Sun and Moon directions for the limits.
const site = geodeticLocation(deg(-16.5097), deg(28.3), meter(2390))
const observer = composeEphemerisPaths(ephemerisPath(SOLAR_SYSTEM_BARYCENTER, naifEphemerisEndpoint(Naif.EARTH), earth), earthObserverEphemerisPath(site, customEphemerisEndpoint('teide')))
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0])
const moonAt = (time: Time) => moon(time)[0]

// Transits between two UTC instants: above 30°, astronomical darkness, 20° from the Moon, 1 h baselines.
const constraints = { minimumAltitude: deg(30), maximumSunAltitude: deg(-18), minimumMoonSeparation: deg(20) }
const { events } = exoplanetTransits(result.ephemeris, eraS2c(result.rightAscension!, result.declination!), observer, site, timeYMDHMS(2026, 10, 18, 19, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), timeYMDHMS(2026, 10, 20, 7, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), { constraints, sunAt, moonAt, baselineBefore: 1 / 24, baselineAfter: 1 / 24 })

for (const e of events) {
	// Cycle, BJD_TDB center and its 1σ (days), observed UTC ingress, and whether enough of it is visible.
	console.log(e.cycle, e.center, e.centerUncertainty, timeToDate(e.observedIngress), e.feasible)
}

// σ(Tn) for n = 10000, σ(T0) = 32e-6 d, σ(P) = 18e-9 d, in days.
console.log(transitTimingUncertainty(10000, 0.000032, 0.000000018) * 86400) // 15.80 — seconds, the period error dominates

// One cycle on the ephemeris' own clock, with σ in seconds.
const cycle = transitEphemerisUncertainty(result.ephemeris, 3414)
```

### Exposure Timing

A camera timestamp usually marks a command, not the light: the shutter opens some latency after the open command and closes some latency after the close command. Timing work needs the actual photon-collection interval and, above all, its midpoint, the instant to refer a measurement to (for example in [Barycentric Julian Date](#barycentric-julian-date)). FITS header keywords give these inputs; see [FITS Observation Timing and Location](#fits-observation-timing-and-location).

An exposure is described either by one recorded timestamp, labelled as the open command, the commanded midpoint, or the close command, with the commanded duration, or by the recorded open and close timestamps. Shutter latencies, the clock uncertainty, and the timestamp resolution are in seconds. The midpoint is the nominal temporal midpoint of the collection interval, not a photon-weighted one: it is the flux-weighted mean time only for constant flux. A shutter that takes a finite time to uncover the aperture can be modeled by adding half its opening (closing) time to the open (close) latency.

All offsets are SI seconds of the recording clock, applied on TAI and converted back to the timestamp's scale, so the same physical instant gives the same physical interval in every scale: a UTC exposure across a leap second keeps its SI length and can start, end, or be centered on 23:59:60.

```ts
import { exposureInterval } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/exposure'
import { Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

// A 300 s exposure stamped when the shutter was commanded closed.
const stamped = exposureInterval({ time: timeYMDHMS(2024, 3, 10, 3, 5, 0, Timescale.UTC), reference: 'end', duration: 300 })

console.log(timeToDate(stamped.midpoint)) // [2024, 3, 10, 3, 2, 30, 0]

// 1 s commanded at 23:59:59.5 UTC on the 2016-12-31 leap-second day, with shutter latencies and clock uncertainty (s).
const leap = exposureInterval({ time: timeYMDHMS(2016, 12, 31, 23, 59, 59.5, Timescale.UTC), reference: 'start', duration: 1, openLatency: 0.1, closeLatency: 0.02, uncertainty: 0.002 })

console.log(timeToDate(leap.midpoint)) // [2016, 12, 31, 23, 59, 60, 60] — inside the leap second
console.log(leap.duration) // 0.92 — seconds of collection

// DATE-BEG and DATE-END style span: 1 s apart on the clock labels, 2 SI seconds across the leap second.
const span = exposureInterval({ start: timeYMDHMS(2016, 12, 31, 23, 59, 59.5, Timescale.UTC), end: timeYMDHMS(2017, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0.5, Timescale.UTC) })

console.log(span.duration.toFixed(6)) // 2.000000 — seconds
```

### FK5 Precession and ICRS Frame Bias

FK5 is the J2000 mean-equator-and-equinox catalog frame. ICRS differs from it by a small constant frame bias of a few tens of milliarcseconds, and FK5 positions at another equinox differ by precession. Both are rotations, so they preserve the length of a vector. Older catalogs and many instruments still give positions referred to a mean equinox of date, which must be precessed before they can be compared with ICRS positions.

Precession uses the IAU 2006 model (Capitaine), with equinoxes given as instants interpreted in TT. The frame bias between ICRS and FK5 is constant, so an FK5 position at another equinox must be precessed to J2000 before the bias is applied. The FK5 equinox-of-date `Frame` combines bias and precession for use with the frame functions, so it differs slightly from precession alone.

```ts
import { fk5, precessFk5, precessFk5FromJ2000 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/fk5'
import { fk5Frame, frameAt, icrsToFk5 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/frame'
import { icrs } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/icrs'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecAngle } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { deg, toArcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// FK5 J2000 Cartesian vector for RA 10.625°, Dec +41.2° at distance 1.
const position = fk5(deg(10.625), deg(41.2), 1)

console.log(position) // [0.73951, 0.13873, 0.65869]

// Mean place at the equinox of 1975.0 (TT); precessFk5ToJ2000 is the inverse.
const equinox = timeYMDHMS(1975, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

console.log(precessFk5FromJ2000(position, equinox)) // [0.74188, 0.13459, 0.65689]

// Between two arbitrary equinoxes (TT).
console.log(precessFk5(position, equinox, timeYMDHMS(2050, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.TT))) // [0.73226, 0.15107, 0.66405]

// The frame bias moves an ICRS direction by a few tens of milliarcseconds; fk5ToIcrs is the inverse.
const direction = icrs(deg(10.625), deg(41.2), 1)

console.log(toArcsec(vecAngle(direction, icrsToFk5(direction)))) // 0.0317 — arcseconds for this direction

// The FK5 equinox-of-date Frame (frame bias plus precession) applied to the ICRS direction.
console.log(frameAt(direction, fk5Frame(equinox), equinox)) // [0.74188, 0.13459, 0.65689] — mean place of 1975.0
```

### Galactocentric Frame

The Galactocentric frame is Cartesian with its origin at the Galactic center, x pointing from the Sun toward the center (so the Sun sits near x = −8.1 kpc), and z toward the north Galactic pole. The Sun is slightly above the Galactic midplane, which the frame accounts for by tilting about y by `asin(zSun / distance)`. The construction mirrors Astropy: rotate ICRS so x points at the center, apply an optional roll about that line, then the Sun-height tilt. It is the natural frame for Galactic structure and stellar kinematics.

The frame is an affine frame (see [Affine Origin Frames](#affine-origin-frames)), parameterized by the ICRS position of the Galactic center, the Sun-center distance, the Sun's height above the midplane, and the roll. The defaults are the Astropy "latest" values: center at (266.4051°, −28.936175°), 8.122 kpc, 20.8 pc, roll 0. The frame is constant in time and has no origin velocity, so velocities are rotated but receive no solar-motion offset. It needs absolute positions with a real distance, never normalized directions.

```ts
import { affineFromBase, affineToBase, galactocentricFrame, GALACTOCENTRIC_DEFAULTS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/affine'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { ONE_KILOPARSEC } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC) // the frame does not depend on time

// Astropy defaults.
const frame = galactocentricFrame()

// ICRS position in AU (here 1, 2, 3 kpc along the ICRS axes) -> Galactocentric Cartesian, AU.
const [x, y, z] = affineFromBase([1 * ONE_KILOPARSEC, 2 * ONE_KILOPARSEC, 3 * ONE_KILOPARSEC], frame, time)

console.log(x / ONE_KILOPARSEC, y / ONE_KILOPARSEC, z / ONE_KILOPARSEC) // -11.3749 1.8454 0.1333 — kpc

// Exact inverse: Galactocentric -> ICRS.
console.log(affineToBase([x, y, z], frame, time)) // the original ICRS position, in AU

// A different Sun-center distance, in AU.
const far = galactocentricFrame({ ...GALACTOCENTRIC_DEFAULTS, galcenDistance: 8.2 * ONE_KILOPARSEC })

console.log(affineFromBase([0, 0, 0], far, time)[0] / ONE_KILOPARSEC) // -8.19997 — kpc, the Sun's x
```

### Galilean Satellite Phenomena

Every few days each Galilean satellite crosses in front of Jupiter (a **transit**), casts its shadow on the cloud tops (a **shadow transit**), passes behind the planet (an **occultation**) and enters Jupiter's shadow (an **eclipse**). Callisto can miss the disk and the shadow entirely in the years when the Earth and the Sun stand a few degrees from Jupiter's equatorial plane. These events are the classic targets of planetary imaging and visual observation, and their timings were historically used to measure the speed of light.

The phenomena are found with the geometry of [Jovian Satellite Geometry](#jovian-satellite-geometry), taking every position from one [Jovian ephemeris source](#jovian-ephemeris-sources); wrapping the source in an interpolated one makes the search faster. Each phenomenon reports its conjunction (the maximum), its depth, and the contacts that are actually reached: external contacts when the disks or shadows touch from outside, internal contacts when the moon or its shadow is wholly on or behind the disk, and center contacts when the center crosses the limb (for an eclipse, the edge of the umbra: the almanac disappearance and reappearance). A phenomenon without internal contacts is partial, and a near-tangency is reported as a zero-duration grazing event.

The instants are geocentric observed times in TDB, with Jupiter, each moon, and both kinds of shadow light-time corrected; they are not topocentric. With the analytical source the contacts agree with JPL Horizons (JUP365) to within about 15 s for Io, Europa, and Ganymede and about a minute for Callisto, whose high paths are where Horizons' spherical Jupiter differs most from the oblate one used here.

```ts
import { analyticalJovianEphemeris, interpolatedJovianEphemeris } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/jovian'
import { jovianPhenomena } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/jupiter.phenomena'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS, utc } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

const format = (time?: Time) => (time ? timeToDate(utc(time)).slice(3, 6).join(':') : '—')

// The L1.2 analytical source, interpolated for speed.
const ephemeris = interpolatedJovianEphemeris(analyticalJovianEphemeris)

// Phenomena whose maximum falls in the window, with their first external contact, maximum, and last external contact.
for (const p of jovianPhenomena(ephemeris, timeYMDHMS(2026, 12, 1, 6, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), timeYMDHMS(2026, 12, 1, 10, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC))) {
	console.log(p.moon, p.kind, format(p.external1), format(p.maximum), format(p.external2))
}
// io shadowTransit 6:32:56 7:43:49 8:54:43 — before opposition the shadow leads the moon
// europa satelliteTransit 6:7:34 7:36:14 9:4:55
// io satelliteTransit 7:46:26 8:56:54 10:7:23
```

### Galilean Satellite Theory (L1.2)

L1.2 (Lainey, Vienne, and Duriez) is the IMCCE analytical theory of the four Galilean satellites. For each body, trigonometric series give equinoctial elements (semi-major axis, mean longitude, and the eccentricity and inclination vectors), degree-8 Chebyshev polynomials add the official long-period corrections, and Kepler's equation is solved for the position. The result is rotated into the J2000 equatorial frame.

The states are Jovicentric, in AU and AU/day, in J2000 equatorial axes, at any time scale (converted to TT). The long-period corrections apply only inside the theory's validity window of about the years 1140 to 2760; outside it they are omitted, matching the official approximate-ephemeris path. The returned vectors are internal buffers overwritten by the next computation, so copy them before computing another state. Add the result to Jupiter's barycentric state for an inertial position; for the Great Red Spot and the central meridian see [Jupiter Central Meridian](#jupiter-central-meridian).

```ts
import { callisto, compute, europa, ganymede, io } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/l12'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const instant = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Jovicentric [position (AU), velocity (AU/day)]; copy before the next call.
const [position, velocity] = io(instant).map((v) => [...v])

console.log(position) // [-0.0028234, -0.000024337, -0.000055447] — AU, Jovicentric
console.log(velocity) // [0.00020049, -0.0090228, -0.0042977] — AU/day
console.log(toKilometer(Math.hypot(...position))) // 422475 — km, close to Io's orbital radius

// The other satellites have the same contract.
console.log(europa(instant)[0], ganymede(instant)[0], callisto(instant)[0]) // AU, Jovicentric positions

// The shared function: index 0 Io, 1 Europa, 2 Ganymede, 3 Callisto.
console.log(compute(instant, 0)[0]) // [-0.0028234, -0.000024337, -0.000055447] — AU, Io again
```

### Gauss Angles-Only Orbit Determination

Gauss's method is the classical way to get a first orbit from just three observations of angles. Three right ascensions and declinations, with the observer's position at each time, fix the unknown distances through an eighth-degree polynomial in the middle range. It then reconstructs the three position vectors and recovers the middle velocity with Gibbs or, for short arcs, Herrick-Gibbs. The result is a rough state meant to seed a least-squares refinement such as [Differential Orbit Correction](#differential-orbit-correction), not a final orbit.

The angles are radians in an inertial frame, and the observer position is in the same frame and in the length unit of the gravitational parameter (AU and the Sun's GM for a heliocentric orbit with an Earth-based observer). The times must strictly increase. The range polynomial can have several positive roots, each a different orbit; the candidates are scored by how well they reproduce the lines of sight, but with multiple roots or a small angular separation between the observations the chosen state can be wrong, so check the warnings in the diagnostics before trusting it.

```ts
import { gauss } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/determination/gauss'
import { GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005 } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'

// obs1, obs2, obs3: GaussObservation — time, right ascension and declination (radians), and the observer's heliocentric position (AU).
// mu in AU³/day².
const result = gauss(obs1, obs2, obs3, { mu: GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005 })

console.log(result.state.r, result.state.v) // AU and AU/day, heliocentric, at the middle epoch
console.log(result.ranges.rho2) // AU, observer-to-target distance at the middle epoch
console.log(result.diagnostics.warnings) // e.g. ['MULTIPLE_POSITIVE_ROOTS']
```

### GCRS to ITRS Rotation

The geocentric celestial frame (GCRS, ICRS-oriented and non-rotating) and the Earth-fixed ITRS are related by Earth orientation: frame bias, precession, and nutation, then the Earth's rotation by the Greenwich apparent sidereal time, then polar motion. Composed, they form a single 3×3 rotation `R` with `v_itrs = R · v_gcrs`; its transpose goes back. It is what places a celestial direction over a point of the ground, and a ground station in inertial space.

It is the same rotation the `ITRS` frame uses (see [Celestial and Terrestrial Reference Frames](#celestial-and-terrestrial-reference-frames)), so prefer the frame functions when you also need velocities. The matrix depends on UT1 and polar motion, which come from the loaded Earth orientation data and are 0 without it (see [Earth Orientation Parameters](#earth-orientation-parameters)). It is cached on the `Time` and shared, so treat it as read-only.

```ts
import { gcrsToItrsRotationMatrix, Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { matMulVec, matTransposeMulVec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/mat3'

// A UT1 instant, so the example does not depend on loaded Earth orientation data.
const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UT1)

// The GCRS to ITRS rotation, a row-major 3×3 matrix.
const rotation = gcrsToItrsRotationMatrix(time)

// A GCRS direction in Earth-fixed axes, and back with the transpose.
const itrs = matMulVec(rotation, [1, 0, 0])

console.log(itrs) // [0.11758, 0.99306, 0.00259] — the same direction in Earth-fixed axes
console.log(matTransposeMulVec(rotation, itrs)) // [1, 0, 0] — back to GCRS
```

### Geographic Observer

An observer on the Earth is a point on a reference ellipsoid: geodetic latitude (north-positive), longitude (east-positive), and height above the ellipsoid. The geodetic latitude is the angle of the local vertical, normal to the ellipsoid, not of the line to the Earth's center; the difference reaches about 0.19° at mid-latitudes and matters for parallax and for anything referred to the zenith. The library supports the GRS80, WGS72, WGS84, and IERS2010 ellipsoids, with IERS2010 as the default.

A site is built from geodetic coordinates or from an Earth-centered Cartesian (ITRS) position. Angles are radians and the elevation is in AU, so convert heights with `meter`; note that longitude comes before latitude. The local sidereal time at the site is apparent by default (mean on request), and its UT1 comes from the loaded Earth orientation data (see [Earth Orientation Parameters](#earth-orientation-parameters)). The geocentric parallax terms `ρ·cos φ′` and `ρ·sin φ′`, in Earth equatorial radii, are what topocentric parallax formulas such as Meeus's use.

```ts
import { itrs } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/itrs'
import { Ellipsoid, geocentricLocation, geodeticLocation, localSiderealTime, polarRadius, rhoCosPhi, rhoSinPhi } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter, toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// longitude, latitude, elevation (radians and AU): La Silla Observatory on the IERS2010 ellipsoid.
const site = geodeticLocation(deg(-70.7313), deg(-29.2563), meter(2400))

// The same site from its ITRS Cartesian position, in AU.
const xyz = itrs(site)
const fromXyz = geocentricLocation(xyz[0], xyz[1], xyz[2])

// Local sidereal time at the site: apparent by default, mean when the third argument is true.
const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 4, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

console.log(toHour(localSiderealTime(time, site))) // 17.7685 — hours, apparent
console.log(toHour(localSiderealTime(time, site.longitude, true))) // 17.7683 — hours, mean

// Geocentric parallax terms ρ·cos φ′ and ρ·sin φ′, in Earth equatorial radii.
console.log(rhoCosPhi(site), rhoSinPhi(site))

// Polar radius of an ellipsoid, in AU.
console.log(toKilometer(polarRadius(Ellipsoid.IERS2010))) // 6356.752 — km
```

### Geographic Sub-point

The sub-point of a celestial position is the point on the Earth's surface directly beneath it: the geodetic longitude and latitude where the ellipsoid normal through the position meets the ellipsoid, plus the height above it. It is how a satellite, the Moon, or any geocentric vector is placed on a map.

`subpoint` takes a geocentric position in GCRS (ICRS-oriented) axes, in AU, rotates it into ITRS with the full Earth orientation at the instant, and converts it to geodetic coordinates on the ellipsoid (IERS2010 by default). The longitude is east-positive in `(−π, π]`. Earth rotation, and so UT1, comes from the loaded Earth orientation data (see [Earth Orientation Parameters](#earth-orientation-parameters)). For satellites tracked with SGP4 see [Satellite Sub-point](#satellite-sub-point); for sub-points on other bodies see [Sub-Observer and Sub-Solar Points](#sub-observer-and-sub-solar-points).

```ts
import { subpoint } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 4, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Geocentric position in AU, GCRS axes (about 10 600 km above the surface).
const point = subpoint([1e-4, 2e-5, 5e-5], time)

console.log(toDeg(point.longitude)) // 34.41 — degrees east
console.log(toDeg(point.latitude)) // 26.32 — degrees north, geodetic
console.log(toKilometer(point.elevation)) // 10617 — km above the ellipsoid
```

### Gibbs Orbit Determination

The Gibbs method finds the velocity of a body at the middle of three position vectors, assuming two-body motion and using no time information. Three coplanar position vectors relative to the central body fix the orbit's plane and shape, and with them the velocity at the middle point. It is the classical choice when the points are widely separated in angle (roughly 1° to 60° apart); for closely spaced points with known times use [Herrick-Gibbs Orbit Determination](#herrick-gibbs-orbit-determination), and for raw right ascension and declination use [Gauss Angles-Only Orbit Determination](#gauss-angles-only-orbit-determination).

The result is a state at the middle epoch, usually the seed of a later fit. Units must be consistent: positions in AU and the gravitational parameter in AU³/day² give a velocity in AU/day. Poor coplanarity or a degenerate geometry make the method unreliable, and the function reports or rejects such a solution rather than returning a silently wrong velocity.

```ts
import { KeplerOrbit } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/asteroid'
import { gibbs } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/determination/gibbs'
import { Timescale, timeShift, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005 } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'
import { matIdentity } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/mat3'

// A synthetic heliocentric orbit sampled 15 days before, at, and 15 days after the epoch.
const epoch = timeYMDHMS(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)
const orbit = KeplerOrbit.trueAnomaly(1.9, 0.18, 0.12, 0.8, 1.1, 0.35, epoch, GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005, matIdentity())
const [r1, r2, r3] = [orbit.at(timeShift(epoch, -15))[0], orbit.at(epoch)[0], orbit.at(timeShift(epoch, 15))[0]]

// Velocity at the middle position from three positions (AU) and the Sun's GM (AU³/day²).
const { r, v, diagnostics } = gibbs(r1, r2, r3, GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005)

console.log(r) // [-1.01258, 1.25644, 0.19314] — AU, the middle position
console.log(v) // [-0.011823, -0.0085783, 0.00030201] — AU/day, equal to the true velocity to about 1e-14 relative
console.log(diagnostics.reliability) // good
```

### Great Red Spot Transits

The Great Red Spot is a long-lived anticyclone in Jupiter's southern hemisphere, at a System II longitude that drifts slowly. It is best seen when it crosses Jupiter's central meridian, which happens once per System II rotation, about every 9 h 56 m. Its longitude cannot be predicted from theory: it is measured, and published by observer programs such as ALPO and JUPOS. The drift is under a degree per month, so one value is adequate for a prediction window of a few weeks; a longer window, or a measurement made some time ago, needs a linear drift model.

A transit is the instant the System II central meridian (see [Jupiter Central Meridian](#jupiter-central-meridian)) equals the spot's longitude with the spot on the near side. Longitudes are System II, positive west, in radians, and the drift is in radians per day toward increasing west longitude. The Jupiter-to-observer vector is supplied as a function of time, in AU and ICRF axes, and sets both the light time and the viewing geometry.

```ts
import { earth, jupiter } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { greatRedSpotLongitude, greatRedSpotTransits, greatRedSpotTransitsWithDrift } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/jupiter'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Vector from Jupiter's center to a geocentric observer, AU, ICRF axes.
const jupiterToEarth = (time: Time) => vecMinus(earth(time)[0], jupiter(time)[0])

const start = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
const stop = timeYMDHMS(2026, 7, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Transits of a spot at System II longitude 50° W, in chronological order.
for (const time of greatRedSpotTransits(deg(50), jupiterToEarth, start, stop)) console.log(timeToDate(time).slice(0, 6))
// [2026, 6, 29, 2, 15, 15] — UTC, then every ~9.93 hours: five transits in 48 hours

// A spot measured at 48.5° on 2026-06-01 and drifting 0.05°/day.
const model = { longitude: deg(48.5), epoch: timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), drift: deg(0.05) }

console.log(toDeg(greatRedSpotLongitude(model, start))) // 49.9 — degrees, the extrapolated longitude
console.log(greatRedSpotTransitsWithDrift(model, jupiterToEarth, start, stop).length) // 5
```

### Greatest Solar Eclipse Circumstances

Eclipse tables list two special places for each solar eclipse. The greatest eclipse is the point where the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to the Earth's center; the greatest duration is the point on the central line where totality or annularity lasts longest. They are generally not the same place. Both are computed from the [Solar Eclipse Besselian Elements](#solar-eclipse-besselian-elements) and describe the Sun there: geodetic position, time, the Sun's altitude and azimuth, and, on the central line, the path width and the central duration. For a partial or non-central eclipse the greatest eclipse is the limb point nearest the axis, and there is no greatest duration.

The path width is the one catalogs publish: the distance between the limits of totality or annularity across the central line. It is not the chord of the shadow through a point, which is narrower at a low Sun, where the footprint is a long ellipse.

The instants of the Meeus series and the Moon of the fast analytical provider are approximate: `nearestSolarEclipse` can be about a minute from the published greatest eclipse, and the low-precision Moon up to about 8″ from ELPMPP02. For results to be shown, build the provider with `sunMoonPositionAround`, which corrects the Moon with ELPMPP02 around the eclipse, refine the eclipse with it, and fit the elements to that refined maximum.

```ts
import { nearestSolarEclipse } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/sun'
import { sunMoonPositionAround } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/eclipse'
import { computeGreatestDurationCircumstances, computeGreatestEclipseCircumstances } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/solar/local'
import { computePolynomialBesselianElements, refineSolarEclipse } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/solar/map'
import { Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS, utc } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The total solar eclipse of 8 April 2024, refined with an ELPMPP02-corrected Sun/Moon provider.
const series = nearestSolarEclipse(timeYMDHMS(2024, 4, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), true)
const provider = sunMoonPositionAround(series.maximalTime)
const eclipse = refineSolarEclipse(series, provider)

console.log(timeToDate(utc(eclipse.maximalTime)).slice(0, 6).join('-'), eclipse.gamma) // 2024-4-8-18-17-14 0.34315

// Besselian elements fitted around the refined maximum.
const pbe = computePolynomialBesselianElements(eclipse.maximalTime, provider)

// The greatest eclipse: east-positive longitude and geodetic latitude (radians), TT time, Sun altitude.
const greatest = computeGreatestEclipseCircumstances(pbe)!
console.log(toDeg(greatest.longitude), toDeg(greatest.latitude), toDeg(greatest.sunAltitude))
console.log(greatest.pathWidthKm, greatest.centralDuration) // km, seconds of totality

// The greatest duration on the central line, a little north-east of the greatest eclipse.
const longest = computeGreatestDurationCircumstances(pbe)!
console.log(toDeg(longest.longitude), toDeg(longest.latitude), longest.centralDuration)
```

### HEALPix Object Index

A HEALPix index is an in-memory spatial index: objects with sky positions are bucketed by the HEALPix pixel that contains them, so a region query only examines the few buckets the region touches instead of every object. It is the structure behind fast cone, box, and polygon searches on a large list of stars or targets (see [HEALPix Pixelization and Covers](#healpix-pixelization-and-covers) for the pixel scheme itself), and it implements the star-catalog query interface used by the catalog modules.

The resolution `NSIDE` is a power of two; a higher value gives smaller pixels and fewer objects per bucket. Objects carry an id and optional metadata, and adding an existing id moves it. Right ascension and declination are in radians, polygons must be convex, and a box whose right ascension range wraps through 0 is handled.

```ts
import { HealpixIndex } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/sky/spatial/healpix'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// NSIDE 64 gives pixels about 0.92° across.
const index = new HealpixIndex<{ name: string }>({ nside: 64 })

// Insert objects by id with their RA and Dec (radians) and optional metadata.
index.add('a', hour(10), deg(20), { name: 'A' })
index.add(2, hour(10) + deg(0.5), deg(20.2))
index.add(3n, hour(11), deg(-30), { name: 'C' })

// A batch insert, then the count and a lookup by id.
index.addMany([{ id: 4, rightAscension: hour(10.02), declination: deg(20.1) }])

console.log(index.size, index.get('a')?.metadata) // 4 { name: 'A' }

// The pixel of a position at the index resolution; pixelToBoundary gives its corners.
console.log(index.coordToPixel(hour(10), deg(20)), index.pixelToCenter(4455)) // 4455, and its center [ra, dec] in radians

// Region queries return the matching entries; queryRegion takes a catalog query object.
console.log(index.queryCone(hour(10), deg(20), deg(1)).map((entry) => entry.id)) // ['a', 2, 4]
console.log(index.queryBox(hour(9.9), hour(10.2), deg(19), deg(21)).map((entry) => entry.id)) // ['a', 2, 4]
console.log(index.queryTriangle([hour(9.9), deg(19)], [hour(10.3), deg(19)], [hour(10), deg(22)]).length) // 3
console.log(
	index.queryPolygon([
		[hour(9.9), deg(19)],
		[hour(10.2), deg(19)],
		[hour(10.2), deg(21)],
		[hour(9.9), deg(21)],
	]).length,
) // 3
console.log(index.queryRegion({ kind: 'cone', centerRA: hour(11), centerDEC: deg(-30), radius: deg(1) }).map((entry) => entry.id)) // [3n]

// Moving an object updates its bucket; removing returns whether it existed; clear empties the index.
index.update('a', hour(12), deg(0))
console.log(index.remove(2)) // true
index.clear()
```

### HEALPix Pixelization and Covers

HEALPix (Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization) divides the sphere into 12 base faces, each split into `NSIDE × NSIDE` pixels, for `12 · NSIDE²` pixels of equal area; `NSIDE` must be a power of two, up to 2²⁴. Equal areas make pixel counts directly comparable over the sky, which is why surveys and catalogs (Gaia, Planck, MOC coverage maps) use it. Pixels are numbered in two orderings: nested, a hierarchy in which a pixel's index contains its parent's, which suits multi-resolution work, and ring, which numbers pixels along rings of constant latitude.

A cover is the set of pixels that intersects a region (a cone, a spherical triangle, or a convex polygon), used to prune a catalog search. Covers are conservative: they can include pixels that only touch the region, never fewer. Angles are radians and nested ordering is the default. For a ready-made object index built on these, see [HEALPix Object Index](#healpix-object-index).

```ts
import { circleToPixels, coordToPixel, nestedToRing, pixelToBoundary, pixelToCenter, polygonToPixels, ringToNested, triangleToPixels } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/sky/spatial/healpix'
import { deg, hour, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const nside = 64 // 12 · 64² = 49152 pixels of about 0.84 square degrees

// The pixel under RA 10 h, Dec +20°, in nested and ring ordering.
const nested = coordToPixel(nside, hour(10), deg(20))

console.log(nested, coordToPixel(nside, hour(10), deg(20), 'ring')) // 4455 16107
console.log(nestedToRing(nside, nested)) // 16107 — the orderings convert exactly
console.log(ringToNested(nside, 16107)) // 4455

// The pixel's center and four corners, as [ra, dec] in radians.
console.log(pixelToCenter(nside, nested).map(toDeg)) // [150.47, 20.106] — degrees
console.log(pixelToBoundary(nside, nested).length) // 4

// Conservative covers of a 1° cone, a spherical triangle, and a convex polygon.
console.log(circleToPixels(nside, hour(10), deg(20), deg(1)).length) // 21
console.log(triangleToPixels(nside, [hour(10), deg(20)], [hour(10) + deg(2), deg(20)], [hour(10), deg(22)]).length) // 20
console.log(
	polygonToPixels(nside, [
		[hour(10), deg(20)],
		[hour(10) + deg(2), deg(20)],
		[hour(10) + deg(2), deg(22)],
		[hour(10), deg(22)],
	]).length,
) // 25
```

### Heliacal Events

As the Sun moves along the ecliptic, a fixed star or planet cycles through four classical visibility transitions each year. The heliacal rising is the first morning it is seen rising in the east just before dawn, after months lost in the Sun's glare; the Sothic rising of Sirius, which marked the Egyptian new year, is the famous one. The acronychal rising is the last evening it is seen rising at dusk. The heliacal setting is the last evening it is seen setting in the west after dusk, before it is lost in the glare. The cosmical setting is the first morning it is seen setting in the west before dawn.

The search uses the classical arc-of-vision model: on each day the object's rise or set counts as visible when the Sun is at least the arc of vision (arcus visionis) below the geometric horizon at that instant. A brighter object needs a smaller depression, so the arc of vision stands in for the object's brightness and the sky; the default 11° is the classical value for a first-magnitude star. The model is geometric, with no sky-brightness or extinction model, so it suits calendar-scale dating. The window should span a full year starting near the object's conjunction with the Sun, and the day-by-day scan takes seconds for a year.

```ts
import { eraS2c } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/erfa'
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { heliacalPhases } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/heliacal'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { deg, hour, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const athens = geodeticLocation(deg(23.7275), deg(37.9838), meter(100))

// Geocentric J2000/ICRS directions over time: Sirius (fixed) and the Sun.
const sirius = eraS2c(hour(6.7525), deg(-16.7161))
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0])

// One year starting near Sirius's conjunction with the Sun.
const start = timeYMDHMS(2025, 6, 20, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
const stop = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 20, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// The four transitions in chronological order, with the Sun depression realized (radians).
for (const phase of heliacalPhases(() => sirius, sunAt, athens, start, stop)) console.log(phase.kind, timeToDate(phase.time).slice(0, 5), toDeg(phase.arcusVisionis))
// heliacalRising [2025, 8, 12, 2, 39] 11.28 — UTC, degrees of Sun depression
// cosmicalSetting [2025, 12, 17, 4, 35] 11.40
// acronychalRising [2026, 1, 14, 16, 26] 11.34
// heliacalSetting [2026, 5, 18, 18, 34] 11.48
```

### Herrick-Gibbs Orbit Determination

The Herrick-Gibbs method is the short-arc counterpart of [Gibbs Orbit Determination](#gibbs-orbit-determination): for three positions close together in time and angle, it estimates the middle velocity from a Taylor-series expansion that also uses the three epochs. It stays accurate where the classical Gibbs method becomes ill-conditioned because the points are nearly colinear, typically for separations of a few degrees, as in a single radar or optical tracking pass. Like Gibbs, it needs positions relative to the central body, not angles.

Time differences are taken in days, so the gravitational parameter must be in position-unit³/day² and the velocity comes out in position-unit/day. A geometry outside the method's regime is reported in the diagnostics, which should be checked before the state is used as the seed of a fit.

```ts
import { KeplerOrbit } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/asteroid'
import { herrickGibbs } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/determination/herrickgibbs'
import { Timescale, timeShift, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005 } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'
import { matIdentity } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/mat3'

// A synthetic heliocentric orbit sampled 2 days before, at, and 3 days after the epoch.
const epoch = timeYMDHMS(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)
const orbit = KeplerOrbit.trueAnomaly(1.9, 0.18, 0.12, 0.8, 1.1, 0.35, epoch, GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005, matIdentity())
const [t1, t2, t3] = [timeShift(epoch, -2), epoch, timeShift(epoch, 3)]
const [r1, r2, r3] = [orbit.at(t1)[0], orbit.at(t2)[0], orbit.at(t3)[0]]

// Velocity at the middle epoch from three positions (AU), their times, and GM (AU³/day²).
const { v, diagnostics } = herrickGibbs(r1, r2, r3, t1, t2, t3, GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005)

console.log(v) // [-0.011823, -0.0085783, 0.00030201] — AU/day, within 1e-8 of the true velocity (relative)
console.log(diagnostics.reliable, diagnostics.warnings) // true []
```

### Hour-Angle Windows

The hour angle of a target is local sidereal time minus its right ascension, `H = LST − RA`: zero on the meridian, negative east of it, positive west. A fixed-right-ascension target's hour angle advances at the sidereal rate, one turn per sidereal day of about 23 h 56 m, so how long it stays within hour-angle limits, such as a mount's tracking range before a meridian flip or the span around the meridian where the airmass is low, is simple geometry. These functions ignore the target's own motion.

All angles are radians, with the hour angle normalized to `(−π, π]`, and durations are SI seconds measured from the epoch of the supplied hour angle. A window whose minimum exceeds its maximum crosses the ±π cut, below the pole, for example from +160° through 12 h to −160°.

```ts
import { hourAngle, hourAngleWindows, timeUntilMeridian } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/hourangle'
import { deg, hour, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// LST 20 h, RA 18 h: 2 hours of sidereal time west of the meridian.
console.log(toDeg(hourAngle(hour(20), hour(18)))) // 30 — degrees

// Seconds until the next meridian transit of a target 30° east of the meridian.
console.log(timeUntilMeridian(deg(-30)) / 3600) // 1.9945 — hours

// From hour angle -100°, the stretches of the next day within ±60° of the meridian, in seconds.
console.log(hourAngleWindows(deg(-100), deg(-60), deg(60), 86400)) // [{ startSeconds: 9573.8, endSeconds: 38295.2 }]
```

### IAU Body Orientation

The IAU Working Group on Cartographic Coordinates and Rotational Elements publishes how each body is oriented in space: the right ascension and declination of its north pole as polynomials in time, and the angle `W` of its prime meridian, which grows linearly with time plus small periodic corrections. From those the body-fixed frame follows, with +Z along the north pole and +X toward the prime meridian, through the rotation `Rz(W) · Rx(π/2 − δ) · Rz(π/2 + α)` from ICRF. It is the geometry behind the central meridian, ring tilt, solar disk orientation, and surface points on other bodies.

The library holds the rotation elements of the Sun, the planets (with Jupiter's Systems I, II, and III), and the Moon as constants. They reproduce the bodies to about 0.1° over the modern era; a few minor periodic terms of Mercury and Mars are omitted. Angles are radians, evaluated at TDB. As a `Frame` the orientation also carries its angular rate in radians per day, so it works with the frame functions (see [Celestial and Terrestrial Reference Frames](#celestial-and-terrestrial-reference-frames)) and with surface locations (see [Planetary Surface Locations](#planetary-surface-locations)). For the points beneath an observer or the Sun, see [Sub-Observer and Sub-Solar Points](#sub-observer-and-sub-solar-points).

```ts
import { bodyFixedFrame, bodyFixedMatrix, orientation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/orientation'
import { MARS_ROTATION } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/orientation.data'
import { frameAt } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/frame'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Mars: pole direction in ICRF and prime meridian angle, radians.
const mars = orientation(MARS_ROTATION, time)

console.log(toDeg(mars.poleRa), toDeg(mars.poleDec), toDeg(mars.primeMeridian)) // 317.65 52.87 72.29 — degrees

// The ICRF to Mars body-fixed rotation (row-major 3×3).
console.log(bodyFixedMatrix(MARS_ROTATION, time).slice(0, 3)) // [-0.3563, 0.7365, 0.5750] — the prime-meridian axis in ICRF

// The same orientation as a Frame: an ICRF state expressed in Mars's rotating axes.
const frame = bodyFixedFrame(MARS_ROTATION)
const state = [
	[1, 0, 0],
	[0, 0, 0],
] as const

console.log(frameAt(state, frame, time)) // [[-0.3563, -0.8210, 0.4461], [-5.028, 2.182, ~0]] — position, velocity per day
```

### Instantaneous Earth Spin

When a state is moved between the inertial and Earth-fixed frames, its velocity picks up a rotating-frame term `W · p`, with `W = dR/dt · Rᵀ` for the GCRS to ITRS rotation `R`. The `ITRS` frame uses a constant mean spin rate for it. The instantaneous versions evaluate the real rate, including the small contributions of precession, nutation, and polar motion, by central differences over ±1 second.

`W` is antisymmetric, and the Earth's angular-velocity vector `ω` is in ITRS axes, both in radians per day, with `ω` close to +z (toward the celestial pole) and about `2π × 1.0027379` per day in size. Use them when velocity accuracy at the level of the precession or polar-motion rates matters; otherwise the mean-rate `ITRS` is enough. To apply the exact term to a state, use the `ITRS_INSTANTANEOUS` frame from [Celestial and Terrestrial Reference Frames](#celestial-and-terrestrial-reference-frames).

```ts
import { instantaneousEarthAngularVelocity, instantaneousEarthRotationMatrix, Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

// A UT1 instant, so the example does not depend on loaded Earth orientation data.
const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UT1)

// W = dR/dt · Rᵀ, radians per day, antisymmetric (row-major 3×3).
const w = instantaneousEarthRotationMatrix(time)

console.log(w[1], w[3]) // 6.3004 -6.3004 — the dominant spin term

// ω in ITRS axes, radians per day.
console.log(instantaneousEarthAngularVelocity(time)) // [-5.2e-7, 6.9e-8, 6.30039] — mostly along +z
```

### Jovian Ephemeris Sources

Predicting a phenomenon of Jupiter's system, such as a mutual event or a satellite eclipse, needs the positions of the Sun, the Earth, Jupiter's center, and the four Galilean satellites at many epochs. The events depend on differences of a few hundred kilometers between bodies, so every state of one computation must come from the same source: mixing an analytical Jupiter with a kernel satellite would introduce offsets larger than the effect being predicted. A `JovianEphemeris` is that source, returning barycentric positions in AU and ICRF axes.

Two sources exist. The analytical one uses VSOP87E for the Sun, the Earth, and Jupiter, and adds the L1.2 jovicentric offsets of the satellites (see [Galilean Satellite Theory (L1.2)](#galilean-satellite-theory-l12)); it never fails. The SPK one resolves each body through a prepared kernel set (see [SPK State Kernels](#spk-state-kernels)); Jupiter is NAIF 599, the planet's center, never the system barycenter 5, so a planetary kernel such as DE440s alone is not enough. When a kernel source cannot resolve a body it throws `JovianEphemerisMiss`, so that the caller can rerun the whole computation with another source instead of mixing them. For dense searches, `interpolatedJovianEphemeris` wraps a source with a Lagrange interpolation on a fixed grid, keeping the error below 0.1 km at a fraction of the cost.

```ts
import { analyticalJovianEphemeris, hasJovianTargets, JovianEphemerisMiss, spkJovianEphemeris } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/jovian'
import type { SpkKernelSet } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/spk.kernelset'
import { findGalileanMutualEvents } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/mutual'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

// set: SpkKernelSet — prepared with prepareSpkKernelSet from a JUP satellite kernel and a planetary kernel.
declare const set: SpkKernelSet

const start = timeYMDHMS(2026, 12, 5, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
const stop = timeYMDHMS(2026, 12, 6, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

let events

try {
	// One source for the whole search: every state from the kernels when they hold all seven bodies...
	events = hasJovianTargets(set) ? findGalileanMutualEvents(spkJovianEphemeris(set), start, stop) : findGalileanMutualEvents(analyticalJovianEphemeris, start, stop)
} catch (e) {
	if (!(e instanceof JovianEphemerisMiss)) throw e
	// ...or, after a miss anywhere in the search, every state from the analytical theories.
	events = findGalileanMutualEvents(analyticalJovianEphemeris, start, stop)
}
```

### Jovian Satellite Geometry

Seen from the Earth, Jupiter is a flattened disk about 30″ to 50″ across, with the four Galilean satellites strung along its equator. A satellite can pass in front of the disk (a transit), cast its shadow on the planet (a shadow transit), pass behind the disk (an occultation), or enter Jupiter's shadow (an eclipse). `jovianView` computes this apparent geometry at an observed geocentric instant from one [Jovian ephemeris source](#jovian-ephemeris-sources): the disk's size and pole angle, the central meridians, and for each moon its sky offset from Jupiter's center in Jupiter equatorial radii, its disk and eclipse states, and the position of its shadow.

Jupiter is an oblate spheroid with the IAU 1-bar radii, so its outline is an ellipse whose minor axis follows the projected pole, never a circle. The moons are spheres of their mean radii, each body is light-time retarded separately, and the shadows are cones of the finite Sun; a moon's shadow is cast along the Sun-moon axis, so away from opposition it lies well off the moon's own position. Times are geocentric, not topocentric, and aberration is neglected. The view is meant for display; [Galilean Satellite Phenomena](#galilean-satellite-phenomena) finds the event instants.

```ts
import { analyticalJovianEphemeris } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/jovian'
import { jovianMoonMargins, jovianShadowPoint, jovianSystemState, jovianView, projectJovianSurfacePoint } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/jupiter.geometry'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Apparent geometry of Jupiter and its moons at a geocentric instant.
const view = jovianView(analyticalJovianEphemeris, time)

console.log(toDeg(view.centralMeridian.II), toDeg(view.poleAngle)) // degrees, System II and the projected pole from north through east

// Each moon: east and north offsets in Jupiter equatorial radii, transit/occultation and eclipse states.
for (const moon of view.moons) console.log(moon.moon, moon.east, moon.north, moon.disk, moon.eclipse)

// A feature at System II 50° W and 22° S on the apparent disk, and whether it faces the Earth.
const spot = projectJovianSurfacePoint(view, deg(50), deg(-22))

console.log(spot.visible, spot.east, spot.north)

// The cheaper scanning steps behind the view: the state shared by all moons, then one moon's
// disk, shadow, and eclipse margins (signed distances to contact, in Jupiter equatorial radii).
const state = jovianSystemState(analyticalJovianEphemeris, time)
const io = jovianMoonMargins(analyticalJovianEphemeris, state, 'io')

console.log(io.disk.distance) // 4.887 — Io's centre outside the limb (negative inside)
```
