```ts
// The centre of the moon's shadow on Jupiter, or undefined when the shadow misses the planet.
console.log(jovianShadowPoint(state, io.shadow)) // undefined — Io is about 5.9 radii off the disk as seen from the Sun
```

### Jupiter Central Meridian

The central meridian of Jupiter is the line of longitude that crosses the middle of the disk as the observer sees it, and its longitude tells which part of the planet faces the observer. Jupiter has no solid surface and its atmosphere rotates differentially, so there are three conventional rotation systems. System I (period 9 h 50 m 30 s) covers the equatorial zone, System II (9 h 55 m 41 s) the rest of the visible clouds, where the Great Red Spot lies, and System III (9 h 55 m 30 s) follows the magnetic field and radio emission tied to the interior. Longitudes are measured positive to the west, so the central meridian longitude increases with time.

The observer enters as the Jupiter-to-observer vector in AU and ICRF axes, for example `earth − jupiter` for a geocentric view: its length sets the light-time delay and its direction the sub-observer point. The result agrees with published System I and II longitudes to about 0.001°. Apply it to a feature at a known longitude to see when it faces you, or use [Great Red Spot Transits](#great-red-spot-transits) for the transit instants of one longitude.

```ts
import { earth, jupiter } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { jupiterCentralMeridian } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/jupiter'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Vector from Jupiter's center to a geocentric observer, AU, ICRF axes.
const jupiterToEarth = vecMinus(earth(time)[0], jupiter(time)[0])

// Central meridian longitude, radians in [0, 2π), west-positive.
console.log(toDeg(jupiterCentralMeridian('I', time, jupiterToEarth))) // 15.82 — degrees, System I
console.log(toDeg(jupiterCentralMeridian('II', time, jupiterToEarth))) // 328.28 — degrees, System II
console.log(toDeg(jupiterCentralMeridian('III', time, jupiterToEarth))) // 264.39 — degrees, System III
```

### Kepler Anomalies and Periapsis Timing

The position of a body on its orbit is measured by three angles from periapsis. The true anomaly `v` is the actual angle seen from the focus; the eccentric anomaly `E` is an auxiliary angle (the hyperbolic anomaly `H` for open orbits); and the mean anomaly `M` grows linearly with time at the mean motion `n`. Kepler's equation relates them, and has no closed-form inverse, so going from a time to a position requires solving it iteratively:

```text
ellipse (e < 1):   M = E − e·sin E      tan(v/2) = √((1 + e)/(1 − e)) · tan(E/2)
hyperbola (e > 1): M = e·sinh H − H     tan(v/2) = √((e + 1)/(e − 1)) · tanh(H/2)
parabola (e = 1):  Barker's equation in tan(v/2)
t − T = M / n      (time since periapsis T)
```

All angles are radians, the mean motion is radians per day, and the gravitational parameter AU³/day². The same quantities are available as properties of an orbit (see [Osculating Orbital Elements](#osculating-orbital-elements)); these functions are the building blocks for code that propagates or fits orbits itself.

```ts
import { eccentricAnomaly, eccentricAnomalyFromMean, meanAnomaly, meanMotion, stumpff, timeSincePeriapsis, trueAnomalyClosed, trueAnomalyHyperbolic, trueAnomalyParabolic } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/asteroid'
import { GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005 } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'

// An ellipse with e = 0.3 at eccentric anomaly E = 0.7 rad: mean and true anomalies.
const e = 0.3
const M = meanAnomaly(0.7, e)
const v = trueAnomalyClosed(e, 0.7)

console.log(M, v) // 0.50673 0.92321 — radians

// Kepler's equation solved for E, and E from the true anomaly.
console.log(eccentricAnomalyFromMean(M, e), eccentricAnomaly(v, e)) // 0.7 0.7

// A hyperbola with e = 1.5 and hyperbolic anomaly H = 4.
console.log(trueAnomalyHyperbolic(1.5, 4)) // 2.2729 — radians

// A parabola: true anomaly from its semi-latus rectum p (AU), GM (AU³/day²), and mean anomaly M (radians).
console.log(trueAnomalyParabolic(2, GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005, 0.1)) // 0.53831 — radians

// Stumpff functions c0..c3 of a dimensionless argument, the series of universal-variable propagation.
console.log(stumpff(0.5)) // [0.76024, 0.91873, 0.47951, 0.16255]

// Days since periapsis for a 1 AU, e = 0.3 solar orbit: mean motion (rad/day) and semi-latus rectum (AU).
const n = meanMotion(1, GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005)

console.log(timeSincePeriapsis(M, n, v, 1 * (1 - e * e), GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005)) // 29.458 — days
```

### Light-Time Solution

Light takes time to cross the Solar System, so a body seen at time `t` is where it was at the earlier emission time `t − τ`, with `τ = distance / c` (about 8.3 minutes per AU). Because the distance depends on that earlier position, the solution is a fixed-point iteration: sample the observer at reception, sample the target at the retarded epoch, recompute the distance, and repeat. Three iterations are enough for Solar-System bodies; zero gives the uncorrected geometric direction.

Target and observer are functions of time returning barycentric `[position (AU), velocity (AU/day)]` states with one common origin, typically ICRS/BCRS. The result is the light-time-corrected line of sight, its distance, and the light time in days. No aberration or gravitational deflection is applied, so it is an astrometric geometric direction, not an apparent place; for that use [Apparent Direction](#apparent-direction).

```ts
import { DEFAULT_LIGHT_TIME_ITERATIONS, lightTimeSolution, topocentricDirection } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/astrometry'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 4, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// observer, target: (time) => [position (AU), velocity (AU/day)] — barycentric states with one origin.
const observer = () =>
	[
		[1, 0, 0],
		[0, 0.0172, 0],
	] as const
const target = () =>
	[
		[1.5, 4.5, 0.5],
		[0, 0, 0],
	] as const

// The retarded geometry: target minus observer at reception, its distance, and the light time.
const solution = lightTimeSolution(target, observer, time, DEFAULT_LIGHT_TIME_ITERATIONS)

console.log(solution?.position) // [0.5, 4.5, 0.5] — AU, target minus observer
console.log(solution?.distance, solution?.lightTime) // 4.5552 0.026309 — AU, days

// Only the observer-to-target vector (AU, not normalized).
console.log(topocentricDirection(target, observer, time, DEFAULT_LIGHT_TIME_ITERATIONS)) // [0.5, 4.5, 0.5]
```

### Local ENU Frames

East-North-Up (ENU) is the local Cartesian frame of an observer: +x points east, +y north, and +z toward the zenith, all tangent to the ellipsoid at the site. Azimuth, measured from north through east, and altitude are its spherical angles. ENU vectors are convenient for mount and horizon geometry because a direction needs no spherical formulas, only a rotation from equatorial axes.

The rotation from apparent equatorial axes (the equator of date) to ENU depends only on the geodetic latitude and the local apparent sidereal time, in radians. The matrices are pure rotations: no refraction, aberration, or parallax is applied. For plain azimuth and altitude from right ascension and declination, [Local Horizon Coordinates](#local-horizon-coordinates) is shorter; use these matrices when you already work with vectors, or need many conversions at one instant, building the matrix once.

```ts
import { eraS2c } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/erfa'
import { enuToEquatorialMatrix, enuVectorToHorizontal, equatorialToEnuMatrix, horizontalToEnuVector } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/frame.local'
import { matMulVec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/mat3'
import { deg, hour, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const latitude = deg(-29.2563)
const lst = hour(17.7685) // local apparent sidereal time

// An apparent equatorial direction (RA 16 h, Dec -26°) rotated into ENU.
const enu = matMulVec(equatorialToEnuMatrix(latitude, lst), eraS2c(hour(16), deg(-26)))

console.log(enu) // [-0.4014, 0.01056, 0.9158] — east, north, up

// ENU vector to azimuth (north through east) and altitude, in radians, and back.
const { azimuth, altitude } = enuVectorToHorizontal(enu)

console.log(toDeg(azimuth), toDeg(altitude)) // 271.51 66.32 — degrees
console.log(horizontalToEnuVector(azimuth, altitude)) // [-0.4014, 0.01056, 0.9158]

// The inverse rotation, back to the equatorial vector.
console.log(matMulVec(enuToEquatorialMatrix(latitude, lst), enu)) // [-0.4494, -0.7784, -0.4384]
```

### Local Horizon Coordinates

The horizontal system describes where a source appears for an observer: azimuth measured from north through east, and altitude above the local horizon. Converting from equatorial coordinates needs the local hour angle `H = LST − RA`, where LST is the local apparent sidereal time, and the observer's latitude:

```text
sin h = sin φ · sin δ + cos φ · cos δ · cos H
```

Right ascension and declination must be referred to the equator of date, the same equator as the sidereal time, and all angles are radians. The conversion is pure spherical trigonometry: it applies no refraction, aberration, or parallax, so it is the geometric direction. For a refracted, topocentric place with the ERFA corrections see [Topocentric Observed Place](#topocentric-observed-place).

```ts
import { equatorialToHorizontal, horizontalToEquatorial } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/coordinate'
import { localSiderealTime } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, hour, toDeg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 4, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
const latitude = deg(-29.2563)

// Local apparent sidereal time at an east-positive longitude (radians).
const lst = localSiderealTime(time, deg(-70.7313))

// Equatorial of date (RA 16 h, Dec -26°) to azimuth and altitude.
const [azimuth, altitude] = equatorialToHorizontal(hour(16), deg(-26), latitude, lst)

console.log(toDeg(azimuth), toDeg(altitude)) // 271.51 66.32 — degrees, azimuth north through east

// The inverse recovers the equatorial coordinates.
const [ra, dec] = horizontalToEquatorial(azimuth, altitude, latitude, lst)

console.log(toHour(ra), toDeg(dec)) // 16 -26 — hours, degrees
```

### Local Horizon Mask

A real observing site rarely has a flat, clear horizon: trees, buildings, and hills hide the sky below some altitude that depends on azimuth. A horizon mask records that as a list of azimuths with the minimum altitude a target must reach there to be seen. Between samples the minimum altitude is interpolated linearly around the circle, including the segment from the last azimuth back to the first, and an empty mask hides nothing.

Angles are radians, with azimuth north through east. Besides point tests, the mask finds where a sampled altitude-azimuth path of a target goes behind it (a set) or emerges from it (a rise); the path must be sampled densely enough that each step is a short azimuth arc. To build such a path from an ephemeris, sample the target with [Local Horizon Coordinates](#local-horizon-coordinates).

```ts
import { horizonCrossings, horizonMinimumAltitude, horizonMinimumAltitudeLookup, type HorizonSample, type HorizontalPathSample, isAboveHorizon } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/horizon'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Obstructions: 10° to the north, 25° to the east, 5° to the south, 15° to the west.
const mask: HorizonSample[] = [
	{ azimuth: deg(0), minimumAltitude: deg(10) },
	{ azimuth: deg(90), minimumAltitude: deg(25) },
	{ azimuth: deg(180), minimumAltitude: deg(5) },
	{ azimuth: deg(270), minimumAltitude: deg(15) },
]

// The interpolated minimum altitude at an azimuth, and a visibility test.
console.log(toDeg(horizonMinimumAltitude(mask, deg(45)))) // 17.5 — degrees
console.log(isAboveHorizon(mask, deg(20), deg(45))) // true — 20° is above the 17.5° there

// The mask prepared once as a reusable lookup by azimuth, for many queries.
const minimumAltitude = horizonMinimumAltitudeLookup(mask)

console.log(toDeg(minimumAltitude(deg(200)))) // 7.22 — degrees

// path: samples of { time, altitude, azimuth } — a target rising in the east-northeast.
const rising: HorizontalPathSample[] = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].map((i) => ({ time: i, altitude: deg(5 + 10 * i), azimuth: deg(60 + 20 * i) }))

// Where the path crosses the mask, in time order, with time in the path's own unit.
for (const crossing of horizonCrossings(rising, mask)) console.log(crossing.kind, crossing.time, toDeg(crossing.altitude), toDeg(crossing.azimuth))
// rise 1.846 23.46 96.92 — emerges from behind the mask at 23.5° altitude, azimuth 97°
```

### Local Lunar Eclipse Search

A lunar eclipse happens on the Moon, so it is the same event for everyone on the night side of the Earth; whether a given site sees it depends only on whether the Moon is above its horizon during the eclipse. A site therefore sees about half of all lunar eclipses, sometimes only a part of one when the Moon rises or sets in the middle of it.

`listLocalLunarEclipses` walks the eclipses of a time window with the Meeus series of [Lunar Eclipse Search](#lunar-eclipse-search) and keeps those for which the Moon is above the horizon during some part of the penumbral phase, returning each with its [Lunar Eclipse Local Circumstances](#lunar-eclipse-local-circumstances) for the site. The longitude is east-positive and the latitude geodetic, in radians, and a raised horizon can be given as an altitude.

```ts
import { sunMoonPosition } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/eclipse'
import { listLocalLunarEclipses } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/lunar/local'
import { Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS, utc } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2025, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
const stop = timeYMDHMS(2028, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Lunar eclipses visible from São Paulo, each with its global and local circumstances.
for (const { eclipse, circumstances } of listLocalLunarEclipses(deg(-46.6333), deg(-23.55), start, stop, sunMoonPosition)) {
	console.log(timeToDate(utc(eclipse.maximalTime)).slice(0, 5).join('-'), eclipse.type, circumstances.visibility.kind, circumstances.details.observableDuration)
}
// 2025-3-14-6-59 TOTAL totalVisible 18767.62 — UTC, seconds with the Moon up
// 2026-3-3-11-34 TOTAL penumbralOnlyVisible 598.84
// 2026-8-28-4-13 PARTIAL completelyVisible 20144.43
// 2027-2-20-23-13 PENUMBRAL penumbralOnlyVisible 12885.95
// 2027-8-17-7-14 PENUMBRAL completelyVisible 12990.18

// With a 20° horizon, the eclipse of 3 March 2026, seen only near the horizon, disappears.
console.log(listLocalLunarEclipses(deg(-46.6333), deg(-23.55), start, stop, sunMoonPosition, { horizonAltitude: deg(20) }).length) // 4
```

### Local Lunar Eclipse View Geometry

The local view of a lunar eclipse is the diagram eclipse circulars draw: the Earth's penumbra and umbra as two concentric circles, the Moon's disk at each contact, the path of its center through the shadow, and the observer's horizon. It shows at a glance which part of the Moon is eclipsed first and which contacts happen with the Moon above the horizon.

`computeLocalLunarEclipseViewGeometry` builds it as plain shapes in SVG pixels (circles, a path, a polygon, and a line, with no text or markup) from the events of [Lunar Eclipse Local Circumstances](#lunar-eclipse-local-circumstances). It is a schematic of the Moon plane: the shadow center is fixed at the center of the view, the Moon is placed by its distance from the shadow axis and its position angle at each contact, and the diagram is oriented with the local zenith or celestial north up. The horizon offset uses a mean angular size, so it is meant for judging which side of the horizon a disk is on. SVG `y` grows downward.

```ts
import { nearestLunarEclipse } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/moon'
import { sunMoonPosition } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/eclipse'
import { computeLocalLunarEclipseCircumstances, computeLocalLunarEclipseViewGeometry } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/lunar/local'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The total lunar eclipse of 7 September 2025, seen from Perth.
const eclipse = nearestLunarEclipse(timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), true)
const circumstances = computeLocalLunarEclipseCircumstances(eclipse, deg(115.86), deg(-31.95), sunMoonPosition)

// The diagram at greatest eclipse, zenith up, as shapes in painter order.
const view = computeLocalLunarEclipseViewGeometry(circumstances, eclipse)

console.log(view.shapes.map((shape) => `${shape.kind}:${shape.role}`).join(' '))
// polygon:horizonBand path:trajectoryPath circle:ghostMoonDisk ×6 circle:moonDisk circle:penumbra circle:umbra line:horizonLine

// The start of totality with celestial north up.
const north = computeLocalLunarEclipseViewGeometry(circumstances, eclipse, { selectedEvent: 'U2', orientationMode: 'north' })

console.log(north.selectedEvent) // U2 — the contact drawn as the primary disk
```

### Local Solar Eclipse Circumstances

The local circumstances of a solar eclipse are what an observer at one place sees: the contacts C1 and C4 that begin and end the partial phase, C2 and C3 that bound totality or annularity when the site is inside the central path, the local maximum, the magnitude (the fraction of the Sun's diameter covered), the durations, the Sun's altitude, and the position angles of the contact points on the solar limb. They are what an eclipse expedition plans with, and what eclipse circulars tabulate for cities.

They are computed for a geodetic site (east-positive longitude and latitude, in radians) from the [Solar Eclipse Besselian Elements](#solar-eclipse-besselian-elements), by evaluating the observer's position against the shadow on the fundamental plane. The cubic fit of the elements is valid for a few hours around the maximum. The site is treated geometrically: every contact is computed even with the Sun below the horizon, and only the observability of each contact reflects the horizon, giving a classification of how much of the eclipse is visible. Pass the Sun/Moon provider used for the elements: with it the altitude, position angles, and apparent diameters come from the real Sun and Moon instead of a Besselian approximation.

```ts
import { nearestSolarEclipse } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/sun'
import { sunMoonPosition } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/eclipse'
import { computeLocalSolarEclipseCircumstances } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/solar/local'
import { computePolynomialBesselianElements } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/solar/map'
import { Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS, utc } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The total solar eclipse of 8 April 2024 and its Besselian elements.
const eclipse = nearestSolarEclipse(timeYMDHMS(2024, 4, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), true)
const pbe = computePolynomialBesselianElements(eclipse.maximalTime, sunMoonPosition)

// Local circumstances at Dallas (longitude east-positive, latitude, radians).
const circumstances = computeLocalSolarEclipseCircumstances(pbe, deg(-96.797), deg(32.776), { sunMoonPosition })

console.log(circumstances.visibility.kind) // completelyVisible
console.log(circumstances.details.maximalMagnitude, circumstances.details.centralPhaseDuration) // 1.0154 234.98 — seconds of totality

// The contacts: UTC time, Sun altitude and position angle of the contact point (degrees), magnitude.
for (const event of Object.values(circumstances.events)) {
	console.log(event.kind, timeToDate(utc(event.time)).slice(0, 6).join('-'), toDeg(event.sunAltitude), toDeg(event.positionAngle!), event.magnitude)
}
// C1 2024-4-8-17-23-22 60.57 226.2 -0.0000
// C2 2024-4-8-18-40-44 64.67 20.3 1.0000
// MAX 2024-4-8-18-42-41 64.62 137.3 1.0154
// C3 2024-4-8-18-44-39 64.56 254.2 1.0000
// C4 2024-4-8-20-2-43 56.75 49.2 0.0000
```

### Local Solar Eclipse Search

Unlike a lunar eclipse, a solar eclipse is seen only where the Moon's penumbra touches the Earth, a band a few thousand kilometers wide, so a given site sees a solar eclipse only every few years and a total one only every few centuries on average. Answering "which eclipses will I see from here" requires testing each global eclipse against the site.

`listLocalSolarEclipses` walks the eclipses of a window with the global search of [Solar Eclipse Search and Classification](#solar-eclipse-search-and-classification), fits the Besselian elements of each once, and keeps those whose local magnitude is above zero at some time. The filter is purely geometric: an eclipse is included even when the Sun is below the horizon at the site. Each entry returns its elements, so the full [Local Solar Eclipse Circumstances](#local-solar-eclipse-circumstances) can be computed without refitting them, which is the dominant cost.

```ts
import { sunMoonPosition } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/eclipse'
import { computeLocalSolarEclipseCircumstances, listLocalSolarEclipses } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/solar/local'
import { Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS, utc } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const longitude = deg(-96.797)
const latitude = deg(32.776)
const start = timeYMDHMS(2023, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
const end = timeYMDHMS(2026, 12, 31, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// The solar eclipses whose shadow reaches Dallas, earliest first, with their Besselian elements.
for (const { eclipse, elements } of listLocalSolarEclipses(longitude, latitude, start, end, sunMoonPosition)) {
	// The full local circumstances from the elements already fitted.
	const local = computeLocalSolarEclipseCircumstances(elements, longitude, latitude, { sunMoonPosition })

	console.log(timeToDate(utc(eclipse.maximalTime)).slice(0, 3).join('-'), eclipse.type, local.visibility.kind, local.details.maximalMagnitude)
}
// 2023-10-14 annular completelyVisible 0.862
// 2024-4-8 total completelyVisible 1.015
// 2025-3-29 partial geometricOnlyBelowHorizon 0.617
```

### Local Solar Eclipse View Geometry

The local view of a solar eclipse is the picture of the Sun with the Moon in front of it as the observer sees it: the solar disk, the Moon's disk offset by the local separation of the centers, and the horizon when the Sun is low. Drawn at each contact, it shows where on the solar limb the Moon first touches and how deep the eclipse gets, which is what observers use to aim and frame their instruments.

`computeLocalSolarEclipseViewGeometry` builds it as plain shapes in SVG pixels (circles, a polygon, and a line, with no text or markup) from the events of [Local Solar Eclipse Circumstances](#local-solar-eclipse-circumstances). The Sun is the unit of the diagram: the Moon is placed by the separation of the centers in solar radii, and its radius follows from the Moon/Sun diameter ratio of the event. The diagram is oriented with the local zenith or celestial north up, and east on the right or mirrored as in the naked-eye view. SVG `y` grows downward.

```ts
import { nearestSolarEclipse } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/sun'
import { sunMoonPosition } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/eclipse'
import { computeLocalSolarEclipseCircumstances, computeLocalSolarEclipseViewGeometry } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/solar/local'
import { computePolynomialBesselianElements } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/solar/map'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The total solar eclipse of 8 April 2024, seen from Dallas.
const eclipse = nearestSolarEclipse(timeYMDHMS(2024, 4, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), true)
const pbe = computePolynomialBesselianElements(eclipse.maximalTime, sunMoonPosition)
const circumstances = computeLocalSolarEclipseCircumstances(pbe, deg(-96.797), deg(32.776), { sunMoonPosition })

// The view at the local maximum, zenith up, as shapes in painter order.
const view = computeLocalSolarEclipseViewGeometry(circumstances)

console.log(view.shapes.map((shape) => `${shape.kind}:${shape.role}`).join(' '))
// circle:ghostMoonDisk ×4 circle:sunDisk circle:moonDisk polygon:horizonBand line:horizonLine

// The start of totality with celestial north up and east on the left.
const north = computeLocalSolarEclipseViewGeometry(circumstances, { selectedEvent: 'C2', orientationMode: 'north', handedness: 'eastLeft' })

console.log(north.selectedEvent) // C2 — the contact drawn as the primary state
```

### Local Standard of Rest Frames

The Local Standard of Rest (LSR) is the reference frame that moves with the average motion of the stars in the solar neighborhood, on a near-circular orbit around the Galactic center. The Sun moves relative to it by its peculiar motion of roughly 10 to 20 km/s, so radial velocities of interstellar gas, notably in radio spectroscopy of the 21 cm line, are referred to the LSR to remove the Sun's own motion. Velocities relative to the Sun, in ICRS, are converted to it by adding that solar motion; positions are unchanged, apart from the Galactic variant, which also rotates the axes.

Several definitions coexist, differing in the adopted solar motion: the standard LSR uses (U, V, W) = (11.1, 12.24, 7.25) km/s of Schönrich, Binney and Dehnen (2010), the dynamical LSRD the Delhaye (1965) motion (9, 12, 7) km/s, and the kinematic LSRK the classical solar-apex motion of about 20 km/s. The frames are affine (see [Affine Origin Frames](#affine-origin-frames)) and take full `[position, velocity]` states in AU and AU/day.

```ts
import { affineFromBase, galacticLsrFrame, lsrdFrame, lsrFrame, lsrkFrame } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/affine'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { ONE_PARSEC } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'
import { kilometerPerSecond, toKilometerPerSecond } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/velocity'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// ICRS state: position 100, 200, 50 pc (in AU); velocity 10, -20, 5 km/s (in AU/day).
const state = [
	[100 * ONE_PARSEC, 200 * ONE_PARSEC, 50 * ONE_PARSEC],
	[kilometerPerSecond(10), kilometerPerSecond(-20), kilometerPerSecond(5)],
] as const

// The state in the standard LSR: position unchanged, the Sun's peculiar motion added to the velocity.
console.log(affineFromBase(state, lsrFrame(), time)[1].map(toKilometerPerSecond)) // [9.148, -36.576, 12.078] — km/s

// The dynamical and kinematic LSR, and the LSR in Galactic axes.
console.log(affineFromBase(state, lsrdFrame(), time)[1].map(toKilometerPerSecond)) // [9.362, -34.585, 12.801] — km/s
console.log(affineFromBase(state, lsrkFrame(), time)[1].map(toKilometerPerSecond)) // [10.290, -37.317, 15.001] — km/s
console.log(affineFromBase(state, galacticLsrFrame(), time)[1].map(toKilometerPerSecond)) // [25.601, 29.813, 4.815] — km/s, Galactic axes
```

### Local Taki Frames

The Taki frame, named after Toshimi Taki's matrix method for telescope pointing, is a local equatorial frame used for polar-aligned mounts and pointing models. Its axes are fixed to the observer's meridian and the celestial pole: +x points to the meridian toward the south, +y east, and +z toward the north celestial pole. A direction with west-positive hour angle `H` and declination `δ` is `[cos δ cos H, −cos δ sin H, sin δ]` in it. Unlike the apparent equatorial frame, it does not depend on the sidereal time: it rotates with the Earth, and a target moves through it as its hour angle advances, exactly as it moves on an equatorial mount's hour axis.

The rotation between Taki and East-North-Up (see [Local ENU Frames](#local-enu-frames)) depends only on the geodetic latitude, in radians, and its inverse is the exact transpose. They are pure rotations with no refraction or place corrections; at a pole the Taki frame degenerates into the ENU axes.

```ts
import { enuToTakiMatrix, takiToEnuMatrix } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/frame.local'
import { matMulVec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/mat3'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const latitude = deg(-29.2563)

// A target at hour angle +1.7685 h (west of the meridian) and declination -26°, as a Taki vector.
const hourAngle = hour(17.7685) - hour(16)
const declination = deg(-26)
const taki = [Math.cos(declination) * Math.cos(hourAngle), -Math.cos(declination) * Math.sin(hourAngle), Math.sin(declination)] as const

// Taki to East-North-Up, and back.
const enu = matMulVec(takiToEnuMatrix(latitude), taki)

console.log(enu) // [-0.4014, 0.01056, 0.9158] — east, north, up
console.log(matMulVec(enuToTakiMatrix(latitude), enu)) // [0.8042, -0.4014, -0.4384] — meridian-south, east, north pole
```

### Location GCRS Frame

A site's local horizon axes turn with the Earth, so expressing a geocentric celestial vector in them requires the full Earth orientation at the instant (precession, nutation, rotation, and polar motion) followed by the rotation from the Earth-fixed frame into the site's altazimuth axes. `gcrs(location)` packages that as a `Frame` whose axes are the site's local axes relative to the geocentric celestial frame (GCRS, ICRS-oriented). Because the frame rotates, a full `[position, velocity]` state also receives the rotating-frame term from the instantaneous Earth angular velocity.

Use it with the frame functions (see [Celestial and Terrestrial Reference Frames](#celestial-and-terrestrial-reference-frames)) to express geocentric vectors in a site's horizon axes. It is geometry only, with no refraction, aberration, or origin shift: a geocentric vector stays geocentric, so subtract the observer's position first for topocentric directions, or use [Topocentric Observed Place](#topocentric-observed-place) for a full observed place.

```ts
import { frameAt } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/frame'
import { gcrs, gcrsRotationAt, geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const site = geodeticLocation(deg(-70.7313), deg(-29.2563), meter(2400))
const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 4, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// A unit GCRS direction (RA 200°, Dec 30°).
const direction = [Math.cos(deg(30)) * Math.cos(deg(200)), Math.cos(deg(30)) * Math.sin(deg(200)), Math.sin(deg(30))] as const

// The direction in the site's local axes.
console.log(frameAt(direction, gcrs(site), time)) // [0.6053, -0.7936, 0.0618]

// A state: the Earth's rotation adds the transport term to the velocity (per day).
const [, velocity] = frameAt([direction, [0, 0, 0]] as const, gcrs(site), time)

console.log(velocity) // [-2.4435, -2.2038, -4.3621] — per day, from the rotating frame

// Only the 3×3 rotation at an instant, as a fresh row-major matrix.
console.log(gcrsRotationAt(site, time))
```

### Low-Precision Earth Ephemeris

Many corrections need the Earth's position and velocity but not to kilometer accuracy: the annual aberration, of up to about 20″, depends on the Earth's barycentric velocity, and the light deflection and parallax terms on its distance from the Sun. `eraEpv00` is the ERFA port of the SOFA routine for that purpose, a harmonic series from a simplified version of Bretagnon's VSOP2000 model, rotated onto the DE405 axes. It is fast and approximate, and is best used where the full precision of VSOP87E or an SPK kernel is not needed.

It returns two states of the Earth, in this order: barycentric (relative to the Solar System barycenter) and heliocentric (relative to the Sun), in AU and AU/day in BCRS-oriented axes. The difference between them is the Sun's offset from the barycenter, of order 0.01 AU, mostly due to Jupiter. The date is a two-part TDB Julian date `tdb1 + tdb2`, split in any way.

```ts
import { eraEpv00 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/earth'

// Earth at the SOFA test epoch: JD 2400000.5 + 53411.52501161 TDB.
const [barycentric, heliocentric] = eraEpv00(2400000.5, 53411.52501161)

console.log(barycentric[0]) // [−0.77141, 0.55984, 0.24260] — AU, barycentric position
console.log(barycentric[1]) // [−0.010919, −0.012465, −0.0054048] — AU/day, barycentric velocity
console.log(heliocentric[0]) // [−0.77572, 0.55981, 0.24270] — AU, heliocentric position
```

### Low-Precision Lunar Ephemeris

The Moon moves fast, about 0.5° per hour across the sky, and its orbit is strongly perturbed by the Sun, so even a rough lunar position needs a series of many periodic terms. `eraMoon98` is the ERFA port of the SOFA low-precision lunar theory: an ELP-based series with the additive terms of Meeus' _Astronomical Algorithms_, in the mean arguments of the lunar orbit. It gives the geometric geocentric position and velocity of the Moon, with no light time and no aberration, in AU and AU/day, rotated onto ICRS axes through the IAU 2006 precession and frame bias.

It is an approximation intended for eclipse screening and similar uses where the precision of a full lunar theory such as [ELP/MPP02 Lunar Theory](#elpmpp02-lunar-theory) or a JPL kernel is not needed. The date is a two-part Terrestrial Time Julian date `tt1 + tt2`.

```ts
import { eraMoon98 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/moon'
import { AU_KM } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'

// The geocentric Moon at the SOFA test epoch: JD 2400000.5 + 43999.9 TT.
const [position, velocity] = eraMoon98(2400000.5, 43999.9)

console.log(position) // [−0.0026013, 0.00061398, 0.00026408] — AU, ICRS axes
console.log(velocity) // [−0.00012443, −0.00052191, −0.00017161] — AU/day
console.log(Math.hypot(...position) * AU_KM) // 401787.8 — km, geocentric distance
```

### Lunar Apsides

The Moon's orbit is an ellipse of mean eccentricity 0.055, so its distance from the Earth changes each month between perigee, the closest point, and apogee, the farthest. Solar perturbations make both vary from month to month, with perigee distances from about 356,400 km to 370,400 km and apogee from 404,000 km to 406,700 km; the extreme perigees occur near full or new moon. A full moon near perigee is the popular supermoon, and the distance sets the Moon's apparent size, its parallax, and the tidal range.

The search uses the series of Meeus's chapter 50, with the periodic corrections for the true apsis; the mean apsis, without them, can differ from the true one by up to about a day. Results are accurate to a few minutes near the modern epoch. Each apsis is returned with the geocentric distance in AU and the Moon's apparent angular diameter in radians, and its time is TT: convert with `utc` for a civil clock time. The distance converts to a parallax with `moonParallax` (see [Lunar Parallax and Semidiameter](#lunar-parallax-and-semidiameter)).

```ts
import { nearestLunarApsis, nearestMeanLunarApsis } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/moon'
import { Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toArcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// The next perigee after the start: TT instant, distance (AU), and apparent diameter (radians).
const [time, distance, diameter] = nearestLunarApsis(start, 'PERIGEE', true)

console.log(timeToDate(time).slice(0, 5)) // [2026, 1, 1, 21, 44] — TT
console.log(toKilometer(distance), toArcsec(diameter)) // 360347 1989.6 — km, arcseconds

// The next apogee (pass false for the last one at or before the time).
const [apogee, apogeeDistance] = nearestLunarApsis(start, 'APOGEE', true)

console.log(timeToDate(apogee).slice(0, 5), toKilometer(apogeeDistance)) // [2026, 1, 13, 20, 48] 405436

// The mean apogee, without the periodic corrections: a TT instant only, here about 10 hours after the true one.
console.log(timeToDate(nearestMeanLunarApsis(start, 'APOGEE', true)).slice(0, 5)) // [2026, 1, 14, 6, 24]
```

### Lunar Declination Extrema and Standstills

The Moon's declination swings between a northern and a southern maximum every tropical month, about 13.7 days apart. The size of the swing changes over the 18.6-year cycle of the lunar nodes: at a major lunar standstill the monthly extremes reach about ±28.6° (the obliquity plus the Moon's orbital inclination of 5.1°), and at a minor standstill only about ±18.3° (the obliquity minus the inclination). The standstills set the extreme rising and setting azimuths of the Moon, which many prehistoric monuments appear to mark, and so matter in archaeoastronomy as well as for planning low-Moon observations.

The monthly extremes come from the series of Meeus's chapter 52, and a standstill is the extreme monthly maximum of the 18.6-year envelope, found separately for each hemisphere because the northern and southern ones fall a couple of weeks apart. The declination is the mean geocentric value of a truncated series, accurate to a few arcminutes with times good to about 20 minutes, without nutation or topocentric parallax. Times are TT and declinations radians, negative for a southern maximum.

```ts
import { nearestLunarStandstill, nearestMaxDeclination } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/moon'
import { Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The next northern monthly maximum: TT instant and declination (radians).
const [north, northDeclination] = nearestMaxDeclination(timeYMDHMS(2025, 3, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), 'NORTH', true)

console.log(timeToDate(north).slice(0, 5), toDeg(northDeclination)) // [2025, 3, 7, 15, 57] 28.71 — TT, degrees

// The next major standstill in the north: the largest monthly maximum of the nodal cycle.
const [major, majorDeclination] = nearestLunarStandstill(timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), 'MAJOR', 'NORTH', true)

console.log(timeToDate(major).slice(0, 5), toDeg(majorDeclination)) // [2025, 3, 7, 15, 57] 28.71

// The minor standstill of the 2015 cycle.
const [minor, minorDeclination] = nearestLunarStandstill(timeYMDHMS(2014, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), 'MINOR', 'NORTH', true)

console.log(timeToDate(minor).slice(0, 5), toDeg(minorDeclination)) // [2015, 10, 3, 23, 55] 18.14
```

### Lunar Eclipse Local Circumstances

A lunar eclipse happens on the Moon, so its contact instants are the same for every observer: P1 and P4 when the Moon enters and leaves the penumbra, U1 and U4 for the umbra, U2 and U3 for totality, and the greatest eclipse. What changes with the site is whether the Moon is above the horizon at each contact and during the phases, its altitude and azimuth, and the orientation on the lunar limb of the contact point, given as the P angle (from celestial north through east) and the Z angle (from the local zenith), as in the published contact tables.

The local circumstances are computed from a `LunarEclipse` (see [Lunar Eclipse Search](#lunar-eclipse-search)) and a Sun/Moon position provider, for an east-positive longitude and a geodetic latitude in radians. Altitudes are topocentric, with diurnal parallax and without refraction. The visibility is not judged only at the contacts: the Moon's altitude is sampled across the eclipse, so a Moon that rises or sets in the middle of it is reported as visible for the part above the horizon, and a raised horizon can be given as an altitude.

```ts
import { nearestLunarEclipse } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/moon'
import { sunMoonPosition } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/eclipse'
import { computeLocalLunarEclipseCircumstances, moonAltitudeAt } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/lunar/local'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The total lunar eclipse of 7 September 2025.
const eclipse = nearestLunarEclipse(timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), true)

// Perth (115.86°E, 31.95°S): the Moon is high during the whole eclipse.
const perth = computeLocalLunarEclipseCircumstances(eclipse, deg(115.86), deg(-31.95), sunMoonPosition)

console.log(perth.visibility.kind, perth.details.observableDuration) // completelyVisible 19477.89 — seconds with the Moon up

// The greatest eclipse: topocentric altitude and azimuth, then the P and Z angles (degrees).
const max = perth.events.MAX!

console.log(toDeg(max.altitude), toDeg(max.azimuth)) // 51.72 307.32
console.log(toDeg(max.positionAngle), toDeg(max.zenithAngle)) // 330.93 193.62

// The topocentric Moon altitude (radians) at any instant, such as the last penumbral contact P4.
console.log(toDeg(moonAltitudeAt(eclipse.lastContactPenumbraTime, deg(115.86), deg(-31.95), sunMoonPosition))) // 20.04 — degrees

// Greenwich: the Moon rises during the eclipse, so only the last part is seen.
const greenwich = computeLocalLunarEclipseCircumstances(eclipse, 0, deg(51.48), sunMoonPosition)

console.log(greenwich.visibility.kind, greenwich.details.observableDuration) // totalVisible 8332.34
```

### Lunar Eclipse Map SVG Paths

The visibility map of a lunar eclipse is drawn as one moonrise/moonset curve per contact, the boundary between the regions of the Earth that see that contact with the Moon up and those that do not. `lunarEclipseMapToSvgPaths` projects the curves of [Lunar Eclipse Visibility Geometry](#lunar-eclipse-visibility-geometry) through a cylindrical map projection and returns them as SVG path data, together with the projected sublunar point of each contact.

Each curve is a circle on the globe, and on a cylindrical map it is split at the antimeridian into separate subpaths instead of a line across the whole map. The coordinates are those of the projection: with `PlateCarree`, `x` is the longitude and `y` the latitude, multiplied by the projection scale, with north up; since SVG `y` grows downward, the projection can be set to SVG axes. For shading, the curves can be returned as closed region polygons on the side where the Moon is down or up; they must be rendered with `fill-rule="evenodd"`, and they assume a projection over the full longitude range.

```ts
import { nearestLunarEclipse } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/moon'
import { sunMoonPosition } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/eclipse'
import { computeLunarEclipseMapGeometry, lunarEclipseMapToSvgPaths } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/lunar/map'
import { PlateCarree } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/projections/projection'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

// The total lunar eclipse of 7 September 2025, on a map of 100 pixels per radian with SVG axes (y down).
const eclipse = nearestLunarEclipse(timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), true)
const geometry = computeLunarEclipseMapGeometry(eclipse, sunMoonPosition)
const projection = new PlateCarree(0, { scale: 100, yAxisDirection: 'southUp' })

// One path string per contact, and the projected sublunar points.
const paths = lunarEclipseMapToSvgPaths(geometry, projection)

console.log(paths.sublunarPoints.MAX) // { x: 151.17, y: 10.47 } — where the Moon is at the zenith at greatest eclipse
console.log(paths.moonRiseSet.MAX.slice(0, 59)) // M151.17 -144.88L165.41 -144.76L179.1 -144.39L191.82 -143.81

// Closed polygons of the region where the Moon is below the horizon, for shading with fill-rule="evenodd".
const filled = lunarEclipseMapToSvgPaths(geometry, projection, { fill: true })

console.log(filled.moonRiseSet.MAX.endsWith('Z')) // true — a closed path
```

### Lunar Eclipse Search

A lunar eclipse happens when the Moon passes through the Earth's shadow at full moon, which requires the full moon to fall near one of the lunar nodes (see [Lunar Nodes](#lunar-nodes)). It is total if the Moon enters the dark umbra completely, partial if only a part of it does, and penumbral if it passes only through the faint outer shadow. The eclipse is seen from everywhere the Moon is above the horizon, and its circumstances do not depend on the observer: the contact instants (P1, U1, U2, greatest eclipse, U3, U4, P4), the magnitude, and gamma, the least distance of the Moon's center from the shadow axis in Earth radii. For the view from a site see [Local Lunar Eclipse Search](#local-lunar-eclipse-search).

`nearestLunarEclipse` uses the method of Meeus's chapter 54, about a minute from the published contacts, and its shadow radii differ from the catalogs': the penumbral duration is about 2 minutes short on average, and marginal cases can be misclassified (the very short total eclipse of 2015-04-04 reads as partial). `refineLunarEclipse` replaces the instants, type, magnitude, and gamma with the geometry of the Moon and the Earth's shadow, using Danjon's enlarged shadow radii (`1.01 π_m + π_s ∓ s_s`); it should be used for results to be shown. All times are TT, and a contact that does not exist for the type is a sentinel `Time` whose `day` is 0.

```ts
import { nearestLunarEclipse } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/moon'
import { sunMoonPositionAround } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/eclipse'
import { refineLunarEclipse } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/lunar/map'
import { Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS, utc } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

// The first lunar eclipse after 1 September 2025 (pass false for the last one at or before the time).
const eclipse = nearestLunarEclipse(timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), true)

console.log(eclipse.type, eclipse.magnitude, eclipse.gamma) // TOTAL 1.3606 -0.2758 — umbral magnitude, Earth radii
console.log(timeToDate(utc(eclipse.maximalTime)).slice(0, 5)) // [2025, 9, 7, 18, 12] — greatest eclipse, UTC
console.log(eclipse.sdTotal * 1440) // 40.7 — minutes, half the duration of totality

// Refined with the Moon and the Earth's shadow geometry: 2015-04-04 becomes total.
const series = nearestLunarEclipse(timeYMDHMS(2015, 4, 3, 0, 0, 0), true)
const refined = refineLunarEclipse(series, sunMoonPositionAround(series.maximalTime))!

console.log(series.type, refined.type, refined.magnitude.toFixed(4)) // PARTIAL TOTAL 1.0008
```

### Lunar Eclipse Visibility Geometry

A map of a lunar eclipse cannot show a shadow on the ground, because the shadow falls on the Moon. What a map can show is where on the Earth the Moon is up. For each contact, the boundary between the hemisphere that sees the Moon above the horizon and the one that does not is a small circle centered on the sublunar point, the place where the Moon is at the zenith (latitude equal to the Moon's declination, longitude equal to its right ascension minus the Greenwich apparent sidereal time).

The radius of the circle is not the geocentric 90° of the horizon: the observer stands on the surface, so the Moon seen on the horizon is lower in the sky than its geocentric direction by the lunar parallax, and the radius is about 0.95° smaller:

```text
radius = π/2 − h0 − asin(cos h0 / d)
```

with `h0` the horizon altitude and `d` the Moon's distance in Earth radii. The observer is treated as spherical. The horizon can be lowered for refraction or for the Moon's upper limb instead of its center. The curves stay in geographic coordinates (radians, east-positive longitude); projecting them to a map is the subject of [Lunar Eclipse Map SVG Paths](#lunar-eclipse-map-svg-paths).

```ts
import { nearestLunarEclipse } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/moon'
import { sunMoonPosition } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/eclipse'
import { computeLunarEclipseMapGeometry, lunarEclipseEvents } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/lunar/map'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The total lunar eclipse of 7 September 2025.
const eclipse = nearestLunarEclipse(timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), true)

// The contacts the eclipse has, in chronological order.
console.log(lunarEclipseEvents(eclipse).map((contact) => contact.kind)) // ['P1', 'U1', 'U2', 'MAX', 'U3', 'U4', 'P4']

// The moonrise/moonset circle and the sublunar point of each contact.
const geometry = computeLunarEclipseMapGeometry(eclipse, sunMoonPosition)
const max = geometry.events.find((event) => event.kind === 'MAX')!

console.log(toDeg(max.sublunar.x), toDeg(max.sublunar.y)) // 86.61 -6.00 — degrees, the Moon at the zenith at greatest eclipse
console.log(geometry.lines.moonRiseSet.MAX![0].length) // 361 — one closed ring at 1° spacing

// The horizon lowered by the standard 34′ of refraction.
const refracted = computeLunarEclipseMapGeometry(eclipse, sunMoonPosition, { refraction: true })

console.log(toDeg(refracted.events[3].horizonAltitude)) // -0.5667 — degrees, 34′
```

### Lunar Libration Extrema

The Moon always shows nearly the same face to the Earth, but it seems to nod and sway by a few degrees, so that about 59% of its surface can be seen over time. This optical libration moves the sub-Earth point on the lunar surface in longitude, an east-west sway of up to about 8° caused by the eccentric orbit, and in latitude, a north-south nod of up to about 7° caused by the tilt of the lunar equator to the orbit. When a libration reaches an extreme, the limb regions on that side, such as Mare Orientale or the polar craters, are best seen.

The libration is the planetocentric longitude (east-positive) and latitude (north-positive) of the sub-observer point, from the IAU lunar rotation model evaluated one light time earlier. The observer enters as the Moon-to-observer vector in AU and ICRF axes, so the extrema can be geocentric or topocentric. The search step, in days, must resolve the extrema; a few hours suit a lunar month.

```ts
import { moon } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/elpmpp02'
import { lunarLibrationExtrema } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/lunar'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecNegate } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Moon center to a geocentric observer: the negative of the geocentric Moon vector (AU).
const moonToObserver = (time: Time) => vecNegate(moon(time)[0])

const start = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
const stop = timeYMDHMS(2025, 10, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Local extrema of both librations in chronological order, with a 6-hour scan step.
for (const e of lunarLibrationExtrema(moonToObserver, start, stop, { step: 0.25 })) console.log(e.axis, e.kind, timeToDate(e.time).slice(0, 5), toDeg(e.angle))
// latitude maximum [2025, 9, 1, 3, 3] 6.85 — UTC, degrees
// longitude minimum [2025, 9, 4, 16, 43] -5.68
// latitude minimum [2025, 9, 14, 4, 23] -6.80
// longitude maximum [2025, 9, 17, 21, 52] 5.97
// latitude maximum [2025, 9, 28, 9, 53] 6.83
```

### Lunar Nodes

The lunar nodes are the two points where the Moon's orbit, inclined about 5.1° to the ecliptic, crosses it: the ascending node, where the Moon passes from south to north, and the descending node, where it passes north to south. Eclipses can happen only when a new or full moon falls near a node. The nodes regress westward along the ecliptic, completing a turn in 18.6 years, which sets the eclipse seasons and the cycle of the lunar standstills (see [Lunar Declination Extrema and Standstills](#lunar-declination-extrema-and-standstills)).

The node passages come from the series of Meeus's chapter 51, a truncated series with minute-level accuracy near the modern epoch, as TT instants. The longitude of the mean ascending node, in the mean ecliptic and equinox of date, is Meeus's equation 47.7, without the periodic terms of the true node, which oscillates around it.

```ts
import { moonMeanAscendingNode, nearestLunarNode } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/moon'
import { Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// The next passages through the ascending and descending nodes (pass false for the previous ones).
console.log(timeToDate(nearestLunarNode(time, 'ASCENDING', true)).slice(0, 5)) // [2025, 10, 5, 9, 21] — TT
console.log(timeToDate(nearestLunarNode(time, 'DESCENDING', true)).slice(0, 5)) // [2025, 10, 18, 4, 34] — TT

// Longitude of the mean ascending node, radians in [0, 2π).
console.log(toDeg(moonMeanAscendingNode(time))) // 347.20 — degrees
```

### Lunar Parallax and Semidiameter

The Moon is close enough that its position and size depend on where you stand. Its equatorial horizontal parallax is the angle that the Earth's equatorial radius subtends at the Moon, about 57′ (0.95°), so the Moon seen on the horizon is displaced by nearly two of its own diameters from its geocentric direction. Its semidiameter, the angular radius of the disk, ranges from about 14.7′ to 16.7′ between apogee and perigee. Both scale inversely with the distance:

```text
sin π = a / Δ        s = k · a / Δ  (k = 0.2725, the Moon/Earth radius ratio)
```

The topocentric semidiameter grows when the Moon is high, by up to about 1.7% at the zenith, because the observer is then closer to the Moon than the Earth's center is. The rigorous version follows Meeus (chapter 55) from the hour angle, the declination, and the observer's parallax constants (see [Geographic Observer](#geographic-observer)); a first-order version uses only the altitude. Distances are in AU and angles in radians. For the Sun see [Solar Parallax and Semidiameter](#solar-parallax-and-semidiameter).

```ts
import { crescentWidth, moonParallax, moonSemidiameter, moonTopocentricSemidiameter, moonTopocentricSemidiameterApprox } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/moon'
import { deg, toArcsec, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { kilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const distance = kilometer(384400) // the mean Earth-Moon distance, in AU

// Equatorial horizontal parallax and geocentric semidiameter.
console.log(toDeg(moonParallax(distance))) // 0.9507 — degrees
console.log(toArcsec(moonSemidiameter(distance))) // 932.55 — arcseconds

// Topocentric semidiameter: first order from the altitude (here the zenith), and rigorous from
// declination, west-positive hour angle, and the observer's ρ·sin φ′ and ρ·cos φ′.
console.log(toArcsec(moonTopocentricSemidiameterApprox(distance, deg(90)))) // 948.03 — arcseconds
console.log(toArcsec(moonTopocentricSemidiameter(distance, deg(-20), deg(30), 0.5, 0.8))) // 939.95 — arcseconds

// Width of the illuminated crescent when 10% of the disk is lit.
console.log(toArcsec(crescentWidth(moonSemidiameter(distance), 0.1))) // 186.51 — arcseconds
```

### Lunar Phase and Lunation

The Moon cycles through its phases every synodic month, 29.53 days on average: new, first quarter, full, and last quarter, the instants when the Moon's geocentric ecliptic longitude exceeds the Sun's by 0°, 90°, 180°, and 270°. The synodic month varies by more than half a day because of the eccentricities of the lunar and terrestrial orbits, so the phases need a series, not a fixed period. A lunation is one such cycle, numbered consecutively from a conventional starting point, and different calendars and almanacs use different starting points.

The phases come from the series of Meeus's chapter 49 with its periodic terms, as TT instants; convert them with `utc` for a civil time. Lunation numbers follow the Brown numbering by default; the Meeus index is 0 for the new moon of 6 January 2000, and the Goldstine, Hebrew, Islamic, and Thai conventions are also available, each a constant offset from it. For the illuminated fraction at an instant see [Meeus Algorithms](#meeus-algorithms).

```ts
import { lunation, nearestLunarPhase } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/moon'
import { Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS, utc } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// The next full moon (pass false for the last one at or before the time), as a TT instant.
console.log(timeToDate(utc(nearestLunarPhase(time, 'FULL', true))).slice(0, 5)) // [2025, 10, 7, 3, 47] — UTC
console.log(timeToDate(utc(nearestLunarPhase(time, 'NEW', true))).slice(0, 5)) // [2025, 10, 21, 12, 25] — UTC

// Lunation numbers: Brown (default) and Meeus.
console.log(lunation(time), lunation(time, 'MEEUS')) // 1271 318
```

### Martian Satellite Theory (MARSSAT)

Mars has two small moons close to the planet: Phobos, orbiting about 9400 km from the center in 7.65 hours, faster than Mars rotates, and Deimos, about 23,500 km out in 30.3 hours. Their positions are needed to predict their elongations, transits, and eclipses, and for spacecraft imaging; at Mars's oppositions they are faint targets close to a bright planet.

MARSSAT (Lainey) is an analytical theory of both moons fitted to observations from 1877 to 2005. Trigonometric series perturb each satellite's equinoctial elements, which are converted to rectangular coordinates and rotated through the slowly precessing Laplace-plane node and inclination into the equatorial frame. The result is the Mars-centered position in AU and velocity in AU/day; add it to Mars's barycentric state for an inertial position.

```ts
import { deimos, marssat, phobos } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/marssat'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Mars-centered position (AU) and velocity (AU/day) of Phobos, in equatorial axes.
const [position, velocity] = phobos(time)

console.log(position) // [-0.000038291, 0.000030662, 0.000038326] — AU
console.log(velocity) // [-0.00078355, -0.00096404, -0.000038947] — AU/day
console.log(toKilometer(Math.hypot(...position))) // 9313 — km from Mars's center

// Deimos, the outer moon.
console.log(toKilometer(Math.hypot(...deimos(time)[0]))) // 23451 — km

// The shared function: index 0 Phobos, 1 Deimos.
console.log(toKilometer(Math.hypot(...marssat(time, 1)[0]))) // 23451 — km, Deimos again
```

### Meeus Algorithms

Jean Meeus' _Astronomical Algorithms_ (2nd edition) is the standard practical reference for computing the positions of the Sun, Moon, and planets and the times of astronomical events with modest series. `nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/meeus` is a port of its algorithms, organized as one TypeScript `namespace` per chapter topic: calendars, Easter, and sidereal time; interpolation, fitting, and Kepler's equation; coordinate transformations, precession, nutation, refraction, and rising and setting; the Sun, the equation of time, and solstices; planetary positions, orbits, and planetary events (conjunctions, oppositions, perihelia); physical ephemerides of the Sun, Mars, and Jupiter, Jupiter's and Saturn's moons, and Saturn's rings; and the Moon's position, illumination, and libration. The functions are low-order series meant for the book's accuracy, arcseconds for the Sun, Moon, and planets and minutes of time for events, not a replacement for the JPL ephemerides of the library; the tests of the module reproduce the book's examples.

Unless a function says otherwise, angles are radians and distances AU, and a Julian Day argument named `jde` is on the dynamical (TT) scale while `jd` is UT. Sidereal times are in seconds of time. The longitudes of `Rise` and `Sunrise` are west-positive, as in the book.

```ts
import { AngularSeparation, Base, Easter, Elliptic, Julian, Kepler, MoonPosition, Nutation, PlanetPosition, Precession, SaturnRing, Sidereal, Solar } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/meeus'
import { deg, hms, signedDms, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Calendars: the Julian Day of 2000-01-01 12:00, and Easter Sunday of 1991.
console.log(Julian.calendarGregorianToJD(2000, 1, 1.5)) // 2451545
console.log(Easter.gregorian(1991)) // [ 1991, 3, 31 ] — year, month, day

// Mean and apparent sidereal time at 0h UT of 1987-04-10, in seconds of time.
console.log(Sidereal.mean(2446895.5), Sidereal.apparent(2446895.5)) // 47446.36683 47446.13514
// Also: Julian (calendarJulianToJD, calendarToJD, jdToCalendar, jdToCalendarGregorian, jdToCalendarJulian, jdToDate,
// dateToJD, jdeToDate, dateToJDE, mjdToJD, jdToMJD, dayOfWeek, dayOfYear, dayOfYearGregorian, dayOfYearJulian,
// dayOfYearToCalendar, dayOfYearToCalendarGregorian, dayOfYearToCalendarJulian, isLeapYearJulian, isLeapYearGregorian,
// isJDCalendarGregorian, isCalendarGregorian, deltaTSeconds, setDeltaTProvider, Calendar, CalendarJulian,
// CalendarGregorian), Easter.julian, Sidereal (mean0UT, apparent0UT, jdToCFrac), Base (julianYearToJDE,
// besselianYearToJDE, jdeToBesselianYear, j2000Century, lightTime, illuminated, limb, horner, sincos, sincos2), and
// Sundial (general, equatorial, horizontal, vertical).

// Kepler's equation for e = 0.1 and M = 5° (example 30.b), to 11 decimal places.
console.log(toDeg(Kepler.kepler2(0.1, deg(5), 11))) // 5.554589254 — eccentric anomaly in degrees
// Also: Kepler (kepler1, kepler2a, kepler2b, kepler3, kepler4, trueAnomaly, radius), Interpolation (Len3, Len5,
// iterate, len4Half, len3ForInterpolateX, lagrange, lagrangePoly, linear), Fit (linear, quadratic, func1, func3,
// correlationCoefficient), Iteration (decimalPlaces, fullPrecision, binaryRoot), Line (time, angle, error,
// angleError), and Circle.smallest.

// Nutation in longitude and obliquity (radians), and the mean obliquity.
console.log(Nutation.nutation(2446895.5), toDeg(Nutation.meanObliquity(2446895.5))) // [Δψ, Δε] 23.44094649

// Angular separation of Arcturus and Spica, and precession of a star from J2000 to 2028 November 13.19.
const arcturus = [hms(14, 15, 39.7), signedDms(false, 19, 10, 57)] as const
const spica = [hms(13, 25, 11.6), signedDms(true, 11, 9, 41)] as const
console.log(toDeg(AngularSeparation.sep(arcturus, spica))) // 32.79301034 — degrees

const precessor = new Precession.Precessor(2000, Base.jdeToJulianYear(Julian.calendarGregorianToJD(2028, 11, 13.19)))
console.log(precessor.precess(hms(2, 44, 11.986), signedDms(false, 49, 13, 42.48)).map(toDeg)) // [ 41.5430861, 49.3492074 ] — degrees
// Also: Coords (eclipticToEquatorial, equatorialToEcliptic, equatorialToHorizontal, horizontalToEquatorial,
// equatorialToGalactic, galacticToEquatorial), AngularSeparation (minSep, minSepRect, hav, sepHav, minSepHav,
// sepPauwels, minSepPauwels, relativePosition), Precession (approxAnnualPrecession, mn, approxPosition, position,
// EclipticPrecessor, eclipticPosition, properMotion, properMotion3D), Nutation (approxNutation, meanObliquityLaskar,
// nutationInRA), Apparent (nutation, perihelion, aberration, eclipticAberration, aberrationRonVondrak, position,
// positionRonVondrak), ElementEquinox (reduceB1950ToJ2000, reduceB1950FK4ToJ2000FK5), Refraction (bennett, bennett2,
// saemundsson, gt15True, gt15Apparent), Rise (refraction, stdh0Stellar, stdh0Solar, stdh0Lunar, stdh0LunarMean,
// hourAngle, approxTimes, times, PlanetRise), Parallactic (parallacticAngle, parallacticAngleOnHorizon,
// eclipticAtHorizon, eclipticAtEquator, diurnalPathAtHorizon), Parallax (horizontal, topocentric, topocentric2,
// topocentric3, topocentricEcliptical), Globe (Ellipsoid, oneDegreeOfLongitude, oneDegreeOfLatitude,
// geocentricLatitudeDifference, approxAngularDistance, approxLinearDistance), Stellar (sum, sumN, ratio, difference,
// absoluteByParallax, absoluteByDistance), and BinaryStars (meanAnomaly, position, apparentEccentricity).

// The Sun on 1992-10-13 0h TT (example 25.a): apparent RA and Dec.
console.log(Solar.apparentEquatorial(2448908.5).map(toDeg)) // [ 198.3808252, -7.7850698 ] — degrees
// Also: Solar (trueLongitude, apparentLongitude, meanAnomaly, eccentricity, radius, true2000, trueEquatorial,
// trueVSOP87, apparentVSOP87, apparentEquatorialVSOP87, aberration), EquationOfTime (e, eSmart), Solstice (march,
// june, september, december, march2, june2, september2, december2, longitude), SolarXYZ (position, positionJ2000,
// positionB1950, positionEquinox, longitudeJ2000, xyz), and Sunrise.Sunrise.

// Venus on 1992-12-20 0h TT (example 33.a): heliocentric ecliptic position and apparent RA and Dec.
console.log(PlanetPosition.position('venus', 2448976.5).map(toDeg)) // [ 26.1141192, -2.6206030, 41.5166177 ] — lon, lat in degrees, then the range
console.log(Elliptic.position('venus', 2448976.5).map(toDeg)) // [ 316.1727242, -18.8880108 ] — degrees
// Also: PlanetPosition (position2000, toFK5), Elliptic (astrometricJ2000, velocity, vPerihelion, vAphelion, length1,
// length2, length4), PlanetElements (mean, inc, node), Planetary (mean, sum, ms, sumA, msa, el, mercuryInfConj,
// mercurySupConj, venusInfConj, marsOpp, jupiterOpp, saturnOpp, saturnConj, uranusOpp, neptuneOpp,
// mercuryEastElongation, mercuryWestElongation, marsStation2), Perihelion (perihelion, aphelion, perihelion2,
// aphelion2), Conjunction (planetary, stellar), Node (ellipticAscending, ellipticDescending, elliptic,
// parabolicAscending, parabolicDescending, parabolic), Parabolic.Elements, NearParabolic.Elements, Illuminated
// (phaseAngle, phaseAngle2, phaseAngle3, fraction, fractionVenus, mercury, venus, mars, jupiter, saturn, uranus,
// neptune, mercury84, venus84, mars84, jupiter84, saturn84, uranus84, neptune84, pluto84), and Semidiameter
// (semidiameter, saturnApparentPolar, asteroidDiameter, asteroid).

// Saturn's rings on 1992-12-16 0h TT (example 45.a): B, B', ΔU, P (radians), then the major and minor axes a, b.
console.log(SaturnRing.ring(2448972.50068).slice(0, 4).map(toDeg)) // [ 16.442, 14.679, 4.198, 6.741 ] — degrees
// Also: SaturnRing.ub, SolarDisk (ephemeris, cycle), Mars.physical, Jupiter (physical, physical2), JupiterMoons
// (positions, e5), and SaturnMoons.positions.

// The Moon on 1992-04-12 0h TT (example 47.a): ecliptic longitude, latitude (radians) and distance (AU).
const [lon, lat, distance] = MoonPosition.position(2448724.5)
console.log(toDeg(lon), toDeg(lat), distance) // 133.1626547 -3.2291264 0.0024627
// Also: MoonPosition (perigee, trueNode), Moon (physical, PhysicalEphemeris, selenographic, sunAltitude, sunrise,
// sunset), and MoonIlluminated (phaseAngleEquatorial, phaseAngleEquatorial2, phaseAngleEcliptic,
// phaseAngleEcliptic2, phaseAngle3).
```

### Meteor Activity Profiles

A meteor shower occurs when the Earth crosses the stream of debris left by a comet or asteroid, so its activity is tied to the Earth's position on its orbit, measured by the solar longitude λ☉, and repeats at nearly the same λ☉ every year. Activity is expressed as the zenithal hourly rate (ZHR), the number of meteors an ideal observer would see per hour under a limiting magnitude of 6.5 with the radiant at the zenith. Around its maximum the ZHR of most showers rises and falls roughly exponentially, as published in the IMO profiles:

```text
ZHR(λ☉) = ZHRmax · 10^(−b · |λ☉ − λmax|)   (b in decades per degree, different before and after the maximum)
```

A catalog solution only carries the interval of solar longitude where the shower is active. The ZHR curve itself is explicit, caller-supplied data: a single exponential peak with separate rise and decay slopes, interpolated samples, or a sum of exponential components for showers with several peaks; it is zero outside its support. All longitudes are geocentric solar longitudes in radians (see [Meteor Solar Longitude](#meteor-solar-longitude)), and intervals advance in increasing longitude, so a window such as 350°–20° wraps through 0. Integrated over time, the ZHR gives the meteors an ideal observer would see; for the rates of a real observer see [Meteor Visual Rates](#meteor-visual-rates).

```ts
import {
	integrateMeteorZhr,
	isMeteorShowerActive,
	isMeteorShowerActivityYearLimited,
	meteorActivityFraction,
	meteorActivityIntervalsAboveFraction,
	meteorActivityMaximumSolarLongitude,
	meteorActivityMaximumZhr,
	meteorActivityPhase,
	meteorActivityProgress,
	meteorActivityZhr,
	meteorShowerActivityYearApplies,
} from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/activity'
import type { MeteorActivityProfile, MeteorShowerActivity } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/types'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A single exponential peak of ZHR 120 at λ☉ 100°, rising at 0.1 and decaying at 0.2 decades per degree.
const profile: MeteorActivityProfile = { type: 'exponential', support: { start: deg(90), end: deg(110) }, solarLongitude: deg(100), zhr: 120, slopeBefore: 0.1, slopeAfter: 0.2 }

// Whether the shower is active at a solar longitude, and how far through its support (0 to 1).
console.log(isMeteorShowerActive(profile.support, deg(95)), meteorActivityProgress(profile.support, deg(95))) // true 0.25

// The ZHR there (meteors per hour); meteorExponentialZhr evaluates one exponential component the same way.
console.log(meteorActivityZhr(profile, deg(95)), meteorActivityZhr(profile, deg(105))) // 37.947 12

// The peak ZHR and its solar longitude, and the ZHR as a fraction of the peak.
console.log(meteorActivityMaximumZhr(profile), toDeg(meteorActivityMaximumSolarLongitude(profile)!)) // 120 100
console.log(meteorActivityFraction(profile, deg(95))) // 0.3162

// Activity, progress, and signed distance from the maximum (radians) in one call.
const phase = meteorActivityPhase(profile, deg(95))
console.log(phase.active, phase.progress, toDeg(phase.deltaFromMaximum!)) // true 0.25 -5 — degrees before the peak

// The intervals where the activity is at least half of the peak.
console.log(meteorActivityIntervalsAboveFraction(profile, 0.5).map((interval) => [toDeg(interval.start), toDeg(interval.end)])) // [[96.990, 101.505]] — degrees

// A dated outburst applies only in its catalog years (isMeteorShowerActivityYearLimited tells whether a range applies).
const outburst: MeteorShowerActivity = { kind: 'outburst', source: '2019', years: { start: 2019, end: 2019 } }
console.log(isMeteorShowerActivityYearLimited(outburst), meteorShowerActivityYearApplies(outburst, 2019), meteorShowerActivityYearApplies(outburst, 2024)) // true true false

// The ZHR integrated over a time span, in ZHR·hours.
const quadrantids: MeteorActivityProfile = { type: 'exponential', support: { start: deg(280), end: deg(286) }, solarLongitude: deg(283), zhr: 110, slopeBefore: 0.2, slopeAfter: 0.2 }
console.log(integrateMeteorZhr(quadrantids, timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 3, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 4, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC))) // 2302.26
```

### Meteor Observing Windows

Seeing a meteor shower needs three things at once: the shower must be active, the sky must be dark, and the radiant must be above the horizon, since the observed rate falls with the sine of the radiant altitude and is zero with the radiant below it. Moonlight is a fourth constraint for visual observers, because it raises the sky background and lowers the limiting magnitude. Planning a night therefore means intersecting the activity support with astronomical darkness (the Sun at least 18° below the horizon by default), a minimum radiant altitude, and optional lunar constraints, and every boundary is refined by root search. Altitudes are geometric, so a window opens a few minutes after the refracted rise of the radiant.

With an activity profile (see [Meteor Activity Profiles](#meteor-activity-profiles)), `meteorObservingWindows` also integrates the expected count over each window from the observed hourly rate, and orders the windows by expected count, most productive first, not chronologically. The rate model is the standard visual one, with the limiting magnitude `lm`, the population index `r`, the obstruction factor `F`, and the radiant altitude `h`; nothing penalizes moonlight or clouds unless a rate-correction callback is supplied:

```text
HR = ZHR · sin^γ(h) / (F · r^(6.5 − lm))
```

Most catalog showers have no activity profile, so `meteorGeometricObservingWindows` plans the same constraints without one and returns the windows in chronological order, with a geometric opportunity measure (the integral of the sine of the radiant altitude) that is never a meteor count. The conditions at one instant, the altitudes of the Sun, the Moon, and the radiant, the lunar illumination, and the Moon-radiant separation, are available directly, and are what a rate-correction callback receives.

```ts
import { meteorMoonDirection, meteorMoonIllumination, meteorObservationContext, meteorObservingConditionsAt, meteorSunDirection } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/observation'
import { meteorGeometricObservingWindows, meteorObservingWindows } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/planner'
import type { MeteorActivityProfile, MeteorShowerSolution } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/types'
import { Ellipsoid, geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS, utc } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// Illustrative values close to the Quadrantids: activity support, radiant (radians), and ZHR profile.
const solution: MeteorShowerSolution = { activity: { kind: 'annual', source: 'annual' }, activityInterval: { start: deg(280), end: deg(286) }, referenceSolarLongitude: deg(283.16), rightAscension: deg(230.1), declination: deg(48.5) }
const profile: MeteorActivityProfile = { type: 'exponential', support: { start: deg(280), end: deg(286) }, solarLongitude: deg(283.16), zhr: 110, slopeBefore: 0.2, slopeAfter: 0.2 }

const observer = geodeticLocation(deg(-8), deg(40), meter(100), Ellipsoid.WGS84) // longitude, latitude, height
const start = timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 3, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
const end = timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 5, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Dark-sky windows with their expected counts, most productive first, for a limiting magnitude of 6.0.
const [best] = meteorObservingWindows(solution, profile, observer, start, end, { limitingMagnitude: 6, populationIndex: 2.1, minimumDurationHours: 0.5 })

console.log(best.durationHours, best.expectedCount) // 8.001 220.09 — hours, meteors

// Without a profile: chronological windows with the radiant at least 20° high.
for (const window of meteorGeometricObservingWindows(solution, observer, start, end, { minimumRadiantAltitude: deg(20) })) {
	console.log(timeToDate(utc(window.start)).slice(0, 5), window.durationHours, window.radiantSineHours) // UTC start, hours, and hours of sine-weighted radiant altitude
}

// The Sun, Moon, and radiant at one instant, with the solar longitude and sidereal time computed once in a context.
const instant = timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 4, 3, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
const context = meteorObservationContext(instant, observer)
const conditions = meteorObservingConditionsAt({ rightAscension: deg(230.1), declination: deg(48.5) }, observer, instant, context)

console.log(toDeg(conditions.sunAltitude), conditions.moonIllumination, toDeg(conditions.radiant.altitude)) // −55.22 0.5034 28.70

// The geocentric J2000 Sun and Moon vectors (AU), and the illuminated lunar fraction from them.
console.log(meteorMoonIllumination(meteorSunDirection(instant), meteorMoonDirection(instant))) // 0.5034
```

### Meteor Orbit Reconstruction

A meteoroid is a small body on its own heliocentric orbit, and a shower is a stream of such orbits shed by a common parent comet or asteroid. Recovering the orbit of an observed meteor is what links it to its stream and its parent. The orbit follows from where the meteor comes from and how fast it hits the Earth: the geocentric radiant (equatorial J2000) gives the direction of the incoming velocity and the asymptotic geocentric speed `Vg` its magnitude. At the encounter the meteoroid is at the Earth's position, and its heliocentric velocity is the Earth's heliocentric velocity minus `Vg` along the radiant direction.

States and elements are heliocentric in the **ecliptic J2000** frame, the frame of the stream elements of the IAU Meteor Data Center, with the Earth taken from VSOP87E and the Sun's GM from Pitjeva (2005) by default. The speed must already be free of the Earth's gravity and of the observer's rotation (see [Meteor Trajectory Correction](#meteor-trajectory-correction)). An eccentricity `≥ 1` is an unbound orbit, which usually reveals an inconsistent radiant or speed rather than an interstellar meteoroid.

The inverse question is where a stream with known elements (`q`, `e`, `ω`, `Ω`, `i`, without epoch) meets the Earth. A stream can only produce meteors near one of its two nodes, where its orbit crosses the ecliptic; each node gives a candidate geocentric radiant and speed, and the Earth-node distance tells whether the Earth actually passes close to it. Choosing the distance limit that makes a node a real encounter is left to the caller.

```ts
import { meteorHeliocentricState, meteorOrbitFromRadiant, meteorStreamOrbitNodeEncounters } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/orbit'
import type { MeteorCompleteStreamOrbit, MeteorRadiant } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/types'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { kilometerPerSecond, toKilometerPerSecond } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/velocity'

// A Geminid-like radiant (equatorial J2000) and geocentric speed.
const radiant: MeteorRadiant = { rightAscension: deg(112.5), declination: deg(32.3) }
const speed = kilometerPerSecond(33.8)
const time = timeYMDHMS(2023, 12, 14, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Heliocentric state of the meteoroid (AU, AU/day, ecliptic J2000) and the Earth state used.
const state = meteorHeliocentricState(radiant, speed, time)
console.log(state.position, state.velocity)

// The same state as a Kepler orbit.
const orbit = meteorOrbitFromRadiant(radiant, speed, time)
console.log(orbit.semiMajorAxis, orbit.eccentricity, toDeg(orbit.inclination)) // 1.3517 AU, 0.88773, 22.02°

// Candidate radiants at the two nodes of a stream orbit, with the Earth-node distance (AU).
const stream: MeteorCompleteStreamOrbit = { perihelionDistance: 0.14, eccentricity: 0.89, argumentOfPerihelion: deg(324.3), longitudeOfAscendingNode: deg(261.2), inclination: deg(22.9) }

for (const encounter of meteorStreamOrbitNodeEncounters(stream, time)) {
	console.log(encounter.node, toDeg(encounter.radiant.rightAscension), toDeg(encounter.radiant.declination), toKilometerPerSecond(encounter.geocentricSpeed), encounter.earthNodeDistance)
}
// ascending 152.94 −7.239 131.53 1.138 — the Earth is 1.14 AU from this node
// descending 112.16 32.615 33.912 0.0322 — 0.032 AU away: the shower radiant and speed
```

### Meteor Orbit Similarity

Whether two meteors, or a meteor and a candidate parent body, share an orbit is decided with a dimensionless distance between orbits, a D-criterion: the smaller the value, the more similar the orbits, and a shower association is declared below a threshold chosen for the criterion and the sample.
