The criteria compare only the orbit shape and orientation, perihelion distance `q` (AU), eccentricity `e`, inclination `i`, node `Ω` and argument of perihelion `ω`, all in the same ecliptic J2000 frame; the position on the orbit is irrelevant.

Three classic criteria are available. Southworth and Hawkins' `D_SH` combines the differences of `q` and `e` with the angle `I` between the orbital planes and the separation `Π` of the perihelion longitudes measured from the mutual node. Drummond's `D_D` normalizes the `q` and `e` differences by their sums and uses the angle between the perihelion directions. Jopek's hybrid `D_J` normalizes only `q` and keeps the angular terms of `D_SH`.

```text
D_SH² = (q₂ − q₁)² + (e₂ − e₁)² + (2 sin(I/2))² + (ē · 2 sin(Π/2))²
```

The three values are not on the same scale and must not be compared with each other's thresholds. A criterion is undefined when the geometry is singular, for an orbit in the ecliptic (`i` of 0 or π) whose node does not exist.

```ts
import { meteorComparableOrbitFromKepler, meteorDDrummond, meteorDJopek, meteorDSouthworthHawkins, meteorOrbitFromRadiant } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/orbit'
import type { MeteorComparableOrbit } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/types'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { kilometerPerSecond } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/velocity'

// Orbit reconstructed from a Geminid-like radiant and speed, reduced to the compared elements.
const time = timeYMDHMS(2023, 12, 14, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
const measured = meteorComparableOrbitFromKepler(meteorOrbitFromRadiant({ rightAscension: deg(112.5), declination: deg(32.3) }, kilometerPerSecond(33.8), time))!

// Mean orbit of the stream (AU and radians).
const stream: MeteorComparableOrbit = { perihelionDistance: 0.14, eccentricity: 0.89, inclination: deg(22.9), longitudeOfAscendingNode: deg(261.2), argumentOfPerihelion: deg(324.3) }

// Each criterion on its own scale; undefined for singular geometry.
console.log(meteorDSouthworthHawkins(measured, stream)) // 0.02240
console.log(meteorDDrummond(measured, stream)) // 0.04080
console.log(meteorDJopek(measured, stream)) // 0.04459
```

### Meteor Radiants

A meteor radiant is the point of the sky from which the meteors of a shower appear to diverge: the perspective vanishing point of parallel meteoroid paths. Catalog radiants are geocentric, in equatorial J2000 coordinates, and are referred to a solar longitude (see [Meteor Solar Longitude](#meteor-solar-longitude)). Because the Earth crosses the stream along its orbit, the radiant drifts during the activity period, typically by about a degree per day; a catalog declares that drift either per unit of solar longitude or per day, and the radiant moves linearly away from the reference longitude. Extrapolating a drift far from its reference is reported as such and can be refused.

For a local observer the radiant is precessed and nutated to the true equator of date and rotated to the horizon with the apparent sidereal time; azimuth is measured north through east and no refraction is applied. The radiant altitude governs how many meteors are seen (see [Meteor Visual Rates](#meteor-visual-rates)), so planning needs when the radiant rises, culminates, and sets. The rise and set instants use the standard horizon altitude of the shared event finder, not the geometric crossing of zero altitude.

```ts
import {
	meteorRadiantDegrees,
	meteorRadiantHorizontal,
	meteorRadiantJ2000,
	meteorRadiantMaximumAltitude,
	meteorRadiantOfDate,
	meteorRadiantPath,
	meteorRadiantPathBetween,
	meteorRadiantPathSegmentsBetween,
	meteorRadiantRiseTransitSet,
	meteorRadiantVector,
	meteorRadiantVisibility,
} from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/radiant'
import { meteorComputationContext } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/solar'
import type { MeteorShowerSolution } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/types'
import { Ellipsoid, geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// Illustrative Quadrantid-like solution with a daily drift (radians per day).
const solution: MeteorShowerSolution = {
	activity: { kind: 'annual', source: 'annual' },
	activityInterval: { start: deg(280), end: deg(286) },
	referenceSolarLongitude: deg(283.16),
	rightAscension: deg(230.1),
	declination: deg(48.5),
	radiantDrift: { basis: 'day', rightAscensionRate: deg(1), declinationRate: deg(-0.25) },
}
const observer = geodeticLocation(deg(-8), deg(40), meter(100), Ellipsoid.WGS84) // longitude, latitude, height
const time = timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 4, 5, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Geocentric J2000 radiant at the instant, with the drift applied away from the reference.
const result = meteorRadiantJ2000(solution, meteorComputationContext(time))!
console.log(toDeg(result.radiant.rightAscension), toDeg(result.radiant.declination), result.extrapolated) // 229.924 48.544 true

// A radiant from catalog degrees, and its unit J2000 direction vector.
console.log(meteorRadiantVector(meteorRadiantDegrees(230.1, 48.5))) // [-0.4250, -0.5083, 0.7490]

// Radiant path sampled daily between two instants; the segments variant splits it where the model is unavailable.
const path = meteorRadiantPathBetween(solution, timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 3, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 5, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC))
const segments = meteorRadiantPathSegmentsBetween(solution, timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 3, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 5, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC))

// Radiant path over solar longitude in 1° steps, for a drift declared per radian of solar longitude.
const perLongitude: MeteorShowerSolution = { ...solution, radiantDrift: { basis: 'solarLongitude', rightAscensionRate: 0.8, declinationRate: -0.2 } }
console.log(meteorRadiantPath(perLongitude, deg(280), deg(286), deg(1)).length) // 7 — points from 280° to 286°

// The radiant in the true equator and equinox of date, and its geometric azimuth and altitude (radians) for the observer.
const ofDate = meteorRadiantOfDate(result.radiant, time)
const horizontal = meteorRadiantHorizontal(result.radiant, observer, time)

// Highest altitude in an interval, and the rise, transit, and set instants with their classification.
const highest = meteorRadiantMaximumAltitude(solution, observer, timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 4, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 5, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC))
const events = meteorRadiantRiseTransitSet(solution, observer, time)
console.log(meteorRadiantVisibility(events)) // risesAndSets
```

### Meteor Shower State

Planning a night of meteor observing needs, for each shower, a snapshot of several quantities at once: whether the shower is active, its expected zenithal hourly rate (ZHR), where its radiant is in the sky, and how dark the sky is, from the Sun's depression and the Moon's altitude, phase, and distance to the radiant. These are what decide whether a shower is worth watching at a given hour.

The quantities that do not depend on the shower (solar longitude, sidereal time, Sun and Moon directions and altitudes, lunar illumination) are computed once in a computation context and shared by any number of shower solutions, so a whole catalog costs one ephemeris evaluation. Without an observer the context is geocentric and the state has no local geometry. Activity and ZHR come from the catalog interval and from an optional activity profile; all altitudes are geometric, without refraction.

```ts
import { meteorShowerComputationContext, meteorShowerState, meteorShowerStates } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/state'
import type { MeteorActivityProfile, MeteorShowerSolution } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/types'
import { Ellipsoid, geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// Illustrative Quadrantid-like solution and activity profile; they are not read from a catalog.
const quadrantids: MeteorShowerSolution = { activity: { kind: 'annual', source: 'annual' }, activityInterval: { start: deg(280), end: deg(286) }, referenceSolarLongitude: deg(283.16), rightAscension: deg(230.1), declination: deg(48.5) }
const profile: MeteorActivityProfile = { type: 'exponential', support: { start: deg(280), end: deg(286) }, solarLongitude: deg(283.16), zhr: 110, slopeBefore: 0.2, slopeAfter: 0.2 }

// Shared Sun, Moon, and sidereal-time quantities for one observer and instant.
const observer = geodeticLocation(deg(-8), deg(40), meter(100), Ellipsoid.WGS84) // longitude, latitude, height
const context = meteorShowerComputationContext(timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 4, 5, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), observer)

// Activity, ZHR, radiant, and sky circumstances of one shower.
const state = meteorShowerState(quadrantids, context, { profile })
console.log(state.active, state.zhr) // true 101.28 — meteors per hour
console.log(toDeg(state.horizontal!.altitude), toDeg(state.sunAltitude!)) // 47.321 −32.53 — degrees
console.log(toDeg(state.moonSeparation!), state.moonIllumination) // 62.46 0.4955 — degrees, illuminated fraction

// A batch of showers sharing the same context, each with its own optional profile.
const states = meteorShowerStates([{ solution: quadrantids, profile }], context)
```

### Meteor Solar Longitude

Meteor catalogs locate a shower by the solar longitude `λ☉`, the Sun's ecliptic longitude, rather than by calendar date. A shower happens when the Earth crosses a meteoroid stream, which occurs at a fixed point of the Earth's orbit, so `λ☉` is the same every year, while the calendar date of that point wanders because of leap years and the calendar.

The meteor modules compute it as the geometric geocentric longitude of the Sun in the **J2000 ecliptic**, from the VSOP87E Sun and Earth positions, with no light-time, aberration, or precession to the date, which is the convention of meteor catalogs. Because the frame is fixed at J2000, longitude 0° is reached about eight hours after the 2024 March equinox, not at it. Longitudes are in radians in `[0, 2π)`.

Converting a longitude to a time searches one civil UTC year. A civil year is shorter than the orbital period, so a fraction of a degree of longitude at the year turn (around 280° today) does not occur in a given year; the plain solver throws there, while the crossing solver answers `undefined`. The dates of a shower solution (start, reference, end, and the maximum of an explicit activity profile) are resolved for the occurrence that starts in the requested year, so an interval that wraps through the new year ends in the following year. The catalog reference longitude is the mean activity longitude, not necessarily the ZHR maximum.

```ts
import { meteorShowerDates, meteorSolarLongitude, meteorSolarLongitudeCrossingTimes, meteorSolarLongitudeDelta, meteorSolarLongitudeForwardDelta, meteorSolarLongitudeTimes, meteorSolarState, timeAtMeteorSolarLongitude } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/solar'
import type { MeteorShowerSolution } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/types'
import { Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS, utc } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Solar longitude (J2000 ecliptic) at an instant.
console.log(toDeg(meteorSolarLongitude(timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 4, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)))) // 282.768 — degrees

// The same longitude with the geocentric J2000 equatorial Sun vector (AU) from one ephemeris evaluation.
const state = meteorSolarState(timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 4, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC))

// Signed shortest difference in (−π, π] and forward difference in [0, 2π) of two longitudes, across 0°.
console.log(toDeg(meteorSolarLongitudeDelta(deg(5), deg(355))), toDeg(meteorSolarLongitudeForwardDelta(deg(5), deg(355)))) // 10 350 — degrees

// First instant of the year at which the Sun reaches a longitude; throws if it does not occur.
console.log(timeToDate(utc(timeAtMeteorSolarLongitude(2024, deg(283))))) // [2024, 1, 4, 5, 27, 22, 228]

// Several longitudes at once: meteorSolarLongitudeTimes throws like the single solver, the crossing variant answers undefined.
const solved = meteorSolarLongitudeTimes(2024, [deg(90), deg(283)])
const times = meteorSolarLongitudeCrossingTimes(2024, [0, deg(90), deg(180), deg(270)])

// Start, reference, and end instants of a catalog solution in a civil year.
const solution: MeteorShowerSolution = { activity: { kind: 'annual', source: 'annual' }, activityInterval: { start: deg(280), end: deg(286) }, referenceSolarLongitude: deg(283) }
const dates = meteorShowerDates(solution, 2024)
console.log(timeToDate(utc(dates.start!))) // [2024, 1, 1, 6, 48, 21, 801]
console.log(timeToDate(utc(dates.end!))) // [2024, 1, 7, 4, 5, 28, 443]
```

### Meteor Track Association

A single observed meteor can be tested against a shower by geometry: its trail, extended backwards along its great circle, must pass through the radiant, and the meteor must move away from it. This is how a sporadic meteor is distinguished from a shower member on a camera or visual plot, before any speed or orbit is available.

A track is the great-circle arc between two equatorial J2000 points, start and end in the direction of motion. The association measures the cross-track error, the angular distance of the radiant from the trail's great circle; the radiant distance, from the radiant to the start of the trail; and whether the direction of motion is compatible. It is a geometric screen only: it does not use the speed or the radiant uncertainty, so the thresholds are the caller's. A track whose ends coincide or are antipodal defines no plane and is never compatible.

```ts
import { associateMeteorTrack, meteorRadiantTrackResidual, meteorTrackDirectionCompatible, meteorTrackGreatCircle, meteorTrackLength, meteorTrackPoint, meteorTrackPositionAngle } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/trajectory'
import type { MeteorRadiant, MeteorTrack } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/types'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Trail from start to end (equatorial J2000) and a candidate radiant.
const track: MeteorTrack = { start: { rightAscension: deg(220), declination: deg(55) }, end: { rightAscension: deg(228), declination: deg(48) } }
const radiant: MeteorRadiant = { rightAscension: deg(214.2), declination: deg(61.7) }

// Length of the trail, its midpoint, and the unit pole of its great circle (J2000); undefined for a degenerate track.
console.log(toDeg(meteorTrackLength(track)!)) // 8.58 — degrees
const middle = meteorTrackPoint(track, 0.5)! // RA 224.31°, Dec 51.57°
const pole = meteorTrackGreatCircle(track)!

// Direction of motion at the start, east of north; and the cross-track error of the radiant.
console.log(toDeg(meteorTrackPositionAngle(track.start, track.end))) // 141.37 — degrees
console.log(toDeg(meteorRadiantTrackResidual(radiant, track)!)) // 2.10 — degrees

// Whether the trail moves away from the radiant.
console.log(meteorTrackDirectionCompatible(radiant, track)) // true

// Decision with caller thresholds (radians) on the cross-track error and the radiant distance.
const association = associateMeteorTrack(radiant, track, { maximumCrossTrackError: deg(5), maximumRadiantDistance: deg(30) })
console.log(association.compatible, toDeg(association.radiantDistance)) // true 7.35

// The same trail travelling the other way moves towards the radiant and is rejected.
console.log(associateMeteorTrack(radiant, { start: track.end, end: track.start }).compatible) // false
```

### Meteor Trajectory Correction

The direction in which a meteor is seen is not the direction in which it approached the Earth. The Earth's gravity bends the path and speeds the meteoroid up, so the apparent radiant is displaced towards the zenith (zenith attraction), and an observer on the rotating Earth adds a velocity of their own (diurnal aberration). These corrections link the geocentric radiant of a catalog (equatorial J2000) and the apparent local radiant, and must be removed from an observed radiant before computing an orbit (see [Meteor Orbit Reconstruction](#meteor-orbit-reconstruction)).

The entry speed follows from energy conservation, with `Vg` the asymptotic geocentric speed and `r` the geocentric distance of the entry point. Schiaparelli's zenith attraction `Δz` is the angle by which the apparent zenith angle `z` is smaller than the geocentric one; it grows with the zenith angle and is largest for slow meteors. The correction acts along the vertical, so the azimuth is unchanged. The rotation correction is of the order of the ratio between the rotation speed (up to 0.465 km/s) and the meteor speed: a fraction of a degree for fast meteors, larger for slow ones.

```text
v² = Vg² + 2·GM/r
z_geocentric = z + Δz,   Δz = 2·atan((v − Vg)·tan(z/2) / (v + Vg))
```

Speeds are AU/day and distances AU, the entry altitude is measured from a reference ellipsoid, atmospheric drag is not modeled, and no refraction is applied.

```ts
import {
	apparentMeteorRadiantHorizontal,
	apparentZenithAngleFromGeocentric,
	geocentricMeteorRadiantFromHorizontal,
	geocentricZenithAngleFromApparent,
	meteorGeocentricRadius,
	meteorObserverRotationVelocity,
	meteorRadiantWithEarthRotation,
	meteorSpeedAtDistance,
	meteorSpeedAtGeodeticAltitude,
	meteorZenithAttraction,
} from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/trajectory'
import type { MeteorRadiant } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/types'
import { Ellipsoid, geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { kilometer, meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'
import { kilometerPerSecond, toKilometerPerSecond } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/velocity'

const speed = kilometerPerSecond(41) // asymptotic geocentric speed Vg
const observer = geodeticLocation(deg(-8), deg(40), meter(100), Ellipsoid.WGS84) // longitude, latitude, height
const time = timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 4, 5, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
const radiant: MeteorRadiant = { rightAscension: deg(230.1), declination: deg(48.5) }

// Speed at a 100 km entry height; the same from the geocentric radius (AU) of that point on the ellipsoid.
const entrySpeed = meteorSpeedAtGeodeticAltitude(speed, deg(40), kilometer(100))
console.log(toKilometerPerSecond(entrySpeed)) // 42.476 — km/s
console.log(toKilometerPerSecond(meteorSpeedAtDistance(speed, meteorGeocentricRadius(deg(40), kilometer(100))))) // 42.476

// The zenith attraction at an apparent zenith angle of 60°, the geocentric zenith angle, and the inverse.
console.log(toDeg(meteorZenithAttraction(deg(60), speed, entrySpeed))) // 1.170 — degrees
const geocentricZenith = geocentricZenithAngleFromApparent(deg(60), speed, entrySpeed) // 61.170°
console.log(toDeg(apparentZenithAngleFromGeocentric(geocentricZenith, speed, entrySpeed)!)) // 60 — degrees

// Apparent horizontal radiant of a geocentric J2000 radiant, and the inverse back to the catalog frame.
const options = { geocentricSpeed: speed, entryAltitude: kilometer(100) }
const apparent = apparentMeteorRadiantHorizontal(radiant, observer, time, options)!
console.log(toDeg(apparent.azimuth), toDeg(apparent.altitude)) // 57.973 48.097 — 0.78° above the geometric 47.321°
const recovered = geocentricMeteorRadiantFromHorizontal(apparent, observer, time, options)

// The observer's rotation velocity in GCRS (AU/day), and the radiant shifted by it.
console.log(toKilometerPerSecond(Math.hypot(...meteorObserverRotationVelocity(observer, time)))) // 0.357 — km/s at latitude 40°
const rotated = meteorRadiantWithEarthRotation(radiant, speed, observer, time)!
console.log(toDeg(rotated.rightAscension), toDeg(rotated.declination)) // 230.471 48.177
```

### Meteor Visual Rates

Visual meteor counts depend on the observer's conditions as much as on the shower: a bright sky hides faint meteors, and a low radiant sends fewer meteors through the observer's field. The zenithal hourly rate (ZHR) removes those conditions: it is the rate an ideal observer would see with the radiant at the zenith under a limiting magnitude of 6.5 and an unobstructed sky, so that counts by different observers and nights can be compared and combined into an activity profile.

```text
ZHR = N · F · r^(6.5 − lm) / (T · sin(h)^γ)
```

Here `N` is the count, `F ≥ 1` the obstruction correction, `r` the population index, `lm` the limiting magnitude, `T` the effective observing time in hours, `h` the geometric radiant altitude, and `γ` the altitude exponent (1 by default). The local hourly rate is the inverse: the rate a given ZHR produces under given conditions. Several observations are combined by exposure, total count over total corrected time, not by averaging their ZHRs.

The population index `r` is the ratio of meteor counts between consecutive magnitude classes, `N(m + 1) / N(m)`, and is related to the mass index by `s = 1 + 2.3 · log10(r)`; it is estimated from counts per magnitude bin by a regression of `ln N` on magnitude. Counts are Poisson-distributed, so small counts have wide uncertainties: Garwood's exact interval gives the confidence interval of the expected count, and of the ZHR scaled from it. The expected number of meteors seen over a night integrates an activity profile through the same correction, with the radiant altitude and any weather or lunar losses supplied explicitly.

```ts
import {
	combineMeteorVisualObservations,
	integrateMeteorExpectedCount,
	meteorGarwoodInterval,
	meteorGarwoodZhr,
	meteorLocalHourlyRate,
	meteorMagnitudeRatio,
	meteorMassIndex,
	meteorPopulationIndex,
	meteorPopulationIndexFromMagnitudeBins,
	meteorVisualRate,
	meteorZhrFromObservation,
} from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/observation'
import type { MeteorVisualObservation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/meteors/types'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// 25 meteors in 1.5 h, limiting magnitude 6.0, radiant 40° high.
const observation: MeteorVisualObservation = { count: 25, effectiveTime: 1.5, limitingMagnitude: 6.0, populationIndex: 2.2, obstructionCorrection: 1.1, radiantAltitude: deg(40) }

// ZHR of one observation, its 95% Poisson interval, and the ZHR of several observations combined.
console.log(meteorZhrFromObservation(observation)) // 42.30 — meteors per hour
console.log(meteorGarwoodZhr(observation)) // { lower: 27.38, upper: 62.45 }
console.log(combineMeteorVisualObservations([observation, { ...observation, count: 10, effectiveTime: 1, radiantAltitude: deg(60) }])) // 31.20

// The 95% Garwood interval of the count itself, before scaling to a ZHR.
console.log(meteorGarwoodInterval(25)) // { lower: 16.18, upper: 36.90 } — meteors

// The inverse: the local hourly rate a ZHR of 100 produces under these conditions, and both rates of the observation.
console.log(meteorLocalHourlyRate(100, observation)) // 39.40 — meteors per hour
console.log(meteorVisualRate(observation)) // { zhr: 42.30, localHourlyRate: 16.67, observation } — the rate is 25 / 1.5 h

// Population index and mass index, both ways, and the count ratio N(m + Δm) / N(m) for two magnitudes.
console.log(meteorMassIndex(2.2), meteorPopulationIndex(1.7876)) // 1.7876 2.2
console.log(meteorMagnitudeRatio(2.2, 2)) // 4.84

// Population index from counts per magnitude class.
console.log(
	meteorPopulationIndexFromMagnitudeBins([
		{ magnitude: 1, count: 4 },
		{ magnitude: 2, count: 10 },
		{ magnitude: 3, count: 26 },
		{ magnitude: 4, count: 62 },
	]),
) // 2.474

// Expected meteors in two hours from an activity profile, with a 45° radiant and 20% losses to clouds.
const profile = { type: 'exponential', support: { start: deg(280), end: deg(286) }, solarLongitude: deg(283), zhr: 110, slopeBefore: 0.2, slopeAfter: 0.2 } as const
const count = integrateMeteorExpectedCount(profile, timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 4, 2, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 4, 4, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), { limitingMagnitude: 6.5, populationIndex: 2.1, obstructionCorrection: 1, radiantAltitude: () => deg(45), rateCorrection: () => 0.8 })
console.log(count) // 118.62 — meteors
```

### Minimum Orbit Intersection Distance

The minimum orbit intersection distance (MOID) is the smallest distance between two orbits as geometric curves, minimized independently over the position on each. It does not depend on where either body is, only on the shapes and orientations of the orbits, so it tells whether a close approach is geometrically possible at all. An Earth MOID of at most 0.05 AU, together with an absolute magnitude `H ≤ 22`, is the standard definition of a potentially hazardous asteroid; a small MOID does not mean an encounter will happen, only that the orbits allow it.

The result is the distance in AU and the true anomalies on each orbit where the closest points lie. Both orbits must be bound (`e < 1`) and expressed in the same frame. The search samples both orbits on a grid and refines the local minima, so an unusually narrow closest-approach valley may need a finer grid. The MOID is a property of osculating orbits at one epoch; planetary perturbations change it over time.

```ts
import { KeplerOrbit } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/asteroid'
import { moid } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/moid'
import { Timescale, time } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005 } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'
import { matIdentity } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/mat3'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// Heliocentric ICRF equatorial states at JD 2461200.5 TDB (JPL Horizons): AU and AU/day.
const epoch = time(2461200.5, 0, Timescale.TDB)
const earth = new KeplerOrbit([-0.2139643995461386, -0.910369590875501, -0.3946284477233859], [0.01653870730744617, -0.003392349872193463, -0.001471244370548932], epoch, GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005, matIdentity())
const apophis = new KeplerOrbit([-0.9239966398806005, 0.5636773710014709, 0.1861766030828077], [-0.008138789687781776, -0.01148145591898846, -0.004471286309082429], epoch, GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005, matIdentity())

// Closest distance between the two orbits and where it lies on each.
const result = moid(apophis, earth)

console.log(toKilometer(result.distance)) // 16144 — km, a potentially hazardous geometry
console.log(toDeg(result.trueAnomaly1), toDeg(result.trueAnomaly2)) // 233.48 99.645 — degrees on Apophis and on Earth
```

### MPCORB Parsing

The Minor Planet Center (MPC) distributes the osculating orbits of all known minor planets and comets in fixed-width text files: MPCORB lines for asteroids and CometEls lines for comets. They are the usual source for computing positions of asteroids and comets, for finder charts, and for occultation or close-approach predictions.

Parsing turns one line into a structured record with angles converted to radians and distances in AU, ready to build a Kepler orbit (see [Asteroid and Comet Orbit Construction](#asteroid-and-comet-orbit-construction)). An asteroid line carries the absolute magnitude `H` and slope `G`, and the elements at an osculating epoch given as a five-character packed date (century letter, two-digit year, and month and day in base 32). A comet line carries the perihelion date and distance instead of an epoch and mean anomaly, and the comet magnitude parameters. The mean daily motion keeps its published unit of degrees per day.

```ts
import { mpcorb, mpcorbComet, packDate, unpackDate } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/mpcorb'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// One MPCORB line for (1) Ceres.
const ceres = mpcorb('00001    3.34  0.15 K2555 188.70269   73.27343   80.25221   10.58780  0.0794013  0.21424651   2.7660512  0 E2024-V47  7330 125 1801-2024 0.80 M-v 30k MPCLINUX   4000      (1) Ceres              20241101')!

console.log(ceres.magnitudeH, ceres.magnitudeG) // 3.34 0.15
console.log(unpackDate(ceres.epochPacked)) // [2025, 5, 5] — packed epoch K2555
console.log(packDate(2025, 5, 5)) // K2555 — the inverse, for writing or matching records
console.log(toDeg(ceres.meanAnomaly), ceres.semiMajorAxis) // 188.70269 2.7660512 — degrees, AU

// One CometEls line for 1P/Halley.
const halley = mpcorbComet('0001P         2061 08 31.8266  0.583972  0.967311  112.5470   59.6368  162.2146  20250501   4.0  6.0  1P/Halley                                                 98, 1083')!

console.log(halley.perihelionYear, halley.perihelionMonth, halley.perihelionDay) // 2061 8 31
console.log(halley.perihelionDistance, halley.eccentricity) // 0.583972 0.967311 — AU
```

### Mutual Planetary-Satellite Events

The satellites of a giant planet occult and eclipse each other when the Earth and the Sun cross the planet's equatorial plane, a season that comes around twice per planetary orbit: about every six years for Jupiter and about every fifteen for Saturn, so most windows return nothing. A **mutual occultation** is one moon passing in front of another as seen from Earth, and a **mutual eclipse** is one moon casting its shadow on another. Their timings, measured photometrically, constrain the satellite ephemerides much better than ordinary astrometry, which is why observing campaigns are organized for each season.

The Galilean search covers Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto with the analytical VSOP87E + L1.2 positions, and the Saturnian search the seven main moons (Mimas, Enceladus, Tethys, Dione, Rhea, Titan, and Iapetus; Hyperion is omitted) with TASS 1.7. The same searches run on any Jovian or Saturnian ephemeris source, taking every body from that one source (see [Jovian Ephemeris Sources](#jovian-ephemeris-sources) and [Saturnian Ephemeris Sources](#saturnian-ephemeris-sources)). Occultations use the apparent geocentric directions of the two moons, each corrected for its own light time; eclipses use the heliocentric shadow geometry with the penumbra and are reported at the instant they are seen from Earth.

This is the detection layer only: each event has its kind, the front and back moons, the instants of first contact, maximum, and last contact, and an impact parameter from 0 (central) to 1 (grazing). There is no light curve and no magnitude drop. The search step must be shorter than the duration of a conjunction.

```ts
import { analyticalSaturnianEphemeris } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/saturnian'
import { findSaturnianMutualEvents, galileanMutualEvents, saturnianMutualEvents } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/mutual'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS, utc } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

const format = (time: Time) => timeToDate(utc(time)).slice(0, 6).join('-')

// Jupiter's mutual-event season of 2026-2027: on 2026-12-02 Ganymede casts its shadow on Callisto and on Europa.
for (const event of galileanMutualEvents(timeYMDHMS(2026, 12, 2, 19, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), timeYMDHMS(2026, 12, 2, 22, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC))) {
	console.log(event.kind, event.front, event.back, format(event.middle), event.impactParameter)
}
// eclipse ganymede callisto 2026-12-2-20-51-58 0.0294 — almost central
// eclipse ganymede europa 2026-12-2-21-47-32 0.3122

// Saturn, shortly after the ring-plane crossing of 2025: Titan eclipses Rhea, and occults it a few minutes later.
const saturnStart = timeYMDHMS(2025, 3, 12, 10, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
const saturnStop = timeYMDHMS(2025, 3, 12, 13, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

for (const event of saturnianMutualEvents(saturnStart, saturnStop)) {
	console.log(event.kind, event.front, event.back, format(event.middle), event.impactParameter)
}
// eclipse titan rhea 2025-3-12-11-27-26 0.8338
// occultation titan rhea 2025-3-12-11-34-1 0.2453

// The same search on an explicit ephemeris source, every body from it (findGalileanMutualEvents takes a JovianEphemeris).
console.log(findSaturnianMutualEvents(analyticalSaturnianEphemeris, saturnStart, saturnStop).length) // 2 — the same events
```

### Nutation and Celestial Orientation

Nutation is the short-period wobble of the Earth's rotation axis on top of the slow precession, caused mainly by the lunar and solar torques on the equatorial bulge; its main term has an 18.6-year period and an amplitude of about 17″ in longitude. It is expressed as two small angles: `Δψ`, the nutation in longitude, and `Δε`, the nutation in obliquity. Together with precession and the frame bias it orients the true equator and equinox of date, or the CIO-based Celestial Intermediate frame (CIRS), relative to GCRS.

The angles come from the IAU 2000A model adjusted for IAU 2006. The GCRS to CIRS matrix (frame bias, precession, and nutation, with right ascension measured from the Celestial Intermediate Origin) is the right companion for the CIRS-based observed-place conversions; the equinox-based precession-nutation matrix would offset right ascension by the equation of the origins, which grows by about 50″ per year since J2000. These matrices are cached on the `Time` and shared, so they must be treated as read-only. See [Precession Matrices](#precession-matrices) for the equinox-based matrices.

```ts
import { cirsRotationMatrix, equationOfOrigins, nutationAngles, Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toArcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Nutation in longitude and in obliquity (radians).
const [deltaPsi, deltaEpsilon] = nutationAngles(time)

console.log(toArcsec(deltaPsi), toArcsec(deltaEpsilon)) // 8.046 7.477 — arcseconds

// GCRS to CIRS rotation matrix (shared, read-only).
console.log(cirsRotationMatrix(time).slice(0, 3)) // [0.9999966, -4.8e-9, -0.0025894] — first row

// The same orientation from the equinox-based precession-nutation matrix turned by GAST − ERA (shared, read-only).
console.log(equationOfOrigins(time).slice(0, 3)) // [0.9999966, -4.8e-9, -0.0025894] — first row
```

### Obliquity and Ecliptic Orientation

The obliquity of the ecliptic is the tilt of the ecliptic plane, the plane of the Earth's orbit, relative to the Earth's equator, about 23.44° today and slowly decreasing. It is the angle that converts between equatorial and ecliptic coordinates, the natural frame for the Sun, the planets, and solar-system orbits. The mean obliquity follows precession only; the true obliquity adds the nutation in obliquity `Δε` (see [Nutation and Celestial Orientation](#nutation-and-celestial-orientation)).

The true ecliptic frame of date is the true equator frame of date tilted about the x axis by the true obliquity, so its rotation from GCRS is `Rx(true obliquity)` times the precession-nutation matrix, the same orientation as the `ECLIPTIC` frame. For converting spherical coordinates see [Spherical Coordinate Conversions](#spherical-coordinate-conversions).

```ts
import { meanObliquity, trueEclipticRotation, trueObliquity, Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Mean and true obliquity (radians).
console.log(toDeg(meanObliquity(time))) // 23.43583 — degrees
console.log(toDeg(trueObliquity(time))) // 23.43791 — degrees, mean plus nutation in obliquity

// GCRS -> true ecliptic of date; the z row carries sin/cos of the obliquity.
console.log(trueEclipticRotation(time).slice(6, 9)) // [0.0000054, -0.39772, 0.91751]
```

### Observed Catalog Star

The observed place of a catalog star is where an observer on the Earth's surface sees it at a given instant: catalog position and proper motion carried to the date, parallax, light deflection, aberration, precession and nutation, Earth rotation, polar motion, and optionally atmospheric refraction. It is the end of the astrometric chain for a star, one call that gives azimuth, altitude, hour angle, and the observed (CIRS) right ascension and declination, which is what a mount needs in order to point.

The star comes from its catalog astrometry (see [Stellar Space Motion](#stellar-space-motion)) and is taken as referred to J2000.0. The caller supplies the Earth's barycentric position and velocity (AU, AU/day) and heliocentric position, so any ephemeris can be used, and the site is the geodetic location carried by the `Time`, which is required. UT1 and polar motion come from the loaded Earth orientation data (see [Earth Orientation Parameters](#earth-orientation-parameters)). Azimuth is north through east, and refraction uses standard conditions unless pressure, temperature, humidity, and wavelength are given, or is disabled. For other body types see [Topocentric Observed Place](#topocentric-observed-place).

```ts
import { observeStar, star } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/star'
import { eraEpv00 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/earth'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { tdb, Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { arcsec, deg, hour, toDeg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'
import { kilometerPerSecond } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/velocity'

// Barnard's Star: RA, Dec, proper motions (RA rate, Dec rate), parallax, and radial velocity.
const declination = deg(4.693391)
const mas = (value: number) => arcsec(value / 1000)
const barnard = star(hour(17 + 57 / 60 + 48.4997 / 3600), declination, mas(-797.84) / Math.cos(declination), mas(10328.12), mas(546.98), kilometerPerSecond(-110.51))

// The time carries the site (La Silla).
const time = timeYMDHMS(2025, 7, 1, 3, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
time.location = geodeticLocation(deg(-70.7313), deg(-29.2563), meter(2400))

// The Earth's barycentric [position, velocity] and heliocentric state at that TDB instant.
const [barycentric, heliocentric] = eraEpv00(tdb(time).day, tdb(time).fraction)

// Observed place with standard refraction; pass false as the last argument to disable it.
const observed = observeStar(barnard, time, barycentric, heliocentric[0])

console.log(toDeg(observed.azimuth), toDeg(observed.altitude)) // 27.05 52.65 — degrees, without Earth orientation data
console.log(toHour(observed.rightAscension), toDeg(observed.declination)) // 17.9624 4.7527 — observed (CIRS) place
```

### Observing Visibility Windows

A target is observable when several conditions hold together: it is high enough above the horizon (or, equivalently, seen through little enough air mass), the sky is dark enough, and it is far enough from the Sun and the Moon. Planning a night or a campaign means intersecting those conditions over time, which gives the intervals in which the target can actually be observed.

The windows are computed with the constraint-interval search (see [Time-Constraint Intervals](#time-constraint-intervals)) from direction providers for the target, the Sun, and the Moon; altitudes are geometric and the air-mass limit uses the Kasten–Young formula. A Moon below a chosen horizon can waive the Moon-separation limit, since a set Moon does not light the sky near the target. No origin or correction is applied to the directions: they must share frames and corrections, with topocentric parallax included by the providers when it matters. The search step must be short enough to resolve every crossing of each constraint.

```ts
import { eraS2c } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/erfa'
import { moon } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/elpmpp02'
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { visibilityWindows } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/visibility'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const site = geodeticLocation(deg(-70.7313), deg(-29.2563), meter(2400)) // La Silla
const start = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Direction providers: a fixed star, and the geocentric Sun and Moon.
const star = eraS2c(hour(5.919), deg(7.407))
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0])
const moonAt = (time: Time) => moon(time)[0]

// Intervals in one day with air mass below 2, the Sun below −12°, and the Moon at least 30° away.
const windows = visibilityWindows(() => star, site, start, timeShift(start, 1), { maximumAirmass: 2, maximumSunAltitude: deg(-12), minimumMoonSeparation: deg(30) }, { sunAt, moonAt })

console.log(windows) // [{ start, end }] — 2025-09-28 06:52 to 09:33 UTC
```

### Orbit Covariance Propagation

An orbit fit gives a state and a 6×6 covariance at the fit epoch, and the uncertainty grows as the orbit is propagated away from it, mostly along the track, because a small error in the orbital period accumulates into a growing error in position. Knowing that uncertainty at a later time tells how large a search region is needed to recover the object, or how reliable a predicted close approach or occultation is.

To first order the covariance maps linearly through the state-transition matrix `Φ = ∂state(t)/∂state(epoch)`, which is obtained here by central finite differences of the two-body propagation. The linear-Gaussian model is valid while the uncertainty stays small, over short to medium arcs; very poorly constrained orbits need nonlinear methods. The state is `[x, y, z, vx, vy, vz]` in AU and AU/day, in the frame of the orbit's input state; the position block of the result feeds [Sky-Plane Uncertainty Ellipses](#sky-plane-uncertainty-ellipses), and the epoch covariance normally comes from [Differential Orbit Correction](#differential-orbit-correction).

```text
C(t) = Φ C₀ Φᵀ
```

```ts
import { KeplerOrbit } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/asteroid'
import { propagateStateCovariance, stateTransitionMatrix } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/covariance'
import { Timescale, time } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005 } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'
import { matIdentity } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/mat3'

// Vesta's heliocentric equatorial state at 2025-04-21 12:00 TDB (AU, AU/day).
const epoch = time(2460787, 0, Timescale.TDB)
const orbit = new KeplerOrbit([-1.70317472297052, -1.333843040283118, -0.3086709149679688], [0.007882762615954012, -0.008079478592200335, -0.004254433056153772], epoch, GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005, matIdentity())

// covariance: Matrix — 6×6 epoch covariance of the state, for example from fitOrbit.
const later = time(2460787 + 365, 0, Timescale.TDB) // one year after the epoch

// State-transition matrix Φ (6×6) from the epoch to the later time.
const phi = stateTransitionMatrix(orbit, later)
console.log(phi.get(0, 3)) // 240.55 — d x(later) / d vx(epoch), in days

// Covariance at the later time; the square roots of its diagonal are 1-sigma errors (AU, AU/day).
const propagated = propagateStateCovariance(orbit, covariance, later)
console.log(Math.sqrt(propagated.get(1, 1))) // 1-sigma y, AU
```

### Osculating Orbital Elements

The osculating elements of a body are the Keplerian elements of the two-body orbit that matches its position and velocity at one instant. They describe the conic it would follow if every perturbation vanished at that moment; since perturbations act continuously, they drift with time and are always tied to an epoch. They are the standard compact description of an orbit: size and shape (semi-major axis `a`, eccentricity `e`), orientation (inclination `i`, ascending node `Ω`, argument of periapsis `ω`), and position on the orbit (mean or true anomaly), from which period, periapsis and apoapsis distances, and time of periapsis follow.

A Kepler orbit built from a heliocentric state (AU, AU/day) exposes the full set, with distances in AU, angles in radians, and rates per day; see [Asteroid and Comet Orbit Construction](#asteroid-and-comet-orbit-construction) for the other ways to build one. The elements refer to the frame of the state, so a state in equatorial axes gives elements relative to the equator, not the ecliptic of published element sets. Circular or equatorial orbits have no defined node or periapsis.

The Tisserand parameter with respect to a planet, `T = a_p/a + 2·cos(i)·√((a/a_p)(1 − e²))`, is nearly conserved during an encounter with that planet and classifies small bodies: relative to Jupiter, above 3 is typically asteroidal, between 2 and 3 a Jupiter-family comet, and below 2 a Halley-type or nearly isotropic comet.

```ts
import { argumentOfLatitude, argumentOfPeriapsis, eccentricityVector, inclination, KeplerOrbit, longitudeOfAscendingNode, longitudeOfPeriapsis, meanLongitude, nodeVector, period, semiLatusRectum, semiMajorAxis, tisserandParameter, trueAnomaly } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/asteroid'
import { Timescale, time, timeToDate } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005 } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'
import { vecCross, vecLength } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Heliocentric equatorial state of Vesta from JPL Horizons, 2025-04-21 12:00 TDB: AU and AU/day.
const vesta = new KeplerOrbit([-1.70317472297052, -1.333843040283118, -0.3086709149679688], [0.007882762615954012, -0.008079478592200335, -0.004254433056153772], time(2460787, 0, Timescale.TDB))

// Elements are lazily computed properties.
console.log(vesta.semiMajorAxis, vesta.eccentricity) // 2.3614 0.090099 — AU
console.log(toDeg(vesta.inclination)) // 22.768 — degrees, relative to the equator since the state is equatorial
console.log(vesta.periodInDays) // 1325.4 — days
console.log(timeToDate(vesta.periapsisTime).slice(0, 3)) // [2021, 12, 28] — last perihelion passage (TDB)

// Tisserand parameter relative to Jupiter (a = 5.2044 AU).
console.log(tisserandParameter(vesta.semiMajorAxis, vesta.eccentricity, vesta.inclination, 5.2044)) // 3.4411 — asteroidal

// The point of the orbit at a true anomaly, in the orbit's output frame: here the perihelion.
console.log(Math.hypot(...vesta.positionAtTrueAnomaly(0))) // 2.1486 — AU, the perihelion distance

// The same elements as functions of a state (the building blocks of KeplerOrbit): the eccentricity vector,
// the angular momentum h = r × v, the node vector, and the semi-latus rectum (AU).
const [r, v] = [vesta.position, vesta.velocity]
const h = vecCross(r, v)
const ev = eccentricityVector(r, v, GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005)
const nv = nodeVector(h)
const p = semiLatusRectum(r, v, GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005)
const e = vecLength(ev)

// Orientation and position angles (radians): inclination, node, argument of periapsis, true anomaly.
const i = inclination(h)
const node = longitudeOfAscendingNode(h, i)
const w = argumentOfPeriapsis(ev, nv, h)
const nu = trueAnomaly(ev, r, v, nv)

console.log(toDeg(i), toDeg(node), toDeg(w), toDeg(nu)) // 22.768 18.192 238.53 322.87 — degrees

// Sizes from p and e (AU): semiMajorAxis, and semiMinorAxis, periapsisDistance, apoapsisDistance with the same
// arguments; the period from a and GM (days).
console.log(semiMajorAxis(p, e), period(semiMajorAxis(p, e), GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005)) // 2.3614 1325.4

// Combined angles (radians): argument of latitude, longitude of periapsis, and mean longitude (node + ω + M).
console.log(toDeg(argumentOfLatitude(w, nu)), toDeg(longitudeOfPeriapsis(node, w)), toDeg(meanLongitude(node, w, vesta.meanAnomaly))) // 201.41 256.73 225.51 — degrees
```

### Planetary Apparent Magnitudes (Mallama and Hilton)

The apparent magnitude of a planet depends on how far it is from the Sun and from the observer, through `5·log10(r·Δ)`, and on how much of its lit face is seen, which is set by the phase angle, the Sun-planet-observer angle. Each planet adds its own phase curve and terms: Saturn's brightness includes the rings and depends on how open they are, Uranus's depends on its polar aspect, and Neptune brightened secularly between 1980 and 2000, so its magnitude depends on the year. The model of Mallama and Hilton (2018), adopted by the Astronomical Almanac, gives visual (V) magnitudes from these.

The geometry comes from two vectors in AU in one consistent frame: Sun to planet and observer to planet. The model is undefined outside its fitted range, for example Saturn with rings beyond a 6.5° phase angle, and returns `NaN` there. The Mars rotation and season correction, up to ±0.06 mag, is not modelled. A smaller number is brighter.

```ts
import { planetMagnitude } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/photometry'
import { earth, saturn, sun, venus } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS, toJulianEpoch } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Visual magnitude from the Sun-to-planet and Earth-to-planet vectors (AU); the Julian year feeds Neptune's secular term.
console.log(planetMagnitude('venus', vecMinus(venus(time)[0], sun(time)[0]), vecMinus(venus(time)[0], earth(time)[0]), { year: toJulianEpoch(time) })) // -4.059

// Saturn with and without its rings.
console.log(planetMagnitude('saturn', vecMinus(saturn(time)[0], sun(time)[0]), vecMinus(saturn(time)[0], earth(time)[0]))) // 0.783
console.log(planetMagnitude('saturn', vecMinus(saturn(time)[0], sun(time)[0]), vecMinus(saturn(time)[0], earth(time)[0]), { rings: false })) // 0.846
```

### Planetary Appulses

An appulse is the least angular distance between two bodies as seen from the observer, the instant they look closest in the sky. It is not a conjunction: a conjunction is defined by equal ecliptic longitudes (see [Planetary Longitude Events](#planetary-longitude-events)), and for inclined orbits the two instants differ, by seconds for a slow pair or by hours when one body moves fast in latitude. A pair can also have appulses with no conjunction at all, at the turning points of a retrograde loop.

The appulses are the local minima of the great-circle separation of two observer-relative directions, which must share the observer, axes, and correction stage. A minimum at the edge of the window, or one flatter than the search step, is not reported.

```ts
import { earth, jupiter, saturn } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { planetaryAppulses } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/planetary'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Geocentric geometric vectors (AU) of Jupiter and Saturn.
const jupiterAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(jupiter(time)[0], earth(time)[0])
const saturnAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(saturn(time)[0], earth(time)[0])

// Separation minima in one year, sampled every 2 days.
for (const appulse of planetaryAppulses(jupiterAt, saturnAt, start, timeShift(start, 366), { step: 2 })) console.log(timeToDate(appulse.time).slice(0, 5), toDeg(appulse.separation))
// [2020, 5, 18, 4, 47] 4.697 — degrees, during the retrograde loop, TT
// [2020, 12, 21, 18, 12] 0.102 — the great conjunction's closest approach, 23 s after the longitude conjunction
```

### Planetary Brightness Maxima

A planet's apparent magnitude changes with its distance and phase, and the two effects compete for the inner planets. Venus is brightest not at inferior conjunction, where it is nearest but almost unlit, but about a month before and after it, at its greatest brilliancy near a 120° phase angle, when its crescent is still large and already well lit.

The maxima are the local minima of the magnitude from [Planetary Apparent Magnitudes (Mallama and Hilton)](#planetary-apparent-magnitudes-mallama-and-hilton), with the phase angle reported for each. Every minimum of the model is reported, including shallow ones that are not traditional brilliancies: for Venus, the forward-scattering branch beyond a 163.7° phase angle and the distance term near superior conjunction add extra minima, so keep phase angles between 90° and 163.7° to find the greatest brilliancies. A brightness maximum is flat, so its instant is far less precise than its magnitude.

```ts
import { earth, sun, venus } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { planetaryBrightnessMaxima } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/planetary'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Geocentric vectors (AU) of Venus and the Sun.
const venusAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(venus(time)[0], earth(time)[0])
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0])

// Magnitude minima in one year, kept to the crescent phases of the greatest brilliancies.
const brilliancies = planetaryBrightnessMaxima('venus', venusAt, sunAt, start, timeShift(start, 366), { step: 2 }).filter((event) => event.phaseAngle > deg(90) && event.phaseAngle < deg(163.7))

for (const event of brilliancies) console.log(timeToDate(event.time).slice(0, 3), event.magnitude, toDeg(event.phaseAngle))
// [2020, 5, 2] -4.753 121.7 — magnitude and degrees, evening star, TT
// [2020, 7, 5] -4.717 122.9 — morning star
```

### Planetary Closest Approaches

A planet's distance from the observer is not constant: for Mars it swings from about 0.4 AU at a favorable opposition to over 2.5 AU near conjunction. A closest approach is a local minimum of that distance, the moment of largest apparent diameter and the best time for high-resolution imaging. Because of orbital eccentricity, the closest approach of an outer planet does not coincide exactly with its opposition (see [Planetary Oppositions](#planetary-oppositions)).

The search is the extremum scan of [Time-Domain Extrema Search](#time-domain-extrema-search) on the length of an observer-to-target vector, so the same provider serves geocentric, topocentric, or heliocentric distances. No correction is added: the caller chooses geometric, astrometric, or apparent vectors. A minimum at the edge of the window is not reported.

```ts
import { earth, mars } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { planetaryClosestApproaches } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/planetary'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Geocentric geometric vector (AU) of Mars.
const marsAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(mars(time)[0], earth(time)[0])

// Distance minima in one year, sampled every 2 days.
for (const approach of planetaryClosestApproaches(marsAt, start, timeShift(start, 366), { step: 2 })) console.log(timeToDate(approach.time).slice(0, 5), approach.distance)
// [2020, 10, 6, 14, 19] 0.4149 — TT, AU
```

### Planetary Conjunctions

A planet is in conjunction with the Sun when the two line up as seen from the observer, so the planet is lost in the Sun's glare and cannot be observed. Because planetary orbits are inclined, the planet rarely passes exactly over the Sun's disk, so the event is taken here as the local minimum of the angular separation, which is reported as it is. An inner planet has two kinds: inferior conjunction, between the Earth and the Sun, and superior conjunction, beyond the Sun. An outer planet has only superior conjunctions; its opposite alignment is in [Planetary Oppositions](#planetary-oppositions).

These are separation minima; the almanac conjunction, defined by equal ecliptic longitudes, is in [Planetary Longitude Events](#planetary-longitude-events). Both direction providers return observer-relative vectors (AU) that must share the observer, axes, and correction stage.

```ts
import { earth, sun, venus } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { planetaryConjunctions, planetaryInnerConjunctions } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/planetary'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)
const stop = timeShift(start, 366)

// Geocentric vectors (AU) of Venus and the Sun.
const venusAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(venus(time)[0], earth(time)[0])
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0])

// Separation minima in one year, sampled every 2 days.
const [conjunction] = planetaryConjunctions(venusAt, sunAt, start, stop, { step: 2 })
console.log(timeToDate(conjunction.time).slice(0, 5), toDeg(conjunction.elongation)) // [2020, 6, 3, 18, 43] 0.482 — TT, degrees from the Sun's center

// The same events for an inner planet, classified as inferior or superior.
const [inner] = planetaryInnerConjunctions(venusAt, sunAt, start, stop, { step: 2 })
console.log(inner.kind) // inferior — Venus is nearer the Earth than the Sun
```

### Planetary Disk Transits

A transit is a planet's disk crossing the Sun's disk, possible only for Mercury and Venus at an inferior conjunction that falls near a node of their orbit. Seen from a given site it is a chord across the solar disk, with four contacts: exterior ingress (I, the disk first touches the limb), interior ingress (II, the disk is wholly inside), interior egress (III), and exterior egress (IV). Because the planet is much closer than the Sun, its parallax shifts the contact times by minutes from site to site, so the prediction is made for one topocentric observer; historically, timing the contacts of transits of Venus from distant sites was how the solar parallax was measured.

The prediction uses barycentric states of the planet, the Sun, and the observer, with light time, and the physical radii of the Sun and the planet, which set the two angular disks. A grazing transit, where the planet is never wholly inside the disk, has no interior contacts, and contacts outside the search window are not reported. Aberration is omitted because it cancels in the difference, and light bending near the limb is not modelled.

```ts
import { observerState } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/correction'
import { earth, mercury, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { planetaryTransits } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/transit'
import { Ellipsoid, geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { SUN_RADIUS_AU } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'
import { deg, toArcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { kilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// Greenwich as a topocentric barycentric state: the Earth's state plus the site offset.
const greenwich = geodeticLocation(deg(-0.0015), deg(51.4779), kilometer(0.047), Ellipsoid.WGS84)
const observer = (time: Time) => observerState(time, earth(time), greenwich)

// The 13 November 2032 transit of Mercury; radii in AU.
const [transit] = planetaryTransits(mercury, sun, observer, timeYMDHMS(2032, 11, 13, 5, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), timeYMDHMS(2032, 11, 13, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), { sunRadius: SUN_RADIUS_AU, planetRadius: kilometer(2439.7) })

console.log(timeToDate(transit.exteriorIngress!).slice(0, 6)) // [2032, 11, 13, 6, 41, 35] — contact I, UTC
console.log(timeToDate(transit.time).slice(0, 6)) // [2032, 11, 13, 8, 54, 48] — mid-transit
console.log(timeToDate(transit.exteriorEgress!).slice(0, 6)) // [2032, 11, 13, 11, 7, 59] — contact IV
console.log(toArcsec(transit.minSeparation)) // 569.4 — arcseconds, least distance between the centers
```

### Planetary Greatest Elongations

An inner planet never strays far from the Sun in the sky. Its elongation, the angular separation from the Sun, rises to a maximum and falls again over each synodic period, and that maximum is the greatest elongation: about 18° to 28° for Mercury, depending on its eccentric orbit, and about 45° to 47° for Venus. It is the best time to observe the planet, east of the Sun in the evening sky and west of it in the morning sky.

The events are the elongation maxima between observer-relative directions of the planet and the Sun, which must share the observer, axes, and correction stage; east or west follows from the ecliptic-longitude difference of date. The search is intended for inner planets; for an outer planet use [Planetary Oppositions](#planetary-oppositions) and [Planetary Quadratures](#planetary-quadratures).

```ts
import { earth, sun, venus } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { planetaryGreatestElongations } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/planetary'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Geocentric vectors (AU) of Venus and the Sun.
const venusAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(venus(time)[0], earth(time)[0])
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0])

// Elongation maxima in one year, sampled every 2 days.
for (const event of planetaryGreatestElongations(venusAt, sunAt, start, timeShift(start, 366), { step: 2 })) console.log(timeToDate(event.time).slice(0, 5), toDeg(event.elongation), event.kind)
// [2020, 3, 24, 21, 59] 46.08 east — evening star, TT
// [2020, 8, 13, 0, 0] 45.79 west — morning star
```

### Planetary Illumination Crossings

The illuminated fraction of a planet's disk seen by the observer is `k = (1 + cos i) / 2`, with `i` the Sun-planet-observer phase angle. Mercury and Venus go from full to new and back, and the instant they are half lit, the dichotomy, falls days away from the greatest elongation, which is a separation maximum (see [Planetary Greatest Elongations](#planetary-greatest-elongations)); the observed dichotomy of Venus is known to differ from the predicted one (Schröter's effect), so the computed instant is geometric.

The crossings are the instants at which the illuminated fraction crosses a chosen value, each marked as increasing or decreasing, from observer-relative vectors of the planet and the Sun with the same axes and correction stage. A touch that does not cross the value is not reported.

```ts
import { earth, sun, venus } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { planetaryIlluminationCrossings } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/planetary'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Geocentric vectors (AU) of Venus and the Sun.
const venusAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(venus(time)[0], earth(time)[0])
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0])

// Instants at which the illuminated fraction crosses 0.5 (the dichotomy) in one year.
for (const event of planetaryIlluminationCrossings(venusAt, sunAt, start, timeShift(start, 366), 0.5, { step: 2 })) console.log(timeToDate(event.time).slice(0, 5), event.kind)
// [2020, 3, 27, 0, 47] decreasing — evening dichotomy, two days after greatest elongation, TT
// [2020, 8, 12, 20, 48] increasing — morning dichotomy
```

### Planetary Longitude Events

The almanac defines conjunction, opposition, and quadrature by ecliptic longitude, not by angular distance: two bodies are in conjunction when their true ecliptic longitudes of date are equal, a planet is in opposition when its longitude differs from the Sun's by 180°, and in quadrature at ±90°. For an inclined orbit the separation is not zero or 180° at these instants, and its extremum falls at a different time: Mars's longitude opposition of 2020 comes about 2.7 hours before its separation maximum. The separation-based finders are [Planetary Conjunctions](#planetary-conjunctions), [Planetary Oppositions](#planetary-oppositions), and [Planetary Quadratures](#planetary-quadratures); the least distance of two bodies is in [Planetary Appulses](#planetary-appulses).

The general search finds the instants at which the longitude of a target minus that of a reference equals any chosen offset; conjunctions, oppositions, and quadratures are its offsets 0, 180°, and ±90°, with the kind of each event (inferior or superior, east or west). The observer-relative vectors (AU) of both bodies must share the observer, axes, and correction stage; they are rotated to the true ecliptic of date with precession-nutation and the true obliquity. Each event also reports the actual separation and the latitude difference, the target's ecliptic latitude minus the reference's, positive when the target is north.

```ts
import { earth, jupiter, mars, saturn, sun, venus } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { planetaryLongitudeConjunctions, planetaryLongitudeCrossings, planetaryLongitudeOppositions, planetaryLongitudeQuadratures } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/planetary'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)
const stop = timeShift(start, 366)

// Geocentric vector provider (AU) of a body.
const geocentric = (body: typeof venus) => (time: Time) => vecMinus(body(time)[0], earth(time)[0])
const sunAt = geocentric(sun)

// Equal longitudes of Venus and the Sun, with the latitude difference at that instant.
const [conjunction] = planetaryLongitudeConjunctions(geocentric(venus), sunAt, start, stop, { step: 2 })
console.log(timeToDate(conjunction.time).slice(0, 5), conjunction.kind, toDeg(conjunction.latitudeDifference)) // [2020, 6, 3, 17, 38] inferior 0.487 — TT, degrees north of the Sun

// Longitude opposition and quadratures of Mars.
const [opposition] = planetaryLongitudeOppositions(geocentric(mars), sunAt, start, stop, { step: 2 })
console.log(timeToDate(opposition.time).slice(0, 5), toDeg(opposition.separation)) // [2020, 10, 13, 23, 19] 177.0
const quadratures = planetaryLongitudeQuadratures(geocentric(mars), sunAt, start, stop, { step: 2 })

// The great conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn, a conjunction between two planets.
const [great] = planetaryLongitudeConjunctions(geocentric(jupiter), geocentric(saturn), start, stop, { step: 2 })
console.log(timeToDate(great.time).slice(0, 5), toDeg(great.separation)) // [2020, 12, 21, 18, 12] 0.102

// Any offset: Venus 30° of longitude west of the Sun, on the way out and back.
const crossings = planetaryLongitudeCrossings(geocentric(venus), sunAt, start, stop, deg(-30), { step: 2 })
```

### Planetary Oppositions

An outer planet is in opposition when it lies opposite the Sun in the sky, so it rises at sunset, is up all night, and is near its closest and brightest: the best time to observe it. Because planetary orbits are inclined, the elongation reaches its maximum near, but rarely exactly at, 180°, so the event is taken here as the maximum of the separation on the far side of quadrature, and the reported elongation need not reach 180°.

The almanac opposition, a 180° difference of ecliptic longitudes, is in [Planetary Longitude Events](#planetary-longitude-events), and the least distance, which can differ from opposition by days, in [Planetary Closest Approaches](#planetary-closest-approaches). Both direction providers must share the observer, axes, and correction stage.

```ts
import { earth, mars, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { planetaryOppositions } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/planetary'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Geocentric vectors (AU) of Mars and the Sun.
const marsAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(mars(time)[0], earth(time)[0])
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0])

// Elongation maxima beyond 90° in one year, sampled every 2 days.
const [opposition] = planetaryOppositions(marsAt, sunAt, start, timeShift(start, 366), { step: 2 })

console.log(timeToDate(opposition.time).slice(0, 5)) // [2020, 10, 14, 2, 2] — TT
console.log(toDeg(opposition.elongation)) // 177.0 — degrees: Mars is 3° off the exact opposite direction
```

### Planetary Quadratures

A planet is at quadrature when it is 90° from the Sun as seen from the observer. For an outer planet it is the phase of greatest defect of illumination (Mars then shows a noticeably gibbous disk) and the boundary between the morning and evening halves of its apparition. East quadrature has the planet east of the Sun, in the evening sky, and west quadrature has it west, in the morning sky.

The events are the instants at which the angular separation crosses 90°, with east or west from the ecliptic-longitude difference. The almanac quadrature, a ±90° difference of ecliptic longitudes, is in [Planetary Longitude Events](#planetary-longitude-events). Both direction providers must share the observer, axes, and correction stage.

```ts
import { earth, mars, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { planetaryQuadratures } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/planetary'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Geocentric vectors (AU) of Mars and the Sun.
const marsAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(mars(time)[0], earth(time)[0])
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0])

// 90° separation crossings in one year, sampled every 2 days.
for (const event of planetaryQuadratures(marsAt, sunAt, start, timeShift(start, 366), { step: 2 })) console.log(timeToDate(event.time).slice(0, 5), toDeg(event.elongation), event.kind)
// [2020, 6, 6, 19, 2] 90 west — Mars in the morning sky, TT
```

### Planetary Stations

Seen from the Earth, a planet normally drifts eastward among the stars (direct motion), but around opposition for an outer planet, or inferior conjunction for an inner one, it appears to reverse for weeks (retrograde motion), as the Earth overtakes it or is overtaken. A station is the moment its ecliptic longitude stops changing and the motion reverses, from direct to retrograde and back; the planet then appears nearly motionless against the stars.

Stations are the sign changes of the rate of the true ecliptic longitude of date, estimated by a centered difference of the observer-relative direction, so the provider must cover slightly more than the search window. The longitude at each station is reported in radians in `(−π, π]`.

```ts
import { earth, mars } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { planetaryStations } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/planetary'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Geocentric vector (AU) of Mars.
const marsAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(mars(time)[0], earth(time)[0])

// Stations in one year, sampled every 2 days.
for (const station of planetaryStations(marsAt, start, timeShift(start, 366), { step: 2 })) console.log(station.kind, timeToDate(station.time).slice(0, 5), toDeg(station.longitude))
// directToRetrograde [2020, 9, 9, 22, 19] 28.14 — TT, ecliptic longitude in degrees
// retrogradeToDirect [2020, 11, 14, 0, 32] 15.23
```

### Planetary Surface Locations

A point on the surface of another body, such as a landing site, a crater, or an observatory on Mars, is described by planetocentric east longitude, latitude from the body's equatorial plane, and elevation above a reference triaxial ellipsoid, in the body-fixed frame. Moving it to the inertial frame needs the body's orientation (see [IAU Body Orientation](#iau-body-orientation), or a SPICE or PCK frame) and carries the rotational velocity of the surface. Composed with a body-center ephemeris, the location becomes an ordinary body, so it works anywhere a body ephemeris does (see [Ephemeris Path Adapters](#ephemeris-path-adapters)), for example as an observer for the sky seen from that site.

The ellipsoid is built from three semi-axes in AU, for example the SPICE body radii (see [SPICE Body Radii](#spice-body-radii)). Elevation is a radial offset along the planetocentric direction, not a planetographic or geodetic height, and the surface normal is that of the reference ellipsoid, ignoring relief. The solar altitude at such a location is in [Body-Surface Solar Illumination](#body-surface-solar-illumination).

```ts
import { bodyFixedFrame } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/orientation'
import { MARS_ROTATION } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/orientation.data'
import { mars } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { bodyFixedPosition, bodyShape, bodySurfaceLocation, bodySurfaceNormal, bodySurfacePositionAndVelocity, bodySurfaceState } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/body'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { kilometer, toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Mars as an oblate ellipsoid: 3396.2 km equatorial and 3376.2 km polar radii.
const shape = bodyShape([kilometer(3396.2), kilometer(3396.2), kilometer(3376.2)])

// 18° N, 135° W (225° E), at the reference surface, in the IAU body-fixed frame of Mars.
const location = bodySurfaceLocation(deg(-135), deg(18), 0, shape, bodyFixedFrame(MARS_ROTATION))

// Body-fixed Cartesian position (AU), computed once and cached on the location; do not mutate it.
console.log(bodyFixedPosition(location).map(toKilometer)) // [-2282.6, -2282.6, 1048.9] — km

// Unit outward normal of the ellipsoid in body-fixed axes.
console.log(bodySurfaceNormal(location)) // [-0.6717, -0.6717, 0.3123]

// State relative to Mars's center in ICRF axes (AU, AU/day), with the velocity of Mars's rotation.
const [position, velocity] = bodySurfaceState(location, time)

// Added to Mars's barycentric ephemeris, it becomes an ordinary barycentric body.
const site = bodySurfacePositionAndVelocity(mars, location)
console.log(site(time)[0]) // [1.18438, 0.74857, 0.31160] — AU, barycentric ICRF
```

### Pluto Short Analytical Theory

Pluto's orbit is eccentric, inclined, and locked in a 3:2 mean-motion resonance with Neptune, so a fixed Kepler orbit is a poor model, and the major-planet theories such as VSOP87 do not include it. Meeus (Astronomical Algorithms, chapter 37) gives a short theory that fits the heliocentric longitude, latitude, and radius with 43 periodic terms in the mean longitudes of Jupiter, Saturn, and Pluto. Its stated accuracy is 0.07″ in longitude, 0.02″ in latitude, and 0.000006 AU in radius, and it is valid only from 1885 to 2099; outside that range use an SPK kernel (see [SPK State Kernels](#spk-state-kernels)).

The result is Pluto's heliocentric position in AU, Cartesian in the ICRF equatorial frame by default, with no velocity. In the J2000 ecliptic frame it returns the underlying spherical coordinates `[longitude, latitude, radius]` instead, not Cartesian ecliptic coordinates. For barycentric Pluto, add the Sun's barycentric state.

```ts
import { pluto } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/pluto'
import { Timescale, time, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Heliocentric ICRF equatorial position (AU).
console.log(pluto(timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.TT))) // [18.971, -26.376, -13.945]

// Spherical J2000 ecliptic coordinates; Meeus example 37.a, JD 2448908.5 TT.
const [longitude, latitude, radius] = pluto(time(2448908, 0.5, Timescale.TT), 'eclipticJ2000')

console.log(toDeg(longitude), toDeg(latitude), radius) // 232.74071 14.58782 29.711111 — degrees, degrees, AU
```

### Polar Motion

Polar motion is the motion of the Earth's rotation pole relative to the crust, described by two angles `x` and `y` of a few tenths of an arcsecond (about ten meters on the ground). It is dominated by the free Chandler wobble, with a period of about 433 days, and an annual term forced by the seasons, and it cannot be predicted far ahead, so it is measured and published by the IERS. It tilts the Earth-fixed (ITRS) frame relative to the terrestrial intermediate frame and matters for precise Earth-fixed positions and topocentric work. The tiny TIO locator `s′` completes the rotation.

The angles come from a polar-motion provider, a function of time returning `[x, y]` in radians. By default it is the provider assigned to the `Time`, then the loaded IERS tables, which give zero when nothing is loaded (see [Earth Orientation Parameters](#earth-orientation-parameters)); a provider can be passed for one call, and `NO_POLAR_MOTION` disables it.

```ts
import { NO_POLAR_MOTION, pmAngles, pmMatrix, Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { arcsec, toArcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UT1)

// A custom provider: x = 0.19", y = 0.32" (radians).
const provider = () => [arcsec(0.19), arcsec(0.32)] as [number, number]

// [s′, x, y] in radians, and the 3×3 polar-motion rotation built from them.
console.log(pmAngles(time, provider).map(toArcsec)) // [-0.0000125, 0.19, 0.32] — arcseconds
console.log(pmMatrix(time, provider).slice(0, 3)) // [1, -5.9e-11, 9.2e-7] — first row

// Without polar motion only the TIO locator remains.
console.log(pmAngles(time, NO_POLAR_MOTION).map(toArcsec)) // [-0.0000125, 0, 0]
```

### Precession Matrices

Precession is the slow, steady motion of the Earth's rotation axis, a cone traced in about 26,000 years under the lunar and solar torques on the equatorial bulge, which moves the equator and the equinox of date relative to the fixed GCRS axes by about 50″ per year in longitude. Catalog coordinates refer to a fixed epoch such as J2000, while pointing and apparent places need the equator of date, so every reduction applies it. Nutation adds the short-period wobble on top.
