The precession matrix follows the IAU 2006 model and includes the frame bias, taking a GCRS vector to the mean equator and equinox of date; the precession-nutation matrix adds nutation and gives the true equator and equinox of date (see [Nutation and Celestial Orientation](#nutation-and-celestial-orientation)). Both are cached on the `Time` and shared, so they must be treated as read-only. The precession between two arbitrary equinoxes is a separate matrix, used by the FK5 conversions in [FK5 Precession and ICRS Frame Bias](#fk5-precession-and-icrs-frame-bias). Times are converted to TT internally.

```ts
import { precessionMatrixCapitaine } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/frame'
import { precessionMatrix, precessionNutationMatrix, Timescale, timeJulianYear, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// GCRS -> mean equator and equinox of date (frame bias + precession), read-only.
console.log(precessionMatrix(time).slice(0, 3)) // [0.99997914, -0.0059238, -0.0025737] — first row

// GCRS -> true equator and equinox of date (adds nutation), read-only.
console.log(precessionNutationMatrix(time).slice(0, 3)) // [0.99997889, -0.0059596, -0.0025892] — first row

// Precession only, from the equinox J2000.0 to J2026.5 (both TT), as a fresh matrix.
console.log(precessionMatrixCapitaine(timeJulianYear(2000), timeJulianYear(2026.5)).slice(0, 3)) // [0.99997913, -0.0059259, -0.0025747]
```

### Projected Paths and Polygons

A path across the sky or a map, such as a satellite ground track, an eclipse limit, or a constellation boundary, becomes a set of lines when projected. A map projection is discontinuous somewhere: at the antimeridian of a cylindrical map, at the limb of an orthographic globe, or near a singular point. Where a path crosses such a seam the projected line must be cut rather than drawn straight across the map, and long steps must be densified so that the curvature of the path shows.

The polyline projection splits a path at antimeridian crossings, at points outside the projection's domain (such as the far side of an orthographic view), and at large planar jumps, and can densify long segments first. Polygons are cut ring by ring; a ring that crosses the antimeridian comes back in several pieces that the caller closes or fills. Points are spherical `{ x: longitude, y: latitude }` in radians.

```ts
import { Orthographic, PlateCarree, projectMany, projectPolygon, projectPolyline } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/projections/projection'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const map = new PlateCarree()

// Project points (x = longitude, y = latitude, radians) into planar points.
console.log(
	projectMany(map, [
		{ x: 0, y: 0 },
		{ x: deg(10), y: deg(20) },
	]),
) // [{ x: 0, y: 0 }, { x: 0.1745, y: 0.3491 }]

// A track crossing the 180° meridian is cut into two lines; segments longer than 30° are densified.
const track = [170, 175, -175, -170].map((longitude) => ({ x: deg(longitude), y: deg(10) }))
console.log(projectPolyline(map, track, { maxSegmentRadians: deg(30) }).length) // 2

// On an orthographic globe, points on the far side are dropped.
const visible = projectPolyline(
	new Orthographic(0, 0),
	[0, 40, 80, 120, 160].map((longitude) => ({ x: deg(longitude), y: 0 })),
)

// Polygon rings: one entry per ring, each a list of planar pieces.
const pieces = projectPolygon(map, [
	[
		{ x: deg(170), y: deg(10) },
		{ x: deg(-170), y: deg(10) },
		{ x: deg(-170), y: deg(20) },
		{ x: deg(170), y: deg(20) },
		{ x: deg(170), y: deg(10) },
	],
])
```

### Radial Doppler Shift

The Doppler shift is the change in a received frequency caused by motion along the line of sight: a receding source is redshifted, an approaching one blueshifted. Tracking a satellite or spacecraft by radio means retuning the receiver (and pre-shifting the transmitter) continuously, because the range rate of a low-Earth-orbit satellite reaches several km/s and shifts a VHF downlink by kilohertz during one pass.

The shift is the classical first-order expression, which assumes `|rangeRate| ≪ c` and ignores relativistic and transverse terms, so it suits radio tracking, not high-velocity astrophysical sources. The range rate is the receiver-to-source range derivative in AU/day, positive when receding, and the result is in the unit of the carrier frequency, negative for a receding source.

```text
Δf = −(rangeRate / c) · f
```

```ts
import { radialDopplerShift } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'
import { kilometerPerSecond } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/velocity'

// Shift of a 145.8 MHz carrier for a source receding at 7 km/s (range rate in AU/day).
console.log(radialDopplerShift(kilometerPerSecond(7), 145.8e6)) // -3404.4 — Hz
```

### Radial Velocity Correction

A measured radial velocity includes the observer's own motion: the Earth's orbital velocity (up to about 30 km/s) and its rotation (up to about 0.46 km/s). Before spectra taken on different nights or at different sites can be compared, for example to detect the reflex motion of a star with a planet, the measurement must be referred to the solar-system barycenter or to the Sun. The correction is the projection of the observer's velocity onto the line of sight, `rv_referred = rv_topocentric + correction`, positive when the observer moves toward the source.

The reference center follows the Earth state passed in, barycentric or heliocentric, and a site location adds the diurnal rotation; without it the correction is geocentric. It is a first-order Newtonian projection, enough for ordinary spectroscopy but not for precise radial-velocity work at the m/s level, and does not use the source's own velocity. The direction is ICRS right ascension and declination in radians, and the result is in AU/day. For the timing counterpart, see [Barycentric and Heliocentric Light-Time Correction](#barycentric-and-heliocentric-light-time-correction).

```ts
import { radialVelocityCorrection } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/correction'
import { eraEpv00 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/earth'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { tdb, Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'
import { toKilometerPerSecond } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/velocity'

const location = geodeticLocation(deg(-70.7313), deg(-29.2563), meter(2400)) // La Silla
const time = timeYMDHMS(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// The Earth's barycentric and heliocentric states at that TDB instant.
const [barycentric, heliocentric] = eraEpv00(tdb(time).day, tdb(time).fraction)

// Barycentric correction for a source at RA 5.5 h, Dec −5°, including the site's rotation.
console.log(toKilometerPerSecond(radialVelocityCorrection(hour(5.5), deg(-5), time, barycentric, location))) // -8.061 — km/s

// Heliocentric correction for the same source.
console.log(toKilometerPerSecond(radialVelocityCorrection(hour(5.5), deg(-5), time, heliocentric, location))) // -8.056 — km/s
```

### Refractive Displacement

The atmosphere bends light, so a source appears higher than its geometric position. The displacement depends on the apparent altitude, on the pressure, temperature, and humidity of the air, and on the observing wavelength: about a minute of arc at 45° and roughly 10′ at 1°. It must be removed to point a telescope accurately or to compare a measured position with a catalog.

The displacement is computed at one wavelength with the same ERFA model as the observed-place transforms (see [Topocentric Observed Place](#topocentric-observed-place)), as the amount by which the apparent altitude exceeds the geometric altitude: positive, finite at low altitude, and zero at the zenith. It takes the apparent altitude, strictly above the horizon, and standard conditions unless pressure (hPa), temperature (°C), and relative humidity are given. For a quick estimate without wavelength or weather, see [Approximate Atmospheric Refraction](#approximate-atmospheric-refraction); for the difference between two wavelengths, see [Differential Refraction and Atmospheric Dispersion](#differential-refraction-and-atmospheric-dispersion).

```ts
import { refractiveDisplacement } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/refraction'
import { deg, toArcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Apparent altitude 45°, wavelength 0.55 µm (green), standard conditions.
console.log(toArcsec(refractiveDisplacement(deg(45), 0.55)!)) // 57.11 — arcseconds

// Near the horizon, and in thinner, colder air.
console.log(toArcsec(refractiveDisplacement(deg(1), 0.55)!)) // 646.93 — arcseconds
console.log(toArcsec(refractiveDisplacement(deg(10), 0.55, { pressure: 700, temperature: -5 })!)) // 232.47 — arcseconds
```

### Rise, Transit, and Set

A body rises when its altitude crosses a horizon value going up, sets when it crosses going down, and transits when it reaches its highest altitude on the meridian. The almanac convention measures the crossing against a horizon altitude that folds in the mean refraction at the horizon and the body's apparent size, instead of the geometric zero: `STANDARD_HORIZON` (−34′) is for a point source such as a star or planet, `SUN_HORIZON` (−50′) for the Sun's upper limb, and `CIVIL_TWILIGHT`, `NAUTICAL_TWILIGHT`, and `ASTRONOMICAL_TWILIGHT` (−6°, −12°, −18°) for the Sun's depression angle at the twilight limits.

The altitude is geocentric and geometric, with precession and nutation applied but no aberration or parallax, so for the Moon the horizon must be raised by its horizontal parallax (about 57′) to match almanac values. The transit is the altitude maximum, reported even below the horizon; a body that never crosses the horizon is reported as always up or always down. The search covers one day from the start time by default, so a start in the middle of the day can place the set before the rise; start at local midnight for the usual order. The search is built on [Time-Domain Event Search](#time-domain-event-search) and [Time-Domain Extrema Search](#time-domain-extrema-search).

```ts
import { eraS2c } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/erfa'
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { altitudeOf, riseTransitSet, STANDARD_HORIZON, SUN_HORIZON } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/horizon'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { deg, hour, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const site = geodeticLocation(deg(-70.7313), deg(-29.2563), meter(2400)) // La Silla
const start = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// The Sun: geocentric ICRS direction, measured against the upper-limb horizon.
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0])
const sunEvents = riseTransitSet(sunAt, site, start, { horizon: SUN_HORIZON })

console.log(timeToDate(sunEvents.rise!).slice(0, 5)) // [2025, 9, 28, 10, 24] — UTC
console.log(timeToDate(sunEvents.set!).slice(0, 5)) // [2025, 9, 28, 22, 42]
console.log(toDeg(sunEvents.transitAltitude)) // 63.05 — degrees

// A fixed star (RA 5.919 h, Dec +7.407°) as a constant direction, and its altitude at one instant.
const star = eraS2c(hour(5.919), deg(7.407))
const starEvents = riseTransitSet(() => star, site, start, { horizon: STANDARD_HORIZON })
console.log(toDeg(altitudeOf(star, start, site))) // -56.39 — degrees, below the horizon at 00:00 UTC
```

### Sampled Angular Motion

The angular motion of a moving target on the sky, such as a comet, asteroid, or satellite, can be estimated from a few sampled positions, for example from an ephemeris or from successive plate solutions. It is what a mount needs to track the target instead of the stars (differential tracking), and what sets the longest exposure before the target trails. Two samples give a constant rate; three or more also give an acceleration, which captures the curvature of the track and tells how quickly a tracking rate goes stale.

The rate is the secant from the earliest to the latest sample, with the longitude unwrapped step by step so a crossing of 0 h does not invent a full turn; consecutive samples must be less than half a turn apart. The longitude rate is a coordinate rate, not multiplied by `cos(latitude)`, while the great-circle rate is the true speed on the sky; the position angle of travel is north through east. Samples are in radians with time in days, and only time differences matter.

```ts
import { angularMotionOrDifferentialTrackingRate } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/motion'
import { arcsec, deg, hour, toArcsec, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Positions at 0 h, 1 h, and 2 h (time in days): longitude and latitude are RA and Dec.
const samples = [
	{ longitude: hour(10), latitude: deg(20), timeDays: 0 },
	{ longitude: hour(10) + arcsec(30), latitude: deg(20) - arcsec(10), timeDays: 1 / 24 },
	{ longitude: hour(10) + arcsec(70), latitude: deg(20) - arcsec(30), timeDays: 2 / 24 },
]

// Rates in RA and Dec and on the sky, the direction of travel, and, with three samples, the accelerations.
const motion = angularMotionOrDifferentialTrackingRate(samples)!

console.log(motion.angularRatePerDay) // 0.0042061 — radians/day on the sky
console.log(toDeg(motion.positionAngle)) // degrees, north through east
console.log(motion.angularAccelerationPerDaySquared) // 0.03832 — radians/day²
```

### Saros Series

A saros is a period of about 6585.3 days (18 years 11⅓ days), equal to 223 synodic months, 242 draconic months, and very nearly 239 anomalistic months. After one saros the Sun, the Moon, and the lunar node return to nearly the same geometry, so an eclipse is followed by a very similar one; the extra third of a day shifts it about 120° west in longitude. Eclipses separated by whole saroses are grouped into numbered saros series, each of which typically lasts more than a thousand years, with separate numberings for solar and lunar eclipses.

`solarSaros` returns the solar series number, from 1 to 223 as in the van den Bergh catalog, for the lunation that contains an instant, using the Kluepfel formula on the Meeus lunation index. `lunarSaros` returns the lunar series number, from 1 to 223, counting from the full moon of 18 January 2003 (series 192) and advancing by 38 (modulo 223) per lunation. Both are numberings of the lunation, not tests that an eclipse occurs: not every lunation belongs to a series that produces one, so find the eclipse with [Solar Eclipse Search and Classification](#solar-eclipse-search-and-classification) or [Lunar Eclipse Search](#lunar-eclipse-search) and pass its maximal time here to get its series.

```ts
import { lunarSaros } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/moon'
import { nearestSolarEclipse, solarSaros } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/sun'
import { Timescale, timeYMD, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

// Solar saros series of the lunation containing a date.
console.log(solarSaros(timeYMD(2017, 8, 21))) // 145 — the "Great American" total eclipse of 21 August 2017
console.log(solarSaros(timeYMD(1999, 8, 11))) // 145 — the same series, one saros (18 years) earlier

// The series of the next solar eclipse, from its time of greatest eclipse.
const eclipse = nearestSolarEclipse(timeYMDHMS(2025, 3, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), true)

console.log(solarSaros(eclipse.maximalTime)) // 149 — the partial eclipse of 29 March 2025

// Lunar saros series of the lunation containing a date.
console.log(lunarSaros(timeYMD(2025, 9, 7))) // 128 — the total lunar eclipse of 7 September 2025
console.log(lunarSaros(timeYMD(2026, 3, 3))) // 133 — the total lunar eclipse of 3 March 2026
```

### Satellite Collision Probability

The probability of collision (Pc) of a satellite conjunction is the chance that two objects, whose positions at the time of closest approach (TCA) are uncertain, come within their combined hard-body radius `R`. It is the quantity operators use to decide whether to perform an avoidance maneuver. In the short-encounter model (Foster and Estes 1992, Chan 1997, Alfano 2005) the relative motion is a straight line during the brief encounter and the position errors are independent Gaussians with combined covariance `C = C₁ + C₂`, so the problem collapses onto the **encounter plane** perpendicular to the relative velocity: Pc is the mass of the projected 2D Gaussian, centred at the miss vector, inside a disk of radius `R`.

```text
Pc = 1 / (2π √|C₂ᴰ|) ∬_{|r| ≤ R} exp(−½ (r − m)ᵀ C₂ᴰ⁻¹ (r − m)) dA
```

The integral is evaluated by adaptive quadrature; the small-object approximation, the density at the disk centre times `πR²`, is valid only when `R` is much smaller than the minor sigma of the plane, and its domain is reported. Neither describes the error of the short-encounter model itself, which does not hold for slow encounters with curved relative motion, a covariance that changes during the encounter, or velocity uncertainty; the model diagnostics are screening heuristics, not error bounds.

The covariance comes from orbit determination, typically delivered in a CCSDS Conjunction Data Message (CDM); it is never derived from TLEs, so an SGP4 screen with [Satellite Conjunctions](#satellite-conjunctions) can find a candidate but cannot supply its Pc. The parser reads CCSDS 508.0-B-1 CDMs version 1.0 in KVN form, strictly, since the text is untrusted, and converts them to library units (AU, AU/day, UTC). The RTN covariances are rotated into the message reference frame; Pc does not depend on the orientation of the shared frame. The CDM carries no hard-body radius, so the caller supplies `R`.

```ts
import { parseCDM } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/cdm'
import { cdmCollisionProbability, cdmEncounterStates, collisionProbability, rotateStateCovariance, rtnRotation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/collision'
import { meter, toMeter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// The CCSDS 508.0-B-1 example message as KVN text ("CCSDS_CDM_VERS = 1.0", "TCA = ...", ...), a repository fixture.
const cdm = parseCDM(await Bun.file('data/cdm.kvn').text())

console.log(toMeter(cdm.relative.missDistance)) // 715 — reported miss distance, m

// Pc for a combined hard-body radius of 20 m, with the encounter-plane geometry and covariance checks.
const result = cdmCollisionProbability(cdm, meter(20))

if (result.kind === 'estimate') {
	console.log(result.probability) // 4.7428e-7
	console.log(toMeter(result.geometry.plane.sigmaMajor), toMeter(result.geometry.plane.sigmaMinor)) // 207.49 20.943 — m
}

// The same estimate from two states in one frame at the same epoch.
const [primary, secondary] = cdmEncounterStates(cdm)
const small = collisionProbability(primary, secondary, meter(5))

// RTN axes of a state (rows R, T, N), and its 6×6 covariance rotated into them; the transpose rotates an RTN covariance back to the frame.
const rtn = rtnRotation(primary.position, primary.velocity)!
const covariance = rotateStateCovariance(primary.covariance, rtn)
console.log(toMeter(Math.sqrt(covariance.get(0, 0))), toMeter(Math.sqrt(covariance.get(1, 1)))) // 6.436 50.329 — 1σ radial and along-track, m, as in the message
```

### Satellite Conjunctions

A conjunction, in space-surveillance usage, is a close approach between two orbiting objects. With tens of thousands of tracked objects in Earth orbit, operators screen their satellites against the catalog to find the approaches worth a closer look: the time of closest approach (TCA), the miss distance, and the relative speed, which sets how brief and how energetic an encounter would be.

The screen propagates both objects with SGP4 from their TLEs in the shared TEME frame, so the separation is the direct difference of the two positions, and reports the local minima of the separation, optionally below a distance threshold. It is a geometric screen of the SGP4 states, not a collision probability: TLEs carry no covariance (see [Satellite Collision Probability](#satellite-collision-probability)). SGP4 is only valid near each TLE epoch, so the window should stay within a few days of the epochs of both objects, and the sampling step must be finer than the approach to catch, since a deep and brief minimum at high relative speed can fall between two samples.

```ts
import { satelliteConjunctions } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/satellite'
import { parseTLE, recordFromTLE } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/propagation/sgp4'
import { timeShift } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { AU_KM, DAYSEC } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'
import { kilometer, toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const tle = parseTLE('1 25544U 98067A   20330.54791667  .00016717  00000-0  10270-3 0  9000', '2 25544  51.6442  21.4611 0001363  85.7790 274.3535 15.49180547 25697', 'ISS')
const iss = recordFromTLE(tle)

// A synthetic companion: the ISS elements with the ascending node shifted by +10°, so the orbital planes cross.
const companion = recordFromTLE(parseTLE('1 25545U 98067A   20330.54791667  .00016717  00000-0  10270-3 0  9000', '2 25545  51.6442  31.4611 0001363  85.7790 274.3535 15.49180547 25697', 'COMPANION'))

// Separation minima in the six hours after the epoch, closer than 735 km.
for (const conjunction of satelliteConjunctions(iss, companion, tle.epoch, timeShift(tle.epoch, 0.25), { threshold: kilometer(735) })) {
	console.log(conjunction.time, toKilometer(conjunction.distance), (conjunction.relativeSpeed * AU_KM) / DAYSEC) // TCA, km, km/s
}
```

### Satellite Eclipses

A satellite in low orbit spends part of each revolution in the shadow of the Earth. The eclipses set its power budget and thermal cycle, and for a visual observer they decide whether a satellite above the horizon can be seen at all, since it shines only by reflected sunlight. The shadow model is conical, using the apparent angular radii of the Sun and of the Earth's spherical limb as seen from the satellite: the satellite is in **umbra** when the Earth's disk fully covers the Sun's, in **penumbra** when it covers it partially, and **sunlit** otherwise.

The Earth is a sphere of radius `EARTH_RADIUS_AU` with no atmospheric refraction, and the satellite is propagated with SGP4. The Sun comes from a provider of its geocentric position (AU, ICRS), called at every sample, so a cheap provider matters. An eclipse interval is measured to the umbra or to the penumbra boundary; penumbra does not count as sunlit, and intervals that touch the window edges are clipped to it.

```ts
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { isSatelliteSunlit, satelliteEclipses, satelliteShadowState } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/satellite'
import { parseTLE, recordFromTLE } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/propagation/sgp4'
import { type Time, timeShift } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'

const tle = parseTLE('1 25544U 98067A   20330.54791667  .00016717  00000-0  10270-3 0  9000', '2 25544  51.6442  21.4611 0001363  85.7790 274.3535 15.49180547 25697', 'ISS')
const iss = recordFromTLE(tle)
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0]) // geocentric ICRS, AU

// Shadow state at one instant, and whether the solar disk is wholly unobscured (penumbra is not sunlit).
console.log(satelliteShadowState(iss, sunAt, tle.epoch)) // umbra
console.log(isSatelliteSunlit(iss, sunAt, tle.epoch)) // false

// Umbral eclipses in the six hours after the epoch; the first one has no entry, since the window starts in the shadow.
for (const eclipse of satelliteEclipses(iss, sunAt, tle.epoch, timeShift(tle.epoch, 0.25))) console.log(eclipse.entry, eclipse.exit, eclipse.duration)
// the full eclipses last about 2130 s

// Penumbral eclipses are slightly longer, since they include the partial shadow.
const penumbra = satelliteEclipses(iss, sunAt, tle.epoch, timeShift(tle.epoch, 0.25), { boundary: 'penumbra' })
```

### Satellite Ground Footprint

The ground footprint, or coverage cap, of a satellite is the part of the Earth from which it is above the geometric horizon: the area it can see, and from which it can be seen or contacted by radio. Its size grows with the satellite's height; for the ISS at about 420 km it is a circle of roughly 2250 km radius.

It is an explicit spherical approximation: the Earth is a sphere of a reference radius, so the subpoint latitude is **spherical** (geocentric), not the geodetic latitude of [Satellite Sub-point](#satellite-sub-point), and terrain, refraction, and any elevation mask are ignored. The cap's half-angle, measured at the Earth's center, follows from the satellite's geocentric radius `r`, the reference radius `R`, and the height `h = r − R`; the surface radius is the arc length from the subpoint to the horizon.

```text
halfAngle = atan2(√(h·(r + R)), R) = acos(R / r)
```

```ts
import { satelliteGroundFootprint } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/satellite'
import { parseTLE, recordFromTLE } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/propagation/sgp4'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { kilometer, toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const tle = parseTLE('1 25544U 98067A   20330.54791667  .00016717  00000-0  10270-3 0  9000', '2 25544  51.6442  21.4611 0001363  85.7790 274.3535 15.49180547 25697', 'ISS')
const iss = recordFromTLE(tle)

// Coverage cap at the TLE epoch over the default reference sphere (6378.135 km).
const footprint = satelliteGroundFootprint(iss, tle.epoch)
console.log(toKilometer(footprint.altitude)) // 419.79 — km above the sphere
console.log(toDeg(footprint.halfAngle), toKilometer(footprint.surfaceRadius)) // 20.24 2253.2 — degrees, km of arc

// Over a sphere of mean radius 6371 km the cap is slightly larger.
const mean = satelliteGroundFootprint(iss, tle.epoch, kilometer(6371))
```

### Satellite Look Angles

The look angles of a satellite are where it appears for a ground observer: azimuth, altitude, and slant range. They are what an antenna rotator or a telescope mount points to, and what decides whether the satellite is above the horizon. The satellite is propagated with SGP4 in the TEME frame, rotated to the Earth-fixed ITRS frame, and differenced against the observer's ITRS position; the topocentric vector is then resolved onto the local horizon of the geodetic vertical.

Azimuth is measured from north through east, the altitude is geometric with no refraction (negative below the horizon), and the range is the observer-to-satellite distance in AU. No light time or aberration is applied. SGP4 is only meaningful near the epoch of the element set, so queries should stay within a few days of it.

```ts
import { satelliteLookAngles } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/satellite'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { parseTLE, recordFromTLE } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/propagation/sgp4'
import { timeShift } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const tle = parseTLE('1 25544U 98067A   20330.54791667  .00016717  00000-0  10270-3 0  9000', '2 25544  51.6442  21.4611 0001363  85.7790 274.3535 15.49180547 25697', 'ISS')
const iss = recordFromTLE(tle)
const site = geodeticLocation(deg(-46.6361), deg(-23.5475), 0) // São Paulo: longitude, latitude, height

// Azimuth, altitude, and range one hour after the TLE epoch.
const angles = satelliteLookAngles(iss, site, timeShift(tle.epoch, 1 / 24))
console.log(toDeg(angles.azimuth), toDeg(angles.altitude), toKilometer(angles.range)) // 153.318 3.433 2033.7 — degrees, km
```

### Satellite Orbit Beta Angle

The beta angle of an orbit is the elevation of the Sun above the orbital plane. It controls how long the satellite spends in sunlight: at a beta angle of 0° the Sun lies in the orbital plane and a low orbit crosses the Earth's shadow on every revolution, while a high beta angle shortens or removes the eclipses. It also drives the thermal and power conditions of the spacecraft, and it changes slowly as the orbital plane precesses and the Sun moves along the ecliptic.

The orbit normal is the SGP4 angular momentum `r × v`, rotated from TEME to the geocentric ICRS axes, and `β = asin(n̂·ŝ)` with `ŝ` the direction to the Sun. The sign is positive when the Sun lies on the side of the orbital angular momentum. The value is that of the osculating orbit at the given time, and SGP4 should be used only near the epoch of the element set.

```ts
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { satelliteBetaAngle } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/satellite'
import { parseTLE, recordFromTLE } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/propagation/sgp4'
import { type Time, timeShift } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const tle = parseTLE('1 25544U 98067A   20330.54791667  .00016717  00000-0  10270-3 0  9000', '2 25544  51.6442  21.4611 0001363  85.7790 274.3535 15.49180547 25697', 'ISS')
const iss = recordFromTLE(tle)
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0]) // geocentric ICRS, AU

// Beta angle (radians) at the epoch and one day later.
console.log(toDeg(satelliteBetaAngle(iss, sunAt, tle.epoch))) // 14.62 — degrees
console.log(toDeg(satelliteBetaAngle(iss, sunAt, timeShift(tle.epoch, 1)))) // 17.81 — degrees
```

### Satellite Passes

A pass is one appearance of a satellite above a ground site's horizon, from rise to set, with its culmination, the highest point, in between. A low-orbit satellite such as the ISS makes a few passes a day over a given site, each lasting minutes; the culmination altitude tells how long and how close the pass is, and the azimuths of rise and set tell where to look or point an antenna. A minimum altitude can replace the ideal horizon to model local obstructions or an elevation mask.

Altitudes are geometric, with no refraction, azimuth is north through east, and the range is in AU. The standard search keeps only passes whose rise and set both lie in the window; the window search also keeps the passes the window cuts, marking which bound is the window edge rather than a horizon crossing, and handles a satellite that stays above the limit throughout, such as a geostationary one. The sampling step must be shorter than the shortest pass that matters, or a brief grazing pass can be missed.

```ts
import { satellitePasses, satelliteWindowPasses } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/satellite'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { parseTLE, recordFromTLE } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/propagation/sgp4'
import { timeShift } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const tle = parseTLE('1 25544U 98067A   20330.54791667  .00016717  00000-0  10270-3 0  9000', '2 25544  51.6442  21.4611 0001363  85.7790 274.3535 15.49180547 25697', 'ISS')
const iss = recordFromTLE(tle)
const site = geodeticLocation(deg(-46.6361), deg(-23.5475), 0) // São Paulo

// Passes reaching at least 10° of altitude in the day after the epoch.
for (const pass of satellitePasses(iss, site, tle.epoch, timeShift(tle.epoch, 1), { minAltitude: deg(10) })) {
	console.log(toDeg(pass.rise.azimuth), toDeg(pass.culmination.altitude), toKilometer(pass.culmination.range), toDeg(pass.set.azimuth))
}
// 291.92 32.06 749.5 160.63 — degrees, km
// 203.75 38.78 651.8 62.08

// A window that starts during a pass keeps it, starting at the window start.
const [clipped] = satelliteWindowPasses(iss, site, timeShift(tle.epoch, 53 / 1440), timeShift(tle.epoch, 70 / 1440))
console.log(clipped.startsBeforeWindow, clipped.endsAfterWindow) // true false
```

### Satellite Sub-point

The sub-point of a satellite is the point of the Earth's surface directly beneath it, along the ellipsoid normal. Its succession over time is the ground track drawn on maps, and its height above the ellipsoid is the altitude usually quoted for a satellite. SGP4 gives the position in TEME, which is rotated to the Earth-fixed ITRS frame and converted to geodetic coordinates on the chosen ellipsoid (`Ellipsoid.IERS2010` by default, like the other geographic-position APIs).

The longitude is east-positive in `(−π, π]`, the latitude geodetic, both in radians, and the elevation in AU. For the spherical coverage cap, see [Satellite Ground Footprint](#satellite-ground-footprint). Propagation is only meaningful near the epoch of the element set.

```ts
import { satelliteSubpoint } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/satellite'
import { Ellipsoid } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { parseTLE, recordFromTLE } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/propagation/sgp4'
import { timeShift } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const tle = parseTLE('1 25544U 98067A   20330.54791667  .00016717  00000-0  10270-3 0  9000', '2 25544  51.6442  21.4611 0001363  85.7790 274.3535 15.49180547 25697', 'ISS')
const iss = recordFromTLE(tle)

// Geodetic sub-point at the TLE epoch.
const subpoint = satelliteSubpoint(iss, tle.epoch)
console.log(toDeg(subpoint.longitude), toDeg(subpoint.latitude), toKilometer(subpoint.elevation)) // 119.282 0.01425 419.79 — degrees, km

// 1.5 hours later on the WGS84 ellipsoid.
const wgs84 = satelliteSubpoint(iss, timeShift(tle.epoch, 0.0625), Ellipsoid.WGS84)
console.log(toDeg(wgs84.latitude), toKilometer(wgs84.elevation)) // −8.802 421.535
```

### Satellite Tracking Rates

Following a satellite with a mount or an antenna, or correcting a radio link for the Doppler shift, needs more than its position: it needs the rates. The range rate is the derivative of the slant range, the input of a Doppler correction (see [Radial Doppler Shift](#radial-doppler-shift)); the angular rate is how fast the line of sight sweeps across the sky, which for a low-orbit satellite near culmination reaches tenths of a degree per second, far beyond sidereal tracking.

The SGP4 state is rotated from TEME to the geocentric inertial axes, the observer's position and diurnal velocity are subtracted, and the rates follow analytically from the observer-relative vectors `r` and `v`. The range rate is positive when the satellite recedes. The angular rate is measured in **inertial** axes, so it is the rate at which a mount referenced to the fixed stars must move, not the derivative of azimuth or altitude in the rotating horizon frame. No refraction or light time is applied, and SGP4 is only meaningful near the TLE epoch.

```text
rangeRate = r·v / |r|      angularRate = |r × v| / |r|²
```

```ts
import { satellitePasses, satelliteTrackingState } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/satellite'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { parseTLE, recordFromTLE } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/propagation/sgp4'
import { timeShift } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { AU_KM, DAYSEC } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const tle = parseTLE('1 25544U 98067A   20330.54791667  .00016717  00000-0  10270-3 0  9000', '2 25544  51.6442  21.4611 0001363  85.7790 274.3535 15.49180547 25697', 'ISS')
const iss = recordFromTLE(tle)
const site = geodeticLocation(deg(-46.6361), deg(-23.5475), 0) // São Paulo

// The culmination of the second pass above 10° in the day after the epoch.
const [, pass] = satellitePasses(iss, site, tle.epoch, timeShift(tle.epoch, 1), { minAltitude: deg(10) })

// Look angles plus range rate (AU/day) and inertial angular rate (radians/day).
const state = satelliteTrackingState(iss, site, pass.culmination.time)
console.log((state.rangeRate * AU_KM) / DAYSEC) // −0.0244 — km/s, near zero at the minimum range
console.log(toDeg(state.angularRate) / DAYSEC) // 0.6468 — degrees/s, the fastest point of the pass
```

### Satellite Trail Prediction

Satellites crossing the field of view leave bright streaks on long astronomical exposures, a growing problem with large constellations in low orbit. Predicting whether a satellite will cross the frame during an exposure, where it enters and leaves the sensor, and how long the streak is lets an astrophotographer delay an exposure, mask the trail, or reject the frame.

The prediction is geometric and topocentric for a site on the Earth: the SGP4 track is sampled adaptively and clipped against a gnomonic rectangle, the sensor, centered on the field and rotated by a position angle from celestial north toward east; no light time, aberration, refraction, or illumination is applied. Each visit to the sensor gives the entry and exit points (time, equatorial coordinates, and sensor-plane position), the chord length, the position angle of the motion, and optionally the length in pixels. The length is the chord between entry and exit, a good approximation for the short crossings of a single exposure. For a track the caller already has, such as the ephemeris of another body, the same clipping is available on its own as `sensorTrails`.

```ts
import { customEphemerisEndpoint, relativeEphemerisPath } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/path'
import { earthObserverEphemerisPath, sgp4EphemerisPath } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/path.adapter'
import { ephemerisAt, equatorialPosition } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/position'
import { predictSatelliteTrails, sensorTrails } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/satellite.trail'
import { Ellipsoid, geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { parseTLE, recordFromTLE } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/propagation/sgp4'
import { timeShift, tt } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toArcsec, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const tle = parseTLE('1 25544U 98067A   20330.54791667  .00016717  00000-0  10270-3 0  9000', '2 25544  51.6442  21.4611 0001363  85.7790 274.3535 15.49180547 25697', 'ISS')
const iss = recordFromTLE(tle)
const site = geodeticLocation(deg(-46.6361), deg(-23.5475), 0, Ellipsoid.WGS84) // São Paulo
const at = (seconds: number) => timeShift(tt(tle.epoch), seconds / 86400) // seconds after the TLE epoch

// Field center where the ISS will be 3332 s after the epoch, near its culmination.
const path = relativeEphemerisPath(sgp4EphemerisPath({ ...iss }), earthObserverEphemerisPath(site, customEphemerisEndpoint('site')))
const [rightAscension, declination] = equatorialPosition(ephemerisAt(path, at(3332)))

// A 0.1° square field rotated by 0.7 rad, a 4 s exposure, and an image scale of 2"/pixel.
const [trail] = predictSatelliteTrails(iss, site, rightAscension, declination, { width: deg(0.1), height: deg(0.1), positionAngle: 0.7 }, at(3330), at(3334), { arcsecPerPixel: 2 })
console.log(toArcsec(trail.length), trail.lengthPixels, toDeg(trail.positionAngle)) // 471.80 235.90 179.84 — the crossing lasts 0.23 s

// The clipping alone, for a sampled track (time in any unit, coordinates in radians).
const [crossing] = sensorTrails(0, 0, { width: deg(1), height: deg(1) }, [
	{ time: 0, rightAscension: -deg(1), declination: 0 },
	{ time: 1, rightAscension: deg(1), declination: 0 },
])
console.log(crossing.entry.time, crossing.exit.time) // 0.25 0.75 — on the sensor for half of the track
```

### Satellite Visibility Intervals

A satellite can be seen with the naked eye or a camera only when several conditions hold at once: it is high enough above the horizon, the observer's sky is dark, the satellite itself is still in sunlight rather than in the Earth's umbra, and it is bright enough. That combination is why satellites are seen mostly in the hours after dusk and before dawn. A visibility interval is an unbroken stretch of time throughout which **all** these criteria hold.

The minimum altitude and the maximum solar altitude must be given explicitly, since there is no objective twilight default. The brightness criterion needs the satellite's empirical standard magnitude (see [Satellite Visual Magnitude](#satellite-visual-magnitude)) and a magnitude limit, given together; without them it is dropped. Each interval reports its start, culmination, and end, with the magnitude, the observer's solar altitude, and the shadow state; an interval can end as the satellite enters the umbra. Refraction, extinction, flares, terrain, and penumbral dimming are not modeled, and the scanning step must resolve every crossing.

```ts
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { satelliteVisibleIntervals } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/satellite'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { parseTLE, recordFromTLE } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/propagation/sgp4'
import { type Time, timeShift } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const tle = parseTLE('1 25544U 98067A   20330.54791667  .00016717  00000-0  10270-3 0  9000', '2 25544  51.6442  21.4611 0001363  85.7790 274.3535 15.49180547 25697', 'ISS')
const iss = recordFromTLE(tle)
const site = geodeticLocation(deg(-46.6361), deg(-23.5475), 0) // São Paulo
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0]) // geocentric ICRS, AU

// Higher than 10°, brighter than magnitude 3, with the Sun more than 6° below the horizon, in the day after the epoch.
const [interval] = satelliteVisibleIntervals(iss, site, sunAt, tle.epoch, timeShift(tle.epoch, 1), { standardMagnitude: -1.8, minimumAltitude: deg(10), maximumMagnitude: 3, maximumSunAltitude: deg(-6) })

console.log(interval.start.magnitude, interval.start.shadow) // 0.5436 sunlit
console.log(toDeg(interval.culmination.altitude), interval.culmination.magnitude) // 38.78 −3.057
console.log(interval.end.shadow) // umbra — it fades into the Earth's shadow
```

### Satellite Visual Magnitude

Whether a satellite pass is worth watching depends on how bright it will look, and that depends on the geometry more than on the satellite: its distance from the observer and how much of its sunlit side faces the observer. The standard-magnitude model of Molczan and McCants treats the satellite as a diffuse sphere, `m = m_std − 15.75 + 2.5·log10(range_km² / f)`, where `f = (1 + cos φ) / 2` is the illuminated fraction and `φ` is the Sun-satellite-observer phase angle (zero at full phase). The standard magnitude `m_std` is an empirical constant of each object, its brightness at 1000 km and half illumination (phase angle 90°); about −1.8 is the value usually quoted for the ISS. Smaller magnitudes are brighter.

`satelliteMagnitude` evaluates this model for a ground observer at one instant and reports whether the satellite is sunlit: inside the Earth's umbra it reflects no sunlight and the magnitude is meaningless (penumbra counts as illuminated). The model has no atmospheric extinction, no refraction, no specular flares, and no dependence on the orientation of the satellite, so it is a planning estimate rather than a photometric prediction. Pair it with [Satellite Passes](#satellite-passes) to evaluate a pass at its culmination.

```ts
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { satelliteMagnitude, satellitePasses } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/satellite'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { parseTLE, recordFromTLE } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/propagation/sgp4'
import { type Time, timeShift } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const tle = parseTLE('1 25544U 98067A   20330.54791667  .00016717  00000-0  10270-3 0  9000', '2 25544  51.6442  21.4611 0001363  85.7790 274.3535 15.49180547 25697', 'ISS')
const iss = recordFromTLE(tle)
const site = geodeticLocation(deg(-46.6361), deg(-23.5475), 0) // São Paulo

// Geocentric Sun position (AU, ICRS) at any instant.
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0])

// The second pass of the day above 10°, evaluated at its culmination with a standard magnitude of −1.8.
const [, pass] = satellitePasses(iss, site, tle.epoch, timeShift(tle.epoch, 1), { minAltitude: deg(10) })
const bright = satelliteMagnitude(iss, site, sunAt, pass.culmination.time, -1.8)

console.log(bright.illuminated) // true — the magnitude is meaningful only while sunlit
console.log(bright.magnitude) // −3.057 — visual magnitude
console.log(toDeg(bright.phaseAngle)) // 69.20 — degrees, Sun-satellite-observer
```

### Saturn Ring Geometry

Saturn's rings lie in its equatorial plane, which is tilted about 27° to its orbit, so over Saturn's 29.5-year year the rings swing from wide open to edge-on and back. Their appearance is described by B, the Saturnicentric latitude of the Earth above the ring plane (the opening seen from Earth, positive on the north side), B′, the same latitude of the Sun (which side is lit), and P, the position angle of Saturn's projected north pole from celestial north toward the east. The apparent minor axis of the ring ellipse is the major axis times `|sin B|`. When B and B′ have opposite signs the Earth sees the unlit face of the rings.

Twice per Saturnian year the Earth crosses the ring plane and the rings nearly vanish, and the Sun crosses it at Saturn's equinox; the two crossings are different events, often weeks apart, and the Earth may cross three times in one season. `saturnRingGeometry` computes the apparent geometry at an observed geocentric instant, with Saturn light-time retarded and its IAU pole evaluated at the emission instant; `saturnRingEvents` finds the Earth and solar plane crossings and the extrema of B in a time window. B and B′ are planetocentric latitudes, while JPL Horizons tabulates planetodetic ones, which differ away from zero but cross zero together. The rings are modeled as an infinitely thin annulus without photometry, with the C, B and A rings and the Cassini Division from the NASA NSSDC fact sheet.

Both functions take one [Saturnian ephemeris source](#saturnian-ephemeris-sources), and only the Sun, the Earth and Saturn's centre are evaluated. For multi-year searches, wrap the source in its ring interpolator.

```ts
import { analyticalSaturnianEphemeris, interpolatedSaturnianRingEphemeris } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/saturnian'
import { saturnRingEvents, saturnRingGeometry, saturnRingIllumination, saturnRingOpenings } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/saturn.rings'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 11, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Ring openings B and B′ and pole position angle P at one instant (radians).
const rings = saturnRingGeometry(analyticalSaturnianEphemeris, time)

console.log(toDeg(rings.earthOpening), toDeg(rings.solarOpening), toDeg(rings.polePositionAngle)) // ~-6.58 ~-8.11 ~3.40 — degrees
console.log(rings.illumination) // sameFace — the Earth sees the lit side

// Only B and B′, without the sky geometry: cheap enough for scanning.
const openings = saturnRingOpenings(analyticalSaturnianEphemeris, time)

console.log(toDeg(openings.earthOpening), toDeg(openings.solarOpening)) // ~-6.58 ~-8.11 — degrees

// Which face is seen, from any pair of openings (radians).
console.log(saturnRingIllumination(deg(5), deg(-3))) // oppositeFaces — the Earth sees the unlit side

// Ring-plane crossings and opening extrema in [start, stop), on a coarse ring-only interpolator.
const ephemeris = interpolatedSaturnianRingEphemeris(analyticalSaturnianEphemeris)

for (const event of saturnRingEvents(ephemeris, timeYMDHMS(2038, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), timeYMDHMS(2040, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC))) {
	console.log(event.kind, event.time, toDeg(event.earthOpening)) // three Earth crossings and one solar crossing
}
```

### Saturnian Ephemeris Sources

Every Saturnian computation (ring geometry, moon positions, phenomena) combines the positions of the Sun, the Earth, Saturn's centre, and its seven major moons from Mimas to Iapetus (Hyperion is omitted). Mixing sources inside one computation would introduce inconsistent offsets far larger than the effects being computed, so every state of one computation comes from one `SaturnianEphemeris`, with the same contract as a [Jovian ephemeris](#jovian-ephemeris-sources): barycentric positions in AU and ICRF axes.

Two sources are provided. The analytical source uses VSOP87E for the Sun, the Earth and Saturn, and adds the [TASS 1.7](#saturnian-satellite-theory-tass17) Saturnicentric offsets for the moons; it is always available. The SPK source resolves each body through a prepared [SPK kernel set](#spk-state-kernels): Saturn is NAIF 699, the planet's centre, not the system barycenter 6, and the moons are 601–606 and 608. A planetary kernel that has Saturn's centre, such as NAIF's `sat480.bsp`, is enough for the rings, while the moons need a satellite kernel such as `sat441.bsp`; DE440s has neither. Dense event searches wrap either source in an interpolator.

```ts
import type { SpkKernelSet } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/spk.kernelset'
import { analyticalSaturnianEphemeris, hasSaturnianTargets, interpolatedSaturnianEphemeris, SATURNIAN_RING_BODIES, spkSaturnianEphemeris } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/saturnian'
import { saturnRingGeometry } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/saturn.rings'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

declare const set: SpkKernelSet // prepared with prepareSpkKernelSet from sat480.bsp

// Use the kernels when they hold the bodies the computation needs (here only the Sun, the Earth and Saturn), else the theories.
const source = hasSaturnianTargets(set, SATURNIAN_RING_BODIES) ? spkSaturnianEphemeris(set) : analyticalSaturnianEphemeris

const rings = saturnRingGeometry(source, timeYMDHMS(2026, 11, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC))

// An interpolated source for dense searches of moon events.
const dense = interpolatedSaturnianEphemeris(analyticalSaturnianEphemeris)
```

### Saturnian Satellite Geometry

Through a telescope Saturn's moons appear as points strung around the planet, and identifying them, or planning to catch one in front of or behind the globe, needs their apparent offsets from Saturn's centre. `saturnianView` returns, for one observed geocentric instant, the [ring geometry](#saturn-ring-geometry) together with each moon's offset east and north of Saturn's apparent centre and its depth toward the Earth (in Saturn equatorial radii), its separation and position angle, and whether it is in front of or behind the disk, in Saturn's shadow, or over the projected rings.

The disk, shadow and eclipse geometry is the oblate-planet geometry shared with [Jovian Satellite Geometry](#jovian-satellite-geometry), using Saturn's IAU radii and pole. A ring overlap is only geometric: the rings have no optical depth in this model, and their shadows and the moons' shadows on the rings are not modeled. With the analytical source the offsets agree with JPL Horizons within 0.1″ (0.25″ for Iapetus).

`saturnianSeparationMaxima` finds the greatest elongations of each moon in a window, two per orbit. They are maxima of the angular separation itself, not of an east-west coordinate, which differ for the inclined orbit of Iapetus; a window shorter than half an orbit of a slow moon may hold none.

```ts
import { analyticalSaturnianEphemeris, interpolatedSaturnianEphemeris } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/saturnian'
import { skyBasis } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/satellites.geometry'
import { saturnianMoonView, saturnianSeparationMaxima, saturnianView } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/saturn.geometry'
import { saturnRingGeometryOf, saturnRingOpenings } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/saturn.rings'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 11, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Apparent positions of the seven major moons at one instant.
const view = saturnianView(analyticalSaturnianEphemeris, time)

for (const moon of view.moons) console.log(moon.moon, toDeg(moon.separation) * 3600, moon.disk, moon.ringOverlap) // arcseconds from Saturn's centre

// The steps of the view, to evaluate the system state once while sampling a track: the ring openings
// with their state, the sky basis of the line of sight, the ring geometry, and one moon.
const openings = saturnRingOpenings(analyticalSaturnianEphemeris, time)
const basis = skyBasis(time, openings.state.lineOfSight)
const rings = saturnRingGeometryOf(openings, basis)
const titan = saturnianMoonView(analyticalSaturnianEphemeris, openings.state, basis, 'titan')

console.log(toDeg(rings.polePositionAngle), toDeg(titan.separation) * 3600) // 3.40 28.75 — degrees, and arcseconds as in the view

// Greatest elongations of Titan and Iapetus in November 2026, on an interpolated source.
const ephemeris = interpolatedSaturnianEphemeris(analyticalSaturnianEphemeris)
const maxima = saturnianSeparationMaxima(ephemeris, time, timeYMDHMS(2026, 12, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), ['titan', 'iapetus'])

for (const maximum of maxima) console.log(maximum.moon, maximum.time, toDeg(maximum.separation) * 3600) // Iapetus ~567″ on 2026-11-10
```

### Saturnian Satellite Phenomena

Saturn's major moons orbit in its ring plane, so they pass in front of the planet, cast shadows on it, hide behind it, or enter its shadow only in the seasons around Saturn's equinoxes, when the Earth and the Sun lie close to that plane. These mutual events are rare observing opportunities, and predicting their contacts needs Saturn's oblate disk and its shadow rather than a spherical approximation.

`saturnianPhenomena` finds the transits, shadow transits, occultations, and eclipses of Mimas, Enceladus, Tethys, Dione, Rhea, Titan, and Iapetus whose conjunction lies in a time window, with the same contacts and conventions as [Galilean Satellite Phenomena](#galilean-satellite-phenomena), on Saturn's oblate IAU 1-bar disk (see [Saturnian Satellite Geometry](#saturnian-satellite-geometry)). The rings are not part of this geometry: a moon or a shadow seen across the rings is reported like any other, and the rings' own occultations and shadows are not predicted. Against JPL Horizons, the inner moons' transits, the moons becoming wholly umbral, and the occultation ends agree within about a minute with the analytical source.

```ts
import { analyticalSaturnianEphemeris, interpolatedSaturnianEphemeris } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/saturnian'
import { saturnianPhenomena } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/saturn.phenomena'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

// An interpolated source keeps the dense contact search fast.
const ephemeris = interpolatedSaturnianEphemeris(analyticalSaturnianEphemeris)

// Titan's phenomena in the first half of April 2025, near the 2025 ring-plane crossing.
const phenomena = saturnianPhenomena(ephemeris, timeYMDHMS(2025, 4, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), timeYMDHMS(2025, 4, 14, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), { moons: ['titan'] })

for (const p of phenomena) console.log(p.kind, p.external1, p.maximum, p.external2) // Titan's eclipse and occultation on April 5, its shadow transit and transit on April 13
```

### Saturnian Satellite Theory (TASS1.7)

TASS 1.7 (Vienne and Duriez) is the IMCCE analytical theory of the eight major Saturnian satellites, Mimas to Iapetus and Hyperion. It represents each orbit by equinoctial element series built from integer combinations of the satellites' mean longitudes, which capture the strong mutual resonances of the system (Mimas–Tethys, Enceladus–Dione, Titan–Hyperion), and needs no external data file.

Each satellite function takes a `Time` in any scale (converted to TT) and returns the Saturnicentric position in AU and velocity in AU/day, in J2000 equatorial axes; add Saturn's barycentric state for an inertial position. The returned vectors alias internal buffers, so copy them before computing another state, or the earlier result is silently overwritten. For a complete Saturnian computation, use the [Saturnian Ephemeris Sources](#saturnian-ephemeris-sources) built on this theory.

```ts
import { mimas, tass17, titan } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/tass17'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Saturnicentric J2000 state of Titan; copy it before the next call.
const [position, velocity] = titan(time)

console.log(position) // [0.0078347, 0.0010775, -0.00076689] — AU, Saturnicentric
console.log(velocity) // [-0.00043573, 0.0032733, -0.00018113] — AU/day
console.log(toKilometer(Math.hypot(...position))) // 1188636 — km, close to Titan's orbital radius

// The other satellites have their own functions (enceladus, tethys, dione, rhea, iapetus, hyperion);
// tass17(time, index) is the shared one (0 Mimas … 7 Hyperion).
console.log(toKilometer(Math.hypot(...mimas(time)[0]))) // 184379 — km
console.log(tass17(time, 5)[0]) // Titan again, AU
```

### SGP4/SDP4 Propagation

SGP4 and SDP4 are the standard analytical models for Earth satellites. They propagate mean orbital elements from a two-line element set (TLE) or an Orbit Mean-Elements Message (OMM), including secular gravity terms (J2, J3, J4), atmospheric drag through the `B*` coefficient, and, for deep-space orbits with periods of 225 minutes or more, lunar-solar perturbations and resonance; SGP4 is used for near-Earth objects and SDP4 for deep space, selected automatically. The elements are mean elements fitted to observations by this model: they must be propagated with it, not treated as osculating elements, and accuracy degrades with distance from the epoch, typically over days.

`sgp4` returns the position (AU) and velocity (AU/day) in the TEME frame, the quasi-inertial frame of the model, at any `Time`. It accepts a parsed TLE or OMM, but builds the satellite record on every call; for repeated propagation build the record once (see [TLE, OMM, and SGP4 Record Construction](#tle-omm-and-sgp4-record-construction)). The call throws when the model cannot propagate, such as after decay. TEME is not an Earth-fixed frame: convert it with [TEME and ITRF Conversion](#teme-and-itrf-conversion), or wrap it as a path (see [Ephemeris Path Adapters](#ephemeris-path-adapters)).

```ts
import { parseTLE, recordFromTLE, sgp4 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/propagation/sgp4'
import { timeShift } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'
import { toKilometerPerSecond } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/velocity'

const tle = parseTLE('1 25544U 98067A   23231.51768399  .00014050  00000+0  25837-3 0  9996', '2 25544  51.6415  14.7889 0003559 325.3396 149.4637 15.49477580411611', 'ISS (ZARYA)')

// TEME state at the TLE epoch.
const [position, velocity] = sgp4(tle.epoch, tle)

console.log(position.map(toKilometer)) // [-3737.79, 2970.46, 4831.15] — km, TEME
console.log(velocity.map(toKilometerPerSecond)) // [-6.2140, -3.7036, -2.5222] — km/s

// A prepared record (WGS-72 constants) for repeated propagation, here one day after the epoch.
const record = recordFromTLE(tle)

console.log(sgp4(timeShift(tle.epoch, 1), record)[0].map(toKilometer)) // [3643.22, -3199.15, -4765.94] — km, TEME
```

### Sidereal Time and Earth Rotation Angle

Sidereal time is the hour angle of the equinox: it measures how far the Earth has turned relative to the stars, and it equals the right ascension currently on the local meridian. The Earth rotation angle (ERA) measures the same rotation relative to the Celestial Intermediate Origin instead of the equinox, and is the modern IAU 2000 definition of the rotation. Greenwich mean sidereal time (GMST) uses the mean equinox; apparent sidereal time (GAST) uses the true equinox, so GAST − GMST is the equation of the equinoxes, an arcsecond-scale nutation term.

The functions take a `Time` and return radians, using the IAU 2006/2000A ERFA models; the equation of the equinoxes is wrapped to `[−π, π]` so it stays signed. All depend on UT1, so they use the loaded Earth orientation data; without it UT1 equals UTC and the angle is off by up to about 0.9 s of rotation (see [Earth Orientation Parameters](#earth-orientation-parameters)). For local sidereal time at a site, see [Geographic Observer](#geographic-observer).

```ts
import { earthRotationAngle, equationOfEquinoxes, greenwichApparentSiderealTime, greenwichMeanSiderealTime, Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toArcsec, toDeg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A UT1 instant, so the example does not depend on loaded Earth orientation data.
const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UT1)

// Mean and apparent Greenwich sidereal time, and their difference.
console.log(toHour(greenwichMeanSiderealTime(time))) // 18.4728 — hours
console.log(toHour(greenwichApparentSiderealTime(time))) // 18.4729 — hours
console.log(toArcsec(equationOfEquinoxes(time))) // 7.381 — arcseconds, GAST − GMST

// Earth rotation angle, measured from the CIO.
console.log(toDeg(earthRotationAngle(time))) // 276.752 — degrees
```

### Sky Projections

A map projection flattens the celestial or terrestrial sphere onto a plane, and no projection can preserve shape, area, and distance at once. Azimuthal projections are tangent at a chosen centre and suit fields of view and all-sky charts: the gnomonic projection maps great circles to straight lines (the projection of a camera and of a plate's standard coordinates, limited to less than a hemisphere), the stereographic is conformal, the orthographic shows a globe seen from infinity (one hemisphere), the Lambert azimuthal projection preserves area, and the azimuthal equidistant preserves distances from the centre. Cylindrical projections map the whole sphere and suit sky and world maps: Mercator is conformal and diverges at the poles, the cylindrical equal-area family (Lambert, Behrmann, Gall–Peters) preserves area, and the plate carrée maps longitude and latitude linearly.

Every projection has `project(longitude, latitude)` and its inverse `unproject(x, y)`, with angles in radians, and returns `undefined` for a point outside its domain, such as the far side of a gnomonic view or a pole in Mercator. By default the plane is in units of the sphere radius, which for small offsets equals radians; a scale turns it into arcseconds, pixels, or meters, and a sky chart can make right ascension increase to the left, as seen from inside the sphere. To project paths and polygons that cross the antimeridian, see [Projected Paths and Polygons](#projected-paths-and-polygons).

```ts
import { Gnomonic, Mercator } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/projections/projection'
import { deg, hour, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A tangent projection centered on RA 10 h, Dec +20°, and a point 2° east in RA and 3° north in Dec.
const gnomonic = new Gnomonic(hour(10), deg(20))
const point = gnomonic.project(hour(10) + deg(2), deg(23))!

console.log(point) // { x: 0.032186, y: 0.052628 } — tangent-plane units (radians for small offsets)

// The inverse returns { x: longitude, y: latitude } in radians.
const back = gnomonic.unproject(point.x, point.y)!

console.log(toDeg(back.x), toDeg(back.y)) // 152 23 — degrees of RA and Dec

// A sky chart in arcseconds, with RA increasing to the left.
const chart = new Gnomonic(hour(10), deg(20), { scale: 206264.806, raAxisDirection: 'west' })

console.log(chart.project(hour(10) + deg(2), deg(23))) // { x: -6638.9, y: 10855.2 } — arcseconds
// Other azimuthal projections (AzimuthalProjection, same constructor): Stereographic, Orthographic,
// LambertAzimuthalEqualArea, AzimuthalEquidistant.

// A cylindrical projection of the whole sphere; the pole is outside Mercator's domain.
console.log(new Mercator().project(deg(30), deg(45))) // { x: 0.5236, y: 0.8814 }
console.log(new Mercator().project(0, deg(90))) // undefined
// Other cylindrical projections (CylindricalProjection): WebMercator, EllipsoidalMercator, Miller, CentralCylindrical,
// CylindricalEqualArea with LambertCylindricalEqualArea, Behrmann, GallPeters, HoboDyer, Balthasart, TrystanEdwards,
// CylindricalStereographic with Gall and Braun, and CylindricalEquidistant with PlateCarree.
```

### Sky Surface Brightness (Krisciunas and Schaefer)

The brightness of the night sky sets the background, and therefore the limiting magnitude and the signal-to-noise ratio, of every exposure. This module predicts it in mag/arcsec² with the scattered-moonlight model of Krisciunas and Schaefer (1991, PASP 103, 1033). The sky is the flux sum of three components: the natural dark sky (airglow, zodiacal light, and faint stars), an artificial light-pollution baseline, and moonlight scattered by Rayleigh and aerosol (Mie) processes. The dark components brighten toward the horizon through the scattering airmass and are dimmed by extinction; the moonlight follows the K&S lunar phase law (with the opposition surge near full Moon and the inverse square of the lunar distance), their scattering function of the Moon–target separation, and the extinction along both lines of sight. Fluxes are in nanolamberts.

```text
B(X) = B_zen · X · 10^(−0.4·k·(X − 1))     X = (1 − 0.96·sin²Z)^(−1/2)
B[nL] = 34.08 · exp(20.7233 − 0.92104·m)    m in mag/arcsec²
```

The published calibration is for the V band at Mauna Kea, where the authors report 8–23% rms agreement. The moonlight is a physical prediction only in V; an offset for another band is a heuristic that holds at most at the separation where it was fitted. The two published aerosol fits do not meet at 10° from the Moon, so the brightness jumps there and should not be treated as a smooth function of the separation; the model also does not describe twilight, very high airmass, or the aureole close to the Moon. The light pollution shares the airmass gradient of the natural sky, so it is isotropic, not a dome brighter toward a city; consequently, sky-quality-meter readings calibrate only the sum of the natural and artificial zenith brightness, which `fitSkyBaseline` resolves by keeping the natural zenith fixed. Unlike the [Observation Scores](#observation-scores), which rank targets with dimensionless ramps, this is a photometric prediction.

```ts
import { eraS2c } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/erfa'
import { moon } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/elpmpp02'
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { Ellipsoid, geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { fitSkyBaseline, nanolambertsToSkyMagnitude, skyBrightness, skyBrightnessGeometryAt, skyMagnitudeToNanolamberts } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/sky/brightness'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { kilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// A target 60° high, 45° from a gibbous Moon (phase angle 40°) 40° high, with the V calibration.
const geometry = { altitude: deg(60), sunAltitude: deg(-25), moon: { altitude: deg(40), phaseAngle: deg(40), separation: deg(45) } }
const sky = skyBrightness(geometry)

console.log(sky.total, sky.natural, sky.moon) // 19.131 21.463 19.266 — mag/arcsec²

// The model's linear flux unit: mag/arcsec² to nanolamberts and back (K&S eq. 1).
console.log(skyMagnitudeToNanolamberts(22)) // 54.008 — nL
console.log(nanolambertsToSkyMagnitude(2 * 54.008)) // 21.247 — mag/arcsec², twice the flux is 0.75 mag brighter

// Calibrate the light pollution of a site from SQM readings (geometry plus measured mag/arcsec²).
const fit = fitSkyBaseline([
	{ altitude: deg(90), sunAltitude: deg(-30), measured: 20.2 },
	{ altitude: deg(45), sunAltitude: deg(-25), measured: 19.85 },
])!

console.log(skyBrightness(geometry, fit.model).total) // mag/arcsec² at the calibrated site

// Geometry for a target, a site and an instant, from J2000 directions and geocentric Sun and Moon positions (AU).
const site = geodeticLocation(deg(-70.7375), deg(-30.24), kilometer(2.2), Ellipsoid.WGS84) // Cerro Pachón
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0])
const moonAt = (time: Time) => moon(time)[0]
const lmc = skyBrightness(skyBrightnessGeometryAt(eraS2c(hour(5.5), deg(-69.75)), timeYMDHMS(2026, 10, 26, 4, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), site, { sunAt, moonAt }))

console.log(lmc.total, lmc.moonDelta) // 18.424 -2.784 — mag/arcsec², and the Moon's brightening in mag
```

### Sky-Plane Uncertainty Ellipses

An orbit's position uncertainty is a 3D ellipsoid, but an observer sees only its projection on the plane of the sky. That projection is an error ellipse around the predicted position, which tells how large a field must be to catch the object. The linear position spread across the line of sight is divided by the distance to give angles, and the ellipse axes are the eigenvalues of the 2×2 covariance along East (increasing right ascension) and North (increasing declination); the position angle of the major axis is measured from north through east.

`ephemerisUncertaintyEllipse` takes a covariance whose top-left 3×3 block is the position covariance in AU² (a full 6×6 state covariance from [Orbit Covariance Propagation](#orbit-covariance-propagation) is fine) and the observer-to-object vector in AU, in the same frame, usually ICRF equatorial. The observer's own position is treated as errorless. Near a celestial pole the position angle is arbitrary but the shape is still correct.

```ts
import { ephemerisUncertaintyEllipse } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/covariance'
import { Matrix } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/matrix'
import { toArcsec, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A position covariance in AU²: sigma x = 1e-4, y = 5e-5, z = 2e-5 AU, with a 0.5 x-y correlation.
const covariance = new Matrix(3, 3)

covariance.set(0, 0, 1e-4 ** 2)
covariance.set(1, 1, 5e-5 ** 2)
covariance.set(2, 2, 2e-5 ** 2)
covariance.set(0, 1, 0.5 * 1e-4 * 5e-5)
covariance.set(1, 0, 0.5 * 1e-4 * 5e-5)

// Projects it on the sky at an observer-to-object vector (AU, same frame), 2.62 AU long.
const ellipse = ephemerisUncertaintyEllipse(covariance, [2.1, -1.2, -1.0])

console.log(toArcsec(ellipse.semiMajor), toArcsec(ellipse.semiMinor)) // 6.60 2.10 — arcseconds, 1-sigma
console.log(toDeg(ellipse.positionAngle)) // 73.5 — degrees, major axis from north through east

// The 3-sigma ellipse.
console.log(toArcsec(ephemerisUncertaintyEllipse(covariance, [2.1, -1.2, -1.0], { sigma: 3 }).semiMajor)) // 19.8 — arcseconds
```

### Solar Disk Geometry and Heliographic Coordinates

Locating a sunspot or a prominence on the Sun, and following it from day to day, needs the orientation of the solar disk as seen by the observer. It is described by three angles: P, the position angle of the solar north pole measured from celestial north toward east; B0, the heliographic latitude of the disk centre; and L0, the Carrington longitude of the disk centre. Heliographic latitude is positive toward solar north. Stonyhurst longitude is measured from the observer's central meridian, positive toward the west limb (the direction of rotation), in `(−π, π]`. Carrington longitude is fixed to a Sun rotating rigidly at 14.1844°/day (the IAU prime meridian), in `[0, 2π)`, so Carrington = Stonyhurst + L0, and L0 decreases by about 13.2°/day. L0 is not the fractional [Carrington Rotation](#carrington-rotation) number.

`solarDiskGeometry` takes barycentric ICRS states of the observer (the Earth, or a site through `observerState`, see [Barycentric and Heliocentric Light-Time Correction](#barycentric-and-heliocentric-light-time-correction)) and of the Sun. B0 and L0 use the IAU rotation retarded by the light time and exclude aberration, matching SunPy's defaults; the Astronomical Almanac L0 includes aberration and is about 0.006° smaller. P is referred to the true equator and equinox of date, and a second angle to ICRS north, which is what a J2000/ICRS plate solution measures; they differ by precession and nutation, up to about 0.16° in 2026. A geocentric Meeus approximation (chapter 29) gives P and B0 to a few thousandths of a degree but L0 only to a few hundredths.

The mapping functions place a line of sight on the solar sphere seen from that observer at its finite distance, either from helioprojective angles (from the disk centre, toward solar west and solar north) or from pixels of an ideal, distortion-free image centred on the disk (origin upper left, +Y down), and back. `mu`, the cosine of the heliocentric angle, is 1 at the disk centre and 0 at the limb. Features are carried forward by differential rotation, ω = A + B sin²φ + C sin⁴φ (sidereal, Howard 1990 by default, Snodgrass 1983 and Allen available), relative to the rigid Carrington rate; the latitude is kept, so map the new Carrington longitude through the geometry of the later time.

```ts
import { approximateSolarDiskGeometry, heliographicToHelioprojective, heliographicToSolarImage, helioprojectiveToHeliographic, rotateCarringtonLongitude, solarDiskGeometry, solarImageScale, solarImageToHeliographic, solarRotationRate } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/sun.heliographic'
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { Timescale, timeShift, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { arcsec, deg, toArcsec, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// P, B0 and L0 for a geocentric observer, from barycentric Earth and Sun states.
const geometry = solarDiskGeometry(time, earth(time), sun(time))

console.log(toDeg(geometry.p), toDeg(geometry.b0), toDeg(geometry.l0)) // -3.6155 2.6155 96.8428 — degrees

// The geocentric Meeus approximation, from the time alone.
const approximate = approximateSolarDiskGeometry(time)

console.log(toDeg(approximate.p), toDeg(approximate.b0), toDeg(approximate.l0)) // -3.6143 2.6114 96.8846 — degrees

// A line of sight 300″ west and 200″ north of the disk centre, on the solar sphere.
const point = helioprojectiveToHeliographic(arcsec(300), arcsec(200), geometry)

if (point.onDisk) {
	console.log(toDeg(point.stonyhurstLongitude), toDeg(point.latitude), toDeg(point.carringtonLongitude), point.mu) // 19.100 14.657 115.943 0.924

	// The inverse: a Carrington (or Stonyhurst) point back to helioprojective angles.
	const back = heliographicToHelioprojective(point.carringtonLongitude, point.latitude, 'carrington', geometry)

	console.log(toArcsec(back.tx), toArcsec(back.ty), back.visible) // 300 200 true — arcseconds
}

// Sidereal rotation rate at a latitude (radians/day), Howard 1990 unless another model is passed.
console.log(toDeg(solarRotationRate(deg(30)))) // 13.682 — degrees/day

// A plate-solved image: disk centre at (1024, 1024), radius 960 px, ICRS north up.
const calibration = { centerX: 1024, centerY: 1024, scale: solarImageScale(geometry, 960), positionAngle: 0, north: 'icrs' } as const
const spot = solarImageToHeliographic(1300, 900, geometry, calibration)

if (spot.onDisk) {
	// Two days later the spot has rotated about 26° west; find its pixel then.
	const later = timeShift(time, 2)
	const carrington = rotateCarringtonLongitude(spot.carringtonLongitude, spot.latitude, time, later)

	console.log(heliographicToSolarImage(carrington, spot.latitude, 'carrington', solarDiskGeometry(later, earth(later), sun(later)), calibration)) // { x: 1675.47, y: 907.61, visible: true }
}
```

### Solar Eclipse Besselian Elements

The Besselian elements describe a solar eclipse in the fundamental plane, the plane through the Earth's centre perpendicular to the Moon's shadow axis. Seen in that plane, the eclipse is simple: the shadow axis is a point `(x, y)` moving almost linearly, surrounded by the circular sections of the penumbral cone (radius `l1`) and the umbral cone (radius `l2`, negative for a total eclipse and positive for an annular one). The direction of the axis is given by its declination `d` and Greenwich hour angle `mu`, and the half-angles of the cones by `tan f1` and `tan f2`. Lengths are in equatorial Earth radii and angles in radians. Every other solar eclipse computation of the library (the ground track, the local circumstances) is built on them.

Because the elements vary smoothly, they are published (and computed here) as cubic polynomials in `t`, the time in hours from `time0`, the hour nearest to greatest eclipse, fitted to Sun and Moon positions sampled around it; the radii of the Sun and the Moon follow the NASA/Espenak convention. The polynomials are extrapolated outside the fitted window, so results more than a few hours from `time0` are unreliable. The instantaneous elements can also be computed directly from the Sun and Moon positions, which is useful to check the fit.

```ts
import { nearestSolarEclipse } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/sun'
import { moon } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/elpmpp02'
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { computeSunMoonPositionAt, sunMoonPosition } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/eclipse'
import { computePolynomialBesselianElements, evaluateBesselian, instantBesselianFromSunMoon } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/solar/map'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The total solar eclipse of 8 April 2024.
const eclipse = nearestSolarEclipse(timeYMDHMS(2024, 4, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), true)

// Cubic polynomials of x, y, l1, l2, d and mu in hours from time0.
const pbe = computePolynomialBesselianElements(eclipse.maximalTime, sunMoonPosition)

console.log(pbe.x) // [-0.3188609437, 0.5117079966, 3.2949e-5, -8.4194e-6] — Earth radii, increasing powers of t

// The elements at greatest eclipse: the axis passes 0.343 Earth radii from the centre, and l2 < 0 (total).
const maximum = evaluateBesselian(pbe, eclipse.maximalTime)

console.log(maximum.x, maximum.y, maximum.l2) // -0.157500055 0.305084134 -0.01036006 — Earth radii
console.log(toDeg(maximum.d), toDeg(maximum.mu)) // 7.59086 94.01317 — degrees

// The same instant straight from the Sun and Moon positions, without the polynomial.
const exact = instantBesselianFromSunMoon(eclipse.maximalTime, sunMoonPosition(eclipse.maximalTime))

console.log(exact.x, exact.y) // -0.1575000315 0.3050841577
```
