```ts
// A Sun/Moon provider from other ephemerides: barycentric Sun and Earth and geocentric Moon states (AU, AU/day, ICRF).
const elpmpp02 = (time: Time) => computeSunMoonPositionAt(time, sun, earth, moon)

console.log(evaluateBesselian(computePolynomialBesselianElements(eclipse.maximalTime, elpmpp02), eclipse.maximalTime).x) // -0.15691 — Earth radii, with the ELPMPP02 Moon
```

### Solar Eclipse Ground-Track Geometry

The ground track of a solar eclipse is the familiar eclipse map: the central line of totality or annularity with its northern and southern limits, the northern and southern limits of the partial eclipse, the curves where the eclipse begins or ends at sunrise or sunset, and the named contact points (first and last contact of the penumbra and umbra with the Earth, the ends of the central line, and greatest eclipse). Each curve is where a condition on the shadow, written with the [Solar Eclipse Besselian Elements](#solar-eclipse-besselian-elements), is met on the Earth's surface, and each point carries the instant when the shadow is there.

`computeSolarEclipseMapGeometry` computes all of them in geographic coordinates, with `x` the east-positive longitude and `y` the latitude, in radians; they run across the ±180° meridian and are projected to a map by [Solar Eclipse Map SVG Paths](#solar-eclipse-map-svg-paths). Limits are lists of branches, so that a fold that could not be followed is never joined by a straight line. The points of the central line are tagged total or annular, so a hybrid eclipse can be split into its total and annular runs. By default an empirical refraction lift near the horizon makes the extremes of the partial limits match the published refracted references; a purely geometric solution is also available. The work is synchronous and its cost grows quickly as the steps shrink: the default steps are the accurate setting, and coarse ones are only for previews.

```ts
import { nearestSolarEclipse } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/sun'
import { sunMoonPosition } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/eclipse'
import { computePolynomialBesselianElements, computeSolarEclipseMapGeometry, splitCentralLineByKind } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/solar/map'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The total solar eclipse of 8 April 2024 and its Besselian elements.
const eclipse = nearestSolarEclipse(timeYMDHMS(2024, 4, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), true)
const pbe = computePolynomialBesselianElements(eclipse.maximalTime, sunMoonPosition)

// A preview-quality map: 5° longitude scan and 2° spacing of the points.
const geometry = computeSolarEclipseMapGeometry(eclipse, pbe, { longitudeStep: deg(5), maxAngularStep: deg(2) })

// Greatest eclipse and the first point of the central line, where the axis first touches the Earth.
console.log(toDeg(geometry.points.MAX!.x), toDeg(geometry.points.MAX!.y)) // -104.05 25.40 — degrees
console.log(toDeg(geometry.lines.centerLine[0].x), toDeg(geometry.lines.centerLine[0].y)) // -158.53 -7.81 — degrees

// Total and annular runs of the central line: one total run here, both for a hybrid eclipse.
const kinds = splitCentralLineByKind(geometry.lines.centerLine, pbe)

console.log(kinds.total.length, kinds.annular.length) // 1 0
```

### Solar Eclipse Map SVG Paths

An eclipse map is drawn by projecting the ground track onto a world map. `solarEclipseMapToSvgPaths` turns the geometry of [Solar Eclipse Ground-Track Geometry](#solar-eclipse-ground-track-geometry) into SVG path data, one string per curve, plus the projected position of each named point, through any cylindrical projection of [Sky Projections](#sky-projections) such as the plate carrée. The curves are split at the antimeridian only here: a curve that crosses it becomes several subpaths and no connector is ever drawn across the map.

The coordinates are those of the projection: with a plate carrée, `x` is the longitude and `y` the latitude, in radians multiplied by the projection scale, with north up. SVG `y` grows downward, so ask the projection for south-up axes to get SVG coordinates directly, and set a central meridian to centre the map on another longitude.

```ts
import { nearestSolarEclipse } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/sun'
import { sunMoonPosition } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/eclipse'
import { computePolynomialBesselianElements, computeSolarEclipseMapGeometry, solarEclipseMapToSvgPaths } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/eclipse/solar/map'
import { PlateCarree } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/projections/projection'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The total solar eclipse of 8 April 2024, as a preview-quality geometry.
const eclipse = nearestSolarEclipse(timeYMDHMS(2024, 4, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), true)
const pbe = computePolynomialBesselianElements(eclipse.maximalTime, sunMoonPosition)
const geometry = computeSolarEclipseMapGeometry(eclipse, pbe, { longitudeStep: deg(5), maxAngularStep: deg(2) })

// A map 100 units per radian, with SVG axes (y down).
const paths = solarEclipseMapToSvgPaths(geometry, new PlateCarree(0, { scale: 100, yAxisDirection: 'southUp' }))

console.log(paths.points.MAX) // { x: -181.5986, y: -44.3387 } — greatest eclipse
console.log(paths.centerLine.slice(0, 60)) // M-276.69 13.63L-273.61 13.2L-270.53 12.7L-268.34 12.31L-266. — SVG path data

// The northern partial limit crosses the antimeridian, so it has two subpaths.
console.log((paths.penumbraNorth.match(/M/g) ?? []).length) // 2
```

### Solar Eclipse Search and Classification

A solar eclipse happens at new moon when the Moon's shadow reaches the Earth. It is total when the Moon's umbra reaches the surface (the Moon looks larger than the Sun), annular when only the antumbra does (the Moon looks smaller, leaving a ring), hybrid when the eclipse is annular in part of its track and total in another, and partial when only the penumbra touches the Earth. Two numbers summarize the global circumstances: the magnitude at greatest eclipse (the Moon-to-Sun apparent-diameter ratio for a central eclipse, the fraction of the Sun's diameter covered otherwise) and gamma, the least distance of the shadow axis from the Earth's centre in equatorial Earth radii, signed positive when the axis passes north of it.

`nearestSolarEclipse` finds the next eclipse strictly after an instant, or the last one at or before it, with the series of Meeus chapter 54, accurate to about a minute in time. Its time of greatest eclipse is TT; convert it with `utc` for civil time. It gives only the global classification: for the ground path and the view from a site, see [Solar Eclipse Besselian Elements](#solar-eclipse-besselian-elements) and the local solar eclipse topics.

```ts
import { nearestSolarEclipse } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/sun'
import { Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS, utc } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

// The first solar eclipse after 1 April 2024 (true = next, false = previous).
const eclipse = nearestSolarEclipse(timeYMDHMS(2024, 4, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC), true)

console.log(eclipse.type, eclipse.central) // total true
console.log(timeToDate(utc(eclipse.maximalTime)).slice(0, 6)) // [2024, 4, 8, 18, 17, 46] — greatest eclipse, UTC
console.log(eclipse.magnitude) // 1.0553 — the Moon is 5.5% larger than the Sun
console.log(eclipse.gamma) // 0.3437 — Earth radii, the axis passes north of the centre
```

### Solar Parallax and Semidiameter

The Sun's horizontal parallax is the angle the Earth's equatorial radius subtends at the Sun, and its semidiameter is the angular radius of the solar disk. Both scale inversely with the Earth-Sun distance, so they grow when the Earth is closer to the Sun.

`sunParallax` and `sunSemidiameter` take the distance in AU and return radians, using 8.794143″ and 959.63″ at 1 AU. They are Sun-specific; for the Moon see [Lunar Parallax and Semidiameter](#lunar-parallax-and-semidiameter).

```ts
import { sunParallax, sunSemidiameter } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/sun'
import { toArcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// distance: Earth-Sun distance in AU.
console.log(toArcsec(sunParallax(1))) // 8.794 — arcseconds
console.log(toArcsec(sunSemidiameter(1))) // 959.63 — arcseconds
console.log(toArcsec(sunSemidiameter(0.98329))) // 975.94 — arcseconds, near perihelion
```

### Spherical Coordinate Conversions

The same direction on the sky can be written in several spherical systems. Equatorial uses right ascension and declination, ecliptic uses longitude and latitude relative to the plane of the Earth's orbit, and Galactic uses longitude and latitude relative to the plane of the Milky Way. Converting between them is a fixed rotation for the J2000 systems, or a time-dependent one for systems "of date", which follow precession, nutation, and the obliquity of the ecliptic.

Each function takes and returns radians as a `[longitude-like, latitude-like]` pair. The J2000 conversions need no time; the "of date" ones take a `Time` (the current instant by default): the ecliptic of date uses the true obliquity, and the J2000-to-date equatorial conversion applies the IAU 2006/2000A precession-nutation. Longitudes and right ascensions come back in `(−π, π]`, not wrapped to `[0, 2π)`. These are directions only: for positions or states and the other frames, see [Celestial and Terrestrial Reference Frames](#celestial-and-terrestrial-reference-frames), and for the horizontal system see [Local Horizon Coordinates](#local-horizon-coordinates).

```ts
import { eclipticJ2000ToEquatorial, eclipticToEquatorial, equatorialFromJ2000, equatorialToEcliptic, equatorialToEclipticJ2000, equatorialToGalactic, equatorialToJ2000, galacticToEquatorial } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/coordinate'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, hour, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 4, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// J2000 equatorial RA 10 h, Dec +20° to J2000 ecliptic, and to the ecliptic of date.
const eclipticJ2000 = equatorialToEclipticJ2000(hour(10), deg(20))
const eclipticOfDate = equatorialToEcliptic(hour(10), deg(20), time)

console.log(eclipticJ2000.map(toDeg)) // [145.128, 7.2907] — degrees
console.log(eclipticOfDate.map(toDeg)) // [145.1281, 7.2915] — degrees

// The inverses, ecliptic J2000 and ecliptic of date back to equatorial.
console.log(eclipticJ2000ToEquatorial(...eclipticJ2000).map(toDeg)) // [150, 20] — degrees
console.log(eclipticToEquatorial(...eclipticOfDate, time).map(toDeg)) // [150, 20] — degrees

// The Galactic center region in Galactic coordinates, and the Galactic origin back in equatorial coordinates.
console.log(equatorialToGalactic(hour(17.7611), deg(-28.9362)).map(toDeg)) // [0.0052, -0.0086] — degrees
console.log(galacticToEquatorial(0, 0).map(toDeg)) // [-93.595, -28.936] — degrees (RA 266.405°)

// J2000 to equatorial coordinates of date (precession and nutation), and back.
const [ra, dec] = equatorialFromJ2000(hour(10), deg(20), time)

console.log(toDeg(ra), toDeg(dec)) // 150.369 19.872 — degrees
console.log(equatorialToJ2000(ra, dec, time).map(toDeg)) // [150, 20] — degrees
```

### Spherical State Rates

A Cartesian position and velocity can be rewritten as spherical coordinates and their first derivatives: longitude, latitude, distance, the two angular rates, and the radial speed. This gives the apparent motion of a body on the sky (for example, to set a non-sidereal tracking rate), or its rate in any frame the state is written in. The longitude rate is the rate of the coordinate itself, not multiplied by `cos(latitude)`, so it grows near the poles; at an exact Cartesian pole the chart is singular and the angular rates are undefined. The radial velocity is positive when receding.

`sphericalPositionAndVelocity` converts a state in the frame it is already in. `frameSphericalPositionAndVelocity` first transforms the state into another frame, including the rotating-frame term of a body-fixed frame, so an inertial point at rest sweeps across the Earth-fixed sky at the Earth's spin rate. For plain angle conversions without rates, see [Spherical Coordinate Conversions](#spherical-coordinate-conversions).

```ts
import { frameSphericalPositionAndVelocity, sphericalPositionAndVelocity } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/astrometry'
import { ITRS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/frame'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

// Spherical coordinates and rates of a state: position in AU, velocity in AU/day.
const spherical = sphericalPositionAndVelocity([
	[1, 1, 1],
	[0.01, -0.02, 0.03],
] as const)

console.log(spherical?.longitude, spherical?.latitude, spherical?.distance) // 0.7854 0.6155 1.7321 — radians, radians, AU
console.log(spherical?.longitudeRate, spherical?.latitudeRate) // -0.015 0.016499 — radians/day
console.log(spherical?.radialVelocity) // 0.011547 — AU/day, positive when receding

// The same in an Earth-fixed frame at an instant: an inertial point at rest moves at the Earth's spin rate.
const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 4, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
const fixed = frameSphericalPositionAndVelocity(
	[
		[1, 0, 0],
		[0, 0, 0],
	] as const,
	ITRS,
	time,
)

console.log(fixed?.longitudeRate) // -6.3004 — radians/day
```

### SPICE Body Radii

The shape of a planet or moon is described in SPICE by a triaxial reference ellipsoid. NAIF text PCK kernels list it as `BODY{id}_RADII`, three numbers in kilometers: the x, y, and z semi-axes in the body-fixed frame, usually the two equatorial radii and the polar radius. These radii are what turns a planetographic longitude and latitude into a position on the body, and they change with each IAU report, so reading them from the kernel keeps a computation consistent with the kernels it uses.

`bodyRadii` reads that variable for a NAIF body id from a loaded kernel pool (see [SPICE Text Kernel Pools](#spice-text-kernel-pools)) and returns the semi-axes in AU, or `undefined` when the kernels have no radii for that body. The result feeds the body shape of [Planetary Surface Locations](#planetary-surface-locations).

```ts
import fs from 'fs/promises'
import { bodyRadii } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/frame.kernel'
import { Naif } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/naif'
import { readTextKernel, SpiceKernelPool } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/text.kernel'
import { fileHandleSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/file'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// Load a text PCK with the BODY{id}_RADII values.
const pool = new SpiceKernelPool()

await using tpc = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/pck00008.tpc'))
pool.load(await readTextKernel(tpc))

// The Earth's ellipsoid semi-axes, in AU.
const earth = bodyRadii(pool, Naif.EARTH)!

console.log(toKilometer(earth.x), toKilometer(earth.z)) // 6378.14 6356.75 — km, equatorial and polar
```

### SPICE Frame Resolution

Body-fixed frames, such as the lunar principal-axes and mean-Earth frames, are defined in SPICE by kernels rather than by formulas. A frame kernel (`KPL/FK`) gives each frame a name and an id and says how it is built: from an orientation stored in a binary PCK (class 2), or as a constant rotation relative to another frame (class 4). The lunar mean-Earth frame, for example, is a fixed rotation of the principal-axes frame that comes from the lunar ephemeris. Resolving a frame means following that chain down to the inertial J2000 base.

`SpiceFrames` resolves a SPICE frame name or id, from a loaded text-kernel pool and optionally a binary PCK (see [Binary PCK Rotation](#binary-pck-rotation)), into a library `Frame` that maps J2000/ICRS axes to the body-fixed axes, with its angular rate when the frame rotates. The result works with the frame functions of [Celestial and Terrestrial Reference Frames](#celestial-and-terrestrial-reference-frames) and with planetary surface locations. A class-2 frame reads the PCK on demand, so the PCK source must stay open while the frame is used.

```ts
import fs from 'fs/promises'
import { frameAt } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/frame'
import { readDaf } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/daf'
import { SpiceFrames } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/frame.kernel'
import { readPck } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/pck'
import { readTextKernel, SpiceKernelPool } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/text.kernel'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { fileHandleSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/file'

// The frame kernel (names and ids) and the binary PCK holding the lunar orientation.
const pool = new SpiceKernelPool()

await using fk = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/moon_080317.tf'))
pool.load(await readTextKernel(fk))

await using bpc = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/moon_pa_de421_1900-2050.bpc'))
const pck = readPck(await readDaf(bpc))

await pck.initialize()

// Resolve the mean-Earth frame (class 4) through the principal-axes frame (class 2).
const frames = new SpiceFrames(pool, pck)
const meanEarth = await frames.frame('MOON_ME_DE421')
const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TDB)

console.log(meanEarth.rotationAt(time).slice(0, 3)) // [0.06651, 0.92523, 0.37353] — first row, J2000 to mean-Earth axes

// A J2000 state (AU, AU/day) expressed in the body-fixed frame.
console.log(
	frameAt(
		[
			[1, 0, 0],
			[0, 0, 0],
		] as const,
		meanEarth,
		time,
	),
) // [position, velocity] — AU and AU/day, lunar mean-Earth axes
```

### SPICE Text Kernel Pools

NAIF text kernels (`KPL/PCK` and `KPL/FK`) store constants as `name = value` assignments between `\begindata` and `\begintext` markers: body radii, frame definitions, gravitational parameters, and the like. A value is a number (Fortran `D` exponents allowed), a quoted string, or a parenthesized list. An assignment either replaces a name (`=`) or appends to it (`+=`), so when several kernels set the same name, the order in which they are loaded matters, as in the NAIF toolkit.

`readTextKernel` parses a text kernel into its ordered assignments, and a `SpiceKernelPool` applies them in load order and answers lookups by name, case-insensitively. Unlike the NAIF toolkit, the pool is explicit, not global, so independent computations can hold different kernels. Use it with [SPICE Frame Resolution](#spice-frame-resolution) and [SPICE Body Radii](#spice-body-radii).

```ts
import { readTextKernel, SpiceKernelPool } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/text.kernel'
import { bufferSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'

const text = `KPL/PCK

\\begindata
  BODY301_RADII = ( 1737.4 1737.4 1737.4 )
  FRAME_31000_NAME = 'MOON_PA'
  ITEMS = ( 1 2 )
  ITEMS += ( 3 )
\\begintext
`

// Parse the assignments, then apply them to a pool in order.
const pool = new SpiceKernelPool()

pool.load(await readTextKernel(bufferSource(Buffer.from(text, 'ascii'))))

console.log(pool.get('items')) // [1, 2, 3] — `=` then `+=`, name matched case-insensitively
console.log(pool.numbers('BODY301_RADII')) // [1737.4, 1737.4, 1737.4] — kilometers in the file
console.log(pool.strings('FRAME_31000_NAME')) // ['MOON_PA']
```

### SPK State Kernels

An SPK (Spacecraft and Planet Kernel) is a NAIF binary file of ephemerides: for a set of target bodies, the position and velocity relative to a center body over a time span, stored as numerically fitted (Chebyshev, Lagrange, or modified-difference) segments inside a DAF container (see [DAF Binary Containers](#daf-binary-containers)). JPL planetary ephemerides such as DE421 and DE440, satellite ephemerides, and small-body and spacecraft files are SPKs. Bodies are identified by NAIF integer codes, and a chain of segments links them, for example the solar-system barycenter to the Earth-Moon barycenter to the Earth. A system barycenter is not its planet: DE440s has Jupiter's barycenter (5) but not Jupiter's centre (599).

`readSpk` reads one file and returns the segment between a center and a target, evaluated in TDB and returning AU and AU/day in the segment's own frame, without rotation; J2000 is the frame that matches the library axes. To combine files, `inspectSpk` catalogs the segments of each one, and `prepareSpkKernelSet` merges them in load order, giving precedence to the file loaded last as the NAIF toolkit does, and resolves the barycentric state of any body through its chain of centers. Coverage is never extrapolated, and coefficient records are read on demand, so the sources must stay open while they are used. To use segments with the rest of the library, wrap them with `spkEphemerisPath` (see [Ephemeris Path Adapters](#ephemeris-path-adapters)).

```ts
import fs from 'fs/promises'
import { readDaf } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/daf'
import { extendedPermanentAsteroidNumber, Naif } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/naif'
import { readSpk } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/spk'
import { inspectSpk } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/spk.inspect'
import { prepareSpkKernelSet } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/kernels/spk.kernelset'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { fileHandleSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/file'

// One file: the Earth-Moon barycenter relative to the solar-system barycenter.
await using source = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/de440s.bsp'))
const spk = readSpk(await readDaf(source))
const segment = (await spk.segment(Naif.SSB, Naif.EMB))!

const [position, velocity] = segment.at(timeYMDHMS(2025, 1, 15, 9, 20, 50, Timescale.TDB))

console.log(position, velocity) // [-0.42340, 0.81246, 0.35239] [-0.015849, -0.0067662, -0.0029331] — AU, AU/day, J2000

// Several files: inspect each, then prepare a set in load order (lowest precedence first).
const entries = []

for (const [id, path] of [
	['de440s', 'data/de440s.bsp'],
	['didymos', 'data/65803_Didymos.bsp'],
]) {
	const daf = await readDaf(fileHandleSource(await fs.open(path)))
	const inspection = inspectSpk(daf, (await fs.stat(path)).size)
	if (inspection.ok) entries.push({ id, daf, segments: inspection.segments })
}

const set = await prepareSpkKernelSet(entries)

// NAIF code of a numbered asteroid, 20000000 + number: (65803) Didymos is Naif.DIDYMOS_BARYCENTER. The other schemes are
// extendedPrimaryBodyOfPermanentAsteroidNumber, extendedSatelliteOfPermanentAsteroidNumber, extendedProvisionalAsteroidNumber,
// and, for old kernels, originalPermanentAsteroidNumber and originalProvisionalAsteroidNumber.
const code = extendedPermanentAsteroidNumber(65803) // 20065803

// Barycentric state of Didymos, chained Sun -> Didymos from one file and barycenter -> Sun from the other.
const didymos = set.stateAt(code, timeYMDHMS(2022, 12, 8, 20, 7, 15, Timescale.TDB))

if (didymos.ok) console.log(didymos.state, didymos.kernels) // AU and AU/day in J2000 axes; ['didymos', 'de440s']
```

### Starlight Deflection

General relativity bends light passing a massive body. For a star seen at an angle `θ` from the Sun by an observer at distance `d` from it, the apparent displacement, away from the Sun, is about `(2GM☉ / c²d) · cot(θ/2)`, which is 1.75″ at the solar limb and still about 4 milliarcseconds at 90°; Jupiter and Saturn add much smaller, local terms. Astrometry at the milliarcsecond level, such as Gaia-based reductions, must account for it.

`deflectStarlight` applies the ERFA multi-body model (`eraLdn`) to the observer-to-star direction of a star treated as infinitely distant. It takes a unit direction in ICRS/BCRS axes, the observer's barycentric position in AU, and the deflecting bodies at the observation epoch with their masses (in solar masses), deflection limiters, and barycentric positions and velocities. It must not be used for finite-distance Solar System targets, which need a deflector-to-source geometry; `apparentDirection` handles those (see [Apparent Direction](#apparent-direction), whose module also exports the ERFA constants for the Sun, Jupiter, and Saturn).

```ts
import { deflectStarlight, SUN_LIGHT_DEFLECTOR_LIMITER, SUN_LIGHT_DEFLECTOR_MASS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/apparent'
import { vecAngle } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { toArcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The Sun at the barycenter, at rest: mass (solar masses), limiter, position (AU) and velocity (AU/day).
const sun = { bm: SUN_LIGHT_DEFLECTOR_MASS, dl: SUN_LIGHT_DEFLECTOR_LIMITER, p: [0, 0, 0], v: [0, 0, 0] } as const

// Observer at 1 AU on +x, looking along +z, 90° from the Sun.
const direction = [0, 0, 1] as const
const deflected = deflectStarlight(direction, [1, 0, 0], [sun])

console.log(toArcsec(vecAngle(direction, deflected))) // 0.00407 — arcseconds of deflection at 90° from the Sun
```

### Stellar and Asteroidal Occultations

A body (an asteroid, or the Moon treated as a sphere) occults a star when its disk passes in front of it as seen from one observer. Asteroidal occultations are short, a few seconds, and their timing from several sites measures the size and shape of the asteroid to kilometer precision, so predicting whether a given site will see one matters. Seen from a site, the event is an **appulse**, a minimum of the topocentric angular separation between the body and the star; it is an occultation when that minimum does not exceed the angular radius of the disk, `asin(radius / distance)`, with the star treated as a point. Its duration is the chord across the disk at that impact parameter divided by the relative angular speed.

`occultationCandidates` answers that per-site question directly, without projecting the shadow onto the Earth, by searching the separation minima over a window. The body and the observer are samplers of position and velocity in the same origin and frame, normally barycentric ICRS; the topocentric observer state is what includes the diurnal parallax, which decides which sites see the event. The star direction must already include proper motion and parallax, as the track is only as wide as the body. Light time to the body is iterated, while annual and diurnal aberration are omitted because they shift the star and the body almost equally and cancel in the differential separation. The accuracy is set by the ephemeris of the body and the astrometry of the star, not by this geometry. The sampling step must be finer than the approach one wants to catch. To map where on Earth the event is visible, see [Stellar Occultation Ground Tracks](#stellar-occultation-ground-tracks).

```ts
import { type PositionAndVelocity, type PositionAndVelocityOverTime, zeroPositionAndVelocity } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/astrometry'
import { occultationCandidates } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/occultation'
import { Timescale, time, timeShift, timeSubtract, type Time } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toArcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A synthetic encounter: a body 2 AU away drifts at 2·10⁻⁴ AU/day past a star on +x, missing it by 10⁻⁶ AU.
const crossing: Time = time(2461200.5, 0, Timescale.TDB)
const target: PositionAndVelocityOverTime = (t: Time): PositionAndVelocity => [
	[2, 1e-6, 2e-4 * timeSubtract(t, crossing)],
	[0, 0, 2e-4],
]
const observer: PositionAndVelocityOverTime = () => zeroPositionAndVelocity()

// Appulses in the window, for a body of radius 3·10⁻⁶ AU (about 449 km), without light time.
const [appulse] = occultationCandidates(target, [1, 0, 0], observer, timeShift(crossing, -0.02), timeShift(crossing, 0.02), { radius: 3e-6, lightTimeIterations: 0 })

console.log(appulse.occultation) // true — the minimum separation is inside the disk
console.log(toArcsec(appulse.separation), toArcsec(appulse.angularRadius)) // 0.1031 0.3094 — arcseconds
console.log(appulse.duration) // 2443.8 — seconds
```

### Stellar Occultation Ground Tracks

The shadow that a body casts from a point source sweeps a corridor across the Earth: inside it the source disappears, on its edges it grazes the limb. Where [Stellar and Asteroidal Occultations](#stellar-and-asteroidal-occultations) answers whether one site sees the event, `occultationPath` solves where on Earth it is seen, which is what observers use to position themselves across the path. At each instant it forms the shadow (a cylinder for a source at infinity, a cone for a point source at finite distance, such as the Sun for a solar eclipse), rotates it into the Earth-fixed frame, and intersects the centerline and the two limit lines with the reference ellipsoid. Only causal geometry counts: the light must pass the body before reaching the ground. The body is a sphere and the source a point: refraction, topography, the stellar diameter, diffraction, and limb profiles are not modeled.

The default rigorous mode solves light time to the shadow plane, tilts the shadow axis by the light-time aberration of the moving shadow (worth a few hundred meters on the ground), and places the limits on the true envelope of the shadow over the rotating ground; the classical fundamental-plane construction is available as an approximate mode, off by up to about a kilometer. Against the RASNZ path tables for (307) Nike on 2022-09-23, rebuilt from the published elements, Gaia star position, and DE440s, the centre, limits, and error limits agree within 0.25 km and the times within 0.3 s. Elements published with such predictions are referred to the ecliptic with the IAU 1976 obliquity of 84381.448″, while the default `KeplerOrbit` rotation uses 84381.411″; that 0.037″ difference moves a main-belt shadow by tens of kilometers, so build those orbits with `KeplerOrbit.meanAnomaly(..., mu, matTranspose(matRotX(arcsec(84381.448))))`.

The position covariances of the body and of the star, when given, widen the track into an uncertainty corridor at a chosen sigma, without moving the nominal centerline. The track can be extracted as polylines, broken where a line leaves the Earth and at the antimeridian, ready for SVG or GeoJSON rendering by the caller.

```ts
import { type PositionAndVelocityOverTime, topocentricDirection } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/astrometry'
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { occultationPath, occultationPathPolylines } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/occultation.path'
import { KeplerOrbit } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/asteroid'
import { Timescale, time, timeShift, timeToDate } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { DAYSEC, GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005 } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'
import { matIdentity } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/mat3'
import { vecPlus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { mas } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { kilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// Barycentric Ceres: the VSOP87E Sun plus a heliocentric Kepler state from JPL Horizons at JD 2461200.5 TDB.
const orbit = new KeplerOrbit([1.414905393343522, 2.2479053286939, 7.722476360317566e-1], [-9.08092698547858e-3, 3.499459682146027e-3, 3.499457832664595e-3], time(2461200.5, 0, Timescale.TDB), GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005, matIdentity())
const ceres: PositionAndVelocityOverTime = (t) => {
	const [sunPosition, sunVelocity] = sun(t)
	const [position, velocity] = orbit.at(t)
	return [vecPlus(sunPosition, position), vecPlus(sunVelocity, velocity)]
}

// A synthetic star on the light-time-corrected geocentric direction of Ceres at 07:12 UTC (not a real event).
const anchor = time(2461200.5, 0.3, Timescale.UTC)
const star = topocentricDirection(ceres, earth, anchor, 3)

// The track of a 469 km body, with a 2-sigma corridor from 20 km body and 1 mas star errors (1 sigma per axis).
const error = kilometer(20)
const path = occultationPath(ceres, star, earth, timeShift(anchor, -240 / DAYSEC), timeShift(anchor, 240 / DAYSEC), {
	radius: kilometer(469),
	step: 20 / DAYSEC,
	uncertainty: { body: [error ** 2, 0, 0, 0, error ** 2, 0, 0, 0, error ** 2], source: [mas(1) ** 2, 0, 0, mas(1) ** 2], sigma: 2 },
})

console.log(timeToDate(path.central[0].start)) // [2026, 6, 9, 7, 9, 42, 130] — UTC, the axis first meets the Earth

// The centerline as polylines of geodetic longitude and latitude (radians).
const [centerline] = occultationPathPolylines(path, 'center')

console.log(centerline.length) // 23 — vertices from limb to limb
```

### Stellar Space Motion

Stars move. A catalog gives a star's position at a reference epoch together with its proper motion (the yearly drift across the sky), its parallax (which sets its distance), and its radial velocity (toward or away from us). From those, the star's position and velocity in the barycentric celestial frame can be built and then propagated to another epoch, which matters for nearby, fast stars: Barnard's Star moves more than 10″ per year. Propagating in space rather than adding the proper motion to the angles also captures perspective acceleration, the change of proper motion as a star approaches or recedes. The propagation is a linear space-motion model, not a perturbed orbit.

`star` builds the barycentric state from the catalog values, with angles in radians and the radial velocity in AU/day, positive when receding. The proper motion in right ascension is `dα/dt`, which is the catalog value `μα*` divided by `cos(dec)`, not `μα*` itself; passing `μα*` silently gives the wrong motion. `spaceMotion` propagates the state to another time. For the place an observer sees, with aberration and refraction, see [Observed Catalog Star](#observed-catalog-star).

```ts
import { spaceMotion, star } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/star'
import { equatorial } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/astrometry'
import { Timescale, timeJulianYear } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { arcsec, deg, hour, normalizeAngle, toDeg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { kilometerPerSecond } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/velocity'

// Barnard's Star at J2000.0: μα* -797.84 mas/yr, μδ +10328.12 mas/yr, parallax 546.98 mas, radial velocity -110.51 km/s.
const declination = deg(4.693391)
const mas = (value: number) => arcsec(value / 1000)

const barnard = star(hour(17 + 57 / 60 + 48.4997 / 3600), declination, mas(-797.84) / Math.cos(declination), mas(10328.12), mas(546.98), kilometerPerSecond(-110.51))

console.log(barnard[0]) // [-3594.0, -375815.9, 30855.5] — AU, barycentric ICRS: about 5.95 light-years

// Propagate to J2025.0 and read the angular position.
const [position] = spaceMotion(barnard, timeJulianYear(2025, Timescale.TDB))
const [ra, dec] = equatorial(position)

console.log(toHour(normalizeAngle(ra)), toDeg(dec)) // 17.9631 4.7652 — the star has moved about 4.3' north in 25 years
```

### Sub-Observer and Sub-Solar Points

The sub-observer point is the spot on a body's surface directly beneath the observer, the centre of the disk as seen; its longitude is the central meridian. The sub-solar point is the spot directly beneath the Sun. Their latitudes are the tilt of the pole toward the observer or the Sun, and the longitude difference is the phase geometry. The position angle of the pole gives the orientation of the body's axis on the sky, measured from celestial north toward east; for the Sun it is the classical P angle. The orientation is evaluated one light time earlier, since the body turned while the light was in flight, which matters for fast rotators like Jupiter, whose prime meridian advances about 18° over the light time.

The functions take the IAU rotation elements of the body (see [IAU Body Orientation](#iau-body-orientation)) and the vectors from the body's centre to the observer and to the Sun, in AU and ICRF axes. The points are planetocentric and east-positive; for west-positive (planetographic) longitudes of a prograde body use `2π − longitude`. The position angle is referred to the true equator and equinox of date and neglects aberration. For the Sun's P, B0 and L0 together, with aberration and image mapping, see [Solar Disk Geometry and Heliographic Coordinates](#solar-disk-geometry-and-heliographic-coordinates).

```ts
import { positionAngleOfPole, subObserverPoint, subSolarPoint } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/orientation'
import { MARS_ROTATION } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/orientation.data'
import { earth, mars, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Vectors from Mars's centre to a geocentric observer and to the Sun, in AU and ICRF axes.
const marsToEarth = vecMinus(earth(time)[0], mars(time)[0])
const marsToSun = vecMinus(sun(time)[0], mars(time)[0])

// The disk centre seen from the Earth: east longitude and latitude.
const observer = subObserverPoint(MARS_ROTATION, time, marsToEarth)

console.log(toDeg(observer.longitude), toDeg(observer.latitude)) // 131.85 -9.86 — degrees
console.log(360 - toDeg(observer.longitude)) // 228.15 — degrees west, the central meridian

// The point beneath the Sun, as the observer sees it.
const solar = subSolarPoint(MARS_ROTATION, time, marsToEarth, marsToSun)

console.log(toDeg(solar.longitude), toDeg(solar.latitude)) // 107.57 -19.17 — degrees: the Sun is 19° south of Mars's equator

// The tilt of the Martian axis on the sky, from celestial north toward east.
console.log(toDeg(positionAngleOfPole(MARS_ROTATION, time, marsToEarth))) // -36.98 — degrees
```

### Surface Feature Illumination

Planning an image of a lunar crater or any other surface feature depends on its local lighting and on whether it faces the observer. At the feature, the Sun has an altitude and azimuth on the local horizon. The incidence is the angle between the surface normal and the Sun, the emission is the angle between the normal and the observer, and the phase is the Sun–feature–observer angle; these are the angles of planetary photometry. A low Sun (grazing light) brings out relief, so the best time to image a crater is a few days around its local sunrise or sunset. Libration moves features near the limb in and out of view.

`surfaceFeature` prepares a location of [Planetary Surface Locations](#planetary-surface-locations) with its local horizon frame: up is the reference ellipsoid normal, north is the body's pole projected onto the tangent plane, and azimuth runs north through east. A facet slope and aspect tilt the normal used for incidence and emission, for example a crater wall, and a terrain horizon mask (see [Local Horizon Mask](#local-horizon-mask)) adds occlusion by distant relief. `surfaceFeatureIllumination` gives the geometry at one instant, taken from the feature point, so the observer's parallax is included (up to about 0.26° for the Earth seen from the Moon); `surfaceFeatureWindows` finds the intervals where solar and observer constraints all hold, with the search of [Time-Constraint Intervals](#time-constraint-intervals). Against SPICE `ilumin`, `azlcpo`, and `gfilum` with the same DE421 and MOON_ME kernels, the tests check the angles to 5e-7° and window edges to about half a second.

Without a mask, the feature sits on a smooth ellipsoid, so crater-rim and relief shadows are not predicted; a digital elevation model supplies the mask, the facet, and the cast shadows (see [Digital Elevation Model Terrain](#digital-elevation-model-terrain)).

```ts
import { bodyFixedFrame, MOON_ROTATION } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/bodies/orientation'
import { moon } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/elpmpp02'
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { surfaceFeature, surfaceFeatureIllumination, surfaceFeatureWindows } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/surface'
import { bodyShape, bodySurfaceLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/body'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { kilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const epoch = timeYMDHMS(2024, 1, 15, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TDB)

// Copernicus crater: 20.08° W, 9.62° N, on a sphere of radius 1737.4 km.
const radius = kilometer(1737.4)
const copernicus = surfaceFeature(bodySurfaceLocation(deg(-20.08), deg(9.62), 0, bodyShape([radius, radius, radius]), bodyFixedFrame(MOON_ROTATION)))

// Moon-centre to Sun and to the geocenter, in AU and base axes (geometric).
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0]), moon(time)[0])
const earthAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus([0, 0, 0], moon(time)[0])

// Local lighting at one instant.
const now = surfaceFeatureIllumination(copernicus, sunAt, earthAt, timeShift(epoch, 5.6))

console.log(toDeg(now.solarAltitude), toDeg(now.solarAzimuth)) // 3.99 92.23 — degrees, a low morning Sun in the east
console.log(toDeg(now.incidence), toDeg(now.emission), toDeg(now.phase)) // 86.01 29.50 59.60 — degrees
console.log(now.sunlit, now.visible) // true true

// Grazing-light windows: solar altitude between 2° and 10° while the Earth sees the crater.
const grazing = surfaceFeatureWindows(copernicus, sunAt, earthAt, epoch, timeShift(epoch, 32), { minSolarAltitude: deg(2), maxSolarAltitude: deg(10), step: 0.25 })

console.log(grazing.map((w) => [w.start, w.end])) // the morning and evening windows of the lunation
```

### TEME and ITRF Conversion

SGP4 outputs positions in TEME, the True Equator, Mean Equinox frame: an Earth-centered frame close to inertial that does not rotate with the Earth. To place a satellite over the ground, or to point an antenna or a telescope at it, the state is converted to ITRF, the Earth-fixed frame, by a rotation about the pole through the Greenwich mean sidereal time, optionally followed by polar motion. A velocity in the Earth-fixed frame also gains the term from the Earth's rotation (with the mean spin rate), so an inertially fixed point appears to move.

The conversions accept a position or a `[position, velocity]` state in any unit (AU and AU/day for SGP4 output) and are exact inverses of each other; variants take a sidereal angle and a polar-motion matrix the caller already has. UT1, and so GMST, comes from the loaded Earth orientation data (see [Earth Orientation Parameters](#earth-orientation-parameters)); without it UT1 equals UTC, which moves a low-orbit position by up to about 0.5 km. The general frame machinery gives the same result (see [Celestial and Terrestrial Reference Frames](#celestial-and-terrestrial-reference-frames)).

```ts
import { itrfToTeme, temeToItrf, temeToItrfByGmst } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/frame'
import { parseTLE, sgp4 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/propagation/sgp4'
import { greenwichMeanSiderealTime, pmMatrix } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'
import { toKilometerPerSecond } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/velocity'

// The ISS at its TLE epoch, in TEME (AU, AU/day).
const tle = parseTLE('1 25544U 98067A   23231.51768399  .00014050  00000+0  25837-3 0  9996', '2 25544  51.6415  14.7889 0003559 325.3396 149.4637 15.49477580411611')
const teme = sgp4(tle.epoch, tle)

// TEME to the Earth-fixed frame, with polar motion. The values assume no Earth orientation data (UT1 = UTC).
const [position, velocity] = temeToItrf(teme, tle.epoch)

console.log(position.map(toKilometer)) // [4662.27, -1028.59, 4831.15] — km, ITRF
console.log(velocity.map(toKilometerPerSecond)) // [3.8830, 5.7151, -2.5222] — km/s, relative to the rotating Earth

// Back to TEME.
console.log(itrfToTeme([position, velocity], tle.epoch)[0].map(toKilometer)) // [-3737.79, 2970.46, 4831.15] — km, the SGP4 state

// The same rotation from a GMST (radians) and polar-motion matrix the caller already has; itrfToTemeByGmst is its inverse.
console.log(temeToItrfByGmst(teme, greenwichMeanSiderealTime(tle.epoch), pmMatrix(tle.epoch))[0].map(toKilometer)) // [4662.27, -1028.59, 4831.15] — km, ITRF
```

### Time-Constraint Intervals

Many observing questions are "when are all of these true at once": the target is above 30° altitude, the Sun is below −18°, the Moon is far away. Each condition can be written as a continuous scalar margin that is non-negative while the condition holds, so the answer is the set of time intervals where every margin is at least zero.

`searchIntervals` takes the margins as functions of `Time` and returns the chronological intervals of a window where all are non-negative. The margins are sampled together at a coarse step, so they can share one geometry evaluation, and each sign change is refined independently. The step must resolve every crossing: a tangency, or an interval shorter than one step, can be missed. For single crossings or extrema use [Time-Domain Event Search](#time-domain-event-search) and [Time-Domain Extrema Search](#time-domain-extrema-search).

```ts
import { searchIntervals } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/search'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeSubtract, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { TAU } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)
const days = (time: Time) => timeSubtract(time, start)

// Two margins over three days, scanned every 0.05 day: sin(2πd) >= 0 (the first half of each day) and 0.75 - frac(d) >= 0.
const intervals = searchIntervals([(time) => Math.sin(TAU * days(time)), (time) => 0.75 - (days(time) % 1)], start, timeShift(start, 3), { step: 0.05 })

console.log(intervals.map((i) => [days(i.start), days(i.end)])) // [[0, 0.5], [1, 1.5], [2, 2.5]] — days from the start
```

### Time-Domain Event Search

Many almanac events are instants where some quantity crosses a value: sunrise is where the Sun's altitude crosses zero, a conjunction where an angular difference crosses zero, a station where a rate crosses zero. Writing the quantity minus the target as a continuous function of time turns the event into a root of that function.

`searchRoots` samples the function over a window at a coarse step, finds each sign change between consecutive samples, and refines it, returning the root instants in chronological order. The step must be finer than the spacing of the roots, since two roots inside one step are missed. The function must be continuous: a quantity that wraps (right ascension, longitude, hour angle) must be unwrapped by the caller, for example with `normalizePI` around the target, or the jump at the seam looks like a crossing. This is the foundation of the higher-level event finders, such as [Rise, Transit, and Set](#rise-transit-and-set) and [Planetary Oppositions](#planetary-oppositions).

```ts
import { searchRoots } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/search'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeSubtract, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { TAU } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// A quantity that crosses zero every half day.
const f = (time: Time) => Math.sin(TAU * timeSubtract(time, start))

// Roots in a window of 2.2 days, scanned every 0.1 day.
const roots = searchRoots(f, start, timeShift(start, 2.2), { step: 0.1 })

console.log(roots.map((time) => timeSubtract(time, start))) // [0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2] — days from the start
```

### Time-Domain Extrema Search

Maxima and minima mark events such as greatest elongation, perihelion and aphelion, the Moon's perigee and apogee, and transit (the maximum altitude). They are the points where a scalar function of time has a local extremum, which a root search cannot find because the function does not change sign there.

`searchExtrema` samples the function at a coarse step and refines each local minimum or maximum, returning them in chronological order with their kind and value. The step must be fine enough that the neighbouring samples sit on each side of the extremum: an extremum flatter than a step, or sitting at the edge of the window, is not reported. The function must be continuous, with wrapping quantities unwrapped by the caller.

```ts
import { moon } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/elpmpp02'
import { searchExtrema } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/search'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const start = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)
const stop = timeYMDHMS(2025, 10, 1, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// The geocentric Moon-Earth distance (AU): its minimum is perigee and its maximum is apogee.
const distance = (time: Time) => Math.hypot(...moon(time)[0])

for (const extremum of searchExtrema(distance, start, stop, { step: 0.25 })) {
	console.log(extremum.kind, timeToDate(extremum.time).slice(0, 5), toKilometer(extremum.value)) // minimum [2025, 9, 10, 12, 10] 364777, then maximum [2025, 9, 26, 9, 47] 405548 — TT, km
}
```

### TLE, OMM, and SGP4 Record Construction

Satellite orbital data comes as a two-line element set (TLE), a fixed-column text format used by NORAD and Space-Track, or as an Orbit Mean-Elements Message (OMM), the CCSDS JSON or XML form of the same mean elements, used by CelesTrak and Space-Track. Both carry SGP4 mean elements at an epoch: inclination, right ascension of the ascending node, eccentricity, argument of perigee, mean anomaly, mean motion (in revolutions per day), and the drag term `B*` (in inverse Earth radii). Five-digit TLE catalog numbers have run out, so numbers from 100000 use the Alpha-5 form, a leading letter in place of the first digits. To propagate either with SGP4, the elements are converted once into a record that holds the initialized model state; reusing it for many propagation times is much cheaper than rebuilding it for each call (see [SGP4/SDP4 Propagation](#sgp4sdp4-propagation)).

The record is built with the WGS-72 constants by default, the set operational element sets are fitted with. Elements typed by hand must also be SGP4 mean elements, not osculating ones. Element sets from a network query, a file, or an operator should be validated before they are parsed or propagated: a corrupted TLE line still parses into plausible numbers, which the per-line modulo-10 checksum detects, and an OMM for another frame or theory still builds a record.

```ts
import { type OMM, parseTLE, recordFromOMM, recordFromSgp4Elements, recordFromTLE, sgp4, tleCatalogNumber, tleChecksum, validateOMM, validateTLE } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/propagation/sgp4'
import { TAU } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const line1 = '1 25544U 98067A   23231.51768399  .00014050  00000+0  25837-3 0  9996'
const line2 = '2 25544  51.6415  14.7889 0003559 325.3396 149.4637 15.49477580411611'

// Validate untrusted lines first: the first problem found, or undefined for a usable set.
console.log(validateTLE(line1, line2)) // undefined

// The modulo-10 checksum of a line (its last column), and the decimal catalog number of an Alpha-5 one.
console.log(tleChecksum(line1), tleCatalogNumber('A0001')) // 6 100001

// Parse the TLE (epoch as a UTC Time, angles in radians) and build a reusable record.
const tle = parseTLE(line1, line2, 'ISS (ZARYA)')
const record = recordFromTLE(tle)

console.log(toDeg(tle.inclination), tle.meanMotion) // 51.6415 15.4947758 — degrees, rev/day
console.log(sgp4(tle.epoch, record)[0].map(toKilometer)) // [-3737.79, 2970.46, 4831.15] — km, TEME

// omm: OMM — a CelesTrak or Space-Track JSON record with the same elements; validate it, then build the same record.
declare const omm: OMM
console.log(validateOMM(omm)) // undefined for a usable set
console.log(sgp4(tle.epoch, recordFromOMM(omm))[0].map(toKilometer)) // the same TEME position, km

// Typed mean elements without TLE or OMM text (mean motion in radians/minute); the gravity option selects SGP4_WGS84 or SGP4_WGS72_OLD.
const typed = recordFromSgp4Elements({ epoch: tle.epoch, eccentricity: tle.eccentricity, inclination: tle.inclination, rightAscensionOfAscendingNode: tle.rightAscensionOfAscendingNode, argumentOfPerigee: tle.argumentOfPerigee, meanAnomaly: tle.meanAnomaly, meanMotion: (tle.meanMotion * TAU) / 1440, bstar: tle.bstar })
console.log(sgp4(tle.epoch, typed)[0].map(toKilometer)) // [-3737.79, 2970.46, 4831.15] — km, the same record
```

### Topocentric Observed Place

The observed place of a source is where an observer on the Earth's surface sees it: azimuth and altitude after light deflection, annual and diurnal aberration, precession-nutation, Earth rotation, polar motion, and optionally atmospheric refraction. This is what a telescope must point at. It is computed with the ERFA astrometry pipeline: the ICRS direction goes first to CIRS (geocentric, from the Earth state only) and then to the observed place (from the site, the Earth orientation, and the atmosphere).

`icrsToObserved` does the full chain for a source without parallax or proper motion, from the Earth's barycentric and heliocentric state; the stages `icrsToCirs` and `cirsToObserved`, and their inverses, are available separately. Azimuth is measured north through east, and the hour angle is positive west. Refraction uses the ERFA model with pressure (hPa), temperature (°C), relative humidity, and wavelength (µm), with standard defaults; it can be turned off for the geometric altitude, and applied alone to an altitude. UT1 and polar motion come from the loaded Earth orientation data; without it UT1 equals UTC, so the outputs below are good to a few arcseconds (see [Earth Orientation Parameters](#earth-orientation-parameters)). For a quick refraction estimate without pressure or temperature, see [Approximate Atmospheric Refraction](#approximate-atmospheric-refraction).

```ts
import { cirsToIcrs, cirsToObserved, icrsToCirs, icrsToObserved, observedToCirs, refractedAltitude, unrefractedAltitude } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/astrometry'
import { eraEpv00 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/earth'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { tdb, Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, hour, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const location = geodeticLocation(deg(-70.7313), deg(-29.2563), meter(2400)) // longitude, latitude, elevation
const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 4, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)

// Earth's barycentric state and heliocentric position at the TDB instant.
const t = tdb(time)
const [barycentric, heliocentric] = eraEpv00(t.day, t.fraction)

// ICRS RA 16 h, Dec -26°, with the default refraction (undefined), or without it (false).
const star = [hour(16), deg(-26)] as const
const observed = icrsToObserved(star, time, barycentric, heliocentric[0], undefined, location)

console.log(toDeg(observed.azimuth), toDeg(observed.altitude)) // 271.54 66.71 — degrees, refracted
console.log(toDeg(icrsToObserved(star, time, barycentric, heliocentric[0], false, location).altitude)) // 66.70 — degrees, geometric

// The two stages: ICRS to the geocentric CIRS [RA, Dec], then CIRS to the observed place.
const cirs = icrsToCirs(star, time, barycentric, heliocentric[0])
const stage = cirsToObserved(cirs, time, undefined, location)

console.log(cirs.map(toDeg), toDeg(stage.altitude)) // [240.0674, -26.0767] 66.71 — degrees

// The inverses: observed azimuth and altitude to CIRS, then CIRS to ICRS.
const back = observedToCirs(stage.azimuth, stage.altitude, time, undefined, location)

console.log(cirsToIcrs(back, time, barycentric, heliocentric[0]).map(toDeg)) // [240, -26] — degrees, the ICRS input

// Refraction alone: a true altitude of 10° appears higher, and an apparent altitude of 10° is lower in truth.
console.log(toDeg(refractedAltitude(deg(10)))) // 10.0861 — degrees
console.log(toDeg(unrefractedAltitude(deg(10)))) // 9.9132 — degrees
```

### Topocentric Parallax

A position computed for the Earth's centre differs from what an observer on the surface sees by the topocentric (diurnal) parallax, the change of viewpoint over up to one Earth radius. It is about a degree for the Moon, 8.8″ for a body at 1 AU, several arcseconds for a main-belt asteroid, and far more for a near-Earth one, so a geocentric prediction must be corrected before it is used to point a telescope or to identify a moving object on an image.

`geocentricToTopocentric` moves a geocentric astrometric position (ICRS/GCRS axes, radians) of a body at a known distance (AU) to a site at an instant, by subtracting the site's geocentric position rotated from ITRS to the GCRS axes. Only the parallax is applied: the light time between the geocentre and the site (at most 21 ms) is neglected, and the result stays astrometric, without the site's diurnal aberration. It suits a geocentric prediction that carries the body's distance, such as the answer of a remote service; seen from the Paris Observatory, it agrees with the SkyBoT cone search's own topocentric answer to a few hundredths of an arcsecond.

```ts
import { geocentricToTopocentric } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/astrometry'
import { Ellipsoid, geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { timeUnix } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, formatDEC, formatRA, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// A main-belt asteroid 1.4963 AU from the geocentre, seen from São Paulo on 2026-01-15 at 0h UTC.
const site = geodeticLocation(deg(-46.63), deg(-23.55), meter(760), Ellipsoid.WGS84)
const time = timeUnix(Date.UTC(2026, 0, 15) / 1000, true)

// Geocentric RA and Dec (radians) and distance (AU) to the topocentric RA and Dec.
const [ra, dec] = geocentricToTopocentric(hour(9.9953), deg(11.9831), 1.4963, time, site)

console.log(formatRA(ra), formatDEC(dec)) // topocentric RA and Dec, a few arcseconds from the geocentric ones
```

### Transit Altitude and Hour Angle

For a target of known declination, the geometry of the diurnal circle gives two quick planning numbers without any time scale or ephemeris: the altitude at upper transit, which is the highest the target gets, and the hour angle at which it crosses a chosen altitude, which sets the time it spends above that altitude. Both assume a fixed declination and ignore refraction unless it is folded into the target altitude.

```text
h_transit = 90° − |φ − δ|
cos H = (sin h − sin φ sin δ) / (cos φ cos δ)
```

The body is at altitude `h` at hour angle `−H` (rising, east of the meridian) and `+H` (setting, west), so the time above it is `2H` of hour angle. For rise and set use a small negative altitude that folds in refraction and semidiameter, such as −34′ for a point source. There is no crossing when the body stays above the altitude (as circumpolar targets do) or below it, nor at the geographic poles, where the formula degenerates. All angles are radians. For actual rise, transit, and set instants from an ephemeris, see [Rise, Transit, and Set](#rise-transit-and-set).

```ts
import { altitudeAtTransit, hourAngleAtAltitude } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'
import { deg, toDeg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const latitude = deg(-29.2563)
const declination = deg(7.407)

// Highest altitude of a target at declination +7.407° seen from latitude -29.2563°.
console.log(toDeg(altitudeAtTransit(latitude, declination))) // 53.34 — degrees

// Hour angle at the horizon with -34' of refraction: the target is up between -H and +H.
const h = hourAngleAtAltitude(declination, latitude, deg(-34 / 60))!

console.log(toHour(h)) // 5.7654 — hours, so it rises about 5.77 h of sidereal time before transit

// Circumpolar at latitude +80° for declination +85°: never reaches the horizon.
console.log(hourAngleAtAltitude(deg(85), deg(80), 0)) // undefined
```

### Tube Flexure Pointing Error

Gravity bends the telescope tube, so the optical axis sags away from the zenith by an amount that grows toward the horizon. The sag is `flexure · sin z`, with `z` the zenith distance and `flexure` the droop at the horizon, and it acts along the vertical. Converting a vertical displacement to equatorial coordinates uses the parallactic angle `q`:

```text
Δδ = −flexure·sin z·cos q
ΔH = +flexure·sin z·sin q / cos δ
```

This is the TF term of the TPoint model and is a property of gravity, not of the mount's axes, so it is kept apart from the geometric terms of [Equatorial Mount Geometric Pointing Errors](#equatorial-mount-geometric-pointing-errors). `tubeFlexureError` returns `[ΔH, Δδ]` in radians on the same convention as `equatorialPointingError`, so the two can be summed away from the poles, and `applyTubeFlexureError` returns the direction the axis really points, `[RA − ΔH, dec + Δδ]`. Near the pole, where `1 / cos δ` diverges, the droop is applied as a great-circle offset.

```ts
import { applyTubeFlexureError, tubeFlexureError } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/pointing'
import { arcsec, deg, hour, toArcsec, toDeg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const latitude = deg(-29.2563)
const flexure = arcsec(120) // droop at the horizon

// Pointing error at hour angle 3 h, declination -20°.
const [deltaHourAngle, deltaDeclination] = tubeFlexureError(hour(3), deg(-20), latitude, flexure)

console.log(toArcsec(deltaHourAngle), toArcsec(deltaDeclination)) // 78.78 29.79 — arcseconds in hour angle and declination

// Where the axis really points for RA 10 h, Dec -20° at LST 13 h (hour angle 3 h).
const [ra, dec] = applyTubeFlexureError(hour(10), deg(-20), hour(13), latitude, flexure)

console.log(toHour(ra), toDeg(dec)) // 9.99854 -19.99173 — hours, degrees
```

### Twilight and Darkness Windows

Twilight is the interval around sunrise and sunset when the Sun is below the horizon but still lights the sky, and it is classified by how far the Sun's centre is below the geometric horizon: civil below −6°, nautical below −12°, and astronomical below −18°, when the sky is dark enough for faint-object work. Dark time for deep-sky imaging usually also asks for the Moon to be down or faint.

`darknessWindows` returns, for a site and a time window, the civil, nautical, and astronomical twilight intervals and the dark intervals: the astronomical night, further restricted by the Moon's altitude or illuminated fraction when asked. The Sun's altitude is geometric and geocentric, as in [Rise, Transit, and Set](#rise-transit-and-set). A window that spans an evening and the next morning gives two intervals per night, clipped at the window edges. It is built on [Time-Constraint Intervals](#time-constraint-intervals).

```ts
import { moon } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/elpmpp02'
import { earth, sun } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { darknessWindows } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/events/darkness'
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { type Time, Timescale, timeShift, timeToDate, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { vecMinus } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec3'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const site = geodeticLocation(deg(-70.7313), deg(-29.2563), meter(2400)) // La Silla
const start = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 0, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
const end = timeShift(start, 1)

// Geocentric ICRS directions to the Sun and the Moon.
const sunAt = (time: Time) => vecMinus(sun(time)[0], earth(time)[0])
const moonAt = (time: Time) => moon(time)[0]

// Twilight windows of one UTC day.
const windows = darknessWindows(sunAt, site, start, end)

console.log(windows.astronomical.map((i) => [timeToDate(i.start).slice(0, 5), timeToDate(i.end).slice(0, 5)])) // [[[2025, 9, 28, 0, 1], [2025, 9, 28, 9, 5]]] — UTC

// Dark time with the Moon below the horizon as well.
const dark = darknessWindows(sunAt, site, start, end, { moonAt }).dark

console.log(dark.map((i) => [timeToDate(i.start).slice(0, 5), timeToDate(i.end).slice(0, 5)])) // [[[2025, 9, 28, 4, 15], [2025, 9, 28, 9, 5]]] — UTC
```

### Two-Body Kepler Propagation

Propagating a state under the Sun's gravity alone is the two-body problem: given a position and velocity at one epoch, the state at any other time follows from Kepler's laws, with no perturbations from planets. The library solves it with universal variables and Stumpff functions, a single formulation that holds for elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic orbits, forward or backward in time. It suits asteroids and comets over short spans or at moderate accuracy; it is not a substitute for a numerically integrated ephemeris over long intervals (see [SPK State Kernels](#spk-state-kernels)).

A `KeplerOrbit` is built from a heliocentric state or from orbital elements, and `at` returns the position (AU) and velocity (AU/day) at any time, with the elapsed time measured in TT. The state is rotated by the orbit's rotation, by default from heliocentric ecliptic J2000 into equatorial J2000; pass the identity rotation to keep the input axes. Elements published in the IAU 1976 ecliptic need a different rotation (see [Stellar Occultation Ground Tracks](#stellar-occultation-ground-tracks)).

```ts
import { comet, KeplerOrbit } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/asteroid'
import { Timescale, time, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005 } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'
import { matIdentity } from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/mat3'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Vesta's heliocentric state at 2025-04-21 12:00 TDB (AU, AU/day), kept in the input axes with an identity rotation.
const position = [-1.70317472297052, -1.333843040283118, -0.3086709149679688] as const
const velocity = [0.007882762615954012, -0.008079478592200335, -0.004254433056153772] as const
const orbit = new KeplerOrbit(position, velocity, time(2460787, 0, Timescale.TDB), GM_SUN_PITJEVA_2005, matIdentity())

// The state one year (365 days) later.
const [p, v] = orbit.at(time(2460787 + 365, 0, Timescale.TDB))

console.log(p) // [2.0377, -0.86910, -0.61354] — AU
console.log(v) // [0.0059944, 0.0093565, 0.0029453] — AU/day

// A comet from its elements (semi-latus rectum q·(1 + e) in AU, e, i, Ω, ω, perihelion time), with the default ecliptic-to-equatorial rotation.
const halley = comet(0.5839719999999998 * 1.967311, 0.967311, deg(162.2146), deg(59.6368), deg(112.547), timeYMDHMS(2061, 8, 31, 19, 50, 18, Timescale.TT))

console.log(halley.at(timeYMDHMS(2025, 4, 21, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.TT))[0]) // [-19.630, 29.058, 1.8353] — AU, equatorial J2000
```

### Two-Body Orbit Mechanics

A two-body orbit is fully reproducible from a center's gravitational parameter, an epoch, and either six classical elements or a Cartesian state. The elements need a reference plane, the axes do not: an ellipse is given by its semi-major axis and mean anomaly, while a parabola has no semi-major axis, period, or periodic mean anomaly and is given, like a hyperbola, by its periapsis distance and time of periapsis passage. This layer over [Two-Body Kepler Propagation](#two-body-kepler-propagation) normalizes every definition into one model in J2000 equatorial (ICRF-aligned) axes, so an ecliptic definition is rotated once and a Cartesian state never.

The model gives the exact geometric state relative to the center at any instant, and the inverse problem, the osculating elements of a state referred to the equator or the ecliptic. Some elements are undefined by geometry rather than numerically small: an equatorial orbit has no node, a circular one no periapsis, and such angles are reported as undefined instead of an arbitrary value. Units are AU, days, and AU³/day² for the gravitational parameter; the centers carry DE440 gravitational parameters by NAIF ID. The same model also samples the conic for drawing, with points crowding near periapsis, and tabulates states over an interval dense enough for Hermite interpolation (see [Splines and Interpolation](#splines-and-interpolation)). A residual against a reference state is resolved on its RTN frame (radial, along-track, normal), the natural frame for comparing an orbit with an ephemeris.

```ts
import { conicClass, orbitalElements, orbitCenter, orbitDiagnostics, orbitOf, orbitStateAt, stateResidual } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/mechanics'
import { sampleConic, sampleStates } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/orbits/sampling'
import { Timescale, time } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The Sun by NAIF ID, with its gravitational parameter (AU³/day²).
const sun = orbitCenter(10)!
const epoch = time(2460787, 0, Timescale.TDB)

// Elements on the J2000 ecliptic (angles in radians); the model's states are in equatorial axes.
const model = orbitOf({ kind: 'elliptic', mu: sun.mu, plane: 'ecliptic', semiMajorAxis: 2.7, eccentricity: 0.3, inclination: deg(12), node: deg(80), argumentOfPeriapsis: deg(70), meanAnomaly: deg(40), epoch })
if (!model.ok) throw new Error(model.reason)

// Exact two-body state 100 days later, relative to the center.
const state = orbitStateAt(model.orbit, time(2460787 + 100, 0, Timescale.TDB))
if (!state.ok) throw new Error(state.reason)
console.log(state.position) // [-0.99291, -2.1971, -0.82024] — AU, heliocentric equatorial J2000

// Osculating elements of a state, referred to the ecliptic.
const elements = orbitalElements(state.time, state.position, state.velocity, sun.mu, 'ecliptic')
console.log(elements.conic, elements.period) // elliptic 1620.5 — days
console.log(toDeg(elements.meanAnomaly!)) // 62.216 — degrees, 100 days after 40°

// The conic class of an eccentricity, with the library's circular and parabolic tolerances.
console.log(conicClass(0.3), conicClass(1)) // elliptic parabolic

// Dynamical diagnostics of a state: radius, speeds, specific energy (AU²/day², −GM/2a when bound), angular momentum.
const diagnostics = orbitDiagnostics(state.position, state.velocity, sun.mu)

console.log(diagnostics.radius, diagnostics.escapeSpeed, diagnostics.specificEnergy) // 2.5467 0.015244 -5.4799e-5 — AU, AU/day, AU²/day²

// The curve for drawing, with periapsis, apoapsis, and nodes as markers; states tabulated over a year.
const conic = sampleConic(model.orbit, { plane: 'ecliptic' })
const table = sampleStates(model.orbit, epoch, time(2460787 + 365, 0, Timescale.TDB))

// Model minus reference, resolved on the reference's RTN frame: 0.01 day later is ahead along-track.
const later = orbitStateAt(model.orbit, time(2460787 + 100.01, 0, Timescale.TDB))
if (later.ok) console.log(stateResidual(later.position, later.velocity, state.position, state.velocity).rtnPosition) // [3.2693e-5, 0.00010588, 1.6e-16] — AU
```

### Unix Millisecond Timestamps

Logs, file names, schedules, and user interfaces need wall-clock time rather than an astronomical time scale: a UTC calendar date and clock reading that can be stored as one number, compared, shifted by calendar units, and written or parsed as text. A `Temporal` is that number, the Unix time in milliseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, with calendar fields in the proleptic Gregorian calendar and no dependency on `Date` or a timezone database.

Unix time follows POSIX, so every day has exactly 86400 labelled seconds and a leap second has no reading of its own: the inserted 23:59:60 maps to the next midnight. Use [Civil UTC Timestamps](#civil-utc-timestamps) and the `Time` model wherever the leap second, the time scale, or sub-millisecond precision matters, and convert to `Temporal` only for display and bookkeeping. Calendar arithmetic is in calendar units: adding a month keeps the day of the month and clamps it to the length of the target month. Patterns are fixed-width tokens (`YYYY`, `MM`, `DD`, `HH`, `mm`, `ss`, `SSS`, and month and weekday names); a timezone offset in minutes only shifts the rendered clock, and the literal `Z` of `ISO8601_FORMAT` is correct only with the default offset 0.

```ts
import {
	daysInMonth,
	formatTemporal,
	isLeapYear,
	ISO8601_FORMAT,
	parseTemporal,
	temporalAdd,
	temporalDayOfWeek,
	temporalEndOfDay,
	temporalFromDate,
	temporalFromFractionOfYear,
	temporalFromTime,
	temporalGet,
	temporalNow,
	temporalSet,
	temporalStartOfDay,
	temporalSubtract,
	temporalToDate,
	temporalUnix,
	zellersCongruence,
} from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/temporal'
import { timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

// A UTC timestamp from calendar fields (month 1–12, milliseconds last), and back to fields.
const t = temporalFromDate(2024, 1, 31, 22, 15, 30, 250)
console.log(t) // 1706739330250 — Unix milliseconds
console.log(temporalToDate(t)) // [2024, 1, 31, 22, 15, 30, 250]

// Calendar arithmetic: one month later clamps to the end of February; 90 minutes earlier.
console.log(formatTemporal(temporalAdd(t, 1, 'month'))) // 2024-02-29 22:15:30.250
console.log(formatTemporal(temporalSubtract(t, 90, 'm'))) // 2024-01-31 20:45:30.250

// The bounds of the UTC day, one field read and replaced, and the weekday (0 is Sunday).
console.log(formatTemporal(temporalStartOfDay(t)), formatTemporal(temporalEndOfDay(t))) // 2024-01-31 00:00:00.000 2024-01-31 23:59:59.999
console.log(temporalGet(t, 'hour'), formatTemporal(temporalSet(t, 2023, 'year'))) // 22 2023-01-31 22:15:30.250
console.log(temporalDayOfWeek(t), zellersCongruence(2024, 1, 31)) // 3 3 — Wednesday

// Formatting with patterns, and with a clock shifted 180 minutes west of UTC; parsing is the inverse.
console.log(formatTemporal(t, ISO8601_FORMAT), formatTemporal(t, 'DD/MM/YYYY HH:mm'), formatTemporal(t, 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm', -180)) // 2024-01-31T22:15:30.250Z 31/01/2024 22:15 2024-01-31 19:15
console.log(parseTemporal('2024-01-31 22:15:30.250', 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss.SSS') === t) // true

// From Unix seconds, from a fractional day of the year (1-based), and from an astronomical Time (a leap second maps to the next midnight).
console.log(formatTemporal(temporalUnix(946684800)), formatTemporal(temporalFromFractionOfYear(2024, 32.5))) // 2000-01-01 00:00:00.000 2024-02-01 12:00:00.000
console.log(formatTemporal(temporalFromTime(timeYMDHMS(2016, 12, 31, 23, 59, 60.5)))) // 2017-01-01 00:00:00.000

// Calendar facts of the proleptic Gregorian calendar, and the current time from the system clock.
console.log(isLeapYear(2024), daysInMonth(2024, 2), daysInMonth(2023, 2)) // true 29 28
const now = temporalNow()
```

### Uranian Satellite Theory (GUST86)

GUST86 (Laskar and Jacobson) is the analytical theory of the five major Uranian satellites: Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, and Oberon. Each body builds equinoctial elements from shared fundamental arguments (mean longitude, eccentricity and inclination phasors), converts them to rectangular coordinates, and rotates the result into the J2000 equatorial frame. Being analytical, it needs no data files and serves for finder charts and for identifying the satellites in an image of Uranus.

The result is Uranicentric: position in AU and velocity in AU/day, in J2000 equatorial axes, at a time converted to TT. Add Uranus's barycentric state for an inertial position. The returned vectors alias internal buffers, so copy them before computing another state, or the first result is silently overwritten.

```ts
import { ariel, gust86 } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/gust86'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Ariel's state; miranda, umbriel, titania, and oberon have the same signature.
const [position, velocity] = ariel(time)

console.log(position) // [-0.0011777, 0.00035847, -0.00033843] — AU, Uranicentric
console.log(velocity) // [-0.0010278, -0.00058557, 0.0029526] — AU/day
console.log(toKilometer(Math.hypot(...position))) // 190990 — km

// The shared function: index 0 Ariel, 1 Umbriel, 2 Titania, 3 Oberon, 4 Miranda.
console.log(gust86(time, 0)[0]) // [-0.0011777, 0.00035847, -0.00033843] — AU
```

### VSOP87E Planetary Theory

VSOP87 is the Bretagnon and Francou analytical theory of the motion of the Sun and the eight planets. Version E gives barycentric rectangular coordinates: for each body a table of periodic terms (amplitude, phase, frequency) per power of time and per coordinate is summed, and its time derivative gives the velocity. It needs no data files, and it is accurate enough for planning, finders, and most apparent-place work, though not a substitute for a numerically integrated JPL kernel when sub-arcsecond planetary astrometry is needed.

Every body returns its position (AU) and velocity (AU/day) with the origin at the solar-system barycenter, at a time converted to TT, in ICRF equatorial axes by default or in the theory's native dynamical ecliptic and equinox of J2000. Pluto is not part of VSOP87: see [Pluto Short Analytical Theory](#pluto-short-analytical-theory). For a Moon state see [ELP/MPP02 Lunar Theory](#elpmpp02-lunar-theory), which is geocentric.

```ts
import { earth, jupiter } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/models/analytical/vsop87e'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2025, 9, 28, 12, 0, 0, Timescale.TT)

// Earth, barycentric, ICRF equatorial axes; sun, mercury, venus, mars, jupiter, saturn, uranus, and neptune share the signature.
const [position, velocity] = earth(time)

console.log(position) // [0.99399, 0.079296, 0.034528] — AU
console.log(velocity) // [-0.0018575, 0.015660, 0.0067880] — AU/day

// The same position in the dynamical ecliptic and equinox of J2000.
console.log(earth(time, 'eclipticJ2000')[0]) // [0.99399, 0.086487, 0.00013679] — AU

console.log(jupiter(time)[0]) // [-1.0007, 4.6557, 2.0200] — AU, barycentric
```

### Zenith and Celestial Circle Intersections

Some points on the sky are defined by the observer's meridian rather than by a catalog position: the zenith, the point where the local meridian crosses the celestial equator, and the point where it crosses the ecliptic. They are expressed as equatorial coordinates of date, and their right ascension is always the local apparent sidereal time; the zenith's declination is the latitude.

The meridian-ecliptic point has the declination that solves `tan(dec) = sin(ra) · tan(ε)` with the true obliquity of date, and the equator-ecliptic intersection is whichever equinox node lies within a quarter turn of the meridian. Angles are radians, longitude is east-positive, and the time defaults to the current instant. Convert to azimuth and altitude with [Local Horizon Coordinates](#local-horizon-coordinates) when needed.

```ts
import { equatorEcliptic, meridianEcliptic, meridianEquator, zenith } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/coordinate'
import { Timescale, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const time = timeYMDHMS(2026, 6, 29, 4, 0, 0, Timescale.UTC)
const longitude = deg(-70.7313)
const latitude = deg(-29.2563)

// Each returns [right ascension, declination] of date, in radians.
```
