```ts
console.log(zenith(longitude, latitude, time).map(toDeg)) // [266.527, -29.256] — degrees, RA = LST and Dec = latitude
console.log(meridianEquator(longitude, time).map(toDeg)) // [266.527, 0] — degrees
console.log(meridianEcliptic(longitude, time).map(toDeg)) // [266.527, -23.399] — degrees
console.log(equatorEcliptic(longitude, time).map(toDeg)) // [180, 0] — degrees, the nearer equinox node
```

## 📐 Astrometry

### ASTAP Plate Solving

Plate solving finds where an image points: the sky coordinates of its center, its pixel scale, its orientation, and its parity, by matching the pattern of the stars in the image against a reference star database. ASTAP (Astrometric STAcking Program) is a free external solver that matches quads of stars against its own star databases; with a center, a search radius, and a field-of-view hint it solves in seconds, and without them it searches the whole sky. The result is the WCS that ASTAP writes, summarized as a [Plate Solution](#plate-solution).

This adapter spawns the local `astap` program on a FITS or image file and needs ASTAP and one of its star databases, which are not part of the library. Angles are radians. A center and radius given here replace the position in the FITS header, and a radius alone lets ASTAP take the center from the header. By default SIP distortion terms are requested, and ASTAP's non-canonical constant and linear SIP terms are evaluated as written (see [FITS TAN and SIP Coordinate Mapping](#fits-tan-and-sip-coordinate-mapping)). The call resolves to `undefined` when ASTAP searched and found no solution, and rejects when it could not search at all.

```ts
import { astapPlateSolve } from 'nebulosa/src/astrometry/solvers/astap'
import { deg, hour, toArcmin, toArcsec, toDeg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A solve with hints for the center, the search radius, and the field of view (radians).
const solution = await astapPlateSolve('data/NGC3372--32.1.fit', { rightAscension: hour(10.7345), declination: deg(-59.6022), radius: deg(4), fov: deg(0.54) })

if (solution) {
	console.log(toHour(solution.rightAscension), toDeg(solution.declination)) // 10.7345062 -59.6019829 — image center, ICRS
	console.log(toDeg(solution.orientation), toArcsec(solution.scale), solution.parity) // 110.1218553 2.7361834 NORMAL — degrees, arcsec/pixel
	console.log(toArcmin(solution.width), toArcmin(solution.height)) // 47.2839347 32.2001423 — arcminutes
}
```

### ASTAP Star Detection

Star detection turns an image into a list of point sources with a sub-pixel centroid, a half-flux diameter (HFD), a signal-to-noise ratio, and a flux, the input of focusing, guiding, registration, and plate solving. This adapter runs the `-extract` mode of the local ASTAP program, an independent detector that is useful to compare with or replace the built-in one of [Star Detection](#star-detection); the records have the same shape.

ASTAP numbers pixels from 1, and the positions are converted to the 0-based array indices of the library. The ASTAP binary is required, and ASTAP writes its CSV next to the input, so the input's directory must be writable. An empty list means ASTAP ran and found no stars.

```ts
import { astapDetectStars } from 'nebulosa/src/astrometry/solvers/astap'

// The five stars with the highest SNR of an image (file of the repository).
const stars = await astapDetectStars('data/apod4.jpg', { maxStars: 5 })

console.log(stars[0]) // { x: 464.9656, y: 119.9062, hfd: 7.5315, snr: 295, flux: 3022214 } — 0-based pixels, HFD in pixels
```

### Astrometry.net Index Selection

An astrometry.net solver needs index files, each of which stores star quads whose diameters fall in a narrow interval, and a field is solvable when the indexes hold quads of roughly 10 % to 100 % of the image size. Knowing the focal length, the pixel pitch, and the sensor size gives the pixel scale and the field, and so the few index scales that the solver will actually use; with an approximate pointing, only the sky tiles around the field are needed. This turns a download of tens of gigabytes into the minimum practical set.

`selectAstrometryIndexes` is a pure computation: it never reads the filesystem or the network and only returns descriptors of the files and why each is needed. The manifest covers the 5200 series (quads from 2′ to 22′, tiled at HEALPix resolution 2, 48 tiles per scale) and the 4100 series (22′ to 2000′, one all-sky file per scale), so a very long or very short focal length can be only partially covered or not at all. The tile numbers are the HEALPix XY identifiers of astrometry.net, which are not the RING or NESTED numbers of standard HEALPix.

```ts
import { coordinateToTile, distanceToTile, selectAstrometryIndexes, tileIntersectsDisc } from 'nebulosa/src/astrometry/solvers/astrometrynet.index'
import { deg, hour, toArcsec, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A 1000 mm telescope (focal length in mm) with a 3.76 µm camera of 4144 × 2822 pixels, no position known.
const plan = selectAstrometryIndexes({ focalLength: 1000, pixelPitch: 3.76, width: 4144, height: 2822 })

console.log(toArcsec(plan.pixelScale)) // 0.7755557 — arcsec/pixel
console.log(plan.scales.map((s) => s.indexNumber)) // [ 5202, 5203, 5204, 5205, 5206, 4107, 4108, 4109 ]
console.log(plan.files.length, plan.files[0].filename) // 243 index-5202-00.fits — every tile of each scale

// The same camera near the Carina Nebula with 1° of pointing error: only the tiles near the field.
const center = { rightAscension: hour(10.7345), declination: deg(-59.6022) }
const near = selectAstrometryIndexes({ focalLength: 1000, pixelPitch: 3.76, width: 4144, height: 2822, center, pointingUncertainty: deg(1) })

console.log(near.files.length) // 13

// The astrometry.net HEALPix XY tile of a position, at resolution 2.
console.log(coordinateToTile(center.rightAscension, center.declination, 2)) // 38

// The angular distance from the position to a neighboring tile, and whether a disc of 1° (radians) touches it.
console.log(toDeg(distanceToTile(36, 2, center.rightAscension, center.declination)), tileIntersectsDisc(36, 2, center.rightAscension, center.declination, deg(1))) // 0.3133201 true — degrees
```

### Catalog Crossmatching

Crossmatching identifies which catalog star each detected image star is. It is the step between detection and anything that needs a known star: photometric calibration against catalog magnitudes, labeling stars, measuring residuals against a reference catalog, or recovering an approximate solution when only the mount's pointing is known. Detections are in pixels and catalog stars in equatorial coordinates, so the catalog stars around the approximate pointing are projected on a gnomonic plane (see [Sky Projections](#sky-projections)) and the two point sets are matched geometrically, without knowing scale or rotation in advance (see [Star Pattern Matching](#star-pattern-matching)).

`crossMatchStars` queries a cone of a [Star Catalog Interface and Spatial Query](#star-catalog-interface-and-spatial-query) around the approximate center, matches, and moves the projection center to the fitted image center until it converges. The cone must cover the field and the pointing error, and a camera's pixel size and focal length give the expected scale. The solution is a similarity fit on a tangent plane (center, scale, rotation, parity), not a WCS with distortion, so it is a starting point for a refined solve. A failed match is reported in the result, not thrown.

```ts
import { crossMatchStars } from 'nebulosa/src/astrometry/matching/star.crossmatching'
import { deg, hour, toArcsec, toDeg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// detected: DetectedStar[] — image stars (pixels, origin at the top-left, y down) with their flux.
// catalog: StarCatalog — any catalog with a cone query, such as a local tiled catalog.
// Pointing within the cone of 1° around RA 5.5 h, Dec −5°; the camera gives the nominal scale (µm, mm).
const result = await crossMatchStars(detected, catalog, { centerRA: hour(5.5), centerDEC: deg(-5), radius: deg(1), camera: { width: 1600, height: 1200, pixelSize: 3.76, focalLength: 387 } })

if (result.success) {
	const solution = result.solution!
	console.log(toHour(solution.rightAscension), toDeg(solution.declination)) // fitted image center, hours and degrees
	console.log(toArcsec(solution.scale), toDeg(solution.rotation), solution.mirrored) // arcsec/pixel, degrees, parity
	console.log(result.matches[0].catalogStar) // the catalog star paired with the first detection
}
```

### FITS TAN and SIP Coordinate Mapping

The FITS World Coordinate System (Greisen and Calabretta) describes in header keywords how image pixels map to the sky. Almost every plate solver writes the gnomonic (`TAN`) projection: pixel offsets from the reference pixel `CRPIX` are turned by the linear `CD` matrix (degrees per pixel, absorbing scale, rotation, and parity) into intermediate coordinates on the plane tangent to the sky at `CRVAL`, which are then deprojected to right ascension and declination. Real optics are not perfectly gnomonic, and the Simple Imaging Polynomial convention (Shupe et al. 2005) adds a 2D polynomial distortion to the pixel offsets before the matrix, marked by `-SIP` in `CTYPE`.

These pure TypeScript functions read a plain `FitsHeader` object, from a file or written by hand, and convert between pixels and the sky for `RA---TAN`/`DEC--TAN` and their `-SIP` forms; for any other projection (`SIN`, `ARC`, `TPV`...) use [WCSLIB Equatorial Projection](#wcslib-equatorial-projection). Pixel coordinates are FITS ones, 1-based with the center of the first pixel at (1, 1); header values are degrees and results radians. The linear part may be given as `CD`, as `PC` with `CDELT`, or as `CDELT` with `CROTA2`. Sky to pixel uses the inverse `AP`/`BP` polynomials when present and otherwise inverts the forward polynomial iteratively, so a SIP round trip is exact only as far as that inverse goes. Non-zero constant and linear SIP terms, as ASTAP writes them, are evaluated as written, so the reference pixel then does not map exactly to `CRVAL`. A malformed SIP header gives `undefined` rather than a silent fallback to plain TAN.

```ts
import { cd, cdFromCdelt, cdMatrix, DEC_TAN, DEC_TAN_SIP, hasCd, isWcsFitsKeyword, matrixKind, pc2cd, RA_TAN, RA_TAN_SIP, tanProject, tanUnproject } from 'nebulosa/src/astrometry/wcs/fits.wcs'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A TAN header of 0.0005°/pixel (1.8″), centered at RA 83.8°, Dec -5.4°, with the reference pixel at (500.5, 400.5).
const header = { CTYPE1: RA_TAN, CTYPE2: DEC_TAN, CRPIX1: 500.5, CRPIX2: 400.5, CRVAL1: 83.8, CRVAL2: -5.4, CD1_1: -0.0005, CD1_2: 0, CD2_1: 0, CD2_2: 0.0005 }

// The linear part as a row-major CD matrix (degrees per pixel), whichever convention the header uses.
console.log(cdMatrix(header)) // [ -0.0005, 0, 0, 0.0005 ]

// The convention of the linear part (cd, pc, crota or none), whether there is one, and one CD element (1-based i, j).
console.log(matrixKind(header), hasCd(header), cd(header, 2, 2)) // cd true 0.0005
console.log(matrixKind({ CDELT1: -0.0005, CDELT2: 0.0005, CROTA2: 30 })) // crota

// The older conventions converted to CD: CDELT with a rotation (radians), and a PC matrix with CDELT.
console.log(cdFromCdelt(-0.0005, 0.0005, deg(30))) // [ -0.000433, -0.00025, -0.00025, 0.000433 ] — to rounding
console.log(pc2cd(0.866, -0.5, 0.5, 0.866, -0.0005, 0.0005)) // [ -0.000433, 0.00025, 0.00025, 0.000433 ]

// The WCS keywords of a header, for example to copy or strip a solution.
console.log(Object.keys({ ...header, EXPTIME: 30 }).filter(isWcsFitsKeyword)) // every key except EXPTIME

// Sky (radians) to FITS pixel, and back; undefined beyond the tangent plane.
const [x, y] = tanProject(header, deg(83.85), deg(-5.3))!
console.log(x, y) // 400.9273535770926 600.4961898691276
console.log(tanUnproject(header, x, y)!.map(toDeg)) // [ 83.85, -5.3 ] — degrees, to rounding

// The same header with an order-2 SIP distortion.
const sip = { ...header, CTYPE1: RA_TAN_SIP, CTYPE2: DEC_TAN_SIP, A_ORDER: 2, B_ORDER: 2, A_2_0: 1e-5, A_1_1: -2e-6, B_0_2: 1.5e-5, B_1_1: 3e-6 }
console.log(tanProject(sip, deg(83.85), deg(-5.3))) // [ 400.7881521810434, 599.9590962083622 ] — no AP/BP, inverted by iteration
```

### FITS WCS Geometry Updates

A plate solution is tied to the pixel grid it was solved on. When the image is later flipped, binned, resampled, or cropped, the WCS keywords must be transformed the same way, or every annotation, catalog overlay, and pixel-to-sky conversion lands on the wrong star. A flip mirrors the reference pixel and the linear matrix and changes the signs of the SIP coefficients according to the parity of each term; a resize divides the matrix by the scale and rescales the SIP coefficients; a crop only moves the reference pixel.

`reflectFitsWcs` and `scaleAndCropFitsWcs` handle the primary two-axis TAN or TAN-SIP solution in the FITS 1-based pixel frame. They change the header in place and return it, so clone it first to keep the original solution. A resized linear part is always written as a `CD` matrix, and a WCS that cannot be resized exactly (distortion tables, `PV` terms, other projections) loses its WCS keywords instead of keeping a wrong solution. The image size is not part of the WCS, so `NAXIS1` and `NAXIS2` are left to the caller.

```ts
import { DEC_TAN_SIP, RA_TAN_SIP, reflectFitsWcs, scaleAndCropFitsWcs, tanProject } from 'nebulosa/src/astrometry/wcs/fits.wcs'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A 1000 × 800 image with a TAN-SIP solution of 0.0005°/pixel, a small rotation term, and an order-2 distortion.
const header = { CTYPE1: RA_TAN_SIP, CTYPE2: DEC_TAN_SIP, CRPIX1: 500.5, CRPIX2: 400.5, CRVAL1: 83.8, CRVAL2: -5.4, CD1_1: -0.0005, CD1_2: 0.00005, CD2_1: 0.00005, CD2_2: 0.0005, A_ORDER: 2, B_ORDER: 2, A_2_0: 1e-5, A_1_1: -2e-6, B_0_2: 1.5e-5, B_1_1: 3e-6 }
console.log(tanProject(header, deg(83.85), deg(-5.3))) // [ 421.61990320356387, 607.7792875222979 ] — FITS pixels

// The image flipped horizontally (width, height in pixels): the star moves to x' = 1001 − x.
const horizontal = reflectFitsWcs({ ...header }, 1000, 800, true, false)
console.log(tanProject(horizontal, deg(83.85), deg(-5.3))) // [ 579.3800967964362, 607.7792875222979 ]

// The image halved and then cropped by 10 columns and 20 rows: p' = (p − 0.5)·0.5 + 0.5 − offset.
const half = scaleAndCropFitsWcs({ ...header }, 0.5, 0.5, 10, 20)
console.log(tanProject(half, deg(83.85), deg(-5.3))) // [ 201.05995160178193, 284.13964376114893 ]
```

### Local Astrometry.net Plate Solving

Astrometry.net (Lang et al. 2010) solves an image blindly, with no hint of position or scale, by geometric hashing: the relative positions of each quad of four stars form a code that does not depend on scale, rotation, or translation, and the codes of the image are looked up in index files built from a reference catalog. A matching quad proposes a solution, which is then verified against the other stars. This adapter runs the `solve-field` program of a local astrometry.net installation and summarizes its WCS as a [Plate Solution](#plate-solution).

`solve-field` detects the stars itself, so the input is a path to an image file. The program and its index files are required (see [Astrometry.net Index Selection](#astrometrynet-index-selection)); a configuration file can point it to them. A field-of-view hint narrows the scale search, a center with a radius narrows the sky search (both are needed for the window), and the timeout is also the program's CPU limit. The call resolves to `undefined` when `solve-field` finished without a solution, and rejects when it could not run.

```ts
import { localAstrometryNetPlateSolve } from 'nebulosa/src/astrometry/solvers/astrometrynet'
import { deg, toArcsec, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A blind solve: the scale is guessed and the sky is not constrained.
const blind = await localAstrometryNetPlateSolve('image.fits', { executable: 'solve-field' })

// A hinted solve: a 1° field of view inside a radius around RA 10°, Dec +20° (radians), with a time limit in ms.
const hinted = await localAstrometryNetPlateSolve('image.fits', { executable: 'solve-field', fov: deg(1), rightAscension: deg(10), declination: deg(20), radius: deg(2.2), timeout: 90000 })

if (hinted) console.log(toDeg(hinted.rightAscension), toDeg(hinted.declination), toArcsec(hinted.scale)) // center in degrees, arcsec/pixel
```

### Native libastrometry Plate Solving

The astrometry.net solver (see [Local Astrometry.net Plate Solving](#local-astrometrynet-plate-solving) for the method) is also compiled into a native library and called in process through `bun:ffi`, so no external program is spawned and no image file is written. Instead of an image it takes the already measured star list, typically from [Star Detection](#star-detection), ordered by flux, with 0-based pixel positions and the image size; this suits a capture pipeline that has detected stars anyway.

The index files are given as paths or directories (see [Astrometry.net Index Selection](#astrometrynet-index-selection)); a field of view or scale and a center with a radius narrow the search, and the solution is refined with a SIP polynomial by default. The result is a [Plate Solution](#plate-solution), or `undefined` when the field is not matched. The native library must exist for the platform, and the solve runs synchronously inside the native call, so a blind solve against many indexes blocks the thread for its whole duration. The `AstrometryNet` class keeps one native solver for several solves and is released with `using`.

```ts
import { AstrometryNet, astrometryNetIndexFiles, libAstrometryNetPlateSolve, unload } from 'nebulosa/src/bindings/astrometry/libastrometry'
import { readImageFromJpeg } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/model/image'
import { detectStars } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/stars/detector'
import { deg, toArcsec, toDeg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A 719 × 507 JPEG of the northern sky, and its detected stars.
const image = readImageFromJpeg(Buffer.from(await Bun.file('data/apod4.jpg').arrayBuffer()), undefined, 'GRAY')!
const stars = detectStars(image, { maxStars: 200 })

// A hinted solve with the 4116 index: a field 34° wide, ±20 % on the scale, SIP order 2.
const solution = await libAstrometryNetPlateSolve(stars, image.metadata.width, image.metadata.height, { indexes: 'data/index-4116.fits', fov: deg(34), scaleError: 0.2, tweakOrder: 2, maxStars: 200 })

if (solution) {
	console.log(toHour(solution.rightAscension), toDeg(solution.declination)) // 12.4786163 56.7126013 — hours, degrees, J2000
	console.log(toArcsec(solution.scale), solution.CTYPE1) // 170.8421226 RA---TAN-SIP — arcsec/pixel
}

// The index files that a path or directory list resolves to (directories are scanned recursively).
console.log(await astrometryNetIndexFiles('data')) // [ "data/index-4116.fits" ] — with the platform's path separator

// One native solver reused for several solves, released at the end of its scope (or by dispose()).
{
	using solver = new AstrometryNet()
	await solver.solve(stars, image.metadata.width, image.metadata.height, { indexes: 'data' })
}

// Closes the cached native library once no solver is alive; the next solver opens it again.
unload()
```

### Nova Astrometry.net Plate Solving

nova.astrometry.net is the public web service of astrometry.net (see [Local Astrometry.net Plate Solving](#local-astrometrynet-plate-solving) for the method): it solves an uploaded image against the complete index set, with no local installation, at the cost of the network round trips and a queue that can take minutes. The same API is served by a self-hosted astrometry.net server, whose URL can replace the public one.

The image is sent to a third-party service; it is submitted privately, without permission for commercial use or modification, unless the options say otherwise, and an API key of the user's account is needed beyond the anonymous one. The input is a URL or a `Blob`. A solve logs in, uploads, polls the submission and its job, and downloads the WCS, which is summarized as a [Plate Solution](#plate-solution); the timeout bounds the whole solve. The individual steps are exported to drive a solve by hand, for example to show the submission and job ids while it runs.

```ts
import { jobStatus, login, novaAstrometryNetPlateSolve, submissionStatus, upload, wcsFile } from 'nebulosa/src/astrometry/solvers/astrometrynet'
import { deg, toArcsec, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// file: Blob — the image to solve.
// End to end, with a 1° search radius (radians) and a time limit in ms.
const solution = await novaAstrometryNetPlateSolve(file, { radius: deg(1), timeout: 120000 })

if (solution) console.log(toDeg(solution.rightAscension), toDeg(solution.declination), toArcsec(solution.scale)) // center in degrees, arcsec/pixel

// The steps by hand against a self-hosted server: session, submission, job, and the WCS FITS file.
const apiUrl = 'http://localhost:8080'
const session = await login({ apiUrl })
const submission = await upload({ input: file, session, apiUrl })
const jobId = (await submissionStatus(submission!, { session, apiUrl }))?.jobs.find((id) => typeof id === 'number')
const job = jobId === undefined ? undefined : await jobStatus(jobId, { session, apiUrl })
const wcs = job?.status === 'success' ? await wcsFile(jobId!, { session, apiUrl }) : undefined // Blob
```

### Planar Similarity and Affine Transforms

Two images of the same field, or an image and a projected catalog, are related in the image plane by a 2D transform. Between frames of the same camera and telescope the relation is a similarity: a rotation, a uniform scale, a translation, and possibly a mirror (an odd number of reflections in the optical train, such as a star diagonal, flips the frame). When the scale differs between the axes or the frame is sheared, for example between different optics or under differential refraction, the affine transform with six free parameters is needed. With `a = scale·cos(rotation)` and `b = scale·sin(rotation)`:

```text
similarity:  x' = a·x − b·y + tx      y' = b·x + a·y + ty
mirrored:    x' = a·x + b·y + tx      y' = b·x − a·y + ty
affine:      x' = m00·x + m01·y + tx  y' = m10·x + m11·y + ty
```

The transforms are plain objects in image pixels, used by [Star Pattern Matching](#star-pattern-matching) and [Star List Registration](#star-list-registration). The fits find the least-squares transform that sends matched `current` points onto their `reference` points, from at least 2 pairs for a similarity and 3 for an affine. The points must be spread over the field: collinear or coincident points give a degenerate fit.

```ts
import { applyAffineTransformToPoint, applySimilarityTransformToPoint, applyTransformToPoint, applyTransformToStars, fitAffineTransform, fitSimilarityTransform, invertAffineTransform, invertSimilarityTransform, invertTransform } from 'nebulosa/src/astrometry/matching/star.matching'

// current, reference: { x, y }[] — pixel positions of the same stars in two frames, in the same order.
// stars: DetectedStar[] — stars of the current frame.
// Least-squares similarity from current to reference; pass true to fit the mirrored branch.
const similarity = fitSimilarityTransform(current, reference)!
console.log(Math.hypot(similarity.a, similarity.b), Math.atan2(similarity.b, similarity.a)) // scale, rotation in radians

// The full affine map, with shear and different axis scales.
const affine = fitAffineTransform(current, reference)!

// Map a point or a star list (other fields kept) into the reference frame, and go back.
console.log(applyTransformToPoint(100, 120, affine)) // { x, y } in reference pixels
const aligned = applyTransformToStars(stars, similarity)
const inverse = invertTransform(similarity) // undefined when singular

// The typed forms of the same operations, for a transform known to be a similarity or an affine.
console.log(applySimilarityTransformToPoint(100, 120, similarity), applyAffineTransformToPoint(100, 120, affine)) // { x, y } in reference pixels
console.log(invertSimilarityTransform(similarity), invertAffineTransform(affine)) // the inverse maps, or undefined
```

### Plate Solution

A plate solution is the compact answer to where an image points: the ICRS coordinates of its center, the pixel scale, the orientation of the field, its angular width, height, and radius, and its parity (whether the image is mirrored relative to the sky). It is what every solver of the library returns, and what centering, framing, and annotation need; the full WCS header is kept alongside it for pixel-level conversions (see [FITS TAN and SIP Coordinate Mapping](#fits-tan-and-sip-coordinate-mapping)).

`plateSolutionFrom` derives it from an equatorial `TAN` or `TAN-SIP` header in ICRS or FK5 J2000, which is taken as ICRS (they agree to about 0.03″); other projections and frames give `undefined`. The center is the sky position of the central pixel with the distortion applied, not `CRVAL`, which is the center only when the reference pixel is. The scale is the geometric mean of the two pixel scales, the square root of the absolute determinant of the CD matrix, so it stays meaningful for non-square or sheared pixels; scale, size, orientation, and parity come from the CD matrix alone, and the parity is `FLIPPED` when its determinant is negative. The solvers are [ASTAP Plate Solving](#astap-plate-solving), [Local Astrometry.net Plate Solving](#local-astrometrynet-plate-solving), [Nova Astrometry.net Plate Solving](#nova-astrometrynet-plate-solving), and [Native libastrometry Plate Solving](#native-libastrometry-plate-solving).

```ts
import { plateSolutionFrom } from 'nebulosa/src/astrometry/solvers/platesolver'
import { toArcmin, toArcsec, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A 1000 × 800 TAN header with 1.8″ pixels whose central pixel is the reference RA 83.8221°, Dec −5.3911°.
const header = { CTYPE1: 'RA---TAN', CTYPE2: 'DEC--TAN', NAXIS1: 1000, NAXIS2: 800, CRPIX1: 500.5, CRPIX2: 400.5, CRVAL1: 83.8221, CRVAL2: -5.3911, CD1_1: -0.0005, CD1_2: 0, CD2_1: 0, CD2_2: 0.0005 }

// The summary of the header; angles in radians.
const solution = plateSolutionFrom(header)!

console.log(toDeg(solution.rightAscension), toDeg(solution.declination)) // 83.8221 -5.3911 — image center, degrees
console.log(toArcsec(solution.scale), toArcmin(solution.width), toArcmin(solution.height), toArcmin(solution.radius)) // 1.8 30 24 19.2093727
console.log(toDeg(solution.orientation), solution.parity) // 180 FLIPPED — a negative CD determinant
```

### SIP Distortion Fitting

A linear TAN solution places stars correctly only near the reference pixel: field curvature, the distortion of reducers and flatteners, and wide fields bend the mapping, so the residuals between measured and predicted star positions grow toward the corners. The Simple Imaging Polynomial (SIP) convention models this as a correction added to the pixel offsets `u = x − CRPIX1` and `v = y − CRPIX2` before the CD matrix, with one polynomial per axis:

```text
x_ref − x = Σ A_i_j · u^i · v^j      y_ref − y = Σ B_i_j · u^i · v^j      2 ≤ i + j ≤ order
```

The terms of degree 0 and 1 belong to `CRVAL` and the CD matrix, so the model starts at degree 2. `fitSipDistortion` fits both polynomials by weighted least squares from matched stars, each with its measured pixel and the pixel where the linear WCS puts its catalog position, and rejects outliers by iterative sigma clipping. A higher order needs more stars and a good spread across the field, otherwise the polynomial extrapolates wildly in the empty regions; when the image size is known, the fit refuses a poor distribution unless told otherwise. The model belongs to the reference pixel of the linear WCS and must be refit when `CRPIX` changes. Writing it into a header promotes `TAN` to `TAN-SIP`; the inverse polynomials are not fitted, so sky to pixel is then computed by iteration (see [FITS TAN and SIP Coordinate Mapping](#fits-tan-and-sip-coordinate-mapping)).

```ts
import { applySipCorrection, countSipTerms, evaluateSipCorrection, fitSipDistortion, listSipTerms, sipModelIntoFitsHeader } from 'nebulosa/src/astrometry/wcs/sip.fit'

// stars: MatchedStar[] — measured pixel (x, y) and the pixel (xRef, yRef) predicted by the linear WCS from the catalog.
// header: FitsHeader — the linear TAN solution of the image.
const wcs = { crpix1: 500.5, crpix2: 400.5, width: 1000, height: 800 }

// The number of coefficients per axis of an order, the unknowns that the matched stars must outnumber, and their (i, j) powers.
console.log(countSipTerms(2), countSipTerms(3), listSipTerms(2)) // 3 7 [ { i: 2, j: 0 }, { i: 1, j: 1 }, { i: 0, j: 2 } ]

// Order-2 fit with sigma clipping; the result has the A and B coefficients and the RMS residual in pixels.
const fit = fitSipDistortion(stars, wcs, { order: 2 })
console.log(fit.A, fit.B, fit.rmsTotal) // { A_2_0, A_1_1, A_0_2 }, { B_2_0, B_1_1, B_0_2 }, pixels

// The correction at a measured pixel, and the corrected position.
console.log(evaluateSipCorrection(900, 700, fit.model, wcs)) // { dx, dy } in pixels
console.log(applySipCorrection(900, 700, fit.model, wcs)) // { x, y } in pixels

// Write A_ORDER, B_ORDER, and the coefficients into a TAN header, which becomes TAN-SIP.
sipModelIntoFitsHeader(fit.model, header)
```

### Star Pattern Matching

Registering two star fields means finding which star of one is which star of the other, without knowing the scale, rotation, or offset between them. The classic answer is triangle matching: the ratios of the sides of a triangle of stars do not change with translation, rotation, or uniform scale, so triangles built from neighboring stars give descriptors that can be compared directly between the two lists; the orientation of a triangle (its chirality) flips in a mirrored field. Matching descriptors vote for star pairs, the best hypotheses are verified against the whole field with outlier rejection, and the result is a transform (see [Planar Similarity and Affine Transforms](#planar-similarity-and-affine-transforms)) and the list of matched pairs.

`matchStars` returns a similarity (rotation, uniform scale, optional mirror, translation), or an affine transform when it fits materially better, that maps the current stars into the frame of the reference stars, in pixels; a scale below 1 means the current frame is the larger one. It is deterministic and meant for tens to a few hundred stars with a scale ratio near 1 (0.8 to 1.2 by default). Nearly collinear or symmetric fields give few stable patterns, and a failure is reported in the result, not thrown. Registration of frames for stacking builds on it in [Star List Registration](#star-list-registration).

```ts
import { matchStars } from 'nebulosa/src/astrometry/matching/star.matching'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// reference, current: DetectedStar[] — the stars of two frames (x, y, flux, snr, hfd), in the same pixel convention.
// Here current is reference rotated by 10°, scaled by 1.05, and shifted.
const match = matchStars(reference, current)

console.log(match.success, match.model) // true similarity
console.log(match.similarity!.scale, toDeg(match.similarity!.rotation), match.similarity!.mirrored) // 0.952381 -10.0000 false — current to reference
console.log(match.matches[0]) // { currentIndex, referenceIndex, residual } — indices into the inputs, residual in pixels
```

### WCSLIB Equatorial Projection

The FITS WCS standard defines more than twenty sky projections besides the gnomonic one: orthographic (`SIN`, common in radio astronomy), zenithal equidistant (`ARC`), zenithal equal-area (`ZEA`), Hammer-Aitoff (`AIT`) for all-sky maps, and others. WCSLIB (Calabretta) is the reference implementation of the standard. `Wcs` binds the native WCSLIB through `bun:ffi` and converts between pixels and equatorial coordinates for any projection it knows, where the pure TypeScript [FITS TAN and SIP Coordinate Mapping](#fits-tan-and-sip-coordinate-mapping) only knows `TAN`.

The sky side is always `[rightAscension, declination]` in radians, whatever the order of the FITS axes, and the pixel side is the FITS one, 1-based. Only a single two-axis equatorial solution is accepted; galactic or ecliptic axes are refused. SIP is not applied by this class: a `-SIP` header is parsed but its transforms fail, so use `tanProject` and `tanUnproject` for TAN-SIP. The class owns native memory and must be released with `using` or `[Symbol.dispose]()`, and the native library must exist for the platform.

```ts
import { unload, Wcs } from 'nebulosa/src/bindings/astrometry/libwcs'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A SIN header of 0.0005°/pixel with a small rotation term, centered at RA 83.8°, Dec -5.4°.
const header = { CTYPE1: 'RA---SIN', CTYPE2: 'DEC--SIN', CRPIX1: 500.5, CRPIX2: 400.5, CRVAL1: 83.8, CRVAL2: -5.4, CD1_1: -0.0005, CD1_2: 0.00005, CD2_1: 0.00005, CD2_2: 0.0005, RADESYS: 'ICRS', EQUINOX: 2000 }

{
	// Parse the header; released at the end of the scope.
	using wcs = new Wcs(header)

	// FITS pixel to [RA, Dec] in radians, and sky to pixel.
	console.log(wcs.pixToSky(700, 600)!.map(toDeg)) // [ 83.70984091889542, -5.290268285694518 ] — degrees
	console.log(wcs.skyToPix(deg(83.85), deg(-5.3))) // [ 421.7149740557992, 608.3743123612096 ] — FITS pixels

	// Replace the solution held by the same instance with another header.
	wcs.load({ ...header, CRVAL1: 84 })
}

// Closes the cached native library once no Wcs is alive.
unload()
```

## 🖼️ Imaging

Plan telescope and camera combinations, then work with captured or synthetic images.

### Aberration Focus Scan

A single frame shows where the stars degrade but not why: a tilted sensor, a curved field, and a wrong backfocus can all leave the corners soft (see [Aberration Inspector](#aberration-inspector)). A focus scan, a run of frames stepped through focus, separates them, because each region of the sensor reaches its own best focus: a tilt makes the best focus change linearly across the field, field curvature makes it change quadratically from the center to the edges, and a wrong spacing to a flattener shows as an offset between the center and the periphery.

`inspectAberrationFocusScan` reports the whole aberration family of a focus run at once: it inspects every frame by region, fits a focus curve per region (see [Focus Curve Fitting](#focus-curve-fitting)), fits a quadratic best-focus surface through the regional minima that separates tilt from field curvature (see [Focus Surface Analysis](#focus-surface-analysis)), and derives from it the plane and its tilt (see [Sensor Tilt Estimator](#sensor-tilt-estimator)), the curvature (see [Focus Field Curvature](#focus-field-curvature)), and the field offset (see [Backfocus Correction Estimates](#backfocus-correction-estimates)). A physical scale converts the tilt into angles, a backfocus calibration permits backfocus findings, and the stars can optionally be registered across the frames and tracked, each with its own focus curve. Findings are statistical and published only at about 3 sigma, so a surface fitted from few regions never reports a pattern; like the surface, they say where the focus is best, not which part causes it. The frames must bracket the best focus of every region, with enough stars in each.

```ts
import { inspectAberrationFocusScan } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/aberration/scan'

// frames: AberrationFocusFrame[] — { position, image } or { position, profiles, width, height } along a focus run (focuser steps).
// Pixel pitch (binning included) and focal-plane displacement per focuser step, both in mm.
const physicalScale = { pixelSize: 0.004, focusDisplacement: 0.001 }

// Regional focus curves on a 4 × 4 grid, the best-focus surface, and what derives from it.
const scan = inspectAberrationFocusScan(frames, { regions: { columns: 4, rows: 4 }, physicalScale })

console.log(scan.regions.map((region) => [region.u, region.v, region.bestFocus])) // normalized sensor position, and best focus in steps
console.log(scan.plane, scan.curvature, scan.fieldOffset?.centerToEdge) // focus gradients, principal curvatures, and periphery minus center, in steps
console.log(scan.tilt?.significant, scan.tilt?.physical) // whether the tilt is significant, and its angles in radians
console.log(scan.findings.map((finding) => finding.kind)) // e.g. sensorTiltPattern, fieldCurvature

// The same run with the stars registered across the frames into tracks, each with its own focus curve.
console.log(inspectAberrationFocusScan(frames, { tracking: {} }).tracks?.length)
```

### Aberration Inspector

The optical defects of an imaging train show in the stars across the field: field curvature makes the stars grow toward the corners, sensor tilt makes one side larger than the other, a wrong flattener spacing elongates the corner stars radially or tangentially, and coma or miscollimation elongates them in a coherent direction. Measuring the size (HFD, FWHM) and the shape (eccentricity, elongation, axis orientation) of many stars and summarizing them by region of the sensor turns a single frame into a map of where and how the optics degrade.

The inspector detects the stars and measures their profiles (see [Star Profile Measurement](#star-profile-measurement)), or takes profiles already measured, selects a balanced set over the field, and summarizes each region with robust medians. It reports per-region metrics, orientation vectors where the long axes agree, and findings such as field degradation or radial or tangential elongation, each with a likelihood, a confidence, and its limitations. A finding describes a pattern in one frame and does not name a mechanical cause: tilt, curvature, and a collimation error cannot be told apart from a single frame, which is the job of a focus scan (see [Aberration Focus Scan](#aberration-focus-scan)). The result is only as good as the profiles: false stars of the detector are not filtered here.

```ts
import { buildAberrationField } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/aberration/region'
import { inspectAberration, inspectAberrationProfiles } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/aberration/single'

// image: Image — a frame with many stars over the whole field.
// Detect, profile, select, and summarize by region (a 3 × 3 grid by default).
const result = inspectAberration(image)

console.log(result.regions.map((region) => [region.id, region.medianHFD])) // median HFD of each region, pixels
console.log(result.vectors) // coherent long-axis orientation per region, radians in [0, π), clockwise (y down)
console.log(result.findings.map((finding) => [finding.kind, finding.likelihood, finding.limitations])) // e.g. fieldDegradation, radialElongation

// A finer map of one metric for display: the median HFD of the selected stars in each cell of a 6 × 4 grid.
const field = buildAberrationField(result.stars, 'hfd', { columns: 6, rows: 4 })
console.log(field.map((cell) => [cell.column, cell.row, cell.value, cell.count])) // pixels, undefined in a cell with too few stars

// profiles: StarProfile[] — profiles already measured on a 1000 × 800 frame.
const fromProfiles = inspectAberrationProfiles(1000, 800, profiles)
```

### Aperture Photometry

Aperture photometry measures the light of a source as the sum of the pixels inside an aperture minus the sky level times the aperture area, `flux = sum − background · area`, with the sky taken from an annulus around the source after rejecting the stars and cosmic rays in it. Its uncertainty follows the CCD equation (Merline & Howell 1995): the shot noise of the source and the sky, the read noise and the dark shot noise of every aperture pixel, plus the uncertainty of the sky estimate, which is common to all the pixels of the aperture and so grows with the square of the area. This is the measurement behind light curves of variable stars and exoplanet transits, and calibrated magnitudes.

Positions are zero-based pixel centers, the same convention as [Star Detection](#star-detection) and Photutils, and apertures are circles or ellipses with an optional sky annulus; partial pixels on the aperture edge are weighted by their exact overlap by default, and the sums and areas agree with Photutils. Fluxes are in the sample unit of the image, naturally DN for a frame read in its digital scale (see [Scientific Image Loading and Export](#scientific-image-loading-and-export)). The error needs a variance source: an uncertainty map, or a noise model with the gain in electrons per sample unit (see [Photon Transfer and Read Noise](#photon-transfer-and-read-noise)), the read noise, and the dark current; otherwise only the annulus scatter is known. Pixels are assumed independent, so a resampled, registered, or drizzled frame needs a noise correlation factor or its errors are underestimated. Saturated pixels are kept in the sum, so a saturated flux is only a lower limit. Unlike the background-limited SNR of star detection, this API is meant for calibrated measurements with physical uncertainties.

```ts
import { aperturePhotometry } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/stars/photometry'

// image: DigitalImage — a calibrated frame in DN; positions: { x, y }[] — zero-based pixel centers of the sources.
// CCD noise model: gain 1.5 e-/DN, read noise 8 e-, dark current 0.02 e-/s/pixel over 300 s.
const noise = { gain: 1.5, readNoise: 8, dark: { current: 0.02, exposureTime: 300 } }

// Circular apertures of 6 pixels with a sky annulus from 9 to 14 pixels, shared by all the sources.
const [star] = aperturePhotometry(image, positions, { shape: 'circle', radius: 6, annulus: { inner: 9, outer: 14 } }, { noise })

console.log(star.flux, star.fluxError, star.snr) // DN, DN, and signal-to-noise ratio
console.log(star.background, star.area, star.flags) // sky in DN per pixel, aperture area in pixels², and flags such as saturated or truncated
```

### Arcsinh Stretch

A linear astronomical image keeps its faint signal in the lowest few percent of the range, so it must be stretched nonlinearly to be seen. The inverse hyperbolic sine stretch (Lupton et al. 2004) is linear for faint values and logarithmic for bright ones, which lifts the faint nebulosity without saturating the stars. Applied to the luminance of an RGB image, with all three channels of a pixel multiplied by the same factor, it keeps the color ratios, so star cores stay colored instead of turning white as with a per-channel stretch. This is the PixInsight-style form on a normalized 0..1 buffer:

```text
y = asinh(β · x') / asinh(β)      x' = (x − blackPoint) / (1 − blackPoint)
```

where `β` grows with the stretch factor and the black point clips the shadows. The image is modified in place. Pixels that exceed 1 after the stretch are clipped per channel, which changes their color, unless the highlights are protected by rescaling the whole image. An arcsinh stretch that approximates a displayed [Screen Transfer Function](#screen-transfer-function) can be searched, to turn the preview into a color-preserving stretch; the match of the two curves is approximate.

```ts
import { approximateArcsinhStretchParameters, arcsinhStretch } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/arcsinh'

// image: Image — a linear mono or RGB image normalized to 0..1.
// Stretch through the luminance, keeping the color ratios; the image is modified and returned.
arcsinhStretch(image, { stretchFactor: 20, blackPoint: 0.05, protectHighlights: true })

// The stretch factor and black point whose curve best approximates an STF of midtone 0.1, shadow 0.02, highlight 0.9.
console.log(approximateArcsinhStretchParameters(0.1, 0.02, 0.9)) // { stretchFactor: 12.697700249709829, blackPoint: 0.02 }
```

### Automatic Background Extraction

The sky behind deep-sky objects is rarely flat: light pollution, moonlight, and airglow add a gradient that changes with the altitude and azimuth of the field, and residual vignetting that flat frames did not remove darkens the corners. A smooth surface fitted to sky samples across the frame, away from stars and nebulosity, models that background, which is then subtracted (an additive gradient such as light pollution) or divided out (a multiplicative effect such as vignetting). Removing it before stretching and color calibration is what makes faint extended signal visible and the background color uniform.

`automaticBackgroundExtraction` samples a grid of box medians, rejects the samples that lie above the surface (stars, nebulosity), fits a Chebyshev polynomial for smooth gradients or a smoothing thin-plate spline for irregular ones, per channel or on the luminance, and removes it while restoring a chosen background level; the fit, evaluation, and application are also exported as separate steps. The image is modified in place. The box medians do not model extended nebulosity: an object that fills most of the frame is absorbed by the background unless it is excluded with a mask, for example the disks around detected stars.

```ts
import { applyBackground, automaticBackgroundExtraction, backgroundExclusionMaskFromStars, evaluateBackgroundModel, fitBackgroundSurface } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/background'

// image: Image — a linear frame normalized to 0..1; stars: DetectedStar[] — its detected stars.
// Fit a degree-4 polynomial per channel and subtract it, restoring the mean level of the model.
const result = automaticBackgroundExtraction(image)

console.log(result.background) // the background model, an image of the same shape
console.log(result.channels[0].acceptedSamples, result.channels[0].residual) // samples used, robust residual dispersion

// Fit only, with a thin-plate spline and the stars kept out of the samples.
const mask = backgroundExclusionMaskFromStars(image.metadata.width, image.metadata.height, stars)
const model = fitBackgroundSurface(image, { model: 'thinPlateSpline', exclusionMask: mask })

// The fitted model as a new image of the same geometry, then divided out of the frame in place (vignetting).
const background = evaluateBackgroundModel(model, image)
console.log(applyBackground(image, background, { correction: 'divide' })) // per channel, the corrected range before clipping
```

### Backfocus Correction Estimates

A field flattener or reducer is designed to work at one distance from the sensor, its back focus. At the wrong spacing the focal surface is curved: the corners reach best focus at a different focuser position than the center, and the corner stars are bloated or elongated. A focus scan that finds the best focus of each region of the sensor measures this as the difference between the best focus of the periphery and of the center.

`measureFocusFieldOffset` takes the best focus of regions at normalized sensor positions (`u`, `v` in −0.5..0.5) and returns the center-to-edge offset in focuser units, the periphery minus the center, with a confidence. `estimateBackfocusCorrection` converts it to a spacing change with `correction = −centerToEdge / response`, where `response` is the change of the offset per unit of added spacing, calibrated by the user on that train (for example by changing the spacing by a known amount and repeating the scan); the correction has the unit and sign convention of that calibration. Nothing here knows the optical design, a linear response is assumed, and the offset mixes field curvature with sensor tilt, which makes it depend on which edge is sampled (see [Sensor Tilt Estimator](#sensor-tilt-estimator) and [Focus Field Curvature](#focus-field-curvature)).

```ts
import { estimateBackfocusCorrection, measureFocusFieldOffset } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/aberration/physical'

// Best focus (focuser steps) of the center and corner regions of a focus scan, at normalized sensor positions.
const samples = [
	{ u: 0, v: 0, bestFocus: 4500, confidence: 0.9 },
	{ u: -0.45, v: -0.45, bestFocus: 4562, confidence: 0.8 },
	{ u: 0.45, v: -0.45, bestFocus: 4558, confidence: 0.8 },
	{ u: -0.45, v: 0.45, bestFocus: 4561, confidence: 0.8 },
	{ u: 0.45, v: 0.45, bestFocus: 4559, confidence: 0.8 },
	{ u: 0.1, v: 0.1, bestFocus: 4502, confidence: 0.9 },
]

// The periphery minus the center, in focuser steps.
const offset = measureFocusFieldOffset(samples)!
console.log(offset.centerToEdge) // 59

// A calibration of 80 steps of offset per 1 mm of added spacing: the spacing change in mm.
console.log(estimateBackfocusCorrection(offset, { response: 80 })) // { correction: -0.7375 } — reduce the spacing by 0.74 mm
```

### Background Estimate

The sky level and its noise are the first numbers to know about a frame: they tell whether the exposure is long enough to swamp the read noise, whether the sky is brightening with dawn or the Moon, and whether anything stands out from the background at all. A robust estimate takes medians, so that stars and hot pixels do not bias it, and converts the median absolute deviation to a Gaussian standard deviation for the noise.

`estimateBackground` returns the background level, the noise, and a rough signal-to-noise ratio of the brightest region, in the sample scale of the image, without star detection. It reads a bounded lattice of pixels in a grid of cells, so its cost does not grow with the frame and it is meant for a quick quality check; a star smaller than the lattice step can be missed. A color image is read through its luminance, and a raw CFA mosaic as raw photosite values. Because the background is a median of cells, a nebula or gradient that covers most of the frame raises it; for a background model use [Automatic Background Extraction](#automatic-background-extraction).

```ts
import { estimateBackground } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/background'

// image: Image — any frame, mono, RGB, or a raw CFA mosaic.
const { background, noise, snr } = estimateBackground(image)

console.log(background, noise) // sky level and its robust standard deviation, in the sample scale of the image
console.log(snr) // brightest cell above the background, in units of the noise
```

### Background Neutralization

The sky background of a color image should be neutral gray, but light pollution, airglow, and the unequal sensitivity of the three channels give it a cast, typically orange or green. Background neutralization measures the median of each channel over the pixels whose values fall in a reference range around the sky level and shifts each channel additively so that the three medians coincide, the additive form of the PixInsight tool. It is usually applied after [Automatic Background Extraction](#automatic-background-extraction) and before color calibration.

The shift is applied to an interleaved RGB image of normalized 0..1 samples in place, and a mono image is returned unchanged. The shift can push values out of 0..1, and the mode decides whether the image is then rescaled, truncated, or placed at a target background level. The reference range is a range of brightness, not a region of the image: on an image with large bright areas choose a narrow range around the sky level, or the medians include the object.

```ts
import { backgroundNeutralization } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/neutralization'

// image: Image — an interleaved RGB image normalized to 0..1.
// Channel medians over the sky range 0.05..0.3 are moved to a common background of 0.1; the image is modified and returned.
backgroundNeutralization(image, { mode: 'targetBackground', lowerLimit: 0.05, upperLimit: 0.3, targetBackground: 0.1 })
```

### Bahtinov Chromatic Comparison

A lens does not bring all wavelengths to the same focus: the longitudinal chromatic aberration of a refractor or of a corrector puts the red, green, and blue focal planes at slightly different distances, which shows as colored halos around the stars and limits the sharpness of one-shot-color and broadband images. Measuring the Bahtinov focus error (see [Bahtinov Focus Analysis](#bahtinov-focus-analysis)) separately on the red, green, and blue planes of one image gives this focus shift directly, and the displacement of the pattern between the planes gives the lateral color.

`compareBahtinovChromatic` analyzes the three planes of a registered RGB image with the same region, workspace, and options, and reports the red and blue focus errors relative to green, in pixels, the span of the three, and the lateral offsets of the reference points; a CFA image has to be debayered first. It succeeds only when every plane is measured and the three patterns agree in orientation, and it never makes up a number. The signs of the differences follow the central normal of the green plane, whose canonical angle can fall at either end of `[0, π)`, so the magnitudes and the span are the stable numbers. Converting pixels of focus error into a focuser distance is a calibration of the user.

```ts
import { compareBahtinovChromatic } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/bahtinov/chromatic'
import { createBahtinovWorkspace } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/bahtinov/preprocess'

// image: Image — a registered RGB frame of a star through a Bahtinov mask, the star near (100, 100).
// A reusable workspace for a region of up to 160 × 160 pixels.
const workspace = createBahtinovWorkspace(160, 160)

const result = compareBahtinovChromatic({ image, center: { x: 100, y: 100 }, size: 160 }, workspace)

if (result.success) {
	console.log(result.redMinusGreen, result.blueMinusGreen, result.focusSpan) // focus differences and span, pixels of focus error
	console.log(result.redReferenceOffset, result.blueReferenceOffset) // lateral color, image pixels
}
```

### Bahtinov Focus Analysis

A Bahtinov mask (Pavel Bahtinov, 2005) placed in front of the telescope has three gratings at slightly different angles, and turns a bright star into three diffraction spikes. When the star is in focus the central spike passes exactly through the intersection of the two outer ones; out of focus it shifts to one side, by an amount proportional to the defocus and with a sign that tells the direction. The offset is visible to the eye at the sub-pixel level, which makes the mask one of the most precise manual focusing aids.

`analyzeBahtinov` finds the three spikes in a region around the star (a ridge filter and a Hough transform, then robust line fits), checks that the outer spikes are symmetric about the central one, and measures the signed distance, in pixels, from the central spike to the intersection of the outer ones, with its uncertainty, a confidence, and a focus state (focused, defocused, or indeterminate against a tolerance). Positions are full-image pixel centers. It works on mono, RGB, or CFA images; the workspace holds reusable buffers and must not be shared by two analyses at once. The measurement is geometric and does not know the focuser, so the sign and scale of a focuser move per pixel of error are a calibration of the user. A failure is a result with a reason, not an exception, and no line is made up. See [Bahtinov Chromatic Comparison](#bahtinov-chromatic-comparison) for the color planes, [Bahtinov Overlay Geometry](#bahtinov-overlay-geometry) for drawing, and [Synthetic Bahtinov Spikes](#synthetic-bahtinov-spikes) for test patterns.

```ts
import { analyzeBahtinov } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/bahtinov/bahtinov'
import { createBahtinovWorkspace } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/bahtinov/preprocess'

// image: Image — a frame of a star through a Bahtinov mask, the star near (100, 100).
// A reusable workspace for a region of up to 160 × 160 pixels.
const workspace = createBahtinovWorkspace(160, 160)

// Analyze a 160-pixel square region around the approximate star center.
const result = analyzeBahtinov({ image, center: { x: 100, y: 100 }, size: 160 }, workspace)

if (result.success) {
	console.log(result.error, result.uncertainty) // signed focus error and its uncertainty, pixels
	console.log(result.focusState, result.confidence) // focused, defocused, or indeterminate; evidence score in 0..1
	console.log(result.reference) // intersection of the outer spikes, image pixels
} else {
	console.log(result.reason) // e.g. patternNotFound, lowSignal, saturated
}
```

### Bahtinov Overlay Geometry

A focusing tool shows the Bahtinov measurement over the live image so the user can see the spikes that were found and how far the central one is from the crossing of the others. This turns a successful [Bahtinov Focus Analysis](#bahtinov-focus-analysis) into drawing primitives: the three spike segments clipped to the region, the reference point, its projection on the central spike, the error segment between them, two small circles at its ends, and a guide circle around the reference.

Everything is in full-image pixel coordinates and independent of any renderer, zoom, or display transform, and the objects are fresh copies of the analysis. The circle radii are only visual and never scale the error, so the circles of a focused pattern overlap and those of a defocused one separate. Only a successful analysis can be given.

```ts
import { analyzeBahtinov } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/bahtinov/bahtinov'
import { createBahtinovOverlayGeometry } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/bahtinov/overlay'
import { createBahtinovWorkspace } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/bahtinov/preprocess'

// image: Image — a frame of a star through a Bahtinov mask, the star near (100, 100).
const analysis = analyzeBahtinov({ image, center: { x: 100, y: 100 }, size: 160 }, createBahtinovWorkspace(160, 160))
if (!analysis.success) throw new Error(analysis.reason)

// The primitives to draw, with error circles of 6 pixels and a guide circle of 40 pixels.
const overlay = createBahtinovOverlayGeometry(analysis, { errorCircleRadius: 6, focusRegionRadius: 40 })

console.log(overlay.spikes.map((spike) => spike.role)) // [ 'central', 'external0', 'external1' ], each with a clipped segment
console.log(overlay.errorSegment) // from the projection on the central spike to the reference, image pixels
```

### Bounded Robust Sampling

The median and the median absolute deviation (MAD) are the robust statistics of image analysis: unlike the mean and standard deviation they are not pulled by stars, hot pixels, and cosmic rays, and the MAD times 1.4826 estimates the standard deviation of Gaussian noise. Computing them exactly needs every value in memory, which for a large frame or a stack is expensive. Reservoir sampling keeps a uniform random sample of fixed size from a stream of any length, so the statistics are estimated in bounded memory.

`RobustReservoir` stores every value exactly until it holds 65536 of them and samples uniformly beyond that, so its statistics are then estimates that differ slightly from the exact ones. Its random generator is deterministic and restored by a reset, so the same sequence always gives the same result. Non-finite values are ignored. Besides the median, percentiles, and MAD, it gives a robust standard deviation computed after dropping the values more than five normalized MADs from the median.

```ts
import { RobustReservoir } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/robust'

// A reservoir for a population of 16 values, kept exactly.
const reservoir = new RobustReservoir(16)
for (const value of [10, 11, 9, 10, 12, 8, 10, 11, 9, 1000]) reservoir.push(value)

// The median, the MAD normalized to a Gaussian standard deviation, and the standard deviation without the outlier.
console.log(reservoir.median(), reservoir.mad(true), reservoir.robustStandardDeviation()) // 10 1.482602218505602 1.154700538379252

// The 90th percentile (a fraction in 0..1, interpolated between ranks), and the normalized MAD around a known center.
console.log(reservoir.percentile(0.9), reservoir.madAround(10, true)) // ≈ 110.8 (pulled by the outlier) 1.482602218505602

// Values seen and values retained; approximate is true once more values were seen than retained.
console.log(reservoir.seenCount, reservoir.retainedCount, reservoir.approximate) // 10 10 false

// Empties the reservoir and restores its random generator, for the next population.
reservoir.reset()
```

### Celestial Streak Tracks

A streak in an image is the track of something that moved during the exposure: an artificial satellite, a meteor, an aircraft, or a fast asteroid. Its pixel endpoints mean little by themselves; mapped through the plate solution they become a segment of a great circle on the sky, which can be compared with a predicted track, for example a satellite pass computed from its orbit (see [Satellite Trail Prediction](#satellite-trail-prediction)), to identify the object. This is the trajectory evidence used by [Streak Classification](#streak-classification).

`celestialStreakTrack` maps the endpoints of a measured streak through a TAN or TAN-SIP header and returns them in radians with the great-circle length and the position angle (east of north). A still image cannot tell which way the object moved, so the track has no direction and a reversed prediction matches the same line. `matchPredictedStreakTrack` compares the track with a predicted great-circle segment by the cross-track residual, the overlap along the track, and the angle between the two planes, combined in a score; with the exposure times and a timed prediction in the same timescale, only the part of the prediction flown during the exposure is compared. The comparison is geometric: it propagates no orbit, and a long predicted arc that curves on the sky differs from a great circle.

```ts
import { celestialStreakTrack, matchPredictedStreakTrack } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/streak/celestial'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// streak: Streak — a measured streak from (10, 20) to (90, 70), zero-based pixels.
// A TAN header of 0.05°/pixel at RA 0, Dec 0, with RA increasing to the left.
const wcs = { CTYPE1: 'RA---TAN', CTYPE2: 'DEC--TAN', CRPIX1: 50.5, CRPIX2: 50.5, CRVAL1: 0, CRVAL2: 0, CD1_1: -0.05, CD1_2: 0, CD2_1: 0, CD2_2: 0.05 }

// The streak on the sky: endpoints [RA, Dec] in radians, great-circle length, and position angle.
const observed = celestialStreakTrack(streak, wcs)!
console.log(observed.start.map(toDeg), observed.end.map(toDeg)) // [1.9742, -1.4738] [357.9758, 1.0243] — degrees
console.log(toDeg(observed.length), toDeg(observed.positionAngle)) // 4.7143 301.98 — degrees, east of north

// predicted: PredictedStreakTrack — start and end [RA, Dec] in radians, optionally with times.
// exposure: { start: Time, end: Time } — the exposure window.
const comparison = matchPredictedStreakTrack(observed, predicted, exposure)
console.log(comparison?.crossTrack, comparison?.overlap, comparison?.score) // radians, fraction 0..1, score 0..1
```

### Channel Composition

Mono-filter imaging integrates one linear master per filter and then maps the masters to color: broadband R, G and B to red, green and blue, or narrowband palettes such as SHO (SII, Ha and OIII to red, green and blue, the "Hubble palette") and HOO (Ha to red, OIII to both green and blue), optionally with a separate luminance master (LRGB, LSHO). The mapping is a choice of the imager: the weights are an artistic mix, not a flux calibration, and no balance between filters is applied unless the caller asks for it with a per-master gain and offset.

`imaging/processing/channel.composition` composes registered masters that share one pixel grid, linearly and a strip of rows at a time, so a caller bounds its memory: nothing is clipped, stretched or rescaled per image, and the result stays a scientific linear RGB that a display stretch can then show (see [Screen Transfer Function](#screen-transfer-function)). Each output channel is the weighted mean of its corrected masters, `Σ w·(gain·x + offset) / Σ w`, with a denominator fixed by the mix, so the color of a pixel never depends on which masters cover it; a pixel is valid only where every master used by the mix is valid. A palette that names a missing filter is a problem for the caller to report, never filled in from another master.

A luminance master is not a fourth channel. It is first matched robustly to the BT.709 luminance `Y` of the mixed RGB (by the 25th percentile and the interquartile span, as in [Global Image Normalization](#global-image-normalization)), and then blended into it: the target luminance `Yt = (1 − alpha)·Y + alpha·M` is reached by scaling the three channels by `Yt/Y`, which keeps their ratios and so the hue, except in the noisy shadows, where the difference is added instead of an unstable ratio. The BT.709 weights describe a display RGB, not the passbands of narrowband filters, so the luminance of a narrowband palette is a convention.

```ts
import { blendLuminanceRows, type ChannelMix, collectLuminanceSamples, createCompositionCounters, createLuminanceSamples, mixChannelRows, solveLuminanceMatch, validateChannelMix } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/channel.composition'

// planes: CompositionPlane[] — strips of the registered Ha (0) and OIII (1) masters: { raw, valid, gain, offset }
// lum: CompositionPlane — the same strip of a luminance master; pixels: number of pixels in the strip

// HOO: Ha drives red, the one OIII master drives both green and blue.
const hoo: ChannelMix = { red: [{ plane: 0, weight: 1 }], green: [{ plane: 1, weight: 1 }], blue: [{ plane: 1, weight: 1 }] }
console.log(validateChannelMix(hoo, planes)) // [] when the mix is usable, otherwise every problem found

// Writes interleaved linear RGB; unsupported pixels are NaN with a zero valid byte.
const rgb = new Float64Array(pixels * 3)
const valid = new Uint8Array(pixels)
const counters = createCompositionCounters()
mixChannelRows(planes, hoo, pixels, rgb, valid, counters)

// LRGB: match the luminance master to the luminance of the mix, then replace it fully (alpha 1).
const samples = createLuminanceSamples(pixels)
collectLuminanceSamples(samples, rgb, valid, lum, pixels)
const match = solveLuminanceMatch(samples, 'robustLinear')
blendLuminanceRows(rgb, valid, lum, match, 1, pixels, counters)

console.log(counters) // valid, unsupported and non-finite pixel counts accumulated over the strips
```

### Collimation Sequence Summary

The geometry of a single defocused star is disturbed by seeing, noise and tube currents, so the offset of the obstruction shadow measured on one frame (see [Defocused Annular Geometry Analysis](#defocused-annular-geometry-analysis)) is not a reliable basis for turning a collimation screw. Repeating the measurement over a short run of frames and summarizing it robustly separates the persistent offset, which is the optics, from the frame-to-frame scatter.

`summarizeCollimationSequence` combines the analyses of one run into the approximate geometric median of the offset vectors, in image pixels and relative to the outer radius, with the dispersion of the frames about it; a direction is reported only when the offset clearly exceeds that dispersion and the resolution floor of the measurement. Failed frames, frames whose outer center lies outside the field reference, and frames without a stability estimate are kept in the per-frame entries but do not enter the median, and at least five usable frames are required. The frames must be of the same target, optical configuration, plane, orientation, sampling, focus side and defocus, with no adjustment in between: the function only sees numbers in one image frame and cannot check that. The dispersion is descriptive, not a confidence interval, and an optional tolerance is compared with it, so it is a statement about repeatability, not about collimation.

```ts
import { analyzeCollimation } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/collimation/collimation'
import { createCollimationWorkspace } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/collimation/preprocess'
import { summarizeCollimationSequence } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/collimation/sequence'

// images: Image[] — consecutive linear frames of the same defocused star, each fully inside `area`
const area = { left: 10, top: 10, right: 190, bottom: 190 }
const workspace = createCollimationWorkspace(200, 200)
const analyses = images.map((image) => analyzeCollimation({ image, area }, { workspace }))

// The median offset of the shadow and the repeatability of the run (tolerance: normalized dispersion).
const summary = summarizeCollimationSequence(analyses, { tolerance: 0.01 })

if (summary.success) {
	console.log(summary.offset, summary.normalizedDistance) // pixels (+X right, +Y down), and the distance over the outer radius
	console.log(summary.dispersion, summary.direction) // pixels, and radians in [0, TAU) or undefined when not resolved
	console.log(summary.dispersionExceedsTolerance) // whether the frames scatter more than the tolerance
} else {
	console.log(summary.reason, summary.entries) // why no summary, and the status of each frame
}
```

### Cosmetic Correction

Every sensor has a few defective pixels: hot pixels with a high dark current, cold or dead pixels with little or no response, and sometimes whole bad columns or rows. They are fixed in position, so a master dark or a defect map from the camera records them, but some remain after calibration, and in a stack without dithering they survive the combination as bright or dark dots and, after registration, as short streaks. Cosmetic correction replaces those samples, in place, with the median of their neighbourhood.

`cosmeticCorrection` combines three detectors. The automatic one flags a pixel that deviates from the local median by several times the robust noise of the channel, but only when it is isolated: a pixel whose immediate neighbour is also elevated is taken as part of a real source, which protects the peak of a star whose profile spills into the adjacent pixels. A master dark flags the pixels that are hot in the dark, and a defect map of pixels, columns and rows is repaired unconditionally. On a raw CFA mosaic the neighbourhood is taken within the same color phase, so the alternating colors of a uniform scene are not taken for defects.

A star confined to a single pixel cannot be told from a hot pixel in one frame; pass a protection mask for such cases. The method repairs single pixels and thin lines, not clusters, and since the repair is a median it does not recover the detail that was under the defect.

```ts
import { cosmeticCorrection } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/cosmetic'

// image: Image — a normalized light frame; masterDark: Image — a master dark of the same geometry

// Repairs isolated hot and cold pixels with the median of their 3x3 neighbourhood, in place.
const result = cosmeticCorrection(image)
console.log(result.corrected, result.hot, result.cold) // number of samples replaced, in total and by each detector

// Adds the hot pixels of a master dark and a known bad column (0-based), with the automatic detector off.
cosmeticCorrection(image, { hotSigma: 0, coldSigma: 0, masterDark, defects: { pixels: [[3, 5]], columns: [8], rows: [] } })
```

### Critical Focus Zone

The critical focus zone is the range of focuser travel over which a star image stays as sharp as diffraction allows. Its width grows with the square of the focal ratio `N` and linearly with the wavelength, and it does not depend on the aperture or the focal length alone, so a fast telescope has a much narrower zone: about 67 µm at f/5 in green light, but only about 11 µm at f/2. Comparing it with the step size and the backlash of the focuser tells whether the focuser can actually hold focus (see [Focuser Backlash Calibration](#focuser-backlash-calibration)), and comparing it with the physical focus offsets that the aberration analyses measure across the field, such as a sensor tilt or a field curvature expressed as a focal-plane displacement (see [Sensor Tilt Estimator](#sensor-tilt-estimator) and [Backfocus Correction Estimates](#backfocus-correction-estimates)), tells whether such an offset matters.

Two functions named `criticalFocusZone` use two conventions that must not be mixed. The one in `astronomy/formulas` is the common planning rule `CFZ ≈ 4.88 · λ · N²`, a full width in micrometers for a wavelength in micrometers (about 0.55 µm for visual or luminance light). The one in `imaging/analysis/aberration/physical` is the focus tolerance of the analyses, a semi-amplitude: the displacement on one side of best focus that the optics tolerate. Its diffraction criterion is `λ · N²`, in whatever length unit the wavelength is given in, and its caller-provided criterion returns a tolerance fixed by the camera, the seeing or the manual of the instrument. Both are optical depths of focus, not focuser settings, and they ignore the seeing, the sensor and its pixel size, field curvature and mechanical slop.

```ts
import { criticalFocusZone } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'
import { criticalFocusZone as focusTolerance } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/aberration/physical'

// Planning rule: the full width of the zone of an f/5 telescope in green light (0.55 µm), in micrometers.
console.log(criticalFocusZone(0.55, 5)) // 67.1 µm

// The zone follows N²: 25 times wider at f/10 than at f/2.
console.log(criticalFocusZone(0.55, 10) / criticalFocusZone(0.55, 2)) // 25

// Analysis tolerance: the diffraction semi-amplitude of the same telescope, in micrometers.
console.log(focusTolerance({ focalRatio: 5, wavelength: 0.55 })) // { tolerance: 13.75, criterion: 'diffraction' }

// A tolerance fixed by the caller, in the same unit as the focus offsets it will be compared with.
console.log(focusTolerance({ criterion: 'callerProvided', tolerance: 15 })) // { tolerance: 15, criterion: 'callerProvided' }
```

### Curves

A tone curve maps each input brightness to an output brightness, from black (0) to white (1). After a linear image has been stretched, curves adjust its contrast: an S-curve deepens the shadows and brightens the highlights, a lifted midpoint brings out faint nebulosity, and a curve on one color channel corrects a color cast. `curvesTransformation` applies such curves in place, as the CurvesTransformation tool of PixInsight does.

A curve is defined by control points in 0..1, with the end points (0, 0) and (1, 1) added when missing, and is interpolated by a spline (a monotone cubic Hermite by default, or Akima, Catmull-Rom or natural cubic); the lookup table is clipped to 0..1 and kept monotone, so a spline overshoot cannot invert the tones. A curve acts on one RGB channel or on a luminance of the whole pixel. A luminance curve preserves the color ratios: a darkened pixel is scaled by the ratio, and a brightened one is blended toward white so the requested luminance is reached. Several curves are applied in order.

```ts
import { curvesTransformation } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/curves'

// image: Image — a stretched, normalized RGB image (modified in place)

// An S-curve on the BT.709 luminance: darker shadows and brighter highlights, color ratios preserved.
curvesTransformation(image, { curves: [{ channel: 'BT709', x: [0.25, 0.5, 0.75], y: [0.15, 0.5, 0.85] }] })

// A curve on one color channel lowers the red midtones only, interpolated with an Akima spline.
curvesTransformation(image, { interpolation: 'akima', curves: [{ channel: 'RED', x: [0.5], y: [0.42] }] })
```

### Dark Current

Thermal agitation in the silicon frees electrons even in the dark. This dark current accumulates linearly with the exposure time, roughly doubles every 5 to 7 °C, and adds both a signal and, because it is a Poisson process, a shot noise whose variance equals the number of dark electrons. Knowing it in electrons per pixel per second tells how much cooling a camera needs and when dark noise starts to compete with the sky; localized excesses reveal amplifier glow.

`measureSensorDarkCurrent` estimates it from pairs of dark frames taken at three or more exposure times, all undebayered digital-number images (read with the digital sample scale, see [Scientific Image Loading and Export](#scientific-image-loading-and-export)). Each pair gives a mean and a temporal variance, and two independent weighted regressions against the exposure, with an unknown intercept for the bias and read noise, give the result: the slope of the mean times the conversion gain, and the slope of the variance times the gain squared. The two should agree for a clean sensor; a disagreement suggests a wrong gain or a non-Poisson contribution. The conversion gain in electrons per DN comes from [Photon Transfer and Read Noise](#photon-transfer-and-read-noise). The model is linear in the exposure, so it does not hold where pixels clip or the dark signal is not linear, and a CFA mosaic is measured one plane at a time (see [Image Analysis Planes](#image-analysis-planes)).

```ts
import { measureSensorDarkCurrent } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/sensor/dark'
import type { SensorFrameSet } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/sensor/types'

// darks: SensorFrameSet[] — for each exposure (s), at least two dark frames and optionally the temperature (°C)
// Conversion gain of 2 e-/DN, measured beforehand by photon transfer.
const result = measureSensorDarkCurrent(darks, 2)

console.log(result.mean) // dark current from the mean signal, e-/pixel/s
console.log(result.variance) // dark current from the shot-noise variance, e-/pixel/s (undefined when not measurable)
console.log(result.temperature) // mean recorded temperature, °C
console.log(result.ampGlow?.ratio) // hottest tile over the median tile: localized amplifier glow
```

### Debayering

A one-shot color camera places a color filter array (CFA), usually a Bayer pattern, over its sensor, so each photosite records only red, green or blue, with twice as many green as red or blue sites. The raw frame is a single-channel mosaic, and a color image needs the two missing colors of each pixel to be interpolated. The pattern is read as the colors of the 2×2 block at the origin of the buffer, row by row (`RGGB`, `BGGR`, `GBRG`, `GRBG`, ...), and the origin must already include any region-of-interest shift: a crop starting at an odd column or row changes the pattern.

`debayer` reconstructs a three-channel RGB image from a mosaic by bilinear interpolation, filling each missing color with the average of the nearest samples of that color in the 3×3 neighbourhood; `bayer` does the opposite, sampling one color per pixel from an RGB image, which is useful for tests and simulations. Both return new images. Bilinear interpolation is simple and preserves the photometry of smooth regions, but it shows zippering and false color at sharp edges; quantitative analyses that must not mix colors work on the native CFA planes instead (see [Image Analysis Planes](#image-analysis-planes)).

```ts
import { bayer, debayer } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/debayer'

// mosaic: Image — a single-channel raw frame whose metadata.bayer is 'RGGB'

// The pattern is taken from the metadata; the result is undefined for an image that is not a mosaic.
const rgb = debayer(mosaic)
console.log(rgb?.metadata.channels) // 3

// An explicit pattern overrides the metadata (a wrong phase swaps the colors).
const swapped = debayer(mosaic, 'BGGR')

// Samples an RGB image back into a mosaic with the given pattern.
const resampled = bayer(rgb!, 'RGGB')
```

### Defocused Annular Geometry Analysis

A reflector with a central obstruction images a defocused star as a bright annulus with a dark central shadow. When the optics are collimated and the star is on the optical axis, the shadow is concentric with the outer edge; a tilted mirror displaces it. Measuring that displacement on the image turns the familiar visual "donut" test into numbers that can be compared from one adjustment to the next.
