Off the optical axis, field aberrations also displace the shadow, which is why the measurement can be checked against a known field reference: the middle of the image or of the sensor does not imply the optical axis.

`analyzeCollimation` fits the outer boundary and the obstruction shadow of one complete, isolated annulus in a linear, unstretched image as two independent ellipses, and reports the offset of the shadow center from the outer center in image pixels, its distance relative to the outer radius, the apparent obstruction ratio and, when resolved, the direction. It also reports the signal-to-noise, the stability of the offset when angular blocks of the boundary are removed, and, when a tolerance on the relative offset is given, a geometric assessment. It is a geometric diagnostic: it does not certify the collimation of a telescope, and the offset is in the sampling grid of the image, with no correction for non-square pixels or binning. A frame where the pattern is cropped, saturated, ambiguous or too faint fails with a reason instead of returning a partial geometry.

The defocus must be large enough for the obstruction to be resolved, and frames to be compared must share sampling and orientation. Several frames are combined in [Collimation Sequence Summary](#collimation-sequence-summary), and test images can be drawn with [Synthetic Defocused Collimation Patterns](#synthetic-defocused-collimation-patterns).

```ts
import { analyzeCollimation } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/collimation/collimation'
import { createCollimationWorkspace } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/collimation/preprocess'

// image: Image — a 200x200 linear frame with one complete defocused star inside `area` (half-open, pixels)
const area = { left: 10, top: 10, right: 190, bottom: 190 }

// A reusable workspace sized for the frame; one analysis at a time.
const workspace = createCollimationWorkspace(200, 200)

// Fits both boundaries; a field reference and a tolerance on the relative offset are optional.
const result = analyzeCollimation({ image, area, field: { center: { x: 101, y: 99 }, maximumDistance: 5 } }, { workspace, tolerance: 0.05 })

if (result.success) {
	console.log(result.geometry.offset, result.geometry.normalizedDistance) // shadow minus outer center (pixels), and over the outer radius
	console.log(result.geometry.direction) // radians in [0, TAU), +X toward +Y; undefined when not resolved
	console.log(result.assessment) // withinTolerance, outsideTolerance or inconclusive
} else {
	console.log(result.reason) // why the pattern could not be measured
}
```

### Differential Photometry and Light Curves

Differential photometry measures a target against comparison stars in the same frames, so that clouds, extinction, exposure time and gain, which dim every star by the same factor, cancel in the ratio. Ensemble photometry combines several comparisons into an artificial comparison star, which lowers its noise and keeps working when one comparison is missing or variable. The result is a light curve: the relative flux of the target against time, and its differential magnitude `-2.5 log10(relativeFlux)`, 0 at the median level and positive when fainter.

`differentialLightCurve` builds it from per-frame star measurements matched by a stable id, not by position; an [Aperture Photometry](#aperture-photometry) result with an id fits directly. Each comparison is divided by its own reference flux, so a missing comparison does not bias the ensemble, and the transparency of each frame is the inverse-variance weighted mean of these ratios, each weight including the comparison's excess scatter beyond its stated errors (Broeg, Fernández & Neuhäuser 2005). With three or more comparisons, a comparison that scatters too much is rejected as variable and a single deviating measurement is clipped from its frame. The epochs are passed through unchanged, so a light curve in TDB or BJD needs TDB epochs.

Frames are tied together only by a chain of shared comparisons: if the comparison set changes completely, the transmission between the two sets is unmeasured, and only one linked set is reported, the others being flagged as disconnected. An optional detrending fits the relative flux against airmass, FWHM or the target centroid; it also absorbs any real variability correlated with those quantities.

```ts
import { differentialLightCurve } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/stars/photometry.differential'

// frames: DifferentialPhotometryFrame[] — { time, airmass?, stars: [{ id, flux, fluxError }] } per frame, one timescale

// Every other star is a candidate comparison; variable ones are rejected automatically.
const curve = differentialLightCurve(frames, 'V')
console.log(curve.points[0].relativeFlux, curve.points[0].magnitude) // flux over the median level, and differential magnitude
console.log(curve.points[0].transparency) // relative transmission of the frame, median 1
console.log(curve.rejectedComparisonIds) // comparisons rejected as variable

// Chosen comparisons and an airmass detrending of the relative flux.
const detrended = differentialLightCurve(frames, 'V', ['A', 'B', 'D'], { detrend: { covariates: ['airmass'] } })
console.log(detrended.points[0].detrended?.relativeFlux) // relative flux with the airmass trend removed
```

### Diffraction and Seeing Sampling

The size of a star image is set by the atmosphere (the seeing, a FWHM in arcseconds) and by diffraction (the Airy disk of the aperture). A camera samples it well when the FWHM spans about two to three pixels: fewer pixels lose resolution and give blocky, poorly centroided stars (undersampling), while more spread the light over pixels that add read noise without adding detail (oversampling). These bands are a convention for long-exposure imaging, not a limit of the sensor.

`astronomy/formulas` relates the image scale to the star size: `samplingRatio` is the seeing over the image scale, the FWHM in pixels, and `fwhmPixelsToSeeing` is its inverse, the seeing implied by a measured star width (see [Star Profile Measurement](#star-profile-measurement); a FWHM from a defocused, trailed or optically limited star is not the seeing). `recommendedFocalLength` is the focal length `206.265 · pixel / (seeing / sampling)` in millimeters that gives the chosen number of pixels across the seeing, the inverse of the pixel scale of [Image Scale and Field of View](#image-scale-and-field-of-view). `airyDiskSize` is `2.44 · λ · N`, the diameter of the first dark ring of a clear circular aperture, which is larger than the FWHM of the diffraction pattern. These are planning formulas: an obstruction, aberrations, guiding and the atmosphere are not combined, and the diffraction limit is not the resolution of a long exposure.

```ts
import { airyDiskInPixels, airyDiskSize, classifyFWHMSampling, fwhmPixelsToSeeing, recommendedFocalLength, samplingRatio } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'

// A seeing of 2.4" at 1.0"/px spans 2.4 pixels, an optimal sampling.
const pixels = samplingRatio(2.4, 1)
console.log(pixels, classifyFWHMSampling(pixels), fwhmPixelsToSeeing(pixels, 1)) // 2.4 'optimal' 2.4 (arcsec)

// The focal length (mm) that puts 2 pixels of 3.76 µm across a 2.4" seeing.
console.log(recommendedFocalLength(3.76, 2, 2.4)) // 646.3 mm

// The Airy disk of an f/5 train at 0.55 µm, in micrometers and in pixels of 3.76 µm.
console.log(airyDiskSize(0.55, 5), airyDiskInPixels(airyDiskSize(0.55, 5), 3.76)) // 6.71 µm, 1.785 px
```

### Disk Limb Fitting

The limb is the outer edge of a bright disk (the Sun, the Moon or a planet) against a darker background. Fitting it gives the geometric center of the disk even when the surface features change, rotate or are lost in the seeing, which is what a solar-system guider needs as an absolute anchor (see [Solar System Guide Tracking](#solar-system-guide-tracking)). An ellipse rather than a circle accounts for the oblateness of Jupiter or Saturn and for non-square sampling.

`measureLimb` casts radial profiles from a starting center, finds on each one the strongest object-to-background transition with subpixel precision, keeps the edges that agree on a dominant limb (so a terminator, a prominence or a ring edge does not pull the fit) and passes them to the robust fit of [Ellipse Fitting](#ellipse-fitting). It works on one analysis plane (see [Image Analysis Planes](#image-analysis-planes)) inside an area, and can start from the previous limb with a continuity check, so a sudden jump fails instead of being followed. `locateBrightObject` is the coarse acquisition: the centroid and equivalent radius of the bright component, which a phase, rings or clipping bias, so it is not a physical disk center.

The object must be brighter than its background. The measured edge is the steepest transition, so a strongly limb-darkened or blurred disk fits slightly inside its geometric edge, and a crescent leaves too large a gap and fails rather than guessing a center.

```ts
import { DEFAULT_LIMB_TRACKING_OPTIONS, locateBrightObject, measureLimb } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/tracking/limb'
import { SurfaceTrackingWorkspace } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/tracking/workspace'

// frame, next: Image — consecutive frames of a planet on a dark sky; area: the search Rect in pixels
const workspace = new SurfaceTrackingWorkspace()

// The coarse centroid and equivalent radius (pixels) of the bright component.
console.log(locateBrightObject(frame, 'mono', area, workspace)) // { center, radius }, or undefined without contrast

// The limb ellipse: center, semi-axes and orientation in pixels and radians.
const first = measureLimb(frame, 'mono', area, workspace)

if (first.success) {
	console.log(first.limb.center, first.limb.semiMajor, first.limb.semiMinor, first.limb.confidence)

	// The next frame, searched around the previous limb; a jump outside the window fails.
	const tracked = measureLimb(next, 'mono', area, workspace, DEFAULT_LIMB_TRACKING_OPTIONS, { prior: first.limb, continuity: true })
	console.log(tracked.success ? tracked.limb.center : tracked.reason)
}
```

### Display Stretch Parameter Estimation

A linear astronomical image keeps almost all of its information in the darkest few percent of the range: the sky background and faint nebulosity sit just above zero. To be seen on a screen it must be stretched, and a good automatic stretch is derived from the statistics of the sky: clip the shadows a few noise units below the background, and choose a midtone that places the background at a fixed display brightness. The parameters are `[midtone, shadow, highlight]`, each in 0..1, the arguments of the midtones transfer function applied by `stf` (see [Screen Transfer Function](#screen-transfer-function)).

`adf` follows the Adaptive Display Function of the XISF specification, from the median and the normalized median absolute deviation of the image (see [Image Statistics](#image-statistics)): the shadow is the median plus a negative clipping point times the deviation, and the midtone sends the shifted median to a target mean background (0.25 by default). A bright or inverted frame mirrors the roles of the shadow and the highlight. A color image is analysed through its grayscale reduction, so one triple serves the three channels (a linked stretch); an unlinked stretch calls it once per channel. The estimate assumes that the median and the deviation describe the sky, so a frame mostly covered by a nebula or a gradient is stretched for that instead.

`autoStf` picks the parameters by a named profile: `low`, `medium` (exactly `adf` with its defaults) and `high` for sky frames, and `moon` and `planet`, which instead send a chosen quantile of a bright disk to a target level and need an area around the disk, since a frame of black sky would dominate the quantiles. None of these functions changes the image; estimate from the original and apply the stretch to a display copy.

```ts
import { adf } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/computation'
import { stf } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/stf'
import { autoStf } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/stf.presets'

// image: Image — a linear, normalized frame; planet: Image — a frame with a bright disk inside `area`

// The automatic stretch of the sky: midtone, shadow and highlight in 0..1.
const [midtone, shadow, highlight] = adf(image)

// Applied to a display copy, the sky background lands near 0.25.
const display = stf({ ...image, raw: image.raw.slice() }, midtone, shadow, highlight)

// A stronger profile for faint targets, and a planetary profile measured around the disk.
console.log(autoStf(image, 'high')) // [midtone, shadow, highlight]
console.log(autoStf(planet, 'planet', { area: { left: 18, top: 18, right: 46, bottom: 46 } }))
```

### Drizzle Integration

Drizzle (Fruchter and Hook, arXiv astro-ph/9808087) reconstructs a set of dithered frames onto a finer output grid. Each input pixel is shrunk to a square drop, mapped onto the output grid, and its value is deposited into every output cell it overlaps, weighted by the overlap area. Unlike interpolation, this does not correlate the noise of neighbouring pixels, and with enough sub-pixel dithers it recovers resolution lost to undersampling (see [Diffraction and Seeing Sampling](#diffraction-and-seeing-sampling)). The drop size `pixfrac`, in input pixels in (0, 1], trades sharpness against coverage: a smaller drop is sharper but needs more dithered frames to fill every output cell.

`imaging/processing/drizzle` holds the primitives that [Image Stacking](#image-stacking) and [Live Stacking](#live-stacking) use for their drizzle reconstruction. An accumulator holds the output grid (the reference size times the scale) as weighted sums and weights, so the result of a pixel is `sum / weights`; the transform of each frame to the reference, `x' = m00 x + m01 y + tx`, gives the footprint of its drops; each sample is normalized photometrically by a per-channel `v · scale + offset` before it is deposited; and a raw CFA mosaic can be drizzled directly, each photosite going to its own color with no interpolation. Coordinates are zero-based pixel centers, x to the right and y down. The accumulator is checked against a memory budget before it is allocated.

```ts
import type { AffineTransform } from 'nebulosa/src/astrometry/matching/star.matching'
import { createDrizzleAccumulator, depositDrizzle, drizzleMemoryBytes, drizzleNormalization, drizzleOverlap, prepareDrizzleFootprint } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/drizzle'

// reference: Image — the 4x4 mono reference frame
// frames: { image: Image; transform: AffineTransform; inverse: AffineTransform }[] — registered frames, input to reference

// The peak bytes of a 2x grid (64 output pixels), mono, with coverage counts and Float64 samples, fixed scratch included.
console.log(drizzleMemoryBytes(64, 1, 1, true, false, 8)) // 789568

// A 2x output grid with coverage counts, Float64 samples and a 1 GiB memory budget.
const state = createDrizzleAccumulator(4, 4, 1, false, 2, true, false, 8, 2 ** 30)

// The fraction of the 4x4 reference area that a 4x4 frame shifted by 1 pixel covers, with the scratch of the state.
console.log(drizzleOverlap({ m00: 1, m01: 0, tx: 1, m10: 0, m11: 1, ty: 0 }, 4, 4, 4, 4, state.polygon, state.clipped)) // 0.75

frames.forEach(({ image, transform, inverse }, i) => {
	// The drop of each input pixel on the output grid, for a pixfrac of 0.7.
	const footprint = prepareDrizzleFootprint(transform, state.scaleX, state.scaleY, 0.7, 4, 4)
	// Photometric scale and offset of the frame against the reference.
	const normalization = drizzleNormalization(state, reference, image, inverse, 'background-scale', 'per-channel')
	// Deposits the frame with weight 1; the generation (1-based) counts each frame once per cell.
	if (footprint && normalization) depositDrizzle(state, image, footprint, normalization.scales, normalization.offsets, 1, i + 1)
})

console.log(state.sum[0] / state.weights[0]) // the drizzled value of the first output pixel
```

### Elliptical Moffat Fitting

The image of a star after the atmosphere is not a Gaussian: it has extended wings from the turbulence. The Moffat (1969) profile, `background + amplitude · (1 + u²/αmajor² + v²/αminor²)^(−β)`, describes it well; `β` controls the wings (a small `β` has heavy wings, and the profile tends to a Gaussian as `β` grows), and the FWHM along an axis is `2α·sqrt(2^(1/β) − 1)` pixels. An elliptical form, with `u` and `v` along and across a major axis rotated by `θ`, captures elongation from tracking errors, tilt or off-axis aberrations.

`fitEllipticalMoffat` fits one such component by damped nonlinear least squares to the unsaturated, finite samples of a circular aperture around a star in a single-channel image, starting from a moment measurement; it is the optional refinement behind the Moffat model of [Star Profile Measurement](#star-profile-measurement). The orientation `θ` is in radians from +X toward +Y (clockwise on screen, since Y grows downward) and is omitted for a round star, whose direction is not meaningful. The fit is local and describes one component: it needs a start close to the truth, a neighbour in the aperture or a strongly non-Moffat profile is absorbed or rejected, `α` and `β` are strongly correlated for small or noisy stars, and the result is not a measurement of the seeing.

```ts
import { createMoffatFitWorkspace, fitEllipticalMoffat, moffatProfileValue } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/stars/profile.moffat'

// image: Image — a single-channel frame; the start comes from a moment measurement of the star.
// Positions, radius and FWHM in pixels; background, deviation, peak and saturation in sample units; theta in radians.
const input = { x: 25, y: 23, radius: 12, background: 0.1, deviation: 0.002, peak: 0.8, major: 6, minor: 4, theta: 0.4, saturationLevel: 1 }

// A reusable workspace for a batch of fits, one fit at a time.
const workspace = createMoffatFitWorkspace()
const fit = fitEllipticalMoffat(image, input, workspace)

if (fit.success) {
	console.log(fit.centerX, fit.centerY, fit.alphaMajor, fit.alphaMinor, fit.beta) // sub-pixel center, alphas (pixels) and beta
	console.log(2 * fit.alphaMajor * Math.sqrt(2 ** (1 / fit.beta) - 1)) // FWHM along the major axis, pixels
	console.log(moffatProfileValue(fit, 25, 23)) // the model at a pixel, background included, sample units
} else {
	console.log(fit.reason)
}
```

### Eyepiece Magnification and Exit Pupil

Visual observing is governed by a few relations of the telescope and the eyepiece. The magnification is the ratio of the focal lengths, `M = F / f`. The exit pupil, the diameter of the beam leaving the eyepiece, is `D / M`, or equivalently `f / N` with `N` the focal ratio: one larger than the pupil of the eye (about 7 mm, decreasing with age) wastes light, and one below about 0.5 mm magnifies the defects of the eye and of the seeing. The true field of view is the apparent field of the eyepiece divided by the magnification, or more accurately the field stop diameter over the telescope focal length.

`astronomy/formulas` has these planning formulas, in millimeters and degrees, for ideal optics: the exit pupil takes no obstruction into account, and the apparent-field estimate of the true field is the usual approximation, not the exact tangent relation, so it can disagree with the field-stop value for a given eyepiece. `exitPupil` has two overloads with the same types and different meanings; the named forms `exitPupilFromApertureAndMagnification` and `exitPupilFromEyepieceAndFocalRatio` avoid mixing the arguments. No limits are applied and the inputs are not validated.

```ts
import { exitPupil, eyepieceTrueFovViaFieldStop, eyepieceView, exitPupilFromApertureAndMagnification, exitPupilFromEyepieceAndFocalRatio, magnification } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'

// A 200 mm f/5 reflector (1000 mm) with a 25 mm eyepiece: 40x.
const power = magnification(1000, 25)

// The exit pupil (mm) from the aperture and magnification, or from the eyepiece and focal ratio.
console.log(exitPupilFromApertureAndMagnification(200, power), exitPupilFromEyepieceAndFocalRatio(25, 5)) // 5 5

// The overloaded form behind both: a length divided by a magnification or a focal ratio.
console.log(exitPupil(200, power)) // 5

// The whole view with a 52° apparent field: magnification, true field (degrees) and exit pupil (mm).
console.log(eyepieceView(1000, 200, 25, 52)) // { magnification: 40, trueFieldOfViewDegrees: 1.3, exitPupilMm: 5 }

// The true field (degrees) from a 27 mm field stop.
console.log(eyepieceTrueFovViaFieldStop(27, 1000)) // 1.547
```

### FFT Image Filter

Filtering in the frequency domain separates structures by scale. A Fourier transform turns an image into spatial frequencies: low frequencies carry the large, smooth structures (gradients, nebulosity), and high frequencies carry the fine ones (stars, detail and pixel noise). A low-pass filter keeps the large structures and smooths the noise; a high-pass filter removes the background and keeps the fine detail.

`fft` filters each channel of a normalized image in place with a centered radial Butterworth mask of second order, whose cutoff is the normalized radius of the −3 dB point, from 0 (zero frequency) to 1 (the Nyquist frequency of each axis). The image is padded with its border pixels to a power of two in each axis, so a star near an edge is not mirrored, and a weight blends the filtered result with the original. A low-pass result is stretched back to the range of the input; a high-pass result is not, so it removes the mean and has positive and negative pixels. A reusable `FFTWorkspace` holds the transform buffers for any image up to its size, and the cost grows as N log N with the padded pixel count.

```ts
import { fft, FFTWorkspace } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/fft'

// image, frame: Image — normalized frames of up to 30x20 pixels (modified in place)

// A workspace padded to powers of two, reused for every frame of a batch.
const workspace = new FFTWorkspace(30, 20)
console.log(workspace.width, workspace.height) // 32 32

// The radial Butterworth gain (0..1) of a filter on the padded grid, cached for the next call with the same filter.
console.log(workspace.mask('lowPass', 0.15).mask) // Float64Array of 32 x 32 gains

// A low-pass at 0.15 of Nyquist smooths the noise and keeps the gradients and the input range.
fft(image, workspace, 'lowPass', 0.15)

// A high-pass at half Nyquist, blended at 50% with the original, keeps the fine structures.
fft(frame, workspace, 'highPass', 0.5, 0.5)
```

### Flat Exposure Estimate

A flat frame should place the signal well inside the linear range of the sensor, typically between a third and a half of full scale, far above the bias and the read noise and far below saturation. The right exposure depends on the light source, the filter and the optics, so a flat run searches for it: take a frame, measure its level, and adjust the exposure.

`estimateFlatExposure` recommends the next exposure from the levels of the frames already taken, for one explicitly chosen plane (the level comes from [Flat-Frame Quality](#flat-frame-quality)). It is a pure scalar model that assumes a signal linear in the exposure, so the source must be stable and the sensor linear in the range. A level from which the bias was already subtracted is proportional to the exposure, and one frame suffices; an observed level includes an unknown pedestal, and the model needs at least two frames to fit a line, or interpolates between the frames that bracket the target. The recommendation aims at the middle of the target interval, respecting the allowed exposure range and an optional maximum step; it is a recommendation, not a measurement, so the next frame must be analysed again.

```ts
import { estimateFlatExposure } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/flat/exposure'

const targetRange = [28000, 36000] as const // DN, the middle is 32000
const exposureRange = [0.1, 10] as const // seconds

// A first frame of 1 s at 8000 DN above the bias: a corrected level scales with the exposure.
console.log(estimateFlatExposure({ observations: [{ exposure: 1, level: 8000 }], levelMode: 'corrected', targetRange, exposureRange })) // increase, ratio model, 4 s predicted at 32000 DN

// Observed levels with a pedestal need two frames for a line through them.
const observations = [
	{ exposure: 0.5, level: 5000 },
	{ exposure: 1, level: 8000 },
]
console.log(estimateFlatExposure({ observations, levelMode: 'observed', targetRange, exposureRange })) // increase, affine model, 5 s predicted at 32000 DN
```

### Flat Sequence Stability

A master flat assumes that the flats it combines record the same illumination. A light panel that warms up, twilight that fades, or a mote of dust that settles during the run makes them differ, and the master then corrects none of the frames exactly. This check measures, over three or more final flats of one configuration, how much the signal, the spatial pattern and the row and column profiles vary and drift in time, from the per-frame measurements of [Flat-Frame Quality](#flat-frame-quality). An exposure search belongs to [Flat Exposure Estimate](#flat-exposure-estimate), not here.

`analyzeFlatSequence` reports for each plane the robust variation and the drift per frame and per second, optional outliers, and a verdict from the limits the caller configures: a limit that is not given is not evaluated, so a variation without a limit cannot reject. Frames that are known to be incompatible (different geometry, exposure, filter, camera settings or temperature) are an error rather than a verdict, and missing metadata is reported as unproven homogeneity. A capture loop can call `measureFlatSequenceFrame` on each flat as it arrives, keeping a compact sample whose size does not grow with the pixels and releasing the image, and `finalizeFlatSequence` gives the same result as the whole-stack analysis, provided every sample uses the same reference, mask and options. The dispersion describes the frames in hand, not a confidence interval, and a drift of the light source cannot be told from one of the sensor.

```ts
import { analyzeFlatSequence, finalizeFlatSequence, measureFlatSequenceFrame } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/flat/sequence'

// frames: FlatFrame[] — final flats in acquisition order: { id, image, exposure, timestamp, filter, operatingPoint }
// Fractional limits on the signal variation and on the drift per frame.
const options = { maximumSignalVariation: 0.01, maximumDriftPerFrame: 0.005 }

// The whole stack at once.
const result = analyzeFlatSequence({ frames }, options)
console.log(result.assessment.verdict, result.assessment.reasons) // accepted, rejected or inconclusive, and why
console.log(result.planes[0].signalVariation, result.planes[0].driftPerFrame) // robust fractional variation and signed drift

// The same analysis while capturing: each image can be released once its sample is kept.
const samples = frames.map((frame) => measureFlatSequenceFrame({ frame }, options))
console.log(finalizeFlatSequence(samples, options).assessment.verdict)
```

### Flat-Frame Quality

A flat frame records the multiplicative response of the optical train and the sensor: vignetting, dust shadows and the pixel-to-pixel sensitivity. Dividing by it is only valid if the flat itself is good: its signal must be in the linear range, no pixel may be clipped, and its spatial pattern should be the expected smooth falloff. `analyzeFlat` measures one already captured flat in source digital numbers and reports, per physical plane (mono, RGB or the native CFA planes, see [Image Analysis Planes](#image-analysis-planes)), the signal statistics, the clipping and the spatial response.

The spatial response describes the illumination: a uniformity ratio of the dimmest to the brightest tiles, the falloff from the center to the edges and corners, the fitted gradient, the center of the illumination from a smooth second-degree model, and optionally the row and column profiles and dust candidates. With a bias or dark-flat master, the signal is also measured after subtracting it. The verdict comes only from the checks the caller configures (a target level and the allowed clipped and non-finite fractions): without criteria nothing can fail and the verdict stays inconclusive. Clipping can be proven only with the effective clipping codes of the camera, since the storage range of the format can show clipping but never its absence. The measurement concerns the digital frame only: a spatial structure is not attributed to dust, vignetting or the sensor. The exposure of the next flat is in [Flat Exposure Estimate](#flat-exposure-estimate) and a series is compared in [Flat Sequence Stability](#flat-sequence-stability).

```ts
import { analyzeFlat } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/flat/flat'

// image: Image — a captured flat in DN; bias: Image — a bias master of the same geometry
// The bias-corrected level must be within 20000..32000 DN, with no clipped or non-finite samples.
const criteria = { targets: { mono: { levelMode: 'corrected', range: [20000, 32000] } }, maximumClippedFraction: 0, maximumNonFiniteFraction: 0 } as const

const result = analyzeFlat({ frame: { image, exposure: 2 }, reference: { kind: 'bias', image: bias } }, { effectiveClip: { lower: 0, upper: 65535 }, criteria })

const plane = result.planes[0]
console.log(plane.corrected?.median) // bias-subtracted median level, DN
console.log(plane.spatial.uniformity, plane.spatial.cornerFalloff) // dimmest over brightest tiles, and corner falloff from the center
console.log(result.assessment.verdict, result.assessment.reasons) // accepted, rejected or inconclusive, and why
```

### Focus Curve Fitting

Moving the focuser through focus and measuring the star size at each position (the half-flux diameter or the FWHM, in pixels) gives a focus curve. Away from focus the blur grows linearly with the displacement, and near focus it levels off at the size set by seeing and diffraction, so the curve is close to a hyperbola, `sqrt(a² + (b·(x − x0))²)`, a V with a rounded bottom. Fitting the curve finds the best focus `x0` more precisely than any single measurement, and is the core of autofocus.

`fitAberrationFocusCurve` fits a robust parabola (the default), a hyperbola, or two trend lines on the two sides of the V that cross at the minimum, or picks automatically the model with the lowest penalized error; outliers are down-weighted and flagged. The minimum of a model is the minimum of that model: a parabola is biased on a V-shaped curve, and the crossing of the trend lines can lie below every measured value. The points must bracket the minimum and use one metric, and by default a fit whose minimum is outside the sampled range fails rather than extrapolating. The points can be the aggregate of a whole frame or of one region (see [Aberration Inspector](#aberration-inspector)); combining the regional minima is [Focus Surface Analysis](#focus-surface-analysis).

```ts
import { fitAberrationFocusCurve } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/aberration/focus'

// points: AberrationFocusPoint[] — { position, value } with the focuser position (steps) and the HFD (pixels)

// Fits each model and keeps the one with the lowest penalized error.
const fit = fitAberrationFocusCurve(points, { model: 'auto' })

if (fit.success) {
	console.log(fit.model, fit.minimum.x) // chosen model and best focus, focuser steps
	console.log(fit.minimum.y, fit.r2) // HFD at the minimum (pixels) and goodness of fit
	console.log(fit.warnings.map((warning) => warning.code)) // e.g. robustOutliers, minimumNearRangeEdge
} else {
	console.log(fit.reason)
}
```

### Focus Field Curvature

Few optical systems have a flat focal surface: without a field flattener, a refractor focuses the edges of the field closer to or farther from the objective than the center, so stars are sharp in the middle and soft at the corners. On a focus surface fitted over the sensor (see [Focus Surface Analysis](#focus-surface-analysis)), `z(u, v) = c + ax·u + ay·v + qxx·u² + qxy·u·v + qyy·v²` in normalized coordinates `u, v` in −0.5..0.5, the quadratic terms are that curvature, and the linear ones are a tilt.

`analyzeFocusCurvature` analyses the quadratic part through its Hessian `[[2 qxx, qxy], [qxy, 2 qyy]]`: its eigenvalues are the larger and smaller principal curvatures, in focuser units per normalized unit squared, positive when the best focus grows from the center toward the edge; their orientation and relative difference describe an astigmatic field; the center-to-edge value is the mean corner focus minus the center focus due to curvature alone; and the stationary point is where the full surface has its extremum. `analyzePhysicalCurvature` converts the curvature to the inverse of a length unit, given the effective pixel pitch and the focal-plane displacement per focuser unit, with the radii of curvature as reciprocals, in the small-slope approximation. The result does not separate the design curvature of the optics from a spacing or mechanical effect, and the error of the caller's calibration is not propagated.

```ts
import { analyzePhysicalCurvature } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/aberration/physical'
import { analyzeFocusCurvature } from 'nebulosa/src/math/numerical/surface.fit'

// A bowl-shaped field (focuser steps): the best focus at the corners is 100 steps above the center.
const bowl = { c: 4500, ax: 0, ay: 0, qxx: 200, qxy: 0, qyy: 200 }
console.log(analyzeFocusCurvature(bowl)) // principalX = principalY = 400, centerToEdge 100 steps, stationary point at the center

// On a 4000x3000 sensor of 0.004 mm pixels, where one step moves the focal plane by 0.001 mm.
console.log(analyzePhysicalCurvature(bowl, 4000, 3000, { pixelSize: 0.004, focusDisplacement: 0.001 })) // radii of 359.76 and 639.68 mm
```

### Focus Surface Analysis

The best focus is not the same everywhere on the sensor. A sensor tilted relative to the focal plane makes it change linearly across the field, and field curvature makes it change quadratically from the center to the edges. Measuring the best focus in several regions of a focus run (the minimum of each regional curve, see [Focus Curve Fitting](#focus-curve-fitting)) and fitting a surface through those values reveals both.

`fitFocusSurface` fits `z(u, v) = c + ax·u + ay·v + qxx·u² + qxy·u·v + qyy·v²` in the focuser unit, over normalized sensor coordinates `u` (to the right) and `v` (downward) in −0.5..0.5, robustly and with optional per-sample weights or uncertainties. Simpler models fit a plane or a single radial curvature. `analyzeFocusPlane` gives the planar part, its direction of increasing focus and its corner-to-corner effect; `focusSurfaceEffect` is the full range of the surface over the sensor; and `buildFocusSurfaceMap` samples the fit on a grid of cells, with the uncertainty of the prediction when a covariance is available. The map samples the model at cell centers, so its extrema are smaller than the analytic range. A surface says where the focus is best, not why (a tilt, a curvature and a decentered element can look alike): the physical interpretation is in [Sensor Tilt Estimator](#sensor-tilt-estimator), [Focus Field Curvature](#focus-field-curvature) and [Backfocus Correction Estimates](#backfocus-correction-estimates).

```ts
import { buildFocusSurfaceMap } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/aberration/surface'
import { analyzeFocusPlane, evaluateFocusSurface, fitFocusSurface, focusSurfaceEffect } from 'nebulosa/src/math/numerical/surface.fit'

// samples: FocusSurfaceSample[] — { u, v, focus, uncertainty? } with the best focus (steps) of each region

// The full quadratic surface, robust to outlying regions.
const fit = fitFocusSurface(samples)

if (fit.success) {
	console.log(fit.coefficients, fit.rms) // c, ax, ay, qxx, qxy, qyy (steps) and the residual scatter
	console.log(evaluateFocusSurface(fit.coefficients, 0.5, 0.5)) // best focus at the bottom-right corner, steps
	console.log(analyzeFocusPlane(fit.coefficients)) // gradients, direction of increasing focus (radians) and effect
	console.log(focusSurfaceEffect(fit.coefficients)) // full range over the sensor, steps

	// A 3x3 map of the model for display.
	console.log(buildFocusSurfaceMap(fit, { columns: 3, rows: 3 }).cells)
}
```

### Frame Saturation

A pixel saturates when its well is full or the converter reaches its maximum: the recorded value no longer grows with the light, so its photometry, centroid and profile are wrong. Counting the saturated pixels tells whether an exposure is too long, and testing the stars of interest tells whether they can be measured at all.

`analyzeSaturation` counts, without modifying the frame, the pixels with any channel at or above a level (1 by default, the top of the normalized scale; pass the clipping level when the full well is reached below the digital maximum), returns their fraction and a mask, and counts the stars whose nearest pixel is saturated. The star test examines that one pixel only, not the whole profile, so a star saturated in a pixel beside its centroid is not counted. A raw CFA mosaic is analysed photosite by photosite, and a stretched image has its own clipping.

```ts
import { analyzeSaturation } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/saturation'

// image: Image — a linear, normalized frame; stars: { x, y }[] — centroids in pixels

// Pixels at or above the default level of 1.
const result = analyzeSaturation(image)
console.log(result.saturatedPixels, result.fraction) // count, and fraction of the frame
console.log(result.mask) // width * height bytes, 1 where saturated

// A camera that clips at 0.95 of the scale, and the stars whose nearest pixel is saturated.
console.log(analyzeSaturation(image, { level: 0.95, stars }).saturatedStars)
```

### Global Image Normalization

Frames of the same field taken during a night differ photometrically: the sky background changes with the Moon, twilight and light pollution, and the transparency changes with airmass and thin clouds. Before they are combined or compared, each is matched to a reference with a linear transform, `reference ≈ scale · current + offset`, in the units of the image (normalized 0..1 for an `Image`, see [Scientific Image Model](#scientific-image-model)), without clamping. Without it, a stack mixes different backgrounds and the outlier rejection rejects good pixels.

`solveGlobalNormalization` finds the transform from the overlapping pixel values of the two frames by matching their distributions by quantile, not pixel by pixel, which tolerates a residual misregistration that would bias a paired regression. The `scale` estimator is the ratio of the medians, with no offset; `background-scale` matches the 25th percentile (the background) and the 25th–75th percentile span; `percentile` matches the 10th percentile and the 10th–90th span, which tolerates bright structure better. `solveGlobalNormalizationPlanes` runs it on the raw buffers of two registered frames, per channel or once on the luminance, and `applyGlobalNormalizationInPlace` applies the result. The estimators need both frames to show the same sky: a different field, a satellite trail or a cloud over a large part of a frame biases them, and a differential gradient needs [Local Image Normalization](#local-image-normalization).

```ts
import { applyGlobalNormalizationInPlace, broadcastNormalizationPlanes, solveGlobalNormalization, solveGlobalNormalizationPlanes } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/normalization'

// A reference ramp and the same sky at 0.8 of the gain plus a pedestal of 0.05.
const reference = Array.from({ length: 101 }, (_, i) => 0.1 + (0.4 * i) / 100)
const current = reference.map((value) => (value - 0.05) / 0.8)
console.log(solveGlobalNormalization(reference, current, 'scale')) // { scale: 0.96, offset: 0 }: the median ratio cannot remove a pedestal
console.log(solveGlobalNormalization(reference, current, 'background-scale')) // scale ≈ 0.8, offset ≈ 0.05

// currentRaw, referenceRaw: registered RGB buffers of width x height; valid: one byte per pixel, nonzero is usable
const planes = solveGlobalNormalizationPlanes(currentRaw, valid, referenceRaw, 3, width, height, 'background-scale', 'per-channel')
const { scales, offsets } = broadcastNormalizationPlanes(planes, 3)
applyGlobalNormalizationInPlace(currentRaw, valid, 3, scales, offsets)
```

### Grayscale Image Conversion

Many analyses (star detection, plate solving, focus measurement, statistics) work on a single plane. A color image is reduced to it either by extracting one channel, which keeps a clean measurement through one filter, or by forming a luminance, a weighted sum of red, green and blue that approximates perceived brightness. The weights depend on the standard: BT.709 (the default, about 0.21, 0.72 and 0.07), the NTSC `Y` (0.299, 0.587, 0.114), or explicit weights that sum to 1. The named weights are the constants of [Scientific Image Model](#scientific-image-model).

`grayscale` converts an interleaved RGB image into a new single-channel image with the precision of the input, and its header loses the third axis and the CFA pattern; a mono input is returned unchanged, as the same object.

```ts
import { grayscale } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/geometry'

// rgb: Image — an interleaved RGB image with the pixels (1, 0, 0) and (0, 0.5, 1)

// The BT.709 luminance (default) and the NTSC Y luminance.
console.log(grayscale(rgb).raw, grayscale(rgb, 'Y').raw) // [0.2125, 0.4298] [0.299, 0.4075]

// One channel extracted without weighting, and explicit weights.
console.log(grayscale(rgb, 'GREEN').raw, grayscale(rgb, { red: 0.5, green: 0.5, blue: 0 }).raw) // [0, 0.5] [0.5, 0.25]
```

### Image Analysis Planes

Quantitative analyses of a sensor, such as noise, dark current, flat uniformity or saturation, must look at the samples as the sensor recorded them. On a color filter array each photosite sees a different filter with its own response, so the red, the two green and the blue photosites of a Bayer mosaic are four separate planes, each sampled every second pixel; debayering would interpolate between them and correlate their noise, and a luminance would mix them. The analyses of `imaging/analysis/plane` therefore work on one plane at a time: `mono`, one interleaved RGB plane (`red`, `green`, `blue`), or one native CFA plane (`red`, `green1`, `green2`, `blue`), of a `DigitalImage` in digital numbers (see [Scientific Image Loading and Export](#scientific-image-loading-and-export)).

A plane inside a rectangular area (left and top inclusive, right and bottom exclusive, in image pixels) is described by its geometry: the first source pixel, the step between samples in the source (1 for mono and RGB, 2 for a CFA plane), the size in samples, and the raw-buffer layout, so sample `(x, y)` is `raw[rawStart + y·rawRowStep + x·rawColumnStep]`. The CFA pattern of the metadata is local to the image: a crop of a full-sensor mosaic that starts at an odd column or row has a shifted pattern, which a `cfaOffset` in unbinned sensor pixels corrects once.

```ts
import { resolveAnalysisArea, resolveImageAnalysisPlanes, resolveImagePlaneGeometry, resolveLocalCfaPattern } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/plane'

// mosaic: DigitalImage — a 6x4 RGGB mosaic in digital numbers

// The planes of the layout, and the whole frame as the default area.
console.log(resolveImageAnalysisPlanes(mosaic)) // ['red', 'green1', 'green2', 'blue']
const area = resolveAnalysisArea(undefined, 6, 4)

// The blue plane: source pixel (1, 1), step 2, 3x2 samples. resolveOptionalImagePlaneGeometry returns undefined instead
// when a CFA plane has no sample in the area, and imagePlaneGeometry does the same from metadata already validated.
const blue = resolveImagePlaneGeometry(mosaic, area, 'blue')
console.log(mosaic.raw[blue.rawStart + 1 * blue.rawRowStep + 1 * blue.rawColumnStep]) // blue sample (1, 1), source pixel (3, 3)

// A crop that starts one column to the right sees the pattern shifted.
console.log(resolveLocalCfaPattern(mosaic, [1, 0])) // 'GRBG'
```

### Image Arithmetic

Calibration and many processing steps are sample-by-sample arithmetic on whole frames: a master dark is subtracted from a light, the result is divided by a normalized flat, frames are summed or averaged, and a pedestal is added or a frame rescaled. See [Image Calibration](#image-calibration) for the complete calibration. These operations run in the full floating-point range, without clipping, so results may leave 0..1 and the caller decides when to clamp or renormalize.

`plus`, `subtract`, `multiply` and `divide` combine two images of the same width, height, channels and CFA pattern; `plusScalar`, `subtractScalar`, `multiplyScalar` and `divideScalar` combine an image and a number. The last argument is the output image, and it defaults to the first operand, which is then overwritten in place: pass an explicit output to keep the input. `divide` writes 0 where the divisor is 0 instead of an infinity. Cloning and copying are in [Image Cloning and Copying](#image-cloning-and-copying).

```ts
import { divide, divideScalar, multiply, multiplyScalar, plus, plusScalar, subtract, subtractScalar } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/arithmetic'

// light, dark, flat, other, mask: Image — frames of the same geometry; calibrated: Image — an output image of the same geometry

// light - dark into a separate output, keeping the light frame.
subtract(light, dark, calibrated)

// Divided by the flat, in place in `calibrated` (a zero flat sample gives 0).
divide(calibrated, flat)

// Sample-by-sample sum and product with another image, in place.
plus(calibrated, other)
multiply(calibrated, mask)

// With a number: a pedestal added and removed, and a rescale by 2 and back, in place.
plusScalar(calibrated, 0.01)
subtractScalar(calibrated, 0.01)
multiplyScalar(calibrated, 2)
divideScalar(calibrated, 2)
```

### Image Calibration

A raw light frame is the sky signal plus everything the sensor and the optics add to it: the bias pedestal of the readout electronics, the thermal dark current that grows with exposure and temperature (with its hot pixels and amp glow), and a multiplicative response that varies across the field because of vignetting, dust shadows, and the pixel-to-pixel sensitivity of the sensor. Calibration removes the additive terms by subtracting master dark and bias frames and the multiplicative term by dividing by a normalized master flat, so that a pixel value becomes proportional to the light that reached it. It must happen before debayering, registration, and stacking, while every pixel is still in sensor coordinates.

`calibrate` applies the masters to a light frame in place, in the normalized 0..1 units of `Image` (see [Scientific Image Model](#scientific-image-model)). With raw masters, as stacked, the dark keeps its bias pedestal and the flat its bias and dark current, and the result is:

```text
L' = (L - D) · mean(F - Fd) / (F - Fd)
```

where `Fd` is the dark-flat, or the bias when there is none. The flat mean is taken per channel of a color image and per phase of an undebayered CFA mosaic. A flat that is already a corrected, normalized response (the product of [Image Calibration Master Integration](#image-calibration-master-integration)) is used as a plain divisor. When the dark exposure differs from the light, only the dark current `D - B` is scaled by the ratio of `EXPTIME`, which needs a bias and assumes a dark current linear in time at the same temperature; the function cannot check that. The masters must match the light in geometry, CFA pattern, binning, subframe, gain, and offset. The result is not clipped, so the noise around zero keeps its sign.

All frames must share one scale. A master kept in digital numbers must be read with the digital sample scale, because the normalized read of a floating-point file whose values leave 0..1 applies a min-max rescale of its own, and then converted by the digital full scale of the frames it came from (1 for a dimensionless flat).

```ts
import { calibrate, calibrationMasterImage, invalidFlatMask } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/calibration'

// light, other, flat, bias: Image — normalized frames of the same sensor setup, with EXPTIME in their headers.
// digitalDark: DigitalImage — a master dark in DN of a 16-bit camera, read with sampleScale: 'digital'.
// Converts it to the normalized units of the lights (DN divided by the full scale).
const dark = calibrationMasterImage(digitalDark, 65535)

// Subtracts the dark (scaled by exposure when it differs) and divides by the bias-corrected, normalized flat, in place.
calibrate(light, { dark, flat, bias })

console.log(light.raw) // calibrated samples, normalized units, not clipped

// normalizedFlat: Image — a calibrated, unit-median flat response.
// Pixels with no valid flat response stay uncorrected; the mask names them, so a stacker can reject them.
calibrate(other, { flat: normalizedFlat, flatRepresentation: 'calibratedNormalized', invalidFlat: 'passthrough' })
console.log(invalidFlatMask(normalizedFlat).count) // number of pixels with a non-finite or non-positive flat
```

### Image Calibration Master Integration

A calibration master combines many frames of the same sensor setup to lower their random noise, so that calibration does not add noise to every light frame. It differs from [Image Stacking](#image-stacking) in what it must preserve: a dark, a bias, or a dark-flat keeps its pedestal, amp glow, and hot pixels, so frames are never registered, interpolated, debayered, or normalized, and the samples of each pixel are combined across frames in sensor coordinates. A hot pixel is stable in time and survives; a cosmic ray hits one frame and is rejected by a sigma clip around the median.

The integration works on rows, one buffer per frame, so a caller can stream an image of any size in pieces and the result does not depend on the pieces. Below three frames a sigma clip degrades to a plain mean, and a quantized pixel whose samples are mostly equal must not see a neighboring code as an outlier, which is why the robust deviation has a lower limit in sample units.

A flat is the one master that is normalized. Each raw flat is corrected by its dark-flat or bias, then divided by its own median per plane (the four phases of a mosaic in image-local coordinates, or the channels), which removes the change of illumination between flats and keeps the vignetting and the dust. The integrated result is the `flatRepresentation: 'calibratedNormalized'` input of [Image Calibration](#image-calibration). Medians make it unity per plane, while the raw branch of `calibrate` uses means, so the two agree up to a constant per plane.

```ts
import { CalibrationPlaneLevels, calibrationPlane, calibrationPlaneCount, createCalibrationIntegrationDiagnostics, divideCalibrationPlanes, effectiveCalibrationCombination, integrateCalibrationRows, subtractCalibrationRows } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/calibration.integration'

// Five dark frames of two pixels, in digital numbers: the second is hot, and a cosmic ray hits the first in the last frame.
const rows = [new Float32Array([1000, 4000]), new Float32Array([1002, 4001]), new Float32Array([998, 3999]), new Float32Array([1001, 4000]), new Float32Array([60000, 4000])]
const output = new Float32Array(2)
const diagnostics = createCalibrationIntegrationDiagnostics(rows.length)

// Combines the samples of each pixel across frames with sigma-clipping rejection.
integrateCalibrationRows(rows, 2, output, { method: 'sigmaClip' }, diagnostics)
console.log(output) // [1000.25, 4000] — DN, the hot pixel stays and the cosmic ray does not

// The method really applied: below three frames a sigma clip is a plain mean, to be reported as a low count.
console.log(effectiveCalibrationCombination('sigmaClip', 2)) // 'mean'

// The independent planes of an image (4 CFA phases of a mosaic, or the channels), and the plane of a sample (x, y).
console.log(calibrationPlaneCount(true, 1), calibrationPlane(1, 1, true, 0)) // 4 3

// One raw 2x2 flat corrected by its pedestal, then normalized to its median.
const flat = new Float64Array([1100, 2100, 1600, 2600])
subtractCalibrationRows(flat, new Float64Array([100, 100, 100, 100]), 4)

const levels = new CalibrationPlaneLevels(calibrationPlaneCount(false, 1), 4, false)
levels.push(flat, 2, 2, 0)
const [{ median }] = levels.levels()
divideCalibrationPlanes(flat, 2, 2, 0, [median], false)

console.log(median, flat) // 1750 [0.5714, 1.1429, 0.8571, 1.4286] — DN, dimensionless
```

### Image Cloning and Copying

Most processing functions modify an `Image` in place to avoid allocating a frame-sized buffer per step. A pipeline that must keep the original (to compare before and after, to try several stretches, or to reuse a calibrated frame) clones it first, and a long-lived buffer can receive the samples of another image of the same shape without a new allocation.

`clone` returns an independent image whose header, metadata, and samples are copies with the same precision. `copyInto` copies only the samples into a destination of the same width, height, channels, and CFA pattern, leaving the header and metadata of the destination alone.

```ts
import { clone, copyInto } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/arithmetic'

// source: Image — any image.
// An independent copy: changing it never touches the source.
const copy = clone(source)
copy.raw[0] = 9

// target: Image — an existing image of the same shape.
// Copies the samples of the source into it and returns the target.
copyInto(source, target)
```

### Image Convolution

Convolution replaces each pixel with a weighted sum of its neighbors, the weights being a kernel. It is the basic linear filter of image processing: a kernel with positive weights summing to one smooths the image and suppresses high spatial frequencies (noise), a kernel with weights summing to zero responds only to change (edges), and a kernel that adds a scaled Laplacian to the identity sharpens. In astronomy, a Gaussian kernel close to the point spread function is the matched filter for star detection, and a dilated ("à trous") smoothing is the building block of the wavelet layers of [Multiscale Linear Transform](#multiscale-linear-transform).

The kernel is normalized by its divisor, the sum of its weights unless one is given, and the pixels outside the image are not read: at a border the kernel is truncated and, by default, renormalized by the weights that fall inside, so a smoothing kernel keeps its gain to the edge. A zero-sum kernel such as edges or emboss is centered at 0.5, so its negative response remains visible. Every channel of an interleaved color image is convolved on its own, in place, and the result is not clipped. The named filters (box and pyramid blurs, Gaussian blur, sharpen, edges, emboss) are fixed kernels of this one operation, and a separable smoothing applies a one-dimensional kernel along rows and then columns at a cost independent of the dilation step.

```ts
import { blur, blurConvolutionKernel, convolution, convolutionKernel, edges, emboss, gaussianBlur, gaussianBlurKernel, mean, meanConvolutionKernel, separableSmoothing, separableSmoothingKernel, sharpen } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/convolution'

// image: Image — a normalized mono or RGB image; every call modifies it in place.
// A Gaussian smoothing, sigma in pixels and an odd kernel size.
gaussianBlur(image, { sigma: 1.4, size: 5 })

// A box (mean) blur and a pyramid blur of an odd size in pixels; mean3x3, mean5x5, mean7x7, blur3x3, blur5x5, and blur7x7 are the fixed sizes.
mean(image, 5)
blur(image, 3)

// The fixed sharpening, edge-detection, and emboss kernels.
sharpen(image)
edges(image)
emboss(image)

// A custom 3x3 kernel; its divisor is the sum of the weights (16).
convolution(image, convolutionKernel([1, 2, 1, 2, 4, 2, 1, 2, 1], 3))

// The kernels of the named filters, for a convolution call: Gaussian (sigma, size), box, and pyramid of a given size.
convolution(image, gaussianBlurKernel(2, 7))
convolution(image, meanConvolutionKernel(9))
convolution(image, blurConvolutionKernel(9))

// A dilated binomial smoothing [1, 4, 6, 4, 1] / 16 with taps 2 pixels apart, from source into output.
// source, output, intermediate: separate buffers of the image's length.
separableSmoothing(source, output, intermediate, image.metadata, separableSmoothingKernel([1, 4, 6, 4, 1]), { step: 2 })
```

### Image Intensity Inversion

Inverting an image produces its negative, `1 - v` for a sample `v` in normalized units. Astronomers inspect negatives because faint nebulosity, tidal tails, and low-contrast structure are often easier to see as dark on a light background, and the convention of printed photographic atlases is a negative.

`invert` works in place on a normalized mono or RGB image. It does not clip, so a sample outside 0..1 maps outside it as well, and applying it twice gives back the original samples up to rounding.

```ts
import { invert } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/geometry'

// image: Image — normalized samples [0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 1.5].
// Replaces each sample v with 1 - v, in place.
invert(image)

console.log(image.raw) // [1, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, -0.5]
```

### Image Mirroring

Images come mirrored for optical and mechanical reasons: a star diagonal or a Newtonian with an odd number of reflections mirrors the field, and a camera may read its rows bottom-up, so the image must be flipped to match the sky or a reference frame. A horizontal flip reverses the columns (left becomes right) and a vertical flip reverses the rows.

A flip keeps the metadata consistent with the pixels. The FITS WCS keywords (`CRPIX` and the linear transformation terms) are reflected, so every star keeps its sky coordinates, and the CFA pattern of a raw mosaic is shifted when the reflection moves its origin to an odd pixel: with an even width `RGGB` becomes `GRBG` after a horizontal flip, and with an even height `GBRG` after a vertical one. Two flips along the same axis restore the image.

```ts
import { horizontalFlip, verticalFlip } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/geometry'

// mosaic: Image — a 4x2 RGGB mosaic with a WCS (CRPIX1 = 1, CD1_1 = -0.001).
// Reverses the columns in place and reflects the WCS and the CFA pattern.
horizontalFlip(mosaic)
console.log(mosaic.header.CRPIX1, mosaic.header.CD1_1, mosaic.metadata.bayer) // 4 0.001 GRBG

// Reverses the rows in place.
verticalFlip(mosaic)
```

### Image Plane Statistics

An image inspector must report what the pixels hold, not what a stretch shows: the true minimum and maximum, the median sky level, the noise, and how many samples are saturated or invalid. These statistics are measured one plane at a time on the original samples, in normalized units: the mono plane, the red, green, and blue channels of an RGB image plus a BT.709 luminance of the linear samples (not a calibrated photometric luminance), or the four photosite phases of a mosaic when its trusted image-local CFA pattern is given, so the two greens stay apart (see [Image Analysis Planes](#image-analysis-planes)).

Each plane reports the exact extremes, the mean, and the population standard deviation, and robust order statistics: the median, the MAD, `robustSigma = 1.4826 · MAD`, and the 1st and 99th percentiles. The robust sigma is the dispersion of the whole population, not a background noise; the per-plane background noise comes from [Local Background Noise](#local-background-noise). Order statistics are exact for small populations and for integer 8 or 16-bit codes, and otherwise estimated from the bounded reservoir of [Bounded Robust Sampling](#bounded-robust-sampling). NaN and infinities are counted but never enter a reduction, and a count of samples at normalized 0 or 1 does not by itself prove saturation, because only the caller knows the representable limits of the source. Two chart histograms, one over the robust P0.1..P99.9 domain and one over the full range, accompany each plane; the quantized histogram of [Image Statistics](#image-statistics) is still the one display stretches use.

The analysis can also run as an incremental scan, advanced a few rows at a time between event-loop turns, with a result identical for any chunking.

```ts
import { analyzeImageStatistics, createImageStatisticsScan } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/statistics'

// image: Image — a normalized frame; area is left/top inclusive and right/bottom exclusive.
// Statistics of every plane of the area, in normalized units.
const { planes } = analyzeImageStatistics(image, { area: { left: 0, top: 0, right: 64, bottom: 64 }, numericLimits: true })
console.log(planes[0].median, planes[0].robustSigma) // median sky level and robust dispersion, normalized units

// One plane per photosite phase of a trusted RGGB mosaic.
console.log(analyzeImageStatistics(image, { cfa: 'RGGB' }).planes.map((p) => p.plane)) // ['red', 'green1', 'green2', 'blue']

// The same computation advanced 8 rows at a time, between event-loop turns; consumeRows also returns done.
const scan = createImageStatisticsScan(image)
while (!scan.done) scan.consumeRows(8)
console.log(scan.finish().planes[0].median) // identical to the one-shot result
```

### Image Scale and Field of View

The image scale ties the pixels to the sky. A telescope of focal length `F` projects one radian of sky onto `F` of focal plane, so one millimeter covers `206265 / F` arcseconds and a pixel of size `p` covers:

```text
scale [arcsec/px] = 206.265 · p [µm] / F [mm]
```

The scale decides the sampling of the seeing (about two to three pixels across the star FWHM is the usual target), the field a sensor covers, and how many panels a mosaic needs. These are closed-form planning estimates of an ideal train: a thin lens without distortion, a flat focal plane, and the small-angle approximation for the field along one axis, which overestimates a wide field (by about 4% for a 36 mm side at 50 mm); the diagonal field is the exact `2 atan(d / 2F)`. Binning multiplies the effective pixel size. The sensor field is not the usable field, because vignetting and the corrector or reducer are not modeled, and the formulas do not validate their inputs.

```ts
import { focalLength, focalRatio, mosaicPanelCount, pixelScale, plateScale, sensorDiagonalFov, sensorFieldOfView } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'

// A 200 mm aperture at f/5, and the inverse relation (mm, dimensionless).
const f = focalLength(200, 5)
console.log(f, focalRatio(f, 200)) // 1000 5

// Focal-plane scale (arcsec/mm) and the scale of a 3.76 µm pixel (arcsec/px).
console.log(plateScale(f), pixelScale(3.76, f)) // 206.265 0.7756

// Field of a 23.5 mm sensor side (degrees, small-angle) and of its 28.26 mm diagonal (radians, exact).
console.log(sensorFieldOfView(23.5, f), sensorDiagonalFov(Math.hypot(23.5, 15.7), f)) // 1.3465 degrees, then radians

// Panels along one axis: a 6° target with a 1.35° camera and 20% overlap.
console.log(mosaicPanelCount(6, 1.35, 0.2)) // 6
```

### Image Stacking

A single sub-exposure of a faint target is dominated by noise: sky shot noise, read noise, and thermal signal. Every frame of the same field carries the same signal but independent noise, so averaging `N` frames improves the signal-to-noise ratio by about `√N`. Combining the samples of each pixel with outlier rejection also removes what appears in only a few frames, such as cosmic-ray hits, satellite and aircraft trails, and residual hot pixels, which a plain mean would keep at `1/N` of their brightness.

Frames can only be combined after they agree geometrically and photometrically. Registration fits a transform (translation, similarity, or affine) between the stars of each frame and those of a reference frame and resamples the frame onto the reference grid; normalization removes the changes of sky level and transparency during the night, which would otherwise bias the combination and defeat the rejection; and weighting lets sharper or less noisy frames contribute more. A median or a sigma-clipped mean rejects outliers at the cost of keeping every aligned frame in memory, while a sum or a (weighted) mean accumulates frame by frame and is what [Live Stacking](#live-stacking) and [Drizzle Integration](#drizzle-integration) use.

`stackFrames` runs the whole pipeline against a reference frame: star matching (see [Star List Registration](#star-list-registration)), resampling (see [Image Warp](#image-warp)), normalization (see [Global Image Normalization](#global-image-normalization)), weighting, and combination. Frames that cannot be registered are rejected rather than combined, and the result reports why. The work is synchronous, so a long stack of large frames blocks for its whole duration. For an integrator that registers frames itself and must bound its memory, `stacking.combination` exposes the same combination a strip of rows at a time, with identical results.

```ts
import { referenceQualityScore, stackFrames } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/stacker'
import { accumulateSamples, combineSamples, combineStrip, coverageBounds, coverageThreshold, createCombinationScratch, finalizeOnlineSamples, frameWeight, isOnlineCombinationMethod, resolveCombinationParameters } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/stacking.combination'

// frames: StackingFrame[] — normalized images of one field with their detected stars (zero-based pixel centers).
// Registers every frame to the reference, normalizes, weights, and combines with sigma-clipping rejection.
const stack = stackFrames(frames, { combinationMethod: 'sigma-clip', weightingMode: 'quality' })

console.log(stack.finalImage) // the combined image, or undefined when no frame could be used
console.log(stack.acceptedFrames, stack.rejectedFrames) // frames combined and frames rejected
console.log(stack.diagnostics[1]) // per-frame transform, overlap, quality, and rejection reason
console.log(stack.coverageMap) // number of frames that contribute to each output pixel

// The score that ranks a frame as reference candidate (higher is better, within one setup), with 10 stars expected.
const quality = stack.diagnostics[1].quality
console.log(referenceQualityScore(quality, 10))

// The building blocks of an integrator that registers frames itself. The weight of a frame from its quality.
const weight = frameWeight(1, quality, 'quality', 10)

// Sum, average and weighted average accumulate exactly, frame by frame; the rejection methods need every sample.
console.log(isOnlineCombinationMethod('average'), isOnlineCombinationMethod('sigma-clip')) // true false

// raw, valid: one aligned mono frame and its validity bytes; sum, weightSum: Float64Array accumulators of the grid;
// coverage: Uint32Array frames per pixel. Adds the frame to the running average.
accumulateSamples(1, raw, valid, sum, weightSum, coverage, 'average', weight)

// The frames a pixel needs (half of 10 accepted frames), and the inclusive box of the pixels that reach it.
const threshold = coverageThreshold(10, 'union', 0.5) // 5
console.log(coverageBounds(width, height, coverage, threshold)) // { left, top, right, bottom, width, height }, or undefined

// Writes the average of the pixels that reach the threshold into out (a pixel buffer of the grid).
finalizeOnlineSamples(sum, weightSum, coverage, 1, threshold, 'average', out)

// The samples of one pixel across 5 frames, combined by sigma clipping: the outlier 0.9 is rejected.
console.log(combineSamples('sigma-clip', new Float64Array([0.2, 0.21, 0.19, 0.2, 0.9]), new Float64Array(5).fill(1), 5, resolveCombinationParameters())) // 0.2

// strips: aligned frames on one grid ({ raw, valid, weight }) starting at the same row.
// Combines `width` pixels of one channel, keeping only pixels covered by at least 2 frames.
combineStrip(strips, width, 1, coverage, 2, 'sigma-clip', resolveCombinationParameters(), out, createCombinationScratch(strips.length))
```

### Image Statistics

The display stretches and the clipped sky estimators need the median, the mean, and the dispersion of an image quickly and many times. They read the normalized `[0, 1]` samples through a histogram of `2^bits` bins (16 bits by default), so every value is quantized to a bin and the statistics are histogram estimates, exact only to the width of a bin (`2^-bits`), not exact order statistics of the floating-point samples; for sample-exact quantiles see [Descriptive Statistics](#descriptive-statistics), and for an inspector report see [Image Plane Statistics](#image-plane-statistics).

A color image is reduced to one channel or to its grayscale luminance, and the statistics can be restricted to an inclusive rectangle, transformed before binning, or computed with the pixels of a sigma-clipping mask left out (see [Pixel Sigma Clipping and Background Levels](#pixel-sigma-clipping-and-background-levels)). The median absolute deviation, multiplied by the Gaussian consistency factor 1.4826, is a robust estimate of the standard deviation that bright stars do not inflate. The display auto-stretch is built on these (see [Display Stretch Parameter Estimation](#display-stretch-parameter-estimation)).

```ts
import { histogram, median, medianAbsoluteDeviation } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/computation'

// image: Image — a normalized RGB sky of 0.2, 0.25, and 0.3 with noise and 40 bright stars.
// The histogram of the grayscale reduction (a Histogram, see Histogram Analysis): normalized mean, median, deviation, and quantiles.
const gray = histogram(image)
console.log(gray.median, gray.standardDeviation, gray.quantile(0.75)) // normalized units

// The median of one channel, and of a region of interest (inclusive rectangle).
const m = median(image, { channel: 'RED' })
console.log(median(image, { channel: 'GREEN', area: { left: 0, top: 0, right: 31, bottom: 31 } }))

// The MAD about the median, normalized (×1.4826) to be comparable to a standard deviation.
console.log(medianAbsoluteDeviation(image, m, true, { channel: 'RED' })) // normalized units
```

### Image Warp

Warping resamples an image onto the pixel grid of another one through a geometric transform, the step that puts registered frames on a common grid before they are compared or combined. It is the resampling half of registration: [Star List Registration](#star-list-registration) fits the transform, and [Image Stacking](#image-stacking) runs the whole pipeline.

The transform is given in its inverse form, mapping each output pixel of the reference grid to a position in the source, so that every output pixel receives exactly one interpolated value. It is a similarity (`x' = a x - b y + tx`, `y' = b x + a y + ty`, optionally mirrored) or a general affine transform. Pixel coordinates have an integer at the center of a pixel and the origin at the center of the first pixel, so a pure translation `tx = 2` makes output pixel `x` the source pixel `x + 2`. The nearest-neighbor, bilinear, and bicubic kernels trade smoothing for fidelity, and interpolation attenuates the noise by an amount that depends on the subpixel phase, which matters for any later noise statistics (see [Local Image Normalization](#local-image-normalization)). A validity mask marks the output pixels whose whole kernel falls inside the source and touches no rejected pixel (a streak or cosmic-ray mask); the other samples are zero. A singular transform is not detected.

```ts
import { composeTransforms, summarizeTransform, toAffineMatrix, warpImage } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/registration'

// source, reference: Image — a 6x4 source whose value is x + 10 y, and any 6x4 grid.
// Resamples the source onto the reference grid, here shifted by 2 pixels (bilinear by default).
const shifted = warpImage(source, reference, { a: 1, b: 0, tx: 2, ty: 0, mirrored: false })
console.log(Array.from(shifted.image.raw.slice(0, 6))) // [2, 3, 4, 5, 0, 0]
console.log(Array.from(shifted.validityMask.slice(0, 6))) // [1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0] — the last columns fall outside the source

// rejectionMask: Uint8Array — one byte per source pixel, nonzero for a streak or cosmic ray.
// A half-pixel shift with the bicubic kernel; outputs whose kernel touches a rejected pixel are invalid.
warpImage(source, reference, { a: 1, b: 0, tx: 0.5, ty: 0, mirrored: false }, { interpolationMode: 'bicubic', rejectionMask })

// The affine matrix equivalent to a similarity transform (a quarter turn).
console.log(toAffineMatrix({ a: 0, b: 1, tx: 0, ty: 0, mirrored: false })) // { m00: 0, m01: -1, tx: 0, m10: 1, m11: 0, ty: 0 }

// One affine applying a shift by (2, 3) first and then a quarter turn with tx = 5, so the frame is resampled once.
const turn = { a: 0, b: 1, tx: 5, ty: 0, mirrored: false }
console.log(composeTransforms(turn, { a: 1, b: 0, tx: 2, ty: 3, mirrored: false })) // { m00: 0, m01: -1, tx: 2, m10: 1, m11: 0, ty: 2 }

// The readable form of a transform: translation (pixels), scales, rotation (radians), shear, parity, with 12 inliers and 0.3 px RMS.
console.log(summarizeTransform(turn, 12, 0.3)) // { model: 'similarity', translationX: 5, translationY: 0, scaleX: 1, rotation: 1.5708, mirrored: false, ... }
```

### Live Stacking

Live stacking builds a stack one frame at a time as frames arrive from the camera and shows the current result at any moment, the technique of electronically assisted astronomy and outreach sessions, and a way to watch the integration of a long acquisition grow. Its memory depends on the frame size and not on the number of frames, because each accepted frame is registered, normalized, and accumulated into a per-pixel sum and weight, and its pixels are not retained.

That restricts it to the combinations that can be accumulated exactly: the sum, the average, and the weighted average, with resampling or the [Drizzle Integration](#drizzle-integration) reconstruction. Median and sigma-clipping rejection need every sample of a pixel at once and are only available in a batch [Image Stacking](#image-stacking), which shares the registration, normalization, and weighting options. The first accepted frame is the reference. A snapshot is a copy of the accumulators, so the stack goes on after it, at the price of one pass over the image per preview. `add` is synchronous and CPU-bound, so a long session on large frames is better run away from a UI thread.

Several live stacks can share one geometric field, for example one stack per filter of a narrowband sequence that will be composed into color later. Every frame of each stack is then registered against the field stars and resampled onto the field grid, so all stacks are on the same pixels, while each stack is normalized to its own first accepted frame, never to the brightness of another filter. A shared field needs the resampling reconstruction.

```ts
import { isLiveCombinationMethodSupported, LiveStacker, liveStackerMemoryBytes } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/stacker'

// Whether a combination method can run live: only the exactly accumulated ones.
console.log(isLiveCombinationMethodSupported('average'), isLiveCombinationMethodSupported('sigma-clip')) // true false

// frame: StackingFrame — a normalized image of the field with its detected stars (zero-based pixel centers).
// Registers, normalizes, and accumulates one frame; the first accepted frame is the reference.
const live = new LiveStacker({ combinationMethod: 'average' })
const result = live.add(frame)
console.log(result.accepted, result.reason) // whether the frame was used, and why not

// The current stack, a copy that later frames do not change (undefined before the first accepted frame).
console.log(live.snapshot()?.finalImage)

// Discards the stack and starts again with the same options, or with new options (and optionally a field).
live.reset()
live.initialize({ combinationMethod: 'sum' })

// field: LiveStackingField — { image, stars } of a reference frame; one stack per filter on the same grid.
const red = new LiveStacker({}, field)
const blue = new LiveStacker({}, field)

// Bytes retained by a resampling stack of a 96x96 mono grid with 8-byte samples.
console.log(liveStackerMemoryBytes(96, 96, 1, 8)) // 423936
```

### Local Background Noise

The background noise of a frame is the standard deviation of the sky where there is no source, the quantity that sets the detection threshold of stars, the signal-to-noise ratio of faint structure, and the comparison of exposures. A global standard deviation is dominated by stars, hot pixels, nebulosity, and gradients, and the coarse [Background Estimate](#background-estimate) is fast but approximate. This estimate is robust to all of them: the plane is split into tiles, each tile is clipped about its median, a plane is fitted and removed so that a smooth gradient does not count as noise, the noise of the tile is the MAD of the residuals scaled by 1.4826, and tiles dominated by structure are rejected. The level and the noise are the medians over the accepted tiles, in the sample units of the image.

The result reports whether the estimate was measured, is uncertain, or is unavailable (too few usable tiles), with warnings for strong gradients, structure, clipping, quantization, and spatially correlated noise. Each photosite phase of a mosaic can be measured on its own when its trusted image-local CFA pattern is given, instead of mixing the levels of the colors. [Image Plane Statistics](#image-plane-statistics) computes the same estimate for each native plane during its scan.

This is a spatial estimate on one frame. It is not a read noise, a gain, or a temporal noise (see [Photon Transfer and Read Noise](#photon-transfer-and-read-noise)), and it does not know whether the baseline is a sky, a bias, or a flat. Debayered, resampled, or denoised pixels have correlated noise and bias it low, and contamination that covers more than half of every tile cannot be told from noise.

```ts
import { BackgroundNoiseCollector, estimateBackgroundNoise } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/background.noise'

// sky: Image — a 400x300 sky of 0.1 with a noise of 0.01, a gradient of 0.3 across the frame, and 500 bright stars.
// The background level and spatial noise of the mono plane, in normalized units.
const noise = estimateBackgroundNoise(sky)
console.log(noise.status, noise.noiseSigma) // 'measured', close to the injected 0.01 (the gradient and the stars are not counted)

// mosaic: Image — a raw RGGB mosaic; the blue photosites are measured alone.
console.log(estimateBackgroundNoise(mosaic, { plane: 'blue', cfa: 'RGGB' }).level) // normalized units

// The same estimate fed row by row, for example while a file is decoded: a plane grid of 400x300 samples,
// each row given by its first raw index and the step between its samples.
const collector = new BackgroundNoiseCollector(400, 300)
for (let row = 0; row < 300; row++) collector.collectRow(sky.raw, row * 400, 1, row)
console.log(collector.totalTiles, collector.finish().noiseSigma) // tiles of the grid, and the same noise as estimateBackgroundNoise(sky)
```

### Local Image Normalization

Frames of one field taken during a night differ by more than a global scale and offset: moonlight, drifting light pollution, and a transparency that changes across the field add gradients that differ from frame to frame. A global normalization (see [Global Image Normalization](#global-image-normalization)) is right on average and wrong in the corners, and the residual gradients defeat outlier rejection and leave blotches in the stack. Local normalization matches a registered frame to a reference with a smoothly varying offset and, where the data support it, a smoothly varying gain.

The model keeps the global solution as an anchor and describes only the smooth residual.
