The frame is divided into a grid of cells, each cell estimates its residual offset (and gain, when it has enough dynamic range) from paired statistics of the same pixels in both frames, and polynomial or spline surfaces are fitted over the cells with outlier rejection. The local gain is limited to a range around the anchor, so a legitimate global exposure difference is never truncated, and a plane that cannot be modeled falls back to the global solution, to identity, or rejects the frame. Both images must already be registered onto the same grid. The fit needs a smooth residual and clean sky: a nebula that fills the frame, or frames that are not registered, will be modeled as gradient.

```ts
import { applyLocalNormalization, applyLocalNormalizationInPlace, fitLocalNormalization, fitLocalNormalizationRaw, isLocalNormalizationFallback, localNormalization, localNormalizationFailureReason, localNormalizationSummary, resolveLocalNormalizationOptions } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/normalization'

// reference, frame, other: Image — registered frames of the same field and geometry; frame adds a sky gradient.
// Fits the model and applies it to the frame in place.
const result = localNormalization(reference, frame)
console.log(result.applied) // false only when the fallback policy rejected the frame
console.log(localNormalizationSummary(result.model)) // compact per-plane record of cells, residual, and fallback

// Whether a plane runs on the fallback policy, and the first reason (undefined when every plane was modeled).
console.log(isLocalNormalizationFallback(result.model), localNormalizationFailureReason(result.model))

// The two steps apart: a coarser grid and a quadratic offset surface, applied to another frame of the same geometry.
const model = fitLocalNormalization(reference, frame, { gridSize: 8, offsetDegree: 2 })
applyLocalNormalization(other, model)

// The same on raw RGB buffers of width x height, with resolved options; valid: one byte per pixel, nonzero is usable.
const rawModel = fitLocalNormalizationRaw(referenceRaw, currentRaw, width, height, 3, 'per-channel', valid, resolveLocalNormalizationOptions({ gridSize: 8 }))
applyLocalNormalizationInPlace(currentRaw, valid, rawModel)
```

### Multiscale Linear Transform

A multiscale transform separates an image into detail layers of increasing spatial scale plus a smooth residual, so that each scale can be processed on its own: noise lives in the finest layers, stars and fine structure in the middle ones, nebulosity in the coarse ones, and the background in the residual. Sharpening a scale, suppressing the noise of another, or removing the background is then a change of the coefficients of one layer before the layers are added back.

This is the redundant à trous wavelet transform (undecimated, so every layer has the size of the image) with a cubic B-spline scaling function, the kernel `[1, 4, 6, 4, 1] / 16` applied along each axis with its taps dilated by `2^k` on layer `k`. With `smooth_0` the image and `smooth_(k+1)` the smoothing of `smooth_k`:

```text
detail_k = smooth_k - smooth_(k+1)        image = Σ detail_k + smooth_n
```

Layer 0 holds the finest detail (about 1 to 2 pixels) and each following layer doubles the scale. Each layer can be denoised by a soft threshold in multiples of its robust standard deviation, or scaled by `1 + bias` (a positive bias sharpens the layer, -1 removes it), and the residual has its own gain. With the default options the reconstruction is the original image up to rounding, the image is modified in place, and nothing is clamped, so a sharpened image can leave 0..1. The linear kernel spreads a bright star into its surroundings at every scale, which causes ringing around it when a layer is boosted; [Multiscale Median Transform](#multiscale-median-transform) avoids that.

```ts
import { multiscaleLinearTransform } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/mlt'

// image: Image — a normalized mono or RGB image; every call modifies it in place.
// Doubles the coefficients of the two finest layers of four (sharpening).
multiscaleLinearTransform(image, { layers: 4, detailLayers: [{ bias: 1 }, { bias: 1 }] })

// Denoises the finest layer: coefficients below 3 robust sigmas are removed.
multiscaleLinearTransform(image, { layers: 3, detailLayers: [{ threshold: 3, amount: 1 }] })

// Removes the large-scale background (the residual of five layers).
multiscaleLinearTransform(image, { layers: 5, residualGain: 0 })
```

### Multiscale Median Transform

The multiscale median transform has the same decomposition and the same layer controls as the [Multiscale Linear Transform](#multiscale-linear-transform), similar to the transform of the same name in PixInsight, but each smoothing is a sliding square median of radius `2^k` pixels on layer `k` instead of the B-spline. The median does not blur edges and ignores isolated outliers, so a small bright object is not spread to its surroundings, and the layers separate structure from noise and stars from a smooth background better, without the ringing of linear wavelets around bright stars. The price is a transform that is not linear even without thresholds and layers whose coefficients are not exactly zero-mean.

The median is computed on a histogram quantized to 14 bits between the minimum and maximum of each channel, so it is exact to 1/16383 of the channel range: an image with a very large dynamic range (a bright star over a faint background) gets a coarser median of the background and a correspondingly coarse layer split, although the layers still add up exactly to the image. As in the linear transform, the image is modified in place, nothing is clamped, and the default options reconstruct the original.

```ts
import { multiscaleMedianTransform } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/mmt'

// image: Image — a normalized mono or RGB image; every call modifies it in place.
// Removes the finest layer (bias -1): lowers the noise without spreading stars.
multiscaleMedianTransform(image, { layers: 3, detailLayers: [{ bias: -1 }] })

// Sharpens the second layer, and removes the large-scale component of five layers.
multiscaleMedianTransform(image, { layers: 4, detailLayers: [{}, { bias: 1 }] })
multiscaleMedianTransform(image, { layers: 5, residualGain: 0 })
```

### Photon Transfer and Read Noise

The photon transfer curve is the standard way to measure a camera's gain and read noise from its own images, with no calibrated light source. Light arrives as a Poisson process, so a signal of `N` electrons has a shot-noise variance of `N` electrons squared. Converted to digital numbers by the system gain `K` (DN per electron), the temporal variance of a uniformly illuminated pixel grows linearly with its dark-corrected signal `S`:

```text
σ²(S) = K · S + σ²₀        (S in DN, σ² in DN²; conversion gain = 1/K e⁻/DN)
```

The slope is the system gain and the intercept holds the read and dark noise. Each point of the curve comes from a pair of frames taken under the same conditions: their difference cancels the fixed pattern, and half its variance is the temporal variance. The read noise is the RMS temporal noise of a pair of bias or short dark frames, converted to electrons by the conversion gain, and optionally corrected for the uniform quantization noise `step² / 12`. The fit uses only the unclipped points within a range of the largest signal, away from the read-noise floor and from saturation. The model holds only for a linear sensor whose pixel-response non-uniformity is removed by the pair difference; [Sensor Characterization](#sensor-characterization) runs this stage with the others.

```ts
import { aggregateSensorPairs, measureSensorPair } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/sensor/pair'
import { characterizeSensorTemporal, fitPhotonTransferGain, measureSensorReadNoise } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/sensor/ptc'

// a, b: DigitalImage — two frames in DN of one setup; the temporal variance is half the variance of their difference.
const pair = measureSensorPair(a, b)
console.log(pair.mean, pair.variance) // DN, DN²

// pairs: SensorPairStatistics[] — several pairs of one level, combined by sample count with their scatter between pairs.
const level = aggregateSensorPairs(pairs)
console.log(level.mean, level.variance, level.pairCount) // DN, DN², number of pairs

// biasPairs: SensorPairStatistics[] — pairs of bias frames of 2 DN RMS noise.
// Read noise with a conversion gain of 2 e-/DN and a quantization step of 1 DN.
console.log(measureSensorReadNoise(biasPairs, 2, 1)) // { digital: 2, totalElectrons: 4, sensorElectrons: 3.958, ... }

// bias: SensorFrameSet, flats: SensorFlatFrameSet[] — a bias pair and flat pairs at increasing illumination.
// The whole chain for one plane: photon transfer points, gain fit, and read noise.
const { photonTransfer, gain, readNoise } = characterizeSensorTemporal(bias, flats, { digitalClip: 60000 })
console.log(gain?.system, gain?.conversion) // DN/e-, e-/DN

// The gain fit alone, restricted to 10–30% of the largest signal.
const [points, refit] = fitPhotonTransferGain(photonTransfer, [0.1, 0.3])
```

### Pixel Sigma Clipping and Background Levels

The sky level of an astronomical image is the value of the pixels where there is no source, but every pixel statistic is pulled up by the stars, hot pixels, and nebulosity that sit on it. Iterative sigma clipping rejects the pixels outside `[center − k_low σ, center + k_high σ]`, recomputes the center and dispersion of the survivors, and repeats until nothing changes. A mean and standard deviation clip is itself pulled by the outliers it is meant to reject, so for a sky with bright stars the median and MAD pair converges to the sky with fewer iterations. The result is a rejection mask of one byte per pixel (a color pixel is rejected as a whole when its grayscale value is), computed with the histogram statistics of [Image Statistics](#image-statistics), which can then exclude the same pixels from another statistic.

`estimateBackground` is the median of the pixels that survive a median and MAD clip, the sky level in the sample units of the image. `estimateBackgroundUsingMode` is the empirical mode approximation `2.5 median − 1.5 mean` of the whole histogram, with no clipping, which is only meaningful for a unimodal sky and biased when many pixels are bright. Both differ from the quick grid estimator of [Background Estimate](#background-estimate), which also returns the noise, and from the spatial model of [Automatic Background Extraction](#automatic-background-extraction).

```ts
import { estimateBackground, estimateBackgroundUsingMode, median, sigmaClip } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/computation'

// image: Image — a normalized RGB sky with bright stars.
// Rejects the stars of the red channel with a median/MAD clip; 1 is rejected.
const mask = sigmaClip(image, { channel: 'RED', centerMethod: 'median', dispersionMethod: 'mad', sigmaLower: 5, sigmaUpper: 2 })

// The median of the remaining sky.
console.log(median(image, { channel: 'RED', sigmaClip: mask })) // normalized units

// The sky level from a clipped median, and from the empirical mode.
console.log(estimateBackground(image, { channel: 'RED' }), estimateBackgroundUsingMode(image, { channel: 'RED' })) // normalized units
```

### PSF Filter

A matched filter correlates an image with the shape of the signal it looks for, which maximizes the signal-to-noise ratio of that shape against white noise. Guiding software applies one to find guide stars in short, noisy exposures: a star-sized peak gets a strong response while a flat background and single-pixel noise do not. This is the point-spread-function filter of the KStars internal guider, a fixed 9x9 stencil (radius 4 pixels) of ring weights decreasing from the center, minus a constant that makes the sum of all weights zero.

Because the weights sum to zero, a uniform region gives 0 and the result is not a brightness image: it is positive on a star, around zero on the sky, and negative next to bright structure. The image is modified in place, each channel of an RGB image is filtered on its own, the four-pixel border keeps its original values, and a raw CFA mosaic must be converted to an intensity image first.

```ts
import { psf } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/psf'

// image: Image — a 21x21 sky of 0.2 with a Gaussian star (sigma 1.2 pixels, peak 0.6) at (10, 10).
// Applies the matched filter in place.
psf(image)

console.log(image.raw[10 * 21 + 10]) // 2.024 — the response peaks on the star; the sky goes to about 0
```

### Scalar Surface Fitting

Many imaging corrections need a smooth surface through scattered measurements: the sky background sampled between the stars, the illumination of a flat, a gradient left by light pollution, or the residual offset of a normalization. A surface `z(x, y)` is fitted to weighted samples over the pixel plane and then evaluated on the whole grid, which is the engine under the background, flat-field, and gradient models of the imaging pipeline (see [Automatic Background Extraction](#automatic-background-extraction)).

Two models are available. A polynomial in a tensor Chebyshev basis of a total degree, with coordinates normalized to `[-1, 1]` over the domain for numerical conditioning, is fitted by weighted least squares with optional iterative rejection of residual outliers (stars or cosmic rays among the samples). A thin-plate smoothing spline follows a more complex shape, with a smoothing parameter that goes from exact interpolation to a stiff surface; it never rejects by residual, because a flexible surface would read the structure it is meant to model as outliers. Rejection starts from a least-squares fit that still includes the outliers, so it needs well more samples than basis terms `(d + 1)(d + 2) / 2`: with fewer than about 2.5 times that number, an outlier near an edge or corner pulls the first fit toward itself and survives the rejection. A fit that cannot be solved returns a failure result instead of throwing. The surface is only meaningful inside the area spanned by the samples: far from them a high-degree polynomial or the affine tail of a spline extrapolates freely, and the domain should be restricted to the bounding box of a partially covered frame.

```ts
import { createScalarSurfaceEvaluator, createScalarSurfacePointEvaluator, createSurfaceColumnTable, evaluateScalarSurfaceInto, fitScalarSurface, isExactThinPlateSpline } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/surface'

// samples: SurfaceSample[] — { x, y, value, weight? } in pixels of a 64x48 plane, with one outlier.
// A degree-2 polynomial with symmetric 3-sigma rejection of the outliers.
const fit = fitScalarSurface(samples, 64, 48, { degree: 2, rejection: { mode: 'symmetric', low: 3, high: 3, iterations: 3 } })

if (fit.ok) {
	// The whole plane in row-major order.
	const plane = new Float64Array(64 * 48)
	evaluateScalarSurfaceInto(fit.model, plane)

	// The surface at a fractional position.
	console.log(createScalarSurfacePointEvaluator(fit.model).at(20.5, 13.25)) // unit of the samples

	// A row evaluator over a Chebyshev basis of 16 columns from x = 0 every 4 pixels, shared by every row.
	const rows = createScalarSurfaceEvaluator(fit.model, createSurfaceColumnTable(fit.model.degree, fit.model.domain, 16, 0, 4))
	const row = new Float64Array(16)
	rows.fillRow(10, row, 0, 1) // the surface along row y = 10
}

// A thin-plate spline that interpolates every sample exactly.
const spline = fitScalarSurface(samples, 64, 48, { model: 'thinPlateSpline', smoothing: 0 })
if (spline.ok) console.log(isExactThinPlateSpline(spline.model)) // true: the spline passes through the samples
```

### Scientific Image Loading and Export

Astronomical images come as FITS, the standard of professional astronomy, XISF, the format of PixInsight, or JPEG for previews. The readers detect the format by content and turn the first image of a file into an `Image` (see [Scientific Image Model](#scientific-image-model)), and the writers serialize an `Image` back to FITS, XISF, or JPEG.

A reader produces either normalized samples, where 0..1 is the nominal range of the source, for processing and display, or a `DigitalImage` that keeps the digital numbers after the scaling of the format, for measurements in DN such as sensor analysis and calibration masters. A floating-point source whose samples leave 0..1 (a stack or a master in ADU) is rescaled by its minimum and maximum when read as normalized, and the rescale is recorded in the metadata so that a writer can restore the scale of the source on request; otherwise the samples are written as they are. JPEG samples are scaled to 8 bits and clamped, and JPEG has no digital mode.

```ts
import { open } from 'fs/promises'
import { readImageFromBuffer, readImageFromFileHandle, readImageFromFits, readImageFromJpeg, readImageFromPath, readImageFromSource, readImageFromXisf, writeImageToFits, writeImageToFormat, writeImageToXisf } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/model/image'
import { readFits } from 'nebulosa/src/io/formats/fits/fits'
import { readXisf } from 'nebulosa/src/io/formats/xisf/xisf'
import { bufferSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'

// Detects the format by content and returns normalized samples (a 1037x706 RGB 16-bit FITS).
const image = (await readImageFromPath('data/NGC3372-16.3.fit'))!
console.log(image.metadata.width, image.metadata.height, image.metadata.channels) // 1037 706 3

// The digital numbers of a 16-bit XISF, in a 32-bit buffer.
const digital = (await readImageFromPath('data/NGC3372-16.1.xisf', { sampleScale: 'digital', raw: 32 }))!
console.log(digital.digitalRange, digital.quantizationStep) // [0, 65535] 1 — DN

// The same detection from a Buffer, a seekable Source, or an open FileHandle, with the same options.
const buffer = Buffer.from(await Bun.file('data/NGC3372-16.1.xisf').arrayBuffer())
console.log((await readImageFromBuffer(buffer))!.metadata.channels) // 1
console.log((await readImageFromSource(bufferSource(buffer), { sampleScale: 'digital' }))!.digitalRange) // [0, 65535]
await using handle = await open('data/NGC3372-8.1.fit', 'r')
console.log((await readImageFromFileHandle(handle))!.metadata.bitpix) // 8

// The image of an already parsed container: a FITS HDU, or an XISF file, read from its source.
const fitsSource = bufferSource(Buffer.from(await Bun.file('data/NGC3372-16.3.fit').arrayBuffer()))
const fits = (await readFits(fitsSource))!
console.log((await readImageFromFits(fits.hdus[0], fitsSource))!.metadata.channels) // 3
const xisfSource = bufferSource(buffer)
console.log((await readImageFromXisf((await readXisf(xisfSource))!, xisfSource))!.metadata.width) // 1037

// A JPEG decoded into normalized samples (8-bit codes divided by 255).
const decoded = readImageFromJpeg(Buffer.from(await Bun.file('data/apod4.jpg').arrayBuffer()))!
console.log(decoded.metadata.width, decoded.metadata.height, decoded.metadata.channels) // 719 507 3

// Writes FITS into a buffer large enough (or a Sink), restoring the scale of a rescaled source.
await writeImageToFits(image, Buffer.alloc(8e6), { sourceScale: true })

// Writes XISF, and a JPEG for preview.
const size = await writeImageToXisf(image, Buffer.alloc(8e6), { pixelStorage: 'Normal', compression: false })
const jpeg = writeImageToFormat(image, 'jpeg', { jpeg: { quality: 80, chrominanceSubsampling: '4:2:0' } })
```

### Scientific Image Model

Every imaging function works on an `Image`: a FITS-compatible header, the metadata that the header implies, and a flat buffer of `Float32Array` or `Float64Array` samples. The layout is row-major, with the origin at the first sample of the first row and the channels of a pixel interleaved:

```text
raw[(y · width + x) · channels + c]        stride = width · channels
```

An image has 1 (grayscale) or 3 (RGB) channels, or a single channel that is a color filter array mosaic when its CFA pattern (the 2x2 tile read row by row, such as `RGGB`) is set; the pattern describes the origin of the buffer, so a crop at an odd offset shifts it. The samples are in a normalized full-scale unit, where 0..1 is the nominal range of the source, and the results of processing may leave that range. A `DigitalImage` is the read-only counterpart for measurements: its samples keep the digital numbers of the source after the FITS `BZERO` and `BSCALE` scaling, with the representable range and the quantization step in DN for integer sources. It is not an input of the writers.

```ts
import { readImageFromPath } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/model/image'
import { cfaChannelAt, channelIndex, grayscaleFromChannel, isImage, makeImageRawTypedArray, shiftCfaPattern } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/model/types'

// A 1037x706 color image with three interleaved channels.
const image = (await readImageFromPath('data/NGC3372-16.3.fit'))!
const { width, channels } = image.metadata

// The normalized green sample of the pixel (500, 300).
console.log(image.raw[(300 * width + 500) * channels + channelIndex('GREEN')]) // within 0..1

// A DigitalImage keeps the DN of the source and is not an Image.
const digital = (await readImageFromPath('data/NGC3372-16.3.fit', { sampleScale: 'digital' }))!
console.log(isImage(digital), isImage(image)) // false true

// The color (0 red, 1 green, 2 blue) of a raw coordinate, and the pattern after moving the origin by one column.
console.log(cfaChannelAt('RGGB', 1, 0), shiftCfaPattern('RGGB', 1, 0)) // 1 GRBG

// The grayscale weights of a channel or a named luminance (BT.709 when omitted).
console.log(grayscaleFromChannel('GREEN'), grayscaleFromChannel()) // { red: 0, green: 1, blue: 0 } { red: 0.2125, green: 0.7154, blue: 0.0721 }

// A zeroed sample buffer of a precision (32 or 64 bits) for 2x1 RGB pixels, or of the type of another buffer.
console.log(makeImageRawTypedArray(32, 6)) // Float32Array(6)
```

### SCNR

Subtractive Chromatic Noise Reduction, as in PixInsight, removes a color cast of one channel, almost always green. Few astronomical objects emit a dominant green that is not accompanied by blue or red (doubly ionized oxygen is teal), so a green excess in a color-balanced astrophotograph is usually noise or a calibration residual, and the green channel can be pulled down where it exceeds a reference built from the other two channels.

The protection methods differ in that reference. The mask methods attenuate the selected channel `a` by an amount and protect it in proportion to a mask `m` built from the other two channels (their maximum, or their sum clipped to 1), `a' = a (1 − amount)(1 − m) + m a`, so a bright neighbor keeps its value. The neutral methods only touch the pixels where the selected channel exceeds the average, the maximum, or the minimum of the other two, and blend it toward that reference. The other channels and the luminance are not rebalanced, so a pixel gets darker where the cast is removed. The image is modified in place, and a mono image is returned unchanged.

```ts
import { scnr } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/scnr'

// image: Image — normalized RGB pixels [0.1, 0.2, 0.1] (green-cast sky), [0.5, 0.5, 0.5], and [0.05, 0.9, 0.05].
// Green with the full amount: the neutral average replaces the excess green by the mean of red and blue.
scnr(image, 'GREEN', 1, 'AVERAGE_NEUTRAL')

console.log(image.raw) // [0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.05, 0.05, 0.05]
```

### Screen Transfer Function

A linear astronomical image is almost black on a screen: the sky and the faint structure occupy the first few percent of the range, while stars reach the top. The screen transfer function of PixInsight stretches it for display with a shadows clip `s`, a highlights clip `h`, and the midtones transfer function of balance `m`:

```text
d  = (v − s) / (h − s)        (0 below s, 1 above h)
v' = (m − 1) d / ((2m − 1) d − m)
```

The value `d = m` is mapped to 0.5, so a midtone below 0.5 brightens (an autostretch typically uses 0.1 to 0.25), above 0.5 darkens, and 0.5 is the identity. The parameters are estimated from the data by [Display Stretch Parameter Estimation](#display-stretch-parameter-estimation). The curve is evaluated exactly for each sample in place, with no lookup table, on every channel or on one, and it destroys the linear data, so it is applied on a copy used for display.

```ts
import { stf } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/stf'

// image: Image — normalized samples [0, 0.02, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1].
// A midtone of 0.1: the sample 0.1 becomes 0.5, while 0 and 1 stay fixed.
stf(image, 0.1)
console.log(image.raw) // [0, 0.1552, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 1]

// rgb: Image — a midtone of 0.2 with shadows at 0 and highlights at 1, on the red channel only.
stf(rgb, 0.2, 0, 1, { channel: 'RED' })
```

### Sensor Characterization

A camera's datasheet values for gain, read noise, full well, dark current, and uniformity are typical, not those of the individual sensor at the gain, offset, temperature, and readout mode actually used. Characterizing the sensor from its own frames, following the method of the EMVA 1288 standard, gives the numbers that matter for choosing exposures, gain, and binning, for estimating the signal-to-noise ratio of a target, and for comparing cameras or operating points.

The characterization works on the digital frames of one operating point: a bias set at the shortest exposure, flat pairs at increasing illumination (with matching darks, and optionally the photon count and wavelength of a calibrated source), darks at several exposures, and a dark and a flat stack for the spatial noise. It combines [Photon Transfer and Read Noise](#photon-transfer-and-read-noise) (gain and read noise), [Sensor Linearity](#sensor-linearity) (linearity, saturation, dynamic range, and quantum efficiency), [Dark Current](#dark-current), [Sensor Fixed-Pattern Noise](#sensor-fixed-pattern-noise), and [Sensor Stack Defects](#sensor-stack-defects), with one result per plane (mono, or each photosite phase of an undebayered mosaic). Every frame is a single-channel `DigitalImage` in DN (see [Scientific Image Loading and Export](#scientific-image-loading-and-export)). A stage that cannot run is omitted, and problems with the data, such as too few levels, a mixed operating point, a temperature drift, or a poor fit, are reported as diagnostics rather than thrown. The analysis reads every pixel of every frame synchronously, so a full-resolution characterization is a long task better run away from a UI thread.

```ts
import { characterizeSensor } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/sensor/characterization'

// bias: SensorFrameSet; flats: SensorFlatFrameSet[] — ten levels with darks, photons, and a 550 nm wavelength;
// darks: SensorFrameSet[] — six exposures at -10 °C. All frames are DigitalImage in DN.
const result = characterizeSensor({ operatingPoint: { gain: 100, temperature: -10 }, bias, flats, darks }, { digitalClip: 65535 })
const [mono] = result.planes

console.log(mono.gain?.conversion, mono.readNoise.sensorElectrons) // e-/DN, e- RMS
console.log(mono.saturation?.capacity, mono.dynamicRange?.practical.stops) // e-, stops
console.log(mono.quantumEfficiency, mono.darkCurrent?.mean) // electrons per photon, e-/pixel/s
console.log(result.diagnostics) // what was short or suspicious in the data
```

### Sensor Fixed-Pattern Noise

Fixed-pattern noise is the part of the noise that is the same in every frame: each pixel has its own dark signal offset and its own sensitivity. EMVA 1288 calls them the dark signal non-uniformity (DSNU), the spatial standard deviation of the dark signal in electrons, and the photo response non-uniformity (PRNU), the spatial standard deviation of the response as a fraction of the mean signal. Averaging frames does not reduce them; calibration with darks and flats does, which is why they matter for choosing the calibration of a camera.

The measurement takes a dark and a bright (flat) stack of digital frames at the same exposure, averages each stack to remove the temporal noise (the residual temporal variance of the average is subtracted), and keeps the high-pass residual of the EMVA box filters, so a slow gradient of illumination or of the dark signal does not count as noise. Both figures are split into row-correlated, column-correlated, and per-pixel components. For a flat that is not perfectly uniform, a fitted plane or second-order polynomial can be removed instead, as a practical figure next to the EMVA one. A stack of few frames leaves temporal noise in the means, which no correction can remove: a spatial analysis wants tens of frames (the characterization warns below 100), and the figures only mean something for a linear, unsaturated flat.

```ts
import { measureSensorSpatial } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/sensor/spatial'

// dark, flat: SensorFrameSet — stacks of DigitalImage in DN at the same exposure; 2 e-/DN conversion gain.
// DSNU in electrons and PRNU as a fraction, with a fitted plane removed from the flat as well.
const result = measureSensorSpatial(dark, flat, 2, { spatialDetrend: 'plane' })

console.log(result.dsnu.overall, result.dsnu.rows, result.dsnu.columns) // e- RMS
console.log(result.prnu.emva.overall, result.prnu.corrected?.overall) // fraction of the mean signal
```

### Sensor Linearity

An ideal sensor converts light to digital numbers proportionally until it saturates. Linearity matters for photometry and for flat-field calibration, which assumes the response does not depend on the signal level, and the saturation point bounds the useful exposure. The linearity fit takes the dark-corrected photon transfer points (see [Photon Transfer and Read Noise](#photon-transfer-and-read-noise)) within a fraction of the saturation signal and fits `signal = slope · input + intercept`, where the input is the incident photons per pixel when every level is calibrated, otherwise the exposure times the relative intensity. The relative residuals measure the non-linearity, only within the selected range, so a response that bends below or above it is not seen. With photon counts the slope is the responsivity in DN per photon, and divided by the system gain (DN per electron) it is the quantum efficiency in electrons per photon, which depends on the calibration of the photon counts as much as on the sensor.

The output saturation is found from the strongest available evidence: the last level before the samples clip at the digital limit, the collapse of the photon-transfer variance, the fall of the response slope, or a plateau of the signal. It is the charge observed at the output saturation, not a claim about the physical full well. The dynamic range divides that capacity by the read noise in electrons (practical), or, as in EMVA 1288, by the absolute sensitivity threshold `sqrt(σ² + 1/4) + 1/2` electrons, as a ratio, in stops, and in decibels (`20 log10`).

```ts
import { measureSensorLinearity } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/sensor/linearity'
import { characterizeSensorTemporal } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/sensor/ptc'
import { computeSensorDynamicRange, detectSensorSaturation } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/sensor/saturation'

// bias: SensorFrameSet, flats: SensorFlatFrameSet[] — flat pairs with photons per pixel and a 550 nm wavelength.
const { photonTransfer, gain, readNoise } = characterizeSensorTemporal(bias, flats)

// Output saturation (DN and electrons) of a 16-bit converter, and the dynamic range.
const saturation = detectSensorSaturation(photonTransfer, gain, 65535)
if (saturation) console.log(computeSensorDynamicRange(saturation, readNoise)) // practical and EMVA: ratio, stops, decibels

// Linear fit of the response within a fraction of that saturation, its relative residuals, and the quantum efficiency.
const response = measureSensorLinearity(photonTransfer, flats, saturation, gain)
console.log(response.linearity?.rms, response.responsivity, response.quantumEfficiency) // fraction, DN/photon, e-/photon
```

### Sensor Operating-Point Series

The gain setting of a CMOS camera is a device number in arbitrary units, while the quantity that matters for calibration and exposure planning is the measured system gain, the digital numbers produced per photoelectron. The setting at which one electron gives one DN is the usual "unity gain": below it a single electron is smaller than a quantization step, and above it the full well no longer fits in the converter range. Finding it requires characterizing the same camera at several settings (see [Sensor Characterization](#sensor-characterization)) and comparing the results.

`characterizeSensorSeries` takes those profiles, checks that they describe the same camera, readout mode, geometry, and temperature, sorts them by configured gain, and interpolates the configured gain where the measured system gain crosses 1 DN/e-. The estimate is only interpolated, never extrapolated: the measured points must bracket unity, and the curve is assumed linear between the two points around the crossing. Cameras that switch to a high conversion gain mode at some setting have a step that a straight line cannot describe, so a sharp change of slope next to the bracket refuses the estimate instead of placing it wrongly. The result is as good as the measured gains and is not a substitute for characterizing the camera at the interpolated setting.

```ts
import { characterizeSensorSeries } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/sensor/series'

// profiles: SensorCharacterization[] — characterizeSensor results of one camera at several configured gain settings.
const series = characterizeSensorSeries(profiles)

console.log(series.profiles.map((p) => p.operatingPoint.gain)) // configured gains, ascending
console.log(series.unityGain?.configuredGain) // device gain setting where the system gain is 1 DN/e-, or undefined
console.log(series.diagnostics) // why the comparison or the interpolation was limited (incompatible profiles, regime change, no bracket)
```

### Sensor Stack Defects

A real sensor has pixels that do not behave like the rest of the array. Hot pixels have an elevated dark current, cold or dead pixels respond weakly to light, noisy pixels have an excess temporal variance, and some of those are unstable: a random telegraph signal makes them switch between discrete levels, so their noise is not Gaussian and calibration frames cannot remove it. Whole rows and columns can also be defective, from the readout electronics. Knowing these defects is the basis of a defect map used to reject pixels during calibration and stacking.

`measureSensorDefects` classifies the pixels of one plane from two matched stacks of digital frames, a dark stack and a flat stack at the same exposure. For every pixel it computes the stack mean and the temporal variance (DN and DN²), and flags pixels that deviate from the robust median of the plane by a number of median absolute deviations; unstable pixels are the noisy ones whose time series fails a Gaussian test, and a row or column is flagged when many of its pixels are defective or its mean response deviates from the other profiles. Because the thresholds come from the plane itself, a mostly defective sensor or a flat with a strong illumination gradient shifts the classification: the flat should be uniform, and the stacks should hold tens of frames for the temporal tests to mean anything. For defects of a single light frame without calibration stacks, see [Single-Frame Bad-Pixel Map](#single-frame-bad-pixel-map). Memory stays bounded (see [Bounded Robust Sampling](#bounded-robust-sampling)), and a CFA plane can be selected as in [Dark Current](#dark-current).

```ts
import { measureSensorDefects, SENSOR_DEFECT_HOT, SENSOR_DEFECT_UNSTABLE } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/sensor/defects'

// dark, flat: SensorFrameSet — stacks of digital frames ({ frames, exposure } in seconds) with the same exposure and geometry.
// The result is retained only when a map is requested (or caller buffers are given); otherwise it is undefined.
const defects = measureSensorDefects(dark, flat, { maps: 'defects' })

console.log(defects?.hot, defects?.cold, defects?.noisy, defects?.unstable) // pixel counts of each class
console.log(defects?.rows, defects?.columns) // defective row and column indices on the plane grid
// index: a row-major pixel index on the plane grid; the mask holds one defect bit per class
// (also SENSOR_DEFECT_COLD, SENSOR_DEFECT_NOISY, and SENSOR_DEFECT_SATURATED).
console.log((defects!.mask![index] & SENSOR_DEFECT_HOT) !== 0, (defects!.mask![index] & SENSOR_DEFECT_UNSTABLE) !== 0)
```

### Sensor Tilt Estimator

When the sensor is not perpendicular to the optical axis, the best focus changes across the field: one side of the frame is sharp while the opposite side is not. A focus run measured over regions of the frame gives a best-focus surface (see [Focus Surface Analysis](#focus-surface-analysis)), and its linear part, the plane, is the tilt. A tilted best-focus surface is not a diagnosis of a part: the same plane comes from a tilted sensor, focuser, or field lens, so the result is a measurement of the surface, which the user must interpret.

The plane is measured in focuser units across the sensor, for example by [Aberration Focus Scan](#aberration-focus-scan), which also converts it in the same step. Converting it into a physical angle needs two calibrations of the user: the effective pixel pitch (binning included) and the signed displacement of the focal plane per focuser unit, in the same length unit. The small-angle slope is `gradient * focusDisplacement / ((size - 1) * pixelSize)`; the result is the right-handed rotation around the sensor X axis (from the Y slope), around the Y axis (from minus the X slope), and their magnitude, in radians. Reversing the sign of the focuser displacement flips the angles. Given the covariance of the gradients, the first-order uncertainty of the angles is propagated too, while the scale itself is taken as exact.

```ts
import { analyzePhysicalTilt, estimatePhysicalSensorTilt } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/aberration/physical'

// Pixel pitch (binning included) and focal-plane displacement per focuser step, both in mm.
const scale = { pixelSize: 0.004, focusDisplacement: 0.001 }

// A best-focus plane (120 and 60 steps across a 4000x3000 sensor), such as the plane of a focus scan, converted into radians.
const plane = { gradientX: 120, gradientY: 60, direction: 0.4636, effect: 180 }
console.log(analyzePhysicalTilt(plane, 4000, 3000, scale)) // { x: 0.005002, y: -0.007502, magnitude: 0.009016 }

// The same with the standard uncertainties of the gradients and their covariance (steps and steps²).
console.log(estimatePhysicalSensorTilt(plane, 4000, 3000, scale, { x: 10, y: 10, covarianceXY: 20 })) // angles with their uncertainties, in radians
```

### Signal-to-Noise and Dynamic Range Estimates

The CCD equation predicts the signal-to-noise ratio of a measurement from the electrons it collects. The signal `S` carries its own shot noise, and each of the `n` pixels of the measurement aperture adds the background and dark electrons accumulated during the exposure (not rates) and the read noise squared:

```text
SNR = S / sqrt(S + n (B + D + RN²))
```

Every input is in electrons, not ADU, and the model has no flat-field or calibration noise, scintillation, or quantization noise. These figures plan an exposure; the measured counterparts of the camera are in [Photon Transfer and Read Noise](#photon-transfer-and-read-noise).

Stacking `N` equal frames ideally improves the ratio by `sqrt(N)`, which is a gain of `1.25 log10(N)` magnitudes in the limiting magnitude; this is the gain of a sky- or shot-noise limited stack, since every frame adds its own read noise. The dynamic range of a single exposure is the full well over the read noise, often given in stops (its base-2 logarithm); a camera whose converter saturates before the well is limited by the converter instead. The saturation time is the exposure that fills the well at a constant rate, and the sky-limited exposure `10 RN² / sky` is the rule of thumb for the exposure at which the accumulated sky is ten times the read variance, so its shot noise is about three times the read noise and dominates it. Times are in seconds.

```ts
import { dynamicRange, dynamicRangeInStops, saturationTime, signalToNoiseRatio, skyLimitedExposure, stackingMagnitudeGain, stackingSnrGain } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'

// A star of 20000 e- in 30 pixels with 400 e- of sky and 2 e- of dark current each, and 1.6 e- of read noise.
console.log(signalToNoiseRatio(20000, 30, 400, 2, 1.6)) // 111.565

// Ideal gain of 25 stacked frames, in SNR and in limiting magnitude.
console.log(stackingSnrGain(25), stackingMagnitudeGain(25)) // 5 1.747

// A 50000 e- full well with 1.6 e- of read noise: the ratio and the stops.
console.log(dynamicRange(50000, 1.6), dynamicRangeInStops(50000, 1.6)) // 31250 14.932

// Seconds to fill that well at 400 e-/s, and the sky-limited exposure under a sky of 0.5 e-/s per pixel.
console.log(saturationTime(50000, 400), skyLimitedExposure(1.6, 0.5)) // 125 51.2
```

### Single-Frame Bad-Pixel Map

Hot and cold pixels survive in light frames when no dark or flat calibration is available, or when the calibration frames are stale. They are then a nuisance for star detection (a hot pixel can look like a faint star), for registration, and for display. A single-frame map finds the isolated defects of one frame without calibration stacks; for the full classification from dark and flat stacks, see [Sensor Stack Defects](#sensor-stack-defects).

`detectBadPixels` flags a pixel when it exceeds, or falls below, the median of its neighbors by a number of robust noise sigmas, the noise coming from the background estimate of the frame (see [Background Estimate](#background-estimate)), and only when it is isolated: no neighbor reaches halfway from the local median to the pixel, which is what tells a one-pixel defect from the peak of a star. A color frame is judged on its luminance and a Bayer mosaic per color phase, so the different pedestals of the colors are not defects. The frame is in normalized samples (see [Scientific Image Model](#scientific-image-model)). It is a heuristic: clustered defects and columns are not isolated and are missed, an undersampled star can be mistaken for a hot pixel, and a noiseless flat image flags any pixel that differs, however slightly.

```ts
import { BAD_PIXEL_COLD, BAD_PIXEL_HOT, detectBadPixels } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/badpixel'

// image: Image — one light frame in normalized samples (mono, RGB, or a Bayer mosaic).
const map = detectBadPixels(image)

console.log(map.hot, map.cold) // number of hot and cold pixels
// index: a row-major pixel index; the mask is 0 for a clean pixel.
console.log(map.mask[index] === BAD_PIXEL_HOT, map.mask[index] === BAD_PIXEL_COLD)

// A stricter threshold for hot pixels, in robust noise sigmas.
console.log(detectBadPixels(image, { hotSigma: 8 }).hot)
```

### Star Detection

Finding the stars of a frame is the first step of plate solving, guiding, autofocus, registration, and stacking. Each detected star is a position and a few measurements: the centroid, the flux, the signal-to-noise ratio, the half-flux diameter (HFD, the diameter of the circle that holds half of the star's flux, the usual focus metric), the FWHM, and the shape of its second moments (see [Star Shape Statistics](#star-shape-statistics)). Positions are zero-based pixel coordinates of the sample centers: origin at the upper-left sample, x to the right, y down.

`detectStars` decides which stars exist with a port of the star extraction of ASTAP (its `-extract` command), so it returns the stars that ASTAP returns for the same minimum SNR, and then measures each one with an aperture suited to guiding and focusing. It works on a mono copy of the image in ADU, as ASTAP loads it. The flux and SNR are ASTAP's: the summed signal above the local sky over the star radius, and `flux / sqrt(flux + πr²σ²)` with an assumed gain of 1 e-/ADU, so the SNR ranks stars rather than predicts a calibrated noise. The list is sorted by decreasing flux and bounded by `maxStars`.

The limitations follow ASTAP. No star starts within a border of the frame (`starDetectionBorder`), so a region cropped for detection must extend that far beyond a star. A single hot pixel is not a star, but a 2x2 defect clump can be, so calibrate or fix bad pixels first (see [Single-Frame Bad-Pixel Map](#single-frame-bad-pixel-map)). A trail longer than about 14 pixels is left out. The default fixed aperture holds only the core of a large star, so it underestimates the HFD of stars above about 4 pixels; for focusing and defocused stars, pass `maximumRadius`, which lets each aperture grow to hold the whole star, at the cost of more work. The `searchRegion` option is the PHD2 uniqueness filter for a guide star, not a crop. To measure a known position without detection, `measureStarPhotometry` returns the flux, SNR, HFD, and FWHM there without recentering; for calibrated photometry with masks and uncertainties, use [Aperture Photometry](#aperture-photometry).

```ts
import { detectStars, measureStarPhotometry, STAR_SIGNAL_RADIUS, starDetectionBorder } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/stars/detector'

// image: Image — a light frame in normalized samples.
// Detects the stars, brightest first, with ASTAP's detection and an aperture measurement.
const stars = detectStars(image, { minSNR: 10, maxStars: 500 })
const star = stars[0]

console.log(star.x, star.y) // centroid, zero-based pixels
console.log(star.flux, star.snr, star.hfd, star.fwhm) // flux in normalized samples, SNR, HFD and FWHM in pixels

// Focusing: let the aperture grow up to 20 pixels to measure large or defocused stars whole.
const defocused = detectStars(image, { maximumRadius: 20 })

// Pixels along each border where no star starts.
console.log(starDetectionBorder()) // 16

// [flux, snr, hfd, fwhm] at a known centroid, with an aperture of radius 4 pixels.
const [flux, snr, hfd, fwhm] = measureStarPhotometry(image, star.x, star.y, STAR_SIGNAL_RADIUS)
```

### Star List Registration

Frames of the same field never land on exactly the same pixels: dithering, drift, flexure, and a meridian flip move, rotate, and sometimes mirror the field. Registration recovers the transform between a frame and a reference from their stars and resamples the frame onto the reference grid, which is what makes stacking and frame comparison possible. The star correspondences come from [Star Pattern Matching](#star-pattern-matching); this capability turns them into a validated frame-to-frame transform, a similarity (shift, rotation, uniform scale, optional mirror) or an affine.

The transform maps target pixels to reference pixels, `x' = m00 x + m01 y + tx`, so a frame whose stars moved by `(+3, -2)` pixels has the translation `(-3, +2)`. Resampling needs the inverse, reference to target, because every output pixel of the reference grid pulls its value from the target. Both star lists must share the pixel origin and axis directions. `registerStars` registers the stars alone, without touching pixels, and validates the match against optional limits on the residual and the transform; `registerImage` also warps the target onto the reference grid, returning a validity mask of the output pixels that the source covered. `warpImage` is the resampling alone, from an inverse transform (see [Image Warp](#image-warp)).

Every resampling interpolates and smooths the noise, so a frame registered to an intermediate frame (the reference of its own filter, say), and that frame registered to a final reference, should be chained into one transform and resampled once. `composeRegistrationTransforms` does that, combining the residuals of both registrations as independent errors.

```ts
import { composeRegistrationTransforms, registerImage, registerStars } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/registration'

// referenceStars, targetStars: DetectedStar[] — the stars of two frames of the same field (zero-based pixels).
const result = registerStars(referenceStars, targetStars)

if (result.success) {
	const { summary } = result.transform
	console.log(summary.model, summary.translationX, summary.translationY) // target-to-reference shift, pixels
	console.log(summary.rotation, summary.scaleX, summary.mirrored, summary.rmsError) // radians, scale, parity, inlier RMS in pixels
}

// reference, target: { image, stars } — registers and resamples the target onto the reference grid.
const registered = registerImage(reference, target)
if (registered.success) console.log(registered.image, registered.validityMask) // aligned image and per-pixel coverage (1 valid, 0 not)

// Chains target → intermediate and intermediate → reference into one transform, to resample once.
const chained = composeRegistrationTransforms(toIntermediate.transform, toReference.transform)
```

### Star Profile Measurement

The optical quality of a frame is read from its star profiles: focus from the half-flux diameter, tracking from elongation and orientation, and collimation or tilt from how these vary over the field. [Star Detection](#star-detection) measures every star quickly with a fixed recipe; this capability measures given positions with more care and with flags that say how far each measurement can be trusted, for focus, tracking, and optical-quality work.

`measureStarProfile` estimates the local sky from an annulus around the star (its median and a robust deviation), takes the signal above it in a circular aperture, recenters on the flux-weighted centroid, and grows the aperture while the star continues past it, including over the flat face of a defocused star. It reports the refined center, the flux and SNR (against the sky noise, in normalized samples), the HFD, a Gaussian-equivalent FWHM and the FWHM along the principal axes, the eccentricity and elongation, and the orientation `theta`, in radians in `[0, π)` from +X toward +Y, which is clockwise on the screen because y grows downward. A profile is invalid when it is saturated, clipped by the border, or too faint; a blend with a neighbor or a nearby border only lowers its quality. The shape comes from second moments, which a bright companion, the noise at the aperture edge, or truncation can bias. A position without a star does not give a meaningful profile, so measure detected positions.

Second moments understate the wings of a real star. The `moffat` model refines the profile with an elliptical Moffat fit (see [Elliptical Moffat Fitting](#elliptical-moffat-fitting)), which keeps the moment profile when the fit fails. `measureStarProfiles` measures a list of positions, and `detectStarProfiles` detects stars and measures them in one call.

```ts
import { detectStarProfiles, measureStarProfile, measureStarProfiles } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/stars/profile'

// image: Image — a frame in normalized samples. Measures the star near an approximate position (pixels).
const profile = measureStarProfile(image, { x: 41, y: 31 })

console.log(profile.valid, profile.flags, profile.quality) // usable or not, why, and a 0..1 quality
console.log(profile.x, profile.y, profile.hfd, profile.fwhm) // refined center, HFD and FWHM in pixels
console.log(profile.major, profile.minor, profile.elongation, profile.theta) // axis FWHMs in pixels, ratio, orientation in radians

// Refines the shape with an elliptical Moffat fit, for stars with extended wings.
const fitted = measureStarProfile(image, { x: 41, y: 31 }, { model: 'moffat' })

// stars: DetectedStar[] — measures a list of positions in order.
const profiles = measureStarProfiles(image, stars)

// Detects the stars and measures their profiles.
const detected = detectStarProfiles(image, { maxStars: 50 })
```

### Star Shape Statistics

A star image is an ellipse to first order, and its second moments describe it. The flux-weighted variances along x and y and their covariance form a 2x2 matrix whose eigenvalues are the variances along the major and minor axes and whose eigenvectors give the orientation. From them come the eccentricity `sqrt(1 - minor / major)` (0 for a round star, toward 1 for a line), the elongation `sqrt(major / minor)` (at least 1), and the major-axis angle `theta` in radians in `[0, π)`, measured from +X toward +Y (clockwise on the screen, since y grows downward). The orientation of a nearly round star is noise. This is how the star detector and the profile measurement read elongation (see [Star Detection](#star-detection) and [Star Profile Measurement](#star-profile-measurement)), and the result describes the moments, not a fitted profile.

Over a whole field, the shapes tell what elongated the stars. A shared axis is the signature of a tracking error, wind, or flexure; stars elongated without a common axis point to an optical effect such as astigmatism or tilt. Because an axis at `theta` and at `theta + π` is the same line, the field orientation is an axial mean taken on the doubled angle, and its coherence, from 0 to 1, says how strongly the stars share an axis. `starShapeStatistics` summarizes the median eccentricity and elongation, that axial mean, and an assessment of the field as round, aligned, mixed, or insufficient. The thresholds are heuristic and should be adjusted to the setup, and the assessment does not prove a cause; the position of the stars over the field is not part of this summary.

```ts
import { starMomentShape, starShapeStatistics } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/stars/shape'

// Moments of a Gaussian with sigma 3 along x and 1.5 along y (variances in pixels², no covariance).
const shape = starMomentShape(9, 0, 2.25)
console.log(shape.majorVariance, shape.minorVariance, shape.elongation, shape.eccentricity, shape.theta) // 9 2.25 2 0.8660 0

// stars: DetectedStar[] or StarProfile[] — anything with eccentricity, elongation and theta.
const field = starShapeStatistics(stars)
console.log(field.medianEccentricity, field.medianElongation) // typical shape of the field
console.log(field.orientation, field.coherence, field.assessment) // shared axis in radians, 0..1 agreement, and the verdict
```

### Straight Streak Detection

Long exposures collect straight luminous trails: satellites (more each year with the large constellations), aircraft, meteors, and slow moving objects. They must be found to mask them before stacking, to report them, or to identify them. Many other structures are also locally straight, such as diffraction spikes, edges, and chains of stars, so this capability finds the trails without deciding what they are; [Streak Classification](#streak-classification) interprets them.

`detectStreaks` works on one plane of the image. It subtracts a local background, keeps significant pixels and edges, sets aside compact sources such as stars, votes the remaining edges in a Hough accumulator, and refines and merges the candidate lines into measured streaks. Stars are recognized because their gradients have no common orientation, which the body of a trail has (the coherence of the structure tensor), so a star lying on a trail is not part of its flux, and two fragments split by a star are still merged. A dotted trail whose dashes are as short and round as stars is set aside with them, so it needs `minCoherence: 0` and a `minCoverage` below its duty cycle.

Coordinates are pixels of the image (origin at the center of the upper-left sample, x right, y down), and angles are axial, in radians in `[0, π)` from +X toward +Y, so a trail has no direction of motion. A streak reports its endpoints, length, width (FWHM), linearity, the fraction of its length that has support, its photometry above the background, and a confidence that is a quality score of the detection, not a probability that the object is real. It is a straight-line model: curved trails, trails fainter than the noise, very wide smears, and the edges of nebulae and halos are outside what it separates, and in a very crowded field chance alignments of stars can still be reported. A preallocated workspace avoids allocation on a series of frames, and `createStreakMask` rasterizes the streaks into a mask that the stacker can exclude (see [Streak-Aware Stacking](#streak-aware-stacking)).

```ts
import { detectStreaks } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/streak/detector'
import { createStreakMask } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/streak/mask'
import { createStreakDetectionWorkspace } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/streak/workspace'

// image: Image — a light frame in normalized samples. Finds the straight trails, strongest first.
const streaks = detectStreaks(image, { minLength: 40 })
const streak = streaks[0]

console.log(streak.start, streak.end, streak.length, streak.width) // endpoints, length and FWHM in pixels
console.log(streak.angle, streak.coverage, streak.snr, streak.confidence) // axial angle in radians, supported fraction, SNR, 0..1 detection quality

// A workspace sized for the frames of a series, reused by every call.
const workspace = createStreakDetectionWorkspace(image.metadata.width, image.metadata.height)
const next = detectStreaks(nextImage, {}, workspace)

// A mask of the trails (1 masked), widened by 2 pixels on each side.
const mask = createStreakMask(image.metadata.width, image.metadata.height, streaks, { dilation: 2 })
console.log(mask.maskedPixels, mask.maskedFraction)
```

### Streak Classification

Knowing what a trail is decides what to do with it: a satellite or an airplane is masked, a meteor may be the target, a moving object may be a discovery, a tracking failure or a defective sensor line is a problem of the setup, and a diffraction spike is part of a star. The shape of a trail alone cannot tell these apart: a long thin line can be a satellite, a meteor, or a sensor column. The classification therefore relies on context that only the caller has, such as predicted satellite tracks, meteor radiants, a tracking measurement, and earlier frames.

`classifyStreaks` interprets the streaks of [Straight Streak Detection](#straight-streak-detection) with a rule-based vote, not a trained model. Each evidence provider votes for one class with a weight, either as a primary cue (a geometric or field identification: a predicted track or a radiant matched through the WCS of the image, elongated field stars, two spikes crossing at one star, a defective line repeated across frames) or as a secondary cue (the morphology and the intensity profile). A class is named only when its primary evidence is strong enough and leads the others; otherwise the result is `unknown`, with the morphology among the alternatives, so a trail that only looks like a satellite is never named from its shape. The scores are uncalibrated weights, not probabilities, and should be validated on the images of the setup. No provider performs network or catalog access: missing context lowers the confidence instead of being looked up. Predicted tracks come from [Celestial Streak Tracks](#celestial-streak-tracks).

```ts
import { classifyStreak, classifyStreaks } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/streak/classifier'
import { MorphologyStreakEvidence, TrajectoryStreakEvidence } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/streak/evidence'

// streaks: Streak[] — from detectStreaks. image, stars: the frame and its detected stars.
// wcs: the TAN or TAN-SIP header of the frame; satelliteTracks: [{ id, start, end }] with [ra, dec] endpoints in radians;
// meteorRadiants: [{ id, rightAscension, declination }] in radians.
const classifications = classifyStreaks(streaks, { image, stars, wcs, satelliteTracks, meteorRadiants })

for (const c of classifications) {
	console.log(c.class, c.confidence) // e.g. satellite with its total weight, or unknown
	console.log(c.alternatives) // the other classes with a positive score, highest first
	console.log(c.evidence.map((e) => [e.kind, e.score, e.id])) // the cues behind the decision, with the track or radiant id
}

// One streak with a replaced provider list. The built-in defaultStreakEvidenceProviders are MorphologyStreakEvidence,
// IntensityStreakEvidence, TrajectoryStreakEvidence, MeteorRadiantStreakEvidence, FieldCoherenceStreakEvidence, OpticalStreakEvidence, and SensorStreakEvidence.
const geometric = classifyStreak(streaks[0], { wcs, satelliteTracks }, { providers: [new TrajectoryStreakEvidence(), new MorphologyStreakEvidence()] })
console.log(geometric.class) // satellite when a predicted track matches strongly; the morphology alone leaves it unknown

// The votes of one provider for a streak, given the context and the other streaks of the frame.
console.log(new MorphologyStreakEvidence().evaluate(streaks[0], { stars }, streaks)) // e.g. a secondary satellite vote for a long, narrow trail
```

### Streak-Aware Stacking

Pixel rejection during combination (see [Image Stacking](#image-stacking)) removes a satellite or meteor trail only when enough other frames outvote it, and a bright trail still leaves a faint residue in a short stack or in an average. Streak-aware stacking instead excludes the pixels of each trail explicitly, so the stack at those pixels comes from the other frames. It is opt-in, for `stackFrames` and the [Live Stacking](#live-stacking) integrator, and no detector or classifier runs while it is disabled.

For every frame the stacker takes the trail mask from, in order of priority: a mask that the frame supplies, else the streaks already detected for the frame, else its own run of [Straight Streak Detection](#straight-streak-detection); the streaks are rasterized with a configurable widening, and can be restricted to some classes of [Streak Classification](#streak-classification). The mask is applied in the source frame before registration, and the masked pixels are excluded from the combination, from the interpolation support of the resampling, from drizzle drops, and from the pairs of the photometric normalization. A frame whose masked fraction is too large can be rejected as a whole. A trail that the detector misses, or that is fainter than the noise, is not removed, and the detector can mistake chains of bright stars for trails, so tune its thresholds or supply the streaks.

```ts
import { createStreakMask } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/streak/mask'
import { stackFrames, type StackingFrame } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/stacker'

// frames: StackingFrame[] — images with their stars; each may carry its detected streaks or an authoritative streakMask.
// Masks the trails (widened by 2 pixels) and rejects frames with more than 5% of their pixels masked.
const stack = stackFrames(frames, { combinationMethod: 'average', streaks: { enabled: true, mask: { dilation: 2 }, maxMaskedFraction: 0.05 } })

console.log(stack.finalImage) // combined image without the trails
console.log(stack.diagnostics[2].streaks) // streaks found, masked pixels, and masked fraction of that frame

// frame: StackingFrame; streaks: Streak[] measured elsewhere — rasterized into an authoritative mask (1 masked) on the grid of the frame.
const masked: StackingFrame = { ...frame, streakMask: createStreakMask(frame.image.metadata.width, frame.image.metadata.height, streaks) }
```

### Sub-Exposure and Integration Planning

The depth of an astronomical image is set by its total integration time, the sum of all its sub-exposures, while the length of each sub-exposure is a separate choice that balances read noise, saturation, and the risk of losing a frame. Planning a session is converting between the two: how many frames of a given length reach a total integration. `totalIntegrationTime` is `N * t`, `subframeCount` is `T / t` as a real number (a fractional count tells how far the plan is from a whole number of frames), and `requiredSubframeCount` is its ceiling, the whole frames that reach at least the requested time, so the last frame overshoots unless the division is exact. All times are in seconds.

These are integration times, not clock times: they do not include the dead time between frames (readout, download, dithering, autofocus), the frames lost to bad guiding or clouds, or the calibration frames. The choice of the sub-exposure itself (the sky-limited exposure, the saturation time, and the stacking gain) is in [Signal-to-Noise and Dynamic Range Estimates](#signal-to-noise-and-dynamic-range-estimates), and the trailing limit in [Trailing and Smear Limits](#trailing-and-smear-limits).

```ts
import { requiredSubframeCount, subframeCount, totalIntegrationTime } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'

// 36 frames of 300 s: 3 hours of integration, in seconds.
console.log(totalIntegrationTime(36, 300)) // 10800

// Frames of 420 s for 3 hours: a fractional count, and the whole frames that reach it.
console.log(subframeCount(10800, 420), requiredSubframeCount(10800, 420)) // 25.714 26

// The ceiling overshoots: 26 frames of 420 s give 10920 s, 2 minutes more than the plan.
console.log(totalIntegrationTime(requiredSubframeCount(10800, 420), 420)) // 10920
```

### Subframe Selector

Not every frame of a night deserves to be stacked: clouds raise the background and lower the star count, poor seeing or a focus drift swells the stars, and wind or a tracking error elongates them. Grading the frames before stacking keeps the bad ones from degrading the result, and weighting the good ones lets the sharpest contribute most. The grade comes from the detected stars of each frame (see [Star Detection](#star-detection)) and a coarse sky estimate (see [Background Estimate](#background-estimate)): the star count, the median SNR, HFD, FWHM, eccentricity, and elongation (widths in pixels), the sky background, and its noise.

`measureSubframeQuality` measures one frame and gives two scores. The quality score, `sqrt(starCount) * max(medianSNR, 1) / max(medianHFD, 0.5)`, is unbounded and is what the stacker uses to weight frames and choose a reference (see [Image Stacking](#image-stacking)). The normalized score on `0..1` is the geometric mean of factors for the star count, sharpness, roundness, SNR, background, and noise (`imageQualityScore`), so a single bad factor drags it down hard; its defaults are tuned for normalized samples and a typical pixel scale, so adjust them to the setup. `selectSubframes` grades a collection against thresholds that the caller sets: nothing is rejected by default, and the selection never reorders or changes the frames. A maximum set on a metric that the stars do not provide rejects the frame instead of skipping the test. `subframeRejectionReasons` applies new thresholds to metrics measured earlier, without the pixels.

```ts
import { imageQualityScore, measureSubframeQuality, selectSubframes, subframeRejectionReasons } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/subframe.selector'

// frame: SubframeInput — { image, stars } with the detected stars of the image.
const metrics = measureSubframeQuality(frame)
console.log(metrics.starCount, metrics.medianHFD, metrics.medianSNR) // count, HFD in pixels, SNR
console.log(metrics.qualityScore, metrics.normalizedScore) // stacking weight, and 0..1 grade

// The 0..1 grade of measurements made elsewhere (HFD in pixels).
console.log(imageQualityScore({ starCount: 50, medianHFD: 5, medianSNR: 25 })) // 0.5

// frames: SubframeInput[] — keeps the frames that pass every threshold, in their original order.
const selection = selectSubframes(frames, { minStars: 20, maxMedianHFD: 4, maxBackground: 0.3 })
console.log(
	selection.accepted.length,
	selection.results.map((r) => r.reasons),
) // passing frames, and why each other one failed

// The same metrics graded again under other thresholds.
console.log(subframeRejectionReasons(selection.results[0].metrics, { maxMedianHFD: 3 }))
```

### Surface Registration

The Moon, the Sun, and the planets fill the field with extended texture (craters, granulation and active regions, cloud bands) instead of point stars, so star-based registration does not apply. Guiding on them, or aligning the frames of a lunar or solar sequence, needs to measure how the texture itself moved. Surface registration estimates a proper rigid transform, `q = R(rotation)·p + translation`, which maps a reference pixel `p` to the current pixel `q`; the rotation is in radians from +X toward +Y (clockwise on a displayed image) and the translation in pixels, with pixel centers at integers, origin at the upper left, x right, and y down.

`createSurfaceReference` builds a reference over an area of the frame: it selects one analysis plane (`selectSurfacePlane` picks the channel with the best usable contrast), normalizes it, removes the illumination gradient, and chooses high-structure patches spread over the area. `registerSurface` searches every patch in a new frame by zero-mean normalized cross-correlation around a predicted transform, rejects weak or ambiguous matches, and fits the rigid transform by robust reweighted least squares, so moving features and differential seeing become outliers; with patches too close together to constrain a rotation, it falls back to a translation. It reports the residual, a deformation spread that acts as a differential-seeing proxy, a heuristic uncertainty, and a confidence. A displacement beyond the patch search fails, and `reacquireSurface` then finds it by coarse phase correlation and registers from there. The model is rigid: a change of scale (focus, a changing apparent diameter) or a large deformation is not fitted, and repeated or featureless texture is rejected rather than matched.

The module `imaging/analysis/tracking/registration` exposes the translation primitives underneath: whole-plane phase correlation refined to subpixel by a localized DFT (Guizar-Sicairos), patch matching by ZNCC, and enhanced correlation coefficient refinement (Evangelidis and Psarakis). [Solar System Guide Tracking](#solar-system-guide-tracking) builds a guide tracker on these functions.

```ts
import { applyRigidTransform, composeRigidTransforms, createSurfaceReference, IDENTITY_RIGID_TRANSFORM, invertRigidTransform, reacquireSurface, registerSurface, rigidTransformThrough, scoreSurfacePlane, selectSurfacePlane, surfaceAnalysisPlanes } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/tracking/surface'
import { SurfaceTrackingWorkspace } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/tracking/workspace'

// first, next: Image — two RGB frames of a lunar or solar surface. The workspace owns buffers reused by every call.
const workspace = new SurfaceTrackingWorkspace()
const area = { left: 32, top: 32, right: 288, bottom: 288 } // pixels, right and bottom exclusive

// The candidate planes of the layout, and the texture score of one (usable fraction times contrast over noise).
console.log(surfaceAnalysisPlanes(first)) // ['red', 'green', 'blue']
console.log(scoreSurfacePlane(first, area, 'green', workspace).score) // dimensionless, 0 when unusable

// Builds the reference over the area, on the plane with the best texture.
const plane = selectSurfacePlane(first, area, workspace)!
const created = createSurfaceReference(first, area, plane, workspace)
if (!created.success) throw new Error(created.reason)

// Registers the next frame from a predicted transform, here no motion.
const registered = registerSurface(created.reference, next, IDENTITY_RIGID_TRANSFORM, workspace)

if (registered.success) {
	console.log(registered.transform) // { rotation: radians, translation: [dx, dy] pixels }, reference to current
	console.log(registered.rmsResidual, registered.uncertainty, registered.confidence) // pixels, pixels, 0..1
	console.log(applyRigidTransform(registered.transform, 100, 200)) // where reference pixel (100, 200) is now
} else {
	// A jump beyond the patch search: coarse phase correlation finds it again.
	const recovered = reacquireSurface(created.reference, next, IDENTITY_RIGID_TRANSFORM, workspace)
}

// Transform algebra: the rigid transform of a given rotation (radians) that moves pixel (100, 200) by (3, -2) pixels.
const step = rigidTransformThrough(0.1, 100, 200, 3, -2)
console.log(applyRigidTransform(step, 100, 200)) // [103, 198]

// Chains two motions (the inner one first) and inverts one: a transform composed with its inverse is the identity.
console.log(composeRigidTransforms(step, invertRigidTransform(step))) // { rotation: 0, translation: [≈ 0, ≈ 0] }
```

### Synthetic Bahtinov Spikes

A Bahtinov mask placed in front of a telescope turns a star into three diffraction spikes: two external spikes that cross, and a central one that passes exactly through their intersection only at best focus. Away from focus, the central spike shifts sideways by an amount proportional to the focus error, which makes the mask a precise focusing aid. Testing [Bahtinov Focus Analysis](#bahtinov-focus-analysis), or a simulator, needs images of that pattern with a known focus error.

`plotBahtinovSpikes` adds the three spikes to an existing mono or interleaved RGB buffer. The pattern is centered at the intersection of the two external spikes (pixel centers), its integrated signal is the given flux, and the error is the signed offset in pixels of the central spike from that intersection, along its normal, in the sign convention that the analysis recovers. The spikes are additive, so the caller draws the background, noise, star core, and saturation. A B-V color index weights the channels of an RGB buffer. The pattern is an idealization: each spike is a Gaussian line with tapered ends, without diffraction orders and without dependence on the mask geometry beyond the spike angles (by default the external spikes cross at 15 degrees from the central one).

```ts
import { plotBahtinovSpikes } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/stars/bahtinov'

const width = 200
const height = 200

// A mono buffer with a 0.05 pedestal; spikes crossing at (100, 100) with a flux of 40 and the central spike 1.5 pixels off.
const mono = new Float64Array(width * height).fill(0.05)
console.log(plotBahtinovSpikes(mono, width, height, 1, 100, 100, 40, 1.5)) // true when something was drawn
console.log(mono.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) - 0.05 * width * height) // 40.0, the added signal is the flux

// An interleaved RGB buffer of a star with B-V 1.8: the channels are weighted by its color.
const rgb = new Float32Array(width * height * 3)
plotBahtinovSpikes(rgb, width, height, 3, 100, 100, 40, 0, 1.8)
```

### Synthetic Defocused Collimation Patterns

A defocused star seen through a telescope with a central obstruction is a bright annulus with a dark shadow: the out-of-focus image of the illuminated pupil. When the optics are collimated, the shadow of the secondary sits at the center of the outer ring; an offset shadow, an elliptical ring, or uneven brightness around the ring reveal miscollimation, astigmatism, or tube currents. Testing [Defocused Annular Geometry Analysis](#defocused-annular-geometry-analysis) needs images of these patterns with a known geometry.

`generateSyntheticCollimationImage` renders a deterministic image of one such pattern in normalized Float32 samples. The pattern is described by its outer boundary and obstruction boundary as ellipses (center in pixels with y down, semi-axes in pixels, orientation in radians, clockwise because y grows downward, and a soft edge), the total annulus signal, the background, and Gaussian noise from a seed, with optional seeing and tracking blur, azimuthal brightness harmonics, spider vanes, a thermal plume, saturation, hot pixels, and a crop. `renderSyntheticCollimationPattern` adds one annulus to an existing buffer, for scenes with several stars. It is an idealization of a geometric annulus: no diffraction rings, chromatic effects, or optical model, and the harmonics, spider, and plume are brightness modulations, not physical simulations.

```ts
import { applySyntheticCollimationBlur, applySyntheticCollimationSaturation, generateSyntheticCollimationImage, renderSyntheticCollimationPattern, type SyntheticCollimationPattern } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/synthetic/collimation'

// An annulus with semi-axes 60x58 pixels and an obstruction of 24x23 offset by (4, -2), on 200x200 pixels.
const pattern: SyntheticCollimationPattern = {
	width: 200,
	height: 200,
	outer: { center: { x: 100, y: 100 }, semiMajor: 60, semiMinor: 58, theta: 0.3, softness: 1.2 },
	obstruction: { center: { x: 104, y: 98 }, semiMajor: 24, semiMinor: 23, theta: 0.3, softness: 1.2 },
	signal: 2000,
	background: 0.05,
	noise: 0.002,
}

// A normalized Float32 image; the same pattern and seed always give the same samples.
const image = generateSyntheticCollimationImage(pattern)
console.log(image.raw.reduce((sum, value) => sum + value - 0.05, 0)) // 2000, the sum above the background is the signal

// Seeing of 2 pixels and four spider vanes.
const blurred = generateSyntheticCollimationImage({ ...pattern, seeing: 2, spider: { vanes: 4, angle: Math.PI / 2, width: 4, attenuation: 0.8 } })

// Adds one annulus to an existing buffer; false when nothing was drawn.
const raw = new Float32Array(200 * 200)
console.log(renderSyntheticCollimationPattern(raw, { ...pattern, noise: 0, background: 0 })) // true

// After every annulus of a scene is drawn: seeing of 2 pixels and a 4-pixel tracking smear along +X, then clipping at 0.5, in place.
applySyntheticCollimationBlur(raw, 200, 200, 1, 2, { length: 4, angle: 0 })
applySyntheticCollimationSaturation(raw, 0.5)
```

### Synthetic Flats

A flat field records how the optical train and the sensor modulate a uniform illumination: vignetting that darkens the corners, dust on filters and windows that casts out-of-focus shadows ("dust donuts"), illumination gradients, row and column banding, and the fixed pixel-to-pixel response non-uniformity (PRNU) of the sensor. Testing [Flat-Frame Quality](#flat-frame-quality) and [Flat Sequence Stability](#flat-sequence-stability) needs flats with these effects at known strengths.

`generateSyntheticFlatImage` renders a deterministic digital flat: a bias pedestal plus a signal (in DN) modulated by quadratic vignetting around a possibly offset illumination center, a linear gradient, Gaussian dust shadows, sinusoidal banding, a fixed PRNU pattern, per-channel responses, and temporal Gaussian noise, followed by quantization and clipping. The noise changes with the frame index while the fixed effects never do, so a sequence shares its PRNU and dust. Every spatial effect is evaluated in unbinned sensor coordinates, so a crop or a binned frame of the same sensor shows consistent fixed patterns. `renderSyntheticFlat` fills a buffer that the caller owns. It is a model of the flat in the digital domain: the shot noise of the signal is not simulated (the noise has a constant sigma), and the dust, banding, and vignetting are descriptive shapes, not an optical simulation.

```ts
import { generateSyntheticFlatImage, renderSyntheticFlat } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/synthetic/flat'

// A 101x101 flat with 1000 DN of signal and a 30% quadratic vignetting at the corners.
const vignetted = generateSyntheticFlatImage({ width: 101, height: 101, bias: 0, signal: 1000, vignetting: 0.3 })
console.log(vignetted.raw[50 * 101 + 50], vignetted.raw[0]) // 1000 at the center and 700 at the corner

// A realistic frame: bias, PRNU of 1%, noise in DN, a dust shadow, and 16-bit clipping; frameIndex changes only the noise.
const flat = generateSyntheticFlatImage({
	width: 64,
	height: 64,
	bias: 100,
	signal: 30000,
	vignetting: 0.2,
	prnu: 0.01,
	noise: 50,
	seed: 7,
	frameIndex: 1,
	dustMotes: [{ center: { x: 32, y: 32 }, sigmaX: 6, sigmaY: 6, contrast: 0.4 }],
	lowerClip: 0,
	upperClip: 65535,
})

// Fills a caller-owned buffer of width * height * channels samples.
const buffer = renderSyntheticFlat(new Float32Array(16 * 16), { width: 16, height: 16, bias: 10, signal: 100, vignetting: 0 })
```

### Synthetic Image Noise
