The noise of an astronomical exposure has several physical sources: the Poisson shot noise of the sky background (airglow, light pollution, moonlight, zodiacal light), the dark current of the sensor, which roughly doubles every few degrees Celsius, the read noise of the electronics, the bias pedestal, fixed-pattern row and column noise, amplifier glow, and hot, warm, and dead pixels. Detectors, calibration, and stacking code need a deterministic and tunable input that has all of them.

`generateNoiseImage` models these effects in electrons for an exposure, from a seed, and adds them in place to a normalized image buffer, whose sample is the electrons over the saturation level (the smaller of the full well and the converter limit). Anything already drawn in the buffer, such as stars from [Synthetic Star Fields](#synthetic-star-fields), is kept and receives the noise on top, so draw the stars first. It returns statistics of the generated frame. It is a phenomenological model, not a calibrated sensor: the defaults are plausible values, not those of a real camera, and the sky, moon, and atmosphere terms are tuning knobs rather than photometry.

```ts
import { generateNoiseImage } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/synthetic/generator'

// raw: a 64x64 mono buffer, possibly holding drawn stars; adds the default 60 s exposure noise in place.
const raw = new Float64Array(64 * 64)
const { stats } = generateNoiseImage(raw, 64, 64, 1, { seed: 7 })
console.log(stats.saturationElectrons, stats.saturatedPixels, stats.hotPixelCount) // electrons at sample 1, and generated defects

// A colder sensor, a 120 s exposure, a moonlit sky, and an interleaved RGB frame.
const rgb = new Float64Array(64 * 64 * 3)
generateNoiseImage(rgb, 64, 64, 3, {
	seed: 7,
	exposure: { exposureTime: 120 },
	sensor: { readNoise: 1.6, temperature: -20 },
	moon: { enabled: true, illuminationFraction: 1, altitude: 0.9, angularDistance: 0.5 },
})
```

### Synthetic Optical Aberration

Real optics do not form the same star everywhere on the sensor. A tilted sensor and field curvature move the best focus across the field; a wrong backfocus to a field flattener or corrector elongates corner stars radially or tangentially; coma and astigmatism shape them, and a miscollimated or decentered optical axis moves the zero of these effects. Synthetic star fields (see [Synthetic Star Fields](#synthetic-star-fields)) use this model to give each star the aberrations of its position, for tests and simulators of focus, tilt, and backfocus analysis.

The model is phenomenological, not an optical simulation: no wavefront, diffraction, or ray tracing, and the strengths are tuning scales. Coordinates and blur sizes are in unbinned sensor pixels and focus values in focuser steps. `resolveSyntheticAberration` validates and clamps a configuration once per frame, and `evaluateSyntheticAberration` gives the aberration at one sensor position: the local best-focus offset (the tilt along its direction plus the curvature with the square of the normalized radius from the optical axis), the normalized defocus at the current focus, an additive Gaussian blur covariance from backfocus and astigmatism, and the coma strength and direction. It writes into a caller-owned object and never allocates, so a large catalog can be processed. The position must be in the same unbinned coordinates as the sensor size.

```ts
import { evaluateSyntheticAberration, resolveSyntheticAberration, type SyntheticAberrationConfig, type SyntheticStarAberration } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/synthetic/aberration'

// config: SyntheticAberrationConfig — the per-effect switches and strengths, here with a tilt of 200 steps toward +X
// and a field curvature of 100 steps at the corners (focusRange: the steps that make a normalized defocus of one).
const resolved = resolveSyntheticAberration({ ...config, tilt: 200, tiltAngle: 0, curvature: 100, focusRange: 1000 })

// The aberration of a star at the right edge of a 4000x3000 sensor, with the focuser at 5100 and the global best focus at 5000.
const out: SyntheticStarAberration = { defocus: 0, focusOffset: 0, covarianceXX: 0, covarianceXY: 0, covarianceYY: 0, coma: 0, comaTheta: 0 }
evaluateSyntheticAberration(3999, 1500, 4000, 3000, 5100, 5000, resolved, out)

console.log(out.focusOffset, out.defocus) // local best-focus offset in steps, and normalized defocus 0..1
console.log(out.covarianceXX, out.covarianceXY, out.covarianceYY) // additive blur covariance, pixels²
console.log(out.coma, out.comaTheta) // coma strength 0..1 and direction in radians
```

### Synthetic Star Fields

Star detection, focus metrics, guide trackers and plate solvers are best tested on images whose truth is known: the exact position, flux and width of every star. A synthetic star field renders a list of stars as analytic point-spread functions into a normalized image buffer and then adds the sensor noise of [Synthetic Image Noise](#synthetic-image-noise), so the output of an algorithm can be compared with the stars it was given.

Each star has a centroid and a half-flux diameter (HFD) in pixels, an SNR, and a flux that is the total integrated signal in the normalized units of the buffer; an optional B-V color index sets the weights of the RGB channels. The profile is a Gaussian or a Moffat core (whose wings are closer to a real seeing disk), optionally elongated, with a halo or coma, and the atmospheric seeing adds a blur. A global focuser position relative to the best focus widens the star, lowers its peak and adds a halo, which is what an autofocus test needs, and the field-dependent shapes of an optical model, such as the output of [Synthetic Optical Aberration](#synthetic-optical-aberration), can be spread into each star.

The stars are drawn analytically, not ray traced: the HFD is the scale of the profile, not a measurement made on the result, so a detector measures a slightly different value after sampling, seeing and noise, and a faint star can be buried by the noise.

```ts
import { colorIndexToRgbWeights, gaussianSigmaFromHfd, plotStar } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/stars/generator'
import { generateStarImage, type AstronomicalImageStar } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/synthetic/generator'

const width = 64
const height = 64

// Positions and HFD in pixels, flux as the total signal in normalized units; colorIndex is B-V (used by RGB images only).
const stars: AstronomicalImageStar[] = [
	{ x: 20, y: 30, hfd: 3, snr: 40, flux: 8 },
	{ x: 45.4, y: 12.7, hfd: 4, snr: 15, flux: 2, colorIndex: 1.2 },
]

// Renders the stars into a mono buffer with 1 pixel of seeing, then adds reproducible sensor noise.
const raw = new Float64Array(width * height)
const { stats } = generateStarImage(raw, width, height, 1, stars, 1, { seed: 5, sensor: { readNoise: 0.5 } })
console.log(stats.seed) // 5, the seed of the noise pass

// Draws one noise-free Moffat star at focuser position 7500 when the best focus is 5000: wider, fainter, with a halo.
const defocused = new Float64Array(width * height)
plotStar(defocused, width, height, 1, 32, 32, 4, 3, 30, 1, undefined, { psfModel: 'moffat', beta: 2.5, focusStep: 7500, bestFocus: 5000, maxFocusStep: 10000 })

// The conversions of the model: the RGB weights of a B-V index, and the sigma of the Gaussian of an HFD (pixels).
// effectiveGaussianSigma adds the seeing and softening terms, and focusDefocusAmount normalizes a focuser offset to 0..1.
console.log(colorIndexToRgbWeights(1.2), gaussianSigmaFromHfd(3)) // [0.447, 0.325, 0.227] 1.274
```

### Synthetic Straight Streaks

Satellites, aircraft, meteors and fast asteroids cross a long exposure as straight trails. The detector, the classifier and the streak-aware stacker (see [Straight Streak Detection](#straight-streak-detection), [Streak Classification](#streak-classification) and [Streak-Aware Stacking](#streak-aware-stacking)) are tested on images that contain a trail of known geometry and brightness.

The trail is analytic: a Gaussian transverse profile of the distance `d` from each pixel center to a finite segment, so the ends are rounded, modulated along the segment by a longitudinal profile evaluated at the closest point:

```text
signal = intensity · profile(s) · exp(−d² / (2σ²)),   σ = width / (2 √(2 ln 2))
```

`width` is the full width at half maximum in pixels, `intensity` the peak signal on the centerline in the units of the image, and `s` the normalized position from 0 at the start to 1 at the end. The longitudinal profile can be constant, a linear fade, a Gaussian flare, or a set of intervals for a flashing or interrupted trail. The endpoints are subpixel pixel coordinates (origin at the center of the first sample, x to the right, y down) and may lie outside the frame.

The trail is added to the samples already in the image, so calls accumulate, and every channel of an RGB image receives the same signal (a white trail). It adds no noise and has no wings beyond the Gaussian, no scintillation, and no color of a Bayer pixel.

```ts
import type { Image } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/model/types'
import { renderSyntheticStreak } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/synthetic/streak'

// image: Image — a zeroed mono frame of 40 × 20 pixels (or a noisy frame to receive the trail).
// Adds a horizontal trail on row 10 from x = 5 to 35, with a FWHM of 4 pixels and a peak of 0.5.
renderSyntheticStreak(image, { start: { x: 5, y: 10 }, end: { x: 35, y: 10 }, width: 4, intensity: 0.5 })
console.log(image.raw[10 * 40 + 20], image.raw[12 * 40 + 20]) // 0.5 on the centerline, 0.25 (the half maximum) 2 pixels away

// A flashing satellite: two bright intervals along the trail (positions 0 to 1), clamped at the saturation level after the addition.
renderSyntheticStreak(image, {
	start: { x: 2, y: 2 },
	end: { x: 38, y: 18 },
	width: 2,
	intensity: 1,
	profile: {
		type: 'segments',
		intervals: [
			{ start: 0, end: 0.3 },
			{ start: 0.6, end: 1, intensity: 2 },
		],
	},
	saturationLevel: 1,
})
```

### Telescope Resolution and Light Grasp

An aperture of diameter `D` limits two things: how close two stars can be and still be separated, and how faint a star can be seen. Diffraction spreads a point into an Airy disk whose first dark ring is at `1.22 λ / D`; the Rayleigh criterion places two equal stars at that separation, which for visual light (about 550 nm) is `138 / D` arcseconds with `D` in millimeters. The Dawes limit, `116 / D`, is the empirical separation at which experienced observers just split equal double stars, so it is smaller than the Rayleigh value. The collected light grows with the area, so the light grasp of two apertures is `(D₁ / D₂)²`, and the visual limiting magnitude under a dark sky is approximately `2.7 + 5 log10(D)`.

A central obstruction of diameter `d` (the secondary mirror of a reflector) removes light and contrast: the unobstructed aperture of the same area is `sqrt(D² − d²)`, and the obstruction is quoted as `100 d / D` percent of the aperture.

These are visual rules of thumb, not measurements of an instrument: they ignore the seeing (which usually limits the resolution of apertures above about 100 mm), the optical quality, the sensor, and the diffraction pattern of the obstruction and the spider vanes. The limiting magnitude is visual, not that of a long exposure (see [Signal-to-Noise and Dynamic Range Estimates](#signal-to-noise-and-dynamic-range-estimates) and [Sub-Exposure and Integration Planning](#sub-exposure-and-integration-planning)).

```ts
import { dawesLimit, effectiveApertureWithObstruction, lightGraspRatio, limitingMagnitude, obstructionRatio, rayleighLimit } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'

// A 200 mm aperture: the resolving power by each criterion (arcseconds) and the visual limiting magnitude.
console.log(dawesLimit(200), rayleighLimit(200), limitingMagnitude(200)) // 0.58 0.69 14.21

// A 200 mm reflector against an 80 mm refractor: the ratio of the collecting areas.
console.log(lightGraspRatio(200, 80)) // 6.25

// A 200 mm reflector with a 70 mm secondary: the obstruction in percent of the diameter, and the equal-area unobstructed aperture (millimeters).
console.log(obstructionRatio(200, 70), effectiveApertureWithObstruction(200, 70)) // 35 187.35
```

### Tone Mapping

Once linear data has been stretched for display (see [Arcsinh Stretch](#arcsinh-stretch)), small tonal adjustments make the result readable: brightness multiplies every sample, a linear map applies `slope · v + intercept`, contrast scales the distance of each sample from mid-gray 0.5, gamma applies the encoding `v^(1/γ)` (a value above 1 lifts the midtones, below 1 darkens them), and saturation scales the chroma of an RGB pixel around its luminance, `gray + (c − gray) · value`, where `gray` is the weighted sum of the channels with the weights of a named grayscale (BT.709 by default) or explicit weights.

The functions work on the normalized display range and clip their output to 0..1, so they are meant for stretched data, not for linear data that must keep values outside that range. They modify the image in place and return the same object: copy the image first when the original samples are still needed.

```ts
import { brightness, contrast, gamma, linear, saturation } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/processing/tone'

// image: Image — a stretched mono or RGB image with samples in 0..1; every call modifies it and returns it.
// Multiplies every sample by 1.5, clipped at 1.
brightness(image, 1.5)

// Maps v to 0.5 · v + 0.25, then doubles the distance of every sample from mid-gray 0.5.
linear(image, 0.5, 0.25)
contrast(image, 2)

// Applies v^(1/2): a sample of 0.25 becomes 0.5.
gamma(image, 2)

// Boosts the chroma of an RGB image by half around its BT.709 luminance (1 changes nothing, 0 gives gray; a mono image is unchanged).
saturation(image, 1.5)
```

### Tracking Quality

A tracking error during an exposure (a drift from polar misalignment, periodic error, a wind gust or a cable snag) moves the whole field, so every star smears along the same direction by about the same amount. Optical aberrations also elongate stars, but differently: coma and tilt produce elongations whose direction changes across the field (radially, for instance) or that appear only near the edges. `measureTrackingQuality` judges from the shapes of the stars of one frame whether the mount tracked, by looking for a coherent elongation spread over the whole field.

The trail of each star comes from its second moments: a uniform trail of length `L` convolved with a symmetric point-spread function adds `L² / 12` to the variance along the trail, so `L = sqrt(12 (σ²major − σ²minor))` pixels. It is a shape proxy, not a subpixel measurement of the displacement, and undersampling, asymmetric optics and truncated apertures bias it. The stars are detections with their moments (see [Star Detection](#star-detection)), with pixel coordinates from the upper left, +X right and +Y down, and angles from +X toward +Y. The score from 0 to 1 combines the fraction of elongated stars, the coherence of their direction, the coverage of the field and the trail length; it is a bounded heuristic, not a calibrated probability.

With a TAN WCS header or a pixel-to-sky matrix the trail is also expressed on the sky. A trail axis has no head, so the signs of its east and north components are a convention. Streaks detected in the same frame (see [Straight Streak Detection](#straight-streak-detection)) remove the stars that sit on a satellite trail.

```ts
import { measureTrackingQuality } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/analysis/tracking/quality'
import { arcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// image: Image — the frame (read only for its size); stars: DetectedStar[] — the detections with their second moments.
// Measures the field-wide elongation of the frame.
const quality = measureTrackingQuality(image, stars)

console.log(quality.score) // 0 for round or incoherent stars, up to 1 for a coherent trail across the whole field
console.log(quality.angle, quality.medianTrail) // the trail axis in radians from +X toward +Y, in [0, π), and its median length in pixels
console.log(quality.diagnostics.opticalPatternSuspected) // true when the elongation looks optical (incoherent or only at the edges)

// streaks: Streak[] — the trails detected in the frame. A plate scale of 1.5″/px with east toward −X and north toward −Y (north up, not mirrored),
// as the matrix [east/X, east/Y, north/X, north/Y] in radians per pixel.
const scale = arcsec(1.5)
const sky = measureTrackingQuality(image, stars, {}, { streaks, pixelToSky: [-scale, 0, 0, -scale] }).sky
console.log(sky?.angle, sky?.medianTrail) // the trail axis measured from east toward north in [0, π), and its median length, both in radians
```

### Trailing and Smear Limits

The image of a target moves on the sensor whenever the mount does not follow it exactly. For an untracked mount a star drifts at the sidereal rate, about 15.041 arcseconds per second of time, scaled by `cos δ`, so the trail of an exposure `t` at an image scale `s` is

```text
L = 15.041 · cos δ · t / s   pixels
```

and the longest exposure for a trail budget is its inverse; at the celestial pole an untracked star does not move and the limit is unbounded, so the inverse is not defined there. The same proportion holds for any body that moves at a rate `ω` relative to the tracking, such as a comet, an asteroid or a satellite: the smear is `ω · t / s` pixels, whatever the sign of the rate (see [Mount Tracking Rates](#mount-tracking-rates) for the sidereal, lunar and solar rates). An RMS guiding error or a periodic error of the mount, in arcseconds, converts to pixels by the image scale the same way.

All of these are straight proportions of a uniform motion in the small-angle approximation. Refraction, field rotation, polar misalignment and the non-uniform motion of a real mount are not modeled, and a budget in arcseconds is not a statement about the FWHM of the stars.

```ts
import { exposureSmearPixels, guidingErrorInPixels, maxExposureBeforeTrail, maxExposureForSmear, periodicErrorInPixels, starTrailLength } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'

const deg = Math.PI / 180

// An untracked star at a 2″/px scale: the trail of a 10 s exposure (pixels) at the equator and at declination 60° (half as long).
console.log(starTrailLength(0, 10, 2), starTrailLength(60 * deg, 10, 2)) // 75.205 37.603

// The exposure (seconds) that keeps the trail within one pixel, at the equator and at 60°.
console.log(maxExposureBeforeTrail(1, 2, 0), maxExposureBeforeTrail(1, 2, 60 * deg)) // 0.133 0.266

// A comet moving 30″ per hour (arcseconds per second) at 1.5″/px: the smear of a 300 s exposure, and the exposure for one pixel of smear.
const rate = 30 / 3600
console.log(exposureSmearPixels(rate, 300, 1.5), maxExposureForSmear(rate, 1, 1.5)) // 1.667 180.0

// A guiding RMS of 0.8″ and a periodic error of 12″ at 1.5″/px, in pixels.
console.log(guidingErrorInPixels(0.8, 1.5), periodicErrorInPixels(12, 1.5)) // 0.533 8
```

## 🔭 Observation

Evaluate observing conditions and target suitability before scheduling or controlling an observation.

### Autofocus

The best focus of a camera on a telescope is where the stars are smallest. The half-flux diameter (HFD, in pixels), the diameter of the circle that holds half of the flux of a star, is a robust measure of that size: far from focus it grows linearly with the focuser offset, and near focus it flattens at the minimum set by the seeing and the optics. Plotted against the focuser position (in steps), the HFD draws a V-curve whose actual shape is a hyperbola, and an autofocus samples it on both sides of the minimum and fits it to find the best position, which usually lies between the sampled ones.

The best focus can be taken as the intersection of two robust (Theil-Sen) lines fitted to the sides of the V, as the vertex of a parabola (biased on a wide V-curve), as the minimum of a hyperbola (the physical shape, which needs more points; see [Hyperbolic Regression](#hyperbolic-regression)), or as the midpoint between a curve and the line intersection. A fit can be rejected when its residual relative to the minimum HFD is too large.

`AutoFocus` is a state machine with no I/O: the caller owns the focuser, the camera and the HFD measurement (see [Star Detection](#star-detection)), calls `add(position, hfd)` after each frame and executes the step it returns. It first moves out by a number of steps and then samples back in through the starting position, and it keeps sampling on the side of the minimum that has too few points. A frame without a star (an HFD of 0 or NaN) is left out of the fits. A focuser with backlash must be moved the same way for every step (see [Focuser Backlash Compensation](#focuser-backlash-compensation)), and a run needs a stable seeing and a star that stays in the frame. [Autofocus Runner](#autofocus-runner) runs this loop on real devices.

```ts
import { AutoFocus, type AutoFocusStep } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/focus/autofocus'

// measureAt(position): number — the caller moves the focuser there, captures a frame and returns the HFD in pixels (0 without a star).
// Samples 7 steps of 50 on each side of the start and fits a hyperbola, rejecting a fit whose relative RMSD is above 0.1.
const autofocus = new AutoFocus({ initialOffsetSteps: 7, stepSize: 50, fittingMode: 'HYPERBOLIC', rmsdThreshold: 0.1, reversed: false, maxPosition: 10000 })

// The first add() records the starting position (its HFD is ignored); each MOVE is executed and measured until the run ends.
let position = 5100
let step: AutoFocusStep = autofocus.add(position, 0)
while (step.type === 'MOVE') {
	position = step.absolute ?? position + step.relative!
	step = autofocus.add(position, measureAt(position))
}

console.log(step.type, step.absolute) // COMPLETED with the best-focus position to move to, or FAILED with the starting position to restore
console.log(autofocus.hyperbolic?.minimum) // the fitted vertex: x in steps, y the HFD in pixels

// The best focus of the selected fitting mode, and the other fits (trendLine, parabolic) of the same samples.
console.log(autofocus.focusPoint, autofocus.trendLine, autofocus.parabolic)

// The leftmost and rightmost sampled points: x in steps, y the HFD in pixels.
console.log(autofocus.minimum, autofocus.maximum)
```

### Autofocus Runner

Running [Autofocus](#autofocus) on real devices adds requirements that the state machine does not have: nothing else may move the focuser between a move and the frame measured there, every frame must be captured at a known position, the star measurement can be slow and must not block, and a failed run should leave the focuser where it started.

`runAutoFocus` runs the loop inside an operation `autofocus` that holds the focuser for the whole run (see [Device Operations](#device-operations)), so no other client moves it, while the [Device Camera Capture](#device-camera-capture) capturer leases the camera per frame. It moves the focuser through a `FocuserMover`, the focuser commander or a service that compensates the backlash, and every position is in that mover's counter. At each position it captures one FITS frame (with the focuser position in its header) and hands only its path to the caller's measurer, which returns the HFD in pixels or `undefined` for an unusable frame; the measurement has a cooperative timeout, as in [Device Command Waiting](#device-command-waiting), and is where the star detection runs, ideally off the event loop.

The run resolves without throwing: on success the focuser stands at the best focus, rounded to whole steps; on a failure it is moved back to the start. A cancelled run commands nothing more and leaves the focuser at an unknown position, so a caller that needs the original one reads it before the run and moves back afterwards.

```ts
import { tmpdir } from 'os'
import { join } from 'path'
import { abortableDelay } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/operation.wait'
import { runAutoFocus } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/focus/autofocus.runner'

// coordinator, focuserCommander, cameraCapturer, focuser and camera as in Device Commanders and Device Camera Capture;
// measureHfd(path, signal) is the caller's star measurement, for example in a Worker.
const result = await runAutoFocus(
	coordinator,
	focuser,
	camera,
	{
		// The options of the AutoFocus state machine; the travel limit comes from the focuser.
		algorithm: { initialOffsetSteps: 7, stepSize: 50, fittingMode: 'HYPERBOLIC', rmsdThreshold: 0.1, reversed: false },
		capture: { exposureTime: 3, exposureTimeUnit: 'second', frameType: 'LIGHT', x: 0, y: 0, width: 0, height: 0, subframe: false, binX: 2, binY: 2, frameFormat: '', gain: 100, offset: 10, compressed: false },
		// Seconds before the measurement is asked to abort, and before an unfinished one is reported unresponsive.
		measureTimeout: 30,
		abortGrace: 5,
	},
	{
		focuserMover: focuserCommander,
		cameraCapturer,
		measurer: (frame, signal) => measureHfd(frame.path, signal),
		auxiliaryPath: (capture) => join(tmpdir(), `autofocus.${capture}.fit`),
		clock: { wallNow: () => Date.now(), monotonicNow: () => performance.now(), delay: abortableDelay },
	},
)

console.log(result) // { ok: true, value: { position, hfd, initialPosition, captures } }: the best focus in steps, its HFD in pixels, the start and the frames taken
```

### Challis Polar Alignment

The drift method aligns the polar axis of an equatorial mount from how a tracked star moves in declination: a polar axis that points exactly at the celestial pole keeps every star at a constant declination, while a misaligned one makes it drift in a pattern that depends on the hour angle. In the small-angle model of Challis and Taki, a polar error with components `u` and `v` makes the apparent declination of a star vary as

```text
δ(H) = δ₀ + u cos H − v sin H
```

where `H` is the west-positive hour angle, `δ₀` is an intercept of each star (its true declination plus any fixed offset of the reading), and `u`, `v` are shared by all the stars. Fitting readings of one or more stars at several hour angles gives `u` and `v`, and from them the position of the mount pole and the signed corrections along the azimuth and altitude knobs. The method needs no camera or plate solution: the readings are mount declinations, taken from the encoders or the hand controller after centering the star. All angles are radians, and the fit works in both hemispheres from the sign of the latitude.

The fit is a weighted least squares, or a robust one (Huber or Tukey) when a reading is wild, such as a mis-centered star. On a real sky the readings also contain the refraction, which changes with the hour angle; `challisRefractionCorrection` gives the apparent minus true declination of a direction, to be subtracted through the correction of each reading. The readings must cover a wide range of hour angles (a coverage under 30° is reported as weak), and the model is linear: an error above a few degrees, a star near the pole, a wrong latitude or a mount flexure that changes the declination with the hour angle are not represented.

```ts
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { challisRefractionCorrection, fitChallisPolarAlignment, type ChallisObservation } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/challis'

const latitude = deg(40)

// readDeclination(hourAngle): Angle — the mount declination after centering the star again at that hour angle.
// Readings of one star near declination 20° over 120° of hour angle, with the refraction increment of each one as its correction.
const observations: ChallisObservation[] = [-60, -30, 0, 30, 60].map((h) => ({
	star: 'alpha',
	hourAngle: deg(h),
	mountDeclination: readDeclination(deg(h)),
	correction: challisRefractionCorrection(deg(h), deg(20), latitude),
}))

// Fits u and v with a Huber loss and converts them to the mount pole.
const fit = fitChallisPolarAlignment(observations, latitude, { robust: 'huber' })

console.log(fit.u, fit.v, fit.totalError) // the Taki components and the distance of the mount pole from the celestial pole, in radians
console.log(fit.azimuthError, fit.altitudeError) // signed corrections along the positive azimuth and altitude knob directions (radians; undefined when singular)
console.log(fit.warnings) // weak hour-angle coverage, ill-conditioned fit, or an error outside the small-angle model
```

### DARV Exposure Planning

DARV (Drift Alignment by Robert Vice) measures polar misalignment from a single long exposure: during the first half the mount moves in right ascension at a guide rate, and during the second half it moves back. A perfectly aligned mount retraces the same line; a polar error makes the stars drift in declination, so the return trail separates from the outbound one and every star draws a narrow V whose opening shows the size and the sign of the error. A star near the meridian is sensitive to the azimuth error and one far to the east or west to the altitude error.

The exposure has to satisfy two conditions: the RA trail must be long enough to measure, and the declination drift caused by the smallest error worth correcting must separate the two legs by a visible number of pixels. The drift of a fixed star, divided by the sidereal rate, is a geometry factor times each polar error: for the azimuth it is proportional to `cos φ cos H` (largest on the meridian, zero six hours from it) and for the altitude to `sin H`, the other way around, with `φ` the latitude and `H` the west-positive hour angle. `estimateDarvExposure` combines the image scale, the guide rate (with the `cos δ` of the RA motion), the geometry and a preset of trail length, separation and target error into a recommended leg time and exposure; built-in presets cover the coarse, medium and fine stages of an alignment.

Choose the star by its hour angle for the knob being set: in the wrong part of the sky, or very close to the pole, the drift is too small to plan for and the estimate is refused rather than made longer. The factors are valid for small errors, short exposures, no DEC guiding and no refraction (the altitude error refers to the geometric pole). The drift of a measured frame is in [DARV Image Analysis](#darv-image-analysis), and its inversion into a polar error in [DARV Polar Error Estimation](#darv-polar-error-estimation).

```ts
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { darvGeometryFactors, estimateDarvExposure, MEDIUM_DARV_EXPOSURE_PRESET } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/darv'

// The [azimuth, altitude] factors at latitude 40° for a star on the meridian: only the azimuth error makes it drift.
console.log(darvGeometryFactors(deg(40), 0)) // [ -0.766, 0 ]

// The exposure to set the azimuth with the medium preset: a 3.76 µm camera on a 400 mm telescope, a star on the meridian at declination 0°.
const estimate = estimateDarvExposure({ focalLength: 400, pixelSize: 3.76, declination: 0, hourAngle: 0, latitude: deg(40), mode: 'azimuth', preset: MEDIUM_DARV_EXPOSURE_PRESET })

console.log(estimate.imageScale, estimate.driftDec) // 1.939″/px, and the expected drift of the target error in arcseconds per second
console.log(estimate.recommendedLegTime, estimate.recommendedExposure) // 173.557 347.114 (seconds: one leg, and both legs)
```

### DARV Image Analysis

Reading the V of a [DARV Exposure Planning](#darv-exposure-planning) frame by eye gives the sign and a rough size of the error; measuring it gives a number. `analyzeDarvImage` finds the two legs of each star (the outbound and the return trails, with the detector of [Straight Streak Detection](#straight-streak-detection) or precomputed streaks), pairs them, measures how far the return leg lies from the outbound one across the trail, and turns that separation into a north drift rate in radians per second, aggregated over the stars with a median and its robust scatter. Pixel positions are zero-based centers with +X right and +Y down, times are seconds and sky offsets are east and north radians.

The measurement needs the timing of the frame, since only the time the mount moved enters the drift (stationary time before, between and after the legs is excluded), the first commanded direction, and the exposure-start position of the stars, which tells the two close outer ends of a trail apart when the legs are equally long. A locally linear pixel-to-sky transform (a matrix, the current guiding calibration, or the WCS of the frame) gives the drift its sign and its angular scale; without one the frame only gives an unsigned magnitude in pixels per second, which is not a measurement of the polar error. With the latitude and hour angle of the star, the drift is also converted into one polar-error component (see [DARV Polar Error Estimation](#darv-polar-error-estimation)).

A result without a signed drift (partial or inconclusive) must never be read as a zero error. Trails that touch the border are excluded from the aggregate, a trail whose legs cannot be resolved only gives an upper limit, and the confidence is a quality score, not a probability.

```ts
import { arcsec, deg, toArcmin } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { analyzeDarvImage } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/darv.analysis'
import { DarvMatrixTransform } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/darv.transform'

// image: Image — the DARV frame; starts: Point[] — the positions of the stars at the start of the exposure, in pixels.
// A 200 s exposure of two 100 s legs, the mount moving west first, at 1″/px with east toward +X and north toward +Y.
const result = analyzeDarvImage({
	image,
	exposure: 200,
	legDuration: 100,
	firstDirection: 'west',
	starts,
	transform: new DarvMatrixTransform([arcsec(1), 0, 0, arcsec(1)]),
	// Converts the drift of a star on the meridian at latitude 40° into the azimuth error.
	geometry: { latitude: deg(40), hourAngle: 0, mode: 'azimuth' },
})

console.log(result.status, result.drift) // 'ok' with the signed north drift in radians per second; otherwise the drift may be undefined
console.log(result.trails.length, result.inliers) // the paired trails, and those kept in the aggregate
if (result.component?.status === 'ok') console.log(toArcmin(result.component.error)) // the signed azimuth error, in arcminutes

// Every transform maps a pixel offset to an [east, north] sky offset in radians. DarvCalibrationTransform reads the
// current guiding calibration and axis scales, and DarvWcsTransform the WCS of the frame (new DarvWcsTransform(() => header, reference)).
console.log(new DarvMatrixTransform([arcsec(1), 0, 0, arcsec(1)]).imageOffsetToSky(10, 0)) // 10″ east, in radians
```

### DARV Polar Error Estimation

A DARV drift is the effect of the polar error; this topic inverts it. With the RA motion cancelled, the north drift of a star is the sidereal rate times the geometry factors of [DARV Exposure Planning](#darv-exposure-planning) applied to the two components of the error:

```text
drift = ω_sidereal · (f_az(φ, H) · azimuthError + f_alt(φ, H) · altitudeError)
```

with the drift in radians per second, `φ` the latitude, `H` the west-positive hour angle at the exposure midpoint, and the errors in radians in the convention of the three-point alignment (azimuth north through east; altitude the mount pole minus the target, relative to the geometric pole; see [Polar Alignment Geometry](#polar-alignment-geometry) to convert a refracted display).

A single frame gives one equation, so `estimateDarvPolarErrorComponent` isolates one knob by assuming the other error is negligible, which is the classic DARV practice: the azimuth from a star near the meridian, the altitude from one near the east or west. Where the chosen knob has almost no effect (the altitude on the meridian, the azimuth six hours away, or either at the geographic pole) a measurement would amplify the noise a hundred-fold, and the estimate is refused as degenerate. `solveDarvPolarError` solves both knobs at once from two or more drifts at well-separated hour angles by weighted least squares, optionally with a Huber reweighting that needs at least three rows to identify an inconsistent one. The two-knob fit cannot tell a bias common to all rows (such as a drift measured with DEC guiding on) from a polar error. The drift of a frame comes from [DARV Image Analysis](#darv-image-analysis).

```ts
import { arcsec, deg, hour, toArcmin } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { estimateDarvPolarErrorComponent, solveDarvPolarError, type DarvDriftObservation } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/darv.solve'

// driftAt(hourAngle): the north drift, in radians per second, measured by DARV frames of a mount whose pole is 10′ off in azimuth and −5′ in altitude.
const latitude = deg(40)
const meridian: DarvDriftObservation = { drift: driftAt(0), hourAngle: 0, latitude, uncertainty: arcsec(0.0005) }
const west: DarvDriftObservation = { drift: driftAt(hour(6)), hourAngle: hour(6), latitude }

// One knob from one frame: on the meridian only the azimuth error makes the star drift.
const component = estimateDarvPolarErrorComponent(meridian, 'azimuth')
if (component.status === 'ok') console.log(toArcmin(component.error), component.uncertainty) // 10 (arcminutes), and the propagated uncertainty in radians

// Both knobs from two frames at hour angles 0 and 6 h.
const solution = solveDarvPolarError([meridian, west])
if (solution.status === 'ok') console.log(toArcmin(solution.azimuthError), toArcmin(solution.altitudeError), solution.conditionNumber) // 10 −5 (arcminutes), and the conditioning of the geometry
```

### DARV Runner

A DARV frame is only meaningful if the mount motions happen while the shutter is open and are timed precisely: a stationary lead after the exposure starts, the outbound RA motion for the leg duration, a stop, the return motion for the same duration, a stop, and a trailing margin before the shutter closes. `runDarv` performs that sequence as one operation over the device commanders: it checks that the mount can do it (a connected, unparked equatorial mount tracking at the sidereal rate that can move west and east, abort, and offers the requested slew-rate preset, the same check as [Three-Point Polar Alignment](#three-point-polar-alignment)), applies the slew rate, starts one LIGHT exposure long enough for both legs and three margins, and drives the motions once the camera reports the exposure.

Any failure or cancellation after the exposure started aborts it, so an incomplete sequence never yields a frame, and a return motion that ended after the earliest possible end of the shutter fails the run. The result carries the written frame and the measured timing in seconds, from the monotonic clock shared with the capturer, which are the durations [DARV Image Analysis](#darv-image-analysis) takes. The runner leases nothing itself (the commander and the capturer lease the mount and the camera per command), and it changes the slew rate without restoring it: the listener reports the preset it replaced.

```ts
import { tmpdir } from 'os'
import { join } from 'path'
import { abortableDelay } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/operation.wait'
import { darvExposureTime } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/darv'
import { analyzeDarvImage } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/darv.analysis'
import { runDarv } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/darv.runner'
import { polarAlignmentMountRefusal } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/polaralignment'

// The shutter time of a 60 s leg with the default margins, in seconds.
console.log(darvExposureTime(60)) // 129

// coordinator, mountCommander, cameraCapturer, mount and camera as in Device Commanders and Device Camera Capture.
// The check the run makes first, also usable to disable a control: undefined when the mount can run the motions at GUIDE.
console.log(polarAlignmentMountRefusal(mount, 'GUIDE')) // undefined, or why the mount cannot
// Applies the GUIDE slew rate, opens the exposure, and moves the mount west for 60 s and back east for 60 s while the shutter is open.
const run = await runDarv(
	coordinator,
	mount,
	camera,
	{ direction: 'WEST', slewRate: 'GUIDE', legDuration: 60, capture: { x: 0, y: 0, width: 0, height: 0, subframe: false, binX: 1, binY: 1, frameFormat: '', gain: 100, offset: 10, compressed: false } },
	{
		mountCommander,
		cameraCapturer,
		clock: { wallNow: () => Date.now(), monotonicNow: () => performance.now(), delay: abortableDelay },
		framePath: join(tmpdir(), 'darv.fit'),
		listener: (event) => console.log(event), // the replaced slew rate, then the phases of the sequence
	},
)

if (run.ok) {
	// image: Image — the frame read from the frame path; transform: the pixel-to-sky transform of DARV Image Analysis.
	const { timing } = run.value
	const analysis = analyzeDarvImage({ image, exposure: timing.exposure, legDuration: 60, leadingDuration: timing.leading, outboundDuration: timing.outbound, turnaroundDuration: timing.turnaround, returnDuration: timing.inbound, trailingDuration: timing.trailing, firstDirection: 'west', transform })
	console.log(analysis.drift) // the signed north drift, in radians per second
}
```

### Direction Alignment

The axes of a mount are referenced to its own base, which is never exactly level or turned to north. Before the encoder angles can be converted into directions on the sky, the rotation from the mount base frame to the world frame (the local east, north, up frame of the observer) must be known. Pointing at a few known stars gives pairs of directions, the one the mount reports and the one the star really has, and the rotation that best maps one set onto the other is the classic attitude problem of star trackers (Wahba's problem).

`fitDirectionAlignment` starts from a TRIAD rotation built from the best-conditioned pair of samples, which is exact for two noise-free, non-collinear pairs, and refines it by least squares of the angular residuals over all samples, optionally with a Huber or Tukey loss that downweights a misidentified star. Directions are 3-vectors whose length is ignored, the rotation is a row-major matrix, and residuals are radians. `fitMountAlignment` builds the samples from encoder positions and the observed azimuth (north through east) and altitude of each star, already converted to the place of the observer and refracted, and `applyDirectionAlignment` puts the fitted rotation into a mount geometry (see [Mount Kinematics](#mount-kinematics)).

Only the orientation of the base is fitted: the errors of the mount axes themselves (non-perpendicularity, index offsets, flexure) belong to [Pointing Model Fit and Correction](#pointing-model-fit-and-correction). At least two samples with positive weight that are neither collinear nor antipodal are needed, a direction pair does not distinguish a rotation from a mirrored frame, and a robust fit of very few samples can reject a good one.

```ts
import { applyDirectionAlignment, fitDirectionAlignment, fitMountAlignment, predictMountDirection, predictWorldDirection } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/mount/alignment'

// samples: DirectionAlignmentSample[] — pairs of the same direction in the mount base frame (mount) and in the east-north-up frame (world).
// Fits the base rotation, with a Tukey loss that gives a misidentified star a zero weight.
const fit = fitDirectionAlignment(samples, { robust: 'tukey' })
console.log(fit.rms, fit.maximumResidual, fit.rejectedCount) // weighted RMS and largest angular residual in radians, and the samples rejected

// Rotates a mount-frame direction into the world frame, as a unit vector, and a world direction back into the mount frame.
console.log(predictWorldDirection(fit, [1, 1, 0]))
console.log(predictMountDirection(fit, [0, 0, 1])) // the local zenith in the mount base frame

// geometry: TwoAxisMountGeometry (see Mount Kinematics); observations: MountAlignmentObservation[] — encoder positions with the observed azimuth and altitude.
// Fits the base orientation from the encoders and puts it into the geometry (its translation in meters is kept).
const aligned = applyDirectionAlignment(geometry, fitMountAlignment(geometry, observations))
```

### Dither Guide Pulses

A dither does not need a running guide loop: when imaging unguided, or between guiding sessions, the mount can be moved by the small offset of [Dither Offsets](#dither-offsets) with one timed guide pulse per axis, whose duration is the offset divided by the rate at which a pulse moves the image. Two sources give that rate. A solved guiding calibration (see [Guiding Calibration](#guiding-calibration)) gives it in pixels per millisecond along each axis, for an offset in pixels of the camera that was calibrated; it must still apply, so the same guide output and optical train, and flipped after a meridian flip, since it carries no device or pier side to prove it. Without a calibration, the guide rate of the mount, as a fraction of the sidereal rate, gives it for an offset in radians on the sky; the RA rate is scaled by `cos δ` at the dither declination, and the caller states which physical direction a positive offset moves, because a guide rate has only magnitudes.

A plan is refused when a rate is unusable or a pulse would exceed the maximum duration. The dispatch hands the pulses to an INDI guide output (see [INDI Guide Output](#indi-guide-output)) back to back; success only means the commands reached the transport, since there is no completion signal, and an abort stops the dispatch but not a pulse the hardware already accepted. The conversion is a vector approximation: backlash, acceleration and a guide rate that differs from the one configured in the mount are not modeled.

```ts
import { arcsec, deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { dispatchDitherPulses } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/dither.executor'
import { ditherPulsePlanFromCalibration, ditherPulsePlanFromGuideRate } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/dither.pulse'

// calibration: GuidingCalibrationResult — a solved calibration of the same guide output and optical train.
// Converts a dither of 3 px in RA and −2 px in DEC into one pulse per axis, refusing any pulse above 2000 ms.
const plan = ditherPulsePlanFromCalibration({ rightAscension: 3, declination: -2 }, calibration, 2000)

// From the guide rate (0.5× sidereal) at declination 60°: an offset in radians and the physical direction of a positive offset.
const context = { guideRate: { rightAscension: 0.5, declination: 0.5 }, declination: deg(60), rightAscensionDirection: 'WEST', declinationDirection: 'NORTH' } as const
console.log(ditherPulsePlanFromGuideRate({ rightAscension: arcsec(10), declination: -arcsec(10) }, context, 5000)) // 2659 ms WEST (longer by 1 / cos 60°) and 1330 ms SOUTH

// guideOutputManager and guideOutput: the connected INDI guide output. Returns whether the pulses were handed to the transport.
if (plan) dispatchDitherPulses(guideOutputManager, guideOutput, plan)
```

### Dither Offsets

The sensor of a camera has a fixed pattern: hot and warm pixels, bad columns and a residual of the calibration that stays at the same pixels in every frame. When the pointing does not change, that pattern lands on the same sky positions in every sub-exposure and survives the stack, often as "walking noise" streaks when the field drifts slowly. Dithering moves the pointing by a few pixels between frames, so the pattern falls on different sky pixels and is rejected when the frames are registered and combined (see [Image Stacking](#image-stacking)).

`DitherGenerator` produces the sequence of offsets for one pattern: the uniform random draws of PHD2, the PHD2 lattice spiral, a golden-angle disk whose `n`-th point is at the radius `amount · √n` (so the points stay evenly spread as the sequence grows), or the border cells of growing square rings. Each offset is an increment along the mount axes from the previous point, not an absolute position, in the unit of the amount (pixels for a guider, radians for a sky-plane dither). An RA-only mode holds the declination at zero, which avoids declination reversals on a mount with backlash. A seeded source makes the random pattern reproducible (see [Seeded Random Sources](#seeded-random-sources)).

The generator knows neither the mount nor the field, and the sum of the offsets drifts like a random walk or an unbounded pattern, so the caller re-centers when that matters. Turning offsets into guide pulses is in [Dither Guide Pulses](#dither-guide-pulses).

```ts
import { DitherGenerator } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/dither'
import { GoldenDitherGenerator } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/dither.golden'

// A golden-angle disk pattern; the random source (a function returning [0, 1), Math.random by default) is used by the random pattern only.
const dither = new DitherGenerator({ mode: 'golden' })
console.log(dither.mode) // 'golden'

// The next increment from the previous point, in the unit of the amount (here 5 guide-camera pixels).
console.log(dither.next(5)) // { rightAscension, declination }: a step, not an absolute position

// RA-only: the declination increment is zero.
console.log(dither.next(5, true))

// Switches to the PHD2 spiral with a fresh sequence; reset() restarts the active pattern from its origin.
dither.setMode('spiral')
dither.reset()

// Each pattern is also a class with the same next() and reset(): RandomDitherGenerator (built with a random source),
// SpiralDitherGenerator, GoldenDitherGenerator and GridDitherGenerator.
console.log(new GoldenDitherGenerator().next(5))
```

### Dome Slit Geometry

A telescope in a dome rarely has its optical axis through the center of the dome: a German equatorial mount carries the tube beside its axes, and the pier may be off center. Opening the slit at the azimuth the telescope points to is then wrong, especially at high altitude, where the offset of the tube can put the optics behind the dome wall. The slit must be placed where the optical axis, starting from its real origin, pierces the dome.

`solveDomeSlit` intersects the optical ray with a spherical dome and returns the azimuth and altitude of that point as seen from the dome center, plus the azimuth to command, mapped by the zero offset and the counting direction of the controller. Points and distances are meters in a shared east, north, up frame and azimuths are radians north through east. `solveDomeSlitFromMount` takes the ray from the forward kinematics of the mount (see [Mount Kinematics](#mount-kinematics)), so the pivot offsets and the optical origin are accounted for. To follow the telescope, the dome azimuth error is the shortest signed correction across north, and a move is needed only when it exceeds a tolerance.

The dome is a sphere and the slit a point: the width of the slit, the shadow of the dome on the aperture and a dome that is not spherical are not modeled.

```ts
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { domeAzimuthError, isDomeMoveRequired, solveDomeSlit, solveDomeSlitFromMount } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/dome/slit'
import { createCanonicalEquatorialGeometry } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/mount/kinematics'

// A dome of 2 m radius centered at the origin, and a ray from its center looking east at an altitude of 30°.
const dome = { center: [0, 0, 0], radius: 2 } as const
const slit = solveDomeSlit({ origin: [0, 0, 0], direction: [Math.cos(deg(30)), 0, Math.sin(deg(30))] }, dome)!
console.log(slit.azimuth, slit.altitude, slit.commandAzimuth) // 90°, 30° and 90°, in radians

// An equatorial head with its pivots 0.4 m above the dome center and the optics 0.25 m off the axis, at the given encoder angles.
const geometry = createCanonicalEquatorialGeometry({ primaryPivot: [0, 0, 0.4], secondaryPivot: [0, 0, 0.4], opticalOrigin: [0.25, 0, 0.4] })
const target = solveDomeSlitFromMount(geometry, { primary: deg(30), secondary: deg(60) }, dome)!
console.log(target.azimuth, target.altitude) // 120° and 65.74°, in radians

// Following: the shortest correction from 350° to 10° is +20°, and a move is needed only beyond the 2° tolerance.
console.log(domeAzimuthError(deg(350), deg(10)), isDomeMoveRequired(deg(359), deg(0.5), deg(2))) // 20° in radians, and false
```

### Focuser Backlash Calibration

Backlash is the dead travel of a drive train when it reverses: the step counter changes but the drawtube does not move until the play of the gears is taken up. To measure it, the focuser is first preloaded in one direction, then reversed and probed in small steps while a metric that depends on the real position is measured, such as the HFD well away from focus, a star position or a laser spot. The metric stays on a plateau while the play is taken up and then changes linearly, so a hinge model fitted to the probe points gives the backlash as its breakpoint `b`:

```text
metric(travel) = intercept + slope · max(0, travel − b)
```

`BacklashCalibration` repeats the probe a few times in each direction, aggregates each direction by the median of its valid runs, refuses a result whose runs disagree, and recommends an overshoot of the larger backlash times a safety factor. It is a synchronous command and event state machine with no device I/O: the caller executes each move or measurement and answers with its result. All positions and distances are focuser steps; the metric is in the caller's units, and its slope per step must be large enough to be seen. `backlashCompensationFromCalibration` turns the result into the settings of [Focuser Backlash Compensation](#focuser-backlash-compensation).

The model has a single breakpoint and a linear response, so a metric that is curved, noisy or near its minimum (the vertex of a V-curve) will not fit, and the backlash is that of the conditions and load of the run.

```ts
import { BacklashCalibration, backlashCompensationFromCalibration, type BacklashCalibrationCommand } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/focus/backlash.calibration'

// focuser: position() returns the counter and move(relative) moves by steps and returns the new counter; measure() returns the metric.
// Probes in steps of 10 up to 200 after a preload of 60, requiring a slope of at least 0.005 metric units per step.
const calibration = new BacklashCalibration({ probeStep: 10, preloadDistance: 60, maximumProbeDistance: 200, minimumSlope: 0.005 })

// Executes each command and answers it with its event until a terminal command.
let command: BacklashCalibrationCommand = calibration.start(focuser.position())
while (command.type === 'move' || command.type === 'measure') {
	if (command.type === 'move') command = calibration.next({ type: 'moved', position: focuser.move(command.relative) })
	else command = calibration.next({ type: 'measured', position: focuser.position(), value: measure() })
	// The phase and the direction of the active run, for a progress display.
	console.log(calibration.state, calibration.currentDirection)
}

// The completed result, also kept by the state machine (undefined before a successful completion).
console.log(calibration.result)

if (command.type === 'completed') {
	console.log(command.result.increasing.steps, command.result.decreasing.steps, command.result.quality) // the backlash of each direction in steps, and the quality
	// Compensation settings that end every move with an OUT approach.
	console.log(backlashCompensationFromCalibration(command.result, { mode: 'OVERSHOOT', finalApproachDirection: 'OUT' }))
}
```

### Focuser Backlash Compensation

A focuser with backlash does not reach the requested position when it reverses: the first steps of the reversal only take up the play. Two strategies absorb it. Overshoot moves past the target by the backlash and comes back, so the last leg of every compensated move approaches from the same side when only one direction has a backlash; this is what autofocus wants, since every sample is then reached the same way. Absolute compensation adds the backlash to the commanded position whenever the direction reverses and keeps the accumulated difference as an offset for every later target, so the driver counter drifts from the requested positions while the optical position stays consistent; the first move has no known direction and is not compensated.

`BacklashCompensator` returns the absolute positions to command, in order, in focuser steps, where OUT is an increasing position. It is stateful: it remembers the direction of the last move it computed, even if the caller does not execute it, and its state can be saved and restored to undo a refused plan or cleared when the counter can no longer be trusted. The positions are never clamped: the caller checks each one against the travel of the focuser before commanding any of them. The backlash itself is measured by [Focuser Backlash Calibration](#focuser-backlash-calibration).

```ts
import { BacklashCompensator } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/focus/backlash'

// OVERSHOOT with 40 steps of backlash IN and 25 OUT: every move goes past the target and returns.
const overshoot = new BacklashCompensator({ mode: 'OVERSHOOT', backlashIn: 40, backlashOut: 25 })
console.log(overshoot.compute(5200, 5000)) // [5225, 5200] (an OUT move from 5000 to 5200)
console.log(overshoot.compute(5100, 5200)) // [5060, 5100] (an IN move back to 5100)

// ABSOLUTE: one move per target, compensated on reversals; the offset carries over (5025 is commanded as 4985).
const absolute = new BacklashCompensator({ mode: 'ABSOLUTE', backlashIn: 40, backlashOut: 25 })
console.log(absolute.compute(5200, 5000), absolute.compute(5000, 5200), absolute.compute(5025, 5000)) // [5200] [4960] [4985]

// Saves the memory before a plan and restores it when the caller refuses the plan.
const saved = absolute.state
absolute.compute(9000, 4985)
absolute.reset(saved)
```

### Guide Pulse Loop

Autoguiding keeps a star at a fixed position on the guide camera by correcting the mount after every frame. The displacement of the star from its target, in pixels, is converted into errors along the RA and DEC axes by the calibration matrix (see [Guiding Calibration](#guiding-calibration)), and each axis error becomes a timed guide pulse. A proportional correction would chase the seeing, so the guider uses the hysteresis controller of PHD2:

```text
correction = aggressiveness · ((1 − hysteresis) · error + hysteresis · lastMove)
```

which is zero for an error below the minimum move of the axis, and the pulse is `|correction|` times the milliseconds per unit, scaled by the frame cadence and clamped to the pulse limits of the axis. Declination has a direction policy (both, north only, south only, or off) and protection against backlash: a reversal is only issued once the error is large and persistent, and an optional adaptive compensation adds the estimated DEC backlash to the first pulse of each accepted reversal, an estimate that tends to stay under the real backlash rather than past it.

`Guider` is a pure state machine with no device I/O: it takes one tracker result per frame (see [Guide Star Tracking](#guide-star-tracking)) and returns the pulses, and the caller sends them (see [INDI Guide Output](#indi-guide-output)). It averages the first good frames into the lock reference, then guides, and reports the star lost after consecutive bad frames (no measurement, low quality or a jump). A dither or a lock shift moves the target, and the calibration and positive directions can be replaced without losing the lock after a meridian flip. When frames arrive much faster than the mount should be corrected, as with a planetary or Lunar camera whose measured motion is mostly seeing (see [Solar System Guide Tracking](#solar-system-guide-tracking)), corrections can be gated to an interval on the capture clock and computed from a robust combination of the buffered errors. The controller has no model of the mount, so its gains and calibration must match the setup.

```ts
import { Guider, hysteresisCorrection } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/guider'
import { trackingResultFromStars } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/tracker'

// The controller equation alone: an error of 1, a last move of 0.5, a hysteresis of 0.1, an aggressiveness of 0.7 and a minimum move of 0.2.
// The other pure steps are applyCalibration (image to axis error), invertCalibration, applyDeadband and aggregateGuideErrors.
console.log(hysteresisCorrection(1, 0.5, 0.1, 0.7, 0.2)) // 0.665, in axis units

// An identity calibration (image X is RA, Y is DEC), a lock averaged over 3 frames, a gain of 1 without hysteresis, 500 ms per pixel.
const guider = new Guider({ lockAveragingFrames: 3, hysteresisRA: 0, hysteresisDEC: 0, aggressivenessRA: 1, aggressivenessDEC: 1, msPerRAUnit: 500, msPerDECUnit: 500 })

// One frame of a 640 × 480 guide camera with the star at (x, y) and a cadence of 1000 ms.
const frame = (x: number, y: number, frameId: number) => ({ tracking: trackingResultFromStars([{ x, y, snr: 40, flux: 1000, hfd: 3 }]), width: 640, height: 480, frameId, cadence: 1000 })

// The first three frames only acquire the lock, at their average position.
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) guider.processFrame(frame(320, 240, i))

// The star moved +1 px in X and −0.5 px in Y; the caller sends the returned pulses.
const command = guider.processFrame(frame(321, 239.5, 3))
console.log(command.state, command.ra, command.dec) // guiding, { direction: 'WEST', duration: 500 } and { direction: 'SOUTH', duration: 250 }
console.log(guider.currentState.referenceX, guider.lastDiagnostics()?.frameId) // the lock at 320 px, and the diagnostics of frame 3

// The pulses that cancel a 2 px error in one move, at full gain and without controller memory, as a recovery move.
console.log(guider.directPulse(2, 0).ra) // { direction: 'WEST', duration: 1000 }

// A dither shifts the target by 3 px in X and starts a settle; setDithering(false) ends the settle and keeps the offset,
// stopDither() returns the target to the lock, and setTargetOffset() shifts it without a settle (a lock shift).
guider.startDither(3, 0)
guider.setDithering(false)
guider.stopDither()
guider.setTargetOffset(1, 1)

// A new exposure time (ms), a DEC policy, and a calibration flipped after a meridian flip, keeping the lock.
guider.setNominalCadence(2000)
guider.setDecMode('north-only')
guider.setCalibration([-1, 0, 0, -1])

// resetControllers() forgets the controller memory and keeps the lock; reset() starts over.
guider.resetControllers()
guider.reset()
```

### Guide Star Tracking

The guider needs, in every frame, the position of the guide star with subpixel precision and the certainty that it is the same star as before. Not every detection is a good guide star: a saturated star has a flat top and a biased centroid, a star near the border can leave the frame, a close double confuses the centroid, and a hot pixel or noise peak can look like a faint star. Averaging the shift of several stars, as the multi-star guiding of PHD2 does, also reduces the effect of the seeing, which moves each star differently.

`StarTracker` runs a detector supplied by the caller (usually [Star Detection](#star-detection) with the sampled peaks of `enrichGuideStars`), filters the detections by SNR, size, shape, saturation and distance to the border, and acquires the best scored isolated star, which is not necessarily the brightest. In the following frames it measures the translation of the field as the robust weighted mean of the shifts of the matched reference stars, added to the acquired position, or follows the single nearest star. Pixel coordinates are from the upper left, +X right and +Y down. The reference only advances when the consumer accepts a frame with `commit()`, so a frame the guider rejects leaves the last good reference. A detector that runs asynchronously, for example in a worker, goes in the `prepare` stage before the synchronous `track`.

The tracker follows a field translation only: rotation, a change of scale and a guide star that changes between frames are not modeled, so check the quality and the star telemetry of each result.

```ts
import { detectStars } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/stars/detector'
import { enrichGuideStars, StarTracker, starTrackingOf } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/tracker.star'

// The caller's detector: the toolkit detector plus the sampled peaks used by the saturation filter.
const tracker = new StarTracker({ detector: (image) => enrichGuideStars(detectStars(image), image) })

// The same stages are exported as pure functions: filterGuideStars, selectGuideStar and estimateTranslation.
// image, nextImage: Image — consecutive 160 × 120 guide frames.
// The first frame acquires the best scored star and measures its position in pixels.
const first = tracker.track({ image, width: 160, height: 120, timestamp: 0, frameId: 0 }, { phase: 'looping', allowAcquisition: true, preserveIdentity: false })
console.log(first.measurement, first.selectionPrimary) // { x, y, confidence }, and the acquired guide star

// A manual selection from that result: the detection nearest a clicked pixel (without a position, the best star of the frame).
console.log(tracker.select(first, [80, 60])) // [x, y] in pixels, or undefined without detections

// The consumer accepts the frame; the next one is detected first by prepare() (which may await a worker),
// then measures the translation of the matched stars from the committed reference.
tracker.commit()
const prepared = await tracker.prepare({ image: nextImage, width: 160, height: 120, timestamp: 1000, frameId: 1 })
const second = tracker.track(prepared, { phase: 'guiding', allowAcquisition: true, preserveIdentity: true })
console.log(second.measurement, second.matches) // the acquired position plus the field translation, and the number of matched stars

// The stellar details of a generic result, as the guide client sees it, and the latest result.
console.log(starTrackingOf(tracker.lastResult)?.selectionPrimary)

// Forgets the guide star and the reference, for a new target.
tracker.reset()
```

### Guider Client

A guiding session couples many parts: camera exposures, decoding of each image, star tracking, calibration, the guide controller, dithering with a settle, and the dispatch of every pulse. PHD2 does this as a separate application; `GuiderClient` does it in-process on local INDI devices, with the method names and the behavior of [PHD2 Client](#phd2-client) (app states, lock position, dithering, lock shift, the calibration flip after a meridian flip, and the [Guiding Assistant](#guiding-assistant)). It drives the tracker (see [Guide Star Tracking](#guide-star-tracking)), the calibrator (see [Guiding Calibration](#guiding-calibration)) and the [Guide Pulse Loop](#guide-pulse-loop), and emits native guiding events to registered handlers; [PHD2 Server](#phd2-server) exposes a client to PHD2 clients over TCP. Distances are pixels and pulse durations milliseconds.

The caller supplies the image decoder and the tracker, so decoding and star detection can run in a worker, and the tracking pass uses the state read after those awaits, so a lock or state change made meanwhile is honored. A frame that arrives while another is being processed is dropped.

The client keeps the source of its calibration apart from the calibration it guides with: a calibration record solved earlier can be restored and transformed for the current declination and side of the pier, and reassessed after a slew, so the next `guide()` does not need to calibrate. A dither moves the lock by the next offset of the dither pattern (see [Dither Offsets](#dither-offsets)), reflected to stay inside the frame, and settles; with fast recenter the star is moved to the new lock by direct pulses rather than through the controller. Every pulse, from guiding, calibration, the assistant or a manual request, goes through one dispatcher that refuses it while paused, and an exclusive pulse admission lets an operation that arbitrates the guide output bound the length of every pulse.

```ts
import type { BlobEncoding } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/types'
import { readImageFromBuffer, readImageFromSource } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/model/image'
import { detectStars } from 'nebulosa/src/imaging/stars/detector'
import { base64Source, bufferSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { GuiderClient, type GuiderClientHandler } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/client'
import { enrichGuideStars, StarTracker } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/tracker.star'

// cameraManager, guideOutputManager, camera and guideOutput: the managers and connected devices of an INDI client (see INDI Guide Output).
// The caller decodes the BLOBs and detects the stars; both may run in a worker.
const decodeImage = (data: Buffer, encoding: BlobEncoding) => (encoding === 'base64' ? readImageFromSource(base64Source(bufferSource(data))) : readImageFromBuffer(data))
const tracker = new StarTracker({ detector: (image) => enrichGuideStars(detectStars(image), image) })
const client = new GuiderClient(cameraManager, guideOutputManager, tracker, { decodeImage })

// Observes the native guiding events (state changes, guide steps, settling, calibration) and receives the camera BLOBs.
const handler: GuiderClientHandler = { event: (_, event) => console.log(event.type) }
client.addHandler(handler)
client.attachHandler()
client.connect(camera, guideOutput, { focalLength: 400, pixelSize: 3.76 })

// The connected devices and the id of the client.
console.log(client.camera?.name, client.guideOutput?.name, client.id)

// Loops 2000 ms exposures; once frames arrive, selects a guide star (findStar is the PHD2 alias of findTarget) and guides,
// calibrating first when needed. startExposureLoop(ms) starts one exposure and keeps its time as the cadence.
client.setExposure(2000)
client.loop()
client.findStar()
client.guide()

// While guiding: dithers by up to 5 px and settles within 1.5 px for 10 s, with a 60 s timeout.
client.dither(5, false, { pixels: 1.5, time: 10, timeout: 60 })

// The lock: an exact position in pixels kept across a new star selection, and a lock shift in pixels per hour.
client.setLockPosition(320, 240, true)
client.setStickyLockPositionEnabled(true)
client.setLockShiftParams({ rate: [3, -1.5], units: 'pixels/hr', axes: 'X/Y' })
client.setLockShiftEnabled(true)

// Settings, each with its getter: getExposure, getDeclinationGuideMode, getDitherMode, getFastRecenterEnabled,
// getGuideOutputEnabled, getLockPosition, getLockShiftEnabled, getLockShiftParams and getStickyLockPositionEnabled.
client.setDeclinationGuideMode('Auto')
client.setDitherMode('spiral')
client.setFastRecenterEnabled(true)
client.setGuideOutputEnabled(true)

// State and telemetry in PHD2 terms; also state, getConnected, getSettling, getCalibrated, getCalibrationData, getSearchRegion,
// getCameraBinning, getCameraFrameSize, and the getStarImage and getTargetImage thumbnails.
console.log(client.getAppState(), client.getPixelScale(), client.getPaused()) // the PHD2 app state such as 'Guiding', arcsec per pixel, and whether paused

// Pauses the pulses (true as the second argument also stops the exposures), resumes, and sends a manual 200 ms pulse west.
client.setPaused(true, false)
client.setPaused(false)
client.guidePulse(200, 'West')

// After a meridian flip: flips the calibration in use and keeps the lock.
client.flipCalibration()

// An operation that arbitrates the guide output bounds every pulse to 1500 ms while it holds the admission.
const admission = client.admitPulses(1500)
admission?.open()
console.log(client.maxPulseDuration(), client.pulseQuiescenceWindow()) // longest pulse of the configuration (ms), and when the delivered pulses end
admission?.[Symbol.dispose]()

// Drops the guide star and returns to looping; while looping, the guiding assistant runs (see Guiding Assistant).
client.deselectStar()
client.startGuidingAssistant({ measureBacklash: false })
client.stopGuidingAssistant()
console.log(client.guidingAssistantResult())

client.stopCapture()

// The calibration with its mount context (declination in radians, pier side), stored and reused in another session or after a slew.
// getCalibrationGeneration() changes whenever the calibration in use does; clearCalibration() forces a new one.
client.setCalibrationContext({ declination: deg(20), pierSide: 'EAST' })
const record = client.exportCalibration()
if (record) console.log(client.restoreCalibration(record, { declination: deg(50), pierSide: 'WEST' }).status)
console.log(client.reassessCalibration({ declination: deg(60), pierSide: 'WEST' }).status)
client.clearCalibration()

client.removeHandler(handler)
client.disconnect()
client.detachHandler()
```

### Guiding Assistant

Before tuning a guider it helps to know what limits it. The motion of a guide star is a mix of high-frequency seeing, which no correction can follow and which a guider only amplifies if it chases it, low-frequency drift and periodic error of the mount, which guiding must correct, a steady declination drift caused by polar misalignment, and the declination backlash that delays every reversal. The Guiding Assistant of PHD2 separates these by watching the unguided star for a few minutes; `GuidingAssistant` is the same passive analysis, with no UI or device coupling.

The caller runs a [Guide Pulse Loop](#guide-pulse-loop) over the tracker results (see [Guide Star Tracking](#guide-star-tracking)) without executing its pulses and gives each frame and its command to the assistant. Per axis it measures the high-frequency RMS (the residual of a straight-line fit against time, so the drift is removed), the peak and the drift rate, in pixels and, with the image scale, in arcseconds; the seeing estimate is the smallest drift-removed DEC RMS over two-minute windows. From these it recommends the minimum moves (from the seeing), an exposure range, a brighter star or better focus when needed, and a polar alignment hint in arcminutes from the DEC drift, `3.8197 · |drift (px/min)| · scale / |cos δ|` as in PHD2. An optional DEC backlash test, driven by the caller, pulses north until the star has moved, then south until it returns: the time of the south pulses that produced no motion is the backlash in milliseconds.

The estimates need a run of at least two minutes to be meaningful, and the polar alignment value is a hint from the drift of one star, not a plate solve or a DARV measurement (see [DARV Polar Error Estimation](#darv-polar-error-estimation)).

```ts
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { GuidingAssistant } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/assistant'
import { Guider } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/guider'

// A guider whose pulses are never sent; frames: GuideFrame[] — at least two minutes of unguided guide frames (see Guide Pulse Loop).
const guider = new Guider({ lockAveragingFrames: 1 })

// A guide scale of 2″/px at declination 30° (for the polar alignment hint), 1 s exposures, and the DEC backlash test enabled.
const assistant = new GuidingAssistant({ imageScale: 2, declination: deg(30), exposure: 1, measureBacklash: true })

// start() opens a fresh run (the first sample also does), and each frame adds its measurement.
assistant.start()
for (const frame of frames) assistant.addSample(frame, guider.processFrame(frame))

const result = assistant.result()
console.log(result.motion.ra.rmsArcsec, result.motion.dec.rmsArcsec) // high-frequency RMS of each axis after the drift is removed, in arcseconds
console.log(result.motion.polarAlignmentError) // the polar alignment hint from the DEC drift, in arcminutes
console.log(result.recommendations) // exposure range, minimum moves, star, focus, polar alignment and backlash advice

// captureFrame(): the next GuideFrame; sendPulse(pulse): executes a pulse on the mount.
// The backlash test, once canMeasureBacklash is true: the origin is the first frame after the start,
// then each returned pulse is executed before the next frame while measuringBacklash is true.
console.log(assistant.canMeasureBacklash)
let pulse = assistant.startBacklashTest().pulse
const origin = await captureFrame()
assistant.alignBacklashOrigin(origin, guider.processFrame(origin))
while (pulse && assistant.measuringBacklash) {
	await sendPulse(pulse)
	const frame = await captureFrame()
	pulse = assistant.addSample(frame, guider.processFrame(frame)).pulse
}

console.log(assistant.result().backlash) // the measured backlash and the recommended compensation, in milliseconds

// Ends the run and freezes its recommendations; abortBacklash(message) aborts a running backlash test and fail(message)
// the whole run, both keeping the measured data.
assistant.complete()
```

### Guiding Calibration

A guider corrects the drift of a star by sending timed pulses to the two mount axes at the guide rate, so it must know how a pulse of one millisecond on each axis moves the star in the guide image. That relation is a 2×2 matrix from axis pulse time to image displacement: each axis has a direction in the image (which depends on the camera rotation) and a rate in pixels per millisecond (which depends on the guide rate, the focal length and, for right ascension, the declination). Its inverse turns a measured guide error in pixels into the RA and DEC pulse durations that cancel it (see [Guide Pulse Loop](#guide-pulse-loop)). Two axes that look nearly parallel in the image, or rates that are too small, cannot be inverted reliably, so the solution is validated before use.

`GuidingCalibrator` measures that matrix in the style of PHD2, as a frame-by-frame state machine with no I/O: the caller feeds it the tracker result of each guide frame (see [Guide Star Tracking](#guide-star-tracking)) and executes the pulse it asks for. It steps the star along RA until it has travelled far enough, brings it back toward the origin (the clearing leg), steps along DEC while the first pulses only take up the gear backlash, solves and validates both axes, and finally returns DEC toward the origin. The result holds the solved axes, the axis-to-image matrix and its inverse in milliseconds per pixel, and the DEC backlash estimate. `assessGuidingCalibration` grades a completed solution like PHD2's calibration sanity check (few steps, short travel, scattered steps, axes far from orthogonal, large backlash), without ever making a valid solution unusable.

A calibration belongs to the optical train, the guide rate, the declination and the side of the pier at which it was measured: recalibrate when the optics or the guide rate change. A meridian flip turns the image by 180 degrees, which `flipGuidingCalibration` applies to the matrix. `effectiveGuidingCalibration` derives the calibration to guide with from a stored record in another context, always from the record so transformations never accumulate: it flips once when the known pier sides differ and, with declination compensation, scales the RA rate by `cos(current) / cos(source)`, since an RA pulse moves the star in proportion to the cosine of the declination; DEC is never scaled. It refuses when a pier side or declination is unknown, and asks for a recalibration near the pole. Turn declination compensation off for a mount whose guide rate already follows the declination, or the pulses are compensated twice.

```ts
import { DEG2RAD } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'
import { assessGuidingCalibration } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/calibration.quality'
import { effectiveGuidingCalibration, GUIDING_CALIBRATION_RECORD_VERSION, type GuidingCalibrationRecord } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/calibration.transform'
import { flipGuidingCalibration, GuidingCalibrator } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/calibrator'

// frame(id): GuideFrame — the tracker result of the latest guide exposure with the image size in pixels.
```
