```ts
// pulse(command): sends the RA and DEC pulses (ms) the calibrator asked for and waits for their end.
const calibrator = new GuidingCalibrator()

// Fast clearing starts the clearing leg back toward the origin with longer pulses, as PHD2's fast recenter.
calibrator.setFastClearing(true)

// Each frame advances the state machine and may ask for the next pulse, until the run completes or fails.
let step = calibrator.processFrame(frame(0))
for (let id = 1; step.completed === undefined && step.failure === undefined; id++) {
	if (step.pulse !== undefined) await pulse(step.pulse)
	step = calibrator.processFrame(frame(id))
	// The phase and step counts, and the diagnostics of the latest step, for a progress display.
	console.log(calibrator.currentState.phase, calibrator.lastDiagnostics())
}

const result = step.completed!
console.log(result.ra.ratePxPerMs, result.ra.angle) // image rate of the RA axis (px/ms) and its image angle (rad)
console.log(result.imageToAxis, result.backlash) // pixel-to-pulse matrix (ms/px, row-major) and DEC backlash (ms)

// Grades the solution as PHD2's calibration sanity check does.
console.log(assessGuidingCalibration(result).quality) // 'good', 'warning' or 'poor'

// The same camera after a meridian flip: the image turned by 180 degrees.
const flipped = flipGuidingCalibration(result)
console.log(flipped.imageMotion) // both axis columns negated; the commanded directions are kept

// A record measured at declination 10° on the east side, reused at declination 50° on the west side.
const record: GuidingCalibrationRecord = { version: GUIDING_CALIBRATION_RECORD_VERSION, calibration: result, context: { declination: 10 * DEG2RAD, pierSide: 'EAST' }, acquiredAt: Date.now() }
const west = effectiveGuidingCalibration(record, { declination: 50 * DEG2RAD, pierSide: 'WEST' }, { declinationCompensation: true, reverseDecOutputAfterMeridianFlip: false })
if (west.status === 'transformed') console.log(west.transformations, west.declinationScale) // ['pierFlip', 'declinationCompensation'] 0.6527

// Starts over for a new calibration run, keeping the configuration.
calibrator.reset()
```

### Guiding Sessions

An automated observing session does not just switch guiding on: it starts guiding and waits until the star settles below a threshold before exposing, pauses guiding before anything else moves the mount (a dither, a meridian flip, a refocus slew), resumes and settles again, and must later know whether guiding was interrupted while a given frame was exposed. A `GuidingSession` is that boundary for the Sequencer. Guiding runs as a long-lived operation under a reservation of the guide devices (see [Device Reservations](#device-reservations)), so no third party can move the mount between two pulses. The loss of a device ends it as `lost`.

The important guarantee is the pause. It resolves only once no new pulse can be emitted and the pulses already sent have physically ended, so the caller may slew as soon as it returns. `LocalGuidingSession` adapts the in-process [Guider Client](#guider-client) and enforces this with a pulse gate that the session alone opens. `PHD2GuidingSession` adapts a [PHD2 Client](#phd2-client), where the guide devices belong to the PHD2 process. There it relies on an operational premise: no actor of that PHD2 sends a pulse longer than the declared maximum. Both sessions are also a `Ditherer` (see [Mount Dithering](#mount-dithering)) that shifts the lock position and waits for the guided settle. Interruptions nobody asked for (a lost star, an external pause, a lost device or connection) are stamped on a monotonic clock and kept in a bounded history, so a frame can be judged against the window of its exposure.

`InteractiveGuidingSession` is the guiding of an application. It is one long session that begins with the first looped guide exposure, then covers target selection, calibration, guiding, pauses and dithers, and ends only when it is stopped or a device is lost. The guide output is held only while guiding, so manual pulses and slews work again after guiding stops, with the loop still running.

```ts
import { OperationCoordinator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/operation'
import { ResourceArbiter } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/resource'
import { PHD2Client } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/phd2/client'
import { LocalGuidingSession } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/session.client'
import { InteractiveGuidingSession } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/session.interactive'
import { PHD2GuidingSession } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/session.phd2'

// client, camera, guideOutput and guideOutputCommander: a local guider client and its devices (see Guider Client); useLocal picks the backend.
const arbiter = new ResourceArbiter()
const coordinator = new OperationCoordinator(arbiter)
const settle = { pixels: 1.5, time: 10, timeout: 60 } // pixels, s, s

// The same session over the local guider (longest pulse 1500 ms, read back as its pulseCeiling) or over a PHD2 process.
const guiding = useLocal ? new LocalGuidingSession(client, camera, guideOutput, guideOutputCommander, { pulseCeiling: 1500 }) : new PHD2GuidingSession(new PHD2Client(), { host: 'localhost', maxGuidePulse: 2000 })

// A sequencer preflight reports every configuration problem; the state is read synchronously.
guiding.preflight((message) => console.log(message))
console.log(guiding.state()) // 'stopped' before the start

// The owner reserves what the session declares, begins the run, then guides under that reservation.
const reserved = arbiter.reserve({ id: 'night-1', kind: 'sequencer' }, guiding.resources().reserve)

if (reserved.ok && guiding.beginRun().ok) {
	const reservation = coordinator.reservedScope(reserved.reservation)
	// Resolves once guiding started and the star settled; operationId() is the id of the long-lived guiding operation.
	await guiding.start(reservation, reservation, { recalibrate: false, settle })
	console.log(guiding.operationId())
	// Resolves ok once no pulse can still be running: the mount may move now. A pause timeout must be at least the bound (ms).
	console.log(guiding.pulseQuiescenceBound())
	await guiding.pause(reservation)
	// After a meridian flip slew, the calibration is flipped before resuming.
	await guiding.flipCalibration(reservation)
	await guiding.resume(reservation, settle)
	// As a Ditherer: whether it supports a request and can dither now, then a shift of the lock by 3 guide-camera pixels and the guided settle.
	const request = { amount: { unit: 'guidePixel', value: 3 }, raOnly: false, settle: { kind: 'guided', ...settle } } as const
	if (guiding.accepts(request) && guiding.ready()) await guiding.dither(reservation, request)
	// Interruptions inside a monotonic window (ms), to judge the frame exposed in it.
	console.log(guiding.interruptions(0, performance.now())) // { interruptions: [], truncated: false }
	await guiding.stop(reservation)
	guiding.endRun()
	reserved.reservation.release()
}

// Interactive guiding: loop, select a star, guide, and stop guiding while still looping.
const session = new InteractiveGuidingSession(client, camera, guideOutput, guideOutputCommander)
await session.startLoop(coordinator, { exposure: 2000 }) // ms
session.selectTarget() // or selectTarget([x, y]) near a pixel; clearTarget() drops it
session.setExposure(1000) // ms
await session.startGuiding(coordinator, coordinator, { recalibrate: true, settle })

// The projection for a UI: state, held guide output, settling, dithering, calibration and lock position;
// lost and admitted tell whether a device was lost and whether a pulse admission is installed.
console.log(session.snapshot(), session.lost, session.admitted)

// The same pause, resume, dither, interruptions, pulseQuiescenceBound, accepts, resources, operationId and beginRun/endRun
// as the sessions above; pause can stop only the corrections and release the guide output for a slew of the same reservation.
await session.pause(coordinator, 'corrections', { releaseGuideOutput: true })
await session.resume(coordinator, settle)

// The calibration of the client, as in Guider Client: flipCalibration, clearCalibration, setCalibrationContext,
// exportCalibration, restoreCalibration and reassessCalibration.
session.flipCalibration()

await session.stopGuiding(coordinator)
await session.stop(coordinator)
```

### iPolar Alignment

An electronic polar scope aligns the right-ascension axis of a mount with the celestial pole from images alone, with the camera rigidly attached to the RA axis. Two plate-solved frames taken before and after a rotation of the RA axis alone calibrate where the mechanical axis points: the rotation that carries the first field onto the second has the mechanical axis as its axis. Every later solved frame of the same sensor geometry then measures the angle between that axis and the pole while the operator adjusts the base, and the error is split into an azimuth component, positive when the axis is east of the pole in either hemisphere, and an altitude component, positive when it is above. The polar error from three frames along a slew is [Three-Point Polar Alignment](#three-point-polar-alignment).

The model is a rigid rotation in the Earth-fixed frame. A grid of sensor pixels goes through each WCS and then through ERFA's observed-place chain at the frame's own mid-exposure instant: light deflection, annual and diurnal aberration, precession-nutation, Earth rotation, polar motion and refraction. The result is the physical direction of the light in ITRS, and the rotation between two frames is fitted on those rays (see [Rotation Fitting](#rotation-fitting)). The frames need not overlap, the axis need not fall inside the image, and the delay between the frames, tracking included, does not bias the result. A fit of the raw ICRS rays would mix in the rotation of the Earth, and a pole without annual aberration would be off by up to about 20″. The observer's `refraction` sets both how the rays are observed and the target: with refraction, the target is the pole raised to its apparent altitude; with `false`, it is the geometric pole.

Two poses cannot prove that the motion was pure RA, so a small mixed RA/DEC motion tilts the axis undetected. An axis found several degrees from the pole is the mark of a declination move or a wrong blind solve, never of a large polar error. A changed binning, subframe, rotator or camera position invalidates the calibration. The convergence threshold is a requested target, not a statement of accuracy, which depends on the solutions, the optics and the mechanics. The runner performs the calibration and the refinement with real devices. In manual mode it waits for the operator to turn the RA axis. In automatic mode it turns the mount with timed motions sized only from the fitted rotation of the solves, never from the motion time. It never restores the slew rate it changed, so the caller does that once the mount is free.

```ts
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { deg, toArcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { advanceIPolarConvergence, calibrateIPolar, IPOLAR_CONVERGENCE_START, measureIPolar } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/ipolar'
import type { IPolarObserver } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/ipolar.geometry'
import { ipolarMountRefusal, runIPolarCalibration, runIPolarRefinement } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/ipolar.runner'

// The site; refraction: false measures against the geometric pole.
const observer: IPolarObserver = { location: geodeticLocation(deg(-45), deg(40)), refraction: false }

// first, second: IPolarFrame — mid-exposure time, plate solution and sensor geometry of two frames separated by an RA-only rotation.
const result = calibrateIPolar(first, second, observer)
if (!result.accepted) throw new Error(result.reason)

// frame: IPolarFrame — a later frame of the same sensor geometry, taken while the base is adjusted.
const measurement = measureIPolar(result.calibration, frame)
if (measurement.valid) console.log(toArcsec(measurement.error.azimuth), toArcsec(measurement.error.altitude)) // arcsec: + east of the pole, + above it

// The streak of consecutive measurements within the threshold.
const convergence = advanceIPolarConvergence(IPOLAR_CONVERGENCE_START, measurement)
console.log(convergence.converged)

// With devices: coordinator, camera and mount as in Device Commanders; services hold the capturer, the solver, the clock and the listener.
// Whether the mount can turn the RA axis in automatic mode at a slew-rate preset: undefined, or why it cannot.
console.log(ipolarMountRefusal(mount, 'SLOW'))
const run = await runIPolarCalibration(coordinator, camera, mount, calibrationOptions, services)
if (run.ok) await runIPolarRefinement(coordinator, camera, mount, run.value.mount, run.value.calibration, { convergence: IPOLAR_CONVERGENCE_START }, refinementOptions, services)
```

### Local Pointing Residuals

A low-order global pointing model (see [Pointing Model Fit and Correction](#pointing-model-fit-and-correction)) describes the mechanics of a mount with a few terms that are smooth functions of hour angle and declination. What it leaves behind can still be systematic: a localized flexure, a mirror that shifts over part of the sky, an irregular worm sector. Such errors are smooth near a sample but are no simple function of the axes. The local layer models them as a k-nearest-neighbour, tricube-weighted average of the residuals the global model leaves at the training samples. Distances are measured on the sphere, and only neighbours on the pier side of the query are used.

It is interpolation, never extrapolation: the contribution is tapered by the local sampling density and decays to zero outside the sampled region, so a target far from every sample falls back to the global model alone. Offsets follow the model convention: `dx` east and `dy` north on the plane tangent at the target, defined as `solved - target`, in radians. The layer is off by default and needs a minimum number of samples, since with few or unevenly spread samples it memorizes the plate-solve noise. `fitPointingModel` and `MountPointing` build and evaluate it when the `local` fit option is enabled; the functions below are for inspecting or composing it.

```ts
import { arcsec, deg, hour, toArcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { fitPointingModel } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/mount/pointing'
import { buildLocalPointingResidual, predictLocalPointingResidual, resolveLocalResidualOptions } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/mount/pointing.local'

// directions: training targets as unit vectors flattened [x0, y0, z0, x1, ...]; pierSides: the side of each;
// residualsDx, residualsDy: the east and north residuals of the global fit at each sample (rad).
const options = resolveLocalResidualOptions({ enabled: true, minimumSamples: 20 })

// Builds the layer, or undefined when disabled or with too few samples (the global model is then kept).
const model = buildLocalPointingResidual(directions, pierSides, residualsDx, residualsDy, options)

// The residual expected at a target on the east side, from its neighbours on that side.
const offset = predictLocalPointingResidual(model!, hour(1), deg(28), 'EAST')
console.log(toArcsec(offset.dx), toArcsec(offset.dy)) // arcsec east and north

// The usual way: the global fit of samples (PointingSample[]) with the local layer enabled.
const pointing = fitPointingModel(samples, { local: { enabled: true } })
```

### Meridian Flip Lifecycle

A meridian flip is not one command but a procedure of several minutes: finish or abort the exposure, pause the guiding, slew to the other side of the pier, verify that the mount really changed side, recenter the target with a plate solve, and let the guiding settle again. The process may be interrupted, and a slew may fail and need one more attempt within a budget. `transitionMeridianFlip` is the persistent half of the engine of [Meridian Flip Planning](#meridian-flip-planning): a pure reducer that advances a plain serializable `MeridianFlipState` when the caller reports that an action ended. Stored after each transition, the state lets a restarted process resume the same cycle with its attempts counted.

The cycle is `WAITING`, `PREPARING`, `READY`, `FLIPPING`, `VERIFYING_PIER_SIDE`, then optionally `RECENTERING` and `SETTLING`, and `COMPLETED`. `FAILED` is reachable from any non-terminal phase, and `RESET` starts a new cycle for the next target or the next night. The caller runs the exposure, the guiding, the slew, the plate solve and the resume, and sends the matching event when each ends. An event that is not valid in the current phase throws, so the caller must drop late or duplicated events of an obsolete cycle. A failed flip is retried only while attempts remain and the hour angle is still past the flip threshold. A mount that publishes no usable pier side can complete a cycle only when the policy allows it, with the flip established from other evidence such as plate solutions. The state then records that the flip was inferred rather than verified.

```ts
import { createMeridianFlipState, evaluateMeridianFlip, transitionMeridianFlip, type MeridianFlipState } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/mount/meridian.flip'

// policy: MeridianFlipPolicy and snapshot(): the current MeridianFlipSnapshot, as in Meridian Flip Planning.
// pauseGuiding, slewToTarget, recenter and resumeGuiding: the caller's actions.
let state: MeridianFlipState = createMeridianFlipState()

// Evaluates, runs the action, and reports its end as an event; the returned state is persisted.
async function step(current: MeridianFlipState): Promise<MeridianFlipState> {
	const decision = evaluateMeridianFlip(policy, snapshot(), current)
	try {
		switch (decision.action) {
			case 'PAUSE_GUIDING':
				await pauseGuiding()
				return transitionMeridianFlip(policy, decision.state, { type: 'PREPARED' })
			case 'START_FLIP': {
				const flipping = transitionMeridianFlip(policy, decision.state, { type: 'FLIP_STARTED' })
				await slewToTarget()
				return transitionMeridianFlip(policy, flipping, { type: 'FLIP_COMPLETED' })
			}
			case 'VERIFY_PIER_SIDE':
				return transitionMeridianFlip(policy, decision.state, { type: 'PIER_SIDE_CONFIRMED' })
			case 'RECENTER':
				await recenter()
				return transitionMeridianFlip(policy, decision.state, { type: 'RECENTER_COMPLETED' })
			case 'RESUME_GUIDING':
				await resumeGuiding()
				return transitionMeridianFlip(policy, decision.state, { type: 'GUIDING_SETTLED' })
			default:
				return decision.state
		}
	} catch {
		// The failure is kept with the attempts; a later evaluation may offer a retry.
		return transitionMeridianFlip(policy, decision.state, { type: 'FAILED', reason: 'EXECUTION_FAILED' })
	}
}

state = await step(state)

// A new cycle for the next target or the next night.
state = transitionMeridianFlip(policy, state, { type: 'RESET' })
```

### Meridian Flip Planning

A German equatorial mount carries the telescope on one side of the pier. As a target crosses the meridian, continuing to track would eventually drive the tube into the pier or the tripod. The mount must therefore "flip": slew the tube to the other side of the pier and point at the same target again. The decision is driven by the hour angle `H = LST − α`, the local apparent sidereal time minus the right ascension, normalized to `(−π, π]`. It is negative east of the meridian, before the transit, and positive after. A policy defines three hour-angle thresholds, `prepareAt ≤ flipAt ≤ latestAt`: where preparation may start, where the flip may start, and the latest safe start, beyond which a running exposure is aborted.

`evaluateMeridianFlip` is a pure function: it opens no device, runs no timer and slews nothing. The caller gives it the policy, a telemetry snapshot (sidereal time, target, reported pier side, and whether the camera is exposing, the guider guiding and the mount slewing) and the persisted state. It returns the action to take next and the signed distances to the thresholds. Before the flip it waits for the exposure or aborts it when overdue, pauses the guiding first, waits for a slewing mount, and then starts the flip. A mount already on its post-flip side completes the cycle. The later phases and their events are in [Meridian Flip Lifecycle](#meridian-flip-lifecycle). `computeLocalSiderealTime` adds an east-positive longitude to the Greenwich apparent sidereal time (see [Sidereal Time and Earth Rotation Angle](#sidereal-time-and-earth-rotation-angle)). The engine assumes it is evaluated near the upper culmination: any hour angle after `flipAt` counts as past the threshold, so do not feed it a target far west of the meridian.

```ts
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { computeHourAngle, computeLocalSiderealTime, evaluateMeridianFlip, type MeridianFlipPolicy, type MeridianFlipSnapshot } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/mount/meridian.flip'

// The local sidereal time from the Greenwich one (10 h) at 45° west, and the hour angle of a target at RA 8 h.
const lst = computeLocalSiderealTime(hour(10), deg(-45))
console.log(lst / hour(1), computeHourAngle(lst, hour(8)) / hour(1)) // 7 -1 (hours; east of the meridian)

// Prepare at -5° of hour angle, flip at the meridian, never after +7.5°; the mount reports EAST before and WEST after.
const policy: MeridianFlipPolicy = { enabled: true, prepareAt: deg(-5), flipAt: 0, latestAt: deg(7.5), beforeFlipPierSide: 'EAST', afterFlipPierSide: 'WEST' }

// A snapshot at a given hour angle of a target at RA 100°.
const target = { rightAscension: deg(100) }
const at = (hourAngle: number, extra: Partial<MeridianFlipSnapshot> = {}): MeridianFlipSnapshot => ({ localSiderealTime: computeLocalSiderealTime(target.rightAscension, hourAngle), target, pierSide: 'EAST', ...extra })

// Inside the preparation window, at the threshold while exposing, and with an idle mount past it.
console.log(evaluateMeridianFlip(policy, at(deg(-2))).action) // PREPARE
console.log(evaluateMeridianFlip(policy, at(deg(0.5), { isExposing: true })).action) // WAIT_FOR_EXPOSURE
const decision = evaluateMeridianFlip(policy, at(deg(0.5)))
console.log(decision.action, decision.untilLatest) // START_FLIP, radians left before the latest threshold
```

### Mosaic Framing

A target larger than the field of view of the camera, such as M31 or a large nebula, is imaged as a mosaic: a grid of panels, each a separate pointing, later registered and blended into one image. Adjacent panels overlap so that the registration has common stars and the blending can hide the seams. Laying the panels out as independent fields side by side in right ascension and declination would distort the grid, because lines of constant right ascension converge toward the pole. `planMosaic` therefore lays every panel out on one shared gnomonic tangent plane centered on the target. It converts angular sizes to plane extents (`2·tan(angle/2)`), spaces the panels on that plane, and projects each center and corner back to equatorial coordinates.

The grid is rotated by an optional position angle (the local y axis from north toward east) and has enough columns and rows to span the requested region with the fractional overlap. Panels come in capture order, row by row, or serpentine, with odd rows reversed to shorten the slews. The plan stays in the frame of the given center, which is not converted. It does not model the plate scale and distortion of the real optics, the rotation of the camera on the mount, whether a mount can reach a panel, or the order that minimizes slew time.

```ts
import { deg, hour, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { planMosaic } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/framing/mosaic.plan'

// A 3 × 2° region around M31 with a camera of 1.2 × 0.9° and 10% overlap on both axes.
const plan = planMosaic({ center: { ra: hour(0.712), dec: deg(41.27) }, panel: { width: deg(1.2), height: deg(0.9) }, region: { width: deg(3), height: deg(2) }, overlap: { x: 0.1, y: 0.1 }, traversal: 'SERPENTINE' })
console.log(plan.columns, plan.rows, plan.panels.length) // 3 3 9

// The spanned coverage, at least the requested region (degrees).
console.log(toDeg(plan.coverage.width), toDeg(plan.coverage.height))

// Each panel: capture index, grid position, equatorial center and the four corners of its footprint (rad).
for (const panel of plan.panels) console.log(panel.index, panel.row, panel.column, panel.center, panel.footprint)
```

### Mount Axis Limits

A real mount cannot point everywhere its axes could turn: cables wrap, the tube can hit the pier or the tripod past some hour angle, a declination range may be blocked, and targets below a minimum altitude are behind trees or in the dome wall. `evaluateMountLimits` is a pure check of a position against such configured axis ranges. It accepts any of hour angle, declination, altitude and azimuth, in radians, and reports every axis outside its closed range. Nothing here commands, parks or stops a mount. Axes with no limit, or not supplied, are skipped.

The hour angle, declination and altitude are linear intervals. A cable wrap may extend beyond ±π, and the hour angle passed must then be the unwrapped angle the mount actually holds, positive west. The azimuth, north through east, is circular by default, so a window that crosses north is written with its minimum above its maximum. `azimuthWrap: 'linear'` compares the raw azimuth instead, for an unwrapped azimuth cable. The check says nothing about the slew path, the pier side or a horizon profile: a target inside the limits may still need a path through a limit.

```ts
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { evaluateMountLimits } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/mount/limits'

// An equatorial mount that goes 6 hours past the meridian on either side, with a declination range and a minimum altitude of 20°.
const limits = { hourAngle: [-Math.PI / 2, Math.PI / 2], declination: [deg(-85), deg(85)], altitude: [deg(20), deg(90)] } as const
console.log(evaluateMountLimits({ hourAngle: deg(40), declination: deg(30), altitude: deg(55) }, limits)) // { accepted: true, violations: [] }

// Every failing axis is reported with its value and range.
console.log(evaluateMountLimits({ hourAngle: deg(100), declination: deg(30), altitude: deg(10) }, limits).violations) // hourAngle and altitude

// A circular azimuth window across north, from 300° to 60°.
console.log(evaluateMountLimits({ azimuth: deg(350) }, { azimuth: [deg(300), deg(60)] }).accepted) // true
```

### Mount Dithering

Dithering moves the pointing by a small random or patterned offset, a few pixels, between exposures. Sensor defects (hot pixels, column defects, residual fixed-pattern noise) then fall on different sky positions in each frame, and outlier rejection removes them when the frames are stacked. A `Ditherer` is the dither boundary of an observation session. When guiding, the guiding session of [Guiding Sessions](#guiding-sessions) shifts the guide lock position and waits for the guided settle. Without a guider, `MountDitherer` moves the mount itself and waits a fixed mechanical settle. Each dither resolves only after the settle, so the next exposure starts on a steady field.

`MountDitherer` takes the next increment of a [Dither Offsets](#dither-offsets) pattern and applies it in one of two ways. As timed guide pulses, it uses the guide rate and the declination (see [Dither Guide Pulses](#dither-guide-pulses)) and sends them through the guide-output commander of [Device Commanders](#device-commanders). As a slew, it goes to `ditherSlewTarget` of the reported pointing. That target is an exact great-circle displacement of `hypot(east, north)` at position angle `atan2(east, north)`. With `raOnly`, it is a move along the parallel by the right ascension that keeps the separation equal to the east offset. It is undefined when the dither disc contains the celestial pole. A mount ditherer must never run while a guider guides the same mount.

```ts
import { arcsec, deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { ditherSlewTarget, MountDitherer } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/ditherer'

// The slew target of a dither of 10″ east and 10″ south from RA 5 h, DEC +60°: about 20″ of RA (1 / cos 60°) and -10″ of DEC.
console.log(ditherSlewTarget(hour(5), deg(60), { rightAscension: arcsec(10), declination: -arcsec(10) }, false))

// mount, guideOutput, guideOutputCommander and coordinator as in Device Commanders.
// A spiral pattern applied as guide pulses of at most 5 s.
const ditherer = new MountDitherer(mount, guideOutput, { guideOutputCommander }, { method: 'pulse', pattern: 'spiral', rightAscensionDirection: 'WEST', declinationDirection: 'NORTH', maxPulseDuration: 5000 })

// What a session reserves for it: the resources that can move the mount (here the guide output, with the worst case in ms
// between cancelling a pulse and releasing it), as movement(settleTimeout) lists them.
console.log(ditherer.resources(), ditherer.movement(0))

// A dither of 15″ followed by a mechanical settle of 5 s, once the ditherer accepts the request and is ready; phases: dithering, dithered, settling, settled.
const request = { amount: { unit: 'angle', value: arcsec(15) }, raOnly: false, settle: { kind: 'mechanical', time: 5 } } as const
if (ditherer.accepts(request) && ditherer.ready()) {
	const result = await ditherer.dither(coordinator, request, (phase) => console.log(phase))
	console.log(result) // { ok: true, value: { kind: 'mount', offset } } — offset along the mount axes (rad, RA positive east)
}

// At startup after a crash: assumes a pulse of the previous process may still run, and waits until it must have ended.
console.log(ditherer.assumeDispatchedPulses()) // { busyAckDeadline, endsBy }, monotonic instants in ms
await ditherer.awaitPulseQuiescence(AbortSignal.timeout(10000))
```

### Mount Kinematics

A telescope mount is a serial chain of two rotations. The primary axis (azimuth or hour angle) carries the secondary axis (altitude or declination), which carries the optics. The forward kinematics gives the direction the optics point at for two encoder angles. The inverse kinematics gives the encoder angles that point at a requested direction. A real mount departs from the ideal head: an axis offset, axes that are not perpendicular, an optical origin displaced from the axes, encoder zero offsets or reversed encoder signs. A `TwoAxisMountGeometry` describes these at encoder zero in the base frame of the mount, with points in metres and angles in radians, and a rigid transform places the base in the world frame. `createIdealAltAzGeometry` gives the ideal altitude-azimuth head in an east, north, up frame. `createCanonicalEquatorialGeometry` gives the ideal equatorial head in the Taki frame, with the primary as the west-positive hour angle and the secondary as the declination (see [Taki Mount Geometry](#taki-mount-geometry)).

`solveMountEncoders` is a local damped Gauss-Newton search. A mount reaches the same direction in several mechanical branches, such as a German equatorial mount on either side of the pier. The solver returns the branch near its initial seed, so the caller passes the seed, and optionally unwrapped axis ranges, of the branch it wants. Near a singular configuration, such as a target at the pole of the primary axis, it returns the best position found without converging, so check `converged` and `residual`. The geometry is only the kinematic model: it does not model flexure, refraction, speeds or tracking.

```ts
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { createCanonicalEquatorialGeometry, createIdealAltAzGeometry, mountDirectionFromEncoders, mountPoseFromEncoders, solveMountEncoders } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/mount/kinematics'

// An ideal alt-az head: azimuth 0 and altitude 0 look north.
const altaz = createIdealAltAzGeometry()
console.log(mountDirectionFromEncoders(altaz, { primary: 0, secondary: 0 })) // [0, 1, 0] (north, in east-north-up)

// An equatorial head whose optics and secondary pivot are displaced from the primary axis (m), with a secondary zero offset.
const equatorial = createCanonicalEquatorialGeometry({ secondaryPivot: [0, 0, 0.1], opticalOrigin: [0.2, 0, 0.1], secondaryIndex: deg(1) })
const pose = mountPoseFromEncoders(equatorial, { primary: deg(30), secondary: deg(20) })
console.log(pose.origin, pose.direction) // optical origin (m) and unit pointing direction in the world frame

// The encoders that point the ideal head at hour angle 40° and declination 25°.
const ideal = createCanonicalEquatorialGeometry()
const target = mountDirectionFromEncoders(ideal, { primary: deg(40), secondary: deg(25) })
const solution = solveMountEncoders(ideal, target)
console.log(solution.converged, solution.primary, solution.secondary, solution.residual) // true, 40° and 25° (rad), residual (rad)

// A seed on the other side of the pier selects the other mechanical branch of the same direction.
const flipped = solveMountEncoders(ideal, target, { initial: { primary: deg(220), secondary: deg(155) } })
```

### Mount Tracking Rates

A mount tracks by turning its right-ascension axis at a constant rate. Which rate depends on the target. The stars need the sidereal rate, one turn per sidereal day of 86164.0905 s, or about 15.041″ per second. The Sun needs one turn per mean solar day of 86400 s, exactly 15″ per second. The Moon's mean rate is the sidereal rate minus the Moon's mean motion over its sidereal month of 27.321661 days. The King rate is the sidereal rate reduced by one part in 3600, the fixed factor of a King drive, not the hour-angle-dependent King formula. `trackingRate` returns these mean rates for the track modes of an INDI mount (see [INDI Mount Control](#indi-mount-control)) in radians per second, arcseconds per second (numerically equal to degrees per hour) and multiples of the sidereal rate, all per SI second. `convertTrackingRate` converts a rate between those units.

These are mean rates of the RA drive. The lunar rate is not the instantaneous topocentric rate of the Moon. The rate of a non-sidereal target (a comet, a satellite, the Moon at its real position) must come from an ephemeris difference or from [Non-Sidereal Guide Tracking](#non-sidereal-guide-tracking) and [Satellite Tracking Rates](#satellite-tracking-rates).

```ts
import { convertTrackingRate, trackingRate } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/formulas'

// The fixed rates, each in rad/s, arcsec/s and sidereal multiples.
console.log(trackingRate('SIDEREAL')) // radiansPerSecond 7.2921e-5, arcsecPerSecond 15.04107, siderealMultiplier 1
console.log(trackingRate('SOLAR')) // radiansPerSecond 7.2722e-5, arcsecPerSecond 15, siderealMultiplier 0.997270
console.log(trackingRate('LUNAR')) // radiansPerSecond 7.0259e-5, arcsecPerSecond 14.49205, siderealMultiplier 0.963499

// A hand controller at 0.5× sidereal, in arcseconds per second.
console.log(convertTrackingRate(0.5, 'siderealMultiplier', 'arcsecPerSecond')) // 7.520534
```

### Non-Sidereal Guide Tracking

A comet, an asteroid or a satellite moves against the stars, so guiding that locks a star keeps the stars round and smears the target. Following the target while still measuring the stars, which are bright and point-like, means moving the lock position along the target's path. The image displacement of the target since an anchor instant is added to the star offset the guider corrects, so the guider (see [Guide Pulse Loop](#guide-pulse-loop)) pulses the mount to follow the target. `NonSiderealTracker` is a decorator of any `GuideTracker` (see [Guide Star Tracking](#guide-star-tracking)) that does exactly this. The base tracker keeps the star detection and identity. The decorator evaluates the target position at each frame's capture time and adds its offset from the anchor, converted to pixels. No rate is integrated, so errors do not accumulate.

The target comes from an ephemeris, typically a table interpolated as in [Equatorial Ephemeris Interpolation](#equatorial-ephemeris-interpolation), and is never extrapolated beyond its validity window. It can also come from a local motion fitted from the images. The sky-to-image transform is built from the guider scale and the RA and DEC image directions of [Guiding Calibration](#guiding-calibration). The rate and acceleration of the target are estimated by finite differences of the ephemeris. With an ephemeris, a feedback estimator and controller (see [Tracking Rate Estimation](#tracking-rate-estimation) and [Tracking Rate Correction](#tracking-rate-correction)) can add a bounded residual rate. The geometry is a local tangent plane around the anchor with a scale-and-rotation image transform. Mount pointing, refraction and field distortion are not modelled, so a long drift needs a new anchor. Each frame must carry its actual capture time, preferably the exposure midpoint. A change of camera orientation, as after a meridian flip, needs a new transform.

```ts
import { linearInterpolator } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/ephemeris/interpolation/ephemeris'
import { arcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { calibratedNonSiderealTransform, estimateNonSiderealDerivative, NonSiderealTracker, nonSiderealAngularOffset, nonSiderealEphemerisFromInterpolator, nonSiderealTrackingOf } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/tracker.nonsidereal'

// points, newerPoints: tabulated target positions ({ time, rightAscension, declination }, TT, rad); base: the star GuideTracker.
const ephemeris = nonSiderealEphemerisFromInterpolator(linearInterpolator(points))

// The adapter is an InterpolatedNonSiderealEphemeris with a TT validity window (JD); update() swaps in a newer table and bumps its generation.
console.log(ephemeris.validTime, ephemeris.generation)
ephemeris.update(linearInterpolator(newerPoints))

// The target rate at an instant by finite differences of the ephemeris (rad/s, east and north).
console.log(estimateNonSiderealDerivative(ephemeris, now).rate)

// The tangent-plane offset of a position from an anchor: east, north and the separation (rad).
console.log(nonSiderealAngularOffset({ rightAscension: 1, declination: 0.3 }, { rightAscension: 1.0001, declination: 0.3 })) // east 9.553e-5 (0.0001 · cos 0.3), north ≈ 0

// 2″ per pixel; positive RA moves the image to +X and positive DEC to -Y.
const transform = calibratedNonSiderealTransform({ pixelScaleArcsecPerPixel: 2, calibration: { rightAscension: { unitX: 1, unitY: 0 }, declination: { unitX: 0, unitY: -1 } } })

// Decorates the star tracker and arms it; the anchor is taken at the first frame after the visual lock.
// arm(ephemeris, transform, { estimator, controller }) adds the residual rate feedback, and arm(provider, transform) follows a fitted local motion.
const tracker = new NonSiderealTracker(base, { maxRate: arcsec(100) })
tracker.arm(ephemeris, transform)

// frame: a GuideTrackerFrame with its captureTime; context: the guider phase with the lock established.
const result = tracker.track(frame, context)
console.log(result.targetOffset, nonSiderealTrackingOf(result)?.state) // pixels the lock moves to follow the target, and 'active'

// The guide client accepts the frame; commit() and select() delegate to the base tracker, and state and lastResult expose the telemetry.
tracker.commit()
console.log(tracker.select(result), tracker.state, tracker.lastResult)

// A new anchor at the current time brings the target offset back to zero.
tracker.reanchor(now)

// A new camera transform (flippedTransform, built from the flipped calibration, as after a meridian flip) invalidates the image fits.
tracker.onCalibrationChanged(flippedTransform)

// reset() keeps the source for the next lock; clear() disables the non-sidereal control.
tracker.reset()
tracker.clear()
```

### Observation Scores

Planning a night means ordering many candidate targets by how well each can be observed now. That depends on its altitude and airmass, on how dark the sky is (the Sun's depression below the horizon), on how much the Moon brightens the sky near it, and on whether enough time remains for the planned integration. `observationScore` combines those few numbers into one dimensionless score from 0 to 1, as the geometric mean of the factors supplied. A single zero factor therefore zeroes the score, and an omitted optional input is left out instead of counting as a failure. The altitude factor rises linearly from the horizon to 60°. The airmass factor uses Kasten and Young when no airmass is given and falls to zero at airmass 3. The twilight factor rises from a Sun at −12° to −18°. `moonInterference` gives the Moon term: the illuminated fraction times the sine of the lunar altitude times a Gaussian of 30° in the separation from the target.

The score evaluates no ephemeris: the altitudes and the lunar geometry come from the caller. Its ramps are planning thresholds, not a photometric sky-brightness model. The Moon term ignores wavelength and transparency, and the airmass is the geometric one, so use the score to order targets, not as a limiting magnitude. [Sky Surface Brightness (Krisciunas and Schaefer)](#sky-surface-brightness-krisciunas-and-schaefer) predicts the sky background itself.

```ts
import { moonInterference, observationScore, observationScoreFactors } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/planning'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A target at 60° with no Moon: only altitude and airmass count.
console.log(observationScore({ altitude: deg(60) })) // 0.9607

// An 80% lit Moon 45° high, 20° from the target.
const moon = moonInterference(0.8, deg(45), deg(20))
console.log(moon) // 0.453

// A full evaluation as a percentage: 50° high, Sun at -19°, that Moon, and 3 of 4 required hours available.
console.log(observationScore({ altitude: deg(50), sunAltitude: deg(-19), moonInterference: moon, availableDurationHours: 3, requiredDurationHours: 4 }, { scale: 100 }))

// The factors behind a score, to tell which one limits it.
console.log(observationScoreFactors({ altitude: deg(60), airmass: 1, sunAltitude: deg(-15) })) // { altitude: 1, airmass: 1, twilight: 0.5, moon: undefined, duration: undefined }
```

### Observing Session Scheduling

A night of imaging several targets is a scheduling problem. Each target is observable only in some windows (see [Observing Visibility Windows](#observing-visibility-windows)), has a priority, and asks for blocks of exposures. Time also goes to overheads: slews, readout, dithers, filter changes, refocusing, and the meridian flip of a German equatorial mount. `scheduleSession` allocates one session to those blocks and returns a timed plan, with the blocks it could not fit and why. It is pure, opens no device, and leaves execution, aborts and retries to the sequencer.

Overheads are explicit costs in seconds supplied by the caller, and the whole of a block, setup included, must fit inside one allowed interval. A time-critical block such as a transit should therefore open early enough to absorb its slew and filter change. Indivisible blocks run in one contiguous chunk. Divisible ones are split into chunks, so focus, priorities and flips are re-evaluated between them. Weather or safety exclusions are supplied intervals, never predictions; they can stop sky blocks only, leaving darks and biases possible. With a meridian, a pre-flip block that reaches the flip hour angle flips after the frame in progress, so leave one exposure of margin as for `latestAt` in [Meridian Flip Planning](#meridian-flip-planning).

The algorithm is a deterministic greedy dispatcher with a one-step look-ahead. Each candidate is charged with the priority-weighted acquisition time it would take from the other blocks' windows, and scored per second elapsed, so overhead and idle waiting lower the score. It is a heuristic, not an optimal schedule. Instants are measured in the time scale of `start`, so pass TT for uniform seconds across a UTC leap second. After an interruption, replan from the new horizon with the completed frames, the current pointing, filter and focus as the initial state.

```ts
import { timeShift, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { scheduleSession, type ScheduleTarget } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/scheduler'

// The night runs from 22:00 UTC to 06:00 UTC; at(h) is h hours after the start.
const start = timeYMDHMS(2026, 1, 15, 22, 0, 0)
const end = timeYMDHMS(2026, 1, 16, 6, 0, 0)
const at = (hours: number) => timeShift(start, hours / 24)

// A long divisible integration in 1 h chunks, a transit between 01:00 and 03:15 UTC, and darks that need neither sky nor mount.
const targets: ScheduleTarget[] = [
	{ id: 'M42', priority: 1, windows: [{ start, end }], pointing: { rightAscension: hour(5.59), declination: deg(-5.4) }, blocks: [{ id: 'M42-L', filter: 'L', exposure: 300, count: 120, divisible: true, maximumFrames: 12, ditherEvery: 3 }] },
	{ id: 'WASP-12', priority: 10, windows: [{ start, end }], pointing: { rightAscension: hour(6.51), declination: deg(29.67) }, blocks: [{ id: 'transit', filter: 'V', exposure: 60, count: 120, notBefore: at(3), notAfter: at(5.25) }] },
	{ id: 'darks', priority: 1, windows: [{ start, end }], sky: false, blocks: [{ id: 'darks-300', exposure: 300, count: 10 }] },
]

// Overheads in seconds (slew rate in rad/s), clouds forecast from 23:30 to 00:30, and a GEM at 45° W flipping 2° past the meridian.
const options = {
	costs: { slewRate: deg(3), slewSettle: 60, readout: 3, dither: 15, filterChange: 8, focus: 180, focusInterval: 2 * 3600 },
	exclusions: [{ start: at(1.5), end: at(2.5), scope: 'sky' as const }],
	meridian: { longitude: deg(-45), flipAt: deg(2) },
	initial: { filter: 'L' },
}

const plan = scheduleSession(targets, start, end, options)
for (const block of plan.blocks) console.log(block.blockId, block.start, block.end, block.frames, block.flags) // setup start and end as Time
console.log(plan.unscheduled) // [{ targetId: 'M42', blockId: 'M42-L', remainingFrames: 67, scheduledFrames: 53, reason: 'partial' }]
console.log(plan.diagnostics.efficiency.toFixed(3)) // 0.906 — exposure time over session duration

// The transit was aborted; replan from 02:00 UTC with 30 frames of M42 done.
const replan = scheduleSession(targets, at(4), end, { ...options, initial: { pointing: targets[1].pointing, filter: 'V', lastFocus: at(3), completedFrames: { 'M42-L': 30, 'darks-300': 10 }, skip: ['transit'] } })
```

### Plate-Solved Centering

A slew lands where the mount believes the target is. The pointing error of the mount (polar misalignment, flexure, cone, a stale sync) can put the field arcminutes away. Centering measures that error on the sky: it exposes a short auxiliary frame, plate solves it, and corrects until a solve **after** the last correction shows the solved center within tolerance of the target. A slew is never taken as proof of arrival.

`centerTarget` runs as an operation of the given scope and leases the camera and the mount per command. The target is a fixed J2000 (ICRS) coordinate. JNOW is not accepted, so a caller holding an equinox-of-date coordinate converts it first. The solver must return the ICRS center of a TAN or TAN-SIP solution (see [Plate Solution](#plate-solution)), which is compared with the target by great-circle distance. Each frame is solved with the astronomical midpoint of its exposure. Off target, the mount is either synced to the solved center and sent to the target, or sent from the position it reports, moved against the measured error. A limit of zero corrections only measures. Corrections that stop shrinking the distance end the run instead of looping.

The solver is a function of the caller (ASTAP, astrometry.net, a Worker, a process). It must yield the event loop and honor its abort signal. The timeout is cooperative: the solve is still awaited after the abort, and a solver that never ends is reported unresponsive and then faulted, so later centerings do not call it again. An observer can follow each step and veto a correction before anything is commanded.

```ts
import { tmpdir } from 'os'
import { join } from 'path'
import { astapPlateSolve } from 'nebulosa/src/astrometry/solvers/astap'
import { abortableDelay } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/operation.wait'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { centerTarget } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/mount/centering'

// coordinator, mountCommander, cameraCapturer, mount and camera as in Device Commanders and Device Camera Capture.
// capture: CenteringCaptureOptions — the exposure, binning and gain of the auxiliary frame.
const target = { frame: 'J2000', rightAscension: hour(5.5881), declination: deg(-5.3911) } as const

// Up to 3 frames and 2 corrections, centered within 1′, syncing the mount to each solution.
const result = await centerTarget(
	coordinator,
	mount,
	camera,
	target,
	{ tolerance: deg(1 / 60), maximumAttempts: 3, maximumCorrections: 2, settle: 2, syncMount: true, capture, solveTimeout: 60, abortGrace: 5 }, // rad, s
	{
		mountCommander,
		cameraCapturer,
		// Solves within 4° of the target, honoring the operation's abort signal.
		solver: (frame, signal) => astapPlateSolve(frame.path, { rightAscension: target.rightAscension, declination: target.declination, radius: deg(4) }, signal),
		auxiliaryPath: (attempt) => join(tmpdir(), `centering.${attempt}.fit`),
		clock: { wallNow: () => Date.now(), monotonicNow: () => performance.now(), delay: abortableDelay },
		observer: { measured: ({ attempt, separation }) => console.log(attempt, separation) }, // separation in rad
	},
)

console.log(result) // { ok: true, value: { attempts, separation, solution } } — final separation in radians
```

### Pointing Model Calibration Plan

A pointing model (see [Pointing Model Fit and Correction](#pointing-model-fit-and-correction)) is only as good as the sky its calibration samples cover. A term the samples do not constrain cannot be trusted, and a model fitted on one side of the pier says nothing about the other. `planPointingWaypoints` chooses where a calibration run should look. The pattern is either rings of altitude with points in proportion to their circumference, or a golden spiral with equal area per point. Waypoints stay within an altitude band, outside a free zone around the upper meridian, and inside a horizon mask and mount limits. The plan is pure and deterministic: it reads no device or clock, and the same options give the same plan.

A waypoint is fixed on the local sky as hour angle (positive west) and declination, so it keeps its azimuth and altitude however long the run takes. The caller turns it into a right ascension with the sidereal time at dispatch. Waypoints come in slew order, one side of the meridian after the other, so the mount flips at most once. The expected pier side is only a geometric prediction, so record the side the mount reports. Some waypoints are held out, spread by azimuth over both sides: they stay out of the fit and measure its predictions on sky it has not seen. When the allowed sky cannot hold the requested count, the plan is simply shorter.

```ts
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { planPointingWaypoints } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/mount/pointing.plan'

// 40 waypoints from Sao Paulo above 25°, 10° of hour angle away from the meridian and within ±75° of declination.
const plan = planPointingWaypoints({ pattern: 'goldenSpiral', count: 40, latitude: deg(-23.5), minimumAltitude: deg(25), meridianAvoidance: deg(10), limits: { declination: [deg(-75), deg(75)] } })
console.log(plan.waypoints.length, plan.heldOutCount, plan.pierSideCounts) // 40 8 and the split per side, about even

// The right ascension of a waypoint at dispatch, from the local sidereal time (rad); held-out waypoints stay out of the fit.
const [first] = plan.waypoints
const lst = deg(150)
console.log(lst - first.hourAngle, first.declination, first.role)
```

### Pointing Model Fit and Correction

A mount never points exactly where it is commanded. Its error is mostly systematic and mechanical: the optical axis is not perpendicular to the declination axis (collimation, `CH`); the encoders have zero-point offsets in hour angle and declination (`IH`, `ID`); the two axes are not perpendicular (`NP`); the polar axis is misaligned in azimuth and elevation (`MA`, `ME`); and the tube sags with the zenith distance (`TF`). These are the TPOINT terms. Fitted on pairs of commanded and plate-solved positions, they predict the error anywhere on the sky, and inverting them makes a command land on the requested position. The error is a tangent-plane offset at the target in radians, `dx` toward east and `dy` toward north, defined as `solved - target`.

`fitPointingModel` fits one of three strategies by weighted, regularized and robust least squares. The semi-physical model has the TPOINT terms above. The empirical model is a linear feature model of hour angle, declination, altitude and pier side. The default hybrid is the semi-physical model plus an empirical residual block. Terms that the observing context or the number of samples cannot support are dropped. Every sample must be in one declared frame, since a frame difference would enter as mechanical error. The leave-one-out RMS from real refits is the number to compare strategies with, because the in-sample RMS can only fall as parameters are added. `selectPointingStrategy` picks the strategy with the smallest one. Predictions report how well the target is surrounded by training samples and flag extrapolation. `correctPointingCoordinate` solves `command + error(command) = target` iteratively and clamps a wildly extrapolating correction. `MountPointing` collects samples and keeps the latest model, and its export can move the model to another instance.

The model describes the mechanics, not the atmosphere: refraction belongs to the astrometric layer, so keep samples and predictions in one frame. A mount without a calibration run of well-spread targets on both pier sides (see [Pointing Model Calibration Plan](#pointing-model-calibration-plan)) should use neither the hybrid empirical block nor the [Local Pointing Residuals](#local-pointing-residuals).

```ts
import { deg, hour, toArcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { applyPointingOffset, computePointingError, correctPointingCoordinate, fitPointingModel, MountPointing, predictPointingModelError, selectPointingStrategy } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/mount/pointing'
import { celestialToEncoders, encodersToCelestial } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/mount/pointing.pipeline'

// The error of one sample: target RA 3 h, DEC 40°, and its plate-solved solvedRightAscension, solvedDeclination (rad).
const error = computePointingError(hour(3), deg(40), solvedRightAscension, solvedDeclination)
console.log(toArcsec(error.dx), toArcsec(error.dy)) // arcsec east and north, solved minus target

// The inverse: the position at that offset from the target, here the solved position again.
console.log(applyPointingOffset(hour(3), deg(40), error.dx, error.dy)) // { rightAscension, declination } in radians

// samples: PointingSample[] — targets and solved positions with time, site and pier side, spread over both sides.
const model = fitPointingModel(samples, { strategy: 'semiPhysical' })
console.log(model.physical!.terms, model.physical!.parameters) // CH IH ID NP MA ME TF and their values (rad)
console.log(toArcsec(model.diagnostics.angularRms), toArcsec(model.diagnostics.looRms!)) // in-sample and leave-one-out RMS (arcsec)

// The strategy with the best leave-one-out RMS.
const best = selectPointingStrategy(samples)

// input: { rightAscension, declination, time, latitude, longitude, pierSide } of a new target.
const prediction = predictPointingModelError(best, input)
console.log(prediction.dx, prediction.dy, prediction.quality.extrapolating) // predicted error (rad) and whether the target is outside the sampled sky

// The command that makes the mount land on the target.
const corrected = correctPointingCoordinate(best, input)
console.log(corrected.rightAscension, corrected.declination, corrected.converged)

// The stateful collector: add samples as they are solved (model(sample, { fit: true }) also refits), fit, and predict or correct with the latest model.
const pointing = new MountPointing({ strategy: 'hybrid' })
for (const sample of samples) pointing.add(sample)
pointing.fit()
console.log(pointing.predictError(input), pointing.correctCoordinate(input))
console.log(pointing.state.sampleCount, pointing.diagnostics) // the collection and fit state, and the diagnostics of the latest fit

// The fitted model as a serializable structure (optionally with its samples), imported into another instance.
const exported = pointing.export({ includeSamples: true })
if (exported) new MountPointing().import(exported)

// chain: MountPointingChain — the mount geometry, its fitted base alignment (see Direction Alignment) and this model.
// The whole chain from a sky position to the encoders that reach it: the model error is inverted on the sky first, then the kinematics.
const encoders = celestialToEncoders(chain, input)
console.log(encoders.primary, encoders.secondary, encoders.correction.clamped) // encoder angles (rad), and whether the correction was truncated

// And back: the sky position the encoders actually point at, the predicted error included.
console.log(encodersToCelestial(chain, encoders, input))
```

### Polar Alignment Exposure Estimator

A residual polar misalignment limits how long a frame can be. The mechanical RA axis is fixed to the Earth, so while it turns at the sidereal rate `ω` around the misaligned axis instead of the true pole, every star moves with the residual angular velocity `ω (p_celestial − p_mount)`. Unguided, a star drifts at up to `2ω sin(e/2)` for a polar error `e`, whatever its direction. Ideal guiding with both axes holds the guide star still, but the field still rotates around it. A star at an angular distance `r` from the guide star then moves at the roll rate times `sin r`, so the sensor corner trails first. The estimator turns a residual polar error into the exposure for which this motion stays below an allowed trail, by default half a pixel.

It concerns only the polar misalignment, not periodic error, flexure or the star trails of an aligned mount that does not track. Directions are unit vectors in the ICRF frame of the plate solutions, and exposures are SI seconds. The unguided limit is reported both for the worst case and for a given target, integrating the changing rate over the exposure. The guided limit protects a field radius around the guide star and is singular for a guide star near the mechanical axis. An exposure of `Infinity` means that the trail is not reached within the search limit, as for an aligned axis; it is not a physically unlimited exposure. The limits are conservative planning values for smooth tracking with no other error, and the guided one assumes ideal guiding with no lag. `polarAlignmentExposureLimitForResult` starts from the result of [Three-Point Polar Alignment](#three-point-polar-alignment), so the target and guide directions must be those of the chosen start epoch.

```ts
import { eraS2c } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/erfa/erfa'
import { deg, toArcmin } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import {
	polarAlignmentExposureLimit,
	polarAlignmentExposureLimitForResult,
	polarAlignmentFieldRadius,
	polarAlignmentGuidedFieldRotationRate,
	polarAlignmentImageScale,
	polarAlignmentResidualAngularVelocity,
	polarAlignmentUnguidedDriftRate,
	polarAlignmentWorstCaseDriftRate,
} from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/exposure'

// mountPole, celestialPole: unit ICRF vectors (see Polar Alignment Geometry).
// The sampling: a 3.76 µm pixel behind a 400 mm telescope, and the corner of a 4144 × 2822 sensor.
const imageScale = polarAlignmentImageScale(3.76, 400) // rad/px, 1.939″
const fieldRadius = polarAlignmentFieldRadius(4144, 2822, imageScale) // rad, 1.35°

// The exposure limits for a target at RA 100°, DEC 20°, guided on a star at RA 103°, DEC 22°.
const target = eraS2c(deg(100), deg(20))
const guide = eraS2c(deg(103), deg(22))
const limit = polarAlignmentExposureLimit({ mountPole, celestialPole, imageScale, target, guiding: { guide, fieldRadius } })
console.log(toArcmin(limit.polarError)) // polar error (arcmin)
console.log(limit.unguided.worstCase, limit.unguided.target) // unguided exposure for any target and for this target (s)
console.log(limit.guided!.exposure) // guided exposure before field rotation trails the sensor corner (s)

// The instantaneous rates behind the limits: the residual angular velocity ω (p_celestial − p_mount) as a vector (rad/s),
// the drift of this target and of the worst target (rad/s), and the field roll around the guide star (rad/s, undefined near the axis).
console.log(polarAlignmentResidualAngularVelocity(mountPole, celestialPole))
console.log(polarAlignmentUnguidedDriftRate(mountPole, celestialPole, target), polarAlignmentWorstCaseDriftRate(mountPole, celestialPole))
console.log(polarAlignmentGuidedFieldRotationRate(mountPole, celestialPole, guide))

// alignment: ThreePointPolarAlignmentResult; the same estimate from its pole and time.
const fromResult = polarAlignmentExposureLimitForResult({ alignment: { pole: alignment.pole, time: alignment.time }, imageScale, target })
```

### Polar Alignment Geometry

Every polar-alignment method compares two directions: the mount pole, the mechanical right-ascension axis fixed to the Earth between adjustments of the base, and the celestial pole the axis should point at. It then expresses the difference as turns of the two knobs of the base, azimuth and altitude. This module holds that shared geometry for [Three-Point Polar Alignment](#three-point-polar-alignment), [DARV Polar Error Estimation](#darv-polar-error-estimation) and [Polar Alignment Overlay](#polar-alignment-overlay). Poles are unit vectors in the inertial ICRF frame of the plate solutions, and angles are radians. The target pole is geometric, or apparent with refraction; refraction raises both the mount pole and the target, so a displayed refracted pole must not be mixed with a geometric one. An Earth-fixed direction such as the mount pole is carried between two instants through ITRS.

The base moves only with its two knobs. The azimuth knob turns it about the local vertical, and the altitude knob turns it about the east axis carried by that rotation, so the knob order matters. Since the pole stands at an altitude equal to the latitude, an azimuth turn moves it on the sky by only the cosine of the latitude times its angle. `decomposePolarErrorGeodesic` splits a finite spherical error into the total separation and signed azimuth and altitude components along the positive knob rotations. Azimuth is measured north through east. The altitude error is the mount pole altitude minus the target altitude in the north, and the opposite in the south, so a hemisphere change flips the signed convention of the knobs. `solveAzAltAdjustment` finds, to small-angle accuracy, the two knob turns that explain the shift of a star. `polarAlignmentError` is the older two-star formula of Ralph Pass with the TPOINT terms. It predicts the right ascension and declination a mount shows for a given pole error.

```ts
import { geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { timeShift, timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { arcmin, deg, hour, toArcmin, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'
import {
	applyInverseMountAdjustment,
	applyMountAdjustment,
	celestialPoleVector,
	convertPolarAlignmentAltitudeError,
	decomposePolarErrorGeodesic,
	mountAdjustmentAxes,
	polarAlignmentError,
	polarAlignmentReferenceAltitude,
	solveAzAltAdjustment,
	transportEarthFixed,
} from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/polaralignment'

// A site at 22° N, 45° W and 800 m, at an instant.
const time = timeYMDHMS(2025, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)
const location = geodeticLocation(deg(-45), deg(22), meter(800))
time.location = location

// The geometric celestial pole (no refraction) and the local up and east axes, as ICRF unit vectors.
const celestialPole = celestialPoleVector(time, location, false)
const { upAxis, eastAxis } = mountAdjustmentAxes(time, location)

// A base 3′ off in azimuth and -10′ in altitude: its pole is the celestial one turned by the two knobs.
const mountPole = applyMountAdjustment(celestialPole, upAxis, eastAxis, arcmin(3), arcmin(-10))

// The total error and its signed components (arcmin); the 3′ knob moves the pole only cos(22°) of it on the sky.
const error = decomposePolarErrorGeodesic(mountPole, celestialPole, upAxis, eastAxis)!
console.log(toArcmin(error.total), toArcmin(error.azimuth), toArcmin(error.altitude)) // 10.38 2.785 -10

// from, to: unit ICRF directions of a star before and after an adjustment of the base; the knob turns that explain the shift.
const knobs = solveAzAltAdjustment(from, to, upAxis, eastAxis)
console.log(knobs.azimuthAdjustment, knobs.altitudeAdjustment) // rad

// The same knob turns undone, in reverse order: the celestial pole again.
console.log(applyInverseMountAdjustment(mountPole, upAxis, eastAxis, arcmin(3), arcmin(-10)))

// The mount pole is fixed to the Earth: the same axis one hour later, as an ICRF vector of that instant.
const later = timeShift(time, 1 / 24)
later.location = location
console.log(transportEarthFixed(mountPole, time, later))

// The altitude of the target pole, geometric (22°) or refracted (22.039°), and a geometric -10′ altitude error as the refracted display shows it.
console.log(toDeg(polarAlignmentReferenceAltitude(deg(22), false)), toDeg(polarAlignmentReferenceAltitude(deg(22))))
console.log(toArcmin(convertPolarAlignmentAltitudeError(arcmin(-10), deg(22)))) // -9.98

// The two-star formula: the RA and DEC (rad) a mount with this pole error shows for a target at RA 6 h, DEC 30°, at a sidereal time of 5 h.
console.log(polarAlignmentError(hour(6), deg(30), deg(22), hour(5), arcmin(3), arcmin(-10)))
```

### Polar Alignment Overlay

After a three-point polar alignment (see [Three-Point Polar Alignment](#three-point-polar-alignment)) measures where the mount pole is, the operator corrects it by turning the two knobs of the base while watching the live image. An on-screen guide makes that practical. It shows where a reference star is now, where the azimuth knob alone should bring it, and where both knobs should bring it. It also draws closed contours of constant residual polar error, so the operator sees how close is close enough. `computeThreePointPolarAlignmentOverlay` computes that geometry from the alignment result and the plate solution of the latest frame. It does no rendering and has no DOM dependency.

The remaining correction is solved in inertial 3D as the two base rotations of [Polar Alignment Geometry](#polar-alignment-geometry), azimuth about local up and then altitude about the carried east axis. They bring the mount pole to the target pole, refracted or geometric. The reference is then projected through the complete TAN or TAN-SIP WCS of the solution (see [Plate Solution](#plate-solution)), so lens distortion is included. The time, the WCS and the pole must describe the same exposure. Points outside the frame keep their true position and get a marker on the border, and a contour that cannot be projected whole is omitted rather than drawn partially. The segments are not the path of the mount: the knob order is azimuth first, then altitude, and for a large error the two components are exact but not additive. Choose a reference star that stays in the frame after the correction.

```ts
import { arcmin, toArcmin } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { computeThreePointPolarAlignmentOverlay } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/tppa.overlay'

// alignment: ThreePointPolarAlignmentResult with the current mount pole; solution: PlateSolution of the latest frame;
// time: its exposure Time carrying the observing location.
// A reference star chosen by pixel, against the geometric pole, with contours at 30″, 1′ and 5′.
const result = computeThreePointPolarAlignmentOverlay(alignment, solution, time, { refraction: false, reference: { type: 'pixel', point: { x: 600, y: 200 } }, tolerances: [arcmin(0.5), arcmin(1), arcmin(5)] })

if (result.success) {
	const { overlay } = result
	// The knob turns still needed (arcmin) and the exact geodesic error.
	console.log(toArcmin(overlay.correction.azimuth), toArcmin(overlay.correction.altitude), toArcmin(overlay.error.total))
	// The star now, after the azimuth knob, and after both knobs (WCS pixels; each point's display keeps its marker inside the frame).
	console.log(overlay.currentPoint.position, overlay.azimuthTargetPoint.position, overlay.targetPoint.position)
	// The segments to draw and the closed contours of constant residual error.
	console.log(overlay.azimuthSegment, overlay.altitudeSegment, overlay.contours)
}
```

### Solar System Guide Tracking

A star is a point source, and its centroid is its position. A planet, the Moon or the Sun is an extended object that often fills the field, has no star around it in a short exposure, and is distorted frame to frame by the seeing, so the guide position has to be measured from the object itself. Two measurements complement each other: [Surface Registration](#surface-registration) follows the relative motion of the surface texture (many textured patches with a robust rigid fit, so field rotation is measured too), and [Disk Limb Fitting](#disk-limb-fitting) anchors the absolute center when the whole disk is visible. Because there is no star detector, the main imaging camera, running short exposures at a high frame rate, can be the guide camera.

`SolarSystemTracker` implements the generic tracker contract of [Guide Star Tracking](#guide-star-tracking), so it plugs into the [Guide Pulse Loop](#guide-pulse-loop) and the guide client like the stellar tracker. Its `planetary` mode publishes the limb-fitted center of the disk, fused with the surface motion; the `lunar` and `solar` modes follow one point of the surface, since the limb of the Moon or the Sun is usually outside a high-resolution field. Without a usable limb, the object center is the apparent bright-object center, which is not the physical center of a crescent or a ringed planet, and a moving terminator or a partial phase biases it. The guide plane can be chosen automatically by contrast, for example red on a one-shot-color H-alpha frame (see [Image Analysis Planes](#image-analysis-planes)).

Coordinates are full-frame image pixels with pixel centers at integers, origin at the upper left, +X right and +Y down; rotations are radians from +X toward +Y. `track()` only stages its updates: the acquisition, the new transform and the keyframes become the reference on `commit()`, which the guide client calls for accepted frames, so a rejected frame never advances the reference. The motion model is rigid (no scale), repeated or featureless texture is rejected as ambiguous, and the limb needs an object brighter than its background.

The tracker measures atmospheric tip-tilt as image motion; it is not adaptive optics. Guide with a correction interval of a second or more and a deadband (see [Guide Pulse Loop](#guide-pulse-loop)), so the seeing jitter is averaged and only the mount drift is corrected. Software guiding does not make Solar observation safe: observe and image the Sun only through appropriate, certified Solar filtration.

```ts
import { GuiderClient } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/client'
import { SolarSystemTracker, solarSystemTrackingOf } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/tracker.solarsystem'

// image0, image1: Image — decoded 320 × 320 short exposures of the Moon, 500 ms apart.
// The Lunar preset follows a surface point; 'planetary' follows the limb-fitted disk center.
const tracker = new SolarSystemTracker({ mode: 'lunar' })

// The first frame acquires the surface, and commit() makes it the anchor.
const first = tracker.track({ image: image0, width: 320, height: 320, timestamp: 0, frameId: 0 }, { phase: 'looping', allowAcquisition: true, preserveIdentity: false })
tracker.commit()
console.log(first.measurement, first.targetEnvelope) // target in pixels, and the bounds inside which it stays measurable

// Later frames register against the reference: the target is carried by the fitted rigid transform.
const next = tracker.track({ image: image1, width: 320, height: 320, timestamp: 500, frameId: 1 }, { phase: 'guiding', allowAcquisition: true, preserveIdentity: true })
tracker.commit()
console.log(next.measurement, solarSystemTrackingOf(next)?.state) // target in pixels; acquiring, tracking, degraded or lost

// A target chosen on that result: the limb center or a clicked surface point inside the measurable envelope (undefined when declined).
console.log(tracker.select(tracker.lastResult!, [160, 120]))

// Forgets the plane, anchor, keyframes and limb model, for a new object.
tracker.reset()

// In a guide session, the guide client drives track() and commit() itself.
// cameraManager, guideOutputManager: the device managers; decodeImage: GuideImageDecoder.
const guider = new GuiderClient(cameraManager, guideOutputManager, new SolarSystemTracker({ mode: 'planetary' }), { decodeImage })
```

### Taki Mount Geometry

A real equatorial or alt-azimuth mount is never built perfectly. Toshimi Taki's matrix method models its three fabrication errors as small rotations: the non-perpendicularity of the secondary axis to the primary axis (Taki D), the collimation (cone) error of the optical axis away from the plane perpendicular to the secondary axis (Taki D'), and the index offset of the secondary encoder (Taki D''). In a classical pointing model the first two appear as hour-angle errors that change with the declination, so a single zero-point offset cannot remove them; modeling them lets a mount point (or be inverted) accurately across the sky.

`applyTakiFabricationErrors` turns those three angles, in radians, into the vector geometry consumed by [Mount Kinematics](#mount-kinematics): it tilts the secondary axis and the optical direction and adds the index offset, keeping the primary axis, so the same kinematic functions compute the pointing of the imperfect mount. The errors are small angles in the sense of equation 5.3-1 of Matrix Method, revision E, and their signs follow that convention and the canonical Taki frame (see [Local Taki Frames](#local-taki-frames)), so errors measured in another convention must be converted. It models only these three errors: the polar misalignment (a rotation of the base) and flexure are not included.

```ts
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { createCanonicalEquatorialGeometry, mountDirectionFromEncoders, solveMountEncoders } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/mount/kinematics'
import { applyTakiFabricationErrors } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/mount/kinematics.taki'

// A mount with 0.1° of non-perpendicularity, 0.2° of collimation and 0.05° of secondary index.
const nominal = createCanonicalEquatorialGeometry()
const real = applyTakiFabricationErrors(nominal, { axisNonPerpendicularity: deg(0.1), collimation: deg(0.2), secondaryIndex: deg(0.05) })

// The pointing at an hour angle of 40° and a declination of 25°, ideal and real (unit vectors).
const encoders = { primary: deg(40), secondary: deg(25) }
const ideal = mountDirectionFromEncoders(nominal, encoders)
const actual = mountDirectionFromEncoders(real, encoders)
console.log(ideal, actual) // [0.694272, -0.582563, 0.422618] and [0.695754, -0.580215, 0.423412], about 596″ apart

// The inverse: the encoders this mount needs to point at the ideal direction.
const solution = solveMountEncoders(real, ideal)
console.log(solution.converged, solution.primary, solution.secondary) // true 0.701169 0.435456 — radians (40.17404° and 24.94982°)
```

### Three-Point Polar Alignment

The right ascension axis of an equatorial mount must be parallel to the Earth's rotation axis, or the stars drift in declination and the field rotates during tracking. Three-point polar alignment measures the misalignment from three plate solves taken while the mount turns only in right ascension, without any knowledge of the stars or the declination readout: the three sky directions lie on a small circle around the mechanical axis, and the normal to their plane is that axis. Comparing it with the celestial pole gives the azimuth and altitude errors that the user corrects with the knobs of the base, and each new plate solve of the same field after a knob turn refreshes the estimate.

The inputs are `[rightAscension, declination, time]` with the ICRF (J2000) coordinates of the solution in radians and the `Time` of the exposure carrying the observer location; the first two points are carried to the epoch of the third through the rotation of the Earth, so the solves may be minutes apart and the mount may track meanwhile. The azimuth error is signed north through east in the northern hemisphere and reversed in the south, and the altitude error is the observed altitude of the mount pole minus that of the target, with the sign reversed in the south. Refraction changes only the displayed azimuth and altitude, not the mechanical axis. Coincident or collinear points do not define a plane and give no estimate.

The precision depends on the rotation between solves: the seed pole error is about `2.4·σ/φ²` for a per-axis astrometric error `σ` and a rotation `φ` between consecutive solves, whatever the declination, and fields within about 10° of the pole do not separate the mechanical rotation from the celestial one. `tppa.geometry` checks those conditions, and `tppa.runner` acquires the three solves automatically with the mount and camera commanders and refines the estimate afterwards; the runner never restores the slew rate it changed, which is left to the caller. The refresh after a knob turn requires no declination motion, guiding, dither, pier side change or tracking rate change between the two exposures, and the tracking rate must match the mount (0 when the tracking is off). The correction is drawn on the image by the [Polar Alignment Overlay](#polar-alignment-overlay), and the shared geometry is in [Polar Alignment Geometry](#polar-alignment-geometry).

```ts
import { deg, toArcmin } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { ThreePointPolarAlignment, threePointPolarAlignmentAfterAdjustment, threePointPolarAlignmentError } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/tppa'
import { polarAlignmentGeometryQuality } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/tppa.geometry'
import { acquireThreePointPolarAlignment, refineThreePointPolarAlignment } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/alignment/tppa.runner'

// p1, p2, p3: ThreePointPolarAlignmentInput — three solves taken while rotating west only in right ascension;
// p4: a new solve of the same field after a knob turn.
// Checks that the rotations and separations give a well-conditioned pole.
console.log(polarAlignmentGeometryQuality(p1, p2, p3, 'WEST').acceptable)

// Fits the mechanical axis and compares it with the observed celestial pole (false for a degenerate triple).
const initial = threePointPolarAlignmentError(p1, p2, p3)

if (initial) {
	console.log(toArcmin(initial.azimuthError), toArcmin(initial.altitudeError)) // arcminutes

	// Infers the knob rotations from the shift of the field and gives the remaining error of the pole.
	const after = threePointPolarAlignmentAfterAdjustment(initial, p3, p4)
```
