```ts
	console.log(toArcmin(after.azimuthError), toArcmin(after.altitudeError)) // arcminutes
}

// The stateful session: false until the third solve, then the estimate, refreshed by every later solve.
const session = new ThreePointPolarAlignment()
for (const [rightAscension, declination, time] of [p1, p2, p3, p4]) console.log(session.add(rightAscension, declination, time))
session.reset()

// With devices: coordinator, mount and camera as in Device Commanders; capture: CenteringCaptureOptions of the auxiliary frames;
// services: the mount commander, camera capturer, solver, auxiliaryPath(stage, index), clock, site location and listener, as in Plate-Solved Centering.
// Turns the RA axis west by timed motions at the SLOW preset until three solves are accepted (durations in seconds).
const acquired = await acquireThreePointPolarAlignment(coordinator, mount, camera, { direction: 'WEST', slewRate: 'SLOW', capture, settle: 1, initialMotion: 2, maximumMotion: 30, maximumAttempts: 6, solveTimeout: 60, abortGrace: 5 }, services)

if (acquired.ok) {
	const { alignment, points, pierSide, result } = acquired.value
	console.log(toArcmin(result.azimuthError), toArcmin(result.altitudeError)) // the initial estimate, in arcminutes
	// Solves new frames while the knobs are turned, until cancelled, reporting each refreshed estimate through the listener; it never moves the mount.
	await refineThreePointPolarAlignment(coordinator, mount, camera, alignment, points[2], pierSide, { capture, delay: 1, maximumFailures: 3, maximumShift: deg(1), solveTimeout: 60, abortGrace: 5 }, services)
}
```

### Tracking Rate Correction

A non-sidereal target (a comet, an asteroid or a satellite) is tracked with a feed-forward rate computed from its ephemeris, but an orbit is never exact: an old orbit solution or TLE leaves a residual drift that the images reveal. The rate controller turns that measured residual (observed minus ephemeris, from [Tracking Rate Estimation](#tracking-rate-estimation)) into a bounded correction added to the feed-forward rate of [Non-Sidereal Guide Tracking](#non-sidereal-guide-tracking), so the images can trim the prediction of a target without ever replacing it.

Rates are sky-plane `[east, north]` vectors in radians per second; the conversion to the rates of the device axes belongs to the mount adapter. The correction follows the residual through a first-order low-pass filter with a deadband, a magnitude clip and a limit on the change per update, so a noisy estimate cannot kick the mount; an estimate that is stale or of low confidence is ignored and the correction decays toward zero instead of holding a value that is no longer verified. Reset the controller for a new target, a change of the camera transform or a meridian flip. The controller knows neither the physical limits of the mount nor the lag of the images, so its limits must be set to rates the mount can follow and the tracker can verify.

```ts
import { arcsec } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { TrackingRateController } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/nonsidereal.rate.controller'

// estimate: TrackingRateEstimate — a residual of [0.3, -0.1] arcsec/s with confidence 1, from TrackingRateEstimator.
// The feed-forward rate of the ephemeris, [east, north] in radians per second.
const feedForward = [arcsec(15), 0] as const
const controller = new TrackingRateController()

// One update every 10 s: the correction moves toward the residual within the limits.
const command = controller.update(feedForward, estimate, 10)
console.log(command?.rate.map((rate) => rate / arcsec(1))) // [15.25, -0.0833] arcsec/s, feed-forward plus correction
console.log(command?.correction, command?.limited) // [east, north] rad/s, and whether a limit altered the request

// A new target, a changed camera transform or a meridian flip starts from zero.
controller.reset()
```

### Tracking Rate Estimation

To follow a moving target, the guider needs its sky motion: the east and north rates, and sometimes their change. The estimator fits that motion to a short series of position observations, which may come from plate-solved positions, the shift of the target in the image, the drift of the background stars (the target moved the opposite way), or a streak trailed during a long exposure. Positions are local east and north offsets in radians from a fixed tangent-plane anchor, times are astronomical times (preferably the exposure midpoint), rates are radians per second and accelerations radians per second squared. Pixel measurements are converted to the sky through an image transform (from a WCS or a guiding calibration, with rotation and parity).

The fit is a robust weighted straight line per axis, which clips outliers; a quadratic is tried for long spans when acceleration fitting is enabled, as for a satellite pass. When each sample also carries the ephemeris prediction, the fit is of the residual observed minus predicted, which is what [Tracking Rate Correction](#tracking-rate-correction) needs; a series cannot mix both modes. A single streak has no sense of direction (its two ends look alike), so a streak without a known direction gives no rate. The estimator models a smooth motion in a local plane: a short or noisy series, a non-smooth maneuver or a transform that does not match the camera give a poor rate, so a consumer must check the confidence and never use a stale estimate. `EstimatorNonSiderealMotionProvider` adapts an ephemeris-free estimator as the local motion source of [Non-Sidereal Guide Tracking](#non-sidereal-guide-tracking).

```ts
import { arcsec, deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { EstimatorNonSiderealMotionProvider, TrackingRateEstimator, trackingMotionSampleFromAstrometry, trackingMotionSampleFromBackgroundStars, trackingMotionSampleFromImage, trackingRateFromStreak, type TrackingImageTransform } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/guiding/nonsidereal.rate'

// A guide camera of 2″ per pixel whose +X is east and +Y is south.
const transform: TrackingImageTransform = { pixelDeltaToSky: ([dx, dy]) => [arcsec(2 * dx), arcsec(-2 * dy)] }

// solves: { time: Time, position: EquatorialCoordinate }[] — plate-solved target positions; now: Time.
const anchor = { rightAscension: deg(100), declination: deg(20) }
const estimator = new TrackingRateEstimator()
for (const { time, position } of solves) estimator.add(trackingMotionSampleFromAstrometry(time, anchor, position))

// A target shift of (5, -3) pixels is another kind of sample.
console.log(trackingMotionSampleFromImage(now, [5, -3], transform)?.offset) // [10″, 6″] east and north, in radians

// So is the median drift of three or more background stars matched by id ({ id, x, y } in pixels): the target moved the opposite way.
const reference = [0, 1, 2].map((id) => ({ id: String(id), x: 40 * id, y: 30 }))
const current = reference.map((star) => ({ ...star, x: star.x - 2 }))
console.log(trackingMotionSampleFromBackgroundStars(now, reference, current, transform)?.offset) // [4″, 0] east and north, in radians

// The fitted motion at a time: rate in rad/s, with its confidence from 0 to 1.
const estimate = estimator.estimate(now)
console.log(estimate?.rate, estimate?.confidence, estimate?.stale)
console.log(estimator.generation) // changes when the series is cleared, so a tracker can drop an anchor of the old series

// A 12-pixel target streak in X during 60 s with a known direction.
console.log(trackingRateFromStreak(now, { axisPixels: [12, 0], exposureSeconds: 60, role: 'target', direction: 1 }, transform)?.rate) // [0.4″/s, 0] in rad/s

// The local motion source of the non-sidereal tracker.
const provider = new EstimatorNonSiderealMotionProvider(estimator)
console.log(provider.motion(now)) // offset, rate and confidence, or undefined without a fresh fit

// A new target starts a new series: provider.reset() clears the estimator it adapts, as estimator.reset() does.
provider.reset()
```

### Weather Quality

Clouds absorb the starlight, humidity and dew fog the optics, wind shakes the telescope and blurs the stars, and rain ends the session. A weather station reports these conditions in physical units, and an imaging session needs one number to decide whether to start, pause or stop. `weatherQualityScore` turns one reading into an imaging quality from 0 (unusable) to 1 (no penalty), independently of the driver that produced it.

Each available sensor gives a factor that falls from 1 to 0 between a safe and an unusable value: cloud cover, relative humidity, the faster of the sustained wind and the gust, and the dew margin (the ambient temperature minus the dew point, in degrees Celsius; optics that cool by radiation below the air temperature dew up before the air reaches saturation). The score is the geometric mean of the factors that were given, so an absent sensor is neither punished nor invented while one bad factor drags the score down; any rain gives 0. The thresholds are planning values for imaging, not a meteorological model or a forecast; they do not know the dome, the wind direction or the telescope, and a stale reading should be discarded by the caller.

```ts
import { weatherQualityScore } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/weather'

// A clear, dry and calm reading has no penalty.
console.log(weatherQualityScore({ cloudCoverPercent: 0, humidityPercent: 50, windSpeedMetersPerSecond: 2, dewMarginCelsius: 8 })) // 1

// Factors combine by the geometric mean: 50% of clouds (0.5) and 85% of humidity (0.5).
console.log(weatherQualityScore({ cloudCoverPercent: 50, humidityPercent: 85 })) // 0.5

// Gusts count as wind, and any rain wins over a clear sky.
console.log(weatherQualityScore({ windSpeedMetersPerSecond: 3, windGustMetersPerSecond: 12 })) // 0.3
console.log(weatherQualityScore({ cloudCoverPercent: 0, rainRateMillimetersPerHour: 0.1 })) // 0
```

## 📖 Catalogs

### ASTAP Tiled Catalog

ASTAP (the plate solver and photometry program) distributes its star databases `d05`, `d20`, `d50` and `d80` as `.1476` files: the sky is cut in 1476 tiles of about 5° (36 declination bands of 5.143° and two polar caps), and each tile `<database>_BBCC.1476` holds the Gaia stars of that region, sorted from the brightest, in the packed record format that [Tiled Sky Catalog](#tiled-sky-catalog) describes. A plate solver reads only the few tiles of its field, and the brightness order lets it stop at a limiting magnitude. The databases differ in star density and limiting magnitude (`d05` is the smallest), the magnitude is the Gaia BP one, and the Gaia color variant also carries a Johnson B−V color.

Positions have the epoch written in the tile header (`Epoch=2025` in the d05 sample) and no proper motion, so they are not J2000 positions. The tile functions select a square field (`|Δα·cos δ| < radius` and `|Δδ| < radius`), not a cone; `AstapCatalog` exposes the tiles through the exact geometry of [Star Catalog Interface and Spatial Query](#star-catalog-interface-and-spatial-query). A query returns only what the tiles in the collection have, so a field whose tiles are not loaded is empty or partial without an error.

```ts
import { astap1476AreaFile, findAstap1476Areas, findAstap1476Region, findAstap1476Stars, openAstapCatalog, readAstap1476Area, readAstap1476Header } from 'nebulosa/src/catalogs/stars/astap'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The tile files of a square field of 1° half width at RA 0.1°, Dec 0°, and the tile of an area number (1 to 1476).
console.log(findAstap1476Areas(deg(0.1), deg(0), deg(1)).map((area) => area.fileName)) // [ "1901.1476", "1969.1476", "1801.1476", "1869.1476" ]
console.log(astap1476AreaFile(1476).fileName) // 3601.1476 — the north polar cap

// files: tile buffers or File objects keyed by name; here the d05 south polar cap.
const files = { 'd05_0101.1476': Buffer.from(await Bun.file('data/d05_0101.1476').arrayBuffer()) }

// The stars of a square field, sorted from the brightest, down to magnitude 10.5.
const query = { rightAscension: 0, declination: deg(-89.5), radius: deg(0.5), magnitudeLimit: 10.5 }
const bright = await findAstap1476Stars(files, 'd05', query)
console.log(bright.length) // 4

// The same search with the touched areas and their headers; findAstap1476Stars keeps only its stars.
console.log((await findAstap1476Region(files, 'd05', query)).areas.length) // 1

// One tile by hand: its header (description, record size, epoch), then the stars of the field in it.
const header = readAstap1476Header(files['d05_0101.1476'])
console.log(header.epoch, [...readAstap1476Area(header, files['d05_0101.1476'], 1, query)].length) // 2025 4

// The same tiles as a star catalog with an exact cone.
using catalog = openAstapCatalog(files, 'd05')
console.log((await catalog.queryCone(0, deg(-89.5), deg(0.5))).length) // 374
```

### Hipparcos Catalog

The ESA Hipparcos satellite (1989–1993) made the first space astrometry survey, and its main catalog (`hip_main.dat`, CDS I/239) has about 118 thousand stars with positions, parallaxes and proper motions at the milliarcsecond level, in the ICRS at the epoch J1991.25. It is the reference for the bright stars and the source of many later catalogs. The reader streams the pipe-delimited file in constant memory and gives positions in radians, the V magnitude, the parallax in radians (a negative value is kept as measured) and the proper motions in radians per Julian year; rows with a missing identifier or position are skipped. There is no radial velocity.

The catalog publishes `μα* = dα/dt·cos δ`, and the reader divides by `cos δ` so that `pmRA` is `dα/dt`, as the other catalogs and `star` expect; at a pole that direction is undefined and `pmRA` is left out. `HipparcosCatalog` indexes the entries for the queries of [HEALPix Object Index](#healpix-object-index) and [Star Catalog Interface and Spatial Query](#star-catalog-interface-and-spatial-query). The positions are at J1991.25: to compare them with a J2000 or current-date sky, apply the proper motion first (see [Stellar Space Motion](#stellar-space-motion)).

```ts
import fs from 'fs/promises'
import { HipparcosCatalog, readHipparcosCatalog } from 'nebulosa/src/catalogs/stars/hipparcos'
import { fileHandleSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/file'
import { deg, toMas } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Streams the file, keeping only the entry being read.
await using source = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/hip_main.dat', 'r'))

for await (const entry of readHipparcosCatalog(source)) {
	if (entry.id === 32349) console.log(entry.epoch, entry.magnitude, toMas(entry.parallax!), toMas(entry.pmDEC!)) // 1991.25 -1.44 379.21 -1223.08 (Sirius, mas and mas/yr)
}

// Indexes the whole catalog and queries a cone of 5° around Sirius.
await using file = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/hip_main.dat', 'r'))
const catalog = new HipparcosCatalog({ nside: 16 })
await catalog.load(file)

const stars = catalog.queryCone(deg(101.28854105), deg(-16.71314306), deg(5))
console.log(stars.length, catalog.get(32349)?.metadata?.magnitude) // 255 -1.44
```

### HNSKY Tiled Catalog

HNSKY (and the Cartes du Ciel / SkyChart programs) use the `.290` star databases `g14` and `g16`, which hold the Gaia stars up to magnitude 14 and 16: the sky is cut in 290 tiles (18 declination bands, with caps of 4.8° and equatorial bands of 12.8°), and each file `<database>_BBCC.290` holds the stars of one tile, sorted from the brightest, in the packed format described in [Tiled Sky Catalog](#tiled-sky-catalog). Depending on the record size, a tile also carries a Gaia BP−RP color or a packed Tycho-2 (`TYC 1234-42-1`) or UCAC4 (`UCAC4 321-12345`) designation. The magnitude is the Gaia BP one, the positions have the `Epoch=` of the file (J2000 when absent), and there is no proper motion.

The functions mirror those of [ASTAP Tiled Catalog](#astap-tiled-catalog): the tile functions select a square field (`|Δα·cos δ| < radius`, `|Δδ| < radius`), and `HnskyCatalog` exposes the tiles through the exact geometry of [Star Catalog Interface and Spatial Query](#star-catalog-interface-and-spatial-query). A tile that is not in the collection is skipped without an error, so a field whose tiles are missing is empty or partial.

```ts
import { decodeHnsky290Designation, findHnsky290Areas, findHnsky290Region, findHnsky290Stars, hnsky290AreaFile, openHnskyCatalog, readHnsky290Area, readHnsky290Header } from 'nebulosa/src/catalogs/stars/hnsky'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The tiles of a square field of 4° half width across a right ascension cell border, and the tile of an area number (1 to 290).
console.log(findHnsky290Areas(deg(11.1), deg(5), deg(4)).map((area) => area.fileName)) // [ "1002.290", "1001.290" ]
console.log(hnsky290AreaFile(1).fileName) // 0101.290 — the south polar cap

// The g14 database as a Map of File objects keyed g14_0201.290, read from its tar archive.
const files = await new Bun.Archive(await Bun.file('data/HNSKY_g14.tar').arrayBuffer()).files()

// The stars of a square field of 0.5° half width at RA 0, Dec 0, sorted from the brightest.
const query = { rightAscension: 0, declination: 0, radius: deg(0.5) }
const stars = await findHnsky290Stars(files, 'g14', query)
console.log(stars.length, stars[0].magnitude) // 97 7.1

// The same search with the touched areas and their headers.
const region = await findHnsky290Region(files, 'g14', query)
console.log(region.areas.map((area) => area.fileName)) // [ "1001.290", "1032.290", "0901.290", "0932.290" ]

// One tile by hand: its header (description, record size, epoch), then the stars of the field in it.
const area = region.areas[0]
const buffer = Buffer.from(await files.get(`g14_${area.fileName}`)!.arrayBuffer())
const header = readHnsky290Header(buffer)
console.log(header.epoch, [...readHnsky290Area(header, buffer, area.area, query)].length) // 2025 27 — Julian year, stars of the field in this tile

// The same tiles as a star catalog with an exact cone.
using catalog = openHnskyCatalog(files, 'g14')
console.log((await catalog.queryCone(0, 0, deg(0.5))).length) // 84

// A packed designation: UCAC4 for a non-negative value, Tycho-2 otherwise.
console.log(decodeHnsky290Designation((321 << 20) | 12345).label) // UCAC4 321-12345
```

### HYG Catalog

The HYG database merges the Hipparcos, Yale Bright Star and Gliese catalogs into one CSV of about 119 thousand stars with identifiers and physical data, which makes it the catalog to use when a star needs a name: proper names, Bayer and Flamsteed designations, HIP, HD and HR numbers, the constellation, the spectral type and the distance. The astrometry is at J2000, with positions and proper motions in radians and radians per year, the radial velocity in AU per day (converted from the km/s of the file) and the distance in AU; there is no parallax.

The file publishes `μα* = dα/dt·cos δ` and the reader divides by `cos δ`, so `pmRA` is `dα/dt` (0 at a pole). A blank or out-of-range distance and a blank radial velocity are read as 0, so they cannot be told from a measured zero, and a missing magnitude is 99. `HygCatalog` indexes the rows for the queries of [HEALPix Object Index](#healpix-object-index) and [Star Catalog Interface and Spatial Query](#star-catalog-interface-and-spatial-query), keyed by the HYG `id`, which is not the HIP number.

```ts
import fs from 'fs/promises'
import { HygCatalog, readHygCatalog } from 'nebulosa/src/catalogs/stars/hyg'
import { fileHandleSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/file'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Streams the CSV until Sirius, the star with the HYG id 32263.
await using source = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/hyg_v42.csv', 'r'))

for await (const star of readHygCatalog(source)) {
	if (star.id !== 32263) continue
	console.log(star.name, star.hip, star.bayer, star.constellation, star.spType, star.magnitude) // Sirius 32349 Alp CMA A0m... -1.44
	break
}

// Indexes every row: a lookup by HYG id and the named stars of a cone of 1° around the Orion Nebula.
await using file = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/hyg_v42.csv', 'r'))
const catalog = new HygCatalog()
await catalog.load(file)

console.log(catalog.get(0)?.metadata?.name) // Sol
console.log(
	catalog
		.queryCone(deg(83.8), deg(-5.39), deg(1))
		.map((star) => star.metadata!.name)
		.filter(Boolean),
) // [ "Hatysa" ]
```

### SAO Catalog

The Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory (SAO) star catalog, compiled in the 1960s, has about 259 thousand stars to roughly magnitude 9 with a two-character spectral type, and is distributed as the binary file `SAO.pc.dat` (the Harvard TDC layout, little endian for the PC files and big endian for the UNIX ones, which the reader must be told). Its positions are B1950 mean positions in the FK4 system, not J2000, and must be converted (see [Celestial and Terrestrial Reference Frames](#celestial-and-terrestrial-reference-frames)) before they are compared with a modern frame or catalog.

The proper motion of the file is already `dα/dt` in radians per year, so unlike the other catalogs it is not divided by `cos δ`. `SaoCatalog` indexes the stars by SAO number for the queries of [HEALPix Object Index](#healpix-object-index) and [Star Catalog Interface and Spatial Query](#star-catalog-interface-and-spatial-query), and a cone is therefore a cone in the B1950 frame.

```ts
import fs from 'fs/promises'
import { readSaoCatalog, SaoCatalog } from 'nebulosa/src/catalogs/stars/sao'
import { fileHandleSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/file'
import { deg, formatDEC, formatRA } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Streams the little-endian PC file.
await using source = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/SAO.pc.dat'))

for await (const star of readSaoCatalog(source, false)) {
	if (star.id === 1) console.log(star.epoch, formatRA(star.rightAscension), formatDEC(star.declination), star.magnitude, star.spType) // B1950 00 00 05.10 +82 41 41.82 7.2 A0
}

// Indexes the whole file: a cone of 1° around the Orion Nebula, in B1950 coordinates.
await using file = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/SAO.pc.dat'))
const catalog = new SaoCatalog()
await catalog.load(file, false)

console.log(catalog.size, catalog.queryCone(deg(83.8), deg(-5.39), deg(1)).length) // 258997 55
```

### Star Catalog Interface and Spatial Query

Every star catalog of the toolkit, local or remote, answers the same `StarCatalog` interface, so the code that consumes stars (crossmatching, framing, annotation) does not depend on where they come from. An entry is an equatorial position, `rightAscension` and `declination` in radians (J2000 unless the catalog says otherwise), with an optional epoch (Julian year), magnitude, proper motion (radians per year, `pmRA` as `dα/dt`), radial velocity and parallax. A region is a cone, a box, a triangle or a convex polygon, given to its own method or as a tagged query, which may also bound the magnitude and limit the count; `streamRegion` yields the same entries one by one, so a dense field does not have to be held in memory.

The geometry is exact and the same for every catalog. A cone is a spherical cap, and a box spans a declination range and a right ascension range that may wrap across 0 (as in `359.7°` to `0.3°`). A triangle or a polygon is tested on a tangent plane centered on its vertices, so it suits fields of tens of degrees or less, except that a region that contains or touches a pole is tested with great-circle edges; a non-convex polygon is not supported.

`BaseStarCatalog` is the base class of the concrete catalogs: a subclass only streams the candidate entries that fall in one or two non-wrapping RA/Dec preselection boxes covering the region, tolerantly at their edges, and the base class applies the exact test, the magnitude bounds and the limit. A remote provider may also send those boxes and bounds to its service.

```ts
import { BaseStarCatalog, type NormalizedStarCatalogQuery, normalizeStarCatalogQuery, type StarCatalogEntry } from 'nebulosa/src/catalogs/stars/catalog'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// An in-memory catalog: it streams the stars inside the preselection boxes, and the base class does the rest.
class ListCatalog extends BaseStarCatalog<StarCatalogEntry> {
	constructor(readonly stars: readonly StarCatalogEntry[]) {
		super()
	}

	protected *streamCandidateEntries(query: NormalizedStarCatalogQuery) {
		for (const star of this.stars) {
			if (query.preselectionBoxes.some((box) => star.rightAscension >= box.minRA && star.rightAscension <= box.maxRA && star.declination >= box.minDEC && star.declination <= box.maxDEC)) yield star
		}
	}
}

const catalog = new ListCatalog([
	{ rightAscension: deg(0.1), declination: deg(5) },
	{ rightAscension: deg(359.9), declination: 0 },
	{ rightAscension: deg(120), declination: 0 },
])

// A cone of 10° around RA 120°, Dec 0°, and a box that wraps across RA 0.
console.log((await catalog.queryCone(deg(120), 0, deg(10))).length) // 1
console.log((await catalog.queryBox(deg(359.7), deg(0.3), deg(-0.1), deg(10))).length) // 2

// A triangle and a convex polygon, with [rightAscension, declination] vertices in radians.
console.log((await catalog.queryTriangle([deg(110), deg(-5)], [deg(130), deg(-5)], [deg(120), deg(10)])).length) // 1
console.log(
	(
		await catalog.queryPolygon([
			[deg(358), deg(-2)],
			[deg(2), deg(-2)],
			[deg(2), deg(8)],
			[deg(358), deg(8)],
		])
	).length,
) // 2

// The tagged form with filters, collected or streamed one entry at a time.
console.log((await catalog.queryRegion({ kind: 'cone', centerRA: 0, centerDEC: 0, radius: deg(10), limit: 1 })).length) // 1
for await (const star of catalog.streamRegion({ kind: 'box', minRA: deg(90), maxRA: deg(140), minDEC: 0, maxDEC: deg(20), limit: 1 })) console.log(star)

// What a provider receives: a cone at RA 2° reaches across 0 and is split in two boxes.
console.log(normalizeStarCatalogQuery({ kind: 'cone', centerRA: deg(2), centerDEC: deg(40), radius: deg(5) }).preselectionBoxes.length) // 2
```

### Stellarium Geodesic Grid

The Stellarium geodesic grid divides the unit sphere into 20 icosahedron faces, each recursively split into four spherical triangles. Level L has 20 × 4^L local zones, numbered from zero; the four children of zone z are 4z through 4z + 3. Equatorial Cartesian directions have x toward RA 0, y toward RA 90° and z toward the north pole. Use this module to locate directions or select candidate zones for custom spatial queries; the file-backed reader is documented in [Stellarium Star Catalog](#stellarium-star-catalog).

A direction on a shared boundary is assigned deterministically with Stellarium's own tests and tie order. The catalog also has an extra global zone, numbered `stellariumLocalZoneCount(level)`, which has no triangle: locating a direction on the grid does not tell whether its star record is stored in that global zone, so catalog readers must always scan it.

A zone cover walks the subdivision tree without materializing the full grid and returns, per level, ascending runs of zones that are either wholly inside the region or candidates that still require an exact per-object test; the selection is conservative and can include zones with no matching object. The built-in classifiers select a cone or a union of non-wrapping RA/Dec boxes (split a box crossing RA 0 in two, or use the preselection boxes of [Star Catalog Interface and Spatial Query](#star-catalog-interface-and-spatial-query)); a custom classifier receives a bounding cap of a zone and returns `outside` only when the cap cannot intersect the region, `inside` only when the whole cap passes, and `border` otherwise.

```ts
import { stellariumBoxesClassifier, stellariumConeClassifier, stellariumLocalZoneCount, stellariumZoneCover, stellariumZoneForPoint, stellariumZoneTriangle } from 'nebulosa/src/catalogs/stars/stellarium/geodesic'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The zone of a unit direction (RA 0, Dec 0) at level 2, and the index of the global zone.
const direction = [1, 0, 0] as const
const zone = stellariumZoneForPoint(direction, 2)
console.log(zone, stellariumLocalZoneCount(2)) // 1 320
console.log(stellariumZoneTriangle(2, zone)) // three unit corner vectors, counterclockwise from outside

// The zones of levels 2 and 4 that a cone of 1° may touch, as [start, end) runs.
const cone = stellariumZoneCover(stellariumConeClassifier(direction, deg(1)), [2, 4])
console.log(cone.ranges.get(2)?.map(({ start, end }) => [start, end])) // [ [ 1, 2 ], [ 4, 5 ], [ 14, 15 ], [ 17, 18 ], [ 20, 21 ], [ 30, 31 ] ]

// The zones of a union of RA/Dec boxes (radians).
const boxes = stellariumZoneCover(stellariumBoxesClassifier([{ minRA: 0, maxRA: deg(1), minDEC: deg(-1), maxDEC: deg(1) }]), [2])
console.log(boxes.ranges.get(2)) // runs of { start, end, inside }
```

### Stellarium Nebulae Catalog

Stellarium's deep-sky catalog is a binary `catalog.dat` of about 95 thousand objects (galaxies, clusters, nebulae and some stars) with their cross-identifiers in the NGC, IC, Messier, Caldwell, Barnard, Sharpless, PGC, UGC and many other catalogs, the morphological type, the angular size and orientation, and the redshift or distance when known; `names.dat` is the text file with the common names of some of them. It is the catalog to use to annotate deep-sky objects or to resolve a designation such as M 42 into a position. The positions are J2000, with no proper motion.

Each entry is identified by its record number in the file, not by an NGC or Messier number; an identifier of 0 (or `undefined` for text designations) means that the object has none, and the magnitude is V, or B when V is absent. An object can have several common names. `StellariumNebulaeCatalog` indexes the objects for the queries of [HEALPix Object Index](#healpix-object-index) and [Star Catalog Interface and Spatial Query](#star-catalog-interface-and-spatial-query) by their center only, so a cone selects a large object when its center is inside, even if its extent crosses the border.

```ts
import fs from 'fs/promises'
import { readCatalogDat, readNamesDat, StellariumNebulaeCatalog, StellariumObjectType } from 'nebulosa/src/catalogs/stars/stellarium/nebulae'
import { fileHandleSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/file'
import { deg, toArcmin } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Streams the big-endian records: the Orion Nebula (M 42 = NGC 1976).
await using source = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/catalog.dat'))

for await (const entry of readCatalogDat(source)) {
	if (entry.m === 42) console.log(entry.ngc, StellariumObjectType[entry.type], entry.magnitude, toArcmin(entry.majorAxis)) // 1976 HII_REGION 4 90
}

// Indexes the catalog: a cone of 1° around the Orion Nebula, with the entry as the metadata of each result.
await using file = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/catalog.dat'))
const catalog = new StellariumNebulaeCatalog()
await catalog.load(file)
console.log(catalog.queryCone(deg(83.8), deg(-5.39), deg(1)).length) // 11

// The common names, by catalog prefix and designation.
await using namesFile = fileHandleSource(await fs.open('data/names.dat'))

for await (const { prefix, id, name } of readNamesDat(namesFile)) {
	if (prefix === 'NGC' && id === '1976') console.log(name) // Great Orion Nebula, Orion Nebula, Orion A
}
```

### Stellarium Star Catalog

Since version 25.1, Stellarium distributes its star catalog (Gaia DR3 merged with Hipparcos) as one binary file per level, `stars_<level>_<type>v<major>_<minor>.cat`, in the `stars/hip_gaia3` directory of the installation, with a manifest (`defaultStarsConfig.json`, or the user's `starsConfig.json`) that lists the files and their MD5 checksums. Each level is a faintness slice (level 0 holds the stars brighter than about V = 6, level 5 those from V = 12 to about 13.75) indexed by the [Stellarium Geodesic Grid](#stellarium-geodesic-grid) subdivided `level` times, plus one global zone for the stars that Stellarium keeps outside the triangles, such as Sirius. Inside a zone the records are sorted by increasing magnitude. Bright levels use a record with the full space motion and the Hipparcos number, fainter levels a compact one with position, proper motion and parallax, and the faintest level only the position. The files must be obtained from a Stellarium installation or its download page; Nebulosa does not download them.

The catalog opens the files in place and reads only the headers and zone tables (a few megabytes for all levels); a query reads, with positional reads, only the zones whose bounding cap may touch the region, stops each zone at the magnitude bound, and applies the exact geometry of [Star Catalog Interface and Spatial Query](#star-catalog-interface-and-spatial-query). Results come level by level and zone by zone, so a `limit` keeps the first matches and not the brightest ones.

Positions are astrometric ICRS directions at the catalog epoch of the file (J2016.0 for the current files) and are not propagated, so a query selects stars by their position at that epoch. The magnitude is the V magnitude of the Stellarium processing, not Gaia G, `pmRA` is `dα/dt`, and a stored zero means a missing value, as in Stellarium: a zero parallax, radial velocity or proper motion is `undefined`. This provider is unrelated to the deep-sky [Stellarium Nebulae Catalog](#stellarium-nebulae-catalog).

```ts
import { openStellariumStarCatalog } from 'nebulosa/src/catalogs/stars/stellarium/star.catalog'
import { deg, toMas } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The stars/hip_gaia3 directory of Stellarium 25.x with the levels 0 to 5 installed; levels 0 to 2 are required.
// Same as await new StellariumStarCatalog(options).open(root); closed by close() or at the end of the scope.
await using catalog = await openStellariumStarCatalog('/path/to/stars/hip_gaia3', { requiredLevels: [0, 1, 2] })
console.log(catalog.isOpen, catalog.root) // true and the opened directory
console.log(
	catalog.levels.map((level) => [level.level, level.recordCount]),
	catalog.missingLevels,
) // records per opened level, and [ 6, 7, 8 ]

// Sirius: a Hipparcos star of the level 0 global zone, at the J2016.0 catalog epoch.
const [sirius] = await catalog.queryRegion({ kind: 'cone', centerRA: deg(101.287), centerDEC: deg(-16.716), radius: deg(0.05), magnitudeMax: 0 })
console.log(sirius.hipId, sirius.magnitude, toMas(sirius.parallax!)) // 32349 -1.46 379.2

// A streamed field toward the Galactic center: only the zones around it are read.
for await (const star of catalog.streamRegion({ kind: 'cone', centerRA: deg(266.4), centerDEC: deg(-29), radius: deg(0.25), magnitudeMax: 12 })) console.log(star.gaiaId, star.magnitude)

// One record by its address, and the MD5 audit of the opened files against the manifest.
console.log((await catalog.get(sirius.level, sirius.zone, sirius.recordNumber))?.hipId) // 32349
console.log((await catalog.verifyChecksums()).map((result) => result.matches))

// The cumulative I/O counters of the queries (bytes read, zones and records scanned...), and their reset.
console.log(catalog.diagnostics.bytesRead, catalog.diagnostics.zonesScanned)
catalog.resetDiagnostics()
```

### Tiled Sky Catalog

HNSKY and ASTAP distribute their star databases as thousands of small binary files, one per tile of the sky, so that a query reads only the few tiles that it touches. `tiled.catalog` is the engine shared by the two formats (the concrete ones are [ASTAP Tiled Catalog](#astap-tiled-catalog) and [HNSKY Tiled Catalog](#hnsky-tiled-catalog)): it describes a tiling, finds the tiles of a field, decodes the packed records and exposes the result as a star catalog. A tiling is a list of declination bands from the south to the north pole, each divided in a number of equal right ascension cells; the tiles are numbered from 1, band after band, and a tile file is named by its 1-based band and cell as `BBCC` plus the extension (`0203.1476`), prefixed by the database inside a collection (`d05_0203.1476`).

Each tile file has a 110-byte header (a text description, a version byte and the record size) followed by records sorted by magnitude, so a reader can stop at a limiting magnitude. A record packs a 24-bit right ascension (a full circle over 2²⁴−1) and a signed 24-bit declination (a quarter circle over 2²³−1), a resolution of about 0.08″ and 0.04″; the magnitude and the high byte of the declination are shared with the following records through special records, and larger sizes add a color byte or a packed designation. The epoch of the positions is the `Epoch=` tag of the description, or the default of the format, and no proper motion is applied.

The tile functions select a square field of half width `radius` in declination and in right ascension times `cos δ`, so the longitude span grows toward the poles; the catalog class applies the exact geometry of [Star Catalog Interface and Spatial Query](#star-catalog-interface-and-spatial-query). The record scanner reuses one cursor object for every record, so copy what you need before the iterator advances.

```ts
import type { StarCatalogEntry } from 'nebulosa/src/catalogs/stars/catalog'
import {
	createTiledSkyGeometry,
	createTiledStarRawRecord,
	findTiledStarAreas,
	findTiledStarRegion,
	readTiledStarArea,
	readTiledStarHeader,
	scanTiledStarRecords,
	TILED_STAR_DEC_SCALE,
	TILED_STAR_RA_SCALE,
	tiledStarAreaFile,
	TiledStarCatalog,
	type TiledStarFileHeader,
	type TiledStarRawRecord,
} from 'nebulosa/src/catalogs/stars/tiled.catalog'
import { PIOVERTWO } from 'nebulosa/src/core/constants'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A tiling of a south cap, a band of 4 cells between -30° and +30°, and a north cap (boundaries in radians).
const geometry = createTiledSkyGeometry([1, 4, 1], [-PIOVERTWO, -deg(30), deg(30), PIOVERTWO], '.demo')
console.log(findTiledStarAreas(geometry, deg(100), 0, deg(2)).map((area) => area.fileName)) // [ "0202.demo" ]

// The descriptor of a 1-based area number: its band, its cell and its file name.
console.log(tiledStarAreaFile(geometry, 3)) // { area: 3, ring: 2, index: 2, fileName: "0202.demo", ... }

// A real tile: the south polar cap of the ASTAP d05 database, scanned record by record.
const buffer = Buffer.from(await Bun.file('data/d05_0101.1476').arrayBuffer())
const header = readTiledStarHeader(buffer, 2000, 'ASTAP .1476')
console.log(header.recordSize, header.epoch) // 5 2025

for (const record of scanTiledStarRecords(header, buffer, createTiledStarRawRecord())) {
	console.log(record.raRaw * TILED_STAR_RA_SCALE, record.decRaw * TILED_STAR_DEC_SCALE, record.magnitude) // radians and magnitude
	break
}

// A materializer turns the reused cursor into a star; the square field of a tile, and of a tile collection.
const star = (area: number, record: Readonly<TiledStarRawRecord>) => ({ area, rightAscension: record.raRaw * TILED_STAR_RA_SCALE, declination: record.decRaw * TILED_STAR_DEC_SCALE, magnitude: record.magnitude })
const query = { rightAscension: 0, declination: deg(-89.5), radius: deg(0.5), magnitudeLimit: 10.5 }
console.log([...readTiledStarArea(header, buffer, 1, query, star)].length) // 4
const capGeometry = createTiledSkyGeometry([1, 1], [-PIOVERTWO, deg(-87.42857143), PIOVERTWO], '.1476')
console.log((await findTiledStarRegion({ 'd05_0101.1476': buffer }, 'd05', capGeometry, query, 2000, 'demo .1476', star)).stars.length) // 4

// A catalog on top of the engine: the geometry, the default epoch, a label and the database; only buildEntry is needed.
class DemoCatalog extends TiledStarCatalog<StarCatalogEntry, 'd05'> {
	constructor() {
		super(capGeometry, 2000, 'demo .1476', 'd05')
	}

	protected buildEntry(record: Readonly<TiledStarRawRecord>, header: TiledStarFileHeader) {
		return { epoch: header.epoch, rightAscension: record.raRaw * TILED_STAR_RA_SCALE, declination: record.decRaw * TILED_STAR_DEC_SCALE, magnitude: record.magnitude }
	}
}

const catalog = new DemoCatalog()
catalog.open({ 'd05_0101.1476': buffer })
console.log((await catalog.queryCone(0, deg(-89.5), deg(0.5))).length) // 374

// The database, whether any of its tiles is present, one tile loaded and cached, and one record by area and record number.
console.log(catalog.database, catalog.hasAnyAreaFile(), (await catalog.loadArea(2)) === undefined) // d05 true true — tile 2 is absent
console.log(await catalog.get('d05', 1, 173)) // the entry of record 173 of tile 1, or undefined

catalog.close()
```

### UCAC4 Catalog

UCAC4 (the fourth USNO CCD Astrograph Catalog) has about 113 million stars to roughly magnitude 16, with J2000 ICRS positions and proper motions over the whole sky, which makes it a dense astrometric reference for plate solving and crossmatching faint fields. Its native distribution is a directory of 900 binary zone files `z001` to `z900`, each one a strip of 0.2° of declination (zone = floor((δ + 90°) / 0.2°) + 1, with 900 for the north pole) whose 78-byte records are sorted by right ascension.

The catalog does not load the files in memory: it opens the root directory, finds the zone files (in the root or in the `u4b`, `u4s` and `u4n` subdirectories), and reads only the records that a query may touch, through the exact geometry of [Star Catalog Interface and Spatial Query](#star-catalog-interface-and-spatial-query). The optional `u4index.unf` narrows the records read from a zone to the right ascension cells of the field, and the optional `u4hpm.dat` supplies the proper motion of the stars faster than the record can store (above 3276.7 mas/yr); without it those stars have no proper motion. The stored `μα·cos δ` is divided by `cos δ`, so `pmRA` is `dα/dt`, and the magnitude is the UCAC aperture magnitude, else the model one, else the 2MASS J. The files of the real catalog have to be downloaded from USNO.

```ts
import { openUcac4Catalog, ucac4ZoneForDec } from 'nebulosa/src/catalogs/stars/ucac4'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The zone of a declination: 0.2° strips from the south pole.
console.log(ucac4ZoneForDec(deg(-90)), ucac4ZoneForDec(deg(0)), ucac4ZoneForDec(deg(0.2)), ucac4ZoneForDec(deg(90))) // 1 451 452 900

// Opens the root directory of the downloaded catalog; same as await new Ucac4Catalog().open(root).
const catalog = await openUcac4Catalog('/path/to/ucac4')

// The opened directory, and whether it holds at least one zone file.
console.log(catalog.root, await catalog.hasAnyZoneFile())

// A cone of 0.1°: each entry carries its native zone and record number.
const cone = await catalog.queryCone(deg(10), deg(0.07), deg(0.1))
console.log(cone.map((entry) => [entry.zone, entry.recordNumber, entry.magnitude]))

// One star by its zone and record number (from 1), or undefined beyond the end of the zone; readRawRecord is the same read.
console.log(await catalog.get(451, 1))

await catalog.close()
```

## 🖲️ Devices

### ASCOM Alpaca Device Adapter

ASCOM Alpaca is the network form of the ASCOM device standard: every camera, mount, focuser or other device is reached over HTTP, independently of the operating system that runs the driver. The library's device model, however, follows INDI. `AlpacaClient` is the bridge between the two: it connects to a remote Alpaca server and presents its devices as if they came from an INDI server, so the same device managers (camera, mount, focuser, wheel, cover, flat panel, rotator, dome, safety monitor and weather) work unchanged. See [ASCOM Alpaca REST API](#ascom-alpaca-rest-api) for the HTTP layer it uses and [ASCOM Alpaca Server](#ascom-alpaca-server) for the other direction.

Alpaca has no events, so everything a device reports comes from polling: a property changes at most once per polling interval, and a capability (the ability to slew, or to move a focuser to an absolute position) shows up only after the first polls that follow the connection, so wait for it before commanding. The library keeps angles in radians; the conversion to the Alpaca units (right ascension in hours, declination in degrees) happens at the boundary. An Alpaca station that implements several interfaces lists the same name once per type, so each interface is published as its own INDI device named `<DeviceName> (<Type> <DeviceNumber>)`. A slew or sync that the driver refuses is published as an `Alert` on the mount coordinates, so a waiting goto fails at once instead of running until its timeout.

Images are downloaded in the binary ImageBytes encoding, and `makeFitsFromImageBytes` turns them into an in-memory FITS whose header is stamped from the connected devices, with the mount coordinates of date converted to J2000. Polling and downloads run over plain HTTP.

```ts
import { timeYMDHMS } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { AlpacaClient, makeFitsFromImageBytes } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/alpaca/client'
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { MountManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/mount'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Managers fed by the client's INDI events, and a provider that resolves the devices it creates.
const mountManager = new MountManager()
const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet([mountManager])
const provider = { get: (client: never, name: string) => mountManager.get(client, name) }

// Reads the configured devices of the server (the address is an example) and polls them every 1000 ms.
const client = new AlpacaClient('http://localhost:11111', { handler, poolingInterval: 1000 }, provider)
await client.start()

// Replays every device definition to the handler, like an INDI getProperties; the managers reach the
// devices through the client's sendText, sendNumber and sendSwitch.
client.getProperties()

// Connecting through the manager becomes a REST call; capabilities appear after the next polls.
const mount = mountManager.get(client, 'Mount Simulator (Mount 0)')!
mountManager.connect(mount)
await Bun.sleep(5000)

// Radians in the INDI model, sent as hours and degrees on the wire.
mountManager.syncTo(mount, hour(5), deg(20))

// Stops polling and forgets the devices.
client.stop()

// data: ArrayBuffer — an Alpaca ImageBytes download; camera: Camera — the connected camera.
// Converts it to FITS, stamping the instrument, the 30 s exposure and the J2000 mount coordinates.
const fits = makeFitsFromImageBytes(data, timeYMDHMS(2026, 2, 18, 12, 0, 0), camera, mount, undefined, undefined, undefined, 30)
```

### ASCOM Alpaca Discovery Client

Alpaca servers announce themselves through the Alpaca Discovery protocol, so a client can find them without knowing their address. The client sends the UDP datagram `alpacadiscovery1` to port 32227, as an IPv4 broadcast on every local interface or to the link-scoped IPv6 multicast group `ff12::a1:9aca`, and each server answers with a JSON datagram `{"AlpacaPort":N}` naming the HTTP port of its management API. `AlpacaDiscoveryClient` is that probing side (see [ASCOM Alpaca Discovery Server](#ascom-alpaca-discovery-server) for the responder).

For every response, the client reports the sender address, the announced port and, unless fetching is turned off, the configured devices read from the management API of that server (see [ASCOM Alpaca REST API](#ascom-alpaca-rest-api)). Responses arrive during a listen window. A server can be reported more than once when it answers the probe of several interfaces. UDP broadcast and multicast are not guaranteed to be delivered, and many networks block them, so a discovery that finds nothing does not prove that there is no server.

```ts
import { AlpacaDiscoveryClient } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/alpaca/discovery'

const client = new AlpacaDiscoveryClient()

// Probes over IPv4 and waits for the 5000 ms listen window to close.
// The callback receives the server address, its management port and its configured devices.
await client.discovery((server) => console.log(server.address, server.port, server.devices), { timeout: 5000, wait: true })

// The same probe over IPv6 multicast.
await client.discovery((server) => console.log(server.address, server.port), { family: 'IPv6', timeout: 5000, wait: true })

client.close()
```

### ASCOM Alpaca Discovery Server

`AlpacaDiscoveryServer` is the responder side of the Alpaca Discovery protocol: a UDP socket on port 32227 that answers every datagram starting with `alpacadiscovery1` with one `{"AlpacaPort":N}` datagram for each registered HTTP port, sent back to the sender. It lets Alpaca clients on the network find a server without being configured with its address (see [ASCOM Alpaca Discovery Client](#ascom-alpaca-discovery-client) for the probing side).

The socket shares its port, so several Alpaca servers on one machine can answer the same probe, and probes from a loopback address are ignored by default. Binding an IPv6 address joins the discovery multicast group on every external IPv6 interface. It only announces ports: the HTTP server that answers the management and device requests is a separate component (see [ASCOM Alpaca Server](#ascom-alpaca-server)), and on a network that blocks UDP broadcast or multicast clients will not find it.

```ts
import { AlpacaDiscoveryServer } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/alpaca/discovery'

const discovery = new AlpacaDiscoveryServer()

// Registers the HTTP port of an Alpaca server to announce; ports can be added and removed while it runs.
discovery.addPort(11111)

// Binds 0.0.0.0 on the discovery port 32227 and answers each probe with {"AlpacaPort":11111}.
await discovery.start()
console.log(discovery.running, discovery.host, discovery.port) // whether it runs, the bound address (also ip), and the bound UDP port

// Stops announcing a port; the socket keeps answering for the others.
discovery.removePort(11111)

discovery.stop()
```

### ASCOM Alpaca REST API

The Alpaca device API is plain HTTP: a property is read with `GET /api/v1/<devicetype>/<devicenumber>/<member>` and parameters in the query string, a property is set or an operation started with a `PUT` and a form-encoded body, and every answer is a JSON envelope with the `Value`, an `ErrorNumber` and an `ErrorMessage`. The management API under `/management/v1/` lists the configured devices. Values are in the units of the ASCOM specification: right ascension in hours; declination, azimuth, altitude and position angles in degrees; exposure durations in seconds and guide pulses in milliseconds; temperatures in degrees Celsius.

`devices/alpaca/api` is a thin typed client of that API: one class per device type, one method per Alpaca member, and the values passed through unchanged. The conversion from the library radians is done by the adapter and the server (see [ASCOM Alpaca Device Adapter](#ascom-alpaca-device-adapter) and [ASCOM Alpaca Server](#ascom-alpaca-server)). `AlpacaApi` bundles one instance of each class on the same server. Every call resolves a result instead of throwing, so a missing optional member or an offline driver is a value to check. The calls are single requests: a long operation such as a slew or an exposure is started and then polled through its state, and the camera image is returned raw in the binary ImageBytes encoding for the caller to decode.

```ts
import { AlpacaApi } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/alpaca/api'
import { AlpacaGuideDirection } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/alpaca/types'

// One wrapper per device type on the same Alpaca server (the address is an example).
const api = new AlpacaApi('http://localhost:11111')

// AlpacaManagementApi: the configured devices, with name, type, device number and unique ID.
const devices = await api.management.configuredDevices()
if (devices.ok) console.log(devices.value)

// Every device member takes the zero-based device number first and resolves { ok, value } or an error.
// AlpacaDeviceApi, the base of every class: connect, disconnect, isConnected and the bulk deviceState.
await api.telescope.connect(0)
console.log(await api.telescope.deviceState(0))

// The members are named after the ASCOM ones, with get, set, is and can prefixes for properties.
// AlpacaTelescopeApi: an asynchronous slew in ASCOM units (right ascension in hours, declination in degrees), then its state.
await api.telescope.slewToCoordinatesAsync(0, 5.5, -20)
console.log(await api.telescope.isSlewing(0))

// AlpacaCameraApi: a 1.5 s light exposure and a 500 ms guide pulse to the east.
await api.camera.startExposure(0, 1.5, true)
await api.camera.pulseGuide(0, AlpacaGuideDirection.EAST, 500)

// Once isImageReady is true, the frame in the ImageBytes encoding, as an ArrayBuffer.
const image = await api.camera.getImageArray(0)

// AlpacaFilterWheelApi, AlpacaFocuserApi and AlpacaRotatorApi: a slot, an absolute position in steps, and a sky angle in degrees.
await api.filterWheel.setPosition(0, 2)
await api.focuser.move(0, 12000)
await api.rotator.moveAbsolute(0, 90)

// AlpacaCoverCalibratorApi and AlpacaDomeApi: open the cover, light the panel at brightness 128, and turn the dome to azimuth 180°.
await api.coverCalibrator.open(0)
await api.coverCalibrator.on(0, 128)
await api.dome.slewToAzimuth(0, 180)

// AlpacaSafetyMonitorApi and AlpacaObservingConditionsApi: the safe flag and the ambient temperature in °C.
console.log(await api.safetyMonitor.isSafe(0), await api.observingConditions.getTemperature(0))
```

### ASCOM Alpaca Server

`AlpacaServer` is the reverse of the [ASCOM Alpaca Device Adapter](#ascom-alpaca-device-adapter): it exposes the INDI devices known to the application's device managers through the [ASCOM Alpaca REST API](#ascom-alpaca-rest-api), so external Alpaca software can control equipment that is driven through INDI. Each manager maps to an Alpaca device type (a mount is a `telescope`, covers and flat panels are both `covercalibrator`, a weather device is `observingconditions`), and the server only sees the devices its managers know about, so the managers must be fed by an INDI client.

Alpaca clients address a device by its type and number, so each device gets a number that is by default a stable hash of its type and name and survives restarts. Values are converted to the Alpaca units at the boundary (the mount reports right ascension in hours and declination in degrees, while the INDI side keeps radians), and exposures are delivered in the ImageBytes encoding, which `makeImageBytesFromFits` produces from an in-memory FITS. Announce the port with an [ASCOM Alpaca Discovery Server](#ascom-alpaca-discovery-server) so clients find it. The server listens on plain HTTP without authentication, so bind it to a trusted interface.

```ts
import { AlpacaDiscoveryServer } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/alpaca/discovery'
import { AlpacaServer, makeImageBytesFromFits } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/alpaca/server'
import { defaultDeviceNumberProvider } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/alpaca/types'
import { IndiClient, IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { FocuserManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/focuser'
import { MountManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/mount'

// Managers fed by a client of an INDI server (the address is an example).
const mountManager = new MountManager()
const focuserManager = new FocuserManager()
using client = new IndiClient({ handler: new IndiClientHandlerSet([mountManager, focuserManager]) })
await client.connect('localhost', 7624)

// Serves the mount and the focuser over Alpaca on an ephemeral port of the loopback.
const server = new AlpacaServer({ mount: mountManager, focuser: focuserManager })
server.start('localhost', 0)
console.log(server.running, server.host, server.port) // whether it listens, the bound host and HTTP port

// The devices as /management/v1/configureddevices lists them.
console.log(server.configuredDevices())

// The device number a client addresses: by default this stable hash of the type and the name.
const [mount] = mountManager.list()
console.log(defaultDeviceNumberProvider(mount, 'telescope'))

// Announces the HTTP port to Alpaca discovery probes.
const discovery = new AlpacaDiscoveryServer()
discovery.addPort(server.port)
await discovery.start()

// The ImageBytes encoding of a FITS image: a metadata header, then the pixels in column-major order.
const bytes = makeImageBytesFromFits(Buffer.from(await Bun.file('data/NGC3372-16.1.fit').arrayBuffer()))

discovery.stop()
server.stop()

// Embedded in an existing Bun.serve instead of start(): serve server.routes and subscribe to the managers
// with listen(); unlisten() unsubscribes and forgets the devices.
using http = Bun.serve({ hostname: 'localhost', port: 0, routes: server.routes })
server.listen()
server.unlisten()
```

### Device Availability Lifecycle

An INDI device that is listed by its manager is not automatically safe to command: it may be disconnected, or connected but still slewing, exposing, or moving a motor that someone else started, from a hand controller or another client. `DeviceLifecycle` closes that gap. It observes the INDI device managers and keeps the availability of each device in the [Device Resource Arbitration](#device-resource-arbitration) up to date, so a [Device Operations](#device-operations) tree can acquire a device only while it is connected and physically quiescent, and every operation holding it is cancelled the moment it disconnects or disappears.

Availability is tracked per capability. An exposing camera blocks itself and its integrated filter wheel or focuser, because they are one physical device, but not its ST4 guide port, which can pulse while the sensor exposes. The default verifier treats a device as quiescent when it is connected and not exposing, slewing, parking, homing, pulsing or moving; a custom verifier can replace it. Whole clients can also be blocked, for example while their server reconnects.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { FocuserManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/focuser'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { FocuserSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/focuser'
import { affectsDeviceQuiescence, DeviceLifecycle, isDeviceQuiescent } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/device.lifecycle'
import { OperationCoordinator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/operation'
import { ResourceArbiter, resourceKey } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/resource'

const focuserManager = new FocuserManager()
const arbiter = new ResourceArbiter()
const coordinator = new OperationCoordinator(arbiter)
const lifecycle = new DeviceLifecycle(arbiter, coordinator)

// Observes the manager before the client publishes devices; returns a disposer for this observation.
const stop = lifecycle.observe(focuserManager)

const client = new ClientSimulator('Client Simulator', new IndiClientHandlerSet([focuserManager]))
const simulator = new FocuserSimulator('Focuser Simulator', client)
const focuser = focuserManager.get(client, 'Focuser Simulator')!
const key = resourceKey(focuser)

console.log(arbiter.availability(key)) // 'unavailable' — listed but not connected

focuserManager.connect(focuser)
console.log(arbiter.availability(key)) // 'available'

// A move started outside any operation blocks acquisition until the motor stops.
focuserManager.moveIn(focuser, 500)
console.log(arbiter.availability(key)) // 'unavailable'

// The default verifier, and whether a changed device field can alter its answer.
console.log(isDeviceQuiescent(focuser), affectsDeviceQuiescence(focuser, 'moving')) // false true

stop()
lifecycle.dispose()
simulator.dispose()
```

### Device Camera Capture

An INDI camera exposure ends in two separate messages: the `CCD_EXPOSURE` vector turning `Ok` and the BLOB carrying the frame, in either order and with no operation id. `CameraCapturer` turns that into a [Device Operations](#device-operations) capture: it acquires the camera, configures it, exposes frame after frame, pairs each exposure completion with its BLOB, decodes and saves the frame, and stops and quiesces the camera before releasing it. A capture is a single frame, a fixed count, or a loop until stopped, with an optional delay between frames.

Stopping and cancelling differ: `stop()` lets the exposure in flight finish and keeps its frame, while `cancel()` aborts it and loses it. Each frame records when its exposure was dispatched, first reported `Busy`, and finished, both as wall-clock Unix milliseconds and on a monotonic clock. The dispatch instant is a lower bound of the physical start and the first `Busy` follows the shutter opening, so use the latter for the exposure midpoint, and the monotonic values for durations, since the wall clock may jump. A frame that was exposed but whose BLOB never arrived quarantines the camera, because the next capture would otherwise read the stale payload.

Auto-saved frames are named after the local time they were commanded and grouped in a folder per night: in `noon` mode the folder is the local date 12 hours earlier, so a whole night stays in the folder of the evening it began. A capture started as suspendable can pause between two frames and lend its camera to a [Device Reservations](#device-reservations) owner, such as a meridian flip that needs it for plate solving, and then resume as the same session. The capturer never dithers; a dither belongs to whoever sequences the frames.

```ts
import { tmpdir } from 'os'
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { CameraManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/camera'
import { CameraSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/camera'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { DeviceLifecycle } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/device.lifecycle'
import { OperationCoordinator, successfulOperationResult } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/operation'
import { ResourceArbiter, resourceKey } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/resource'
import { autoSubFolderName, CameraCapturer, configureCameraExposure } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/capture/capture'
import { type CameraCaptureStart, DEFAULT_CAMERA_CAPTURE_START, exposureTimeIn } from 'nebulosa/src/observation/capture/types'

const cameraManager = new CameraManager()
const arbiter = new ResourceArbiter()
const coordinator = new OperationCoordinator(arbiter)
const lifecycle = new DeviceLifecycle(arbiter, coordinator)
lifecycle.observe(cameraManager)

// The capturer listens to the camera manager; publish receives every decoded frame and its path.
// The write and decode hooks default to writeFrameExclusively and decodeCameraBlobFromBase64.
using capturer = new CameraCapturer(cameraManager, arbiter, { capturesDir: tmpdir(), publish: (frame, path) => console.log(path) })

const client = new ClientSimulator('Client Simulator', new IndiClientHandlerSet([cameraManager]))
const simulator = new CameraSimulator('Camera Simulator', client)
const camera = cameraManager.get(client, 'Camera Simulator')!
cameraManager.connect(camera)
while (arbiter.availability(resourceKey(camera)) !== 'available') await Bun.sleep(10)

// Two 100 ms frames, 0.5 s apart, auto-saved under a folder per night.
const request: CameraCaptureStart = { ...structuredClone(DEFAULT_CAMERA_CAPTURE_START), exposureTime: 100, exposureTimeUnit: 'millisecond', exposureMode: 'fixed', count: 2, delay: 0.5, autoSave: true, autoSubFolderMode: 'noon' }
console.log(exposureTimeIn(request.exposureTime, request.exposureTimeUnit, 'second')) // 0.1 s

// Device events of a camera no capture owns go to its watcher; the call returns the unregistration.
const unwatch = capturer.watch(camera, { updated: (_, property) => console.log(property) })

// A feature that owns the camera applies the sensor settings of a request without exposing.
await coordinator.start('preview', [{ key: resourceKey(camera), device: camera }], () => {
	configureCameraExposure(cameraManager, camera, request)
	return successfulOperationResult(undefined)
}).result
unwatch()

// Runs as its own operation tree; started resolves when the first exposure is Busy.
const capture = capturer.start(coordinator, camera, request, { listener: (event) => console.log(event.state) })
await capture.started

// Resolves after cleanup and release; each frame carries its path and exposure instants (ms).
const result = await capture.result
if (result.ok) console.log(result.value.frameCount, result.value.frames[0].exposureStartedMonotonic)

// A suspendable loop pauses after the frame in flight and lends the camera to a reservation, then resumes.
const loop = capturer.start(coordinator, camera, { ...request, exposureMode: 'loop' }, { suspendable: true })
await loop.started
const flip = arbiter.reserve({ id: 'flip-1', kind: 'meridianFlip' }, [])
const paused = flip.ok ? await loop.suspend(flip.reservation, new AbortController().signal) : undefined
if (paused?.ok) paused.suspension.resume()

// stop() keeps the frame in flight; cancel() would abort it.
loop.stop()
await loop.result
if (flip.ok) flip.reservation.release()

// 02:00 UTC on 2026-10-10 at offset 0 min belongs to the night of October 9.
console.log(autoSubFolderName(Date.UTC(2026, 9, 10, 2), 'noon', 0)) // '2026-10-09'

lifecycle.dispose()
simulator.dispose()
```

### Device Command Waiting

A device command usually completes long after it is sent: the driver accepts a move and later reports the motor stopped at the target, or reports `Alert`. Waiting for that confirmation has three traps: the confirming update can arrive before the command call returns, the wait must stop on cancellation and on timeout, and a failed wait must stop the hardware before the caller releases it. `waitForDeviceState` handles all three and returns an `OperationResult` instead of throwing: it subscribes before sending the command, evaluates every update as pending, successful or a failure reason, and on any non-successful outcome runs the physical abort before settling.

Some work cannot be cancelled at all, such as an external plate solver or an HFD measurement reading a frame from disk. `awaitCooperativeJob` gives it a strictly cooperative timeout: the job receives a signal that aborts at the deadline, and is then still awaited until it ends, so a file it reads is never moved while it runs; a job that ignores the abort is reported as unresponsive. These waits are the building blocks of the [Device Commanders](#device-commanders) and usually run inside the signal of a [Device Operations](#device-operations) context.

```ts
import { abortableDelay, abortReason, awaitCooperativeJob, settlesWithin, settleWithSignal, waitForDeviceState } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/operation.wait'

// A toy device whose position reaches 100 steps 50 ms after the command.
const listeners = new Set<(position: number) => void>()
let position = 0

// Subscribes, sends the command, and resolves when evaluate answers 'success', or fails after timeout ms.
const moved = await waitForDeviceState({
	signal: new AbortController().signal,
	timeout: 1000,
	subscribe: (listener: (position: number) => void) => {
		listeners.add(listener)
		return () => void listeners.delete(listener)
	},
	current: () => position,
	evaluate: (value: number): 'success' | 'pending' => (value === 100 ? 'success' : 'pending'),
	command: () => void setTimeout(() => listeners.forEach((listener) => listener((position = 100))), 50),
	abort: () => console.log('halt'), // runs on every non-successful outcome
})

console.log(moved) // { ok: true, value: 100 }

// A job that ignores its signal: aborted at 50 ms, still awaited until it ends at 120 ms.
console.log(await awaitCooperativeJob(() => Bun.sleep(120), { signal: new AbortController().signal, timeout: 50, abortGrace: 50 })) // { kind: 'timeout', unresponsive: true }

// A delay that ends early as a failed result when the signal aborts, mapped by abortReason to a failure reason.
const controller = new AbortController()
setTimeout(() => controller.abort('timeout'), 10)
console.log(await abortableDelay(1000, controller.signal), abortReason(controller.signal)) // { ok: false, reason: 'timeout' } timeout

// Whether a promise settles within 50 ms, without cancelling it; and a promise that rejects once a signal aborts.
console.log(await settlesWithin(Bun.sleep(120), 50)) // false
await settleWithSignal(Bun.sleep(10), new AbortController().signal)
```

### Device Commanders

The INDI managers send a command and return at once: `FocuserManager.moveTo` only writes the target, and the model changes later when the driver reports it. Commanders are the operation-aware layer above them, one per device type (camera cooling, cover, dew heater, dome, flat panel, focuser, guide output, mount, power, rotator, weather and filter wheel). Each command acquires the device, checks the capability and the connection, sends the command, waits until the driver reports the expected state (see [Device Command Waiting](#device-command-waiting)), and resolves an `OperationResult` without throwing. This holds even for commands that move nothing, so a command the driver ignores ends as a timeout rather than as a success.

Every command takes an `OperationScope` first: the `OperationCoordinator` runs it as its own operation tree, an `OperationContext` nests it in a larger feature that already holds the device, and a [Device Reservations](#device-reservations) scope runs it inside a session. A device that is moving, leased elsewhere, or not yet verified by the [Device Availability Lifecycle](#device-availability-lifecycle) is refused as `busy`. When a motion fails, times out or is cancelled, the commander stops the device and waits for it to settle before the lease is released. `stopMotion` is the emergency stop: it takes no scope and acquires nothing, so it also reaches a device moving under another owner. A target is first resolved to one the driver can reach and will echo back, since a value outside the device range would only end in a timeout. The mount and the guide output have their own topics, [Mount Commander](#mount-commander) and [Guide Output Commander](#guide-output-commander). Commanders listen to their manager's device events, so dispose of one only after the operations that use it have settled.

```ts
import { CameraCommander } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/commanders/camera'
import { CoverCommander } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/commanders/cover'
import { DewHeaterCommander } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/commanders/dewheater'
import { DomeCommander, domeAzimuth } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/commanders/dome'
import { FlatPanelCommander } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/commanders/flatpanel'
import { FocuserCommander, focuserPosition } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/commanders/focuser'
import { PowerCommander } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/commanders/power'
import { RotatorCommander, rotatorAngle } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/commanders/rotator'
import { WeatherCommander } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/commanders/weather'
import { WheelCommander, wheelSlot } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/commanders/wheel'
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { FocuserManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/focuser'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { FocuserSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/focuser'
import { DeviceLifecycle } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/device.lifecycle'
import { OperationCoordinator, successfulOperationResult } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/operation'
import { ResourceArbiter, resourceKey } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/resource'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const focuserManager = new FocuserManager()
const arbiter = new ResourceArbiter()
const coordinator = new OperationCoordinator(arbiter)
const lifecycle = new DeviceLifecycle(arbiter, coordinator)
lifecycle.observe(focuserManager)
using focuserCommander = new FocuserCommander(focuserManager)

const client = new ClientSimulator('Client Simulator', new IndiClientHandlerSet([focuserManager]))
const simulator = new FocuserSimulator('Focuser Simulator', client)
const focuser = focuserManager.get(client, 'Focuser Simulator')!
focuserManager.connect(focuser)

// A top-level command: resolves only after the focuser stopped at the target, in steps.
console.log(await focuserCommander.moveTo(coordinator, focuser, 1000)) // { ok: true, value: undefined }

// Composed: the feature holds the focuser and each step reacquires it reentrantly.
const scan = coordinator.start('focusScan', [{ key: resourceKey(focuser), device: focuser }], async (context) => {
	for (const position of [1100, 1200]) {
		const moved = await focuserCommander.moveTo(context, focuser, position)
		if (!moved.ok) return moved
	}

	return successfulOperationResult(focuser.position.value)
})

console.log(await scan.result) // { ok: true, value: 1200 }

// Relative moves in steps; syncTo, reverse and setBacklash are confirmed the same way, and position reads the steps.
await focuserCommander.moveIn(coordinator, focuser, 100)
await focuserCommander.moveOut(coordinator, focuser, 50)
console.log(focuserCommander.position(focuser)) // 1150

// The emergency stop needs no scope.
await focuserCommander.stopMotion(focuser)

// cameraManager, coverManager, dewHeaterManager, domeManager, flatPanelManager, powerManager, rotatorManager,
// weatherManager, wheelManager: the managers of the other devices, observed by the same lifecycle; camera, cover,
// dewHeater, dome, panel, power, rotator, weather and wheel: connected devices of those managers.
using cameraCommander = new CameraCommander(cameraManager)
using coverCommander = new CoverCommander(coverManager)
using dewHeaterCommander = new DewHeaterCommander(dewHeaterManager)
using domeCommander = new DomeCommander(domeManager)
using flatPanelCommander = new FlatPanelCommander(flatPanelManager)
using powerCommander = new PowerCommander(powerManager)
using rotatorCommander = new RotatorCommander(rotatorManager)
using weatherCommander = new WeatherCommander(weatherManager)
using wheelCommander = new WheelCommander(wheelManager)

// Camera cooling: the cooler switch, then a sensor set-point in °C.
await cameraCommander.cooler(coordinator, camera, true)
await cameraCommander.temperature(coordinator, camera, -10)

// Cover: park closes and unpark opens; stopMotion halts it.
await coverCommander.park(coordinator, cover)

// Dew heater and flat panel: a duty cycle and an intensity in the driver's range; the panel also has enable, disable and toggle.
await dewHeaterCommander.dutyCycle(coordinator, dewHeater, 60)
await flatPanelCommander.intensity(coordinator, panel, 128)

// Dome azimuth in radians; also moveToAltitude, moveBy, move, syncTo, home, park, unpark, setPark, openShutter,
// closeShutter, slave, setSpeed, setBacklash, setBacklashSteps and stopMotion.
await domeCommander.moveTo(coordinator, dome, deg(90))

// An open-ended manual rotation keeps the dome leased until stopped; manualMove and manualMoveOf reach it later.
const rotation = await domeCommander.startManualMove(coordinator, dome, 'CLOCKWISE')
if (rotation.ok) await rotation.value.stop()

// Power box: switch a channel; voltage and dutyCycle set the variable and dew outputs.
await powerCommander.toggle(coordinator, power, power.dc[0], true)

// Rotator angle in degrees; also home, syncTo, reverse and stopMotion.
await rotatorCommander.moveTo(coordinator, rotator, 45)

// Weather station controls: the update period in seconds, the averaging window in hours, and a forced re-read.
await weatherCommander.setUpdatePeriod(coordinator, weather, 30)
await weatherCommander.setAveragePeriod(coordinator, weather, 0)
await weatherCommander.refresh(coordinator, weather)

// Filter wheel: a 0-based slot, and the slot names that later captures stamp into their frames.
await wheelCommander.moveTo(coordinator, wheel, 3)
await wheelCommander.setNames(coordinator, wheel, ['L', 'R', 'G', 'B', 'Ha', 'SII', 'OIII', 'Dark'])

// The targets the commands resolve: a focuser position (steps), a wheel slot, a rotator angle (degrees) and a
// dome azimuth (radians), each rounded, wrapped or clamped to the device; domeAltitude does the same for altitude.
console.log(focuserPosition(focuser, 1e9), wheelSlot(wheel, 2.6), rotatorAngle(rotator, 370), toDeg(domeAzimuth(dome, deg(-10)))) // 100000 3 10 350 with the simulators

lifecycle.dispose()
simulator.dispose()
```

### Device Operations

Observatory features compose: an autofocus run moves the focuser and takes exposures, a flat wizard drives a panel and a camera, and either may be cancelled by the user or by a disconnect at any time. `OperationCoordinator` gives each such feature an operation tree that owns its devices for its whole duration, propagates cancellation to every nested step, undoes registered work in reverse order, and only then releases the devices. Every outcome is an `OperationResult` (see [Device Command Waiting](#device-command-waiting) for the reasons), so callers never handle rejections.

An operation acquires all its resources atomically from the [Device Resource Arbitration](#device-resource-arbitration) arbiter, or fails at once as `busy` without waiting or queueing. Inside it, nested scopes reacquire what an ancestor holds, while two sibling scopes conflict, so two parallel steps can never command one device. Cleanups run once, last registered first, after the nested scopes have finished and whatever the outcome; a cleanup that fails turns the result into a failure because the device may not be quiescent. Operations can be cancelled one by one or by resource, device, client, or all at once. Services take an `OperationScope` (anything with `start`), so the same service runs at top level, nested in a feature, or inside a [Device Reservations](#device-reservations) scope.

```ts
import { failedOperationResult, OperationCoordinator, type OperationContext, type OperationResult, successfulOperationResult } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/operation'
import { ResourceArbiter } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/resource'

const coordinator = new OperationCoordinator(new ResourceArbiter())

// Acquires the camera and the focuser atomically and runs the executor.
const autoFocus = coordinator.start('autoFocus', [{ key: 'camera' }, { key: 'focuser' }], async (context) => {
	// Cleanups run in reverse order after the nested scopes finished.
	context.onCleanup(() => console.log('restore focuser'))

	// A nested scope reacquires the focuser its root already holds.
	const move = context.start('focuserMove', [{ key: 'focuser' }], () => successfulOperationResult(1200))
	return await move.result
})

console.log(await autoFocus.result) // logs the cleanup, then { ok: true, value: 1200 }

// An executor that stops on cancellation; a second capture of the same camera is refused as busy.
const waitForAbort = (context: OperationContext) => new Promise<OperationResult<void>>((resolve) => context.signal.addEventListener('abort', () => resolve(failedOperationResult('aborted')), { once: true }))
const capture = coordinator.start('capture', [{ key: 'camera' }], waitForAbort)
console.log((await coordinator.start('capture', [{ key: 'camera' }], waitForAbort).result).ok) // false

// A running tree by its id; completed trees are no longer retained.
console.log(coordinator.get(capture.id)?.kind) // 'capture'

// Cancelling resolves once cleanup finished; the result reports the cancellation reason.
await capture.cancel('timeout')
console.log(await capture.result) // { ok: false, reason: 'timeout' }

// Bulk cancellation: by id, by resource key, by physical device key, by client id, or every tree.
await coordinator.cancel(capture.id)
await coordinator.cancelByResource('camera')
await coordinator.cancelByDevice('camera')
await coordinator.cancelByClient('client-id')
await coordinator.cancelAll('disconnected')
```

### Device Reservations
