A lease lasts as long as one operation tree, but a session such as an imaging sequence needs its mount and camera for hours, across many operations and pauses, without a manual command slipping in between two of them. A reservation is that durable ownership. It is held by an owner (`{ id, kind }`), it is not itself an operation, and only operations started with its token may acquire the resources it covers. A reservation covers every requested resource or none, and an unavailable device can be reserved but stays unacquirable until it becomes available. The token is matched by object identity and must never be serialized.

A reservation can also take a resource from a session that is still running without any instant at which a third owner could grab it. A request may name a guest, the root context of a running tree: the guest keeps its lease, and when the lease ends the key stays reserved instead of becoming available, while the guest may acquire it again, as a paused session resuming does. Keys can also be transferred between two live reservations, so a session can lend what it reserved and get it back.

Draining cancels every tree of a reservation and leaves it open for the work that follows, as in a pause; cancelling closes it for good and is the call to make before releasing. Running trees are explained in [Device Operations](#device-operations) and keys and conflicts in [Device Resource Arbitration](#device-resource-arbitration).

```ts
import { failedOperationResult, OperationCoordinator, type OperationResult, successfulOperationResult } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/operation'
import { ResourceArbiter } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/resource'

const arbiter = new ResourceArbiter()
const coordinator = new OperationCoordinator(arbiter)
const session = { id: 'sequence-1', kind: 'sequencer' }

// Reserves the mount and the camera for the session, all or nothing.
const reserved = arbiter.reserve(session, [{ key: 'mount' }, { key: 'camera' }])
if (!reserved.ok) throw new Error('devices in use')
const { reservation } = reserved
console.log(arbiter.reservationOwnerOf('mount')) // { id: 'sequence-1', kind: 'sequencer' }

// Outside the reservation, a manual slew is refused.
console.log(await coordinator.start('slew', [{ key: 'mount' }], () => successfulOperationResult(undefined)).result) // { ok: false, reason: 'busy', error: 'mount is reserved by sequencer sequence-1' }

// A scope whose trees acquire under the reservation token; tokenScope(reservation.token) builds the same from the token alone.
const scope = coordinator.reservedScope(reservation)
const capture = scope.start('capture', [{ key: 'camera' }], (context) => new Promise<OperationResult<void>>((resolve) => context.signal.addEventListener('abort', () => resolve(failedOperationResult('aborted')), { once: true })))

// Pause: cancels the running trees and keeps the reservation usable.
await coordinator.drainByReservationOwner(session)
console.log(await capture.result) // { ok: false, reason: 'aborted' }

// Grows the same reservation, then lends the focuser to another live reservation without freeing it in between.
reservation.extend([{ key: 'focuser' }])
const flip = arbiter.reserve({ id: 'flip-1', kind: 'meridianFlip' }, [])
if (flip.ok) arbiter.transfer(reservation, flip.reservation, ['focuser'])
console.log(arbiter.reservationOwnerOf('focuser')) // { id: 'flip-1', kind: 'meridianFlip' }

// Stop: closes the reservation to new trees, then releases the devices.
await coordinator.cancelByReservationOwner(session)
reservation.release()
console.log(arbiter.availability('mount')) // 'available'
```

### Device Resource Arbitration

Two features must not command the same hardware at once: a filter that turns during an exposure ruins the frame, and a focus move during an exposure trails every star. `ResourceArbiter` is the single authority that decides who may use what. It grants leases atomically and without waiting: a request either gets every resource or none, and a conflict is reported immediately instead of being queued or preempting the holder. Most code reaches it through [Device Operations](#device-operations), which acquire and release leases around each operation tree.

A resource is identified by a string key. `resourceKey(device)` is the key an operation acquires to command a device, normally its hardware id, which every INDI interface of one physical device shares: a camera and its integrated wheel, a focuser and the rotator of a combined unit, or a cover and the flat panel of a flip-flat are one resource. The exception is the ST4 guide port of a camera, which has a key of its own so guiding can pulse while the same camera exposes. Resources with no device behind them, such as a remote guiding session, use a `logical:` key.

A key is unavailable for independent causes: the device lifecycle (disconnected or busy, see [Device Availability Lifecycle](#device-availability-lifecycle)), a quarantine (a pending driver payload that must be discarded first), and a guide pulse whose end was not yet observed (see [Guide Output Commander](#guide-output-commander)). Clearing one cause leaves the others in place. Durable ownership across operations is covered by [Device Reservations](#device-reservations).

```ts
import { deviceKey, guideOutputKey, ResourceArbiter, resourceDevice, resourceKey } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/resource'

const arbiter = new ResourceArbiter()
const capture = { id: 'capture-1', kind: 'capture' }
const focus = { id: 'focus-1', kind: 'autoFocus' }

// Physical keys normally come from resourceKey(device) and carry the device: { key, device }.
const camera = 'camera-hardware-id'

// Acquires every requested key or none; the owner is compared by identity.
const acquired = arbiter.acquire(capture, [{ key: camera }, { key: 'logical:guider:local' }])
if (!acquired.ok) throw new Error('busy')
console.log(arbiter.availability(camera)) // 'leased'

// Who holds what: by owner and key, the holders of a key, and the keys of an owner.
console.log(arbiter.owns(capture, camera), arbiter.ownersOf(camera), arbiter.resourcesOf(capture)) // true [{ id: 'capture-1', kind: 'capture' }] ['camera-hardware-id', 'logical:guider:local']

// All or nothing: the free focuser is not taken because the camera is refused.
const refused = arbiter.acquire(focus, [{ key: camera }, { key: 'focuser-hardware-id' }])
console.log(refused.ok ? [] : refused.conflicts) // [{ key: 'camera-hardware-id', by: 'lease', ownerId: 'capture-1', ownerKind: 'capture', causes: [] }]

acquired.lease.release()

// Unavailability causes are independent: clearing quarantine leaves lifecycle in place.
arbiter.markUnavailable(camera, 'quarantine')
arbiter.markUnavailable(camera)
arbiter.markAvailable(camera, 'quarantine')
console.log(arbiter.snapshot(camera).causes) // ['lifecycle']

// device: Device — a managed INDI device. Its keys: the capability, the guide port, and the physical device;
// resourceDevice resolves a sub-device proxy to its parent.
console.log(resourceKey(device), guideOutputKey(device), deviceKey(device), resourceDevice(device).name) // for a focuser: its hardware id, '<hardwareId>:guideOutput', its hardware id, and its own name

// What the lifecycle does on device events: block every capability of one physical device, or one capability
// (markCapabilityAvailable clears it), and drop a device's association with a key.
arbiter.markDeviceUnavailable(deviceKey(device))
arbiter.markCapabilityUnavailable(resourceKey(device))
arbiter.markCapabilityAvailable(resourceKey(device))
arbiter.disassociate(resourceKey(device), device)

// A whole client while its server reconnects, and the owners a disconnect must reach (by device or by client).
arbiter.markClientUnavailable('client-id')
console.log(arbiter.ownersOfDevice(deviceKey(device)), arbiter.ownersOfClient('client-id'))
arbiter.markClientAvailable('client-id')
```

### Firmata Accelerometer

An inertial measurement unit combines an accelerometer, which measures specific force (gravity included, so at rest it reads about 9.81 m/s² along the vertical and reveals the tilt of the sensor), and a gyroscope, which measures angular velocity. Attached to a telescope tube or a mount, it gives the inclination or the motion of the instrument without encoders.

`MPU6050` drives the InvenSense MPU-6050 six-axis IMU over I2C and implements both `Accelerometer` (`ax`, `ay`, `az` in m/s²) and `Gyroscope` (`gx`, `gy`, `gz` in rad/s). The full-scale ranges trade resolution for headroom: ±2 to ±16 g for the accelerometer and ±250 to ±2000 °/s for the gyroscope. The values are in the sensor frame: no gravity removal, offset calibration or filtering is applied, and the gyroscope bias of an individual chip is not corrected, so integrating the angular velocity drifts.

```ts
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { MPU6050 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/sensors/accelerometer'

// A client over TCP to a board that runs Firmata (the address and port are an example).
const client = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await client.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// ±16 g and ±2000 °/s on the default address 0x68, polled every 50 ms.
const imu = new MPU6050(client, MPU6050.ADDRESS, 50, { accelerometerRange: 16, gyroscopeRange: 2000 })

// The listener receives the acceleration in m/s² and the angular velocity in rad/s, in the sensor frame.
imu.addListener((device) => console.log(device.ax, device.ay, device.az, device.gx, device.gy, device.gz))

// Wakes the chip, writes the ranges and polls the measurement registers.
imu.start()
imu.stop()
```

### Firmata Ammeter

A Hall-effect current sensor carries the current through a conductor next to a Hall element and outputs a voltage proportional to it, centred on a zero-current voltage (half the supply) so both directions of flow can be read. The current is `I = (V - V0) / S`, where `V0` is the zero-current voltage and `S` the sensitivity of the variant in V/A. The DC current of a dew heater, a focuser or a whole observatory power line is the typical use.

`ACS712` reads an Allegro ACS712 on one analog pin and implements `Ammeter` (`current` in amperes, signed by the direction of the flow). It is an analog peripheral (see [Firmata Peripheral Base](#firmata-peripheral-base)): every ADC report is converted with the reference voltage and resolution of the board's converter. The sensor offset varies with the supply and the unit, so give the actual ADC reference and the measured no-load voltage. No filtering is applied: a reading is the instantaneous value and does not average an AC waveform.

```ts
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { ACS712 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/sensors/ammeter'

// A client over TCP to a board that runs Firmata (the address and port are an example).
const client = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await client.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// The 30 A variant (0.066 V/A) on analog pin 0, a 3.3 V reference, a 12-bit converter and a measured 1.64 V zero.
const ammeter = new ACS712(client, 0, { range: 30, aref: 3.3, adcResolution: 4095, zeroCurrentVoltage: 1.64 })

// The listener receives the current in amperes on every new sample.
ammeter.addListener((device) => console.log(device.current))
ammeter.start()
ammeter.stop()
```

### Firmata Analog Thermometer

The LM35 is a linear analog temperature sensor whose output rises 10 mV per degree Celsius from 0 V at 0 °C, so the temperature follows directly from the ADC count: `T = aref * 100 * raw / 1023` for a 10-bit converter. It is a cheap way to monitor the ambient or the optics temperature, for example to follow the focus drift of a cooling telescope.

`LM35` reads it on one analog pin and implements `Thermometer` (`temperature` in degrees Celsius). It is an analog peripheral (see [Firmata Peripheral Base](#firmata-peripheral-base)), and the ADC reference voltage must match the real reference of the board. The plain LM35 reads from about 2 °C to 150 °C and has no negative range without a bias network, which matters on cold nights; no averaging is applied, so the ADC noise of the board shows in the reading. For a one-wire digital sensor with a wider range see [Firmata Digital Thermometer](#firmata-digital-thermometer).

```ts
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { LM35 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/sensors/thermometer'

// A client over TCP to a board that runs Firmata (the address and port are an example).
const client = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await client.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// An LM35 on analog pin 0 with a 3.3 V ADC reference.
const thermometer = new LM35(client, 0, 3.3)

// The listener receives the temperature in degrees Celsius on every change.
thermometer.addListener((device) => console.log(device.temperature))
thermometer.start()
thermometer.stop()
```

### Firmata Barometer and Altimeter

The atmospheric pressure at the site, together with the temperature, is what an atmospheric refraction correction needs, and its trend is a simple weather indicator. A barometric sensor also gives a pressure altitude: the height at which the International Standard Atmosphere (15 °C and 1013.25 hPa at sea level, with the standard temperature lapse rate) would have the measured pressure. That altitude changes with the weather and no sea-level reduction is applied, so it is not a substitute for the surveyed site elevation.

`BMP180` and `BMP280` are the Bosch barometric pressure sensors over I2C. Both implement `Barometer` (`pressure` in hPa, equal to millibar), `Altimeter` (`altitude`, a `Distance` in astronomical units like every distance of the library; `toMeter` converts it) and `Thermometer` (`temperature` in degrees Celsius). Readings are compensated with the factory calibration of each chip, which the driver reads first; polling begins only when that block arrives, so a board that never answers stays silent. The BMP280 adds configurable oversampling, an IIR filter and a forced (one-shot) mode.

```ts
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { BMP180, BMP180Mode, BMP280 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/sensors/barometer'
import { toMeter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// A client over TCP to a board that runs Firmata (the address and port are an example).
const client = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await client.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// A BMP280 at 0x76 in normal mode: hPa, pressure altitude in metres, and °C.
const bmp280 = new BMP280(client)
bmp280.addListener((device) => console.log(device.pressure, toMeter(device.altitude), device.temperature))

// Reads the calibration block, then polls the measurements.
bmp280.start()
bmp280.stop()

// A BMP180 with the highest oversampling.
const bmp180 = new BMP180(client, BMP180Mode.ULTRA_HIGH_RESOLUTION)
bmp180.start()
bmp180.stop()
```

### Firmata Character Display

The Hitachi HD44780 controller drives the common 16x2 and 20x4 character LCDs, and these modules usually come with an I2C backpack, a PCF8574 I/O expander wired to the control and data lines of the display (see [Firmata IO Expander](#firmata-io-expander)). On an observatory controller it shows readings or state without a computer screen.

`HD44780` runs the display in 4-bit mode following the LiquidCrystal power-on sequence and translates every command or character into expander writes, mirroring the Arduino LiquidCrystal API (cursor, display and blink control, scrolling, text direction, backlight and eight custom 5x8 glyphs). `begin()` must be called once first: its initialization blocks the thread for about 60 ms. Text is not wrapped between lines, and only the characters of the controller character set (ASCII and its ROM extensions) display properly. Nothing is read back, so a display that is not connected simply does not answer.

```ts
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { HD44780 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/components/display'
import { PCF8574 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/components/io'

// A client over TCP to a board that runs Firmata (the address and port are an example).
const client = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await client.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// A 16x2 module on a PCF8574 backpack at 0x27 (polling disabled), with the common backpack wiring.
const lcd = new HD44780(new PCF8574(client, 0x27, 0))

// Starts the expander and runs the 4-bit initialization (blocking, about 60 ms) for 16 columns and 2 rows.
lcd.begin(16, 2)

// Writes text at a column and row (zero-based).
lcd.setCursor(0, 0)
lcd.print('T 12.5 C')
lcd.setCursor(0, 1)
lcd.print('RH 64 %')

// A custom glyph in slot 0 (a heart), then written by its code.
lcd.createChar(0, [0x00, 0x0a, 0x1f, 0x1f, 0x1f, 0x0e, 0x04, 0x00])
lcd.write(0)

// A blinking block at the cursor; cursor/noCursor, display/noDisplay and noBlink toggle the other display controls.
lcd.blink()

// Shifts the whole display one column; scrollDisplayRight shifts the other way.
lcd.scrollDisplayLeft()

// Text direction and automatic shift on write; leftToRight and noAutoscroll restore the defaults.
lcd.rightToLeft()
lcd.autoscroll()

// Returns the cursor and the shift home, then clears the screen.
lcd.home()
lcd.clear()

// Turns the backlight off; backlight() turns it on.
lcd.noBacklight()
lcd.stop()
```

### Firmata DAC

A digital-to-analog converter turns a number into a voltage, for example to dim a flat panel driven by an analog input or to provide an adjustable reference. The Microchip MCP4725 is a 12-bit I2C DAC whose output is `V = value / 4095 * Vdd`, so its resolution is about 0.8 mV on a 3.3 V supply. When not needed, the output can be powered down and pulled to ground through an internal resistor.

`MCP4725` drives it as a write-only device: nothing is ever read back from the chip. The code and the power-down mode are properties, and a change is written immediately once the peripheral is started (staged before that). `persist()` also writes them to the EEPROM of the chip so the output powers up in that state; the EEPROM has a limited number of write cycles, so persisting is a configuration step, not a per-sample operation.

```ts
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { MCP4725 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/components/dac'

// A client over TCP to a board that runs Firmata (the address and port are an example).
const client = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await client.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// Half scale (code 2048 of 4095, about 1.65 V on a 3.3 V supply), written by start().
const dac = new MCP4725(client, MCP4725.ADDRESS, { value: 2048 })
dac.start()

// A new code is written at once; the output can be released through a 100 kΩ pull-down.
dac.value = 4095
dac.powerDownMode = '100k'

// Stores the code and the power-down mode in the EEPROM as the power-up state.
dac.persist()
dac.stop()
```

### Firmata Digital Thermometer

The Dallas/Maxim DS18B20 is a digital thermometer on the 1-Wire bus: each sensor has a unique 64-bit ROM address (family code 0x28), so several can share one pin, for example to measure the ambient air, the primary mirror and the tube at once and follow the thermal equilibrium of a telescope. It reads from −55 °C to +125 °C with a programmable resolution of 9 to 12 bits, at 0.0625 °C per least significant bit in 12-bit mode, and a higher resolution takes longer to convert (up to 750 ms).

`DS18B20` reads it through the One-Wire feature of the client (see [Firmata One-Wire](#firmata-one-wire)) and implements `Thermometer` (`temperature` in degrees Celsius). Without a ROM address it searches the bus and adopts the first DS18B20 found; SKIP ROM addresses a lone sensor without a search and is valid only with a single device on the bus. Each reading starts a conversion, waits for it, and accepts the scratchpad only with a valid CRC.

```ts
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { DS18B20 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/sensors/thermometer'

// A client over TCP to a board that runs Firmata (the address and port are an example).
const client = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await client.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// A known sensor on pin D4, by its 8-byte ROM address, at 9-bit resolution (0.5 °C, 94 ms conversion), polled every 1000 ms.
const rom = Buffer.from([0x28, 0xff, 0x64, 0x1e, 0x0f, 0x16, 0x03, 0x4b])
const sensor = new DS18B20(client, ESP8266.D4, 1000, { address: rom, resolution: 9 })

// The listener receives the temperature in degrees Celsius.
sensor.addListener((device) => console.log(device.temperature))
sensor.start()
sensor.stop()

// Without an address, start() searches the bus and adopts the first DS18B20.
const found = new DS18B20(client, ESP8266.D4)
found.start()
found.stop()
```

### Firmata FM Receivers

The FM broadcast band spans 87.5 to 108 MHz in most of the world and 76 to 91 MHz in Japan, with stations on a fixed channel grid. The NXP TEA5767 and the RDA Microelectronics RDA5807 are single-chip FM receivers controlled over I2C: the host tunes them, reads the received signal strength and the stereo indication, and seeks the next station, while the demodulated audio leaves through the analog pins of the module and never reaches the host.

`TEA5767` and `RDA5807` implement `RadioTuner`. Frequencies are in MHz and are snapped to the grid of the chip (100 kHz for the TEA5767, the configured channel spacing for the RDA5807). The state read from the chip is refreshed on a polling timer, so after a change it is stale until the next status frame arrives. The signal strength is an uncalibrated 0 to 127 scale, not a field strength. The RDA5807 seeks in hardware and has a volume control; the TEA5767 seek is done by the driver one step at a time, and that chip has no volume control.

```ts
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { RDA5807, TEA5767 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/components/radio'

// A client over TCP to a board that runs Firmata (the address and port are an example).
const client = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await client.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// An RDA5807 tuned to 104.3 MHz; the listener receives the frequency (MHz), stereo, signal strength (0–127) and station flag.
const rda = new RDA5807(client)
rda.addListener((device) => console.log(device.frequency, device.stereo, device.rssi, device.station))
rda.start()
rda.frequency = 104.3

// A hardware seek up to the next station, and one channel down (frequencyUp moves one channel up).
rda.seek('up')
rda.frequencyDown()

// The volume (0–100, in 16 chip steps); volumeUp and volumeDown move one chip step.
rda.volume = 50
rda.volumeUp()

// Mutes and unmutes the audio (the same as the muted property); stereo = false forces mono.
rda.mute()
rda.unmute()
rda.stereo = false

// Chip-specific audio settings: the bass boost and the high-impedance audio output.
rda.bassBoost = true
rda.audioOutputHighZ = false
rda.stop()

// A TEA5767 on the Japanese band; frequencyUp() and frequencyDown() move one 100 kHz step.
const tea = new TEA5767(client, TEA5767.ADDRESS, 1000, { frequency: 80, band: 'japan' })
tea.start()
tea.frequencyUp()

// A software seek, one step at a time, down to the next station, wrapping at the band edge.
tea.seek('down', true)

// Receiver settings of the TEA5767: soft mute; highCutControl, stereoNoiseCancelling and highSideInjection likewise.
tea.softMute = true
tea.stop()
```

### Firmata FM Transmitter

The KT Micro KT0803L is a single-chip FM stereo transmitter controlled over I2C: it modulates the audio on its analog inputs onto a carrier between 70 and 108 MHz, on 50 kHz channels. Transmitting is regulated by law in most places, so the output power, the frequency and the use of the transmitter must comply with the local rules.

`KT0803L` implements `RadioTransmitter`. It is write-only: the driver keeps the configuration, writes the registers on `start()` and on each change, and never reads anything back, so nothing confirms that the chip received a write. Frequencies are in MHz, rounded to the nearest channel and clamped to the band. The audio gain is in dB, while the transmit power is the RF gain code of the datasheet (0 to 15), not a calibrated power. `stop()` puts the chip in standby.

```ts
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { KT0803L } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/components/radio'

// A client over TCP to a board that runs Firmata (the address and port are an example).
const client = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await client.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// Transmits mono at 100.1 MHz with a low RF gain code and the 50 µs pre-emphasis used in Europe.
const transmitter = new KT0803L(client, KT0803L.ADDRESS, { frequency: 100.1, stereo: false, transmitPower: 4, preEmphasis: 50 })
transmitter.start()

// Each change rewrites the registers that carry it: one 50 kHz channel up (frequencyDown moves down), and +6 dB of audio gain.
transmitter.frequencyUp()
transmitter.gain = 6

// Mutes and unmutes the audio input (the same as the muted property); stereo = true enables the stereo encoder.
transmitter.mute()
transmitter.unmute()
transmitter.stereo = true

// The RF gain code and the bass boost in dB; preEmphasis, deviation, pilotToneHigh, automaticLevelControl,
// automaticPowerDown, powerAmplifierBias and audioEnhancement are set the same way.
transmitter.transmitPower = 8
transmitter.bassBoost = 5

// Standby.
transmitter.stop()
```

### Firmata Hygrometer

Relative humidity, together with the air temperature, gives the dew point: when a surface cools below it, dew forms, and an optical surface radiating to the clear night sky cools below the air. A humidity sensor near the telescope therefore tells when the dew heaters are needed and when it is time to close.

`AM2320` and `SHT21` are I2C humidity and temperature sensors; both implement `Hygrometer` (`humidity`, relative humidity in percent) and `Thermometer` (`temperature` in degrees Celsius) and are polled no faster than once per second. The AM2320 frame is accepted only with a valid CRC, while the SHT21 reading is converted with the datasheet formulas without checking its CRC. Neither driver applies a calibration offset.

```ts
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { AM2320, SHT21 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/sensors/hygrometer'

// A client over TCP to a board that runs Firmata (the address and port are an example).
const client = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await client.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// An SHT21 at 0x40: the listener receives the relative humidity in percent and the temperature in °C.
const sht21 = new SHT21(client)
sht21.addListener((device) => console.log(device.humidity, device.temperature))
sht21.start()

// Sends the soft-reset command to the SHT21.
sht21.reset()
sht21.stop()

// An AM2320 at 0x5C, read the same way.
const am2320 = new AM2320(client)
am2320.start()
am2320.stop()
```

### Firmata IO Expander

A board runs out of digital pins quickly; an I2C I/O expander adds eight more lines on two shared wires, for relays, switches, limit sensors or an LCD backpack. The NXP/TI PCF8574 is quasi-bidirectional: it has no direction register, and a pin reads as an input only while it is written high (released), so the byte written to the chip is the output byte with every input pin forced high.

`PCF8574` implements `IOExpander`. Pins are numbered 0 to 7, pin n being bit n of the port. Writes can be batched and sent with a single flush. Reads return the logic level of the latest port snapshot without a bus transaction, so they reflect the chip only after a reply, and input changes are seen at the polling period, since the interrupt line of the chip is not used.

```ts
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { PCF8574 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/components/io'
import { PinMode } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/types'

// A client over TCP to a board that runs Firmata (the address and port are an example).
const client = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await client.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// An expander at 0x20 polled every 1000 ms, every pin released as an input.
const expander = new PCF8574(client, PCF8574.ADDRESS, 1000)
expander.addListener((device) => console.log(device.pinRead(7)))
expander.start()

// Pins 0 and 1 become outputs; the two writes are sent together by flush().
expander.pinWrite(0, false, false)
expander.pinWrite(1, true, false)
expander.flush()

// Pin 0 back to an input, and the level of pin 7 from the latest snapshot.
expander.pinMode(0, PinMode.INPUT)
console.log(expander.pinRead(7))

// Requests a fresh port snapshot without waiting for the next poll.
expander.refresh()
expander.stop()
```

### Firmata Light Sensors

Illuminance, in lux, is the luminous flux per unit area weighted by the photopic sensitivity of the human eye. It ranges from about 100000 lx in sunlight to below 0.01 lx on a moonless night, so a light sensor can tell day, twilight and night apart, detect dawn to close an observatory, or monitor the brightness of a flat panel. It is not a sky brightness in mag/arcsec²: the conversions here are those of the datasheets, with no spectral, cosine or absolute calibration, so the readings suit relative monitoring rather than photometry.

`BH1750`, `TSL2561` and `MAX44009` (I2C) and `TEMT6000` (analog) implement `Luxmeter` (`lux` in lux). The BH1750 is a 16-bit sensor whose sensitivity is set by its measurement time. The TSL2561 measures a broadband and an infrared channel and derives the illuminance from both; when a channel clips it reports the sentinel `TSL2561.SATURATED_LUX`, which is not a measurement and must be filtered out. The MAX44009 covers a very wide range, from 0.045 lx to about 188000 lx. The TEMT6000 is a phototransistor whose current, proportional to the illuminance, is read as a voltage across a load resistor.

```ts
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { BH1750, MAX44009, TEMT6000, TSL2561 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/sensors/luxmeter'

// A client over TCP to a board that runs Firmata (the address and port are an example).
const client = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await client.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// A BH1750 in continuous high-resolution mode; the listener receives the illuminance in lux.
const bh1750 = new BH1750(client)
bh1750.addListener((device) => console.log(device.lux))
bh1750.start()

// Clears the data register of the BH1750.
bh1750.reset()
bh1750.stop()

// A MAX44009 at 0x4A in continuous mode, polled every 1000 ms, for the widest range.
const max44009 = new MAX44009(client, MAX44009.ADDRESS, 1000, { continuousMode: true })
max44009.start()
max44009.stop()

// A TSL2561 at 16x gain and 101 ms integration, for dim light; a clipped reading is SATURATED_LUX.
const tsl2561 = new TSL2561(client, TSL2561.ADDRESS, 1000, { gain: 16, integrationTime: 101 })
tsl2561.addListener((device) => console.log(device.lux === TSL2561.SATURATED_LUX ? 'saturated' : device.lux))
tsl2561.start()
tsl2561.stop()

// A TEMT6000 on analog pin 0 with the default 5 V reference and 10 kΩ load.
const temt6000 = new TEMT6000(client, 0)
temt6000.start()
temt6000.stop()
```

### Firmata Magnetometer

A three-axis magnetometer measures the local magnetic field vector; the Earth's field is about 0.25 to 0.65 gauss, and its horizontal component points to magnetic north, so the sensor can give a rough azimuth for a mount or a dome. Turning it into a true heading needs a hard-iron and soft-iron calibration (the offsets and distortions of nearby metal and currents), a tilt compensation, and the magnetic declination of the site.

`HMC5883L` drives the Honeywell HMC5883L over I2C and implements `Magnetometer` (`x`, `y` and `z` in gauss, in the sensor frame). The full-scale range (0.88 to 8.1 gauss) trades resolution for headroom, and the output data rate and averaging set how fast and how smooth the samples are; a sample in which an axis overflows is dropped. The driver applies no calibration and no declination: the reading is the raw field.

```ts
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { HMC5883L } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/sensors/magnetometer'

// A client over TCP to a board that runs Firmata (the address and port are an example).
const client = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await client.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// Eight-sample averaging at 15 Hz with the 1.3 gauss range, polled every 100 ms.
const compass = new HMC5883L(client, HMC5883L.ADDRESS, 100, { sampleAveraging: 8, dataRate: 15, range: 1.3 })

// The listener receives the raw field in gauss, in the sensor frame.
compass.addListener((device) => console.log(device.x, device.y, device.z))
compass.start()
compass.stop()
```

### Firmata Peripheral Base

Firmata turns a microcontroller board into a remote set of pins and buses controlled from the host, and the library builds sensor and actuator drivers on top of it. `devices/firmata/peripheral` defines what every such peripheral is and the base classes that implement the common plumbing. A peripheral has a name, its client, `start()` and `stop()`, and is disposable. The measurement contracts fix the units every driver reports: `Thermometer` (°C), `Hygrometer` (% relative humidity), `Barometer` (hPa), `Altimeter` (a `Distance` in AU), `Luxmeter` (lux), `Ammeter` (A), `Accelerometer` (m/s²), `Gyroscope` (rad/s) and `Magnetometer` (gauss), plus the radio, clock, I/O expander and display contracts of the following topics.

Listeners are called with the peripheral on every change of its reading, and a listener added later still gets its first reading even when the value did not change. A sample counter counts every completed reading, changed or not, so a consumer can tell a sensor that holds a steady value from one that stopped answering. `ADCPeripheral` is the base of the analog sensors: a subclass declares its pin and a `calculate(raw)` that converts the raw count of the Firmata analog report to the physical quantity and returns whether it changed. `PeripheralBase` is the base of the bus-attached ones and queues register reads over I2C.

```ts
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import type { FirmataClient } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { ADCPeripheral, type Thermometer } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/peripheral'

// A client over TCP to a board that runs Firmata (the address and port are an example).
const client = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await client.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// An analog sensor of 10 mV per °C on pin 0, with a 3.3 V reference and a 10-bit converter.
class Probe extends ADCPeripheral<Probe> implements Thermometer {
	readonly name = 'Probe'
	readonly pin = 0
	temperature = 0

	constructor(readonly client: FirmataClient) {
		super()
	}

	// Converts the raw count to °C and reports whether the reading changed.
	calculate(raw: number) {
		const temperature = ((raw / 1023) * 3.3) / 0.01
		const changed = temperature !== this.temperature
		this.temperature = temperature
		return changed
	}
}

// The listener receives the reading on every change; samples counts every completed reading.
const probe = new Probe(client)
const listener = (device: Probe) => console.log(device.temperature, device.samples)
probe.addListener(listener)

// start() puts the pin in analog mode and enables its reports, which then feed calculate().
probe.start()

// Whether every attached listener has received its first reading.
console.log(probe.initialized)

// Detaches the listener; stop() disables the reports, and disposing the peripheral (using) also stops it.
probe.removeListener(listener)
probe.stop()
```

### Firmata Real-Time Clock

A real-time clock keeps the calendar time on a coin cell while the board is off, so a controller without network access still knows the date. The Maxim DS3231 is temperature-compensated and much more stable than the DS1307, which runs from a plain external crystal whose rate drifts with temperature. Neither chip has a sub-second register, so the time is known to the second at best.

`DS3231` and `DS1307` are I2C real-time clocks implementing `RealTimeClock`, with the calendar fields year, month (1 to 12), day, day of week, hour (0 to 23), minute and second. The time is the wall-clock time the chip was programmed with, normally local time: the drivers carry no time zone or UTC offset, so convert to UTC before using it for astronomy. `sync()` writes the fields of a `Date` in the local time zone of the host. The DS1307 has no century bit and always reports years from 2000 to 2099.

```ts
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { DS1307, DS3231 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/components/rtc'

// A client over TCP to a board that runs Firmata (the address and port are an example).
const client = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await client.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// Reads the 7 calendar registers every second; the listener receives the decoded wall-clock time.
const rtc = new DS3231(client)
rtc.addListener((device) => console.log(device.year, device.month, device.day, device.hour, device.minute, device.second))
rtc.start()

// Sets 2026-10-05 (day of week 1) 21:30:15 in the chip's own wall-clock time.
rtc.update(2026, 10, 5, 1, 21, 30, 15)

// Sets it from the host clock in the host's local time zone.
rtc.sync()
rtc.stop()

// A DS1307 in place of the DS3231 (both answer at 0x68) has the same fields, update() and sync().
const ds1307 = new DS1307(client)
ds1307.start()
ds1307.sync(new Date())
ds1307.stop()
```

### Firmata-to-INDI Bridge

The application's device managers, weather safety and auxiliary views consume INDI devices. `FirmataIndiClient` lets a board attached over Firmata take part without an INDI server: it is a local, network-free implementation of the INDI client contract that exposes Firmata peripherals as virtual INDI devices, publishing standard INDI properties through a handler.

`createPeripheral(peripheral)` chooses the device from the interfaces the peripheral implements. A sensor becomes a device with read-only measurement vectors: `WEATHER_PARAMETERS` with the temperature (°C), the relative humidity (%) and the pressure (hPa, at the sensor altitude, not reduced to sea level) for whichever of them it reports, which makes it a Weather device, and `ALTITUDE` (m), `CURRENT` (A), `ILLUMINANCE` (lx), `ACCELERATION` (m/s²), `ANGULAR_VELOCITY` (rad/s) and `MAGNETIC_FIELD` (G) as Auxiliary vectors. A real-time clock becomes an auxiliary device with a writable `TIME` vector and a `TIME_SYNC` switch that writes the host clock.

Devices are connected with the usual INDI `CONNECTION` switch. A measurement vector is published Busy and settles to Idle only with its first real reading, so a value not yet known is never presented as a measurement; the weather vector is also republished periodically so its consumers can tell the sensor is alive. A board reset or a transport close disconnects every device, and a later ready makes them connectable again.

```ts
import { FirmataIndiClient } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/adapters/indi.client'
import { ESP8266 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/board'
import { FirmataClientOverTcp } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/client.tcp'
import { DS3231 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/components/rtc'
import { SHT21 } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/firmata/sensors/hygrometer'

// A Firmata client over TCP to a board (the address and port are an example).
const firmata = new FirmataClientOverTcp(new ESP8266())
await firmata.connect('192.168.0.50', 3030)

// The bridge publishes INDI events to the handler, normally the device managers.
const bridge = new FirmataIndiClient(firmata, 'esp8266', { handler: { setNumberVector: (_, message) => console.log(message.device, message.name, message.elements) } })

// Resolves true once the board finished its initialization; ready is the current state.
await bridge.whenReady()
console.log(bridge.ready)

// An SHT21 becomes the Weather and Auxiliary device 'SHT21' with WEATHER_PARAMETERS.
const weather = bridge.createPeripheral(new SHT21(firmata))

// The same as the INDI CONNECTION switch: starts the peripheral and publishes its vectors.
bridge.sendSwitch({ device: 'SHT21', name: 'CONNECTION', elements: { CONNECT: true, DISCONNECT: false } })

// A DS3231 becomes the writable clock device 'DS3231', connected directly.
const clock = bridge.createPeripheral(new DS3231(firmata))
await clock.connect()
console.log(clock.isConnected)

// Writes the TIME vector to the clock (sendText routes text vectors the same way), and TIME_SYNC writes the host clock.
bridge.sendNumber({ device: 'DS3231', name: 'TIME', elements: { YEAR: 2026, MONTH: 10, DAY: 5, HOUR: 21, MINUTE: 30, SECOND: 15 } })
bridge.sendSwitch({ device: 'DS3231', name: 'TIME_SYNC', elements: { SYNC: true } })

// Replays the definitions and current values of every device (or of one, by device and property name).
bridge.getProperties()

// Disconnects one device, removes another, then tears every device down.
weather.disconnect()
clock.dispose()
bridge.dispose()
```

### Guide Output Commander

A guide pulse is a timed command: the mount or the camera ST4 port drives one axis for the requested milliseconds and stops by itself. The driver reports the pulse Busy and later Idle, but both reports may be late or missing, and a pulse cannot always be cut short, because the standard INDI guider interface and the Alpaca bridge ignore a zero-duration stop. A pulse therefore has a quiescence window, computed from the instant it was dispatched: a Busy may still begin until its acknowledgement deadline, and the axis is surely stopped by its end. Until the end of a pulse has been observed on the device, its guide output stays blocked in the [Device Resource Arbitration](#device-resource-arbitration), so no other operation starts with an axis still drifting.

`GuideOutputCommander` turns pulses into operations under the guide port key (`guideOutputKey`): a mount's guide output and the mount are one resource, while a camera's ST4 port is separate and pulses while the camera exposes. A single pulse resolves after the device reported it busy and then stopped, perpendicular pulses of one correction run together, and a cancelled pulse holds the device until it has ended. A guiding loop that issues one correction per frame dispatches it synchronously inside the operation that already holds the port. The windows are in milliseconds of `performance.now()`. [Guide Pulse Loop](#guide-pulse-loop) and [Guiding Calibration](#guiding-calibration) are built on it, and [INDI Guide Output](#indi-guide-output) is the manager below it.

```ts
import { GuideOutputCommander, guidePulseReleaseBound, guidePulseWindow } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/commanders/guideoutput'
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { GuideOutputManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/guideoutput'
import { MountManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/mount'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { MountSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/mount'
import { DeviceLifecycle } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/device.lifecycle'
import { OperationCoordinator, successfulOperationResult } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/operation'
import { guideOutputKey, ResourceArbiter } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/resource'

const mountManager = new MountManager()
const guideOutputManager = new GuideOutputManager(mountManager)
const arbiter = new ResourceArbiter()
const coordinator = new OperationCoordinator(arbiter)
const lifecycle = new DeviceLifecycle(arbiter, coordinator)
lifecycle.observe(mountManager)
lifecycle.observe(guideOutputManager)

// The commander needs the arbiter to block a guide port whose pulse end was not yet observed.
using guideCommander = new GuideOutputCommander(guideOutputManager, arbiter)

const client = new ClientSimulator('Client Simulator', new IndiClientHandlerSet([mountManager, guideOutputManager]))
const simulator = new MountSimulator('Mount Simulator', client)
mountManager.connect(mountManager.get(client, simulator.name)!)
const guide = guideOutputManager.get(client, simulator.name)!
while (arbiter.availability(guideOutputKey(guide)) !== 'available') await Bun.sleep(10)

// The window of a 2000 ms pulse dispatched at 0 ms, and the longest wait to release the port after stopping one of 2500 ms.
console.log(guidePulseWindow(0, 2000), guidePulseReleaseBound(2500)) // { busyAckDeadline: 2250, endsBy: 4500 } 20500

// Guide rates as fractions of the sidereal rate (right ascension, declination), confirmed by the driver.
await guideCommander.setGuideRate(coordinator, guide, 0.5, 0.5)

// A 500 ms pulse north, then perpendicular pulses of one correction in one operation.
console.log(await guideCommander.pulse(coordinator, guide, 'NORTH', 500)) // { ok: true, value: undefined }
await guideCommander.pulseAxes(coordinator, guide, [
	{ direction: 'NORTH', duration: 300 },
	{ direction: 'EAST', duration: 600 },
])

// Inside an operation that holds the port: dispatch sends at once and returns the pulse window.
await coordinator.start('guiding', [{ key: guideOutputKey(guide), device: guide }], (context) => {
	console.log(guideCommander.dispatch(context, guide, 'WEST', 200), guideCommander.dispatchedPulseWindow(guide)) // { busyAckDeadline, endsBy } in ms, twice
	return successfulOperationResult(undefined)
}).result

// Emergency stops that acquire nothing: one direction, or several.
await guideCommander.stopPulse(guide, 'NORTH')
await guideCommander.stopPulses(guide, ['NORTH', 'EAST'])

// A pulse sent by someone else, of at most 1000 ms: blocks the port until its end is observed.
guideCommander.assumeDispatchedPulse(guide, 1000)
console.log(arbiter.snapshot(guideOutputKey(guide)).causes) // ['guidePulse']

lifecycle.dispose()
simulator.dispose()
```

### INDI Camera Control

An astronomical camera is more than a shutter: its sensor is usually cooled, because the dark current (thermal electrons that accumulate even without light) roughly doubles every few degrees, and a stable set-point lets dark frames taken later match the lights. A capture also chooses the kind of frame (`LIGHT`, `DARK`, `FLAT` or `BIAS`, the calibration set described in the imaging topics), a subframe and binning in unbinned sensor pixels, and gain and offset in the driver's own units (not electrons per ADU). The pixel size (micrometres) and the colour filter array of a one-shot-colour sensor describe how the image must be interpreted downstream.

`CameraManager` builds a `Camera` device from the INDI CCD interface and reflects its vectors onto the shared model that also serves the Alpaca camera. The image arrives as the `CCD1` BLOB, forwarded to the handlers added with `addHandler` once BLOB delivery is enabled; when the driver offers no transfer formats (as an Alpaca camera), only FITS can be relied on. `snoop` tells the driver which mount, focuser, filter wheel and rotator to read, so that their state can describe the frame. The sensor temperature is read through [INDI Thermometer](#indi-thermometer), the guide port through [INDI Guide Output](#indi-guide-output), and a heater through [INDI Dew Heater](#indi-dew-heater). Like every INDI manager, the state follows the driver: a command becomes visible only after the driver reports it.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { CameraManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/camera'
import { CameraSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/camera'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'

const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const manager = new CameraManager()
handler.add(manager)

// The in-process simulator stands for an INDI server; with real hardware only the client changes.
using client = new ClientSimulator('camera', handler)
using simulator = new CameraSimulator('Camera Simulator', client)
const camera = manager.get(client, simulator.name)!

// Each finished exposure is delivered as a Buffer holding the FITS (or XISF) file.
manager.addHandler({ added() {}, removed() {}, blobReceived: (_, data, encoding) => console.log(data.length, encoding) })

// waitUntil(condition): a local helper that awaits Bun.sleep until condition() is true.
manager.connect(camera)
await waitUntil(() => camera.connected)
manager.enableBlob(camera)

// mount, focuser, wheel, rotator: optional devices of their managers, whose state the driver stamps into the frame header.
manager.snoop(camera, mount, focuser, wheel, rotator)

// Cool the sensor to -10 °C; camera.coolerPower is in percent.
manager.cooler(camera, true)
manager.temperature(camera, -10)

// Subframe in unbinned pixels, 2×2 binning, gain and offset in driver units, frame type and file format.
manager.frame(camera, 100, 50, 640, 480)
manager.bin(camera, 2, 2)
manager.gain(camera, 120)
manager.offset(camera, 10)
manager.frameType(camera, 'LIGHT')
manager.transferFormat(camera, 'FITS')

// The capture format by name (one of camera.frameFormats, such as MONO or RGB on the simulator) and BLOB compression.
manager.frameFormat(camera, camera.frameFormats[0].name)
manager.compression(camera, false)

// A 1 s exposure: exposuring is true while it runs, and the image reaches the handler when it ends.
manager.startExposure(camera, 1)
await waitUntil(() => camera.exposuring)
await waitUntil(() => !camera.exposuring)

// Aborts an exposure in progress without an image, then stops BLOB delivery.
manager.stopExposure(camera)
manager.disableBlob(camera)
```

### INDI Camera Simulator

Imaging software (calibration, stacking, plate solving, autofocus, guiding) needs images whose content is known and reproducible, which a real sky never gives. `CameraSimulator` is an in-process INDI camera that renders physically plausible frames: a 16-bit sensor of 1280 × 1024 pixels of 5.2 µm with a cooler, the full CCD vector set of a real driver, and the image delivered as a FITS or XISF `CCD1` BLOB with its header.

The frame types differ as in a real camera: a bias holds only the offset and the read noise, a dark adds a dark current that grows with the sensor temperature (doubling over a fixed interval), a flat is a vignetted illumination with dust and banding, and a light adds the sky background, the stars and optional moon, light pollution and amp glow. Star fluxes and sky level scale linearly with the exposure time, and an exposure lasts its real duration. The stars come from a seeded random field or from a catalog projected through the pointing of the snooped mount; the star profile follows the snooped focuser position (so autofocus has a real V-curve), the field turns with the rotator, the filter dims the flux, and the stars trail along the recorded path of the mount during the exposure, so mount errors from [INDI Mount Simulator](#indi-mount-simulator) appear in the image. The scene, the noise and the optical aberrations are tuned through simulator-only INDI vectors, so any INDI client can change them; the shared connection and configuration behaviour is in [INDI Client Simulator](#indi-client-simulator).

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { CameraManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/camera'
import { MountManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/mount'
import { CameraSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/camera'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { MountSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/mount'

const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const mounts = new MountManager()
const cameras = new CameraManager()
handler.add(mounts)
handler.add(cameras)

// The camera reads the snooped devices through their managers: here the field centre follows the mount.
using client = new ClientSimulator('camera', handler)
using mount = new MountSimulator('Mount Simulator', client)
using simulator = new CameraSimulator('Camera Simulator', client, { mountManager: mounts, focalLength: 500, aperture: 80 })
mount.connect()
simulator.connect()
client.sendText({ device: simulator.name, name: 'ACTIVE_DEVICES', elements: { ACTIVE_TELESCOPE: mount.name } })

// A denser random star field; the seed of SIMULATOR_SCENE makes every frame reproducible.
client.sendNumber({ device: simulator.name, name: 'SIMULATOR_SCENE', elements: { STAR_DENSITY: 0.003 } })

// The methods are the INDI actions: a subframe in unbinned pixels, binning, and the cooler target in °C.
simulator.setFrame(0, 0, 256, 256)
simulator.setBin(2, 2)
simulator.setTargetTemperature(-10)
console.log(simulator.imageWidth, simulator.imageHeight) // 128 128 (binned pixels)

// What the next frame is rendered from: the sensor, the snooped mount and its centre (radians), and the scene.
console.log(simulator.sensorWidth, simulator.sensorHeight, simulator.frameType, simulator.cfaPattern, simulator.channels)
// activeMountSimulator is the simulator behind the mount, and sceneTime the instant of its simulated clock.
console.log(simulator.activeMount?.name, simulator.reportedCenter, simulator.sceneTime, simulator.activeFocuser, simulator.activeRotator, simulator.activeFilter)
console.log(simulator.catalogSourceType, simulator.seeing, simulator.telescopeFocalLength, simulator.telescopeAperture) // focal length and aperture in mm

// A 0.5 s exposure; the image reaches CameraManager handlers as the CCD1 BLOB when it ends.
simulator.startExposure(0.5)
console.log(simulator.isExposuring) // true

// abortExposure ends it without a frame; pulse drives the ST4 port of the camera, in ms.
simulator.abortExposure()
simulator.pulse('NORTH', 500)
console.log(simulator.isPulsing) // true
```

### INDI Client Simulator

The simulator backend runs INDI devices inside the process, with no server and no network, so the device managers and everything built on them (capture, mount control, guiding, focusing) can be exercised deterministically in tests and demonstrations. `ClientSimulator` implements the same `Client` contract as the TCP client of [INDI Protocol Client](#indi-protocol-client): the managers send their commands to it, and it routes each one to the registered simulator with the addressed device name.

Every simulated device shares the `DeviceSimulator` base: on construction it registers itself and publishes `DRIVER_INFO` (from which the managers create the device), `CONNECTION`, `ACTIVE_DEVICES` (the snooped mount, focuser, filter wheel and rotator) and `CONFIG`; connecting defines the device vectors, as a driver does. Persistence is entirely in the caller's hands: the optional `save` and `load` hooks receive and return the savable vectors, which `CONFIG` (or `saveProperties` and the asynchronous `loadProperties`) uses to keep a device's settings across sessions. Each simulator is documented in its own topic.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { FlatPanelManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/flatpanel'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { FlatPanelSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/flatpanel'
import type { SimulatorProperty } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/types'

// Persistence hooks: save receives the savable vectors, load returns those to apply (a real application would use a file).
const storage = new Map<string, readonly SimulatorProperty[]>()
const options = { save: (name: string, properties: readonly SimulatorProperty[]) => storage.set(name, structuredClone(properties)), load: (name: string) => storage.get(name) ?? [] }

const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const manager = new FlatPanelManager()
handler.add(manager)

// Disposing the client disposes every registered simulator.
using client = new ClientSimulator('simulator', handler)
const simulator = new FlatPanelSimulator('Flat Panel Simulator', client, options)

// The constructor registered the simulator under its name (register and unregister do it by hand).
console.log(client.get(simulator.name) === simulator) // true

// The manager created the device from DRIVER_INFO; connecting defines the panel vectors.
const panel = manager.get(client, simulator.name)!
manager.connect(panel)
console.log(simulator.isConnected) // true

// Save the configuration, change it, and load it back (asynchronous).
manager.intensity(panel, 90)
simulator.saveProperties()
manager.intensity(panel, 0)
await simulator.loadProperties()
console.log(panel.intensity.value) // 90

// disconnect() removes the device vectors, as the CONNECTION switch does.
simulator.disconnect()

// dispose disconnects, deletes the device, and unregisters it from the client.
simulator.dispose()
```

### INDI Cover

A motorized dust cap or telescope cover protects the optics between sessions and, closed, turns the telescope into a dark box for dark frames; many covers carry a flat panel on their inner side (see [INDI Flat Panel](#indi-flat-panel)). INDI models a cover as a parkable device through `CAP_PARK`: parking closes the cover and unparking opens it.

`CoverManager` turns these properties into a `Cover` device and sends the commands. A command only requests the movement, so a caller waits for `parked` or `parking` to change; the cover's heater, when present, is described in [INDI Dew Heater](#indi-dew-heater). The example uses [INDI Cover Simulator](#indi-cover-simulator), and with a real INDI server only the client changes.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { CoverManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/cover'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { CoverSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/cover'

const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const manager = new CoverManager()
handler.add(manager)

using client = new ClientSimulator('cover', handler)
using simulator = new CoverSimulator('Dust Cap Simulator', client)

// waitUntil(condition): a local helper that awaits Bun.sleep until condition() is true.
const cover = manager.get(client, simulator.name)!
manager.connect(cover)
await waitUntil(() => cover.connected)

// park() closes the cover; parking is true for the duration of the movement.
manager.park(cover)
await waitUntil(() => cover.parked)

// unpark() opens it, and stop() aborts a movement in progress.
manager.unpark(cover)
manager.stop(cover)
```

### INDI Cover Simulator

`CoverSimulator` is an in-process dust cap for testing observatory automation without hardware. It defines `CAP_PARK` and `CAP_ABORT` and reproduces the sequence a client sees with a real driver: a park or an unpark keeps `CAP_PARK` Busy for half a second and then reports the final position, and an abort stops the movement in place with an Alert. The cover starts open (unparked). The shared connection and configuration behaviour is in [INDI Client Simulator](#indi-client-simulator).

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { COVER_MOVE_TIME_MS } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/constants'
import { CoverSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/cover'

using client = new ClientSimulator('cover', new IndiClientHandlerSet())
using simulator = new CoverSimulator('Dust Cap Simulator', client)
simulator.connect()

// Through the INDI vector, as a client would: Busy during the movement, then Idle and parked.
client.sendSwitch({ device: simulator.name, name: 'CAP_PARK', elements: { PARK: true } })
await Bun.sleep(COVER_MOVE_TIME_MS + 100)

// The direct form of the switches; stop() cancels the movement (Alert, or Idle with stop(false)).
simulator.unpark()
await Bun.sleep(100)
simulator.stop()
simulator.park()
```

### INDI Device Managers

An INDI server publishes devices only as named property vectors, and a device appears, changes and disappears whenever its driver defines, updates or deletes them. A device manager is the layer that turns that stream into typed devices: one manager per device type reads the `DRIVER_INTERFACE` bitmask of `DRIVER_INFO`, creates a device of its type when the matching bit is set, applies every later vector to the device's fields with the library units, and reports each device as added, updated and removed. The same managers serve every `Client` (INDI, Alpaca, Firmata and the simulator), which is why everything above them is backend-independent.

A device has two identities: `id`, unique per interface view, and `hardwareId`, shared by every interface of one physical device (a camera and its built-in filter wheel). A capability that a device of another type publishes, such as the guide port of a mount, the temperature probe of a focuser or the heater of a cover, becomes a sub-device: a proxy of its own type over the parent, created by the capability's manager through a provider that resolves the parent. Each typed topic ([INDI Camera Control](#indi-camera-control), [INDI Mount Control](#indi-mount-control) and the others) adds its commands to this shared lifecycle; the raw vectors stay available in [INDI Property Registry](#indi-property-registry).

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { DeviceInterfaceType, findDeviceTypes, type Focuser, isFocuser, isInterfaceType, isSubDevice, isThermometer } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/device'
import { FocuserManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/focuser'
import { ThermometerManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/thermometer'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { FocuserSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/focuser'

// The thermometer manager takes the focuser manager as the provider of its parent devices.
const focusers = new FocuserManager()
const thermometers = new ThermometerManager(focusers)
const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet([focusers, thermometers])

// Lifecycle events of one device type; updated names the changed field, such as connected or position.
const events = { added: (device: Focuser) => console.log('added', device.name), updated: (device: Focuser, property: string) => property === 'connected' && console.log(device.connected), removed: (device: Focuser) => console.log('removed', device.name) }
focusers.addHandler(events)

using client = new ClientSimulator('focuser', handler)
const simulator = new FocuserSimulator('Focuser Simulator', client) // logs: added Focuser Simulator

// The managed devices (a Set, optionally of one client), their number, and a lookup by id, hardware id or name.
const names = Array.from(focusers.list(client), (e) => e.name)
console.log(names, focusers.length, focusers.has(client, 'Focuser Simulator')) // ['Focuser Simulator'] 1 true
const focuser = focusers.get(client, 'Focuser Simulator')!
console.log(focuser.type, focuser.interfaces) // 'focuser' ['focuser']

// Connect through the CONNECTION switch; ask requests the definitions again; simulation toggles a driver's SIMULATION switch.
focusers.connect(focuser)
focusers.ask(focuser)
focusers.simulation(focuser, false)

// The probe of the focuser is a thermometer sub-device: another id, the same hardware id.
const thermometer = thermometers.get(client, 'Focuser Simulator')!
console.log(isFocuser(focuser), isThermometer(focuser), isSubDevice(thermometer), thermometer.hardwareId === focuser.hardwareId) // true true true true

// The device types of a DRIVER_INTERFACE bitmask, and one bit test; isCamera, isMount and the other is* guards test a device.
console.log(findDeviceTypes(DeviceInterfaceType.CCD | DeviceInterfaceType.FILTER), isInterfaceType(0x1008, DeviceInterfaceType.ROTATOR)) // ['camera', 'wheel'] true

// Disconnect, and the device is removed when its driver deletes it (add and remove register or drop one by hand).
focusers.disconnect(focuser)
simulator.dispose() // logs: removed Focuser Simulator

// removeHandler unsubscribes from the events.
focusers.removeHandler(events)
```

### INDI Dew Heater

A telescope's optics radiate heat to the cold night sky and can fall below the dew point of the air, so moisture condenses on the objective or the corrector and ruins the images. A dew heater keeps the surface a few degrees warmer, and its power is set as a duty cycle. Some devices publish their heater as a generic number vector named `Heater`, as the WandererCover V4 EC does on its cover.

`DewHeaterManager` turns that vector into a `'dewHeater'` proxy device over its parent (resolved by the provider, here the cover manager) and marks the parent with `hasDewHeater`. The duty cycle keeps the unit and range the driver declares, and a command can be given the proxy or the parent. Deleting the vector removes the capability and the proxy. No simulator publishes the vector, so the example defines it by hand, as the driver would.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { CoverManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/cover'
import { DewHeaterManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/dewheater'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { CoverSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/cover'
import { makeNumberVector } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/types'

const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const covers = new CoverManager()
// The provider resolves the parent device of the heater.
const heaters = new DewHeaterManager(covers)
handler.add(covers)
handler.add(heaters)

using client = new ClientSimulator('cover', handler)
using simulator = new CoverSimulator('Wanderer Cover', client)
const cover = covers.get(client, simulator.name)!
covers.connect(cover)

// The driver defines the heater channel, 0 to 150, currently at 50.
handler.numberVector(client, makeNumberVector(simulator.name, 'Heater', 'Heater', 'Main Control', 'rw', ['Heater', 'Heater', 50, 0, 150, 1, '%g']), 'defNumberVector')

const dewHeater = heaters.get(client, simulator.name)!
console.log(dewHeater.dutyCycle.value, dewHeater.dutyCycle.max, cover.hasDewHeater) // 50 150 true

// Request a new duty cycle; the value changes when the driver reports it.
heaters.dutyCycle(dewHeater, 100)
```

### INDI Dome and Roof

An observatory dome must keep its slit in front of the telescope as the sky turns, and both a dome and a roll-off roof must be open before imaging and closed when conditions turn bad. Because the telescope is usually not at the centre of the dome, the dome azimuth that clears the light path differs from the telescope azimuth; drivers that compute it publish the dome measurements (radius, shutter width, mount displacements and OTA offset, in metres), and [Dome Slit Geometry](#dome-slit-geometry) explains that computation.

`DomeManager` builds a `Dome` device from the INDI Dome interface and reflects its vectors onto the shared model that also serves the roll-off roof and the ASCOM dome of the Alpaca backend. Azimuths and altitudes are radians in the model (the driver uses degrees) and the speed is in RPM. `slewing` is true while any part of the dome moves, including the shutter, like the ASCOM `Slewing`. Slaving (`slave`) lets the driver follow the active mount by itself; while it is on, the motion commands are ignored, and every command is ignored when the driver lacks its capability.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { DomeManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/dome'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { DomeSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/dome'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const manager = new DomeManager()
handler.add(manager)

using client = new ClientSimulator('dome', handler)
using simulator = new DomeSimulator('Dome Simulator', client)
const dome = manager.get(client, simulator.name)!

// waitUntil(condition): a local helper that awaits Bun.sleep until condition() is true.
manager.connect(dome)
await waitUntil(() => dome.connected)

// Absolute slew to an azimuth in radians; relative moves are signed.
manager.moveTo(dome, deg(30))
await waitUntil(() => dome.slewing)
await waitUntil(() => !dome.slewing)
console.log(toDeg(dome.azimuth.value)) // ≈ 30
manager.moveBy(dome, deg(-10))

// The shutter altitude, for drivers that publish it, and continuous rotation started and stopped by direction.
manager.moveToAltitude(dome, deg(45))
manager.move(dome, 'CLOCKWISE', true)
manager.move(dome, 'CLOCKWISE', false)

// Sync declares the current azimuth without moving; home slews to the reference position.
manager.syncTo(dome, deg(100))
manager.home(dome)

// Rotation speed in RPM, controller backlash compensation and its size in driver steps, and driver-side slaving.
manager.speed(dome, 3)
manager.backlash(dome, true)
manager.backlashSteps(dome, 20)
manager.slave(dome, false)

// The shutter is asynchronous: OPENING, then OPEN.
manager.openShutter(dome)
await waitUntil(() => dome.shutterState === 'OPEN')

// Store the current azimuth as the park position; unpark releases a parked dome; stop() aborts any motion.
manager.setPark(dome)
manager.unpark(dome)
manager.stop(dome)

// Close and park at the end of the night.
manager.closeShutter(dome)
manager.park(dome)
```

### INDI Dome Simulator

`DomeSimulator` is an in-process dome controller for testing observatory automation. Its azimuth motion and shutter transitions run on a clock from the elapsed wall time, so they are observable through the INDI vectors exactly as with a real driver. Angles are degrees on the INDI side and the speed is in RPM (one RPM is 6°/s); absolute moves take the shortest path, relative moves keep the requested direction across 0°, home and park are slews to their configured azimuths, and the shutter takes 1.5 s to open or close.

Given a `mountManager`, the simulator supports `DOME_AUTOSYNC`: it follows the azimuth of the telescope named by `ACTIVE_TELESCOPE`, computed from the mount's equatorial coordinate, time and site. It does not apply the off-centre geometry: the dome measurements and backlash vectors are stored but do not alter the motion. The shared connection and configuration behaviour is in [INDI Client Simulator](#indi-client-simulator).

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { MountManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/mount'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { DomeSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/dome'

const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const mounts = new MountManager()
handler.add(mounts)

// The mount manager enables autosync with the snooped telescope.
using client = new ClientSimulator('dome', handler)
using simulator = new DomeSimulator('Dome Simulator', client, { mountManager: mounts })
simulator.connect()

// waitUntil(condition): a local helper that awaits Bun.sleep until condition() is true.
// The direct form of the INDI actions, in degrees: +20° from 350° crosses 0° and ends at 10°.
simulator.moveTo(350)
await waitUntil(() => !simulator.isMoving)
simulator.moveBy(20)
await waitUntil(() => !simulator.isMoving)
console.log(simulator.azimuth) // 10

// The same actions through the INDI vectors.
client.sendNumber({ device: simulator.name, name: 'ABS_DOME_POSITION', elements: { DOME_ABSOLUTE_POSITION: 120 } })

// The shutter transition is timed; its target is visible meanwhile.
simulator.openShutter()
console.log(simulator.shutterTarget, simulator.isMoving) // OPEN true

// stop() aborts the motion and the shutter, and turns autosync off; activeMount is the followed mount, if any.
simulator.stop()
console.log(simulator.activeMount)

// Sync declares an azimuth at once; setPark stores the current one as the park position.
simulator.syncTo(200)
simulator.setPark()

// Slews to the home and park azimuths; unpark releases the park, and closeShutter starts the closing transition.
simulator.home()
await waitUntil(() => !simulator.isMoving)
simulator.park()
await waitUntil(() => !simulator.isMoving)
simulator.unpark()
simulator.closeShutter()
```

### INDI Filter Wheel

A filter wheel puts one filter at a time in the light path: luminance and colour filters for broadband imaging, narrowband filters such as Hα, [S II] and [O III] for emission nebulae, and often a dark slot. Each slot has a name, and filters of different thickness can shift the focus, so a capture plan refers to filters by slot and name.

`WheelManager` builds a `Wheel` device from the INDI filter-wheel properties. In the model the slot `position` is **0-based**, while INDI numbers the slots from 1; the manager converts both ways, so a caller never adds or subtracts one. `moving` is true while the wheel turns.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { WheelManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/wheel'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { WheelSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/wheel'

const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const manager = new WheelManager()
handler.add(manager)

using client = new ClientSimulator('wheel', handler)
using simulator = new WheelSimulator('Filter Wheel Simulator', client)
const wheel = manager.get(client, simulator.name)!

// waitUntil(condition): a local helper that awaits Bun.sleep until condition() is true.
manager.connect(wheel)
await waitUntil(() => wheel.connected)
console.log(wheel.count, wheel.names) // 8 ['L', 'R', 'G', 'B', 'Ha', 'SII', 'OIII', 'Dark']

// Move to the fourth slot (0-based index 3) and wait for the wheel to stop.
manager.moveTo(wheel, 3)
await waitUntil(() => wheel.moving)
await waitUntil(() => !wheel.moving)
console.log(wheel.position, wheel.names[wheel.position]) // 3 B

// Rename the slots, one name per slot in order.
manager.slots(wheel, ['Luminance', 'Red', 'Green', 'Blue', 'Ha', 'SII', 'OIII', 'Dark'])
```

### INDI Filter Wheel Simulator

`WheelSimulator` is an in-process filter wheel with eight slots named `L`, `R`, `G`, `B`, `Ha`, `SII`, `OIII` and `Dark`. A move takes a time proportional to the number of slots travelled and keeps `FILTER_SLOT` Busy meanwhile, so sequencing code sees the same timing behaviour as with a real wheel; a requested slot is rounded and clamped to the wheel. On the INDI side, and in the simulator methods, slots are 1-based. The camera simulator dims the stars with the selected filter when it snoops this wheel (see [INDI Camera Simulator](#indi-camera-simulator)).

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { FILTER_WHEEL_MOVE_TIME_MS } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/constants'
import { WheelSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/wheel'

using client = new ClientSimulator('wheel', new IndiClientHandlerSet())
using simulator = new WheelSimulator('Filter Wheel Simulator', client)
simulator.connect()

// Move to the 1-based slot 5 (Ha); the time per slot travelled is FILTER_WHEEL_MOVE_TIME_MS.
simulator.moveTo(5)
await Bun.sleep(FILTER_WHEEL_MOVE_TIME_MS * 8)

// The same through the INDI vectors: a slot and a slot name.
client.sendNumber({ device: simulator.name, name: 'FILTER_SLOT', elements: { FILTER_SLOT_VALUE: 2 } })
client.sendText({ device: simulator.name, name: 'FILTER_NAME', elements: { FILTER_SLOT_NAME_1: 'Luminance' } })
```

### INDI Flat Panel

Flat frames record how the optical system transmits light across the field: vignetting, dust shadows and pixel-to-pixel sensitivity. They are taken against a uniform source, and an electroluminescent or LED flat panel in front of the aperture is the most repeatable one. Its intensity sets the exposure time needed to reach the target signal level, often combined with a motorized cover (see [INDI Cover](#indi-cover)).

`FlatPanelManager` builds a `FlatPanel` device from the INDI light-box properties: `enabled` is the light switch and `intensity` the brightness, in the driver's range. The intensity is sent as is, and the change is seen once the driver reports it.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { FlatPanelManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/flatpanel'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { FlatPanelSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/flatpanel'

const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const manager = new FlatPanelManager()
handler.add(manager)

using client = new ClientSimulator('panel', handler)
using simulator = new FlatPanelSimulator('Flat Panel Simulator', client)
const panel = manager.get(client, simulator.name)!

// waitUntil(condition): a local helper that awaits Bun.sleep until condition() is true.
manager.connect(panel)
await waitUntil(() => panel.connected)
console.log(panel.intensity.min, panel.intensity.max) // 0 255

// Set the brightness, then switch the light on.
manager.intensity(panel, 128)
manager.enable(panel)

// disable() switches it off, and toggle() inverts the current state.
manager.disable(panel)
manager.toggle(panel)
```

### INDI Flat Panel Simulator

`FlatPanelSimulator` is an in-process light box with an on/off switch and an intensity from 0 to 255. The changes are immediate, because a panel has no motion, so both vectors stay Idle; a requested intensity is clamped to the range, and the light switch and the intensity are independent (the light can be on at intensity 0). Both vectors are kept by `CONFIG` (see [INDI Client Simulator](#indi-client-simulator)).

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { FlatPanelManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/flatpanel'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { FlatPanelSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/flatpanel'

const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
```
