```ts
const manager = new FlatPanelManager()
handler.add(manager)

using client = new ClientSimulator('panel', handler)
using simulator = new FlatPanelSimulator('Flat Panel Simulator', client)
const panel = manager.get(client, simulator.name)!
manager.connect(panel)
await Bun.sleep(50)

// The INDI vectors written directly, as a client of a real driver would.
client.sendSwitch({ device: simulator.name, name: 'FLAT_LIGHT_CONTROL', elements: { FLAT_LIGHT_ON: true } })
client.sendNumber({ device: simulator.name, name: 'FLAT_LIGHT_INTENSITY', elements: { FLAT_LIGHT_INTENSITY_VALUE: 1000 } })
console.log(panel.enabled, panel.intensity.value) // true 255 (clamped)
```

### INDI Focuser Control

A focuser moves the camera along the optical axis, in motor steps. The best-focus position is not fixed: it shifts as the tube expands or contracts with temperature and changes with the filter, so focus is measured and corrected during the night (see [Autofocus](#autofocus)). Two mechanical effects matter for repeatability: backlash, the play of the gear train that makes a reversal of direction lose motion, and the direction convention, where moving _in_ decreases the position and _out_ increases it, whatever the motor wiring (`reverse` only inverts the motor).

`FocuserManager` builds a `Focuser` device from the INDI focuser properties. `position` is in steps; `moving` is true while a move runs. A focuser that publishes only one of the absolute and relative position vectors still offers both kinds of move. On an absolute-only driver, relative moves are sent as absolute targets. On a relative-only driver, `position` is a virtual counter kept by the manager (starting at the middle of a configurable range, `virtualRange`): it is an estimate, since an aborted move travelled an unknown distance, moves by other clients are not counted, and it restarts on every connection, so redefine it with `syncTo` when the real position matters. The [ASCOM Alpaca Server](#ascom-alpaca-server) keeps exporting such a focuser as relative, and the [Device Commanders](#device-commanders) move it like any other.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { FocuserManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/focuser'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { FocuserSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/focuser'

const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const manager = new FocuserManager()
handler.add(manager)

using client = new ClientSimulator('focuser', handler)
using simulator = new FocuserSimulator('Focuser Simulator', client)
const focuser = manager.get(client, simulator.name)!

// waitUntil(condition): a local helper that awaits Bun.sleep until condition() is true.
manager.connect(focuser)
await waitUntil(() => focuser.connected)

// Absolute move, in steps.
manager.moveTo(focuser, 52000)
await waitUntil(() => focuser.moving)
await waitUntil(() => !focuser.moving)
console.log(focuser.position.value) // 52000

// Relative moves: inward decreases the position, outward increases it.
manager.moveIn(focuser, 1000)
manager.moveOut(focuser, 500)

// Invert the motor direction, and switch the driver's backlash compensation, when the driver allows it.
manager.reverse(focuser, false)
manager.backlash(focuser, true)

// Sync redefines the current position without moving; stop() aborts a move.
manager.syncTo(focuser, 30000)
manager.stop(focuser)
```

### INDI Focuser Simulator

`FocuserSimulator` is an in-process absolute focuser (0 to 100000 steps, starting at 50000, moving at 20000 steps per second) that the camera simulator reads to blur its stars, which makes it the test bed for autofocus. It also publishes a temperature, a sinusoid of 4 °C amplitude and 40 s period around the ambient temperature, and, with temperature compensation enabled, nudges the focus by a fixed number of steps per degree of drift; this is a simple model, not a calibrated focuser.

The `backlash` option models a rigid gear train with play, in steps: the reported `position` is the motor position and `effectivePosition` the optical position. On a reversal the motor first takes up the slack before the optics follow, so the optics lag by up to `backlash` steps; the loss is the same in both directions and repeated in/out cycles do not drift the optical position. A sync unloads the gear train. The standard backlash vectors of the INDI focuser interface are stored but never applied to the motion, so an algorithm under test must compensate by itself.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { FocuserSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/focuser'

// A focuser with 100 steps of gear play.
using client = new ClientSimulator('focuser', new IndiClientHandlerSet())
using simulator = new FocuserSimulator('Focuser Simulator', client, { backlash: 100 })
simulator.connect()
console.log(simulator.backlash) // 100

// waitUntil(condition): a local helper that awaits Bun.sleep until condition() is true.
// Absolute move, then an outward relative move: the gear train is loaded in the outward direction.
simulator.moveTo(55000)
await waitUntil(() => !simulator.isMoving)
simulator.moveRelative(1000)
await waitUntil(() => !simulator.isMoving)

// Reversing direction first consumes the play: the optics lag the motor by 100 steps.
client.sendSwitch({ device: simulator.name, name: 'FOCUS_MOTION', elements: { FOCUS_INWARD: true } })
simulator.moveRelative(1000)
await waitUntil(() => simulator.isMoving)
await waitUntil(() => !simulator.isMoving)
console.log(simulator.position, simulator.effectivePosition) // 55000 55100

// The simulated temperature, in °C, and whether temperature compensation is on.
console.log(simulator.temperature, simulator.isTemperatureCompensationEnabled)

// A sync redefines the position at once and unloads the gear train; stop() aborts a move (Alert, or Idle with stop(false)).
simulator.syncTo(50000)
simulator.moveTo(60000)
simulator.stop()
```

### INDI Guide Output

Autoguiding corrects the tracking of a mount with short pulses: for a given duration, the mount moves one axis at a guide rate, a fraction of the sidereal rate (about 15″ per second of time), so a pulse of `t` milliseconds at rate `r` shifts the pointing by about `r × 15.04″ × t / 1000`. The pulses go through the mount driver or through the ST-4 port of a camera; [Guiding Calibration](#guiding-calibration) measures their effect on the image and [Guide Pulse Loop](#guide-pulse-loop) issues them.

`GuideOutputManager` exposes the timed-guide vectors of a mount or camera as a `'guideOutput'` proxy device over its parent, resolved by the provider (usually the mount manager), and marks the parent with `canPulseGuide`. `pulsing` follows the Busy state of the timed-guide vectors, so a pulse is complete when it turns false. The guide rate is shown as the driver publishes it; INDI mounts publish a fraction of the sidereal rate. A command can be given the proxy or the parent. [Guide Output Commander](#guide-output-commander) turns these pulses into operations that wait for their end.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { GuideOutputManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/guideoutput'
import { MountManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/mount'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { MountSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/mount'

const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const mounts = new MountManager()
// The provider resolves the parent device that defines the timed-guide vectors.
const guides = new GuideOutputManager(mounts)
handler.add(mounts)
handler.add(guides)

using client = new ClientSimulator('mount', handler)
using simulator = new MountSimulator('Mount Simulator', client)
const mount = mounts.get(client, simulator.name)!

// waitUntil(condition): a local helper that awaits Bun.sleep until condition() is true.
mounts.connect(mount)
await waitUntil(() => mount.connected)

// The guide output is a proxy over the mount; the rate is a fraction of the sidereal rate per axis.
const guide = guides.get(client, simulator.name)!
console.log(guide.canPulseGuide, guide.guideRate) // true { rightAscension: 0.5, declination: 0.5 }

// A 500 ms pulse north (pulseSouth, pulseWest and pulseEast are the other axes); pulsing is true until the driver finishes it.
guides.pulseNorth(guide, 500)
await waitUntil(() => guide.pulsing)
await waitUntil(() => !guide.pulsing)

// The same by direction name, and a new guide rate (right ascension, declination).
guides.pulse(guide, 'EAST', 300)
guides.guideRate(guide, 0.3, 0.4)
```

### INDI Mount Alignment Subsystem

No mount points exactly where it is told: polar misalignment, cone error, non-orthogonal axes and flexure displace the optical axis by amounts that vary across the sky. A pointing model corrects them from a set of alignment points, each pairing a commanded coordinate with the one actually observed (usually by plate solving). The INDI Alignment Subsystem is the pointing-model engine that some telescope drivers embed: a database of alignment points and a selectable math plugin that turns it into a coordinate correction.

`MountManager` mirrors only what the driver advertises in `mount.alignment`: whether the subsystem is available and active, the math plugins and the selected one, and the number of points. It carries neither the points nor the model, and the state changes only when the driver reports it, because the driver may refuse a command. The commands do nothing while the subsystem is not available. A database change (deleting a point, clearing, loading) is committed and the plugin re-initialised afterwards. Deleting the last point undoes a sync only if the sync appended a point, which not every driver does.

```ts
import { MountManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/mount'

const manager = new MountManager()
// mount: Mount — a device of this manager whose driver defines the ALIGNMENT_SUBSYSTEM_* vectors.

// The subsystem as the driver advertises it: availability, math plugins by name, and the number of points.
console.log(
	mount.alignment.available,
	mount.alignment.plugins.map((e) => e.name),
	mount.alignment.pointCount,
)

// Turn the subsystem on and select a math plugin by name; both are applied when the driver confirms.
manager.alignmentActive(mount, true)
manager.alignmentPlugin(mount, 'SVD Math Plugin')

// Delete one point by its 0-based index in [0, pointCount), or the last one, then save the database.
manager.alignmentDeletePoint(mount, 1)
manager.alignmentDeleteLastPoint(mount)
manager.alignmentSave(mount)

// Reload the saved database, or clear it; pointCount follows the driver's report.
manager.alignmentLoad(mount)
manager.alignmentClear(mount)

// Re-initialise the math plugin from the current points, as the database commands do afterwards.
manager.alignmentInitialize(mount)
```

### INDI Mount Control

A telescope mount points the optical axis at a celestial coordinate and then tracks it against the Earth's rotation. INDI mounts work in JNOW, equatorial coordinates of the current date, while catalogs give J2000 positions, so a target must be converted before it is sent. A German equatorial mount can reach most of the sky from either side of the pier, and the side matters for the meridian flip (see [Meridian Flip Planning](#meridian-flip-planning)); a sync tells the mount where it really points, typically after a plate solve, without moving it.

`MountManager` builds a `Mount` device from the INDI Telescope interface and reflects its vectors onto the shared model that also serves the Alpaca telescope. Coordinates are radians (JNOW), the site latitude and longitude are radians and the elevation a distance in AU (`meter` and `toMeter` convert it), and the time is UTC epoch milliseconds with an offset in minutes. A `mountType` of `'UNKNOWN'` means the mount has not reported one and must not be read as equatorial, and a zero coordinate before `hasEquatorialCoordinate` is a default, not a position. The goto, flip and sync commands select the `ON_COORD_SET` mode before sending the coordinate, while `equatorialCoordinate` sends only the coordinate and therefore uses whichever mode was set last. `moveTo` accepts a target in J2000, JNOW, horizontal, ecliptic or galactic coordinates, as angles or sexagesimal text, and converts it to JNOW; `mountTargetEquatorial` performs that conversion alone. The model follows the driver, and the position is republished while the mount moves, so read it after the slew has ended. Pulse guiding is described in [INDI Guide Output](#indi-guide-output), the pointing model in [INDI Mount Alignment Subsystem](#indi-mount-alignment-subsystem), and commands that wait for the mount in [Mount Commander](#mount-commander).

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { MountManager, mountTargetEquatorial } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/mount'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { MountSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/mount'
import { deg, hour, toDeg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const manager = new MountManager()
handler.add(manager)

using client = new ClientSimulator('mount', handler)
using simulator = new MountSimulator('Mount Simulator', client)
const mount = manager.get(client, simulator.name)!

// waitUntil(condition): a local helper that awaits Bun.sleep until condition() is true.
manager.connect(mount)
await waitUntil(() => mount.connected)

// The site (radians, elevation as a distance) and the driver clock (UTC epoch ms, offset in minutes).
manager.geographicCoordinate(mount, { latitude: deg(-23), longitude: deg(-46), elevation: meter(760) })
manager.time(mount, { utc: Date.UTC(2026, 9, 5, 12), offset: -180 })

// The tracking rate and the manual slew rate (one of mount.slewRates, by name).
manager.trackMode(mount, 'SIDEREAL')
manager.slewRate(mount, 'SPEED_7')

// Track at the selected rate and slew to a JNOW coordinate in radians.
manager.tracking(mount, true)
manager.goTo(mount, hour(3.5), deg(25))
await waitUntil(() => mount.slewing)
await waitUntil(() => !mount.slewing)
console.log(toHour(mount.equatorialCoordinate.rightAscension), toDeg(mount.equatorialCoordinate.declination), mount.pierSide) // hours and degrees of date, and the side of the pier

// Sync declares the JNOW position without moving; flipTo slews forcing the other side of the pier;
// equatorialCoordinate sends a coordinate with the last selected ON_COORD_SET mode.
manager.syncTo(mount, hour(3.5), deg(25))
manager.flipTo(mount, hour(3.5), deg(25))
manager.equatorialCoordinate(mount, hour(3.5), deg(25))

// A J2000 target as sexagesimal text, converted to JNOW without commanding the mount.
const [rightAscension, declination] = mountTargetEquatorial(mount, { type: 'J2000', J2000: { x: '05 35 17', y: '-05 23 28' } })
console.log(toHour(rightAscension), toDeg(declination)) // ≈ 5.610 -5.373 in 2026 — hours and degrees of date

// moveTo converts and slews in one call ('goto', 'flip' or 'sync'); stop() aborts the slew.
manager.moveTo(mount, 'goto', { type: 'J2000', J2000: { x: '05 35 17', y: '-05 23 28' } })
manager.stop(mount)

// Manual motion at the slew rate, on and off per direction (moveSouth, moveWest and moveEast likewise).
manager.moveNorth(mount, true)
manager.moveNorth(mount, false)

// Home: store the current position, search the mechanical index, or slew to the stored home.
manager.setHome(mount)
manager.findHome(mount)
manager.home(mount)

// Store the current position as the park position and unpark; park at the end of the night, which stops tracking.
manager.setPark(mount)
manager.unpark(mount)
manager.park(mount)
```

### INDI Mount Simulator

`MountSimulator` is an in-process German equatorial mount for testing pointing, tracking, guiding and meridian-flip logic. It distinguishes three directions: the reported coordinate (radians, JNOW) that the controller believes and an INDI client sees, the mechanical orientation of its axes, and the boresight where the optical axis really points. With every imperfection off they coincide; turned on, they diverge as on a real mount. The simulator models goto, flip and sync, manual motion at seven slew rates, sidereal, solar, lunar and King tracking, home and park, the site and clock, and pulse guiding at a guide rate that is a fraction of the sidereal rate. The side of the pier follows the placement of the axes.

The imperfections are independent families switched on by `SIMULATOR_ERROR_FEATURES`, each configured by its own number vector: polar misalignment, cone and non-orthogonality and index errors (alignment), periodic error of the worm with optional PEC playback, backlash and stiction of the gears, guiding latency and quantization, settling ring-down after a stop, tube flexure, wind deflection, and tracking-rate bias and drift. The recorded boresight path is what the camera simulator uses to trail the stars of an exposure (see [INDI Camera Simulator](#indi-camera-simulator)). The simulated clock advances in real time, and `pauseAutomaticTicking` hands it to the caller, who drives it with `advance(seconds)` so that every step is deterministic.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { MountSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/mount'
import { deg, hour, toArcsec, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

using client = new ClientSimulator('mount', new IndiClientHandlerSet())
using simulator = new MountSimulator('Mount Simulator', client)

// Connect, then take over the clock: the mount only moves when advance(seconds) is called.
simulator.connect()
simulator.pauseAutomaticTicking()
simulator.setTime({ utc: Date.UTC(2026, 9, 5, 0), offset: 0 })
client.sendNumber({ device: simulator.name, name: 'GEOGRAPHIC_COORD', elements: { LAT: -23, LONG: 314, ELEV: 760 } })
console.log(simulator.utcTime, simulator.latitude, simulator.longitude, simulator.elevation) // simulated UTC ms, and the site

// The local sidereal time of the site at a simulated instant, in radians.
console.log(toHour(simulator.siderealTimeAt(simulator.utcTime))) // hours

// Tracking mode and manual slew rate; the presets are SPEED_1 (0.5°/s) to SPEED_7 (32°/s).
simulator.setTrackMode('SIDEREAL')
simulator.setSlewRate('SPEED_7')
console.log(simulator.trackMode, simulator.slewRate) // SIDEREAL SPEED_7

// Sync places the axes, then a goto (radians, JNOW) advanced in 0.1 s steps until the slew ends.
simulator.syncTo(hour(3), deg(20))
simulator.setTrackingEnabled(true)
simulator.goTo(hour(4), deg(30))
while (simulator.isSlewing) simulator.advance(0.1)
console.log(simulator.isTracking, simulator.pierSide, simulator.mechanical) // tracking, the side of the pier, and the axes (radians)

// flipTo slews to a coordinate on the other side of the pier.
simulator.flipTo(hour(4), deg(30))
while (simulator.isSlewing) simulator.advance(0.1)

// Manual motion on one axis at the slew rate (moveSouth, moveWest and moveEast likewise); stop() aborts slews and motion.
simulator.moveNorth(true)
simulator.advance(1)
simulator.moveNorth(false)
simulator.stop()

// A 1 s pulse north at half the sidereal rate moves the declination by about 0.5 × 15.04 arcsec.
simulator.setGuideRate(0.5, 0.5)
console.log(simulator.guideRateRightAscension, simulator.guideRateDeclination) // 0.5 0.5
const declination = simulator.declination
simulator.pulse('NORTH', 1000)
console.log(simulator.isPulsing) // true
for (let i = 0; i < 30; i++) simulator.advance(0.1)
console.log(toArcsec(simulator.declination - declination)) // ≈ 7.52 arcsec

// Where the optical axis pointed over the last second (simulated ms): its path length in radians, and RA/Dec samples.
const end = simulator.utcTime
const samples = new Float64Array(2 * 16)
console.log(simulator.boresightPathLength(end - 1000, end), simulator.sampleBoresightTrajectory(end - 1000, end, 16, samples)) // radians, samples written
// sampleBoresightPath writes RA, Dec and time-weight triples spaced by path length instead.

// Polar misalignment and periodic error: the optical axis no longer matches the reported coordinate.
client.sendSwitch({ device: simulator.name, name: 'SIMULATOR_ERROR_FEATURES', elements: { ALIGNMENT: true, PERIODIC_ERROR: true } })
const { reported, boresight } = simulator.pointingState
console.log(toArcsec(boresight.declination - reported.declination)) // pointing error in declination, arcsec
console.log(toArcsec(simulator.pointingErrorBound)) // upper bound of the pointing error, arcsec

// The same boresight alone, the geometric pointing model, the worm phase and the tracking-rate drift (radians).
console.log(simulator.boresight, simulator.pointingModel, simulator.wormPhase, simulator.trackingRateOffset)

// Home: store the current pose, seek the home index, or slew to the stored home.
simulator.setHome()
simulator.findHome()
while (simulator.isHoming) simulator.advance(0.1)
simulator.home()
while (simulator.isHoming) simulator.advance(0.1)

// Park: store the current pose as the park position, then park and unpark.
simulator.setPark()
simulator.park()
while (simulator.isParking) simulator.advance(0.1)
console.log(simulator.isParked) // true
simulator.unpark()
```

### INDI Power Channels

A remote or portable observatory feeds every device from a power box: switchable 12 V outputs for the camera and mount, PWM dew-heater outputs, an adjustable-voltage output, and switchable USB ports, plus sensors of the total voltage, current and power. Switching an output is how a hung device is power-cycled remotely and how heaters are adjusted to the dew point.

`PowerManager` builds a `Power` device from the INDI Power interface. The aggregate `voltage` (V), `current` (A) and `power` (W) come from the sensors, and each kind of channel is a list: `dc` (with its current), `dew` (with a duty cycle in percent), `autoDew`, `variableVoltage` (with its voltage) and `usb`, each channel carrying its driver element name and its label. The commands address an element by the channel name, so the vectors of one kind must use the same element names for the same channel. `PowerCommander` (see [Device Commanders](#device-commanders)) runs these commands as operations that clamp the value to the channel range and resolve once the driver reports it.

```ts
import { PowerManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/power'

const manager = new PowerManager()
// power: Power — a device of this manager whose driver defines the INDI Power interface.

console.log(power.voltage.value, power.current.value, power.power.value) // volts, amperes, watts
console.log(power.dc.map((e) => `${e.label} ${e.enabled}`)) // the labelled DC outputs and their switch state

// Switch a channel of any kind; the switch vector is chosen by its kind.
manager.toggle(power, power.dc[1], true)
manager.toggle(power, power.usb[0], false)

// The duty cycle of a dew output (percent) and the voltage of the variable output (volts).
manager.dutyCycle(power, power.dew[0], 75)
manager.voltage(power, power.variableVoltage[0], 12)
```

### INDI Property Registry

A driver publishes far more than the device managers turn into typed state: ports, baud rates, driver options, and the whole of a device whose `DRIVER_INTERFACE` no manager supports. A generic property view or editor needs all of it, and the managers themselves need each vector already merged with the latest update.

`IndiPropertyRegistry` is an `IndiClientHandler` that keeps every vector of every device a client reports, keyed by client and device name. It stores a copy of each definition (other handlers may mutate the parsed message), merges each update into it, and reports every change to its listeners with a kind: `'metadata'` when a numeric range or the timeout changed, `'feedback'` when the state or the message changed, and `'values'` otherwise. BLOB elements keep only the format and size of their latest delivery; the bytes stay with the handler that consumes them. Records are live objects mutated in place, so a listener that keeps one must copy it. A shared registry passed to the manager constructors must be added to the handler set **before** the managers, so that one copy serves them all; without one, each manager keeps a private registry of the devices it manages.

```ts
import { handleDefNumberVector, handleDefSwitchVector, handleSetNumberVector, IndiClient, IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { CameraManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/camera'
import { IndiPropertyRegistry } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/properties'
import { findOnSwitch, makeNumberVector, makeSwitchVector } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/types'

// One registry shared by the managers, registered on the client before them.
const properties = new IndiPropertyRegistry()
const cameras = new CameraManager(properties)
const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet([properties, cameras])
const client = new IndiClient({ handler })

// Listeners receive every change synchronously, after the state is updated; the call returns the remover.
const stop = properties.addListener({ propertyUpdated: (_, device, property, change) => console.log(change.kind, property.name, change.elements) })

// A device of any type is tracked from its first vector, even one no manager supports.
// The handleDef*/handleSet* functions dispatch a parsed message of each kind (Text, Number, Switch, Light, Blob)
// to a handler; handleDelProperty deletes; makeTextVector, makeLightVector and makeBlobVector build the other kinds.
handleDefNumberVector(client, handler, makeNumberVector('Relay Box', 'DELAY', 'Delay', 'Options', 'rw', ['SECONDS', 'Seconds', 1, 0, 60, 0.5, '%.1f'], ['REPEAT', 'Repeat', 3, 1, 10, 1, '%.0f']))
handleDefSwitchVector(client, handler, makeSwitchVector('Relay Box', 'MODE', 'Mode', 'Options', 'OneOfMany', 'rw', ['PULSE', 'Pulse', true], ['LATCH', 'Latch', false]))

// An update merges into the stored copy; the listener reports a 'values' change of the element SECONDS.
handleSetNumberVector(client, handler, { device: 'Relay Box', name: 'DELAY', elements: { SECONDS: { name: 'SECONDS', value: 2.5 } } })

const device = properties.device(client, 'Relay Box')!
console.log(device.properties.DELAY.elementNames, device.properties.DELAY.elements.SECONDS.value) // [ 'SECONDS', 'REPEAT' ] 2.5

// Every device of a client, their count across clients, and one vector by device and name.
console.log(properties.devices(client).length, properties.length, properties.property(client, 'Relay Box', 'DELAY')?.label) // 1 1 Delay

// The names of the members of a switch vector that are on (selectOnSwitch turns one on under the vector rule).
console.log(findOnSwitch(properties.property(client, 'Relay Box', 'MODE') as never)) // ['PULSE']

// has(device) tells whether the physical device behind a managed device has vectors.
stop()
```

### INDI Protocol Client

INDI (Instrument Neutral Distributed Interface) is the device protocol of most Linux astronomy software. An `indiserver` runs one driver per device and speaks XML over TCP (port 7624). A device describes itself as named property vectors of five kinds (text, number, switch, light and BLOB), each with a state (Idle, Ok, Busy or Alert): it announces them with `def*Vector`, updates them with `set*Vector` and withdraws them with `delProperty`, while a client asks for definitions with `getProperties`, chooses BLOB delivery with `enableBLOB`, and requests changes with `new*Vector`. Numbers on the wire may be decimal or sexagesimal (`12:30:36`, `-5 30`) and are in the driver's own units, hours or degrees alike; the format of a `defNumber` is a C printf conversion or INDI's sexagesimal `%<w>.<f>m`.

`IndiClient` is the TCP client: it parses the XML stream in any chunking and dispatches every message to an `IndiClientHandler`; `IndiClientHandlerSet` fans the events out to several handlers, such as the device managers and the [INDI Property Registry](#indi-property-registry). The same `Client` contract is implemented by the Alpaca and Firmata adapters and by the in-process simulator ([INDI Client Simulator](#indi-client-simulator)), which is why the device managers work with all of them (see [INDI Device Managers](#indi-device-managers)). The device model they produce (`nebulosa/src/devices/indi/device`) uses radians for mount, dome and site angles (the rotator angle stays in the driver's degrees) and degrees Celsius for temperatures, and also holds two pieces of mount geometry: the pier side a German equatorial mount would use for a target, and the time until the target's next upper transit. `parseIndiNumber` and `formatIndiNumber` live in `nebulosa/src/devices/indi/number`, which has no runtime dependency and runs in a browser.

```ts
import { DEFAULT_INDI_PORT, IndiClient } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { expectedPierSide, meridianTimeIn } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/device'
import { formatIndiNumber, parseIndiNumber } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/number'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Wire numbers: parse decimal or sexagesimal text, and write a value with the format of its defNumber.
console.log(parseIndiNumber('-10:30:18'), formatIndiNumber(-10.505, '%10.9m'), formatIndiNumber(-3.14159, '%.4f')) // -10.505 -10:30:18.00 -3.1416

// The handler receives every message of the server (an IndiClientHandlerSet fans it out to managers).
const client = new IndiClient({
	handler: {
		setNumberVector: (_, vector) => console.log(vector.device, vector.name, vector.state),
		message: (_, message) => console.log(message.device, message.message),
		close: (_, server) => console.log('closed by the server:', server),
	},
})

// Opens the socket to an indiserver and asks for every property definition.
await client.connect('localhost', DEFAULT_INDI_PORT)
console.log(client.connected, client.id, client.remoteHost, client.remotePort, client.remoteIp, client.localPort) // the endpoint, and an MD5 id derived from it

// Asks again for the definitions of one device (or of all without arguments).
client.getProperties({ device: 'CCD Simulator' })

// Commands are serialized as XML, e.g.
// <newNumberVector device="CCD Simulator" name="CCD_EXPOSURE"><oneNumber name="CCD_EXPOSURE_VALUE">2.5</oneNumber></newNumberVector>
client.enableBlob({ device: 'CCD Simulator', value: 'Also' })
client.sendNumber({ device: 'CCD Simulator', name: 'CCD_EXPOSURE', elements: { CCD_EXPOSURE_VALUE: 2.5 } })

// The other kinds of request: a switch and a text vector.
client.sendSwitch({ device: 'CCD Simulator', name: 'CCD_FRAME_TYPE', elements: { FRAME_DARK: true } })
client.sendText({ device: 'CCD Simulator', name: 'ACTIVE_DEVICES', elements: { ACTIVE_TELESCOPE: 'Telescope Simulator' } })

// Pier side for a target at 3h, +20° with local sidereal time 1h, and seconds until its upper transit.
console.log(expectedPierSide(hour(3), deg(20), hour(1)), meridianTimeIn(hour(3), hour(1))) // WEST 7180.340875

// close() drops the connection without notifying the handler.
client.close()
```

### INDI Rotator

A field rotator turns the camera around the optical axis, which sets the orientation of the image on the sky: framing an elongated target, matching the panels of a mosaic, or returning to the same orientation on another night. The rotator reports a mechanical angle; its relation to the position angle on the sky is fixed by a sync, typically after a plate solve.

`RotatorManager` builds a `Rotator` device from the INDI rotator properties. Unlike the mount and dome angles of the device model, `angle` stays in the driver's **degrees**, and its range and wrapping are left to the driver. `moving` is true while a move or a homing runs, and `reverse` only flips the driver's motor direction.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { RotatorManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/rotator'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { RotatorSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/rotator'

const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const manager = new RotatorManager()
handler.add(manager)

using client = new ClientSimulator('rotator', handler)
using simulator = new RotatorSimulator('Rotator Simulator', client)
const rotator = manager.get(client, simulator.name)!

// waitUntil(condition): a local helper that awaits Bun.sleep until condition() is true.
manager.connect(rotator)
await waitUntil(() => rotator.connected)

// Move to 45 degrees and wait for the rotation to end.
manager.moveTo(rotator, 45)
await waitUntil(() => rotator.moving)
await waitUntil(() => !rotator.moving)
console.log(rotator.angle.value) // 45

// Flip the driver's motor direction.
manager.reverse(rotator, false)

// Sync redefines the current angle without moving, home returns to the reference, stop() aborts.
manager.syncTo(rotator, 100)
manager.home(rotator)
manager.stop(rotator)
```

### INDI Rotator Simulator

`RotatorSimulator` is an in-process field rotator with an angle from 0° to 360° turning at 90° per second, which the camera simulator reads to rotate its star field. A target is wrapped to [0°, 360°) and the rotator takes the shortest way round, so a move from 350° to 10° crosses zero instead of travelling 340°. The reverse and backlash switches are only flags and do not change the simulated motion.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { RotatorSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/rotator'

using client = new ClientSimulator('rotator', new IndiClientHandlerSet())
using simulator = new RotatorSimulator('Rotator Simulator', client)
simulator.connect()

// waitUntil(condition): a local helper that awaits Bun.sleep until condition() is true.
// Sync to 350 degrees, then go to 10: the shortest path crosses 0 and takes 20 / 90 s.
simulator.syncTo(350)
simulator.moveTo(10)
await waitUntil(() => simulator.isMoving)
await waitUntil(() => !simulator.isMoving)
console.log(simulator.angle) // 10

// Turns back to the configured home angle.
simulator.home()

// The same through the INDI vectors; stop() aborts at the angle reached.
client.sendNumber({ device: simulator.name, name: 'ABS_ROTATOR_ANGLE', elements: { ANGLE: 90 } })
simulator.stop()
```

### INDI Safety Monitor

An unattended observatory must close when the conditions become dangerous (rain, wind, clouds, a power fault), and a safety monitor is the single yes/no signal that sequencers, domes and roofs act on. INDI drivers publish it as the `SAFETY_STATUS` light vector.

`SafetyMonitorManager` exposes that vector as a `SafetyMonitor` device whose `safe` flag is true **only** when the state is Ok: Idle, Busy, Alert, an unknown status and a deleted vector are all unsafe, so the flag fails closed. For a dome, mount or weather station that publishes the status, the manager creates a `'safetyMonitor'` proxy over the parent device resolved by its provider; a standalone device is created only when the driver announces the Auxiliary interface (or the client is an Alpaca one). The manager is a passive reader with no commands.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { SafetyMonitorManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/safetymonitor'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { SafetyMonitorSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/safetymonitor'

// No primary devices here, so the provider never finds a parent and the monitor is standalone.
const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const manager = new SafetyMonitorManager({ get: () => undefined })
handler.add(manager)

using client = new ClientSimulator('safety', handler)
using simulator = new SafetyMonitorSimulator('Safety Monitor Simulator', client)
const monitor = manager.get(client, simulator.name)!

// waitUntil(condition): a local helper that awaits Bun.sleep until condition() is true.
manager.connect(monitor)
await waitUntil(() => monitor.connected)
console.log(monitor.safe) // false: the initial condition is unknown

// The flag follows the status the driver reports.
simulator.setSafe(true)
await Bun.sleep(50)
console.log(monitor.safe) // true
```

### INDI Safety Simulator

`SafetyMonitorSimulator` is an in-process Auxiliary driver that publishes the passive `SAFETY_STATUS` light, for testing how automation reacts to a change of conditions. The simulator-only `SIMULATOR_SAFETY` switch selects the condition: `SAFE` (status Ok), `UNSAFE` (Alert), `WARNING` (Busy) or `UNKNOWN` (Idle, the initial condition); only Ok means safe for the managers. The condition is saved by `CONFIG` (see [INDI Client Simulator](#indi-client-simulator)).

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { SafetyMonitorSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/safetymonitor'

using client = new ClientSimulator('safety', new IndiClientHandlerSet())
using simulator = new SafetyMonitorSimulator('Safety Monitor Simulator', client)
simulator.connect()

// Select a condition through the simulator switch, as an interactive session would.
client.sendSwitch({ device: simulator.name, name: 'SIMULATOR_SAFETY', elements: { WARNING: true } })

// setSafe() is the direct form of SAFE and UNSAFE.
simulator.setSafe(true)
```

### INDI Thermometer

Temperature drives two decisions in imaging: the focus position drifts as the tube changes temperature, and dark frames must match the sensor temperature of the lights. A camera reports its sensor temperature in `CCD_TEMPERATURE` and a focuser its probe temperature in `FOCUS_TEMPERATURE`.

`ThermometerManager` exposes either sensor as an independent `'thermometer'` proxy device over its parent, resolved by the provider (usually an object that asks the camera and focuser managers), and marks the parent with `hasThermometer`. The `temperature` (°C) is kept at the precision the driver reports and follows every new reading, on the proxy and on the parent. Deleting the vector removes the capability and the proxy. The sensors are read-only, so the manager has no commands.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { FocuserManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/focuser'
import { ThermometerManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/thermometer'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { FocuserSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/focuser'

// The provider resolves the parent device, here the focuser that publishes FOCUS_TEMPERATURE.
const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const focusers = new FocuserManager()
const thermometers = new ThermometerManager({ get: (client, name) => focusers.get(client, name) })
handler.add(focusers)
handler.add(thermometers)

using client = new ClientSimulator('focuser', handler)
using simulator = new FocuserSimulator('Focuser Simulator', client)
const focuser = focusers.get(client, simulator.name)!
focusers.connect(focuser)
await Bun.sleep(100)

// The proxy exists once the temperature vector is defined; the reading is in °C.
const thermometer = thermometers.get(client, simulator.name)!
console.log(thermometer.temperature, focuser.hasThermometer) // degrees Celsius, true
```

### INDI Weather

Weather decides whether an observatory can open and how good the night is: humidity and the dew point predict dew, wind shakes the telescope, cloud cover (often from a sky-temperature sensor, since clear sky is much colder than cloud) and rain close the roof, and the sky quality in mag/arcsec² measures darkness. INDI weather drivers publish these readings in `WEATHER_PARAMETERS`, but INDI does not standardize their names.

`WeatherManager` builds a `Weather` device (the same model serves the ASCOM ObservingConditions of the Alpaca backend) and maps the parameters to thirteen typed sensors, recognizing the usual names of common drivers: `cloudCover` (%), `dewPoint` (°C), `humidity` (%), `pressure` (hPa, at the station altitude), `rainRate` (mm/h), `skyBrightness` (lx), `skyQuality` (mag/arcsec²), `skyTemperature` (°C), `starFWHM` (arcsec), `temperature` (°C), `windDirection` (radians in [0, 2π), converted from degrees), `windGust` and `windSpeed` (m/s). A sensor the driver does not publish stays `undefined`. The minimum and maximum of a parameter are the driver's alarm thresholds, not a display range, so a reading outside them is kept. Because stale weather is a safety hazard, the time of the last report of each sensor is tracked even when the value repeats, and its age is measured with the monotonic clock. `WeatherCommander` (see [Device Commanders](#device-commanders)) runs the driver controls as operations.

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { WeatherManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/weather'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { WeatherSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/weather'

const handler = new IndiClientHandlerSet()
const manager = new WeatherManager()
handler.add(manager)

using client = new ClientSimulator('weather', handler)
using simulator = new WeatherSimulator('Weather Simulator', client)
const weather = manager.get(client, simulator.name)!

// waitUntil(condition): a local helper that awaits Bun.sleep until condition() is true.
manager.connect(weather)
await waitUntil(() => weather.connected)

// Typed readings in °C, %, hPa and m/s; the wind direction is in radians.
console.log(weather.temperature, weather.humidity, weather.dewPoint, weather.pressure, weather.windSpeed) // 16.8 52 6.9 1013.2 2.6

// Freshness: epoch ms of the last report of a sensor, and ms elapsed since then.
console.log(manager.updatedAt(weather, 'temperature'), manager.elapsedSince(weather, 'temperature'))

// The same for the most recent report of any sensor.
console.log(manager.lastUpdatedAt(weather), manager.lastElapsedSince(weather))

// Which driver controls are writable: the update period, the averaging window and a forced re-read.
console.log(manager.canSetUpdatePeriod(weather), manager.canSetAveragePeriod(weather), manager.canRefresh(weather))

// Driver controls return whether the driver has the writable property: update period (s), averaging window (h) and a forced re-read.
manager.setUpdatePeriod(weather, 30)
manager.setAveragePeriod(weather, 0)
manager.refresh(weather)
```

### INDI Weather Simulator

`WeatherSimulator` is an in-process weather station for testing safety and scheduling logic; it is deterministic, with nothing random. Its initial readings are mutually consistent: 16.8 °C at 52 % humidity with a dew point of 6.9 °C, 1013.2 hPa, 15 % cloud cover, no rain, wind of 2.6 m/s gusting to 4.2 m/s from 135°, a sky of 21.3 mag/arcsec² at -22.4 °C, a star FWHM of 2.4 arcsec and a sky brightness of 0.002 lx. The ranges advertised by its vectors are only plausible bounds of the simulator.

The public `WEATHER_PARAMETERS` are read-only, as on a real station; the simulator-only `SIMULATOR_WEATHER` vector has the same elements and is their source, so writing a control (or calling `setParameter`) changes the public reading at once. The update period is stored but not scheduled, since the simulator has no timer; `refresh` re-publishes the readings even when none changed, as a driver does when asked to read its hardware again. The controls are saved by `CONFIG` (see [INDI Client Simulator](#indi-client-simulator)).

```ts
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { WeatherSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/weather'

using client = new ClientSimulator('weather', new IndiClientHandlerSet())
using simulator = new WeatherSimulator('Weather Simulator', client)
simulator.connect()

// One sensor by its INDI element name, clamped to its range; returns whether a value changed.
console.log(simulator.setParameter('WEATHER_TEMPERATURE', 5), simulator.setParameter('WEATHER_TEMPERATURE', 5)) // true false

// Several sensors at once through the simulator control vector: a windy, rainy spell.
client.sendNumber({ device: simulator.name, name: 'SIMULATOR_WEATHER', elements: { WEATHER_WIND_SPEED: 12, WEATHER_WIND_GUST: 20, WEATHER_RAIN_HOUR: 1.5 } })

// Publish the readings again, which counts as a new report of every sensor.
simulator.refresh()
```

### Mount Commander

Commanding a mount has more traps than any other device. The target of a catalog is in J2000 while the mount takes coordinates of the equinox of date, so a conversion made at one instant and compared with a position computed at another disagrees; a slew can stop short, at the wrong place, or be refused with an `Alert`; and a meridian flip may or may not change the side of the pier, which the driver reports only as its own belief. `MountCommander` is the [Device Commanders](#device-commanders) layer of the mount: every command resolves only once the mount reports the commanded state, as an `OperationResult` without throwing, and a failed, timed-out or cancelled slew stops the mount before its lease is released.

A target may be given in any supported frame (J2000, JNOW, horizontal, ecliptic, galactic) and is converted to the equinox of date at the command time, or at the instant the caller passes so that both sides use the same conversion (see [INDI Mount Control](#indi-mount-control)). A slew resolves with where the mount stopped and its pier side; `flip` reports whether a pier side change could be verified. For a meridian flip, `executeMeridianFlip` sends the flip by one of the strategies the mount supports, the driver's own flip or a forced goto to the same target, and reports the evidence the motion left (whether the pier side changed, where it comes from, and how far from the target the mount stopped) rather than a verdict, which belongs to the caller (see [Meridian Flip Planning](#meridian-flip-planning)). Manual motion is open-ended: its handle keeps the mount leased until every direction is stopped.

```ts
import { meridianFlipStrategies, MountCommander, pierSideProvenance } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/commanders/mount'
import { IndiClientHandlerSet } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/client'
import { MountManager } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/manager/mount'
import { ClientSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/client'
import { MountSimulator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/indi/simulator/mount'
import { DeviceLifecycle } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/device.lifecycle'
import { OperationCoordinator } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/operation'
import { ResourceArbiter, resourceKey } from 'nebulosa/src/devices/orchestration/resource'
import { deg, hour, toDeg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const mountManager = new MountManager()
const arbiter = new ResourceArbiter()
const coordinator = new OperationCoordinator(arbiter)
const lifecycle = new DeviceLifecycle(arbiter, coordinator)
lifecycle.observe(mountManager)
using mountCommander = new MountCommander(mountManager)

const client = new ClientSimulator('Client Simulator', new IndiClientHandlerSet([mountManager]))
const simulator = new MountSimulator('Mount Simulator', client)
const mount = mountManager.get(client, 'Mount Simulator')!
mountManager.connect(mount)
while (arbiter.availability(resourceKey(mount)) !== 'available') await Bun.sleep(10)

// The site (radians, elevation as a distance) and the clock (UTC epoch ms, offset in minutes), each confirmed by the driver.
await mountCommander.setGeographicCoordinate(coordinator, mount, { latitude: deg(-23), longitude: deg(-46), elevation: meter(760) })
await mountCommander.setTime(coordinator, mount, { utc: Date.now(), offset: -180 })

// Tracking rate, manual slew rate (by name) and the tracking switch.
await mountCommander.setTrackMode(coordinator, mount, 'SIDEREAL')
await mountCommander.setSlewRate(coordinator, mount, 'SPEED_7')
await mountCommander.setTracking(coordinator, mount, true)

// Sync declares where the mount points, here in JNOW radians, and resolves once it reports that position.
await mountCommander.sync(coordinator, mount, { type: 'JNOW', JNOW: { x: hour(5), y: deg(-30) } })

// A J2000 goto, converted at the command time; resolves with where the mount stopped, in radians of date.
const slew = await mountCommander.goTo(coordinator, mount, { type: 'J2000', J2000: { x: '05 35 17', y: '-05 23 28' } })
if (slew.ok) console.log(toHour(slew.value.rightAscension), toDeg(slew.value.declination), slew.value.pierSide) // ≈ 5.610 -5.373 WEST

// Open-ended manual motion: the handle adds or stops directions and keeps the mount leased until stopped.
const manual = await mountCommander.startManualMove(coordinator, mount, 'NORTH')
if (manual.ok) {
	await manual.value.move('EAST', true)
	console.log(mountCommander.manualMoveOf(mount)?.directions()) // ['NORTH', 'EAST']

	// manualMove is the direct endpoint for the open motion, as a button release would send it.
	await mountCommander.manualMove(coordinator, mount, 'EAST', false)
	await manual.value.stop()
}

// The flip strategies this mount supports, and where its pier side comes from.
console.log(meridianFlipStrategies(mount), pierSideProvenance(mount)) // ['nativeFlip', 'forcedGoto'] 'simulated'

// A flip to the current target, reporting the pier side before and after and whether the change was verified.
const target = { type: 'JNOW' as const, JNOW: { x: mount.equatorialCoordinate.rightAscension, y: mount.equatorialCoordinate.declination } }
const flip = await mountCommander.flip(coordinator, mount, target)
if (flip.ok) console.log(flip.value.initialPierSide, flip.value.pierSide, flip.value.pierSideVerified) // WEST EAST true

// The meridian flip of a session: the motion's evidence, not a verdict.
const execution = await mountCommander.executeMeridianFlip(coordinator, mount, target, { strategy: meridianFlipStrategies(mount)[0] })
if (execution.ok) console.log(execution.value.outcome, execution.value.pierSideChanged, execution.value.arrivalSeparation) // 'moved' true, and the distance to the target in radians

// Home and park: store the current position, seek or go to home, then park and unpark.
await mountCommander.setHome(coordinator, mount)
await mountCommander.findHome(coordinator, mount)
await mountCommander.home(coordinator, mount)
await mountCommander.setPark(coordinator, mount)
await mountCommander.park(coordinator, mount)
await mountCommander.unpark(coordinator, mount)

// The emergency stop needs no scope and also reaches a mount moving under another owner.
await mountCommander.stopMotion(mount)

lifecycle.dispose()
simulator.dispose()
```

## 🌐 External Services

### ADES Codec

The Astrometry Data Exchange Standard (ADES) is the IAU format in which the Minor Planet Center receives and distributes the astrometry of minor planets and comets. Unlike the fixed-width [MPC1992 Codec](#mpc1992-codec) format it replaces, an ADES record carries what an orbit determination needs to weight each measurement: the uncertainties of the position (the right-ascension one already multiplied by cos δ) and their correlation, the astrometric catalog, the photometric band, an explicit observer position for spacecraft and roving sites, and radar delay and Doppler measurements. ADES is defined as XML and as PSV, a pipe-separated text with `# section` and `! key value` metadata blocks (observatory, submitter, telescope, observers) above a header row and the observation rows.

The codec reads and writes the PSV form and single records, such as the rows of the ADES payload of the [Minor Planet Center API](#minor-planet-center-api), as the `MPCObservation` union discriminated by `type` (`optical`, `offset`, `occultation`, `radar`). Values are converted to library units: the time is a UTC `Time`, the angles and their uncertainties are radians (ADES writes degrees and arcseconds), the radar delay is in seconds and its frequency in hertz, and spacecraft positions are in AU. The writer emits the time with millisecond resolution and never invents a field the record does not hold. The XML form is not supported.

```ts
import { isOpticalObservation, observationDesignation, observationIdentifier, parseADESObservation, parseADESPSV, writeADESPSV } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/orbits/mpc'
import { toArcsec, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// A PSV document: one metadata block and one optical row (degrees for ra/dec, arcseconds for rmsRA/rmsDec).
const psv = `# version=2022
# observatory
! mpcCode 568
permID|obsTime|ra|dec|rmsRA|rmsDec|mag|band|stn|mode|astCat
433|2024-03-05T10:20:30.250Z|123.456789|-12.345678|0.12|0.15|17.4|V|568|CCD|Gaia2
`

// Parses the blocks, each with its context and its observations.
const document = parseADESPSV(psv)
const eros = document.blocks[0].observations[0]
if (isOpticalObservation(eros)) console.log(toDeg(eros.rightAscension), toArcsec(eros.raError!)) // 123.456789 0.12 — degrees; arcseconds of RA·cos δ

// The object of a record (permanent, else provisional, else tracklet id) and its observation id, when given.
console.log(observationDesignation(eros), observationIdentifier(eros)) // 433 undefined

// Parses one record given as an object: an observer on a spacecraft, its position in km converted to AU.
const hubble = parseADESObservation({ obsTime: '2024-03-05T10:20:30Z', stn: 'C51', provID: '2024 AB', ra: 10, dec: 20, sys: 'ICRF_KM', ctr: 399, pos1: 149597870.7, pos2: 0, pos3: 7000 })
if (hubble.type === 'optical' && hubble.observer?.kind === 'spacecraft') console.log(hubble.observer.position) // AU, relative to the NAIF center 399

// Writes a document back to PSV, with the union of the fields of each block as its header.
console.log(writeADESPSV({ version: '2022', blocks: [{ observations: [eros, hubble] }] }))
```

### AstroBin Equipment API

AstroBin, the image-hosting community of astrophotographers, keeps an equipment database of sensors, cameras and telescopes with their published specifications. An imaging application reads it to fill in the pixel size and sensor dimensions of a camera and the aperture and focal length of a telescope, from which it derives the image scale (about `206.265 × pixel size [µm] / focal length [mm]` arcseconds per pixel), the field of view and the focal ratio without asking the user to type them (see [Image Scale and Field of View](#image-scale-and-field-of-view)).

The client reads the AstroBin API v2 with a paged listing and a lookup by id for each kind of equipment; a listing returns the total count and the addresses of the neighbor pages, so a caller walks the database until there is no next page. The decimal specifications (pixel size in µm, aperture and focal lengths in mm) are strings exactly as the API publishes them, and many may be `null`, so a caller converts and checks them.

```ts
import { camera, cameras, sensor, sensors, telescope, telescopes } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/imaging/astrobin'

// One page of sensors: the total count, the records and the address of the next page.
const page = await sensors(1)
const first = page!.results[0]

// The sensor width in mm from the string pixel size (µm) and the width in pixels.
const widthMm = (+first.pixelSize * first.pixelWidth) / 1000

// A sensor by id, then a camera that uses it.
const chip = await sensor(first.id)
const body = await camera(chip!.cameras[0])
console.log(body?.brandName, body?.name, body?.cooled)

// A telescope by id: the focal ratio of a fixed-focal-length instrument from its string specifications.
const scope = await telescope(5)
const focalRatio = +scope!.minFocalLength! / +scope!.aperture!

// The camera and telescope listings page the same way as the sensors.
const [bodies, scopes] = await Promise.all([cameras(1), telescopes(1)])
console.log(bodies?.count, scopes?.next)
```

### Close Approach Data

A close approach is the minimum distance between a small body and a planet or the Moon around an encounter. JPL computes them from the orbit solutions of its Small-Body Database: the nominal distance, its 3-sigma minimum and maximum from the orbit uncertainty, the relative velocity at the approach, and the velocity at infinity (hyperbolic excess) relative to a massless target. They are the basis of the close-approach lists of planetary defense, such as the 2029 encounter of Apophis with the Earth. JPL measures a lunar distance (LD) as 384400 km. The times are TDB: the Julian date and calendar date of an approach are not UTC.

`closeApproaches` is the quick query of the approaches to the Earth in a window of dates, returning the rows as published text in the order of the named fields. For paged queries against any body or the history of one object, `closeApproachesUrl` builds the request and `parseCloseApproaches` reads its JSON into rows with parsed numbers (AU, km/s, km), leaving the transport and the HTTP status check to the caller; a value the service does not publish is absent, never 0.

```ts
import { closeApproaches, closeApproachesUrl, parseCloseApproaches } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/orbits/sbd'

// The approaches to the Earth in the next 7 days within 10 lunar distances; rows of text in `fields` order.
const week = await closeApproaches()
const dist = week.fields.indexOf('dist')
for (const row of week.data) console.log(row[week.fields.indexOf('fullname')], row[dist]) // name, nominal distance in AU

// One page of every approach to the Moon in November (TDB dates), nearest first.
const url = closeApproachesUrl({ selector: 'catalog', dateMin: '2026-11-01', dateMax: '2026-11-30', body: 'Moon', distanceMax: 10, distanceUnit: 'LD', sort: 'dist', limit: 50, offset: 0 })
const response = await fetch(url)

// Parses the page: total matches, and rows with distances in AU (3-sigma bounds) and velocities in km/s.
const moon = parseCloseApproaches(await response.json())
for (const row of moon.rows) console.log(row.designation, row.calendarDate, row.distance, row.distanceMin, row.relativeVelocity)
```

### Gaia DR3 Star Catalog

Gaia DR3 (2022) is the astrometric catalog of the ESA Gaia mission, with positions, proper motions, parallaxes and G-band magnitudes of about 1.8 billion sources; it is the reference for plate solving, field star lists and astrometric calibration. VizieR publishes it as the table `I/355/gaiadr3`, which besides the positions at the Gaia epoch 2016.0 carries positions propagated to the epoch J2000.

`VizierGaiaCatalog` is a star catalog (see [Star Catalog Interface and Spatial Query](#star-catalog-interface-and-spatial-query)) over that table, queried remotely through [VizieR TAP Queries](#vizier-tap-queries). Its entries have the J2000 positions as VizieR gives them (epoch 2000, ICRS, radians), the G magnitude, the proper motion as dα/dt and dδ/dt in radians per year (the published μα·cos δ divided by cos δ), and the radial velocity when known; there is no parallax, and a source without a G magnitude never appears. A region is answered by a single request, so the row limit of the service can truncate a large or crowded region.

```ts
import { VizierGaiaCatalog } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/catalogs/vizier'
import { deg, toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const catalog = new VizierGaiaCatalog({ timeout: 30000 })

// A cone of 3 arcminutes around the Orion Nebula (J2000, radians), ordered by G magnitude.
const stars = await catalog.queryCone(deg(83.8221), deg(-5.3911), deg(0.05))
for (const star of stars) console.log(star.id, toDeg(star.rightAscension), toDeg(star.declination), star.magnitude)

// A region given as a shape, streamed entry by entry.
for await (const star of catalog.streamRegion({ kind: 'box', minRA: deg(83.7), maxRA: deg(84), minDEC: deg(-5.5), maxDEC: deg(-5.3) })) console.log(star.id, star.pmRA, star.pmDEC) // rad/yr

// The same box collected into an array; queryTriangle, queryPolygon and queryRegion take the other shapes.
const box = await catalog.queryBox(deg(83.7), deg(84), deg(-5.5), deg(-5.3))

// One source by its Gaia identifier: a string or bigint keeps every digit of the 64-bit id.
const one = await catalog.get('4472832130942575872')
```

### HiPS Survey Discovery

HiPS (Hierarchical Progressive Surveys) is an IVOA standard that stores an all-sky survey as HEALPix tiles at increasing resolution orders, so any region can be served at any scale. The CDS hosts hundreds of image surveys in this form (DSS2, 2MASS, AllWISE, and many more) and indexes their properties in its MocServer.

`hipsSurveys` lists the CDS image surveys that cover at least a fraction of the sky (0 to 1, 0.99 by default, which keeps the all-sky surveys), with the identifier that [HiPS2FITS Cutouts](#hips2fits-cutouts) takes, the category, the native frame, the wavelength regime, and the native pixel scale in degrees per pixel. It is how a client offers a choice of background surveys or picks one whose resolution suits a field of view.

```ts
import { hipsSurveys } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/sky/hips2fits'

// The surveys that cover at least 99% of the sky.
const surveys = await hipsSurveys()

// Pick the optical ones and their native pixel scale, converted to arcseconds per pixel.
for (const survey of surveys.filter((survey) => survey.regime === 'optical')) console.log(survey.id, survey.frame, survey.pixelScale * 3600)
```

### HiPS2FITS Cutouts

The hips2fits service of the CDS resamples a HiPS survey onto a new image with a chosen center, field of view, size, rotation and WCS projection, and returns it as FITS (with its WCS header) or as JPEG or PNG. It gives a reference image of any field without downloading a survey: to frame a target, compare it with a capture, or test plate solving.

`hips2Fits` asks for a cutout of a survey (see [HiPS Survey Discovery](#hips-survey-discovery)) centered on an ICRS position in radians, with the field of view and rotation in radians, and returns the image as a `Blob`. The FITS cutout carries the WCS of the projection, so it can be read with [FITS Containers and HDUs](#fits-containers-and-hdus) and used as an image with astrometry. The service, not the client, decides whether a combination of options is acceptable.

```ts
import { hips2Fits } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/sky/hips2fits'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// The Orion Nebula from DSS2 with the defaults: 1200 x 900 pixels, 1° field, TAN projection, FITS.
const blob = await hips2Fits('CDS/P/DSS2/color', hour(5.588), deg(-5.39))
if (blob) await Bun.write('orion.fits', blob)

// A 5° JPEG, rotated by 30°, in the stereographic projection.
const wide = await hips2Fits('CDS/P/2MASS/color', deg(83.8), deg(-5.4), { width: 1000, height: 600, fov: deg(5), rotation: deg(30), projection: 'STG', format: 'jpg' })
```

### IAU Meteor Data Center catalog

The IAU Meteor Data Center keeps the official list of meteor showers. Each stream has an IAU number and three-letter code, a status (working list, established, to be established, removed), and one or more solutions published by different authors and techniques: the radiant at a reference solar longitude, its daily drift, the geocentric speed `Vg`, the activity interval in solar longitude, the mean orbit and the parent body. Solutions of the same shower often disagree, so taking the radiant from one and the speed from another produces an inconsistent stream.

The adapter turns the MDC stream document into the meteor shower model of the toolkit (see [Meteor Shower State](#meteor-shower-state) and [Meteor Radiants](#meteor-radiants)) in stages that can be used apart: parsing checks the structure, normalization converts the units (degrees to radians, `Vg` from km/s to AU/day, AU kept) and keeps every missing value `undefined`, never zero, and selection picks one whole solution (the one with the largest sample by default) without mixing fields. The activity text of the catalog (annual, an outburst year, a year range) is interpreted, but no activity profile is invented.

```ts
import { fetchIauMeteorShowerCatalog, normalizeIauMeteorShowerCatalog, parseIauMeteorShowerCatalog, selectMeteorShowerSolution } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/catalogs/iau.meteor.showers'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// json: the streamfulldata.json document of the MDC, as an object or as text.
// Checks the structure, then converts it to showers with their solutions in library units.
const { metadata, showers } = normalizeIauMeteorShowerCatalog(parseIauMeteorShowerCatalog(json))

// One whole solution per shower: the one with the largest number of members.
const perseids = showers.find((shower) => shower.code === 'PER')!
const solution = selectMeteorShowerSolution(perseids)
console.log(toDeg(solution!.rightAscension!), toDeg(solution!.declination!)) // radiant, degrees
console.log(solution!.geocentricSpeed, toDeg(solution!.referenceSolarLongitude!)) // AU/day; solar longitude in degrees

// Downloads, parses and normalizes the current catalog in one call.
const downloaded = await fetchIauMeteorShowerCatalog({ timeout: 30000 })
console.log(downloaded.showers.length, downloaded.metadata.retrievedAt)
```

### JPL Horizons Observer Tables

JPL Horizons is the online solar-system ephemeris service of JPL. It computes the positions of planets, natural satellites, asteroids, comets and spacecraft from the JPL planetary ephemerides and the orbits of its Small-Body Database. An observer table gives the quantities of a target as seen from a site at each step of an interval: astrometric or apparent right ascension and declination, magnitude, range, elongation, phase angle, sky motion, airmass, and many others selected by quantity code. It is the reference to check a local ephemeris, or to obtain one for a body without local data.

`observer` returns the rows of the table as text, one string per column, in the units Horizons defines for the requested quantities, so the caller parses the numbers. The target is a Horizons target string, a TLE, or osculating elements of a body Horizons does not know (see [JPL Horizons Orbital Elements](#jpl-horizons-orbital-elements)); the site is the geocenter or a topocentric `coord@399` site given as longitude and latitude in radians and elevation in AU. The times are Unix milliseconds or a `Time`, and the observer table is in UT. A name that matches several small bodies is retried once with the comet adjustments Horizons suggests. JPL asks automated clients to identify themselves with a `User-Agent`, which `options.headers` sends.

```ts
import { observer, Quantity } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/ephemeris/horizons'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

const start = Date.UTC(2026, 9, 5)
const end = Date.UTC(2026, 9, 5, 2)

// Mars (499) from a site on the Earth: longitude and latitude in radians, elevation in AU.
// Each row has one string per column of the default quantities (position, magnitude, range, ...).
const rows = await observer('499', 'coord@399', [deg(-45.5), deg(-23.2), meter(760)], start, end)

// Ceres from the geocenter with chosen quantities, every 10 minutes.
const ceres = await observer('Ceres;', 'geo', undefined, start, end, [Quantity.APPARENT_RA_DEC, Quantity.AIRMASS_EXTINCTION], { stepSize: 10, stepSizeUnit: 'minutes' })
for (const row of ceres) console.log(row)
```

### JPL Horizons Orbital Elements

Osculating elements are the Keplerian elements of the two-body orbit tangent to the real, perturbed trajectory at one instant (see [Osculating Orbital Elements](#osculating-orbital-elements)). Perturbations make them drift, so Horizons gives them at each step of an interval: eccentricity `EC`, perihelion distance `QR`, inclination `IN`, longitude of the ascending node `OM`, argument of perihelion `W`, time of perihelion `Tp`, mean motion `N`, mean and true anomalies `MA` and `TA`, semi-major axis `A`, aphelion distance `AD` and period `PR`, at Julian dates in TDB and in the units Horizons defines for the chosen output units.

`elements` returns these rows as text. The center is a body, such as `500@10` for heliocentric elements, and the elements are referred to the ecliptic by default. Besides a target string or a TLE, the input can be the osculating elements of a body Horizons does not know, such as a new discovery: an epoch as a Julian date in TDB, the angles in radians, and the size and phase of the orbit given as mean anomaly and semi-major axis (AU), perihelion distance and time, or mean anomaly and mean motion; Horizons then propagates them.

```ts
import { elements } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/ephemeris/horizons'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const start = Date.UTC(2026, 9, 5)
const end = Date.UTC(2026, 9, 7)

// The heliocentric elements of Ceres, one row per day: JDTDB, date, EC, QR, IN, OM, W, Tp, N, MA, TA, A, AD, PR.
const rows = await elements('Ceres;', '500@10', start, end, { stepSize: 1, stepSizeUnit: 'd' })

// Elements of a body Horizons does not know: epoch (JD TDB), angles in radians, mean anomaly and semi-major axis (AU).
await elements({ epoch: 2461000.5, ec: 0.0785, tpqr: { ma: deg(120.5), a: 2.77 }, om: deg(80.25), w: deg(73.6), i: deg(10.59), h: 3.3, g: 0.12 }, '500@10', start, end)
```

### JPL Horizons SPK Downloads

SPK is the binary ephemeris kernel format of the NAIF SPICE system: it stores the trajectory of a body as polynomial segments that are evaluated locally at any instant of their interval. Horizons can integrate the orbit of a small body over an interval and deliver the result as an SPK file, which gives an offline, fast ephemeris for that body instead of one request per epoch; the file is read with [SPK State Kernels](#spk-state-kernels).

`spkFile` requests the kernel of the body with a given SPK id for an interval (Unix milliseconds or `Time` values) and returns either the kernel encoded in Base64 or the error message of Horizons, so the caller checks which one is present and decodes the bytes.

```ts
import { spkFile } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/ephemeris/horizons'

// Ceres (asteroid 1) has the SPK id 2000001; a kernel covering 2026.
const file = await spkFile(2000001, Date.UTC(2026, 0, 1), Date.UTC(2027, 0, 1))

// The kernel arrives as Base64 text: decode it to the bytes of the .bsp file.
if (file.spk) await Bun.write('ceres.bsp', Buffer.from(file.spk, 'base64'))
else console.log(file.error)
```

### JPL Horizons State Vectors

A state vector is the Cartesian position and velocity of a target relative to a center, in a reference frame and plane, at an instant of TDB. Horizons gives it geometric (the true position at the instant), corrected for light time (where the target was when the light left it), or also for stellar aberration (the apparent direction). State vectors seed a numerical integration, cross-check a local ephemeris, and give the distance and velocity of a body in physical units.

`vector` returns the rows as text: the Julian date in TDB, the calendar date, and `X`, `Y`, `Z`, `VX`, `VY`, `VZ` in AU and AU/day by default, in the ICRF equatorial frame unless another plane is asked. The center is a body (`500@10` the Sun, `500@0` the solar-system barycenter, `500@399` the Earth) or a topocentric site given as in [JPL Horizons Observer Tables](#jpl-horizons-observer-tables), and the target forms are the same.

```ts
import { vector } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/ephemeris/horizons'

const start = Date.UTC(2026, 9, 5)
const end = Date.UTC(2026, 9, 5, 2)

// The Earth relative to the Sun, hourly: JDTDB, date, X, Y, Z (AU), VX, VY, VZ (AU/day), ICRF equator.
const rows = await vector('399', '500@10', undefined, start, end)

// Mars from the geocenter, light-time corrected, in the ecliptic, in km and km/s.
await vector('499', 'geo', undefined, start, end, { outputUnits: 'KM-S', vectorCorrection: 'LT', referencePlane: 'ECLIPTIC' })
```

### JPL Small-Body Lookup

The JPL Small-Body Database (SBDB) holds the orbit and physical parameters of every known asteroid and comet: the current orbit solution with its uncertainties, the observation arc, the minimum orbit intersection distance (MOID), the near-Earth and potentially-hazardous flags, the orbit class, and physical parameters such as the absolute magnitude, diameter, albedo and rotation period.

`search` looks a name or designation up and returns one of three shapes: a unique match with the identity, the orbit solution and the physical parameters, a list of candidates for an ambiguous text, or a message when nothing usable is found; a caller tells them apart by their properties. The values are text exactly as published, in the units named by each element (angles in degrees, distances in AU, epochs as Julian dates in TDB).

```ts
import { search } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/orbits/sbd'

// A unique match: identity, orbit solution and physical parameters, as published text.
const ceres = await search('Ceres')
if ('orbit' in ceres)
	console.log(
		ceres.object.spkid,
		ceres.orbit.epoch,
		ceres.orbit.elements.map((e) => `${e.name}=${e.value} ${e.units ?? ''}`),
	)

// An ambiguous text gives the candidates; a comet designation with spaces and a slash is accepted.
const result = await search('C/2023 A3')
if ('list' in result) console.log(result.list.map((item) => item.pdes))
else if ('message' in result) console.log(result.message)
```

### Minor Planet Center API

The Minor Planet Center, under the IAU, is the clearing house for the observations and orbits of minor planets, comets and outer irregular satellites. It assigns the designations, keeps the list of observatory codes, archives every reported observation, publishes the orbit solutions and the lists of objects by dynamical category, and runs the NEO Confirmation Page (NEOCP) for new near-Earth candidates, identified by the temporary designation of their tracklet until they are confirmed. Its API answers these as JSON.

The adapter converts the answers to typed records in radians, AU and UTC; the observatory codes have their own topic, [MPC Observatory Codes](#mpc-observatory-codes). A designation lookup resolves any identifier to the permanent and provisional designations of the object and their packed forms. Observations of a designated object or of a NEOCP tracklet come as the records of the [ADES Codec](#ades-codec), while the low-level queries return the payload in the encodings asked for, such as the 80-column text of the [MPC1992 Codec](#mpc1992-codec). An `mpc_orb` solution yields its heliocentric Cartesian state with covariance and a `KeplerOrbit` (see [Two-Body Kepler Propagation](#two-body-kepler-propagation)). Optical records become the input of the [Differential Orbit Correction](#differential-orbit-correction), but the adapter does not look up station positions: the caller supplies the heliocentric observer position of each observation. The service takes `GET` requests with a JSON body, which Bun's `fetch` refuses, so the adapter uses `node:https` directly.

```ts
import {
	designation,
	designationAliases,
	designations,
	isOpticalObservation,
	list,
	listAll,
	neocpObservations,
	observations,
	observationsToOrbitFit,
	observationToOrbitFitObservation,
	orbit,
	orbitCartesianState,
	orbitToKeplerOrbit,
	parseMPC80Lines,
	primaryDesignation,
	queryNEOCPObservations,
	queryObservations,
} from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/orbits/mpc'

// Up to 100 ids (numbers, provisional designations, names, packed forms) resolved in one request.
for (const record of await designations(['433', '1898 DQ'])) console.log(record.found, primaryDesignation(record))

// One id, only when it matches a single object, and every packed and unpacked form it is known by.
const eros = await designation('Eros')
if (eros) console.log(designationAliases(eros))

// The observations of an object as ADES records (radians, UTC).
const records = await observations('433')

// The raw payload in the encodings asked for: here the 80-column text, read with the MPC1992 codec.
const payload = await queryObservations('433', { outputFormats: ['OBS80'] })
const archived = parseMPC80Lines(payload.obs80 ?? '')

// The observations of a NEOCP tracklet, as ADES records (empty for an unknown tracklet) or as the raw payload.
const candidate = await neocpObservations('P12abcd')
const neocp = await queryNEOCPObservations('P12abcd', { outputFormats: ['ADES_DF'] })

// The orbit fit input: resolve(time, observation) gives the heliocentric observer position in AU.
// resolve: (time: Time, observation: MPCObservation) => Vec3 | undefined
const { observations: fit, rejected } = observationsToOrbitFit(records, resolve)

// The same conversion for one optical record whose observer position is known.
// observer: Vec3 — heliocentric position of the observer at the time of the record, AU
const first = records.find(isOpticalObservation)
if (first) console.log(observationToOrbitFitObservation(first, observer))

// The first mpc_orb solution: heliocentric state (AU, AU/day, with covariance) and a Kepler orbit.
const solution = await orbit('433')
if (solution) console.log(orbitCartesianState(solution)?.position, orbitToKeplerOrbit(solution))

// One page of a List API category, and up to a number of items paged automatically.
const page = await list('neos', { like: '2010%', limit: 2 })
const neos = await listAll('neos', { like: '2010%', maxItems: 5 })
console.log(page.items[0]?.unpackedPrimaryProvisionalDesignation, neos.length)
```

### MPC Observatory Codes

Every site that reports astrometry to the Minor Planet Center has a three-character observatory code, such as `568` for Maunakea or `500` for the geocenter, and the `stn` field of the records of the [ADES Codec](#ades-codec) and the [MPC1992 Codec](#mpc1992-codec) names it. For each fixed site the MPC list gives the east longitude λ and the parallax constants ρ cos φ′ and ρ sin φ′, where ρ is the geocentric distance in units of the Earth's equatorial radius and φ′ the geocentric latitude, so the geocentric position follows from them and the equatorial radius alone, without a height or a flattening:

```text
x = ρ cos φ′ cos λ    y = ρ cos φ′ sin λ    z = ρ sin φ′
```

`observatory` and `observatories` read one code or the whole list from the [Minor Planet Center API](#minor-planet-center-api), and `parseObservatoryCode`, `parseObservatoryCodes` and `writeObservatoryCode` read and write the lines of the fixed-width `ObsCodes.html` list. `observatoryItrsPosition` gives the geocentric ITRS position in AU, scaling ρ by the equatorial radius of an ellipsoid, and `observatoryLocation` the geodetic site derived from it (see [Geographic Observer](#geographic-observer)); both are `undefined` for the geocenter and for a code without fixed geometry, such as a spacecraft, whose observations carry the observer position themselves. The position is Earth-fixed: the heliocentric observer position of an orbit fit also needs the Earth's rotation and heliocentric position at the time of each observation.

