```ts
import { observatories, observatory, observatoryItrsPosition, observatoryLocation, parseObservatoryCode, parseObservatoryCodes, writeObservatoryCode } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/orbits/mpc'
import { toDeg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { toKilometer } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// One line of ObsCodes.html: code, east longitude (degrees), ρ cos φ′, ρ sin φ′ and name.
const line = '310 288.871640.739802+0.670574Minor Planet Center Test Code'
const site = parseObservatoryCode(line)
console.log(site.code, toDeg(site.longitude!), site.rhoCosPhi, site.rhoSinPhi) // 310 288.87164 0.739802 0.670574

// Writes it back in the same columns; a whole list is parsed line by line, skipping blank lines.
console.log(writeObservatoryCode(site) === line, parseObservatoryCodes(`${line}\n\n${line}`).length) // true 2

// The geocentric ITRS position (AU), and the geodetic site derived from it.
console.log(observatoryItrsPosition(site)?.map(toKilometer)) // ≈ [ 1526.2, -4464.9, 4277.0 ] km
const location = observatoryLocation(site)!
console.log(toDeg(location.longitude), toDeg(location.latitude)) // ≈ -71.12836 42.381 — degrees, longitude east-positive

// One code, or every code, from the MPC API, with names and observation type.
const maunakea = await observatory('568')
const all = await observatories()
```

### MPC1992 Codec

The MPC1992 format is the historical fixed-width record of the Minor Planet Center: one line of 80 columns per observation (the "obs80" format), still found in the MPC archive and in many tools. A line holds the packed designation, the discovery mark and notes, the observing mode, the date with a fractional day, the right ascension in sexagesimal hours and the declination in sexagesimal degrees, the magnitude and band, the reference and the station code. Satellite, roving and radar observations add a second line with the observer position or the radar fields. The columns bound the precision (the day fraction has six decimals, about 0.09 s; the declination 0.01″) and leave no room for uncertainties, which is why the [ADES Codec](#ades-codec) replaces it.

Designations are packed into a few characters: `433` is `00433`, `2024 YR4` is `K24Y04R`, and `C/1995 O1` is `CJ95O010`. The codec packs and unpacks designations and reads and writes the 80-column records as the same `MPCObservation` union as ADES, so records can move between the formats; values the format cannot hold, such as uncertainties and catalogs, are not written. The second line of a roving observer stores an east longitude from 0 to 360°, so a west longitude comes back as its east equivalent.

```ts
import { packMPCDesignation, parseADESObservation, parseMPC80, parseMPC80Lines, unpackMPCDesignation, writeMPC80, writeMPC80Lines } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/orbits/mpc'

// Packed and readable designations.
console.log(packMPCDesignation('2024 YR4'), unpackMPCDesignation('K24Y04R')) // K24Y04R 2024 YR4

// An optical record (here from ADES input) written as one 80-column line.
const eros = parseADESObservation({ obsType: 'optical', permID: '433', obsTime: '2024-03-05T10:20:30.250Z', ra: 123.456789, dec: -12.345678, mag: 17.4, band: 'V', stn: '568', disc: '*', ref: 'MPEC1' })
console.log(writeMPC80(eros)) // 00433       * C2024 03 05.43090608 13 49.629-12 20 44.44         17.40VMPEC1 568

// One line read back as a record.
console.log(parseMPC80(writeMPC80(eros)).station) // 568

// A whole file, read back: two-line records are joined, and the time and angles return to UTC and radians.
const records = parseMPC80Lines(writeMPC80Lines([eros]))
console.log(records[0].type, records[0].station) // optical 568
```

### NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP Queries

The NASA Exoplanet Archive publishes two tables of planet parameters. `ps` (Planetary Systems) has one row per published solution, each self-consistent, with `default_flag = 1` on the solution the archive picks as default; `pscomppars` (Planetary Systems Composite Parameters) has one row per planet whose columns can come from different publications, so its epoch, period, and duration are not necessarily one fit. The mid-transit epoch `pl_tranmid` is a Julian Date whose clock and origin are named by `pl_tsystemref` in `ps` and by `pl_tranmid_systemref` in `pscomppars`.

`exoplanetArchiveRows` fetches the transit-ephemeris columns of one of these tables through the archive's synchronous TAP service, for a planet or a host, either the default `ps` solution or every one. Each value stays the string the archive sent and an empty column is `null`, so `pl_tranmid` keeps all its digits and `0` stays distinct from a missing value; no time scale is assumed and nothing is merged or chosen. The rows go to `exoplanetArchiveTransitEphemeris` (see [Exoplanet Transit Prediction](#exoplanet-transit-prediction)), which decides which are usable. `exoplanetArchiveTapQuery` runs any ADQL text verbatim. The archive is live data: values and default solutions change as publications are added.

```ts
import { exoplanetArchiveTransitEphemeris } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/catalogs/exoplanet.archive'
import { exoplanetArchiveRows, exoplanetArchiveTapQuery } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/catalogs/exoplanet.archive.tap'

// Every published `ps` solution of one planet, values as the archive's strings.
const { rows, truncated } = await exoplanetArchiveRows({ table: 'ps', planetName: 'WASP-12 b', solution: 'all', limit: 100 })

// Converts each row to a transit ephemeris, or says why it cannot.
for (const row of rows) {
	const result = exoplanetArchiveTransitEphemeris(row)
	console.log(result.success ? result.ephemeris.period : result.reason) // period in days, or the rejection reason
}

// Any ADQL query: CSV columns and records keyed by column name.
const { columns, records } = await exoplanetArchiveTapQuery("SELECT pl_name, pl_orbper FROM pscomppars WHERE hostname = 'TRAPPIST-1'")
```

### SIMBAD Object Types

SIMBAD classifies every object with a type from a hierarchical taxonomy: stars and their variants, sets of stars, galaxies, sets of galaxies, the interstellar medium, spectral objects, gravitational phenomena, and others. Each type has short codes, and a code ending in `?` marks a candidate rather than a confirmed object (`QSO` is a quasar, `Q?` a quasar candidate). The object type is what a planner filters on to keep galaxies, clusters or variable stars.

`SIMBAD_OBJECT_TYPES` holds the taxonomy as a constant table keyed by an upper-case name, each entry with a numeric id, a description, its broad classification and its codes. The lookups by id and by code resolve both the confirmed and the candidate codes to the same entry. The `type` of a [SIMBAD Star Catalog](#simbad-star-catalog) entry and the `otype` column of a TAP query are such codes.

```ts
import { findSimbadObjectTypeInfoByCode, findSimbadObjectTypeInfoById, SIMBAD_OBJECT_TYPES } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/catalogs/simbad'

// One entry of the table.
console.log(SIMBAD_OBJECT_TYPES.QUASAR) // { id: 213, description: "Quasar", classification: "GALAXY", codes: [ "QSO", "Q?" ] }

// Lookups by id and by code; a candidate code gives the same entry as the confirmed one.
console.log(findSimbadObjectTypeInfoById(213)?.description) // Quasar
console.log(findSimbadObjectTypeInfoByCode('GlC')?.description, findSimbadObjectTypeInfoByCode('Gl?') === findSimbadObjectTypeInfoByCode('GlC')) // Globular Cluster true
```

### SIMBAD Star Catalog

SIMBAD, maintained by the CDS, is the reference database of astronomical objects outside the solar system: identifiers, object type, ICRS position, proper motion, parallax, radial velocity and fluxes, cross-matched over the literature. Unlike a survey catalog such as Gaia, it covers named objects of every kind with their types and V magnitudes, which suits finder charts, target lists and the bright stars of a field.

`SimbadCatalog` is a star catalog (see [Star Catalog Interface and Spatial Query](#star-catalog-interface-and-spatial-query)) over the `basic` and `allfluxes` tables, queried through [SIMBAD TAP Queries](#simbad-tap-queries). Its entries have the ICRS position at J2000 in radians, the V magnitude, the proper motion as dα/dt and dδ/dt in radians per year (the published μα·cos δ divided by cos δ), the parallax in radians, the radial velocity, and the object type code (see [SIMBAD Object Types](#simbad-object-types)); an object without a V magnitude never appears. A region is read page by page, so the stream is complete without repeated rows.

```ts
import { findSimbadObjectTypeInfoByCode, SimbadCatalog } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/catalogs/simbad'
import { deg, toMas } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const catalog = new SimbadCatalog({ timeout: 30000 })

// A cone of 3 arcminutes around the Orion Nebula (radians), ordered by V magnitude.
const stars = await catalog.queryCone(deg(83.8221), deg(-5.3911), deg(0.05))
for (const star of stars) console.log(star.id, star.type && findSimbadObjectTypeInfoByCode(star.type)?.description, star.magnitude, star.parallax && toMas(star.parallax))

// A region streamed through the pages of the service.
for await (const entry of catalog.streamRegion({ kind: 'box', minRA: deg(83.7), maxRA: deg(84), minDEC: deg(-5.5), maxDEC: deg(-5.3) })) console.log(entry.id, entry.magnitude)

// The same box collected into an array; queryTriangle, queryPolygon and queryRegion take the other shapes.
const box = await catalog.queryBox(deg(83.7), deg(84), deg(-5.5), deg(-5.3))

// One object by its SIMBAD oid.
const one = await catalog.get(3755198)
```

### SIMBAD TAP Queries

TAP (Table Access Protocol) is the IVOA protocol through which a client sends an ADQL query, an SQL dialect with spherical-geometry functions such as `CONTAINS` and `CIRCLE`, to an astronomical database; the synchronous endpoint returns the result in the same request. SIMBAD exposes its tables this way: `basic` holds the identity, type, ICRS position `ra` and `dec` in degrees, proper motions `pmra` and `pmdec` in mas/yr, parallax `plx_value` in mas and radial velocity `rvz_radvel` in km/s, and `allfluxes` the magnitudes by band. The service limits the number of rows of an answer.

`simbadQuery` runs an ADQL query against SIMBAD and returns the TSV rows as arrays of strings, with the header line dropped by default, or `undefined` when the request fails; nothing is converted and the ADQL is not validated. It works like [VizieR TAP Queries](#vizier-tap-queries), and the parsing follows [CSV Parsing](#csv-parsing).

```ts
import { SIMBAD_ALTERNATIVE_URL, simbadQuery } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/catalogs/simbad'

const adql = "SELECT TOP 2 oid, main_id, ra, dec FROM basic WHERE main_id IN ('M  42', 'M  31')"

// One array of strings per row; ra and dec are degrees as text.
const rows = await simbadQuery(adql)
for (const row of rows ?? []) console.log(row)

// The mirror host, keeping the header line as the first row.
const data = await simbadQuery(adql, { baseUrl: SIMBAD_ALTERNATIVE_URL, skipFirstLine: false })
```

### SkyBoT Cone Search

SkyBoT, a service of the IMCCE, predicts which known solar-system objects (asteroids, comets, planets and natural satellites) are inside a field of the sky at an instant, computing their positions from the orbits of the whole catalog. It tells which moving objects an image should contain, identifies a moving source, or warns of a bright asteroid crossing a target. [Small-Body Identification](#small-body-identification) is the equivalent JPL service.

`coneSearch` asks for the objects within a radius of a J2000 center at an instant (Unix milliseconds in UTC or a `Time`; angles in radians), seen from an IAU observatory code, the geocenter by default. Each object has its astrometric J2000 position in radians, its dynamical class, and when known the visual magnitude, the position uncertainty, the sky motion in radians per day, and its distances in AU. The service accepts a radius up to 10° and epochs from 1889 to 2060, and requests are sent as given, so a caller checks them first. Although it documents a geographic observer, the service refuses one, so a site without an observatory code takes the geocentric positions and corrects them with [Topocentric Parallax](#topocentric-parallax). An ephemeris the service cannot compute for a planet or satellite fails the whole answer, so a search limited to asteroids and comets is more robust. Answers take seconds.

```ts
import { coneSearch, coneSearchUrl, parseSkybotResponse } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/orbits/skybot'
import { geocentricToTopocentric } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/coordinates/astrometry'
import { Ellipsoid, geodeticLocation } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/observer/location'
import { timeUnix } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// Asteroids and comets within 15′ of RA 10h, Dec +12° on 2026-01-15 at 0h UTC, seen from the geocenter.
const objects = await coneSearch(Date.UTC(2026, 0, 15), hour(10), deg(12), deg(0.25), { objects: { asteroids: true, planets: false, comets: true } })
for (const object of objects) console.log(object.name, object.class, object.magnitude)

// The geocentric positions moved to a site that has no observatory code.
const site = geodeticLocation(deg(-46.63), deg(-23.55), meter(760), Ellipsoid.WGS84)
const at = timeUnix(Date.UTC(2026, 0, 15) / 1000, true)
for (const object of objects) if (object.distance !== undefined) console.log(object.name, geocentricToTopocentric(object.rightAscension, object.declination, object.distance, at, site)) // radians

// The same search through the caller's own transport: the request URL, then the parser of its JSON body (no body when the field is empty).
const response = await fetch(coneSearchUrl(Date.UTC(2026, 0, 15), hour(10), deg(12), deg(0.25)))
const text = await response.text()
const parsed = parseSkybotResponse(text ? JSON.parse(text) : undefined)
```

### Small-Body Identification

`sb_ident` is the JPL service that searches the orbits of its Small-Body Database for the asteroids and comets inside a rectangular field of view, seen from a site at a given time, down to a limiting magnitude. It is the standard check of whether a moving source in an image is a known body. It works in two passes, a fast approximate one and a refined one, and only the refined table is returned. [SkyBoT Cone Search](#skybot-cone-search) is the equivalent IMCCE service.

`identify` takes the time (Unix milliseconds in UTC or a `Time`), the site as east longitude and latitude in radians and elevation in AU, the center of the field in radians, its half-widths in radians (1° by default), and a limiting visual magnitude. It returns the answer of the service: the column names and one row of text per body (name, position, distance, rates, magnitude), as published.

```ts
import { identify, type SmallBodyIdentifySecondPass } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/orbits/sbd'
import { deg, hour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'
import { meter } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/distance'

// The field around the Orion Nebula from a site at 760 m, on 2026-10-05 at 03:00 UTC, with 1° half-widths.
const when = Date.UTC(2026, 9, 5, 3)
const result = (await identify(when, deg(-45.5), deg(-23.2), meter(760), hour(5.588), deg(-5.39))) as SmallBodyIdentifySecondPass
console.log(result.n_second_pass, result.fields_second)
for (const row of result.data_second_pass) console.log(row.join(' | '))

// A 2° x 0.5° half-width field, limit magnitude 20, including bodies of unknown magnitude.
await identify(when, deg(-45.5), deg(-23.2), meter(760), hour(5.588), deg(-5.39), deg(2), deg(0.5), 20, false)
```

### VizieR TAP Queries

VizieR, the catalog service of the CDS, hosts thousands of published astronomical catalogs and tables, such as Gaia DR3 (`I/355/gaiadr3`), 2MASS and Tycho-2, each named by its catalog identifier. Its TAP service accepts ADQL queries over all of them (see [SIMBAD TAP Queries](#simbad-tap-queries) for the protocol), which makes it the general way to fetch columns of any catalog for a field.

`vizierQuery` runs an ADQL query against the synchronous TAP endpoint of VizieR and returns the TSV rows as arrays of strings, with the header line dropped by default, or `undefined` when the request fails. Nothing is converted: the cells are the text of the service, in the units of each catalog, and the parsing follows [CSV Parsing](#csv-parsing). [Gaia DR3 Star Catalog](#gaia-dr3-star-catalog) is a typed catalog built on this call.

```ts
import { vizierQuery } from 'nebulosa/src/adapters/catalogs/vizier'

// A table name with a slash is quoted in ADQL.
const adql = 'SELECT TOP 2 Source, RAJ2000, DEJ2000, Gmag FROM "I/355/gaiadr3" WHERE Gmag < 13 ORDER BY Gmag ASC'

// One array of strings per row: the source id, J2000 position in degrees and G magnitude, as text.
const rows = await vizierQuery(adql)
for (const row of rows ?? []) console.log(row)

// Keep the header line and trim the cells.
const data = await vizierQuery(adql, { skipFirstLine: false, forceTrim: true })
```

## 💾 I/O and Data Formats

### Buffer Byte I/O

The format readers and writers of the toolkit work on the byte-stream contracts of [Byte-Stream Contracts](#byte-stream-contracts), so the same FITS, XISF or CSV code reads a file, a network stream or memory. `BufferSource` and `BufferSink` are the in-memory implementations: they read from and write into a fixed `Buffer` through a seekable `position` cursor in bytes, and report when they are exhausted. They serve to parse downloaded bytes, to write into a preallocated buffer, and to test.

A read returns `0` at the end, and a negative seek counts from the end (`-1` is the last byte). The sink's buffer does not grow: a write returns a smaller count than requested once the buffer is full, so a record of unknown size belongs in [Growable Binary Buffers](#growable-binary-buffers). The buffer is shared, not copied.

```ts
import { bufferSink, bufferSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'

// Reads from a fixed buffer through a cursor (a BufferSource); a read returns the bytes copied, 0 at the end.
const source = bufferSource(Buffer.from('Nebulosa 2026'))
const chunk = Buffer.alloc(8)
console.log(source.readSync(chunk), chunk.toString()) // 8 Nebulosa

// A negative position counts from the end.
source.seek(-4)
console.log(await source.read(chunk), chunk.toString('latin1', 0, 4)) // 4 2026

// Writes strings or buffers into a fixed buffer; the count is short once it is full.
const sink = bufferSink(Buffer.alloc(16))
console.log(sink.write('Hello'), sink.position) // 5 5

// The sink seeks like the source, writeSync is the same write, and exhausted tells whether the end was reached.
sink.seek(0)
sink.writeSync('J')
console.log(sink.buffer.toString('latin1', 0, 5), source.exhausted, sink.exhausted) // Jello true false
```

### Byte Reading, Writing, and Transfer

The `read` of a source and the `write` of a sink may move fewer bytes than requested without having reached the end, like the POSIX `read` and `write` calls (see [Byte-Stream Contracts](#byte-stream-contracts)). Every consumer that needs an exact count must therefore loop, and these helpers implement those loops once, for any adapter.

`readUntil` reads until a buffer is filled or the input ends, `writeFully` repeats short writes until every byte is accepted, `readRemaining` reads to the end into one new buffer (materializing the whole input), and `sourceTransferToSink` copies a source into a sink through one reusable transfer buffer. A sink that stops accepting bytes makes them throw instead of spinning. They neither seek nor close.

```ts
import { bufferSink, bufferSource, readRemaining, readUntil, readUntilSync, sourceTransferToSink, writeFully, writeFullySync } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'

// Fills the buffer, or what is left of the input; the count is smaller only at the end.
const source = bufferSource(Buffer.from('0123456789abcdefghij'))
const buffer = Buffer.alloc(8)
console.log(await readUntil(source, buffer), buffer.toString()) // 8 01234567

// Reads everything that is left as one new buffer.
console.log((await readRemaining(source)).toString()) // 89abcdefghij

// Writes every byte even through a sink that accepts only part of each write.
const sink = bufferSink(Buffer.alloc(64))
await writeFully(sink, Buffer.from('nebulosa'))

// Copies a whole source into a sink in blocks of 16 bytes; returns the bytes copied.
const input = bufferSource(Buffer.from('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog'))
console.log(await sourceTransferToSink(input, bufferSink(Buffer.alloc(64)), 16)) // 43

// The synchronous forms of readUntil and writeFully, for adapters that support synchronous calls.
const head = Buffer.alloc(4)
console.log(readUntilSync(bufferSource(Buffer.from('0123456789')), head), writeFullySync(bufferSink(Buffer.alloc(8)), Buffer.from('nebulosa'))) // 4 8
```

### Byte Shuffling

`byteShuffle(input, output, itemSize)` and `byteUnshuffle(input, output, itemSize)` (`src/io/formats/xisf/xisf.ts`) are the reversible byte reordering that XISF applies before compressing a block of multi-byte samples. For items of `itemSize` bytes, the shuffle writes all the first bytes of the items, then all the second bytes, and so on, so that similar bytes (the high bytes of neighbouring pixels, for instance) end up together, which usually raises the compression ratio of a following codec; the unshuffle restores the original layout. The item size is the sample size of the pixel type (2 for 16-bit integers, 4 for 32-bit integers and floats, 8 for double precision). The XISF codecs apply it when a compression name carries the `+sh` suffix (see [XISF Pixel I/O and Compression](#xisf-pixel-io-and-compression)), usually before [Deflate Compression](#deflate-compression).

Both functions write into a caller buffer of at least the input length and copy any trailing bytes that do not fill a whole item unchanged.

```ts
import { byteShuffle, byteUnshuffle } from 'nebulosa/src/io/formats/xisf/xisf'

// Four 16-bit samples, written big-endian: 0x0102 0x0304 0x0506 0x0708.
const samples = Buffer.from([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8])

// Groups the first bytes of every item, then the second bytes.
const shuffled = Buffer.alloc(samples.byteLength)
byteShuffle(samples, shuffled, 2)
console.log(shuffled) // <Buffer 01 03 05 07 02 04 06 08>

// The inverse restores the original bytes.
const restored = Buffer.alloc(samples.byteLength)
byteUnshuffle(shuffled, restored, 2)
console.log(restored.equals(samples)) // true
```

### Byte-Stream Contracts

`src/io/types.ts` holds the small interfaces that every byte reader and writer of the toolkit implements, so a format codec is written once and works on memory, files, web streams and HTTP. A `Source` reads up to a requested number of bytes into a buffer and returns how many it copied, `0` meaning the end of the input; a `Sink` writes a buffer or a string and returns how many bytes it consumed. Both may answer synchronously or with a promise, so callers `await` them, and each has a synchronous counterpart that a source or sink backed by an asynchronous transport refuses by throwing. The two calls of one object share a single cursor, so they must not run at the same time.

A short read is allowed: a source may return fewer bytes than requested without being at the end, which is why the helpers of [Byte Reading, Writing, and Transfer](#byte-reading-writing-and-transfer) loop. The optional capabilities are separate interfaces, `Seekable` (a position and a seek), `Exhaustible` (whether everything was consumed) and `Flushable`, with runtime guards so generic code uses a capability only when the object has it. The concrete adapters are [Buffer Byte I/O](#buffer-byte-io), [File-Handle Byte I/O](#file-handle-byte-io), [ReadableStream Byte Sources](#readablestream-byte-sources) and [HTTP Range Byte Sources](#http-range-byte-sources).

```ts
import { bufferSource, writeFully } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'
import { isExhaustible, isFlushable, isSeekable, type Sink, type Source } from 'nebulosa/src/io/types'

// Copies any source into any sink through the contracts: a read of 0 is the end, a short read is not.
async function copy(source: Source, sink: Sink) {
	const buffer = Buffer.alloc(4096)
	let n: number
	while ((n = await source.read(buffer)) > 0) await writeFully(sink, buffer, n)

	// Uses an optional capability only when the sink has it.
	if (isFlushable(sink)) sink.flush()
}

// The guards tell which capabilities an object has.
const memory = bufferSource(Buffer.from('nebulosa'))
console.log(isSeekable(memory), isExhaustible(memory), isFlushable(memory)) // true true false
```

### CRC Checksums

A cyclic redundancy check is the remainder of the division of a message, read as a polynomial over GF(2), by a generator polynomial. It detects burst errors and accidental corruption cheaply, and it protects the messages of many device protocols and file formats. A CRC is fully described by its width, polynomial, initial value, bit order (reflection) and final xor; the RevEng catalogue names the standard combinations and gives the check value of each for the ASCII text `123456789`.

`CRC` is a table-driven calculator for any CRC of 1 to 32 bits. The catalogued algorithms are cached static instances named after the catalogue (`CRC.crc32`, `CRC.crc32c`, `CRC.crc16xmodem`, `CRC.crc8`, and so on), and the constructor takes a custom configuration. `compute` returns the checksum as an unsigned integer, and passing the previous result continues a running checksum, so a stream checksummed chunk by chunk gives the same value as the whole.

```ts
import { CRC } from 'nebulosa/src/io/crc'

const text = Buffer.from('123456789')

// Catalogued algorithms; these are their catalogue check values.
console.log(CRC.crc32.compute(text).toString(16)) // cbf43926
console.log(CRC.crc16xmodem.compute(text).toString(16)) // 31c3

// A running checksum: the result of the first 4 bytes continues over the rest.
const first = CRC.crc32.compute(text, undefined, 0, 4)
console.log(CRC.crc32.compute(text, first, 4).toString(16)) // cbf43926

// A custom configuration: width, polynomial, initial value, reflection and final xor (CRC-16/ARC).
console.log(new CRC(16, 0x8005, 0x0000, true, 0x0000).compute(text).toString(16)) // bb3d
```

### CSV Parsing

Delimited text is the answer format of most astronomical services (TAP queries in CSV or TSV, JPL and MPC tables) and of many exported catalogs. The common conventions are those of RFC 4180: a delimiter between fields, quotes around a field that contains the delimiter, a line break or a quote, and a doubled quote inside a quoted field.

`readCsv` parses a whole string into rows of strings, `readCsvStream` parses a byte source (see [Byte-Stream Contracts](#byte-stream-contracts)) incrementally, yielding rows as they complete with multi-byte characters and quoted fields reassembled across chunk boundaries, and `CsvLineParser` splits one line. Unquoted fields are trimmed, comment and blank lines are skipped, and every value stays text: the parser infers no types and no column names. The first row is taken as a header and dropped by default, so a file without a header must say so.

```ts
import { CsvLineParser, readCsv, readCsvStream, TSV_DELIMITER } from 'nebulosa/src/io/csv'
import { bufferSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'

// Parses a document; the header row is dropped and the values are strings.
const csv = 'name,magnitude\nSirius, -1.46\nCanopus,-0.74'
console.log(readCsv(csv)) // [ [ "Sirius", "-1.46" ], [ "Canopus", "-0.74" ] ]

// A delimiter alone can replace the options.
console.log(readCsv('a\tb\n1\t2', TSV_DELIMITER)) // [ [ "1", "2" ] ]

// Streams the rows of a byte source, decoding in chunks.
for await (const row of readCsvStream(bufferSource(Buffer.from('id,name\n1,Café\n2,Zürich\n')))) console.log(row)

// Splits one line; quoted fields keep their delimiters.
console.log(new CsvLineParser({ delimiter: ',' }).parse('1, 2 ,"3,4"')) // [ "1", "2", "3,4" ]
```

### Deflate Compression

Deflate (RFC 1951) is the lossless compression that combines LZ77 back-references with Huffman coding; the zlib format (RFC 1950) wraps a deflate stream with a two-byte header and an Adler-32 checksum. The zlib format is what the XISF `zlib` codec stores in its pixel blocks (see [XISF Pixel I/O and Compression](#xisf-pixel-io-and-compression)), often after [Byte Shuffling](#byte-shuffling) to bring similar bytes together. It is neither raw deflate nor gzip, so those streams cannot be read with it.

`deflate` compresses a buffer, typed array or string to a new zlib buffer at a level from 0 (stored) to 9 (best), and `inflate` restores the original bytes. Both run on the zlib thread pool, so a large block does not block the event loop, and the whole result is held in memory. The FITS tile codec is the separate [FITS Rice Compression](#fits-rice-compression).

```ts
import { deflate, inflate } from 'nebulosa/src/io/compression'

// Compresses a repetitive block at the best level; the result is a zlib stream.
const text = Buffer.from('NEBULOSA '.repeat(500))
const best = await deflate(text, { level: 9 })
console.log(text.byteLength, best.byteLength) // 4500 46

// Restores the original bytes.
console.log((await inflate(best)).equals(text)) // true
```

### File-Handle Byte I/O

`FileHandleSource` and `FileHandleSink` adapt a `FileHandle` of `fs/promises` to the [Byte-Stream Contracts](#byte-stream-contracts), so the format codecs read and write files directly. Each keeps its own cursor in bytes and reads or writes at that explicit position, so the offset of the descriptor does not matter, and the asynchronous and synchronous calls share that cursor as long as they run one after the other. A seek accepts any non-negative position, with no seek from the end, and the end of a file is seen only as a read of `0`.

The adapters take ownership of the handle: closing them, or their `await using` and `using` disposal, closes it.

```ts
import { open } from 'fs/promises'
import { fileHandleSink, fileHandleSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/file'
import { readRemaining } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'

// Writes text and bytes at the cursor; disposal closes the handle.
{
	await using sink = fileHandleSink(await open('data.txt', 'w'))
	await sink.write('Nebulosa')
	sink.writeSync(Buffer.from(' toolkit'))
}

// Reads it back, synchronously or asynchronously, from an explicit position.
{
	await using source = fileHandleSource(await open('data.txt', 'r'))
	const head = Buffer.alloc(2)
	console.log(source.readSync(head), head.toString()) // 2 Ne
	source.seek(4)
	console.log((await readRemaining(source)).toString()) // losa toolkit
}

// Without disposal: seek the sink to overwrite a byte, then close() releases the handle.
const sink = fileHandleSink(await open('data.txt', 'r+'))
sink.seek(0)
await sink.write('n')
await sink.close()
```

### FITS Containers and HDUs

FITS (Flexible Image Transport System) is the standard file format of astronomical data, maintained under the IAU (FITS Standard 4.0). A file is a sequence of header and data units (HDUs) made of 2880-byte blocks: a header of 80-character ASCII cards that ends with `END`, then the data padded to a whole block. The primary unit comes first and extensions (`IMAGE`, `BINTABLE`, and others) follow. Image data are big-endian samples whose type is `BITPIX`: 8 for unsigned bytes, 16, 32 and 64 for signed integers, −32 and −64 for IEEE floats; unsigned 16-bit data are stored as signed integers with `BZERO = 32768`. A tile-compressed image is stored as a binary table extension.

`readFits` indexes a seekable source: it parses every header (see [FITS Header Cards and Metadata](#fits-header-cards-and-metadata)) and only locates each data segment by offset and size, seeking past the data, so a large file is indexed cheaply and the pixels are read afterwards with [FITS Pixel I/O and Rice Tiles](#fits-pixel-io-and-rice-tiles). `writeFits` writes images from the normalized library arrays (0 to 1), scaled to the integer range of an integer `BITPIX` and adding `BZERO` for 16-bit output, and can write them with [FITS Rice Compression](#fits-rice-compression). Only uncompressed images and `RICE_1` tiles are decoded as pixels; other units are indexed but not interpreted.

```ts
import { isFits, readFits, writeFits } from 'nebulosa/src/io/formats/fits/fits'
import { bufferSink, bufferSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'

// raw: Float32Array of 6 x 4 normalized samples (0 to 1), a ramp.
const width = 6
const height = 4
const raw = Float32Array.from({ length: width * height }, (_, i) => i / (width * height - 1))

// Writes one 16-bit image: one block of header and one block of data.
const out = Buffer.alloc(2880 * 4)
const sink = bufferSink(out)
await writeFits(sink, [{ header: { SIMPLE: true, BITPIX: 16, NAXIS: 2, NAXIS1: width, NAXIS2: height, OBJECT: 'M42' }, raw }])
console.log(isFits(out)) // true

// Indexes the file: the headers are parsed, the data are only located (offset and size in bytes).
const fits = (await readFits(bufferSource(out.subarray(0, sink.position))))!
console.log(fits.hdus.length, fits.hdus[0].offset, fits.hdus[0].data) // 1 0 { offset: 2880, size: 48 }
```

### FITS Header Cards and Metadata

A FITS header is a list of 80-character cards: a keyword of up to 8 characters, the value indicator `= `, the value (a quoted string with an embedded quote doubled, `T` or `F` for logicals, or a number), and an optional comment after `/`. `COMMENT` and `HISTORY` cards hold free text, and the `CONTINUE` convention splits a string too long for one card. Beyond the standard keywords, capture software writes the same metadata with different conventions, such as the pointing as degrees in `RA` or as sexagesimal hours in `OBJCTRA`, so a reader has to try several keywords.

`FitsKeywordWriter` formats cards (taking the default comment of the keyword table when a card has none) and `FitsKeywordReader` parses one card or a whole header into a `FitsHeader` object, joining the commentary cards and rebuilding continued strings. The accessors of `util.ts` read a header with a default for a missing key, and the metadata readers return the image geometry, the exposure, the CFA pattern, the pointing in radians (trying `RA`, `OBJCTRA`, `RA_OBJ`, then `CRVAL1`, and the matching declination keywords) and the observation date in Unix milliseconds (UTC). The typed readers of [FITS Instrument Provenance](#fits-instrument-provenance) and [FITS Observation Timing and Location](#fits-observation-timing-and-location) build on them and tell an absent keyword from an unreadable one.

```ts
import { FitsKeywordReader, FitsKeywordWriter } from 'nebulosa/src/io/formats/fits/fits'
import {
	bitpixKeyword,
	booleanKeyword,
	cfaPatternKeyword,
	declinationKeyword,
	exposureTimeKeyword,
	hasKeyword,
	heightKeyword,
	isCompressedImageHeader,
	numberOfAxesKeyword,
	numberOfChannelsKeyword,
	numericKeyword,
	observationDateKeyword,
	rightAscensionKeyword,
	textKeyword,
	uncompressedWidthKeyword,
	widthKeyword,
} from 'nebulosa/src/io/formats/fits/util'
import { toDeg, toHour } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

// Formats cards of 80 characters into a buffer, then the END card.
const writer = new FitsKeywordWriter()
const buffer = Buffer.alloc(80 * 4)
let size = writer.write(['EXPTIME', 120.5], buffer, 0)
size += writer.write(['OBJECT', "Barnard's Star", 'target'], buffer, size)
writer.writeEnd(buffer, size)

// Parses the cards until END into a header object, or one card into its key, value and comment.
const reader = new FitsKeywordReader()
const header = reader.readAll(buffer)
console.log(reader.read(buffer, 80)) // [ "OBJECT", "Barnard's Star", "target" ]

// Formats a whole header object or card list, without the END card; returns the bytes written.
console.log(writer.writeAll(header, Buffer.alloc(80 * 4))) // 160

// The accessors: presence, then text, number and logical values with a default for a missing key.
console.log(hasKeyword(header, 'EXPTIME'), textKeyword(header, 'OBJECT'), numericKeyword(header, 'GAIN', 0), booleanKeyword(header, 'SIMPLE')) // true Barnard's Star 0 false

// The metadata readers: geometry, sample type, exposure (s) and CFA pattern.
const image = { NAXIS: 3, NAXIS1: 100, NAXIS2: 50, NAXIS3: 3, BITPIX: -32, EXPOSURE: 10, BAYERPAT: 'RGGB ', RA: 83.82, DEC: -5.39, 'DATE-OBS': '2026-10-05T03:04:05.250Z' }
console.log(numberOfAxesKeyword(image, 0), widthKeyword(image, 0), heightKeyword(image, 0), numberOfChannelsKeyword(image, 1), bitpixKeyword(image, 0), exposureTimeKeyword(image, 0), cfaPatternKeyword(image)) // 3 100 50 3 -32 10 RGGB

// The pointing in radians and the observation date in Unix milliseconds (UTC).
console.log(toHour(rightAscensionKeyword(image, 0)), toDeg(declinationKeyword(image, 0)), observationDateKeyword(image)) // 5.587999999999999 -5.39 1791169445250

// A tile-compressed image: isCompressedImageHeader, isRiceCompressedImageHeader and compressionTypeKeyword identify it, and
// uncompressedWidthKeyword, uncompressedHeightKeyword, uncompressedNumberOfChannelsKeyword, uncompressedBitpixKeyword,
// uncompressedScaleKeyword and uncompressedZeroKeyword read the image it stores.
console.log(isCompressedImageHeader({ ZIMAGE: true }), uncompressedWidthKeyword({ ZIMAGE: true, ZNAXIS1: 100, NAXIS1: 8 }, 0)) // true 100
```

### FITS Instrument Provenance

Besides the pixels, a FITS header says which telescope, camera and sensor took the frame, which filter was in the beam, the frame's role in calibration, the sensor settings, and which calibration steps were already applied. The Standard defines only a few of these keywords (`TELESCOP`, `INSTRUME`, `OBSERVER`, `OBJECT`, `ORIGIN`); capture software adds the rest with varying spellings, such as `IMAGETYP = 'Light Frame'` or `FRAME = 'Light'`.

`readFitsProvenance` returns a typed record of the instrument names, the filter, the frame type normalized to light, dark, flat, bias or dark flat (and whether it is a master), the binning, the sensor and set temperatures in °C, the gain, offset and readout mode, the calibration already applied, and the pedestal in ADU. `GAIN` is returned as written: capture software stores the camera's gain setting there, while NOAO-style headers store e⁻/ADU, so the conversion factor is `electronGain` (`EGAIN`). Headers are untrusted, so an unreadable or contradictory value is left out or resolved and reported in `diagnostics` instead of throwing. `writeFitsProvenance` writes the record back in place and deletes the provenance keywords it does not define, so a stale `FRAME` cannot contradict the new `IMAGETYP`. Observation times and the site are read by [FITS Observation Timing and Location](#fits-observation-timing-and-location).

```ts
import type { FitsHeader } from 'nebulosa/src/io/formats/fits/fits'
import { readFitsProvenance, writeFitsProvenance } from 'nebulosa/src/io/formats/fits/provenance'

const header: FitsHeader = { SIMPLE: true, INSTRUME: 'ZWO CCD ASI294MM Pro', TELESCOP: 'iOptronV3', IMAGETYP: 'Light Frame', FRAME: 'Light', FILTER: 'L', XBINNING: 4, YBINNING: 4, 'CCD-TEMP': -10.1, 'SET-TEMP': -10, GAIN: 120, OFFSET: 30, EGAIN: 1.0022, CALSTAT: 'BD', OBSERVER: '  ' }

// Reads the typed provenance; blank strings count as absent.
const provenance = readFitsProvenance(header)
console.log(provenance.frameType, provenance.filter, provenance.binning) // light L [4, 4]
console.log(provenance.sensorTemperature, provenance.electronGain, provenance.calibration) // -10.1 1.0022 ["bias", "dark"] — °C, e⁻/ADU

// Writes a modified record back: the owned keywords are replaced, the others kept.
writeFitsProvenance(header, { ...provenance, frameType: 'dark', software: 'nebulosa' })
console.log(header.IMAGETYP, header.FRAME, header.PROGRAM) // Dark Frame undefined nebulosa
```

### FITS Observation Timing and Location

A FITS header records when and where an exposure was taken through several overlapping conventions. FITS 4.0 defines the time scale `TIMESYS` (UTC when absent), the place where the times are valid `TREFPOS` (the topocenter by default), the instants `DATE-BEG`/`MJD-BEG`, `DATE-AVG`/`MJD-AVG` and `DATE-END`/`MJD-END`, the older `DATE-OBS`/`MJD-OBS` (the start unless its comment says otherwise), times relative to `MJDREF`/`JDREF`/`DATEREF` (`TSTART`, `TSTOP`, `TIMEOFFS` in `TIMEUNIT`), the durations `XPOSURE` and `TELAPSE`, the errors `TIMSYER` and `TIMRDER`, and the observatory as ITRS `OBSGEO-X/Y/Z` in meters or geodetic `OBSGEO-B/L/H` on the IAU 1976 ellipsoid; capture software adds `EXPTIME`, `EXPOSURE` and `SITELAT`/`SITELONG`/`SITEELEV`.

`readFitsTime` resolves them into one typed record following the precedence of the Standard, without changing the header. Each instant is a two-part `Time` in the header's own scale (GPS carried on TAI), with the keyword that supplied it and its resolution, one unit of its last written digit in seconds (86400 for a date without time), so a coarse timestamp is never mistaken for a precise one. The start is `DATE-BEG`, else `DATE-OBS` (an assumption that is reported), else `TSTART`; `DATE-OBS` is never taken as the midpoint. The exposure comes from `XPOSURE`, else `EXPTIME`, else `EXPOSURE`, in seconds, and `continuous` tells whether the start and end bound one continuous exposure: two endpoints alone give the observing window, not the integration time, so it is `undefined` whenever the written resolutions cannot separate dead time from rounding. The location comes from `OBSGEO-X/Y/Z`, else `OBSGEO-B/L/H`, else the `SITE` keywords, and is attached to every topocentric `Time`, which enables the topocentric TDB−TT term. When `TREFPOS` is absent, TDB and TCB refer to the barycenter and TCG to the geocenter (FITS 4.0 §4.4.2.2), and the other scales to the topocenter. Headers are untrusted, so bad or contradictory values are reported in `diagnostics` rather than thrown; the file creation date `DATE` is ignored.

Nothing is corrected: a barycentric TDB time is returned as written and a timestamp is not moved to the midpoint. `fitsExposure` hands the instants to [Exposure Timing](#exposure-timing), with the clock errors as its uncertainty, and [Barycentric Julian Date](#barycentric-julian-date) does the light-time correction. `writeFitsTime` is the inverse: it converts only the clock scale, never the origin, so TCG, TDB and TCB are written with `TREFPOS = 'TOPOCENTER'` unless another reference position is given; FITS 4.0 advises against TDB at the topocenter, so local times are best written in TT or UTC, and `'barycenter'` declared only for instants already corrected. It deletes the time keywords the input does not define, so stale values cannot contradict the new ones.

```ts
import { exposureInterval } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/exposure'
import { fitsExposure, formatFitsDateTime, readFitsTime, writeFitsTime } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/fits'
import { timeToDate } from 'nebulosa/src/astronomy/time/time'
import { parseFitsDateTimeFields } from 'nebulosa/src/io/formats/fits/util'

// A capture-software header: DATE-OBS at the shutter opening, a 60 s EXPTIME and the site.
const header = { TIMESYS: 'UTC', 'DATE-OBS': '2016-12-31T23:59:30.250', EXPTIME: 60, SITELAT: '-29 15 22.7', SITELONG: -70.7313, SITEELEV: 2400, OBJECT: 'WASP-12' }

// Resolves the instants, the exposure and the site; each instant has its keyword and resolution in seconds.
const metadata = readFitsTime(header)
console.log(metadata.start!.keyword, metadata.start!.resolution, timeToDate(metadata.start!.time)) // DATE-OBS 0.001 [2016, 12, 31, 23, 59, 30, 250]
console.log(metadata.diagnostics.map((e) => `${e.kind} ${e.keyword}`)) // ["defaulted TREFPOS", "assumed SITELAT", "assumed DATE-OBS"]

// The exposure interval spans the 2016-12-31 leap second: its midpoint is 23:59:60.25 UTC.
const interval = exposureInterval(fitsExposure(metadata)!)
console.log(timeToDate(interval.midpoint)) // [2016, 12, 31, 23, 59, 60, 250]

// The FITS datetime syntax both ways: an instant formatted in its own scale with 3 decimals, and a string split into its fields.
console.log(formatFitsDateTime(interval.midpoint, 3)) // 2016-12-31T23:59:60.250
console.log(parseFitsDateTimeFields('2016-12-31T23:59:60.25')) // { year: 2016, month: 12, day: 31, hour: 23, minute: 59, second: 60.25, resolution: 0.01, ... }

// Writes the interval back with the FITS 4.0 keywords; OBJECT passes through.
const out = writeFitsTime({ OBJECT: 'WASP-12' }, { start: interval.start, end: interval.end, exposure: interval.duration, referencePosition: 'topocenter', location: metadata.location, digits: 3 })
console.log(out['DATE-BEG'], out['DATE-END'], out.TELAPSE) // 2016-12-31T23:59:30.250 2017-01-01T00:00:29.250 60
```

### FITS Pixel I/O and Rice Tiles

FITS stores an image as planes: all the samples of the first channel, then those of the next (`NAXIS3` channels), as big-endian values of the `BITPIX` type, where the physical value is `BZERO + BSCALE × stored`. The imaging code of the toolkit works on channel-interleaved `Float32Array` or `Float64Array` samples, either normalized to 0..1 or digital (the integer values, such as 0 to 65535 for 16 bits). `FitsImageReader` and `FitsImageWriter` convert between the two layouts and scales, with a bounded scratch buffer so a large image does not need a second copy in memory.

The reader takes an HDU indexed by [FITS Containers and HDUs](#fits-containers-and-hdus) and reads a tile-compressed `RICE_1` image through the same call, decoding the tiles with [FITS Rice Compression](#fits-rice-compression); other tile compressions are not supported. The writer writes only the data segment for the `BITPIX` and dimensions of the header, optionally scaling each sample by a normalization (see [Scientific Image Loading and Export](#scientific-image-loading-and-export)). An image too large for one buffer goes through rows: `readRows` reads a range of rows of one channel from an uncompressed image (tile-compressed data are not row-addressable), and `FitsImageRowWriter` writes a floating-point primary image in file order, storing the samples as given.

```ts
import { FitsImageReader, FitsImageRowWriter, FitsImageWriter, readFits, writeFits } from 'nebulosa/src/io/formats/fits/fits'
import { bufferSink, bufferSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'

// raw: Float32Array of 6 x 4 normalized samples (0 to 1), a ramp, written as a 16-bit file.
const width = 6
const height = 4
const raw = Float32Array.from({ length: width * height }, (_, i) => i / (width * height - 1))
const file = Buffer.alloc(2880 * 4)
const sink = bufferSink(file)
await writeFits(sink, [{ header: { SIMPLE: true, BITPIX: 16, NAXIS: 2, NAXIS1: width, NAXIS2: height }, raw }])
const hdu = (await readFits(bufferSource(file.subarray(0, sink.position))))!.hdus[0]

// Reads the pixels in the digital scale (0 to 65535 for 16 bits); 'normalized' is the default.
const digital = new Float32Array(width * height)
await new FitsImageReader(hdu).read(bufferSource(file), digital, 'digital')
console.log(digital.slice(0, 4), digital.at(-1)) // Float32Array(4) [ 0, 2849, 5699, 8548 ] 65535

// Reads 2 rows of channel 0 starting at zero-based row 1, when the data are row-addressable (not tile-compressed).
const reader = new FitsImageReader(hdu)
const rows = new Float32Array(width * 2)
if (reader.rowAddressable) await reader.readRows(bufferSource(file), rows, 1, 2)

// Writes only the data segment for the BITPIX and dimensions of a header, without header or padding; returns its bytes.
const data = bufferSink(Buffer.alloc(width * height * 4))
console.log(await new FitsImageWriter({ SIMPLE: true, BITPIX: -32, NAXIS: 2, NAXIS1: width, NAXIS2: height }).write(raw, data)) // 96

// Writes a 32-bit float image in file order: header, the samples (whole channels in turn), padding.
const writer = new FitsImageRowWriter(bufferSink(Buffer.alloc(2880 * 4)), { SIMPLE: true, BITPIX: -32, NAXIS: 2, NAXIS1: width, NAXIS2: height })
await writer.begin()
await writer.write(raw)
await writer.end()
```

### FITS Rice Compression

Rice coding is a Golomb code with a power-of-two parameter: each value is split into low bits written as they are and a high part written in unary. The FITS tiled-image compression convention (`RICE_1`) applies it to the differences between consecutive integer samples, choosing the number of low bits for each block of samples, so smooth data of small differences compress well and flat blocks cost a few bits. The codec is lossless for integers; the loss of a compressed FITS image comes only from the quantization of float pixels to the integer `BITPIX`. Noise-like data barely shrink, so the compressed size cannot be predicted from the input size.

`compressRice` encodes an 8-, 16- or 32-bit integer typed array in blocks (32 samples by default, the usual `ZVAL1`) and `decompressRice` fills an output of the same type and length, which must be decoded with the same block size. In a FITS file each tile is one such stream in the heap of a binary table; `writeFits` produces them and `FitsImageReader` decodes them (see [FITS Pixel I/O and Rice Tiles](#fits-pixel-io-and-rice-tiles)). When a `BitWriter` is passed to be reused across tiles, the result aliases its storage and is valid only until the next call that uses it.

```ts
import { compressRice, decompressRice } from 'nebulosa/src/io/compression'

// A smooth 16-bit signal: a slow drift with a small repetitive variation.
const signal = new Int16Array(1024)
for (let i = 0; i < signal.length; i++) signal[i] = 1000 + ((i * 37) % 17) - 8 + (i >> 5)

// Encodes in blocks of 32 samples; returns the encoded bytes.
const encoded = compressRice(signal, 32)
console.log(signal.byteLength, encoded.byteLength) // 2048 601

// Decodes into an output of the same type and length, with the same block size.
const decoded = decompressRice(encoded, new Int16Array(signal.length), 32)
console.log(decoded.every((value, i) => value === signal[i])) // true
```

### Growable Binary Buffers

Binary records, such as the messages of a device protocol or a file header, are often assembled field by field before their size is known. `GrowableBuffer` appends integers of 8, 16 and 32 bits, signed or unsigned, little- or big-endian, to a buffer that doubles its capacity whenever a write does not fit, and keeps the written length in bytes. There are no writers for strings or floating-point numbers.

`toBuffer` returns a view of the written region, not a copy: the next write or a `reset` changes it, and a growth leaves it pointing to the old storage, so a caller that keeps the bytes copies them. `toString` decodes the region, optionally trimming the leading and trailing bytes up to 0x20 (spaces, line feeds, zero bytes), and `reset` rewinds to the start while keeping the storage, so one buffer serves many records.

```ts
import { GrowableBuffer } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'

// Starts with 4 bytes of capacity and grows by doubling.
const buffer = new GrowableBuffer(4)
buffer.writeUInt8(0xca)
buffer.writeInt8(-2)
buffer.writeUInt16BE(0x0102)
buffer.writeUInt16LE(0x0102)
console.log(buffer.length, buffer.toBuffer()) // 6 <Buffer ca fe 01 02 02 01>

// Copies the view before the next record reuses the storage.
const record = Buffer.from(buffer.toBuffer())
buffer.reset()
console.log(buffer.length) // 0

// writeInt16LE/BE, writeUInt32LE/BE and writeInt32LE/BE append the other widths and byte orders.
buffer.writeInt32BE(0x204f4b0a)

// Decodes the region, trimming the leading and trailing bytes up to 0x20 (toBuffer(true) trims the same way).
console.log(buffer.toString(true), buffer.toString(true).length) // OK 2
```

### HTTP Range Byte Sources

Astronomical files are large, and often only a small part is needed: the header of a FITS or XISF image, one data block, or a few rows of a catalog. HTTP range requests (RFC 9110) let a client ask a server for an arbitrary byte interval with `Range: bytes=first-last`, and a server that supports them answers `206 Partial Content` with just those bytes. A reader that seeks and reads through ranges can therefore parse a remote file in place, without downloading it whole.

`rangeHttpSource` exposes a remote resource as a seekable source (see [Byte-Stream Contracts](#byte-stream-contracts)), so the same parsers that read local files read remote ones. A seek only moves the cursor; each `read` is one request and one network round trip, so read in blocks of tens of kilobytes rather than a few bytes at a time. The server must honour ranges (a full `200` response is an error), the end of the resource is seen as a read of 0 bytes, and only asynchronous reads are supported. Disposing the source aborts its pending requests.

```ts
import { rangeHttpSource, readRemaining, readUntil } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'

// A seekable source over a remote file; each read is one Range request with a 5 s timeout.
using source = rangeHttpSource('https://example.com/data.bin', { timeout: 5000 })

// Fill a buffer from the start of the file, joining as many requests as needed.
const header = Buffer.alloc(2880)
await readUntil(source, header)

// Jump to a data block: the seek sends nothing, the next read fetches the range.
source.seek(50000)
const block = Buffer.alloc(65536)
console.log(await source.read(block)) // bytes received, 0 at or past the end of the resource

// Everything from a position to the end of the resource.
source.seek(99000)
const tail = await readRemaining(source)
```

### JPEG via TurboJPEG

JPEG is the lossy compression of 8-bit images by the discrete cosine transform: the image is converted to luminance and chrominance (YCbCr), split into 8x8 blocks, and the high-frequency coefficients are quantized according to a quality factor. Because the eye is less sensitive to colour detail, the chrominance can also be subsampled (`4:2:0` halves it in both axes). JPEG is the format of previews, thumbnails and streamed views of stretched images; it is not a format for science data, which needs the full bit depth and exact values of FITS or XISF.

`Jpeg` wraps the native libjpeg-turbo library, a SIMD-accelerated implementation loaded through `bun:ffi` on first use from the shared library bundled for Windows (x64) and Linux (x64 and arm64); no library is bundled for other platforms. It encodes raw 8-bit pixels in a given layout (RGB, BGR, gray, with or without alpha), reads the header without decoding, and decodes to the requested layout. A decoded image differs from the source by the usual lossy error, not just by rounding.

```ts
import { isJpeg, Jpeg, unload } from 'nebulosa/src/bindings/imaging/libturbojpeg'

// rgb: Buffer — 64 x 32 pixels, 3 bytes per pixel (R, G, B), rows tightly packed
const jpeg = new Jpeg()

// The worst-case encoded size in bytes, to preallocate a destination buffer that compress can reuse.
const output = Buffer.alloc(jpeg.estimateBufferSize(64, 32, '4:4:4'))

// Encode with quality 90 (1 to 100) and full-resolution chrominance; the result is a view of the destination.
const encoded = jpeg.compress(rgb, 64, 32, 'RGB', 90, '4:4:4', output)!
console.log(isJpeg(encoded)) // true: the stream starts with the FF D8 start-of-image marker

// Dimensions, chrominance subsampling and colour space, without decoding the pixels.
console.log(jpeg.readHeader(encoded)) // { width: 64, height: 32, subsampling: "4:4:4", colorspace: "YCbCr" }

// Decode to interleaved RGB (the default for colour images) or to another layout.
const decoded = jpeg.decompress(encoded)!
const rgba = jpeg.decompress(encoded, 'RGBA')!

// A lower quality and subsampled chrominance give a smaller preview; without a destination one is allocated.
const preview = jpeg.compress(rgb, 64, 32, 'RGB', 40, '4:2:0')!

// Closes the native library when JPEG work is over; existing Jpeg instances must not be used after it, and a new one loads it again.
unload()
```

### Portable Path Segments

A file name that arrives from outside the process, such as the output name of a capture request, must address exactly one file inside the directory the caller chose. A name containing a separator or `..` escapes that directory (path traversal), and a name that is valid on Linux can be invalid or alias another file on Windows, where a request written on one system may be executed. Validating the name as a single portable segment prevents both problems.

`isPathSegment` accepts a name only when it is one portable file name on every common platform: no separators, no `.` or `..`, no control characters, none of the characters Windows forbids (where `:` would also open an NTFS alternate data stream), no trailing dot or space (which Windows strips), none of the Windows device names such as `CON`, `NUL`, `COM1` or `LPT1` with any extension, and at most 255 UTF-8 bytes. Names are not normalized. `directoryExists` tells whether a path is an existing directory, following symbolic links, and never rejects.

```ts
import { tmpdir } from 'os'
import { directoryExists, isPathSegment } from 'nebulosa/src/io/path'

// Accept a single portable file name, reject traversal and names that are invalid on Windows.
console.log(isPathSegment('m42-lum-0.fit')) // true
console.log(isPathSegment('../m42.fit'), isPathSegment('nul.fit'), isPathSegment('m42.fit.')) // false false false

// Whether the target directory exists (false for a missing path or a regular file).
console.log(await directoryExists(tmpdir())) // true
console.log(await directoryExists('/does/not/exist')) // false
```

### ReadableStream Byte Sources

The web platform delivers bytes as a `ReadableStream<Uint8Array>`: a `fetch` response body, a `Blob` stream, or `Bun.file(...).stream()`. Its chunks have whatever sizes the producer chose, while the parsers of the library pull bytes into buffers of their own through the `Source` contract (see [Byte-Stream Contracts](#byte-stream-contracts)). `readableStreamSource` bridges the two, so a download can be parsed as it arrives, holding one chunk in memory instead of the whole body.

A read returns at most what is left of the current chunk, so it can return fewer bytes than requested; use the helpers of [Byte Reading, Writing, and Transfer](#byte-reading-writing-and-transfer) to fill a buffer exactly. The source is forward-only (not seekable) and asynchronous only, so formats that need random access must be read into memory or a file first. Closing or disposing the source cancels the stream, which stops an unfinished download.

```ts
import { readableStreamSource, readRemaining, readUntil } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'

// Any web stream works; here the body of a Response.
const response = new Response('stellar data from a response')
const source = readableStreamSource(response.body!)

try {
	// Fill a buffer exactly, joining chunks as needed.
	const buffer = Buffer.alloc(7)
	console.log(await readUntil(source, buffer), buffer.toString()) // 7 stellar

	// Read the rest of the stream into one buffer.
	const rest = await readRemaining(source)
} finally {
	// Cancels the stream, as `await using` disposal does; an unfinished download stops here.
	await source.close()
}
```

### Socket Write Backpressure

TCP delivers a byte stream with flow control: when a peer reads more slowly than it is written to, its receive window and the local send buffer fill, and a write can accept only part of the bytes. The sender must then keep the rest, in order, and resume when the socket can take more; this is backpressure. Bun's `socket.write` returns the number of bytes the socket took and drops the rest instead of buffering it, so a protocol message written to a slow peer, such as an INDI XML element or a telescope reply, would arrive truncated in the middle.

`SocketWriteQueue` is the ordered output queue of one socket, which the INDI and Firmata TCP clients and the LX200 and Stellarium servers of the toolkit use. It writes straight through while it is empty and otherwise queues a copy of what the socket did not take, so the caller may reuse its buffer at once; the socket's `drain` handler flushes it. A write reports a stalled peer when more than a limit of bytes is pending, and the caller is expected to close that connection, because the queue would otherwise grow without bound. Create one queue per connection and clear it when the connection ends.

```ts
import { SocketWriteQueue } from 'nebulosa/src/io/socket'

// An echo server whose replies keep their order and integrity whatever the speed of the peer.
const server = Bun.listen<SocketWriteQueue>({
	hostname: 'localhost',
	port: 10001,
	socket: {
		// One queue per connection; a peer with more than 1 MiB pending counts as stalled.
		open(socket) {
			socket.data = new SocketWriteQueue(1024 * 1024)
		},
		// Writes after the queued bytes; false means the peer stopped reading, so the connection ends.
		data(socket, chunk) {
			if (!socket.data.write(socket, chunk)) socket.end()
		},
		// Writes the queued bytes the socket now takes, keeping the rest for the next drain.
		drain(socket) {
			socket.data.drain(socket)
			console.log(socket.data.pending) // bytes still queued
		},
		// Discards what was never delivered.
		close(socket) {
			socket.data.clear()
		},
	},
})
```

### Streaming Base64

Base64 (RFC 4648) represents binary data as text: every 3 bytes become 4 characters of a 64-letter alphabet, with `=` padding for a final partial group, at a cost of one third more size. It is how binary payloads travel inside text formats: INDI BLOBs inside XML messages, XISF data blocks embedded in the XML header, MIME attachments. The URL-safe variant `base64url` replaces `+` and `/` by `-` and `_`.

`base64Source` decodes Base64 text into bytes as a `Source`, and `base64Sink` encodes the bytes written to it and forwards the text to another sink (see [Byte-Stream Contracts](#byte-stream-contracts)). Both work in constant memory, so a large image never exists at once as bytes and as a string a third larger. The source accepts both alphabets and ignores white space and line breaks, as in wrapped MIME lines. The sink holds back the last partial group, so `end()` must be called after the last write, or the encoded text is silently truncated.

```ts
import { base64Sink, base64Source, bufferSink } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'

// Decode Base64 text (a string or another Source); line breaks and spaces are ignored.
const source = base64Source('TmVidWxv\nc2E gdG9v bGtpdA==')
const buffer = Buffer.alloc(32)
const n = await source.read(buffer)
console.log(n, buffer.toString('latin1', 0, n)) // 16 Nebulosa toolkit

// The source seeks in decoded bytes; readSync decodes synchronously from a string or a synchronous source.
source.seek(9)
console.log(source.readSync(buffer), buffer.toString('latin1', 0, 7), source.position) // 7 toolkit 16

// Encode bytes into another sink; end() writes the final group with its padding.
const text = Buffer.alloc(64)
const output = bufferSink(text)
const sink = base64Sink(output)
await sink.write(Buffer.from('Nebulosa!'))
await sink.end()
console.log(text.toString('latin1', 0, output.position), sink.encodedSize) // TmVidWxvc2Eh 12 — encoded characters

// The URL-safe alphabet, written synchronously.
const url = Buffer.alloc(8)
const urlOutput = bufferSink(url)
const urlSink = base64Sink(urlOutput, 'base64url')
urlSink.writeSync(Buffer.from([0xfb, 0xff, 0xfe]))
await urlSink.end()
console.log(url.toString('latin1', 0, urlOutput.position)) // -__-
```

### Streaming Text Lines

Many astronomical data sets are line-oriented text: CSV catalogs, two-line element sets, MPC orbit files, IERS tables. They can be large or remote, so reading them line by line keeps memory bounded by one chunk plus the longest line, whatever the size of the file.

`readLines` is an async generator over any `Source` (see [Byte-Stream Contracts](#byte-stream-contracts)): files, memory, web streams and HTTP ranges. It splits on the line feed and assembles each line as bytes before decoding it, so a multi-byte UTF-8 character that crosses a chunk boundary is decoded whole. A carriage return stays at the end of the line, so CRLF text yields lines ending in `\r` that the caller trims.

```ts
import { bufferSource, readLines, readableStreamSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'

// The lines of an in-memory text, read 1024 bytes at a time.
for await (const line of readLines(bufferSource(Buffer.from('alpha\nbeta\n\ngamma')), 1024)) console.log(line) // alpha, beta, (empty), gamma

// stream: ReadableStream<Uint8Array> — a CSV body "name,mag\nVega,0.03\nSirius,-1.46\n" arriving in arbitrary chunks
await using source = readableStreamSource(stream)

// Read 16 bytes at a time and skip empty lines.
for await (const line of readLines(source, 16, { emptyLines: false })) console.log(line.split(',')) // [ "name", "mag" ] / [ "Vega", "0.03" ] / [ "Sirius", "-1.46" ]
```

### XISF Containers and Metadata

XISF (Extensible Image Serialization Format) is the image format of PixInsight. Unlike FITS, its metadata is an XML header that describes each image (geometry, sample format, colour space, pixel layout, compression) and carries properties and FITS keywords, while the pixels live in binary data blocks. A monolithic file starts with the signature `XISF0100`, a 32-bit little-endian length of the XML header and 4 reserved bytes, then the UTF-8 XML, and then the data blocks that the `location="attachment:offset:size"` attributes point to.

`readXisf` reads the XML header of a seekable source (see [Byte-Stream Contracts](#byte-stream-contracts)) and describes and locates every image without reading its pixels, which is the job of [XISF Pixel I/O and Compression](#xisf-pixel-io-and-compression). Each image gets a FITS-style header built from its geometry, sample format and `FITSKeyword` elements, so the metadata accessors of [FITS Header Cards and Metadata](#fits-header-cards-and-metadata) work on XISF and FITS alike. `writeXisf` writes images described as in [FITS Containers and HDUs](#fits-containers-and-hdus) as a monolithic file. Images in the CIELab colour space or with 64-bit integer samples, and images whose data is not attached to the file, are not supported.

```ts
import { isXisf, readXisf, writeXisf } from 'nebulosa/src/io/formats/xisf/xisf'
import { bufferSink, bufferSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'

// raw: Float32Array — an 8 x 4 RGB image, channel-interleaved, normalized to [0, 1]
// The FITS-style header gives the geometry, the sample format (BITPIX 16 is UInt16) and the keywords to keep.
const header = { SIMPLE: true, BITPIX: 16, NAXIS: 3, NAXIS1: 8, NAXIS2: 4, NAXIS3: 3, OBJECT: 'M42', EXPTIME: 30 }

// Write a monolithic file; its XML header describes the image like this:
// <Image geometry="8:4:3" sampleFormat="UInt16" colorSpace="RGB" location="attachment:338:192" pixelStorage="Planar" byteOrder="little">
//   <FITSKeyword name="OBJECT" value="&apos;M42&apos;" comment=""/><FITSKeyword name="EXPTIME" value="30" comment=""/></Image>
const out = Buffer.alloc(8192)
const sink = bufferSink(out)
await writeXisf(sink, [{ header, raw }])
const file = out.subarray(0, sink.position)
console.log(isXisf(file)) // true

// Read the XML: each image is described and its data block located, not decoded.
const [image] = (await readXisf(bufferSource(file)))!.images
console.log(image.geometry, image.location) // { width: 8, height: 4, channels: 3 } { offset: 338, size: 192 }
console.log(image.sampleFormat, image.colorSpace, image.pixelStorage) // UInt16 RGB Planar
console.log(image.header) // { SIMPLE: true, BITPIX: 16, NAXIS: 3, NAXIS1: 8, NAXIS2: 4, NAXIS3: 3, OBJECT: "M42", EXPTIME: 30 }
```

### XISF Pixel I/O and Compression

An XISF data block stores the samples of an image as unsigned integers (8, 16 or 32 bits) or floating-point numbers (32 or 64 bits), in little- or big-endian byte order, either planar (one channel after the other) or normal (channels interleaved per pixel). A block can be compressed with zlib or Zstandard, optionally after byte shuffling (see [Byte Shuffling](#byte-shuffling)), which groups the bytes of equal significance of the multi-byte samples so that the slowly varying high bytes compress much better.

`XisfImageReader` decodes the block of an image located by `readXisf` (see [XISF Containers and Metadata](#xisf-containers-and-metadata)) into the channel-interleaved `Float32Array` or `Float64Array` used by the imaging code, undoing compression, shuffling, byte order and planar layout. Integer samples are read normalized to [0, 1] or as their stored digital values (0 to 65535 for 16 bits). `XisfImageWriter` does the reverse, and `writeXisf` uses it for whole files. Integer formats quantize the samples, so a 16-bit round trip is accurate to one step (1/65535), while floating-point formats round-trip exactly. Only zlib and Zstandard are supported; LZ4 blocks cannot be read or written.

```ts
import { readXisf, writeXisf, XisfImageReader, XisfImageWriter } from 'nebulosa/src/io/formats/xisf/xisf'
import { bufferSink, bufferSource } from 'nebulosa/src/io/io'

// raw: Float32Array — an 8 x 4 RGB image, channel-interleaved, normalized to [0, 1]
const header = { SIMPLE: true, BITPIX: 16, NAXIS: 3, NAXIS1: 8, NAXIS2: 4, NAXIS3: 3 }

// Write 16-bit samples, byte-shuffled and zlib-compressed.
const out = Buffer.alloc(8192)
const sink = bufferSink(out)
await writeXisf(sink, [{ header, raw }], { compression: { format: 'zlib', shuffled: true } })
const file = out.subarray(0, sink.position)
const [image] = (await readXisf(bufferSource(file)))!.images
console.log(image.compression) // the codec, the shuffling item size and the uncompressed size of the block

// Decode into the interleaved layout, normalized to [0, 1] or as the stored integer values (0 to 65535).
const normalized = new Float32Array(8 * 4 * 3)
await new XisfImageReader(image).read(bufferSource(file), normalized)
const digital = new Float32Array(8 * 4 * 3)
await new XisfImageReader(image).read(bufferSource(file), digital, 'digital')

// Encode one block alone: the bytes and the compression descriptor to declare in the XML.
const writer = new XisfImageWriter({ byteOrder: 'little', bitpix: -32, geometry: { width: 8, height: 4, channels: 3 }, pixelStorage: 'Planar', compression: undefined })
const block = await writer.encode(raw)
console.log(block.data.byteLength) // 384: 8 x 4 x 3 Float32 samples

// Encodes the same way and writes the block to a sink; returns the bytes written.
console.log(await writer.write(raw, bufferSink(Buffer.alloc(384)))) // 384
```

### XML Parsing

The INDI device protocol is a never-ending stream of XML elements over TCP, and socket reads split it at arbitrary bytes, so a message can arrive in many pieces and several messages in one piece. A document parser that expects a complete document does not fit, and BLOB elements can carry megabytes of Base64 text. The XISF header is XML too.

`SimpleXmlParser` is a small incremental parser for plain element, attribute and text documents. It keeps its partial state between calls and returns, at each call, the top-level elements that the chunk completed. An element has its tag name, its attributes, its child elements in order and its text as raw bytes, which the caller decodes (or passes on, for a BLOB) without an intermediate string. Attribute values have their entities and character references decoded; DTDs, CDATA sections and namespaces are not supported, and entities in element text are left as they came. The returned array is reused by the next call, so keep the elements, not the array.

```ts
import { SimpleXmlParser } from 'nebulosa/src/io/xml'

const parser = new SimpleXmlParser()

// Feed chunks cut anywhere (strings, Buffers or Uint8Arrays); an element is returned by the call that closes it.
const chunks = ['<setSwitchVector device="Mount" na', 'me="TELESCOPE_TRACK_STATE"><oneSwitch name="TRACK_ON">O', 'n</oneSwitch></setSwitchVec', 'tor>']

for (const chunk of chunks) {
	for (const node of parser.parse(chunk)) {
		// The tag, the attributes, and the text of each child decoded from its bytes.
		console.log(node.name, node.attributes.name) // setSwitchVector TELESCOPE_TRACK_STATE
		for (const child of node.children) console.log(child.attributes.name, Buffer.from(child.text).toString()) // TRACK_ON On
	}
}

// Discard a partial element and the open elements, for example after a reconnection.
parser.reset()
```

## 🔢 Numerical

### 2D Vectors

Planar vectors appear wherever the library works on an image or a tangent plane: pixel offsets between stars, guiding corrections, displacements on a detector, directions in a projected field. A `Vec2` is a read-only `[x, y]` tuple of plain numbers in whatever unit the caller uses (pixels, millimetres, radians of a tangent plane), and `MutVec2` its mutable form; angles are radians, counterclockwise from +x. See [3D Vectors](#_3d-vectors) for the three-component counterpart.

The helpers cover construction, dot and cross products (the 2D cross product is the z component of the 3D one, positive when the second vector is counterclockwise from the first), length and distance, the unsigned angle between two vectors, the polar angle, rotation, normalization and component-wise arithmetic. A function that builds a vector writes into an optional output, which may be one of its inputs, and allocates a new vector otherwise; the `...Mut` variants work in place. Normalizing the zero vector returns it unchanged instead of `NaN`, and the midpoint direction of two opposite vectors is undefined and returned as zero.

```ts
import {
	type MutVec2,
	vec2Angle,
	vec2Clone,
	vec2Cross,
	vec2CrossLength,
	vec2Distance,
	vec2Div,
	vec2DivScalar,
	vec2DivScalarMut,
	vec2Dot,
	vec2Fill,
	vec2FillWith,
	vec2Length,
	vec2Longitude,
	vec2Midpoint,
	vec2Minus,
	vec2MinusScalar,
	vec2Mul,
	vec2MulScalar,
	vec2Negate,
	vec2NegateMut,
	vec2Normalize,
	vec2NormalizeMut,
	vec2Plus,
	vec2PlusScalar,
	vec2Rot,
	vec2RotMut,
	vec2XAxis,
	vec2YAxis,
	vec2Zero,
} from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/vec2'

const a: MutVec2 = [3, 4]
const b: MutVec2 = [0, 2]

// New vectors: the zero vector and the unit axes.
console.log(vec2Zero(), vec2XAxis(), vec2YAxis()) // [ 0, 0 ] [ 1, 0 ] [ 0, 1 ]

// Length, distance between two points, dot product and the signed cross product (positive: b is counterclockwise from a).
console.log(vec2Length(a), vec2Distance(a, b), vec2Dot(a, b), vec2Cross(a, b)) // 5 3.605551275463989 8 6

// The absolute cross product, the area of the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors.
console.log(vec2CrossLength(b, a)) // 6

// The polar angle from +x in [0, 2π), and the unsigned angle between two vectors in [0, π] (radians).
console.log(vec2Longitude([0, -1]), vec2Angle([1, 0], [0, 1])) // 4.71238898038469 1.5707963267948966

// Element-wise sum into a new vector, or into an output that is returned; difference, product and quotient work alike.
const out: MutVec2 = [0, 0]
console.log(vec2Plus(a, b), vec2Plus(a, b, out) === out) // [ 3, 6 ] true
console.log(vec2Minus(a, b), vec2Mul(a, b), vec2Div(b, a)) // [ 3, 2 ] [ 0, 8 ] [ 0, 0.5 ]

// Arithmetic with a scalar, and the opposite vector.
console.log(vec2PlusScalar(a, 1), vec2MinusScalar(a, 1), vec2MulScalar(a, 2), vec2DivScalar(a, 2), vec2Negate(a)) // [ 4, 5 ] [ 2, 3 ] [ 6, 8 ] [ 1.5, 2 ] [ -3, -4 ]

// Normalize, rotate a quarter turn counterclockwise, and the unit midpoint direction.
console.log(vec2Normalize(a)) // [ 0.6, 0.8 ]
console.log(vec2Rot([1, 0], Math.PI / 2)) // [ 6.123233995736766e-17, 1 ]
console.log(vec2Midpoint([1, 0], [0, 1]).map((v) => Number(v.toFixed(6)))) // [ 0.707107, 0.707107 ]

// In place on a mutable copy: set both components or fill them with one value, then the ...Mut operations.
const v = vec2Clone(a)
vec2Fill(v, 0, 4)
vec2DivScalarMut(v, 2) // [0, 2]
vec2NegateMut(v) // [0, -2]
vec2NormalizeMut(v) // [0, -1]
vec2RotMut(v, Math.PI) // [0, 1] up to roundoff
console.log(vec2FillWith(out, 1)) // [ 1, 1 ]
```

### 2x2 Matrices

A 2x2 matrix is a linear map of the plane: a rotation and scale between two pixel grids, the CD matrix of a WCS solution, the calibration that converts guiding offsets into mount corrections. Here it is a flat row-major tuple `[m00, m01, m10, m11]` (`Mat2` read-only, `MutMat2` mutable), small enough to live without allocation in tight loops.

`mat2Rot(angle)` is the rotation of the coordinate frame by an angle in radians, `[cos, sin, -sin, cos]`, so a vector expressed in the rotated frame turns by the opposite angle; given an existing matrix it returns the product `R·m`. The other helpers are the determinant and trace, transpose, flips, scalar and element-wise arithmetic, the products (including the fused forms with a transposed operand, which avoid building the transpose) and the products with a `Vec2`. A function that builds a matrix writes into an optional output and returns it, and allocates otherwise. There is no inverse here: the general solvers are in [Dense Linear System Solvers](#dense-linear-system-solvers).

```ts
import {
	mat2Clone,
	mat2Copy,
	mat2Determinant,
	mat2DivScalar,
	mat2Fill,
	mat2FlipX,
	mat2FlipY,
	mat2Identity,
	mat2Minus,
	mat2MinusScalar,
	mat2Mul,
	mat2MulScalar,
	mat2MulTranspose,
	mat2MulVec,
	mat2Negate,
	mat2Plus,
	mat2PlusScalar,
	mat2Rot,
	mat2Trace,
	mat2Transpose,
	mat2TransposeMul,
	mat2TransposeMulTranspose,
	mat2TransposeMulVec,
	mat2Zero,
	type MutMat2,
} from 'nebulosa/src/math/linear-algebra/mat2'
import { deg } from 'nebulosa/src/math/units/angle'

const a: MutMat2 = [1, 2, 3, 4]
const b: MutMat2 = [0, 1, 1, 0]

// New matrices: zero and identity.
console.log(mat2Zero(), mat2Identity()) // [ 0, 0, 0, 0 ] [ 1, 0, 0, 1 ]

// Scalar properties and the transpose.
console.log(mat2Determinant(a), mat2Trace(a), mat2Transpose(a)) // -2 5 [ 1, 3, 2, 4 ]

// Swap the rows (flip about the x axis) or the columns (flip about the y axis).
console.log(mat2FlipX(a), mat2FlipY(a)) // [ 3, 4, 1, 2 ] [ 2, 1, 4, 3 ]

// Element-wise sum and difference, the negation, and arithmetic with a scalar.
console.log(mat2Plus(a, b), mat2Minus(a, b), mat2Negate(a)) // [ 1, 3, 4, 4 ] [ 1, 1, 2, 4 ] [ -1, -2, -3, -4 ]
console.log(mat2PlusScalar(a, 1), mat2MinusScalar(a, 1), mat2MulScalar(a, 2), mat2DivScalar(a, 2)) // [ 2, 3, 4, 5 ] [ 0, 1, 2, 3 ] [ 2, 4, 6, 8 ] [ 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 ]

// The product a·b, and the fused aᵀ·b; mat2MulTranspose (a·bᵀ) and mat2TransposeMulTranspose (aᵀ·bᵀ) work alike.
console.log(mat2Mul(a, b), mat2TransposeMul(a, b)) // [ 2, 1, 4, 3 ] [ 3, 1, 4, 2 ]
console.log(mat2MulTranspose(a, b), mat2TransposeMulTranspose(a, b))

// The product with a vector, a·v and aᵀ·v.
console.log(mat2MulVec(a, [1, 1]), mat2TransposeMulVec(a, [1, 1])) // [ 3, 7 ] [ 4, 6 ]

// The frame rotation by 90° (the residues stand for exact zeros).
console.log(mat2Rot(deg(90))) // [ 6.123233995736766e-17, 1, -1, 6.123233995736766e-17 ]

// A mutable copy, overwritten with four elements and copied into an existing output.
const c = mat2Clone(a)
mat2Fill(c, 5, 6, 7, 8)
console.log(mat2Copy(c, mat2Zero())) // [ 5, 6, 7, 8 ]
```

### 3D Vectors

Directions on the celestial sphere and positions in space are three-component vectors: a unit vector toward a star in equatorial or ecliptic axes, the barycentric position of a planet in AU, the geocentric position of a satellite. A `Vec3` is a read-only `[x, y, z]` tuple in the caller's unit and `MutVec3` its mutable form; frames are right-handed and angles are radians. See [2D Vectors](#_2d-vectors) for the planar counterpart.

Besides the products (dot, cross, the triple product as a signed volume), norms and arithmetic, the helpers extract spherical coordinates from a vector of any length: the longitude in the xy plane in [0, 2π), the latitude above it in [-π/2, π/2] and the colatitude from +z, all stable at the poles. The angle between two vectors uses a stable `atan2` form that stays accurate for tiny and nearly opposite separations.
